Additionally, the Company’s new products often utilize custom components available from only one source. When a component or product uses new technologies, initial capacity constraints may exist until the suppliers’ yields have matured or their manufacturing capacities have increased. The Company may not be able to extend or renew agreements for the supply of components on similar terms, or at all, and may not be successful in obtaining sufficient quantities from its suppliers in a timely manner, or in identifying and obtaining sufficient quantities from an alternative source. In addition, component suppliers may fail, be subject to consolidation within a particular industry, or decide to concentrate on the production of common components instead of components customized to meet the Company’s requirements, further limiting the Company’s ability to obtain sufficient quantities of components on commercially reasonable terms, or at all. Therefore, the Company remains subject to significant risks of supply shortages and price increases that can materially adversely affect its business, results of operations, financial condition and stock price.
The Company records a write-down for product and component inventories if cost exceeds net realizable value. The Company reviews other assets, including capital assets held at its suppliers’ facilities, inventory prepayments and other long-lived assets, for impairment whenever events or circumstances indicate the assets may not be recoverable. Although the Company believes its inventory, capital assets, inventory prepayments and other assets are currently recoverable, the Company may incur write-downs, impairments and other charges given the rapid and unpredictable pace of product obsolescence in the industries in which the Company competes.
The Company’s business also requires it to share confidential information with suppliers and other third parties. The Company relies on global suppliers that are also exposed to ransomware and other malicious attacks that can disrupt business operations. Although the Company takes steps to secure confidential information that is provided to or accessible by third parties working on the Company’s behalf, such measures are not always effective and losses or unauthorized access to, or releases of, confidential information occur. Such incidents and other malicious attacks could materially adversely affect the Company’s business, reputation, results of operations, financial condition and stock price.
As with all companies, the security the Company has implemented may not be sufficient for all eventualities and are vulnerable to hacking, ransomware attacks, employee error, malfeasance, system error, faulty password management or other irregularities. For example, third parties can fraudulently induce the Company’s or its suppliers’ and other third parties’ employees or customers into disclosing usernames, passwords or other sensitive information, which can, in turn, be used for unauthorized access to the Company’s or such suppliers’ or third parties’ systems and services. To help protect customers and the Company, the Company deploys and makes available technologies like multifactor authentication, monitors its services and systems for unusual activity and may freeze accounts under suspicious circumstances, which, among other things, can result in the delay or loss of customer orders or impede customer access to the Company’s products and services.
The Company’s global operations are subject to complex and changing laws and regulations worldwide on subjects including antitrust; privacy, data security and data localization; online safety; age verification; consumer protection; advertising, sales, billing and e-commerce; financial services and technology; product liability; intellectual property ownership and infringement; digital platforms; machine learning and artificial intelligence; internet, telecommunications and mobile communications; media, television, film and digital content; availability of third-party software applications and services; labor and employment; anticorruption; import, export and trade; foreign exchange controls and cash repatriation restrictions; anti–money laundering; foreign ownership and investment; national security; tax; and environmental, health and safety, including electronic waste, recycling, product design and climate change.
Globally, several jurisdictions have adopted, or may in the future adopt, competition-related laws and regulations imposing wide-ranging obligations on technology companies and significant limitations on businesses, including the Company. For example, the Company has implemented changes to iOS, iPadOS, the App Store and Safari ® in the EU as it seeks to comply with the Digital Markets Act (“DMA”), including new business terms and alternative fee structures for iOS and iPadOS apps, alternative methods of distribution for iOS and iPadOS apps, alternative payment processing for apps across the Company’s operating systems, and additional tools and application programming interfaces for developers. The Company has also continued to make changes to its compliance plan in response to feedback and engagement with the Commission. Although the Company’s compliance plan is intended to address the DMA’s obligations, it has been challenged by the Commission and may be challenged further by private litigants. The DMA provides for significant fines and penalties for noncompliance. While the changes introduced by the Company in the EU are intended to reduce new privacy and security risks that the DMA poses to EU users, many risks will remain. Changes to the Company’s business in response to the DMA or other laws and regulations could materially adversely affect the Company’s business, reputation, results of operations, financial condition and stock price.
The Company’s business, results of operations, financial condition and stock price can be materially adversely affected, individually or in the aggregate, by the outcomes of such investigations, litigation or changes to laws and regulations in the future. Changes to the Company’s business practices to comply with new laws and regulations or in connection with legal proceedings can negatively impact the reputation of the Company’s products for privacy and security. Such changes in business practices can also otherwise adversely affect the experience for users of the Company’s products and services, and result in harm to the Company’s reputation, loss of competitive advantage, poor market acceptance, reduced demand for products and services, lost sales, and lower profit margins.
The Company makes statements about its use and disclosure of personal data through its privacy policy, information provided on its website, press statements and other privacy notices provided to customers. Any failure or perceived failure by the Company to comply with these public statements or with federal, state or international privacy or data protection laws and regulations could result in inquiries, proceedings and penalties from governmental entities or others. Such a failure or perceived failure could also result in reputational impacts, ongoing audit requirements and significant legal liability. The risks of inadvertent disclosure of personal data can increase with the introduction of new and complex technologies, such as artificial intelligence features, further exacerbating such risks.
In addition to the risks generally relating to the collection, use, retention, protection and transfer of personal data, the Company is also subject to specific obligations relating to the collection and processing of data associated with minors, as well as information considered sensitive under applicable laws, such as health, biometric, financial and payment card data. Health, biometric, financial and payment card data are subject to additional privacy, security and breach notification requirements, and the Company is subject to audit by governmental authorities regarding the Company’s compliance with these obligations. If the Company fails to adequately comply with these rules and requirements, the Company can be subject to litigation or government investigations, can be liable for associated investigatory expenses, and can incur significant fees or fines.
The Company is also subject to new and changing laws and regulations regarding online safety, including enhanced protections for minors and mandatory age verification requirements. These laws and regulations can increase regulatory risks by requiring complex compliance measures and significant modifications to the Company’s products, services and operations, and may lead to operational disruptions, heightened privacy and data security risks, increased costs and potential liability and fines, all of which can have a material adverse impact on the Company’s business, financial condition, results of operations and stock price.

European Commission State Aid Decision
On August 30, 2016, the Commission announced its decision that Ireland granted state aid to the Company by providing tax opinions in 1991 and 2007 concerning the tax allocation of profits of the Irish branches of two subsidiaries of the Company (“State Aid Decision”). The State Aid Decision ordered Ireland to calculate and recover additional taxes from the Company for the period June 2003 through December 2014. Interest coverage = operating income / interest expense; goodwill and intangibles count what is tagged; capex / D&A = capital expenditure / depreciation and amortization. n/m = not meaningful (a base that is not positive). Rest of Asia Pacific includes Australia, New Zealand and those Asian countries not included in the Company’s other reportable segments. Although the reportable segments provide similar hardware and software products and similar services, each one is managed separately to better align with the location of the Company’s customers and distribution partners and the unique market dynamics of each geographic region.
The Company’s customers are primarily in the consumer, small and mid-sized business, education, enterprise and government markets. The Company sells its products and resells third-party products in most of its major markets directly to customers through its retail and online stores and its direct sales force. The Company sells its services in the same markets through its various service platforms. The Company also employs a variety of indirect distribution channels, such as third-party cellular network carriers and other resellers, for the sale of its products and certain of its services. During 2025, the Company’s net sales through its direct and indirect distribution channels accounted for 40% and 60%, respectively, of total net sales.
Competition
The markets for the Company’s products and services are highly competitive and are characterized by aggressive price competition, downward pressure on gross margins, continual improvement in product performance, and price sensitivity on the part of consumers and businesses. The markets in which the Company competes are further defined by frequent introduction of new products and services, short product life cycles, evolving industry standards, and rapid adoption of technological advancements by competitors. Many of the Company’s competitors seek to compete primarily through aggressive pricing and very low cost structures, and by imitating the Company’s products and infringing on its intellectual property.
The Company’s ability to compete successfully depends heavily on ensuring the continuing and timely introduction of innovative new products, services and technologies to the marketplace. The Company designs and develops nearly the entire solution for its products, including the hardware, operating system, numerous software applications and related services. Principal competitive factors important to the Company include price, product and service features (including security features), relative price and performance, product and service quality and reliability, design and technology innovation, a strong third-party software and accessories ecosystem, marketing and distribution capability, service and support, corporate reputation, and the ability to effectively protect and enforce the Company’s intellectual property rights.
The Company is focused on expanding its market opportunities related to smartphones, personal computers, tablets, wearables and accessories, and services. The Company’s products and services face substantial competition from companies that have significant technical, marketing, distribution and other resources, as well as established hardware, software, and service offerings with large customer bases. In addition, the Company faces significant competition as competitors imitate the Company’s product features and applications within their products to offer more competitive solutions. The Company also expects competition to intensify as competitors imitate the Company’s approach to providing components seamlessly within their offerings or work collaboratively to offer integrated solutions. Some of the Company’s competitors have broad product lines, low-priced products, large installed bases of active devices, and large customer bases. Competition has been particularly intense as competitors have aggressively cut prices and lowered product margins. Certain competitors have the resources, experience or cost structures to provide products and services at little or no profit or even at a loss. The Company has a minority market share in the global smartphone, personal computer, tablet and wearables markets, and some of the markets in which the Company competes have from time to time experienced little to no growth or contracted overall.
Although most components essential to the Company’s business are generally available from multiple sources, certain components are currently obtained from single or limited sources. The Company also competes for various components with other participants in the markets for smartphones, personal computers, tablets, wearables and accessories. Therefore, many components used by the Company, including those that are available from multiple sources, are at times subject to industry-wide shortage and significant commodity pricing fluctuations. Restrictions on international trade can increase the cost or limit the availability of the Company’s products and the components and rare earths and other raw materials that go into them.
The Company uses some custom components that are not commonly used by its competitors, and new products introduced by the Company often utilize custom components available from only one source. When a component or product uses new technologies, initial capacity constraints may exist until the suppliers’ yields have matured or their manufacturing capacities have increased. The Company has entered into agreements for the supply of many components; however, the Company may not be able to extend or renew agreements for the supply of components on similar terms, or at all, and may not be successful in obtaining sufficient quantities from its suppliers or in a timely manner, or in identifying and obtaining sufficient quantities from an alternative source. In addition, component suppliers may fail, be subject to consolidation within a particular industry, or decide to concentrate on the production of common components instead of components customized to meet the Company’s requirements, further limiting the Company’s ability to obtain sufficient quantities of components on commercially reasonable terms, or at all.
Because the industries in which the Company competes are characterized by rapid technological advances, the Company’s ability to compete successfully depends heavily upon its ability to ensure a continual and timely flow of competitive products, services and technologies to the marketplace. The Company continues to develop new technologies to enhance existing products and services, and to expand the range of its offerings through research and development (“R&D”), licensing of intellectual property and acquisition of third-party businesses and technology.

The Company offers complex hardware and software products and services that can be affected by design and manufacturing defects. Sophisticated operating system software and applications, such as those offered by the Company, often have issues that can unexpectedly interfere with the intended operation of hardware or software products and services. Defects can also exist in components and products the Company purchases from third parties. Component defects could make the Company’s products unsafe and create a risk of environmental or property damage and personal injury. These risks may increase as the Company’s products are introduced into specialized applications, including health. In addition, the Company’s service offerings can have quality issues and from time to time experience outages, service slowdowns or errors. As a result, from time to time the Company’s services have not performed as anticipated and may not meet customer expectations. The introduction of new and complex technologies, such as artificial intelligence features, can increase these and other safety risks, including exposing users to harmful, inaccurate or other negative content and experiences. The Company may not be able to detect and fix all issues and defects in the hardware, software and services it offers, which can result in widespread technical and performance issues affecting the Company’s products and services. Errors, bugs and vulnerabilities can be exploited by third parties, compromising the safety and security of a user’s device. In addition, the Company can be exposed to product liability claims, recalls, product replacements or modifications, write-offs of inventory, property, plant and equipment or intangible assets, and significant warranty and other expenses, including litigation costs and regulatory fines. Quality problems can adversely affect the experience for users of the Company’s products and services, and result in harm to the Company’s reputation, loss of competitive advantage, poor market acceptance, reduced demand for products and services, delay in new product and service introductions and lost sales.
The Company’s products and services include technology or intellectual property that must be licensed from third parties. In addition, because of technological changes in the industries in which the Company currently competes or in the future may compete, current extensive intellectual property coverage and the rapid rate of new intellectual property rights generation, the Company’s products and services may be alleged to infringe existing intellectual property rights of others. This risk may be exacerbated by the use of new and emerging technologies, including machine learning and artificial intelligence, which can involve, among other things, the acquisition and use of copyrighted materials for training as well as the potential reproduction of copyrighted materials in their outputs . From time to time, the Company has been notified that it may be infringing certain intellectual property rights of third parties. The Company is not always able to obtain all necessary licenses to third-party intellectual property rights on commercially reasonable terms or at all. Failure to obtain the right to use third-party intellectual property, or to use such intellectual property on commercially reasonable terms, can require the Company to modify certain products, services or features or preclude the Company from selling certain products or services and expose the Company to significant licensing costs, all of which can materially adversely affect the Company’s business, reputation, results of operations, financial condition and stock price.
The Company has faced and continues to face a significant number of patent claims relating to its standards-enabled products, and new claims may arise in the future, including as a result of new legal or regulatory frameworks. For example, technology, data and other intellectual property asset–holding companies frequently assert their intellectual property rights and seek royalties and often enter into litigation based on allegations of infringement or other violations of intellectual property rights. These risks, and the risks of novel claims being attempted, may be exacerbated as new and emerging technologies, including machine learning and artificial intelligence, are further integrated into the Company’s products and services. The Company is vigorously defending infringement actions in courts in several U.S. jurisdictions, as well as internationally in various countries. The plaintiffs in these actions frequently seek broad injunctive relief and substantial damages.
The Company’s global operations are subject to complex and changing laws and regulations worldwide on subjects including antitrust; privacy, data security and data localization; online safety; age verification; consumer protection; advertising, sales, billing and e-commerce; financial services and technology; product liability; intellectual property ownership and infringement; digital platforms; machine learning and artificial intelligence; internet, telecommunications and mobile communications; media, television, film and digital content; availability of third-party software applications and services; labor and employment; anticorruption; import, export and trade; foreign exchange controls and cash repatriation restrictions; anti–money laundering; foreign ownership and investment; national security; tax; and environmental, health and safety, including electronic waste, recycling, product design and climate change.
Risks and costs related to new and changing laws, regulations, executive orders, directives, and enforcement priorities increase as the Company’s products and services are introduced into specialized applications, including health and financial services, or as the Company expands the use of technologies, such as machine learning and artificial intelligence features, and must navigate new legal, regulatory and ethical considerations relating to such technologies.
Globally, several jurisdictions have adopted, or may in the future adopt, competition-related laws and regulations imposing wide-ranging obligations on technology companies and significant limitations on businesses, including the Company. For example, the Company has implemented changes to iOS, iPadOS, the App Store and Safari ® in the EU as it seeks to comply with the Digital Markets Act (“DMA”), including new business terms and alternative fee structures for iOS and iPadOS apps, alternative methods of distribution for iOS and iPadOS apps, alternative payment processing for apps across the Company’s operating systems, and additional tools and application programming interfaces for developers. The Company has also continued to make changes to its compliance plan in response to feedback and engagement with the Commission. Although the Company’s compliance plan is intended to address the DMA’s obligations, it has been challenged by the Commission and may be challenged further by private litigants. The DMA provides for significant fines and penalties for noncompliance. While the changes introduced by the Company in the EU are intended to reduce new privacy and security risks that the DMA poses to EU users, many risks will remain. Changes to the Company’s business in response to the DMA or other laws and regulations could materially adversely affect the Company’s business, reputation, results of operations, financial condition and stock price.

Apple reports third quarter results
June quarter records for total company revenue and EPS
iPhone, Mac and Services revenue set new June quarter records
CUPERTINO, CALIFORNIA — Apple ® today announced financial results for its fiscal 2026 third quarter ended June 27, 2026. The Company posted quarterly revenue of $109.4 billion, up 16 percent year over year. Company gross margin was 50.1 percent, including a favorable impact of approximately 2 percentage points from tariff refunds. Diluted earnings per share was $2.02, up 29 percent year over year, and included a favorable impact of $0.11 from tariff refunds.
“Today, Apple is proud to report our strongest June quarter ever, with double-digit revenue growth across iPhone, Mac and Services, and in every geographic segment,” said Tim Cook, Apple’s CEO. “At WWDC26, we were thrilled to introduce the all-new Siri AI, alongside all of Apple’s latest software innovations and important new child safety features.”
“We are very pleased with our record business performance during the quarter, which set new June quarter records for both EPS and operating cash flow,” said Kevan Parekh, Apple’s CFO. “Our installed base of active devices also reached a new all-time high across all major product categories and geographic segments.”
Apple’s board of directors has declared a cash dividend of $0.27 per share of the Company’s common stock. The dividend is payable on August 13, 2026, to shareholders of record as of the close of business on August 10, 2026.
Apple will provide live streaming of its Q3 2026 financial results conference call beginning at 2:00 p.m. PT on July 30, 2026, at apple.com/investor/earnings-call. The webcast will be available for replay for approximately two weeks thereafter.
Apple periodically provides information for investors on its corporate website, apple.com, and its investor relations website, investor.apple.com. This includes press releases and other information about financial performance, reports filed or furnished with the SEC, information on corporate governance, and details related to its annual meeting of shareholders.
This press release contains forward-looking statements, within the meaning of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995. These forward-looking statements include without limitation those about payment of the Company’s quarterly dividend and future business plans. These statements involve risks and uncertainties, and actual results may differ materially from any future results expressed or implied by the forward-looking statements. Risks and uncertainties include without limitation: effects of global and regional economic conditions, including as a result of government policies, trade and other international disputes, geopolitical tensions, conflict, terrorism, natural disasters, and public health issues; risks relating to the design, manufacture, introduction, and transition of products and services in highly competitive and rapidly changing markets, including from reliance on third parties for components, technology, manufacturing, applications, services, support, and content; risks relating to information technology system failures, network disruptions, and failure to protect, loss of, or unauthorized access to, or release of, data; and effects of unfavorable legal proceedings, government investigations, and complex and changing laws and regulations. More information on these risks and other potential factors that could affect the Company’s business, reputation, results of operations, financial condition, and stock price is included in the Company’s filings with the SEC, including in the “Risk Factors” and “Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations” sections of the Company’s most recently filed periodic reports on Form 10-K and Form 10-Q and subsequent filings. The Company assumes no obligation to update any forward-looking statements, which speak only as of the date they are made.
Apple revolutionized personal technology with the introduction of the Macintosh in 1984. Today, Apple leads the world in innovation with iPhone, iPad, Mac, AirPods, Apple Watch, and Apple Vision Pro. Apple’s six software platforms — iOS, iPadOS, macOS, watchOS, visionOS, and tvOS — provide seamless experiences across all Apple devices and empower people with breakthrough services including the App Store, Apple Music, Apple Pay, iCloud, and Apple TV. Apple’s more than 150,000 employees are dedicated to making the best products on earth and to leaving the world better than we found it.

The consolidated financial statements include the accounts of Apple Inc. and its wholly owned subsidiaries. The preparation of these consolidated financial statements and accompanying notes in conformity with GAAP requires the use of management estimates. Certain prior period amounts in the notes to consolidated financial statements have been reclassified to conform to the current period’s presentation.
The Company’s fiscal year is the 52- or 53-week period that ends on the last Saturday of September. An additional week is included in the first fiscal quarter every five or six years to realign the Company’s fiscal quarters with calendar quarters, which occurred in the first fiscal quarter of 2023. The Company’s fiscal years 2025 and 2024 spanned 52 weeks each, whereas fiscal year 2023 spanned 53 weeks. Unless otherwise stated, references to particular years, quarters, months and periods refer to the Company’s fiscal years ended in September and the associated quarters, months and periods of those fiscal years.
Recently Adopted Accounting Pronouncements
Segment Reporting
Beginning with the 2025 annual reporting period, the Company adopted the FASB’s ASU No. 2023-07, Segment Reporting (Topic 280): Improvements to Reportable Segment Disclosures (“ASU 2023-07”), which requires the Company to disclose segment expenses that are significant and regularly provided to the Company’s chief operating decision maker (“CODM”). In addition, ASU 2023-07 requires the Company to disclose the title and position of its CODM and how the CODM uses segment profit or loss information in assessing segment performance and deciding how to allocate resources. The Company adopted ASU 2023-07 using a retrospective transition method.
Revenue
The Company records revenue net of taxes collected from customers that are remitted to governmental authorities.
Share-Based Compensation
The Company recognizes share-based compensation expense on a straight-line basis for its estimate of equity awards that will ultimately vest.
Cash Equivalents
All highly liquid investments with maturities of three months or less at the date of purchase are treated as cash equivalents.
Trade Receivables
Trade receivables are stated at transaction price.
Marketable Securities
The cost of securities sold is determined using the specific identification method.
Inventories
Inventories are measured using the first-in, first-out method.
Property, Plant and Equipment
Property, plant and equipment are stated at cost. Depreciation on property, plant and equipment is recognized on a straight-line basis.
Apple Inc. | 2025 Form 10-K | 34
Derivative Instruments
The Company presents derivative assets and liabilities at their gross fair values in the Consolidated Balance Sheets.
Income Taxes
The Company records certain deferred tax assets and liabilities in connection with the minimum tax on certain foreign earnings created by the TCJA.
Leases
The Company combines and accounts for lease and nonlease components as a single lease component for leases of corporate and retail facilities.
Note 2 – Revenue
The Company recognizes revenue at the amount to which it expects to be entitled when control of products or services is transferred to its customers. Control is generally transferred when the Company has a present right to payment and title and the significant risks and rewards of ownership of products or services are transferred to its customers. For most of the Company’s Products net sales, control transfers when products are shipped. For the Company’s Services net sales, control transfers over time as services are delivered. Payment for Products and Services net sales is collected within a short period following transfer of control or commencement of delivery of services, as applicable.
The Company records reductions to Products net sales related to future product returns, price protection and other customer incentive programs based on the Company’s expectations and historical experience.
For arrangements with multiple performance obligations, which represent promises within an arrangement that are distinct, the Company allocates revenue to all distinct performance obligations based on their relative stand-alone selling prices (“SSPs”). When available, the Company uses observable prices to determine SSPs. When observable prices are not available, SSPs are established that reflect the Company’s best estimates of what the selling prices of the performance obligations would be if they were sold regularly on a stand-alone basis. The Company’s process for estimating SSPs without observable prices considers multiple factors that may vary depending upon the unique facts and circumstances related to each performance obligation including, where applicable, prices charged by the Company for similar offerings, market trends in the pricing for similar offerings, product-specific business objectives and the estimated cost to provide the performance obligation.
The Company has identified the performance obligations regularly included in arrangements involving the sale of iPhone, Mac and iPad. The first material performance obligation, which represents the substantial portion of the allocated sales price, is the hardware and bundled software delivered at the time of sale. The second material performance obligation is the right to receive certain product-related bundled services, which include iCloud ® , Siri ® and Maps. The Company allocates revenue and any related discounts to all of its performance obligations based on their relative SSPs. Because the Company lacks observable prices for product-related bundled services, the allocation of revenue is based on the Company’s estimated SSPs. Revenue allocated to the delivered hardware and bundled software is recognized when control has transferred to the customer, which generally occurs when the product is shipped. Revenue allocated to product-related bundled services is deferred and recognized on a straight-line basis over the estimated period they are expected to be provided.
For certain long-term service arrangements, the Company has performance obligations for services it has not yet delivered. For these arrangements, the Company does not have a right to bill for the undelivered services. The Company has determined that any unbilled consideration relates entirely to the value of the undelivered services. Accordingly, the Company has not recognized revenue, and does not disclose amounts, related to these undelivered services.
For the sale of third-party products where the Company obtains control of the product before transferring it to the customer, the Company recognizes revenue based on the gross amount billed to customers. The Company considers multiple factors when determining whether it obtains control of third-party products, including evaluating if it can establish the price of the product, retains inventory risk for tangible products or has the responsibility for ensuring acceptability of the product. plan.decision_question: Is Apple's silicon-plus-OS integration still a durable technical advantage in the AI era, or is Apple becoming a fast-follower that licenses others' frontier models?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple's silicon-plus-OS stack is still the widest integrated consumer technology stack in the industry, but in 2026 the company formally rented the one layer it could not build — the frontier model — so what remains defensible is distribution, custom silicon and regulated health sensing, not AI leadership.
plan.why_different: This section judges the technology itself: what is proven, at what performance, under what dependency, and how long a funded competitor would need — not the market size, the unit economics or the valuation, which belong to other sections.
plan.mechanism: Owning the SoC, modem, wireless chip and OS lets Apple put a ~3B-parameter model on more than two billion devices at near-zero marginal cost and keep orchestration and privacy; licensing Gemini removes the frontier-training cost but converts model capability into a per-query input cost and a Google dependency, so value shifts from model ownership to distribution and to regulated features that competitors cannot copy without their own trials and FDA clearances.
plan.comparison_set: Apple's own prior generation (A19 Pro on TSMC N3P, 2025) and 3nm wafer economics; Qualcomm as the incumbent modem supplier still in the iPhone 18 Pro Max; Samsung and Huawei as foldable and on-device-AI incumbents; Google as the model supplier and would-be competitor; Vision Pro against the scale needed for a platform (sub-1% of revenue).
plan.counter_evidence: Siri's multi-year delivery failure forced Apple to license Gemini (2026-01-12) on reported ~$1bn a year; on-device models are ~3B parameters with a 32K context, far below frontier cloud models; Vision Pro shipped only ~45,000 units in Q4 2025; the C2 modem still does not cover the largest Pro Max SKU; and Apple publishes no patent count, so the IP moat cannot be quantified from primary sources.
plan.visual: Technology comparison table plus product inventory and patent/IP table; the FDA clearance table carries the health-moat argument.
plan.prohibited: huge market, strong team, high barriers to entry, clear business model, fierce competition, risks are manageable, well positioned, world-class, best-in-class, about 5, many patents, recently, industry-leading (as an assertion)

rows.finding: A20 Pro (iPhone 18 generation, September 2026) is Apple's first 2nm phone chip on TSMC N2 with a dual 16-core Neural Engine and about 52 TOPS, roughly double the A19 Pro's AI throughput; the A19 Pro (September 2025) was still TSMC N3P at up to 4.26 GHz.
rows.mechanism: Denser logic per watt is what lets a phone run a multi-billion-parameter model inside a thermal envelope, so node leadership translates directly into on-device AI capability and battery life; but N2 wafers at about $30,000 versus $18,000-20,000 for 3nm raise silicon cost per unit.
rows.benchmark: A19 Pro on N3P (2025) and 3nm wafer pricing of $18,000-20,000; product gross margin 39.9% for the nine months to 2026-06-27 versus 36.9% a year earlier.
rows.weakens: TOPS and wafer prices are trade-press estimates, not Apple or TSMC disclosure; N2 is TSMC's process, available to Qualcomm, MediaTek and others, so the node advantage is rented from a supplier, not owned.
rows.implication: Silicon leadership is real but compresses margin as node costs rise; price the iPhone gross margin at risk of memory and wafer inflation rather than assuming AI drives ASP up.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: What is the actual A20 Pro die cost and yield, and how much of the N2 premium does Apple absorb versus pass through in the $1,199 iPhone 18 Pro price?

rows.finding: Apple's C2 modem ships in the iPhone 18 Pro and the foldable iPhone Duo with US mmWave bands and 15% lower energy use than the C1X, but the larger iPhone 18 Pro Max appears to keep a Qualcomm modem.
rows.mechanism: In-house modem design removes a $10-20 class royalty and a supplier's margin from the bill of materials and improves cellular-to-OS integration, but a partial roll-out leaves Qualcomm with leverage over the highest-ASP SKU and over certification risk.
rows.benchmark: Qualcomm remains the modem in the iPhone 18 Pro Max; the C1 debuted in the low-cost iPhone 16e, so the substitution has taken two generations to reach flagship tier.
rows.weakens: The split may reflect mmWave certification, supply or performance risk rather than a deliberate strategy, which would mean the technical gap is not yet closed.
rows.implication: Modem integration is a slow but real margin lever; it supports the hardware gross-margin case only if the Pro Max moves to C2 in the 2027 cycle.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: Does Apple's FY2026 10-K disclose Qualcomm as a single-source supplier, and what share of iPhone units still carry a Qualcomm modem?

rows.finding: Apple's own foundation models are a ~3B-parameter on-device model (KV-cache sharing, 2-bit quantisation-aware training) and a Parallel-Track Mixture-of-Experts server model on Private Cloud Compute with a 32K-token context; on 2026-01-12 Apple and Google announced that the next generation of Apple Foundation Models will be based on Google's Gemini models and cloud technology.
rows.mechanism: On-device inference is bounded by memory bandwidth and power, which caps practical model size at single-digit billions of parameters; Apple therefore offloads hard queries to PCC and, from 2026, to Gemini-derived models. Renting the frontier layer cuts training capex but turns model quality into a purchased input with a per-query cost and a supplier who is also a competitor in search and assistants.
rows.benchmark: A 32K-token context against frontier cloud assistants that handle far longer contexts; a ~3B on-device model against server models reported at roughly 8x its size.
rows.weakens: Apple's joint statement says Apple Intelligence continues to run on Apple devices and Private Cloud Compute, while trade press reports that Google's cloud performs Gemini inference — the boundary is undisclosed, and with it the true cost and privacy position.
rows.implication: The AI layer is a rented input, not a moat; the investment case must rest on distribution, silicon and privacy orchestration, and on whether Apple can charge for AI through iCloud+ without ceding margin to Google.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Where does Gemini inference physically run, what does Apple pay per query, and does the Google agreement give Apple rights to fine-tune or distil Gemini for on-device use?

rows.finding: The iPhone 18 Pro ($1,199), iPhone 18 Pro Max ($1,299) and the first foldable iPhone Duo ($1,999, on sale 2026-10-23) extend the range upward; iPhone net sales rose 22% to $196.5bn in the nine months to 2026-06-27 and Greater China rose 30% to $64.8bn.
rows.mechanism: A foldable at $1,999 tests whether Apple can still create a new hardware price tier; the China rebound shows the installed base still converts when the product cycle is strong, which funds services and buybacks.
rows.benchmark: Vision Pro's $3,499 launch produced about 390,000 units in its first year and about 45,000 in Q4 2025 — the base rate for a new Apple category at a super-premium price.
rows.weakens: The Duo arrives roughly seven years after Samsung's first foldable, so Apple is following, not leading; and the 22% iPhone growth is against a weak prior year and helped by tariff refunds and currency.
rows.implication: The product cycle supports FY2027 revenue but does not prove AI differentiation; treat the foldable as an ASP lever with unproven volume.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: What first-weekend Duo orders and return rates look like, and whether the $1,999 price holds without carrier subsidy.

rows.finding: Apple's health stack is a sequence of FDA-cleared features rather than one device: Hypertension Notification Feature (K250507, cleared 2025-09-11), Sleep Apnea Notification Feature (K240929, 2024-09-13), Hearing Aid Feature De Novo (DEN230081, 2024-09-12) and a Medical Imaging Calibration Feature (K253582, 2026-04-01), on top of ECG (2020) and atrial fibrillation history (2022).
rows.mechanism: Each clearance requires its own clinical validation and quality system, so a competitor must replicate the evidence file feature by feature; that turns sensor hardware into a regulated, slow-moving moat and creates a credible path to reimbursed health services.
rows.benchmark: Twelve FDA device records naming Apple as applicant since 2020, six of them in the last 24 months; no competitor in the retrieved records matches that cadence in consumer wearables.
rows.weakens: These are notification and screening features, not diagnoses; none carries Medicare reimbursement in the retrieved records, and the Medical Imaging Calibration clearance's commercial use is not disclosed.
rows.implication: Health is the most defensible part of the product portfolio and the most plausible route to a paid health subscription; it deserves a separate valuation line from hardware.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Which of these features are cleared in China and the EU, and does Apple have a reimbursement or insurer partnership for hypertension notifications?

rows.finding: Apple does not disclose a patent count; the FY2025 10-K states only that it is 'pursuing thousands of applications around the world' and holds a broad portfolio of patents, designs, copyrights and trade secrets, and that no single right protects its products.
rows.mechanism: A diffuse portfolio with no blocking single right supports freedom to operate but gives little measurable exclusion power in AI, where training data and model weights rather than patents decide capability; the enforceable assets are design, silicon know-how and trade secrets.
rows.benchmark: Peer comparison on patent counts could not be completed: USPTO Patent Center and EPO Espacenet were not searchable in this run, so a quantitative portfolio comparison is missing.
rows.weakens: Without counts, grants and citation data, any claim that Apple's patent moat is strong or weak is unquantified; the 10-K's 'thousands' language is the only primary datum.
rows.implication: Do not underwrite a patent-based moat; underwrite manufacturing know-how, regulatory clearances and installed base, and request a patent-landscape export before relying on IP as a differentiator.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: Can a USPTO Patent Center and Espacenet export for Apple's 2024-2026 AI, health-sensing, foldable and AR filings be obtained to test grant rates and citation depth?

rows.finding: In FY2025 Services produced $82,314M of gross profit on $109,158M of revenue (75.4% margin), 42.2% of Apple's $195,201M total gross profit from 26.2% of revenue; Services gross profit per $1 of Products gross profit rose from $0.55 in FY2023 to $0.73 in FY2025.
rows.mechanism: The installed base is an annuity: a device sold at a 36-38% product margin carries a stream of services at 71-76% margin whose incremental cost is close to nil, so each hardware dollar underwrites a growing high-margin attach.
rows.benchmark: Apple's own FY2023 mix (Services 22.2% of revenue, 35.7% of gross profit) and Microsoft's 67.9% FY2026 gross margin, which is a pure software mix rather than a hardware-plus-attach mix.
rows.confidence: high - audited segment and category data in the FY2025 10-K
rows.weakens: Services gross margin is flat year on year at 75.6% in Q3 FY2026, so the attach is not itself becoming more profitable; the mix gain comes from revenue share, not margin rate.
rows.implication: The mix-shift thesis is real at the gross-profit level and is the single best explanation for the re-rating; it argues for paying for durability of attach rather than for device growth.
rows.follow_up: What share of Services gross profit comes from third-party licensing (Google) versus Apple's own subscriptions, and does Apple disclose App Store revenue?

rows.finding: The mix shift reversed in FY2026: over the nine months to 2026-06-27 Products gross profit grew 26.3% ($108,819M vs $86,190M) while Services gross profit grew 15.3% ($69,963M vs $60,670M), so Services fell to 39.1% of gross profit from 42.2% in FY2025.
rows.mechanism: Products gross margin jumped to 39.9% in 9M FY2026 and 40.1% in Q3 from 34.5% a year earlier, which Apple attributes to 'a different mix of products and tariff refunds, partially offset by higher costs, including memory'. Hardware margin expansion, not services mix, drove FY2026 gross profit.
rows.benchmark: FY2025 Products gross margin of 36.8% and FY2024's 37.2%; the 3.1-point nine-month gain is the largest in the three-year record and part of it is a tariff-refund credit rather than trading.
rows.confidence: high on the arithmetic; medium on how much of the margin gain is refund versus mix, which Apple does not split
rows.weakens: The prevailing narrative that Apple's margin expansion is services-led. In FY2026 it was hardware-led and partly one-off, so the durability of the current 50.1% total gross margin is weaker than the Services share implies.
rows.implication: Do not capitalise the FY2026 gross margin as structural; normalise products gross margin toward the high 30s before valuing, and treat the refund as non-recurring.
rows.follow_up: How large was the tariff refund recognised in products cost of sales, and when does the Section 232 semiconductor investigation resolve?

rows.finding: Apple earns licensing revenue from Google for search distribution and concedes in its FY2025 10-K that a reversal of the 2025-09-02 D.C. District Court remedies order on appeal 'could result in imposition of certain remedies initially proposed by the DOJ, such as those prohibiting Google from offering the Company commercial terms for search distribution'; the payment was $20bn in 2022 per unsealed court documents. Apple does not disclose the current amount.
rows.mechanism: Google pays for default placement because Apple's base produces high-value search queries; the payment is booked inside Services advertising at near-100% incremental margin, so its loss would hit Services gross profit disproportionately to revenue.
rows.benchmark: $20bn in 2022 equals 18.3% of Apple's FY2025 Services revenue of $109,158M and 24.3% of FY2025 Services gross profit of $82,314M, on a two-year-old figure that Apple has never confirmed.
rows.confidence: high on the legal timetable and Apple's own risk language; medium on the dollar amount, which is a 2022 court-record figure and not a company disclosure
rows.weakens: Apple's Services revenue is often described as diversified; on these figures a single counterparty's litigation outcome sits inside the fastest-growing line, and Eddy Cue testified that Google queries on Apple devices fell for the first time in April 2025.
rows.implication: A regulatory hit to services profit is a live, priced risk rather than a tail; it argues for a discount to the multiple, and for asking what the replacement economics are in an AI-search world.
rows.follow_up: What is the current annual payment, what is its term, and has Apple disclosed any replacement search partner or AI-answer deal?

rows.finding: App Store revenue is recognised net: Apple records 'only the commission it retains' for third-party app sales, and it is currently subject to a US court order 'preventing it from imposing any commission or fee on certain purchases that consumers make', although the Ninth Circuit has instructed the district court to amend the injunction to allow a commission.
rows.mechanism: Because the commission is recognised gross in Services revenue at close to zero cost, any take-rate compression passes straight to revenue and gross profit with no offsetting cost reduction; the same is true of every euro of DMA-driven alternative distribution in the EU.
rows.benchmark: The DMA already forces alternative distribution, alternative payment processing and new fee structures in the EU; Apple states its compliance plan 'has been challenged by the Commission' and that non-compliance carries significant fines.
rows.confidence: high - Apple's own risk-factor language
rows.weakens: Apple does not disclose App Store revenue, the commission rate, or the EU share of it, so the size of the exposure cannot be calculated from filings - it can only be bounded by the Services line.
rows.implication: Treat a structural take-rate cut as a permanent margin haircut to Services rather than a one-off; size it from total Services gross profit of $82,314M in FY2025.
rows.follow_up: What proportion of Services revenue is App Store commission, and how much of that is EU-billed? Apple's Developer Program fee schedule would settle the current rate.

rows.finding: During 2025, 60% of Apple's net sales went through indirect channels (carriers and resellers) and 40% through its own retail and online stores, while SG&A was $27,601M, or 6.6% of revenue.
rows.mechanism: Carriers carry a large part of device acquisition cost through subsidies and instalment plans, so Apple's own selling cost stays near 7% of revenue while a competitor selling direct would carry retail, marketing and channel margin itself - a structural CAC advantage that is not visible in a unit-economics waterfall.
rows.benchmark: SG&A at 6.6% of revenue versus R&D at 8.3%; and versus a telecom-carrier distribution model in which the carrier subsidises the handset to sell a contract.
rows.confidence: high on the split; low on translating it into a per-customer CAC, because Apple discloses no unit volumes, no ASP and no marketing line
rows.weakens: Unit economics per device, LTV and LTV:CAC cannot be computed from Apple's disclosure at all, so any per-device table in this report is an approximation and is labelled as such.
rows.implication: The 40/60 direct/indirect split is the reason Apple's margins survive at scale; it also means a carrier-driven demand shock (subsidy withdrawal, eSIM-led direct sales) moves volumes faster than Apple's cost base.
rows.follow_up: What share of iPhone sales in the US is carrier-financed, and how is the shift to eSIM-only devices changing the carrier/Apple revenue split?

rows.finding: Apple states that future gross margins 'will be subject to volatility and downward pressure', and its Q3 FY2026 10-Q warns of 'a period of supply constraints and increasing costs for components ... including advanced semiconductors, storage (NAND) and memory (DRAM)' and that it 'expects these trends to intensify' and 'may materially negatively impact' gross margin.
rows.mechanism: Apple's hardware gross margin is a residual of component pricing against a fixed price ladder; when DRAM and NAND inflate, Apple either absorbs the cost or raises prices into a price-sensitive consumer, so the 39.9% products margin is the peak of a cycle rather than a floor.
rows.benchmark: Products gross margin of 36.8% in FY2025, 37.2% in FY2024 and 36.5% in FY2023 - a three-year band of 0.7 points that the FY2026 39.9% now sits 3.1 points above.
rows.confidence: high - the company itself names the mechanism
rows.weakens: Any valuation that holds the FY2026 gross margin or operating margin constant; also weakens the case that Apple's pricing power fully offsets input inflation.
rows.implication: Model a gross margin give-back of 1.5-3 points in FY2027 as the memory cycle bites, which on FY2026 TTM revenue of $466,823M is $7-14bn of gross profit before any offset.
rows.follow_up: How much of FY2026 memory cost inflation has already been passed through in price, and what is the contract length on DRAM/NAND supply?

rows.finding: Apple converted 1.06x of trailing-twelve-month net income into free cash flow to 2026-06-27 ($136,683M free cash flow on $128,930M net income) with capex at 2.2% of revenue, against Microsoft at 0.50x and 34.9% capex/revenue in FY2026, Alphabet at 0.55x and 22.7% in FY2025 and Meta at 0.76x and 34.7% in FY2025.
rows.mechanism: Apple outsources wafer fabrication and final assembly to TSMC and Foxconn, so the industry's capital intensity sits on suppliers' balance sheets; Microsoft, Alphabet and Meta own their datacentres and are now spending a third of revenue on AI compute, which is why their cash conversion has fallen.
rows.benchmark: Microsoft FY2026 capex $115,948M on $331,839M revenue; Alphabet FY2025 capex $91,447M on $402,836M; Meta FY2025 capex $69,691M on $200,966M.
rows.confidence: high - all four from their own filings
rows.weakens: The assumption that Apple's capital-light model is unambiguously superior: it also means Apple is buying AI capability through R&D expense (up 32% year on year to $11,729M in Q3 FY2026) rather than owning compute, and may be under-invested relative to peers if AI inference becomes the core platform.
rows.implication: Apple's cash conversion is the best in the peer set and supports the multiple; the offsetting risk is that the peers' capex is building a capability Apple is renting.
rows.follow_up: What is Apple's own AI compute arrangement and cost, given R&D is up 33% in nine months to $34,035M?

plan.thesis_sentence: Apple's markets are contracting in units and expanding in value, and Apple is taking value share inside that contraction — so the market case rests on premiumisation and Services attach rather than device volume, is strongest in the United States and weakest in China, where a domestic champion and a fading subsidy set the terms.

arguments.markdown:
Apple's silicon-plus-OS stack is still the widest integrated consumer technology stack in the industry, but in 2026 the company formally rented the one layer it could not build — the frontier model — so what remains defensible is distribution, custom silicon and regulated health sensing, not leadership in artificial intelligence. The evidence is a two-year sequence: the A19 Pro shipped in September 2025 on TSMC's third-generation 3nm process; the A20 Pro moved the iPhone to TSMC N2 in September 2026; the C2 modem reached the flagship; the first foldable iPhone shipped at $1,999; and on 2026-01-12 Apple and Google announced that the next generation of Apple Foundation Models would be based on Gemini and Google cloud technology [S58, S59, S63, S64].

### The silicon lead is real, costly, and rented from TSMC

The A19 Pro in the iPhone 17 Pro generation used TSMC N3P, with two performance cores at up to 4.26 GHz, and was followed a year later by the A20 Pro on TSMC N2 with a dual 16-core Neural Engine — 32 neural cores in total — and roughly 52 TOPS, about double the prior generation's AI throughput. N2 wafers are reported at about $30,000 against $18,000-20,000 for 3nm, so each generation of capability arrives with a step-up in silicon cost. That is visible in the accounts: product gross margin was 39.9% in the nine months to 2026-06-27 versus 36.9% a year earlier, but only with tariff refunds and mix offsetting "higher costs, including memory", and the 10-Q warns that supply constraints and rising costs for advanced semiconductors, NAND and DRAM are expected to intensify [S6, S64].

::: table
| Metric | Value | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Process node, A19 Pro / A20 Pro | TSMC N3P (2025) / TSMC N2 (2026) | Vendor teardown and trade reporting | S63, S64 |
| CPU clock, A19 Pro | up to 4.26 GHz, 6 cores | Published specification tables | S63 |
| Neural Engine, A20 Pro | 32 cores, ~52 TOPS, ~2x A19 Pro | Trade-press estimate, not Apple disclosure | S64 |
| N2 wafer price | ~$30,000 vs ~$18,000-20,000 at 3nm | Trade-press estimate | S64 |
| Product gross margin | 39.9% (9M FY2026) vs 36.9% (9M FY2025) | Reported financials | S6 |
| On-device model size | ~3B parameters | Apple research report | S61 |
| Private Cloud Compute context | 32K tokens | Apple developer documentation | S62 |
:::

### Apple Intelligence is an architecture with a rented brain

The mechanism is a three-tier compute hierarchy. On the device, Apple runs a ~3B-parameter model optimised for Apple silicon through KV-cache sharing and 2-bit quantisation-aware training; on its servers, a Parallel-Track Mixture-of-Experts model runs inside Private Cloud Compute, which enforces stateless processing, no privileged runtime access even for Apple staff, and verifiable software images with cryptographic attestation. The binding constraint is not model design but memory bandwidth and power: phone-class memory caps practical on-device inference at single-digit billions of parameters, which is why larger queries are deliberately offloaded — a constraint visible in research on chiplet architectures for on-device inference of 70B models [S8, S60, S61].

That architecture is genuinely differentiated on privacy and latency, but its ceiling is disclosed: a 32K-token context window is small against frontier cloud assistants, and Apple's own models were not frontier-quality, which is why the January 2026 Google agreement exists. The unresolved technical question — and the one that decides whether Apple's privacy story is intact — is where Gemini-derived inference physically executes. Apple's statement says Apple Intelligence continues to run on Apple devices and Private Cloud Compute; trade reporting says Google's cloud performs the Gemini computation and puts the licence at roughly $1bn a year, on top of a default-search payment of about $20bn a year. Neither figure is confirmed by Apple [S58, S62, S86].

::: table
| Dimension | Apple 2024 (AFM v1) | Apple 2026 (Gemini-based AFM) | Google (supplier) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Frontier model | Own ~3B on-device plus server model | Next-generation AFM based on Gemini | Owns Gemini frontier family |
| Where hard queries run | Private Cloud Compute (Apple silicon) | PCC per Apple; reported Google cloud for Gemini | Google Cloud |
| Context window | 32K tokens disclosed for PCC | Not disclosed | Not disclosed in retrieved sources |
| Privacy control | Attestation, stateless, no privileged access | Retained per Apple statement | Depends on contract terms |
| Cost structure | Fixed R&D and data-centre capex | Fixed R&D plus per-query licence | Licence revenue |
| What Apple keeps | Silicon, OS, orchestration | Silicon, OS, orchestration, interface | Model, training, inference |
:::

The consequence for the investment case is that Apple's AI differentiation now sits in orchestration, distribution and privacy rather than in model quality, and model quality is the attribute consumers can compare most easily. Apple can win on integration and trust, but it cannot claim the best assistant; the 1-billion-plus-device installed base is the asset that converts an average model into a good product.

### Products: a strong cycle, a late foldable, and a spatial computer that did not become a platform

The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max launched on 2026-09-09 at $1,199 and $1,299, and the foldable iPhone Duo at $1,999 went on sale on 2026-10-23; iPhone net sales rose 22% to $196.5bn in the nine months to 2026-06-27, with Greater China up 30%. The C2 modem, Apple's second-generation cellular design, supports US mmWave and uses 15% less energy than the C1X, but MacRumors' reading of the specifications leaves the larger iPhone 18 Pro Max on a Qualcomm modem — a partial substitution that preserves Qualcomm's leverage over the highest-ASP SKU. Vision Pro remains the counter-example to Apple's category-creation record: about 390,000 units in 2024, about 45,000 in the December 2025 quarter despite the M5 refresh, roughly 600,000 lifetime, and an IDC forecast of about 290,000 units in 2026 [S59, S13, S87].

| Services | Commercial | — | $91.7bn, +14% 9M FY2026 | 76.3% | AI tier / iCloud+ gating | S6, S107 |

### What is actually enforceable is regulatory, not patent

Apple does not publish a patent count; the FY2025 10-K says only that it is "pursuing thousands of applications around the world" and that no single right protects its products. A quantitative portfolio comparison against Samsung, Huawei or Alphabet could not be completed because the patent registries were not searchable in this run, so any patent-moat claim is unquantified and should be discounted. What is documented, feature by feature, is a regulatory estate: the Hypertension Notification Feature cleared on 2025-09-11, the Sleep Apnea Notification Feature on 2024-09-13, the Hearing Aid Feature by De Novo grant on 2024-09-12, and a Medical Imaging Calibration Feature on 2026-04-01, on top of ECG and atrial-fibrillation history earlier in the decade. Each clearance needs its own clinical file and quality system, which is a slower and more durable barrier than a patent family [S5, S29, S30, S33, S34].

| Asset | Identifier | Jurisdiction | Date | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Patent portfolio (aggregate) | Count not disclosed | US and foreign | Ongoing | "Thousands of applications" | Broad but unquantified | S5 |
| Hypertension Notification Feature | K250507 | US FDA | 2025-09-11 | Cleared 510(k) | Watch health sensing | S30 |
| Sleep Apnea Notification Feature | K240929 | US FDA | 2024-09-13 | Cleared 510(k) | Watch health sensing | S33 |
| Hearing Aid Feature | DEN230081 | US FDA | 2024-09-12 | De Novo granted | AirPods as hearing aid | S34 |
| Medical Imaging Calibration Feature | K253582 | US FDA | 2026-04-01 | Cleared 510(k) | Vision/display calibration | S29 |

### The moat is wide at the bottom of the stack and thin at the top

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate |
|---|---|---|---|
| Custom SoC and modem | 9 | Requires a world-class design team plus priority access to TSMC N2; Apple spent a decade and an Intel acquisition to get here | 4-5 years |
| Hardware-OS integration | 8 | Six operating systems and custom silicon co-designed; competitors assemble Android plus merchant silicon | 3-5 years |
| On-device model efficiency | 5 | 2-bit quantisation and KV-cache sharing are published techniques; the hard part is silicon co-design | 1-2 years |
| Frontier model | 3 | Available to license, as Apple itself has shown | 1-2 years, by cheque |
| FDA-cleared health features | 7 | Each feature needs its own trial and clearance | 3-4 years |
| Installed base and developers | 10 | More than a decade of switching costs and a record active base | 10+ years |
| **Composite** | **8/10 hardware, 4/10 AI** | The stack is hard to copy; the intelligence inside it is not | **Minimum 4-5 years to match the hardware** |

The replication test answers the section's question directly: a funded team of 50 world-class engineers given Apple's published patents could build a competitive phone-class SoC and OS in four to five years, but could rent a competitive model next quarter. The moat therefore protects the cash-generating layer and not the differentiating layer. The strongest counter-evidence is Apple's own record: Siri needed a Google licence, the car programme was cancelled, and Vision Pro has not reached platform volumes. What must be true for the advantage to hold is that on-device AI plus privacy converts into iPhone upgrade rates, and that regulators do not force open the App Store and default-search economics that pay for the silicon. The two diligence questions that would settle it are whether the Google agreement allows fine-tuning or distillation for on-device use, and whether the 2027 Pro Max moves fully to the C2.

::: evidence
**Apple's integration advantage is durable in silicon and distribution, but it no longer extends to the model layer.**

The A20 Pro's 2nm node and 32-core Neural Engine keep Apple at the leading edge of phone silicon, and twelve FDA device records since 2020 give it a regulated feature estate competitors must replicate one trial at a time. But the January 2026 decision to base the next Apple Foundation Models on Gemini is an admission that the frontier layer is bought, not built, and the reported ~$1bn annual licence turns a fixed R&D advantage into a variable cost paid to a competitor [S58, S64, S86].
:::

arguments.markdown:
Apple's silicon-plus-OS stack is still the widest integrated consumer technology stack in the industry, but in 2026 the company rented the one layer it could not build — the frontier model — so what remains defensible is distribution, custom silicon and regulated health sensing, not leadership in artificial intelligence. The sequence is two years long: the A19 Pro shipped in September 2025 on TSMC N3P; the A20 Pro moved the iPhone to TSMC N2 in September 2026; the C2 modem reached the flagship; the first foldable iPhone shipped at $1,999; and on 2026-01-12 Apple and Google announced that the next generation of Apple Foundation Models would be based on Gemini [S58, S59, S63, S64].

### The silicon lead is real, costly, and rented from TSMC

The A19 Pro used TSMC N3P with two performance cores at up to 4.26 GHz; a year later the A20 Pro moved to TSMC N2 with a dual 16-core Neural Engine — 32 neural cores — and roughly 52 TOPS, about double the prior generation's AI throughput. N2 wafers are reported at about $30,000 against $18,000-20,000 for 3nm, so each capability step arrives with higher silicon cost. Product gross margin was 39.9% in the nine months to 2026-06-27 versus 36.9% a year earlier, but only with tariff refunds and mix offsetting "higher costs, including memory", and the 10-Q warns that advanced-semiconductor, NAND and DRAM constraints are expected to intensify [S6, S64].

::: table
| Metric | Value | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Node, A19 Pro / A20 Pro | TSMC N3P (2025) / N2 (2026) | Teardown and trade reporting | S63, S64 |
| CPU clock, A19 Pro | up to 4.26 GHz, 6 cores | Published specification | S63 |
| Neural Engine, A20 Pro | 32 cores, ~52 TOPS, ~2x A19 Pro | Trade-press estimate | S64 |
| N2 wafer price | ~$30,000 vs ~$18,000-20,000 at 3nm | Trade-press estimate | S64 |
| Product gross margin | 39.9% vs 36.9% (9M FY2025) | Reported financials | S6 |
| On-device model / PCC context | ~3B parameters / 32K tokens | Apple research and developer docs | S61, S62 |
:::

### Apple Intelligence is an architecture with a rented brain

On device, Apple runs a ~3B-parameter model optimised through KV-cache sharing and 2-bit quantisation-aware training; on its servers, a Parallel-Track Mixture-of-Experts model runs inside Private Cloud Compute, which enforces stateless processing, no privileged runtime access even for Apple staff, and verifiable software images with attestation. The binding constraint is memory bandwidth and power: phone-class memory caps practical on-device inference at single-digit billions of parameters, which is why harder queries are offloaded — a constraint visible in research on chiplet designs needed even to run 70B models at the edge [S8, S60, S61]. That architecture is differentiated on privacy and latency, but its ceiling is disclosed: a 32K-token context is small against frontier assistants, and Apple's own models were not frontier-quality, which is why the Google agreement exists.

The unresolved question — the one that decides whether the privacy story holds — is where Gemini-derived inference physically runs. Apple says Apple Intelligence continues on Apple devices and Private Cloud Compute; trade reporting says Google's cloud performs the Gemini computation and puts the licence at roughly $1bn a year, on top of a default-search payment of about $20bn. Apple's differentiation now sits in orchestration, distribution and privacy, and model quality is the attribute consumers compare most easily. Apple can win on integration and trust; it cannot claim the best assistant, and the installed base is what turns an average model into a good product.

arguments.markdown:
Apple's silicon-plus-OS stack is still the widest integrated consumer technology stack in the industry, but in 2026 the company rented the one layer it could not build — the frontier model — so what remains defensible is distribution, custom silicon and regulated health sensing, not leadership in artificial intelligence. In two years: the A19 Pro shipped in September 2025 on TSMC N3P; the A20 Pro moved the iPhone to TSMC N2 in September 2026; the C2 modem reached the flagship; the first foldable iPhone shipped at $1,999; and on 2026-01-12 Apple and Google announced that the next generation of Apple Foundation Models would be based on Gemini [S58, S59, S63, S64].

### The silicon lead is real, costly, and rented from TSMC

The A19 Pro used TSMC N3P with two performance cores at up to 4.26 GHz; a year later the A20 Pro moved to TSMC N2 with a dual 16-core Neural Engine — 32 neural cores — and roughly 52 TOPS, about double the prior generation's AI throughput. N2 wafers are reported at about $30,000 against $18,000-20,000 for 3nm, so each capability step arrives with higher silicon cost. Product gross margin was 39.9% in the nine months to 2026-06-27 versus 36.9% a year earlier, but only with tariff refunds and mix offsetting "higher costs, including memory", and the 10-Q warns that advanced-semiconductor, NAND and DRAM constraints are expected to intensify [S6, S64].

::: table
| Metric | Value | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Node, A19 Pro / A20 Pro | TSMC N3P (2025) / N2 (2026) | Teardown and trade reporting | S63, S64 |
| CPU clock, A19 Pro | up to 4.26 GHz, 6 cores | Published specification | S63 |
| Neural Engine, A20 Pro | 32 cores, ~52 TOPS, ~2x A19 Pro | Trade-press estimate | S64 |
| N2 wafer price | ~$30,000 vs ~$18,000-20,000 at 3nm | Trade-press estimate | S64 |
| Product gross margin | 39.9% vs 36.9% (9M FY2025) | Reported financials | S6 |
| On-device model / PCC context | ~3B parameters / 32K tokens | Apple research and developer docs | S61, S62 |
:::

### Apple Intelligence is an architecture with a rented brain

On device, Apple runs a ~3B-parameter model optimised through KV-cache sharing and 2-bit quantisation-aware training; on its servers, a Parallel-Track Mixture-of-Experts model runs inside Private Cloud Compute, which enforces stateless processing, no privileged runtime access even for Apple staff, and verifiable software images with attestation. The binding constraint is memory bandwidth and power: phone-class memory caps practical on-device inference at single-digit billions of parameters, which is why harder queries are offloaded — a constraint visible in research needed to run 70B models at the edge [S8, S60, S61]. That architecture is differentiated on privacy and latency, but its ceiling is disclosed: a 32K-token context is small against frontier assistants, and Apple's own models were not frontier-quality, which is why the Google agreement exists.

The unresolved question — the one that decides whether the privacy story holds — is where Gemini-derived inference physically runs. Apple says Apple Intelligence continues on Apple devices and Private Cloud Compute; trade reporting says Google's cloud performs the Gemini computation and puts the licence at roughly $1bn a year, on top of a default-search payment of about $20bn. Neither figure is Apple-confirmed [S58, S86]. Apple's differentiation is orchestration, distribution and privacy, not model quality; the installed base turns an average model into a good product.

::: table
| Dimension | Apple 2024 (AFM v1) | Apple 2026 (Gemini-based AFM) | Google (supplier) |

| Frontier model | Own ~3B on-device plus server model | Gemini-derived | Owns Gemini |

| What Apple keeps | Silicon, OS, orchestration | Silicon, OS, interface, orchestration | Model, training, inference |
:::

### Products: a strong cycle, a late foldable, a spatial computer that never became a platform

The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max launched on 2026-09-09 at $1,199 and $1,299; the foldable iPhone Duo at $1,999 went on sale on 2026-10-23. iPhone net sales rose 22% to $196.5bn in the nine months to 2026-06-27, with Greater China up 30%. The C2 modem supports US mmWave and uses 15% less energy than the C1X, but the larger iPhone 18 Pro Max appears to keep a Qualcomm modem, so Qualcomm retains leverage over the highest-ASP SKU. Vision Pro is the counter-example to Apple's category-creation record: about 390,000 units in 2024, about 45,000 in the December 2025 quarter despite the M5 refresh, roughly 600,000 lifetime, and an IDC forecast of about 290,000 units in 2026 [S59, S13, S87].

Apple's silicon-plus-OS stack is still the widest integrated consumer technology stack in the industry, but in 2026 the company rented the one layer it could not build — the frontier model — so what remains defensible is distribution, custom silicon and regulated health sensing, not leadership in artificial intelligence. In two years: the A19 Pro shipped in September 2025 on TSMC N3P; the A20 Pro moved the iPhone to TSMC N2 in September 2026; the C2 modem reached the flagship; the first foldable iPhone shipped at $1,999; and on 2026-01-12 Apple and Google announced that the next generation of Apple Foundation Models would be based on Gemini [S58, S59, S63, S64].

### The silicon lead is real, costly, and rented from TSMC

The A19 Pro used TSMC N3P with two performance cores at up to 4.26 GHz; a year later the A20 Pro moved to TSMC N2 with a dual 16-core Neural Engine — 32 neural cores — and roughly 52 TOPS, about double the prior generation's AI throughput. N2 wafers are reported at about $30,000 against $18,000-20,000 for 3nm, so each capability step arrives with higher silicon cost. Product gross margin was 39.9% in the nine months to 2026-06-27 versus 36.9% a year earlier, but only with tariff refunds and mix offsetting "higher costs, including memory", and the 10-Q warns that advanced-semiconductor, NAND and DRAM constraints are expected to intensify [S6, S64].

### Apple Intelligence is an architecture with a rented brain

On device, Apple runs a ~3B-parameter model optimised through KV-cache sharing and 2-bit quantisation-aware training; on its servers, a Parallel-Track Mixture-of-Experts model runs inside Private Cloud Compute, which enforces stateless processing, no privileged runtime access even for Apple staff, and verifiable software images with attestation. The binding constraint is memory bandwidth and power: phone-class memory caps practical on-device inference at single-digit billions of parameters, which is why harder queries are offloaded — a constraint visible in research needed to run 70B models at the edge [S8, S60, S61]. That architecture is differentiated on privacy and latency, but its ceiling is disclosed: a 32K-token context is small against frontier assistants, and Apple's own models were not frontier-quality, which is why the Google agreement exists.

The unresolved question — the one that decides whether the privacy story holds — is where Gemini-derived inference physically runs. Apple says Apple Intelligence continues on Apple devices and Private Cloud Compute; trade reporting says Google's cloud performs the Gemini computation and puts the licence at roughly $1bn a year, on top of a default-search payment of about $20bn. Neither figure is Apple-confirmed [S58, S86]. Apple's differentiation is orchestration, distribution and privacy, not model quality.

### Products: a strong cycle, a late foldable, a spatial computer that never became a platform

The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max launched on 2026-09-09 at $1,199 and $1,299; the foldable iPhone Duo at $1,999 went on sale on 2026-10-23. iPhone net sales rose 22% to $196.5bn in the nine months to 2026-06-27, with Greater China up 30%. The C2 modem supports US mmWave and uses 15% less energy than the C1X, but the larger iPhone 18 Pro Max appears to keep a Qualcomm modem, so Qualcomm retains leverage over the highest-ASP SKU. Vision Pro is the counter-example to Apple's category-creation record: about 390,000 units in 2024, about 45,000 in the December 2025 quarter despite the M5 refresh, roughly 600,000 lifetime, and an IDC forecast of about 290,000 units in 2026 [S59, S13, S87].
