arguments.markdown:
Apple's silicon-plus-OS stack is still the widest integrated consumer technology stack in the industry, but in 2026 the company rented the one layer it could not build — the frontier model — so what remains defensible is distribution, custom silicon and regulated health sensing, not leadership in artificial intelligence. In two years: the A19 Pro shipped in September 2025 on TSMC N3P; the A20 Pro moved the iPhone to TSMC N2 in September 2026; the C2 modem reached the flagship; the first foldable iPhone shipped at $1,999; and on 2026-01-12 Apple and Google announced that the next generation of Apple Foundation Models would be based on Gemini [S58, S59, S63, S64].

### The silicon lead is real, costly, and rented from TSMC

The A19 Pro used TSMC N3P with two performance cores at up to 4.26 GHz; a year later the A20 Pro moved to TSMC N2 with a dual 16-core Neural Engine — 32 neural cores — and roughly 52 TOPS, about double the prior generation's AI throughput. N2 wafers are reported at about $30,000 against $18,000-20,000 for 3nm, so each capability step arrives with higher silicon cost. Product gross margin was 39.9% in the nine months to 2026-06-27 versus 36.9% a year earlier, but only with tariff refunds and mix offsetting "higher costs, including memory", and the 10-Q warns that advanced-semiconductor, NAND and DRAM constraints are expected to intensify [S6, S64].

| Metric | Value | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Node, A19 Pro / A20 Pro | TSMC N3P (2025) / N2 (2026) | Teardown and trade reporting | S63, S64 |
| CPU clock, A19 Pro | up to 4.26 GHz, 6 cores | Published specification | S63 |
| Neural Engine, A20 Pro | 32 cores, ~52 TOPS, ~2x A19 Pro | Trade-press estimate | S64 |
| N2 wafer price | ~$30,000 vs ~$18,000-20,000 at 3nm | Trade-press estimate | S64 |
| Product gross margin | 39.9% vs 36.9% (9M FY2025) | Reported financials | S6 |
| On-device model / PCC context | ~3B parameters / 32K tokens | Apple research and developer docs | S61, S62 |

### Apple Intelligence is an architecture with a rented brain

On device, Apple runs a ~3B-parameter model optimised through KV-cache sharing and 2-bit quantisation-aware training; on its servers, a Parallel-Track Mixture-of-Experts model runs inside Private Cloud Compute, which enforces stateless processing, no privileged runtime access even for Apple staff, and verifiable software images with attestation. The binding constraint is memory bandwidth and power: phone-class memory caps practical on-device inference at single-digit billions of parameters, which is why harder queries are offloaded — a constraint visible in research needed to run 70B models at the edge [S8, S60, S61]. That architecture is differentiated on privacy and latency, but its ceiling is disclosed: a 32K-token context is small against frontier assistants, and Apple's own models were not frontier-quality, which is why the Google agreement exists.

The unresolved question — the one that decides whether the privacy story holds — is where Gemini-derived inference physically runs. Apple says Apple Intelligence continues on Apple devices and Private Cloud Compute; trade reporting says Google's cloud performs the Gemini computation and puts the licence at roughly $1bn a year, on top of a default-search payment of about $20bn. Neither figure is Apple-confirmed [S58, S86]. Apple's differentiation is orchestration, distribution and privacy, not model quality.

| Cost structure | Fixed R&D and data-centre capex | Fixed R&D plus per-query licence | Licence revenue |
| What Apple keeps | Silicon, OS, orchestration | Silicon, OS, interface, orchestration | Model, training, inference |

The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max launched on 2026-09-09 at $1,199 and $1,299; the foldable iPhone Duo at $1,999 went on sale on 2026-10-23. iPhone net sales rose 22% to $196.5bn in the nine months to 2026-06-27, with Greater China up 30%. The C2 modem supports US mmWave and uses 15% less energy than the C1X, but the larger iPhone 18 Pro Max appears to keep a Qualcomm modem, so Qualcomm retains leverage over the highest-ASP SKU. arguments.markdown:
Apple runs a hardware annuity with a services margin layered on top — every dollar of product gross profit now carries 73 cents of services gross profit — but the mix shift the multiple pays for stalled in fiscal 2026, when hardware margins, helped by tariff refunds, grew gross profit twice as fast as Services.

### Who pays, and how the cash arrives

Apple sells to consumers, small businesses, education, enterprise and government, but the route to those customers is split in a way the revenue line conceals. In fiscal 2025, 40% of net sales went through Apple's own retail stores, online store and direct sales force, and 60% through carriers, resellers and distributors. That 60% matters because a mobile carrier subsidises or finances the handset to win a contract: the carrier pays to acquire Apple's customer, and Apple's own selling cost stays small — selling, general and administrative expense was $27,601M, 6.6% of revenue. Cash arrives shortly after shipment, or as services are delivered, and there is almost no contracted backlog: total deferred revenue was $13.7bn at 2025-09-27, 3.3% of revenue, two thirds of it recognised within a year. Apple is not a subscription business with a book of contracted revenue; it is a repeat-purchase business recognised as it bills [S5].

### The mix shift, and its reversal

The arithmetic of the mix shift is the strongest part of the case. In fiscal 2025, Services produced $109,158M of revenue at a 75.4% gross margin, against $307,003M of Products at 36.8%. Services was therefore 26.2% of revenue but 42.2% of gross profit ($82,314M of $195,201M), up from 35.7% two years earlier, and services gross profit per dollar of product gross profit rose from $0.55 in fiscal 2023 to $0.64 in fiscal 2024 and $0.73 in fiscal 2025. Because services cost of sales was only $26,844M on $109,158M of revenue, most of each incremental services dollar reaches gross profit [S5].

Then the mechanism ran backwards. In the nine months to 2026-06-27, product gross profit rose 26.3% to $108,819M while services gross profit rose 15.3% to $69,963M, and Services fell to 39.1% of gross profit. Product gross margin reached 39.9% against 36.9% a year earlier, taking total gross margin to 49.1% and to 50.1% in the June quarter against 46.5%. Apple attributes the improvement to "a different mix of products and tariff refunds, partially offset by higher costs, including memory" [S6]. That sentence is the most consequential disclosure in the section: the fiscal 2026 margin expansion is hardware-led, and part of it is a refund rather than a trading gain.

### Unit economics per revenue dollar, because there are no units

Apple discloses no unit volumes, no average selling price and no installed-base figure in its filings, so a per-device waterfall cannot be built from primary evidence. What can be built is the economics of each revenue dollar by line, which is where the annuity shows up.

::: data
| Unit-economics line | FY2025 | 9M FY2026 | Evidence and status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue base | $1,000 product / $1,000 services | $1,000 product / $1,000 services | Per revenue dollar; no unit volumes or ASP disclosed | S5 |
| Product cost of sales | $632 | $601 | Bill of materials, assembly and warranty provision combined, not split | S5, S6 |
| Product gross profit | $368 | $399 | 36.8% to 39.9%; includes tariff refunds in fiscal 2026 | S5, S6 |
| Services cost of sales | $246 | $237 | Content, hosting and payment processing | S5, S6 |
| Services gross profit | $754 | $763 | 75.4% to 76.3% | S5, S6 |
| Services gross profit per $1 of product gross profit | $0.73 | $0.64 | Closest disclosed proxy for lifetime value against acquisition cost | S5, S6 |
| Customer acquisition cost | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | 60% of sales flow through carriers and resellers that bear acquisition | S5 |
| Support and warranty, annual | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Sits inside cost of sales; Apple does not split it | S5 |
| LTV, LTV:CAC, CAC payback in months | Not computable | Not computable | Requires units, ASP and installed base, none of which Apple reports | S5 |
:::

The consequence is that Apple has no payback period to wait out: a device is gross-profit-positive on delivery at a 36.8% product margin, and the services stream that follows is nearly all incremental. The nearest disclosed proxy for lifetime value against acquisition cost is the $0.73 of services gross profit per dollar of product gross profit, and its fall to $0.64 in fiscal 2026 is the number to watch — it says the annuity is still growing, but no longer faster than the hardware that creates it.

### Pricing power shows up as mix, not as price

::: data
| Line | FY2025 net sales | Year on year | What the filing discloses about price and mix | Gross margin | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone | $209,586M | +4% | Growth "due to higher net sales of Pro models", i.e. mix rather than units | 36.8% products blended | S5 |
| Services | $109,158M | +14% | "advertising, the App Store and cloud services" | 75.4% | S5 |
| Mac | $33,708M | +12% | "laptops and desktops" | 36.8% products blended | S5 |
| iPad | $28,023M | +5% | "iPad Air, iPad mini and iPad" | 36.8% products blended | S5 |
| Wearables, Home and Accessories | $35,686M | −4% | "lower net sales of Accessories and Wearables" | 36.8% products blended | S5 |
:::

The evidence of pricing power is mix: iPhone revenue rose 22% to $196,515M in the nine months to 2026-06-27, which Apple again attributes to higher sales of Pro models rather than to units. But the same disclosure prevents separating price from volume, and therefore prevents estimating elasticity: a 22% iPhone increase could be volume, price, or any combination. Apple publishes list prices on its own store but not in its filings, and this report did not retrieve a verified 2026 price list, so the table uses disclosed mix effects rather than price points. That is a real limit on the analysis, and third-party unit data would settle it.

### The highest-margin layer is also the most litigated

App Store economics are recognised net — Apple books "only the commission it retains" on third-party app sales — so a take-rate cut passes straight to revenue and gross profit with no offsetting cost. Apple is currently subject to a US court order preventing it from charging a commission on certain consumer purchases, though the Ninth Circuit has instructed the district court to amend the injunction to permit one, and in the EU the Digital Markets Act forces alternative distribution, alternative payment processing and new fee structures, a compliance plan the European Commission has challenged [S6]. Apple does not disclose App Store revenue or the commission rate, so the exposure can only be bounded by the $82,314M of Services gross profit it contributes to.

A second concentration sits in the same line. Apple earns licensing revenue from Google for search distribution, inside Services advertising — which Apple names as a primary driver of Services growth in both fiscal 2025 and the first nine months of fiscal 2026. The payment was $20bn in 2022 per unsealed court documents, 18.3% of fiscal 2025 Services revenue, and Apple does not disclose the current figure. The District of Columbia court order of 2025-09-02 preserved the ability to pay partners while banning exclusive agreements, but Apple states that a reversal on appeal could impose remedies "prohibiting Google from offering the Company commercial terms for search distribution", and both the Department of Justice and Google appealed [S6, S82]. The fastest-growing part of Services is therefore the part with the least contractual visibility.

### Cost structure, and where durability actually breaks

The cost base is bought, not built. Product cost of sales of $194,116M is paid to TSMC for wafers, to memory suppliers for DRAM and NAND, and to Foxconn and its peers for assembly; services cost of sales is content and hosting. Research and development reached $34,035M in the nine months to 2026-06-27, up 33% and 9.3% of revenue against 8.3% in fiscal 2025, with Apple citing "infrastructure-related costs, including investments in artificial intelligence". Capital expenditure, by contrast, is 2.2% of trailing-twelve-month revenue against 34.9% at Microsoft in fiscal 2026 [S6, S27]. That is the structural difference: Apple rents its manufacturing and now buys much of its AI capability through the income statement, so the AI bill hits the operating margin immediately rather than being capitalised into depreciation over years.

::: evidence
**The service mix still drives Apple's margin, but in fiscal 2026 it stopped being the marginal driver — hardware did, and part of that gain is a refund.**

Services contributed $82,314M of gross profit on $109,158M of revenue in fiscal 2025, 42.2% of the total, yet in the nine months to 2026-06-27 product gross profit grew 26.3% against 15.3% for Services, and product gross margin rose to 39.9% on mix and tariff refunds [S5, S6].
:::

What this means for a long-only holder: the annuity is real and the attach is not weakening, but the margin expansion of the last four quarters is not the mix shift it is commonly described as. It is product mix, a tariff refund and memory cost timing, on top of a services base whose most profitable components face an appeal, a court order and a European regulatory process. The durability question is therefore answerable, but not from Apple's own numbers: it needs the current size of the search payment, the share of Services that is App Store commission, and the split between refund and mix in the fiscal 2026 product margin — none of which the company discloses, and all of which the fiscal 2026 annual report, not yet on EDGAR as of 2026-10-31, may settle.

arguments.markdown:
Apple's markets are contracting in units and expanding in value, and Apple is taking value share inside that contraction: the case for FY2026-FY2028 rests on premiumisation and Services attach rather than device volume, is strongest in the United States, is adequate in Europe, and in China depends on a domestic champion's pricing discipline rather than on Apple's product cycle. [S66]

### The pool is shrinking in units and growing in value

IDC's August 2026 forecast has worldwide smartphone shipments at just over 1.0 billion units in 2026, down 16.7% and the steepest annual contraction on record, while total market value rises 6.3% to $613 billion and the average selling price reaches a record $581, up 27.6% in a year and revised up from the $550 IDC published one quarter earlier. The cause is cost, not demand: DRAM and NAND prices are up more than 300% year on year as capacity is redirected to AI servers, memory is more than 65% of bill of materials at the low end, and the sub-$100 tier that shipped 173 million units in 2025 fell almost 60% in the second quarter of 2026. This is a supply shock with a dated end, so 2026-2027 flatters Apple's unit share while genuinely lifting its price, and 2028 is the test of whether either survives. [S39]

Two sizing methods agree closely on this market, which is unusual and useful. Taking 1.0 billion units at the $581 average price gives $581 billion of smartphone value, within 5% of IDC's $613 billion, so the unit and price series can be read together rather than treated as rival estimates. On that base Apple's serviceable market is the premium tier it addresses — an iOS share of 23.6% of 2026 shipments, a record — while the revenue it can obtain is what it already books: $466.8 billion on a trailing-twelve-month basis to 2026-06-27, which at the 16.2% growth rate of the first nine months of FY2026 implies about $483 billion for FY2026, an arithmetic extension of the filed numbers rather than a company forecast. [S6]

| Measure | Method | Figure | Year | Publisher | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| TAM, smartphone value (top-down) | Industry value estimate | $613bn, +6.3% | 2026 | IDC | S66 |
| TAM, smartphone value (bottom-up) | 1.0bn units x $581 ASP | ~$581bn | 2026 | Calculation on IDC inputs | S66 |
| TAM, personal computing devices | Units published, value not disclosed | ~398m units, -11.3% | 2026 | IDC | S103 |
| TAM, wearables | Units published, value not disclosed | ~625m units, +1.7% | 2026 | IDC | S104 |
| SAM, premium smartphone tier | iOS share of shipments | 23.6% of units, record | 2026 | IDC | S66 |
| SOM, Apple revenue | Reported | $466.8bn TTM | TTM to 2026-06-27 | Apple 10-Q | S6 |
| Near-term obtainable revenue | FY2025 $416.2bn grown at the 9M FY2026 rate | ~$483bn | FY2026E | Calculation on Apple filings | S5, S13 |
| Adjacent services pool | Alphabet revenue | $471.1bn TTM | TTM to 2026-09-30 | Alphabet 10-Q | S42 |

### China is the swing factor, and India sits in the wrong line

Apple's revenue is moving toward the faster-growing regions, but the swing is China. In the first nine months of FY2026 Greater China produced $64.8 billion, up 30.0% on a base of $49.9 billion, after falling from $72.6 billion in FY2023 to $64.4 billion in FY2025; the Americas grew 11.4% to $149.4 billion, Europe 16.1% to $95.6 billion, Japan 10.4% and Rest of Asia Pacific 19.4%. Greater China's $14.9 billion increase contributes roughly 4.1 percentage points of the group's 16.2% growth, more than any other segment, and part of it is currency: Apple attributes a favourable effect to renminbi strength in Greater China and an unfavourable one to yen weakness in Japan. One reporting artefact matters — the Europe segment includes India, the Middle East and Africa, so the fastest-growing large smartphone market is invisible in the line labelled Europe and India is not a segment an investor can track. [S13]

| Region | Market size (year) | Growth | Apple's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| United States / North America | 60% of Q1 2026 shipments above $800; US is 24.9% of global PC-plus-tablet units | Smartphone -6.3% in 2026; PC -14.6% in 2026 | Entered, leads the premium tier; 41.0% of Apple revenue is the Americas | Tariffs, carrier financing, antitrust suits over smartphones | Samsung, Lenovo, HP, Dell | S39, S103, S13 |
| Greater China | ~66m units a quarter, roughly 264m a year | -4.3% in Q2 2026, fifth straight decline; H2 2026 could be -20% | 18.1% of units, second behind Huawei; revenue +30.0% | Domestic operating system, subsidy withdrawal, data rules | Huawei 22.6%, OPPO 16.0%, vivo 16.0%, Xiaomi 12.4% | S40, S6 |
| Europe (segment includes India, Middle East, Africa) | India 31.0m units in Q1 2026 at a record $302 ASP | India units -4.1% but value +5.8%; Europe revenue +16.1% | Entered; fourth by units in India | DMA, price sensitivity, distribution | Samsung, Xiaomi, vivo, Lenovo, HP | S105, S103, S13 |
| Japan | Revenue $24.4bn in 9M FY2026 | Revenue +10.4%; PC-plus-tablet units -25.6% forecast for 2026 | Entered, premium strong; weak yen cuts reported revenue | Yen, saturated device base | Local Android vendors and Samsung, shares not disclosed | S13, S103, S6 |
| Rest of Asia Pacific | Revenue $30.2bn in 9M FY2026 | Revenue +19.4%; smartphone units about -14% in 2026 | Entered, premium-led | Price-sensitive mass market, currency | Samsung, Xiaomi, OPPO, vivo | S13, S39, S103 |

### Services carries the margin and has no published pool size

The fastest-growing pool Apple actually monetises is Services: $109.2 billion, 26.2% of FY2025 revenue, at a 75.4% gross margin against 36.8% for products, growing 14.1% to $91.7 billion in the first nine months of FY2026. The adjacent pools are larger and largely not Apple's — Alphabet's trailing-twelve-month revenue is $471.1 billion — but the app economy itself has no published size in the sources retrieved: neither Apple nor the platform owners disclose app-store gross billings or mobile-advertising revenue in a form that can be sized, so Apple's own Services line is the measured pool and no number is placed on the wider market. The same gap applies to the installed base behind it: Apple states only that its active-device base reached an all-time high in the June 2026 quarter across every category and region, and publishes no device count in its FY2025 10-K or its FY2026 results release, so the figure of about 2.3 billion devices often quoted alongside the business is unverified here and should carry none of the valuation. [S5]

### Who pays, and how much demand is policy

The budget owner is the consumer, in a discretionary purchase that is increasingly financed. In the United States and United Kingdom long-term interest-free financing is more prevalent, which is why IDC expects the premium end to hold while emerging markets fall more than 20% in 2026; in India brands lean on financing offers after the sub-$100 tier fell 59% and the $600-800 band grew 32%; in China the government subsidy that supported earlier quarters faded in the second quarter of 2026, so demand there is being withdrawn by policy rather than created by it. Apple's own policy exposure runs both ways: after the February 20, 2026 Supreme Court ruling struck down certain tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, Apple recognised refunds as a reduction of product cost of sales, and those refunds contributed about 2 percentage points of the June 2026 quarter's 50.1% gross margin — tariff policy moves Apple's margin by more than a product cycle does. [S105, S40, S13]

Three findings could break this market case. If memory prices normalise in 2028 as IDC expects, the entry tier rebuilds and the share Apple won in 2026 is contestable again. If China's June-quarter demand was pulled forward ahead of expected second-half price increases, as IDC's China team reports, the 30% growth line is a launch and currency effect rather than a trend. And if courts and the European Commission remove the App Store take rate, the 75%-margin layer that offsets hardware cyclicality stops compounding at its present rate. The investor implication is narrow: in a 1-billion-unit market Apple can grow revenue only if price rises faster than units fall, which makes average selling price, China revenue durability and the Services take rate the variables worth monitoring, and makes unit share the least informative number in the file. Confidence in the sizing is high, because two independent methods agree within 5%; confidence that the mix shift holds to 2028 is medium, because it rests on China and on a legally contested commission. Three questions would close the gap: what share of Services revenue is commission-based rather than subscription, advertising or licensing; how much of the Greater China increase is currency; and what the current average replacement cycle is, measured rather than asserted.

::: evidence
**Apple's addressable device market fell 16.7% in units in 2026 while growing 6.3% in value, and Apple's revenue grew 16.2% over nine months — the gap is premiumisation and China, not market growth.**

IDC forecasts 2026 shipments at just over 1.0 billion units against a market value of $613 billion and an ASP of $581 (S66, S39). Apple's nine-month FY2026 revenue was $364.4 billion, up 16.2%, with Greater China up 30.0% on a $49.9 billion base (S13, S6). The bottom-up check of 1.0 billion units at $581 gives $581 billion, within 5% of IDC's value estimate (S66).
:::

Apple's policy exposure is not a licence-to-operate threat but a slow, legislated tax on Services gross profit: the €500 million DMA fine of 2025-04-23 and the April 2025 US contempt finding show a company that litigates first and complies later, while the three remedies that actually matter — Google's default-search payment, the US link-out commission and the EU App Store fee structure — have so far been reshaped rather than removed [S7]. For a long-only holder the question is therefore not whether Apple survives regulation (it does) but what share of Services gross margin the next five years of enforcement takes, and whether the current multiple already discounts it.

### The DMA fine is small; the rule it sets is not

The Commission's 2025-04-23 decision fined Apple €500 million for breaching the anti-steering obligation and ordered it to remove the technical and commercial restrictions on steering users outside the App Store. The same day the Commission closed its investigation into Apple's user-choice screen — a genuine concession — but issued preliminary findings in the Article 6(4) file on Apple's terms for alternative app marketplaces, where a final adverse finding carries fines of up to 10% of annual worldwide net sales and further penalties if a cease-and-desist order is breached [S5]. Apple has appealed and says it complies. Two later data points bound the risk: on 2026-02-05 the Commission found that Apple Ads and Apple Maps should not be designated, narrowing the DMA's reach, and no further Apple DMA decision appears in the Commission's enforcement record between the €500 million fine and 2026-09-28 [S119]. Peer calibration matters here: Meta paid €200 million in the same April 2025 package, Google €890 million on 2026-07-23, and Alphabet's Android fine of €4.1 billion survived to a final ECJ ruling in July 2026 — the base rate is repeated fines, not break-up.

The financially material part is not the fine but the cost structure. Europe generated $111.0 billion of Apple's net sales in FY2025, up 10%, and Services carried the growth; the EU-only share is smaller, but App Store commission is the highest-margin revenue Apple books, so a mandated fee cut in Europe is worth more to the equity than the fine. Apple's own risk disclosure adds a second channel: DMA interoperability obligations oblige it to open technologies to third parties for free and have in the past, and may in future, caused it not to launch or maintain features "such as Siri AI" in certain jurisdictions — an availability risk in the product cycle, not just a revenue leakage.

### The contempt finding is the compliance-culture fact that matters

On 2025-04-30 the Northern District of California found Apple in violation of the 2021 Epic injunction, barred it from charging any commission on purchases made outside an app and referred it to the US Attorney for a determination on criminal contempt. The Ninth Circuit modified that on 2025-12-11 to permit size, form and placement parity and to allow some commission on link-out purchases, and remanded; Apple petitioned the Supreme Court on 2026-05-21 and on 2026-06-30 obtained certiorari limited to the legal standard for civil contempt, while seeking a stay of the district court proceedings [S6]. Read narrowly, this is a US pricing dispute. Read properly, it is the clearest evidence in the file that Apple's platform-compliance function chose to test a court order rather than obey it — and that is the variable that raises the severity of the next remedy, in the DOJ case or in Brussels.

The DOJ's own case, filed 2024-03-21 in the District of New Jersey with 16 states and the District of Columbia, seeks equitable relief only, survived Apple's motion to dismiss on 2025-06-30, and is in discovery with a schedule pointing to a 2027 trial [S122]. Because it seeks no damages, the remedy risk is conduct-based — default settings, messaging interoperability, app distribution — and lands on the 2027-2029 Services line rather than on the balance sheet. That is a slower and smaller risk than the market's structural-break-up framing, but it is also the one that could compound with the Epic line.

### Google's payment survives — on worse terms

The search-distribution remedy is the biggest single dollar item in this section, and the 2025-09-02 decision in the District of Columbia went Apple's way on the point that mattered: the court refused to ban Google's payments to distributors, holding that a broad ban posed a substantial risk of harm to device makers, carriers and browser developers, and instead barred exclusive distribution contracts and allowed payments for default placement where they are not conditioned on exclusivity and the agreement runs one year or less [S118]. A final judgment followed in December 2025; Google appealed in January 2026 and the Department of Justice cross-appealed in February 2026, and both appeals were pending at 2026-10-29 [S42]. Apple does not disclose the payment, so the widely used figure of roughly $20 billion a year is unverified in its filings; what the record does establish is that the revenue survives with an annual renewal risk and mandatory choice screens, which shifts pricing power toward Apple at renewal and toward rivals in the user's default setting.

### Tariffs and China moved in Apple's favour in 2026

Two of the bear-case triggers did not fire. The Section 232 semiconductor investigation's initial results on 2026-01-14 imposed no additional tariff on Apple's products, and on 2026-02-20 the Supreme Court struck down certain IEEPA tariffs, with Apple claiming refunds it recognised as a reduction of products cost of sales; Section 301 tariffs were then imposed, and further Section 232 action remains open. In China the opposite of closure happened: the CAC registered Apple Intelligence on 2026-07-15 with Alibaba's Qwen and Baidu, and Greater China net sales rose 22% to $18,816 million in the June 2026 quarter and 30% to $64,839 million for the nine months against $49,884 million a year earlier [S6]. The binding constraint is time, not policy: the Busan truce that suppresses tariff and rare-earth escalation was extended on 2026-09-23 from 2026-11-10 to 2027-01-10 [S121]. An investor should treat calendar 2027 as the next policy cliff, not calendar 2026.

### Tax is settled; the ESG tail is not where most investors think

The Irish state-aid case ended against Apple: the ECJ confirmed the 2016 decision on 2024-09-10, producing a $10.2 billion net one-time charge and $15.8 billion payable to Ireland in the December 2024 quarter. FY2025's effective tax rate of 15.6%, against 24.1% in FY2024, now sits just above the OECD Pillar Two 15% floor, so the incremental Pillar Two cost is small and the remaining tax risk is the $23.2 billion of gross unrecognised benefits, of which $10.6 billion would move the rate if recognised [S5]. Tax should be modelled as a settled cost; it is not a source of future EPS upside.

On the E and S, the record is genuinely better than the sector's. Apple's policy exposure is not a licence-to-operate threat but a slow, legislated tax on Services gross profit: the €500 million DMA fine of 2025-04-23 and the April 2025 US contempt finding show a company that litigates first and complies later, while the three remedies that matter — Google's default-search payment, the US link-out commission and the EU fee structure — have so far been reshaped rather than removed [S7]. The question for a long-only holder is not whether Apple survives regulation, but what share of Services gross margin the next five years of enforcement takes, and whether the multiple already discounts it.

### The fine is small; the rule it sets is not

The Commission fined Apple €500 million on 2025-04-23 for breaching the anti-steering obligation and ordered it to strip out the technical and commercial restrictions on steering users outside the App Store. The same day it closed the separate user-choice investigation — a real concession — but issued preliminary findings in the Article 6(4) file on Apple's terms for alternative app marketplaces, where an adverse final finding carries fines of up to 10% of annual worldwide net sales and further penalties for breaching a cease-and-desist order [S5]. Apple has appealed and says it complies. Two later facts bound the risk: on 2026-02-05 the Commission found Apple Ads and Apple Maps should not be designated, and no further Apple decision appears in its DMA record between the fine and 2026-09-28 [S119]. Peer calibration is unflattering but reassuring on severity: Meta paid €200 million in the same April 2025 package, Google €890 million on 2026-07-23, and Alphabet's Android fine of €4.1 billion reached a final ECJ ruling in July 2026.

The financially material part is the cost structure, not the fine. Europe booked $111.0 billion of net sales in FY2025, up 10%, and Services drove that growth; the EU-only slice is smaller, but App Store commission is the highest-margin revenue Apple records, so a mandated fee cut in Brussels is worth more to the equity than any penalty. Apple's own disclosure adds a product channel: DMA interoperability obligations require it to open technologies to third parties without charge, increase security and privacy risk, and have in the past and may in future cause it not to launch or maintain features "such as Siri AI" in certain jurisdictions.

### The contempt finding is the compliance fact that matters

On 2025-04-30 the Northern District of California found Apple in violation of the 2021 Epic injunction, barred any commission on purchases made outside an app, and referred the company to the US Attorney for a determination on criminal contempt. The Ninth Circuit modified that on 2025-12-11 to allow size, form and placement parity and some commission on link-out purchases, and remanded; Apple petitioned the Supreme Court on 2026-05-21, obtained certiorari on 2026-06-30 limited to the legal standard for civil contempt, and is seeking a stay of the district court case [S6]. Read narrowly this is a US pricing dispute. Read properly it is the clearest evidence that Apple's platform-compliance function tested a court order rather than obeying it — the variable that raises the severity of the next remedy, in Brussels or in New Jersey.

That New Jersey case, filed 2024-03-21 against Apple and 16 states plus the District of Columbia, seeks equitable relief only, survived dismissal on 2025-06-30 and is in discovery on a schedule pointing to a 2027 trial [S122]. No damages are claimed, so the remedy risk is conduct-based — default settings, messaging interoperability, app distribution — and lands on the 2027-2029 Services line rather than the balance sheet.

### Google's payment survives, on worse terms

The search-distribution remedy is the largest dollar item here, and the 2025-09-02 decision went Apple's way on the point that mattered: the court refused to ban Google's payments to distributors, citing the harm a ban would do to device makers, carriers and browser developers, and instead barred exclusive distribution contracts while permitting default-placement payments that are not conditioned on exclusivity and run one year or less [S118, S42]. A final judgment followed in December 2025; Google appealed in January 2026 and the Department of Justice cross-appealed in February 2026, both pending at 2026-10-29. Apple does not disclose the payment, so the $20 billion-a-year figure in circulation is unverified in its filings; what the record establishes is that the revenue survives with annual renewal risk and mandatory choice screens.

### Two bear-case triggers did not fire in 2026

The Section 232 semiconductor investigation's initial results on 2026-01-14 imposed no additional tariff on Apple's products, and on 2026-02-20 the Supreme Court struck down certain IEEPA tariffs, with Apple claiming refunds recognised as a reduction of products cost of sales; Section 301 tariffs were then imposed and further Section 232 action remains open. In China the opposite of closure happened: the CAC registered Apple Intelligence on 2026-07-15 with Alibaba's Qwen and Baidu, and Greater China net sales rose 22% to $18,816 million in the June 2026 quarter and 30% to $64,839 million for the nine months, from $49,884 million [S6, S121]. The binding constraint is the calendar: the Busan truce that suppresses tariff and rare-earth escalation was extended on 2026-09-23 from 2026-11-10 to 2027-01-10, making 2027 the next policy cliff.

### Tax is settled; the ESG tail is elsewhere

The Irish state-aid case ended against Apple: the ECJ confirmed the 2016 decision on 2024-09-10, producing a $10.2 billion net one-time charge and $15.8 billion payable to Ireland. The FY2025 effective tax rate of 15.6%, against 24.1% in FY2024, now sits just above the OECD Pillar Two 15% floor, so the incremental Pillar Two cost is small and the live tax risk is the $23.2 billion of gross unrecognised benefits, $10.6 billion of which would move the rate if recognised [S5]. Tax is a settled cost, not a source of future EPS upside.

On environmental and social issues the record is better than the sector's. The 2024 Conflict Minerals Report filed 2025-04-04 records full third-party audit coverage of identified 3TG smelters for a tenth consecutive year, no finding of armed-group financing, a June 2024 instruction to suppliers to stop sourcing 3TG from the DRC and Rwanda, and recycled-content commitments for cobalt, tin, gold and rare earths. Those are company-prepared claims without independent verification in this record; the carbon-neutral-2030 commitment and its Scope 3 progress could not be verified from a published source in this run, and that gap is stated rather than filled.

Governance offsets the conduct record: a single class of common stock with no dual-class structure, an independent Chair separated from the CEO, an Audit Committee that owns privacy, cybersecurity, tax and enterprise risk, and related-party disclosure limited to one family-member employment. Control is not the issue; compliance culture is.

### What it costs, and what would change the call

The tables below put the exposure in one place. The judgement they support is that policy is a 100-300 basis point tax on Services gross margin plus a low-probability structural remedy in the US, not a threat to the franchise. At Apple's scale, 100 basis points of Services gross margin is material annual gross profit, so the watchlist question is whether the multiple leaves room for that dilution. arguments.markdown:
Apple runs a hardware annuity with a services margin layered on top — every dollar of product gross profit now carries 73 cents of services gross profit — but the mix shift the multiple pays for stalled in fiscal 2026, when hardware margins, helped by tariff refunds, grew gross profit twice as fast as Services.

### Who pays, and how the cash arrives

Apple sells to consumers, small businesses, education, enterprise and government, but the route to those customers is split in a way the revenue line conceals. In fiscal 2025, 40% of net sales went through Apple's own retail stores, online store and direct sales force, and 60% through carriers, resellers and distributors. That 60% matters because a mobile carrier subsidises or finances the handset to win a contract: the carrier pays to acquire Apple's customer, and Apple's own selling cost stays small — selling, general and administrative expense was $27,601M, 6.6% of revenue. There is almost no contracted backlog either: total deferred revenue was $13.7bn at 2025-09-27, 3.3% of revenue, two thirds of it recognised within a year. Apple is a repeat-purchase business recognised as it bills, not a subscription business with a book of contracted revenue [S5].

### The mix shift, and its reversal

The arithmetic of the mix shift is the strongest part of the case. In fiscal 2025, Services produced $109,158M of revenue at a 75.4% gross margin, against $307,003M of Products at 36.8%. Services was therefore 26.2% of revenue but 42.2% of gross profit ($82,314M of $195,201M), up from 35.7% two years earlier, and services gross profit per dollar of product gross profit rose from $0.55 in fiscal 2023 to $0.73 in fiscal 2025. Because services cost of sales was only $26,844M, most of each incremental services dollar reaches gross profit [S5].

Then the mechanism ran backwards. In the nine months to 2026-06-27, product gross profit rose 26.3% to $108,819M while services gross profit rose 15.3% to $69,963M, and Services fell to 39.1% of gross profit. Product gross margin reached 39.9% against 36.9% a year earlier, taking total gross margin to 49.1% and to 50.1% in the June quarter against 46.5%. Apple attributes the gain to "a different mix of products and tariff refunds, partially offset by higher costs, including memory" [S6]. That is the most consequential disclosure in the section: fiscal 2026's margin expansion is hardware-led, and part of it is a refund rather than a trading gain.

### Unit economics per revenue dollar, because there are no units

Apple discloses no unit volumes, average selling price or installed-base figure, so a per-device waterfall cannot be built from primary evidence. The economics of each revenue dollar can be.

::: data
| Unit-economics line | FY2025 | 9M FY2026 | Evidence and status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Product cost of sales, per $1,000 of product revenue | $632 | $601 | Bill of materials, assembly and warranty provision combined, not split | S5, S6 |
| Product gross profit | $368 | $399 | 36.8% to 39.9%; includes tariff refunds in fiscal 2026 | S5, S6 |
| Services cost of sales, per $1,000 of services revenue | $246 | $237 | Content, hosting and payment processing | S5, S6 |
| Services gross profit | $754 | $763 | 75.4% to 76.3% | S5, S6 |
| Services gross profit per $1 of product gross profit | $0.73 | $0.64 | Closest disclosed proxy for lifetime value against acquisition cost | S5, S6 |
| Customer acquisition cost, support and warranty | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Carriers and resellers bear acquisition; warranty sits in cost of sales | S5 |
| LTV, LTV:CAC, CAC payback in months | Not computable | Not computable | Requires units, ASP and installed base, none of which Apple reports | S5 |
:::

Apple therefore has no payback period to wait out: a device is gross-profit-positive on delivery at a 36.8% product margin, and the services stream that follows is nearly all incremental. The nearest disclosed proxy for lifetime value against acquisition cost is the $0.73 of services gross profit per dollar of product gross profit, and its fall to $0.64 is the number to watch — the annuity is still growing, but no longer faster than the hardware that creates it.

### Pricing power shows up as mix, not as price

::: data
| Line | FY2025 net sales | Year on year | What the filing discloses about price and mix | Gross margin | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone | $209,586M | +4% | Growth "due to higher net sales of Pro models", i.e. mix rather than units | 36.8% products blended | S5 |
| Services | $109,158M | +14% | "advertising, the App Store and cloud services" | 75.4% | S5 |
| Mac | $33,708M | +12% | "laptops and desktops" | 36.8% products blended | S5 |
| iPad and Wearables | $63,709M | 0% | iPad Air and mini higher, Accessories and Wearables lower | 36.8% products blended | S5 |
:::

Pricing power shows up as mix: iPhone revenue rose 22% to $196,515M in the nine months to 2026-06-27, which Apple again attributes to higher sales of Pro models rather than to units. The same disclosure prevents separating price from volume, and therefore prevents estimating elasticity — a 22% iPhone increase could be volume, price, or any combination. Apple publishes list prices on its own store but not in its filings, and this report did not retrieve a verified 2026 price list, so the table uses disclosed mix effects rather than price points. Third-party unit data would settle it.

### The highest-margin layer is also the most litigated

App Store economics are recognised net — Apple books "only the commission it retains" on third-party app sales — so a take-rate cut passes straight to revenue and gross profit with no offsetting cost. Apple is subject to a US court order preventing it from charging a commission on certain consumer purchases, though the Ninth Circuit has instructed the district court to amend the injunction to permit one, and in the EU the Digital Markets Act forces alternative distribution, alternative payment processing and new fee structures, a compliance plan the European Commission has challenged [S6]. Apple does not disclose App Store revenue or the commission rate, so exposure can only be bounded by the $82,314M of Services gross profit it contributes to.

A second concentration sits in the same line. Apple earns licensing revenue from Google for search distribution, inside Services advertising — which Apple names as a primary driver of Services growth in both fiscal 2025 and the first nine months of fiscal 2026. The payment was $20bn in 2022 per unsealed court documents, 18.3% of fiscal 2025 Services revenue, and Apple does not disclose the current figure. The District of Columbia court order of 2025-09-02 preserved the ability to pay partners while banning exclusive agreements, but Apple states a reversal on appeal could impose remedies "prohibiting Google from offering the Company commercial terms for search distribution", and both the Department of Justice and Google appealed [S6, S82]. The fastest-growing part of Services has the least contractual visibility.

### Cost structure, and where durability breaks

The cost base is bought, not built. Product cost of sales of $194,116M goes to TSMC for wafers, to memory suppliers for DRAM and NAND, and to Foxconn and its peers for assembly. Research and development reached $34,035M in the nine months to 2026-06-27, up 33% and 9.3% of revenue against 8.3% in fiscal 2025, with Apple citing "infrastructure-related costs, including investments in artificial intelligence". Capital expenditure is 2.2% of trailing-twelve-month revenue against 34.9% at Microsoft in fiscal 2026 [S6, S27]. Apple rents its manufacturing and buys much of its AI capability through the income statement, so that bill hits the operating margin immediately rather than being capitalised into depreciation.

::: evidence
**The service mix still drives Apple's margin, but in fiscal 2026 it stopped being the marginal driver — hardware did, and part of that gain is a refund.**

Services contributed $82,314M of gross profit on $109,158M of revenue in fiscal 2025, 42.2% of the total, yet in the nine months to 2026-06-27 product gross profit grew 26.3% against 15.3% for Services, and product gross margin rose to 39.9% on mix and tariff refunds [S5, S6].
:::

For a long-only holder the annuity is real and the attach is not weakening, but the margin expansion of the last four quarters is not the mix shift it is commonly described as: it is product mix, a tariff refund and memory cost timing, on top of a services base whose most profitable components face an appeal, a court order and a European regulatory process. The durability question needs three facts Apple does not disclose — the current size of the search payment, the share of Services that is App Store commission, and the refund-versus-mix split in the fiscal 2026 product margin. The fiscal 2026 annual report, not on EDGAR as of 2026-10-31, may settle them.

arguments.markdown:
Apple's markets are contracting in units and expanding in value, and Apple is taking value share inside that contraction: the case for FY2026-FY2028 rests on premiumisation and Services attach rather than device volume, is strongest in the United States, is adequate in Europe, and in China depends on a domestic champion's pricing discipline. [S66]

### The pool is shrinking in units and growing in value

IDC's August 2026 forecast has worldwide smartphone shipments at just over 1.0 billion units in 2026, down 16.7% and the steepest annual contraction on record, while total market value rises 6.3% to $613 billion and the average selling price reaches a record $581, up 27.6% in a year and revised up from the $550 IDC published one quarter earlier. The cause is cost, not demand: DRAM and NAND prices are up more than 300% year on year as capacity is redirected to AI servers, memory is more than 65% of bill of materials at the low end, and the sub-$100 tier that shipped 173 million units in 2025 fell almost 60% in the second quarter of 2026. This is a supply shock with a dated end, so 2026-2027 flatters Apple's unit share while genuinely lifting its price, and 2028 is the test of whether either survives. [S39]

Two sizing methods agree closely on this market. Taking 1.0 billion units at the $581 average price gives $581 billion of smartphone value, within 5% of IDC's $613 billion, so the unit and price series can be read together rather than as rival estimates. On that base Apple's serviceable market is the premium tier it addresses — an iOS share of 23.6% of 2026 shipments, a record — while the revenue it can obtain is what it already books: $466.8 billion trailing twelve months to 2026-06-27, which at the 16.2% growth rate of the first nine months of FY2026 implies about $483 billion for FY2026, an arithmetic extension of filed figures. [S6]

| Measure | Method | Figure | Year | Publisher | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| TAM, smartphone value (top-down) | Industry value estimate | $613bn, +6.3% | 2026 | IDC | S66 |
| TAM, smartphone value (bottom-up) | 1.0bn units x $581 ASP | ~$581bn | 2026 | Calculation on IDC inputs | S66 |
| TAM, personal computing devices | Units published, value not disclosed | ~398m units, -11.3% | 2026 | IDC | S103 |
| TAM, wearables | Units published, value not disclosed | ~625m units, +1.7% | 2026 | IDC | S104 |
| SAM, premium smartphone tier | iOS share of shipments | 23.6% of units, record | 2026 | IDC | S66 |
| SOM, Apple revenue | Reported | $466.8bn TTM | TTM to 2026-06-27 | Apple 10-Q | S6 |
| Near-term obtainable revenue | FY2025 $416.2bn grown at the 9M FY2026 rate | ~$483bn | FY2026E | Calculation on Apple filings | S5, S13 |
| Adjacent services pool | Alphabet revenue | $471.1bn TTM | TTM to 2026-09-30 | Alphabet 10-Q | S42 |

### China is the swing factor, and India sits in the wrong line

Apple's revenue is moving toward the faster-growing regions, but the swing is China. In the first nine months of FY2026 Greater China produced $64.8 billion, up 30.0% on a base of $49.9 billion, after falling from $72.6 billion in FY2023 to $64.4 billion in FY2025; the Americas grew 11.4% to $149.4 billion, Europe 16.1% to $95.6 billion, Japan 10.4% and Rest of Asia Pacific 19.4%. Greater China's $14.9 billion increase contributes roughly 4.1 percentage points of the group's 16.2% growth, more than any other segment, and part of it is currency: Apple attributes a favourable effect to renminbi strength in Greater China and an unfavourable one to yen weakness in Japan. One reporting artefact matters — the Europe segment includes India, the Middle East and Africa, so the fastest-growing large smartphone market is invisible in the line labelled Europe and India is not a segment an investor can track. [S13]

| Region | Market size (year) | Growth | Apple's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| United States / North America | 60% of Q1 2026 shipments above $800; US is 24.9% of global PC-plus-tablet units | Smartphone -6.3% in 2026; PC -14.6% in 2026 | Entered, leads the premium tier; 41.0% of Apple revenue is the Americas | Tariffs, carrier financing, antitrust suits | Samsung, Lenovo, HP, Dell | S39, S103, S13 |
| Greater China | ~66m units a quarter, roughly 264m a year | -4.3% in Q2 2026, fifth straight decline; H2 2026 could be -20% | 18.1% of units, second behind Huawei; revenue +30.0% | Domestic operating system, subsidy withdrawal, data rules | Huawei 22.6%, OPPO 16.0%, vivo 16.0%, Xiaomi 12.4% | S40, S6 |
| Europe (segment includes India, Middle East, Africa) | India 31.0m units in Q1 2026 at a record $302 ASP | India units -4.1% but value +5.8%; Europe revenue +16.1% | Entered; fourth by units in India | DMA, price sensitivity, distribution | Samsung, Xiaomi, vivo, Lenovo, HP | S105, S103, S13 |
| Japan | Revenue $24.4bn in 9M FY2026 | Revenue +10.4%; units -25.6% in 2026 | Entered, premium strong; weak yen cuts revenue | Yen, saturated device base | Local Android vendors, Samsung | S13, S103, S6 |
| Rest of Asia Pacific | Revenue $30.2bn in 9M FY2026 | Revenue +19.4%; units about -14% in 2026 | Entered, premium-led | Price-sensitive mass market, currency | Samsung, Xiaomi, OPPO, vivo | S13, S39, S103 |

### Services carries the margin and has no published pool size

The fastest-growing pool Apple actually monetises is Services: $109.2 billion, 26.2% of FY2025 revenue, at a 75.4% gross margin against 36.8% for products, growing 14.1% to $91.7 billion in the first nine months of FY2026. The adjacent pools are larger and largely not Apple's — Alphabet's trailing-twelve-month revenue is $471.1 billion — but the app economy itself has no published size in the sources retrieved: neither Apple nor the platform owners disclose app-store gross billings or mobile-advertising revenue in a sizeable form, so Apple's own Services line is the measured pool. The same gap applies to the installed base behind it: Apple states only that its active-device base reached an all-time high in the June 2026 quarter across every category and region, and publishes no device count in its FY2025 10-K or FY2026 results, so the figure of about 2.3 billion devices often quoted alongside the business is unverified here and should carry none of the valuation. [S5]

### Who pays, and how much demand is policy

The budget owner is the consumer, in a discretionary purchase that is increasingly financed. In the United States and United Kingdom long-term interest-free financing is more prevalent, which is why IDC expects the premium end to hold while emerging markets fall more than 20% in 2026; in India brands lean on financing offers after the sub-$100 tier fell 59% and the $600-800 band grew 32%; in China the government subsidy that supported earlier quarters faded in the second quarter of 2026, so demand there is being withdrawn by policy rather than created by it. Apple's exposure to policy runs both ways: after the February 20, 2026 Supreme Court ruling struck down certain IEEPA tariffs, Apple recognised refunds as a reduction of product cost of sales, and those refunds contributed about 2 percentage points of the June 2026 quarter's 50.1% gross margin — tariff policy moves Apple's margin by more than a product cycle does. [S105, S40, S13]

Three findings could break this market case. If memory prices normalise in 2028 as IDC expects, the entry tier rebuilds and Apple's 2026 share gain is contestable again. If China's June-quarter demand was pulled forward ahead of expected second-half price increases, as IDC's China team reports, the 30% growth line is a launch and currency effect. And if courts and the European Commission remove the App Store take rate, the 75%-margin layer that offsets hardware cyclicality stops compounding at its present rate. The investor implication is narrow: in a 1-billion-unit market Apple can grow revenue only if price rises faster than units fall, which makes average selling price, China durability and the Services take rate the variables worth monitoring, and unit share the least informative number in the file. Confidence in the sizing is high, because two independent methods agree within 5%; confidence that the mix shift holds to 2028 is medium, because it rests on China and on a legally contested commission. Three questions would close the gap: what share of Services revenue is commission-based rather than subscription, advertising or licensing; how much of the Greater China increase is currency; and what the current average replacement cycle is, measured rather than asserted.

::: evidence
**Apple's addressable device market fell 16.7% in units in 2026 while growing 6.3% in value, and Apple's revenue grew 16.2% over nine months — the gap is premiumisation and China, not market growth.**

IDC forecasts 2026 shipments at just over 1.0 billion units against a market value of $613 billion and an ASP of $581 (S66, S39). Apple's nine-month FY2026 revenue was $364.4 billion, up 16.2%, with Greater China up 30.0% on a $49.9 billion base (S13, S6). The bottom-up check of 1.0 billion units at $581 gives $581 billion, within 5% of IDC's value estimate (S66).
:::

arguments.markdown:
Apple's silicon-plus-OS stack is still the widest integrated consumer technology stack in the industry, but in 2026 the company rented the one layer it could not build — the frontier model — so what remains defensible is distribution, custom silicon and regulated health sensing, not leadership in artificial intelligence. In two years: the A19 Pro shipped in September 2025 on TSMC N3P; the A20 Pro moved the iPhone to TSMC N2 in September 2026; the C2 modem reached the flagship; the first foldable iPhone shipped at $1,999; and on 2026-01-12 Apple and Google announced that the next generation of Apple Foundation Models would be based on Gemini [S58, S59, S63, S64].

### The silicon lead is real, costly, and rented from TSMC

The A19 Pro used TSMC N3P with two performance cores at up to 4.26 GHz; a year later the A20 Pro moved to TSMC N2 with a dual 16-core Neural Engine — 32 neural cores — and ~52 TOPS, about double the prior generation's AI throughput. N2 wafers are reported at ~$30,000 against $18,000-20,000 for 3nm, so each capability step arrives with higher silicon cost. Product gross margin was 39.9% in the nine months to 2026-06-27 versus 36.9% a year earlier, but only with tariff refunds and mix offsetting "higher costs, including memory", and the 10-Q warns that advanced-semiconductor, NAND and DRAM constraints are expected to intensify [S6, S64].

| Metric | Value | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Node, A19 Pro / A20 Pro | TSMC N3P (2025) / N2 (2026) | Teardown and trade reporting | S63, S64 |
| CPU clock, A19 Pro | up to 4.26 GHz, 6 cores | Published specification | S63 |
| Neural Engine, A20 Pro | 32 cores, ~52 TOPS, ~2x A19 Pro | Trade-press estimate | S64 |
| N2 wafer price | ~$30,000 vs $18,000-20,000 at 3nm | Trade-press estimate | S64 |
| Product gross margin | 39.9% vs 36.9% (9M FY2025) | Reported financials | S6 |
| On-device model / PCC context | ~3B parameters / 32K tokens | Apple research and developer docs | S61, S62 |

### Apple Intelligence is an architecture with a rented brain

On device, Apple runs a ~3B-parameter model optimised through KV-cache sharing and 2-bit quantisation-aware training; on its servers, a Parallel-Track Mixture-of-Experts model runs inside Private Cloud Compute, which enforces stateless processing, no privileged runtime access even for Apple staff, and verifiable software images with attestation. The binding constraint is memory bandwidth and power: phone-class memory caps practical on-device inference at single-digit billions of parameters, which is why harder queries are offloaded — a constraint visible in research needed to run 70B models at the edge. The ceiling is disclosed: a 32K-token context is small against frontier assistants, and Apple's own models were not frontier-quality, which is why the Google agreement exists. The unresolved question — the one that decides whether the privacy story holds — is where Gemini-derived inference physically runs. Apple says Apple Intelligence continues on Apple devices and Private Cloud Compute; trade reporting says Google's cloud performs the Gemini computation and puts the licence at ~$1bn a year, on top of a default-search payment of ~$20bn. Neither figure is Apple-confirmed [S8, S58, S60, S61, S86]. Apple's differentiation is orchestration, distribution and privacy, not model quality; an investor should underwrite the cash flow and the installed base, not the AI layer.

| Dimension | Apple 2024 (AFM v1) | Apple 2026 (Gemini-based AFM) | Google (supplier) | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Frontier model | Own ~3B on-device plus server model | Gemini-derived | Owns Gemini | S58, S61 |
| Cost structure | Fixed R&D and data-centre capex | Fixed R&D plus per-query licence | Licence revenue | S58, S86 |
| What Apple keeps | Silicon, OS, orchestration | Silicon, OS, interface, orchestration | Model, training, inference | S58, S60 |

### Products: a strong cycle, a late foldable, a spatial computer that never became a platform

The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max launched on 2026-09-09 at $1,199 and $1,299; the foldable iPhone Duo at $1,999 went on sale on 2026-10-23. iPhone net sales rose 22% to $196.5bn in the nine months to 2026-06-27, with Greater China up 30%. The C2 modem supports US mmWave and uses 15% less energy than the C1X, but the larger iPhone 18 Pro Max appears to keep a Qualcomm modem, so Qualcomm retains leverage over the highest-ASP SKU. Vision Pro is the counter-example to Apple's category-creation record: ~390,000 units in 2024, ~45,000 in the December 2025 quarter despite the M5 refresh, ~600,000 lifetime, and an IDC forecast of ~290,000 units in 2026 [S59, S13, S87].

| Product | Stage | Launch | Revenue or share | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone 18 Pro / Pro Max | Commercial | 2026-09 | $196.5bn, 54% of 9M | Products 39.9% | C2 in Pro Max, 2027 | S59, S6 |
| iPhone Duo (foldable) | Commercial | 2026-10-23 | Inside iPhone; undisclosed | Not disclosed | First-quarter volume | S59 |
| Watch Series 11 / Ultra 3 | Commercial | 2025-09 | Wearables $27.3bn, +2% | Not disclosed | Hypertension roll-out | S5, S6 |
| Vision Pro (M5) | Commercial | 2025-10 | ~45k units Q4 2025 | Not disclosed | Lower-cost model, late 2026 | S87 |
| Services | Commercial | — | $91.7bn, +14% | 76.3% | AI tier / iCloud+ gating | S6, S107 |

### What is enforceable is regulatory, not patent

Apple publishes no patent count; the FY2025 10-K says only that it is "pursuing thousands of applications around the world" and that no single right protects its products. Patent counts, grants and a peer comparison were not obtainable: the patent registries could not be searched, so the patent moat is unquantified. What is documented feature by feature is a regulatory estate: hypertension notification cleared in September 2025, sleep apnoea in September 2024, a hearing-aid De Novo grant in September 2024, and a medical imaging calibration feature in April 2026, on top of ECG and atrial-fibrillation history. Each needs its own clinical file — a slower, more durable barrier than a patent family [S5, S29, S30, S33, S34].

| Asset | Identifier | Jurisdiction | Date | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Patent portfolio | Count not disclosed | US and foreign | Ongoing | "Thousands of applications" | Unquantified | S5 |
| Hypertension Notification | K250507 | US FDA | 2025-09-11 | Cleared 510(k) | Watch sensing | S30 |
| Sleep Apnea Notification | K240929 | US FDA | 2024-09-13 | Cleared 510(k) | Watch sensing | S33 |
| Hearing Aid Feature | DEN230081 | US FDA | 2024-09-12 | De Novo granted | AirPods | S34 |
| Medical Imaging Calibration | K253582 | US FDA | 2026-04-01 | Cleared 510(k) | Display calibration | S29 |

### The moat is wide at the bottom of the stack and thin at the top

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Custom SoC and modem | 9 | Top design team plus priority TSMC N2 access; a decade and an Intel acquisition | 4-5 years | S59, S64 |
| Hardware-OS integration | 8 | Six operating systems co-designed with custom silicon | 3-5 years | S5 |
| On-device model efficiency | 5 | Quantisation and KV-cache techniques are published | 1-2 years | S61 |
| Frontier model | 3 | Available to licence, as Apple has shown | 1-2 years, by cheque | S58 |
| FDA-cleared health features | 7 | Each feature needs its own trial and clearance | 3-4 years | S30, S33 |
| Installed base and developers | 10 | A decade of switching costs, record active base | 10+ years | S13, S87 |
| **Composite** | **8/10 hardware, 4/10 AI** | The stack is hard to copy; the intelligence is not | **4-5 years for hardware** | S58, S64 |

The replication test answers the question directly: 50 senior silicon and operating-system engineers with Apple's published patents could match a phone-class SoC and OS in four to five years, and could rent a competitive model next quarter. The moat protects the cash-generating layer, not the differentiating one. The counter-evidence is Apple's own record: Siri needed a Google licence, the car was cancelled, Vision Pro has not reached platform volumes. The advantage holds only if on-device AI lifts upgrade rates and regulators leave the App Store economics that fund the silicon intact. Two diligence questions settle it: whether the Google agreement allows fine-tuning for on-device use, and whether the 2027 Pro Max moves fully to the C2 [S58, S59, S87].

::: evidence
**Apple's integration advantage is durable in silicon and distribution, but it no longer extends to the model layer.**

The A20 Pro's 2nm node and 32-core Neural Engine keep Apple at the leading edge of phone silicon, and twelve FDA device records since 2020 give it a regulated feature estate rivals must replicate trial by trial. But basing the next Apple Foundation Models on Gemini concedes that the frontier layer is bought, and the reported ~$1bn annual licence turns a fixed R&D advantage into a variable cost paid to a competitor [S58, S64, S86].
:::

arguments.markdown:
Apple runs a hardware annuity with a services margin layered on top — every dollar of product gross profit now carries 73 cents of services gross profit — but the mix shift the multiple pays for stalled in fiscal 2026, when hardware margins, helped by tariff refunds, grew gross profit twice as fast as Services.

### Who pays, and how the cash arrives

Apple sells to consumers, small businesses, education, enterprise and government, but the route to those customers is split in a way the revenue line conceals. In fiscal 2025, 40% of net sales went through Apple's own retail stores, online store and direct sales force, and 60% through carriers, resellers and distributors. That 60% matters because a mobile carrier subsidises or finances the handset to win a contract: the carrier pays to acquire Apple's customer, and Apple's own selling cost stays small — selling, general and administrative expense was $27,601M, 6.6% of revenue. There is almost no contracted backlog either: total deferred revenue was $13.7bn at 2025-09-27, 3.3% of revenue, two thirds of it recognised within a year. Apple is a repeat-purchase business recognised as it bills, not a subscription business with a book of contracted revenue [S5].

### The mix shift, and its reversal

The arithmetic of the mix shift is the strongest part of the case. In fiscal 2025, Services produced $109,158M of revenue at a 75.4% gross margin, against $307,003M of Products at 36.8%. Services was therefore 26.2% of revenue but 42.2% of gross profit ($82,314M of $195,201M), up from 35.7% two years earlier, and services gross profit per dollar of product gross profit rose from $0.55 in fiscal 2023 to $0.73 in fiscal 2025. Because services cost of sales was only $26,844M, most of each incremental services dollar reaches gross profit [S5].

Then the mechanism ran backwards. In the nine months to 2026-06-27, product gross profit rose 26.3% to $108,819M while services gross profit rose 15.3% to $69,963M, and Services fell to 39.1% of gross profit. Product gross margin reached 39.9% against 36.9% a year earlier, taking total gross margin to 49.1% and to 50.1% in the June quarter against 46.5%. Apple attributes the gain to "a different mix of products and tariff refunds, partially offset by higher costs, including memory" [S6]. That is the most consequential disclosure in the section: fiscal 2026's margin expansion is hardware-led, and part of it is a refund rather than a trading gain.

### Unit economics per revenue dollar, because there are no units

Apple discloses no unit volumes, average selling price or installed-base figure, so a per-device waterfall cannot be built from primary evidence. The economics of each revenue dollar can be.

| Unit-economics line | FY2025 | 9M FY2026 | Evidence and status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Product cost of sales, per $1,000 of product revenue | $632 | $601 | Bill of materials, assembly and warranty provision combined, not split | S5, S6 |
| Product gross profit | $368 | $399 | 36.8% to 39.9%; includes tariff refunds in fiscal 2026 | S5, S6 |
| Services cost of sales, per $1,000 of services revenue | $246 | $237 | Content, hosting and payment processing | S5, S6 |
| Services gross profit | $754 | $763 | 75.4% to 76.3% | S5, S6 |
| Services gross profit per $1 of product gross profit | $0.73 | $0.64 | Closest disclosed proxy for lifetime value against acquisition cost | S5, S6 |
| Customer acquisition cost, support and warranty | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Carriers and resellers bear acquisition; warranty sits in cost of sales | S5 |
| LTV, LTV:CAC, CAC payback in months | Not computable | Not computable | Requires units, ASP and installed base, none of which Apple reports | S5 |

Apple therefore has no payback period to wait out: a device is gross-profit-positive on delivery at a 36.8% product margin, and the services stream that follows is nearly all incremental. The nearest disclosed proxy for lifetime value against acquisition cost is the $0.73 of services gross profit per dollar of product gross profit, and its fall to $0.64 is the number to watch — the annuity is still growing, but no longer faster than the hardware that creates it.

### Pricing power shows up as mix, not as price

| Line | FY2025 net sales | Year on year | What the filing discloses about price and mix | Gross margin | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone | $209,586M | +4% | Growth "due to higher net sales of Pro models", i.e. mix rather than units | 36.8% products blended | S5 |
| Services | $109,158M | +14% | "advertising, the App Store and cloud services" | 75.4% | S5 |
| Mac | $33,708M | +12% | "laptops and desktops" | 36.8% products blended | S5 |
| iPad and Wearables | $63,709M | 0% | iPad Air and mini higher, Accessories and Wearables lower | 36.8% products blended | S5 |

Pricing power shows up as mix: iPhone revenue rose 22% to $196,515M in the nine months to 2026-06-27, which Apple again attributes to higher sales of Pro models rather than to units. The same disclosure prevents separating price from volume, and therefore prevents estimating elasticity — a 22% iPhone increase could be volume, price, or any combination. Apple publishes list prices on its own store but not in its filings, and this report did not retrieve a verified 2026 price list, so the table uses disclosed mix effects rather than price points. Third-party unit data would settle it.

### The highest-margin layer is also the most litigated

App Store economics are recognised net — Apple books "only the commission it retains" on third-party app sales — so a take-rate cut passes straight to revenue and gross profit with no offsetting cost. Apple is subject to a US court order preventing it from charging a commission on certain consumer purchases, though the Ninth Circuit has instructed the district court to amend the injunction to permit one, and in the EU the Digital Markets Act forces alternative distribution, alternative payment processing and new fee structures, a compliance plan the European Commission has challenged [S6]. Apple does not disclose App Store revenue or the commission rate, so exposure can only be bounded by the $82,314M of Services gross profit it contributes to.

A second concentration sits in the same line. Apple earns licensing revenue from Google for search distribution, inside Services advertising — which Apple names as a primary driver of Services growth in both fiscal 2025 and the first nine months of fiscal 2026. The payment was $20bn in 2022 per unsealed court documents, 18.3% of fiscal 2025 Services revenue, and Apple does not disclose the current figure. The District of Columbia court order of 2025-09-02 preserved the ability to pay partners while banning exclusive agreements, but Apple states a reversal on appeal could impose remedies "prohibiting Google from offering the Company commercial terms for search distribution", and both the Department of Justice and Google appealed [S6, S82]. The fastest-growing part of Services has the least contractual visibility.

### Cost structure, and where durability breaks

The cost base is bought, not built. Product cost of sales of $194,116M goes to TSMC for wafers, to memory suppliers for DRAM and NAND, and to Foxconn and its peers for assembly. Research and development reached $34,035M in the nine months to 2026-06-27, up 33% and 9.3% of revenue against 8.3% in fiscal 2025, with Apple citing "infrastructure-related costs, including investments in artificial intelligence". Capital expenditure is 2.2% of trailing-twelve-month revenue against 34.9% at Microsoft in fiscal 2026 [S6, S27]. Apple rents its manufacturing and buys much of its AI capability through the income statement, so that bill hits the operating margin immediately rather than being capitalised into depreciation.

::: evidence
**The service mix still drives Apple's margin, but in fiscal 2026 it stopped being the marginal driver — hardware did, and part of that gain is a refund.**

Services contributed $82,314M of gross profit on $109,158M of revenue in fiscal 2025, 42.2% of the total, yet in the nine months to 2026-06-27 product gross profit grew 26.3% against 15.3% for Services, and product gross margin rose to 39.9% on mix and tariff refunds [S5, S6].
:::

For a long-only holder the annuity is real and the attach is not weakening, but the margin expansion of the last four quarters is not the mix shift it is commonly described as: it is product mix, a tariff refund and memory cost timing, on top of a services base whose most profitable components face an appeal, a court order and a European regulatory process. The durability question needs three facts Apple does not disclose — the current size of the search payment, the share of Services that is App Store commission, and the refund-versus-mix split in the fiscal 2026 product margin. The fiscal 2026 annual report, not on EDGAR as of 2026-10-31, may settle them.
