arguments.markdown:
Apple's markets are contracting in units and expanding in value, and Apple is taking value share inside that contraction: the case for FY2026-FY2028 rests on premiumisation and Services attach rather than device volume, is strongest in the United States, is adequate in Europe, and in China depends on a domestic champion's pricing discipline. [S66]

### The pool is shrinking in units and growing in value

IDC's August 2026 forecast has worldwide smartphone shipments at just over 1.0 billion units in 2026, down 16.7% and the steepest annual contraction on record, while total market value rises 6.3% to $613 billion and the average selling price reaches a record $581, up 27.6% in a year and revised up from the $550 IDC published one quarter earlier. The cause is cost, not demand: DRAM and NAND prices are up more than 300% year on year as capacity is redirected to AI servers, memory is more than 65% of bill of materials at the low end, and the sub-$100 tier that shipped 173 million units in 2025 fell almost 60% in the second quarter of 2026. This is a supply shock with a dated end, so 2026-2027 flatters Apple's unit share while genuinely lifting its price, and 2028 is the test of whether either survives. [S39]

Two sizing methods agree closely: 1.0 billion units at the $581 average price gives $581 billion, within 5% of IDC's $613 billion, so the unit and price series can be read together rather than as rival estimates. On that base Apple's serviceable market is the premium tier it addresses — an iOS share of 23.6% of 2026 shipments, a record — while the revenue it can obtain is what it already books: $466.8 billion trailing twelve months to 2026-06-27, which at the 16.2% growth rate of the first nine months of FY2026 implies about $483 billion for FY2026. [S6]

| Measure | Method | Figure | Year | Publisher | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| TAM, smartphone value (top-down) | Industry value estimate | $613bn, +6.3% | 2026 | IDC | S66 |
| TAM, smartphone value (bottom-up) | 1.0bn units x $581 ASP | ~$581bn | 2026 | Calculation on IDC inputs | S66 |
| TAM, personal computing devices | Units published, value not disclosed | ~398m units, -11.3% | 2026 | IDC | S103 |
| SAM, premium smartphone tier | iOS share of shipments | 23.6% of units, record | 2026 | IDC | S66 |
| SOM, Apple revenue | Reported | $466.8bn TTM | TTM to 2026-06-27 | Apple 10-Q | S6 |
| Near-term obtainable revenue | FY2025 $416.2bn grown at the 9M FY2026 rate | ~$483bn | FY2026E | Calculation on Apple filings | S5, S13 |
| Adjacent services pool | Alphabet revenue | $471.1bn TTM | TTM to 2026-09-30 | Alphabet 10-Q | S42 |

### China is the swing factor, and India sits in the wrong line

Apple's revenue is moving toward the faster-growing regions, but the swing is China. In the first nine months of FY2026 Greater China produced $64.8 billion, up 30.0% on a base of $49.9 billion, after falling from $72.6 billion in FY2023 to $64.4 billion in FY2025; the Americas grew 11.4% to $149.4 billion, Europe 16.1% to $95.6 billion, Japan 10.4% and Rest of Asia Pacific 19.4%. Greater China's $14.9 billion increase contributes roughly 4.1 percentage points of the group's 16.2% growth, more than any other segment, and part of it is currency: Apple attributes a favourable effect to renminbi strength in Greater China and an unfavourable one to yen weakness in Japan. One reporting artefact matters: the Europe segment includes India, the Middle East and Africa, so the fastest-growing large smartphone market is invisible in the line labelled Europe and India is not a segment an investor can track. [S13]

| Region | Market size (year) | Growth | Apple's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| United States / North America | 60% of Q1 2026 shipments above $800; US is 24.9% of global PC-plus-tablet units | Smartphone -6.3% in 2026; PC -14.6% in 2026 | Entered, leads the premium tier; 41.0% of Apple revenue is the Americas | Tariffs, carrier financing, antitrust suits | Samsung, Lenovo, HP, Dell | S39, S103, S13 |
| Greater China | ~66m units a quarter, roughly 264m a year | -4.3% in Q2 2026, fifth straight decline; H2 2026 could be -20% | 18.1% of units, second behind Huawei; revenue +30.0% | Domestic operating system, subsidy withdrawal, data rules | Huawei 22.6%, OPPO 16.0%, vivo 16.0%, Xiaomi 12.4% | S40, S6 |
| Europe (segment includes India, Middle East, Africa) | India 31.0m units in Q1 2026 at a record $302 ASP | India units -4.1% but value +5.8%; Europe revenue +16.1% | Entered; fourth by units in India | DMA, price sensitivity, distribution | Samsung, Xiaomi, vivo, Lenovo, HP | S105, S103, S13 |
| Japan | Revenue $24.4bn in 9M FY2026 | Revenue +10.4%; units -25.6% in 2026 | Entered, premium strong; weak yen cuts revenue | Yen, saturated device base | Local Android vendors, Samsung | S13, S103, S6 |
| Rest of Asia Pacific | Revenue $30.2bn in 9M FY2026 | Revenue +19.4%; units about -14% in 2026 | Entered, premium-led | Price-sensitive mass market, currency | Samsung, Xiaomi, OPPO, vivo | S13, S39, S103 |

### Services carries the margin and has no published pool size

The fastest-growing pool Apple actually monetises is Services: $109.2 billion, 26.2% of FY2025 revenue, at a 75.4% gross margin against 36.8% for products, growing 14.1% to $91.7 billion in the first nine months of FY2026. The adjacent pools are larger and largely not Apple's — Alphabet's trailing-twelve-month revenue is $471.1 billion — but the app economy itself has no published size in the sources retrieved: neither Apple nor the platform owners disclose app-store gross billings or mobile-advertising revenue in a sizeable form, so Apple's own Services line is the measured pool. The same gap applies to the installed base behind it: Apple states only that its active-device base reached an all-time high in the June 2026 quarter across every category and region, and publishes no device count in its FY2025 10-K or FY2026 results, so the figure of about 2.3 billion devices often quoted alongside the business is unverified here and should carry none of the valuation. [S5]

### Who pays, and how much demand is policy

The budget owner is the consumer, in a discretionary purchase that is increasingly financed. In the United States and United Kingdom long-term interest-free financing is more prevalent, which is why IDC expects the premium end to hold while emerging markets fall more than 20% in 2026; in India brands lean on financing after the sub-$100 tier fell 59% and the $600-800 band grew 32%; in China the government subsidy that supported earlier quarters faded in the second quarter of 2026, so demand there is being withdrawn by policy rather than created by it. Apple's exposure to policy runs both ways: after the February 20, 2026 Supreme Court ruling struck down certain IEEPA tariffs, Apple recognised refunds as a reduction of product cost of sales, and those refunds contributed about 2 percentage points of the June 2026 quarter's 50.1% gross margin — tariff policy moves Apple's margin by more than a product cycle does. [S105, S40, S13]

Three findings could break the case. If memory prices normalise in 2028 as IDC expects, the entry tier rebuilds and Apple's 2026 share gain is contestable again. If China's June-quarter demand was pulled forward ahead of expected second-half price increases, as IDC's China team reports, the 30% growth line is a launch and currency effect. And if courts and the European Commission remove the App Store take rate, the 75%-margin layer that offsets hardware cyclicality stops compounding at its present rate. The investor implication is narrow: in a 1-billion-unit market Apple can grow revenue only if price rises faster than units fall, making average selling price, China durability and the Services take rate the variables worth monitoring and unit share the least informative number in the file. Confidence in the sizing is high, because two independent methods agree within 5%; confidence that the mix shift holds to 2028 is medium, because it rests on China and on a legally contested commission. Three questions would close the gap: what share of Services revenue is commission-based rather than subscription, advertising or licensing; how much of the Greater China increase is currency; and what the current average replacement cycle is, measured rather than asserted.

::: evidence
**Apple's addressable device market fell 16.7% in units in 2026 while growing 6.3% in value, and Apple's revenue grew 16.2% over nine months — the gap is premiumisation and China, not market growth.**

IDC forecasts 2026 shipments at just over 1.0 billion units against a market value of $613 billion and an ASP of $581 (S66, S39). Apple's nine-month FY2026 revenue was $364.4 billion, up 16.2%, with Greater China up 30.0% on a $49.9 billion base (S13, S6). The bottom-up check of 1.0 billion units at $581 gives $581 billion, within 5% of IDC's value estimate (S66).
:::

arguments.markdown:
Apple's silicon-plus-OS stack is still the widest integrated consumer technology stack in the industry, but in 2026 the company rented the one layer it could not build — the frontier model — so what remains defensible is distribution, custom silicon and regulated health sensing, not leadership in artificial intelligence. In two years: the A19 Pro shipped in September 2025 on TSMC N3P; the A20 Pro moved the iPhone to TSMC N2 in September 2026; the C2 modem reached the flagship; the first foldable iPhone shipped at $1,999; and on 2026-01-12 Apple and Google announced that the next generation of Apple Foundation Models would be based on Gemini [S58, S59, S63, S64].

### The silicon lead is real, costly, and rented from TSMC

The A19 Pro used TSMC N3P with two performance cores at up to 4.26 GHz; a year later the A20 Pro moved to TSMC N2 with a dual 16-core Neural Engine — 32 neural cores — and ~52 TOPS, about double the prior generation's AI throughput. N2 wafers are reported at ~$30,000 against $18,000-20,000 for 3nm, so each capability step arrives with higher silicon cost. Product gross margin was 39.9% in the nine months to 2026-06-27 versus 36.9% a year earlier, but only with tariff refunds and mix offsetting "higher costs, including memory", and the 10-Q warns that advanced-semiconductor, NAND and DRAM constraints are expected to intensify [S6, S64].

| Metric | Value | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Node, A19 Pro / A20 Pro | TSMC N3P (2025) / N2 (2026) | Teardown and trade reporting | S63, S64 |
| CPU clock, A19 Pro | up to 4.26 GHz, 6 cores | Published specification | S63 |
| Neural Engine, A20 Pro | 32 cores, ~52 TOPS, ~2x A19 Pro | Trade-press estimate | S64 |
| N2 wafer price | ~$30,000 vs $18,000-20,000 at 3nm | Trade-press estimate | S64 |
| Product gross margin | 39.9% vs 36.9% (9M FY2025) | Reported financials | S6 |
| On-device model / PCC context | ~3B parameters / 32K tokens | Apple research and developer docs | S61, S62 |

### Apple Intelligence is an architecture with a rented brain

On device, Apple runs a ~3B-parameter model optimised through KV-cache sharing and 2-bit quantisation-aware training; on its servers, a Parallel-Track Mixture-of-Experts model runs inside Private Cloud Compute, which enforces stateless processing, no privileged runtime access even for Apple staff, and verifiable software images with attestation. The binding constraint is memory bandwidth and power: phone-class memory caps practical on-device inference at single-digit billions of parameters, which is why harder queries are offloaded — a constraint visible in research needed to run 70B models at the edge. The ceiling is disclosed: a 32K-token context is small against frontier assistants, and Apple's own models were not frontier-quality, which is why the Google agreement exists. The unresolved question — the one that decides whether the privacy story holds — is where Gemini-derived inference physically runs. Apple says Apple Intelligence continues on Apple devices and Private Cloud Compute; trade reporting says Google's cloud performs the Gemini computation and puts the licence at ~$1bn a year, on top of a default-search payment of ~$20bn. Neither figure is Apple-confirmed [S8, S58, S60, S61, S86]. Apple's differentiation is orchestration, distribution and privacy, not model quality; an investor should underwrite the cash flow and the installed base, not the AI layer.

| Dimension | Apple 2024 (AFM v1) | Apple 2026 (Gemini-based AFM) | Google (supplier) | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Frontier model | Own ~3B on-device plus server model | Gemini-derived | Owns Gemini | S58, S61 |
| Cost structure | Fixed R&D and data-centre capex | Fixed R&D plus per-query licence | Licence revenue | S58, S86 |
| What Apple keeps | Silicon, OS, orchestration | Silicon, OS, interface, orchestration | Model, training, inference | S58, S60 |

### Products: a strong cycle, a late foldable, a spatial computer that never became a platform

The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max launched on 2026-09-09 at $1,199 and $1,299; the foldable iPhone Duo at $1,999 went on sale on 2026-10-23. iPhone net sales rose 22% to $196.5bn in the nine months to 2026-06-27, with Greater China up 30%. The C2 modem supports US mmWave and uses 15% less energy than the C1X, but the larger iPhone 18 Pro Max appears to keep a Qualcomm modem, so Qualcomm retains leverage over the highest-ASP SKU. Vision Pro is the counter-example to Apple's category-creation record: ~390,000 units in 2024, ~45,000 in the December 2025 quarter despite the M5 refresh, ~600,000 lifetime, and an IDC forecast of ~290,000 units in 2026 [S59, S13, S87].

| Product | Stage | Launch | Revenue or share | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone 18 Pro / Pro Max | Commercial | 2026-09 | $196.5bn, 54% of 9M | Products 39.9% | C2 in Pro Max, 2027 | S59, S6 |
| iPhone Duo (foldable) | Commercial | 2026-10-23 | Inside iPhone; undisclosed | Not disclosed | First-quarter volume | S59 |
| Watch Series 11 / Ultra 3 | Commercial | 2025-09 | Wearables $27.3bn, +2% | Not disclosed | Hypertension roll-out | S5, S6 |
| Vision Pro (M5) | Commercial | 2025-10 | ~45k units Q4 2025 | Not disclosed | Lower-cost model, late 2026 | S87 |
| Services | Commercial | — | $91.7bn, +14% | 76.3% | AI tier / iCloud+ gating | S6, S107 |

### What is enforceable is regulatory, not patent

Apple publishes no patent count; the FY2025 10-K says only that it is "pursuing thousands of applications around the world" and that no single right protects its products. Patent counts and peer comparison were not obtainable: the registries could not be searched, so the patent moat is unquantified. What is documented feature by feature is a regulatory estate: hypertension notification cleared in September 2025, sleep apnoea in September 2024, a hearing-aid De Novo grant in September 2024, and a medical imaging calibration feature in April 2026. Each needs its own clinical file — a slower, more durable barrier than a patent family [S5, S29, S30, S33, S34].

| Asset | Identifier | Jurisdiction | Date | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Patent portfolio | Count not disclosed | US and foreign | Ongoing | "Thousands of applications" | Unquantified | S5 |
| Hypertension Notification | K250507 | US FDA | 2025-09-11 | Cleared 510(k) | Watch sensing | S30 |
| Sleep Apnea Notification | K240929 | US FDA | 2024-09-13 | Cleared 510(k) | Watch sensing | S33 |
| Hearing Aid Feature | DEN230081 | US FDA | 2024-09-12 | De Novo granted | AirPods | S34 |
| Medical Imaging Calibration | K253582 | US FDA | 2026-04-01 | Cleared 510(k) | Display calibration | S29 |

### The moat is wide at the bottom of the stack and thin at the top

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Custom SoC and modem | 9 | Top design team plus priority TSMC N2 access; a decade and an Intel acquisition | 4-5 years | S59, S64 |
| Hardware-OS integration | 8 | Six operating systems co-designed with custom silicon | 3-5 years | S5 |
| On-device model efficiency | 5 | Quantisation and KV-cache techniques are published | 1-2 years | S61 |
| Frontier model | 3 | Available to licence, as Apple has shown | 1-2 years, by cheque | S58 |
| FDA-cleared health features | 7 | Each feature needs its own trial and clearance | 3-4 years | S30, S33 |
| Installed base and developers | 10 | A decade of switching costs, record active base | 10+ years | S13, S87 |
| **Composite** | **8/10 hardware, 4/10 AI** | The stack is hard to copy; the intelligence is not | **4-5 years for hardware** | S58, S64 |

The replication test answers the question directly: 50 senior silicon and operating-system engineers with Apple's published patents could match a phone-class SoC and OS in four to five years, and could rent a competitive model next quarter. The moat protects the cash-generating layer, not the differentiating one. The counter-evidence is Apple's own record: Siri needed a Google licence, the car was cancelled, Vision Pro has not reached platform volumes. The advantage holds only if on-device AI lifts upgrade rates and regulators leave the App Store economics that fund the silicon intact. Two diligence questions settle it: whether the Google agreement allows fine-tuning for on-device use, and whether the 2027 Pro Max moves fully to the C2 [S58, S59, S87].

::: evidence
**Apple's integration advantage is durable in silicon and distribution, but it no longer extends to the model layer.**

The A20 Pro's 2nm node and 32-core Neural Engine keep Apple at the leading edge of phone silicon, and twelve FDA device records since 2020 give it a regulated feature estate rivals must replicate trial by trial. But basing the next Apple Foundation Models on Gemini concedes that the frontier layer is bought, and the reported ~$1bn annual licence turns a fixed R&D advantage into a variable cost paid to a competitor [S58, S64, S86].
:::

arguments.markdown:
Apple's policy exposure is not a licence-to-operate threat but a slow, legislated tax on Services gross profit: the €500 million DMA fine of 2025-04-23 and the April 2025 US contempt finding show a company that litigates first and complies later, while the three remedies that matter — Google's default-search payment, the US link-out commission and the EU fee structure — have so far been reshaped rather than removed [S7]. The question for a long-only holder is not whether Apple survives regulation, but how much Services gross margin the next five years of enforcement takes, and whether the multiple already discounts it.

### The DMA fine is small; the cost structure is not

The Commission fined Apple €500 million on 2025-04-23 for breaching the anti-steering obligation and ordered it to remove the technical and commercial restrictions on steering users outside the App Store. The same day it closed the user-choice investigation — a real concession — but issued preliminary findings in the Article 6(4) file on Apple's terms for alternative app marketplaces, where an adverse final finding carries fines of up to 10% of annual worldwide net sales and further penalties for breaching a cease-and-desist order [S5]. Apple has appealed and says it complies. The record bounds the risk on both sides: on 2026-02-05 the Commission found Apple Ads and Apple Maps should not be designated, and no further Apple decision appears in its DMA record between the fine and 2026-09-28. Peer severity is modest — Meta paid €200 million in the same package, Google €890 million on 2026-07-23, and Alphabet's Android fine of €4.1 billion only reached a final ECJ ruling in July 2026 — so repeated fines, not break-up, are the base rate.

The financially material part is the fee, not the penalty. Europe booked $111.0 billion of net sales in FY2025, up 10%, led by Services, and App Store commission is the highest-margin revenue Apple records, so a mandated fee cut in Brussels is worth more to the equity than any fine. Apple also warns that DMA interoperability obligations force it to open technologies to third parties without charge and have in the past, and may in future, caused it not to launch or maintain features "such as Siri AI" in certain jurisdictions — a product-availability risk, not only a revenue leak.

### A contempt finding, then a slow antitrust case

On 2025-04-30 the Northern District of California found Apple in violation of the 2021 Epic injunction, barred any commission on purchases made outside an app, and referred the company to the US Attorney for a determination on criminal contempt. The Ninth Circuit modified that on 2025-12-11 to allow parity requirements and some commission on link-out purchases; Apple petitioned the Supreme Court on 2026-05-21, obtained certiorari on 2026-06-30 limited to the civil-contempt standard, and seeks a stay of the district court case [S6, S122]. Read narrowly this is a US pricing dispute; read properly it is evidence that Apple's platform-compliance function tested a court order rather than obeyed it, which raises the severity of the next remedy. That next remedy is the DOJ's case, filed 2024-03-21 with 16 states and the District of Columbia, which seeks equitable relief only, survived dismissal on 2025-06-30 and is in discovery on a schedule pointing to a 2027 trial. No damages are claimed, so the risk is conduct-based — defaults, messaging, app distribution — and lands on the 2027-2029 Services line rather than the balance sheet.

### Google's payment survives, on worse terms

The search-distribution remedy is the largest dollar item here, and the 2025-09-02 decision went Apple's way on the point that mattered: the court refused to ban Google's payments to distributors, citing harm to device makers and browser developers, and instead barred exclusive contracts while permitting default-placement payments that are not conditioned on exclusivity and run one year or less [S118, S42]. A final judgment followed in December 2025; Google appealed in January 2026 and the Department of Justice cross-appealed in February 2026, both pending at 2026-10-29. Apple does not disclose the payment, so the $20 billion-a-year figure in circulation is unverified in its filings. What the record establishes is that the revenue survives with annual renewal risk and mandatory choice screens, shifting pricing power to Apple at renewal and to rivals in the default setting.

### Two bear-case triggers did not fire in 2026

The Section 232 semiconductor investigation's initial results on 2026-01-14 imposed no additional tariff on Apple's products, and on 2026-02-20 the Supreme Court struck down certain IEEPA tariffs, with Apple claiming refunds it recognised as a reduction of products cost of sales; Section 301 tariffs were then imposed and further Section 232 action remains open. In China the opposite of closure happened: the CAC registered Apple Intelligence on 2026-07-15 with Alibaba's Qwen and Baidu, and Greater China net sales rose 22% to $18,816 million in the June 2026 quarter and 30% to $64,839 million for the nine months, from $49,884 million [S6, S121]. The binding constraint is the calendar: the Busan truce that suppresses tariff and rare-earth escalation was extended on 2026-09-23 from 2026-11-10 to 2027-01-10, which makes 2027 the next policy cliff.

### Tax is settled; the ESG tail is elsewhere

The Irish state-aid case ended against Apple: the ECJ confirmed the 2016 decision on 2024-09-10, producing a $10.2 billion net one-time charge and $15.8 billion payable to Ireland. The FY2025 effective tax rate of 15.6%, against 24.1% in FY2024, now sits just above the OECD Pillar Two 15% floor, so incremental Pillar Two cost is small and the live tax risk is the $23.2 billion of gross unrecognised benefits, $10.6 billion of which would move the rate if recognised [S5]. Tax is a settled cost, not a source of future EPS upside.

On environmental and social issues the record is stronger than the sector's: full third-party audit coverage of identified 3TG smelters for a tenth consecutive year, no finding of armed-group financing, a June 2024 instruction to suppliers to stop sourcing 3TG from the DRC and Rwanda, and recycled-content commitments for cobalt, tin, gold and rare earths. Those claims are company-prepared and not independently verified in this record, and the carbon-neutral-2030 commitment and its Scope 3 progress could not be verified from a published source in this run; that gap is stated, not filled.

Governance offsets the conduct record: a single class of common stock with no dual-class structure, an independent Chair separated from the CEO, an Audit Committee that owns privacy, cybersecurity, tax and enterprise risk, and related-party disclosure limited to one family-member employment. Control is not the issue; compliance culture is.

### What it would change, and what to ask

The tables below collect the exposure. They support a judgement that policy is a 100-300 basis point tax on Services gross margin plus a low-probability structural remedy in the United States, not a threat to the franchise: at Apple's scale, 100 basis points of Services gross margin is material annual gross profit, so the watchlist question is whether the multiple leaves room for that dilution. Three questions decide it: what fee Apple now charges on US link-out purchases after the December 2025 remand and how much spending has moved off in-app purchase; what Apple actually receives from Google at the first one-year renewal; and whether the Article 6(4) file produces a second EU fine before the General Court rules. None is a reason to avoid Apple; each is a reason to demand a price that assumes some of the loss.

arguments.markdown:
Apple's markets are contracting in units and expanding in value, and Apple is taking value share inside that contraction: the case for FY2026-FY2028 rests on premiumisation and Services attach rather than device volume, is strongest in the United States, is adequate in Europe, and in China depends on a domestic champion's pricing discipline.

### The pool is shrinking in units and growing in value

IDC's August 2026 forecast has worldwide smartphone shipments at just over 1.0 billion units in 2026, down 16.7% and the steepest annual contraction on record, while total market value rises 6.3% to $613 billion and the average selling price reaches a record $581, up 27.6% in a year and revised up from the $550 IDC published one quarter earlier. The cause is cost, not demand: DRAM and NAND prices are up more than 300% year on year as capacity is redirected to AI servers, memory is more than 65% of bill of materials at the low end, and the sub-$100 tier that shipped 173 million units in 2025 fell close to 60% in the second quarter of 2026. This is a supply shock with a dated end, so 2026-2027 flatters Apple's unit share while genuinely lifting its price, and 2028 is the test of whether either survives. [S39]

Two sizing methods agree closely: 1.0 billion units at the $581 average price gives $581 billion, within 5% of IDC's $613 billion, so the unit and price series can be read together rather than as rival estimates. On that base Apple's serviceable market is the premium tier it addresses — an iOS share of 23.6% of 2026 shipments, a record — while the revenue it can obtain is what it already books: $466.8 billion trailing twelve months to 2026-06-27, which at the 16.2% growth rate of the first nine months of FY2026 implies $483 billion for FY2026. On IDC's numbers the PC-plus-tablet pool compounds at 1.5% a year from 2026 to 2030, so the device pools are not growth markets at any price. [S6]

| Adjacent services pool | Alphabet revenue | $471.1bn TTM | TTM to 2026-09-30 | Alphabet 10-Q | S42 |

### China is the swing factor, and India sits in the wrong line

Apple's revenue is moving toward the faster-growing regions, but the swing is China. In the first nine months of FY2026 Greater China produced $64.8 billion, up 30.0% on a base of $49.9 billion, after falling from $72.6 billion in FY2023 to $64.4 billion in FY2025; the Americas grew 11.4% to $149.4 billion, Europe 16.1% to $95.6 billion, Japan 10.4% and Rest of Asia Pacific 19.4%. Greater China's $14.9 billion increase contributes 4.1 percentage points of the group's 16.2% growth, more than any other segment, and part of it is currency: a favourable renminbi effect in Greater China, an unfavourable yen effect in Japan. One reporting artefact matters: the Europe segment includes India, the Middle East and Africa, so the fastest-growing large smartphone market is invisible in the line labelled Europe and India is not a segment an investor can track. ### Services carries the margin and has no published pool size

The fastest-growing pool Apple actually monetises is Services: $109.2 billion, 26.2% of FY2025 revenue, at a 75.4% gross margin against 36.8% for products, growing 14.1% to $91.7 billion in the first nine months of FY2026. The adjacent pools are larger and largely not Apple's — Alphabet's trailing-twelve-month revenue is $471.1 billion — but the app economy itself has no published size in the sources retrieved: neither Apple nor the platform owners disclose app-store gross billings or mobile-advertising revenue in a sizeable form, so Apple's own Services line is the measured pool. The installed base behind it has the same gap: Apple states only that its active-device base reached an all-time high in the June 2026 quarter across every category and region, and publishes no device count in its FY2025 10-K or FY2026 results, so the figure of 2.3 billion devices often quoted alongside the business is unverified here and should carry none of the valuation. [S5]

### Who pays, and how much demand is policy

The budget owner is the consumer, in a discretionary purchase that is increasingly financed. In the United States and United Kingdom long-term interest-free financing is more prevalent, so IDC expects the premium end to hold while emerging markets fall more than 20%; in India brands lean on financing after the sub-$100 tier fell 59% and the $600-800 band grew 32%; in China the government subsidy that supported earlier quarters faded in the second quarter of 2026, so demand there is being withdrawn by policy rather than created by it. Apple's exposure to policy runs both ways: after the February 20, 2026 Supreme Court ruling struck down certain IEEPA tariffs, Apple recognised refunds as a reduction of product cost of sales, and those refunds contributed 2.0 percentage points of the June 2026 quarter's 50.1% gross margin — tariff policy moves Apple's margin by more than a product cycle does. [S105, S40, S13]

The counter-evidence is threefold and each strand has a date attached. If memory prices normalise in 2028 as IDC expects, the entry tier rebuilds and Apple's 2026 share gain is contestable again. If China's June-quarter demand was pulled forward ahead of expected second-half price increases, as IDC's China team reports, the 30% growth line is a launch and currency effect. And if courts and the European Commission remove the App Store take rate, the 75%-margin layer that offsets hardware cyclicality stops compounding at its present rate. The investor implication is narrow: in a 1-billion-unit market Apple can grow revenue only if price rises faster than units fall, making average selling price, China durability and the Services take rate the variables worth monitoring. Sizing confidence is high, because two independent methods agree within 5%; confidence that the mix shift holds to 2028 is medium, because it rests on China and a legally contested commission. Three questions would close the gap: what share of Services revenue is commission-based rather than subscription, advertising or licensing; how much of the Greater China increase is currency; and what the current average replacement cycle is, measured rather than asserted. [S66, S40]

::: evidence
**Apple's addressable device market fell 16.7% in units in 2026 while growing 6.3% in value, and Apple's revenue grew 16.2% over nine months — the gap is premiumisation and China, not market growth (S66, S13).**

IDC forecasts 2026 shipments at just over 1.0 billion units against a market value of $613 billion and an ASP of $581 (S66, S39). Apple's nine-month FY2026 revenue was $364.4 billion, up 16.2%, with Greater China up 30.0% on a $49.9 billion base (S13, S6). The bottom-up check of 1.0 billion units at $581 gives $581 billion, within 5% of IDC's value estimate (S66).

arguments.markdown:
Apple's silicon-plus-OS stack is still the widest integrated consumer technology stack in the industry, but in 2026 the company rented the one layer it could not build — the frontier model — so what remains defensible is distribution, custom silicon and regulated health sensing, not leadership in artificial intelligence. In two years: the A19 Pro shipped in September 2025 on TSMC N3P; the A20 Pro moved the iPhone to TSMC N2 in September 2026; the C2 modem reached the flagship; the first foldable iPhone shipped at $1,999; and on 2026-01-12 Apple and Google announced that the next generation of Apple Foundation Models would be based on Gemini [S58, S59, S63, S64].

### The silicon lead is real, costly, and rented from TSMC

The A19 Pro used TSMC N3P with two performance cores at up to 4.26 GHz; a year later the A20 Pro moved to TSMC N2 with a dual 16-core Neural Engine — 32 neural cores — and ~52 TOPS, about double the prior generation's AI throughput. N2 wafers are reported at ~$30,000 against $18,000-20,000 for 3nm, so each capability step arrives with higher silicon cost. Product gross margin was 39.9% in the nine months to 2026-06-27 versus 36.9% a year earlier, but only with tariff refunds and mix offsetting "higher costs, including memory", and the 10-Q warns that advanced-semiconductor, NAND and DRAM constraints are expected to intensify [S6, S64].

| Metric | Value | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Node, A19 Pro / A20 Pro | TSMC N3P (2025) / N2 (2026) | Teardown and trade reporting | S63, S64 |
| CPU clock, A19 Pro | up to 4.26 GHz, 6 cores | Published specification | S63 |
| Neural Engine, A20 Pro | 32 cores, ~52 TOPS, ~2x A19 Pro | Trade-press estimate | S64 |
| N2 wafer price | ~$30,000 vs $18,000-20,000 at 3nm | Trade-press estimate | S64 |
| Product gross margin | 39.9% vs 36.9% (9M FY2025) | Reported financials | S6 |
| On-device model / PCC context | ~3B parameters / 32K tokens | Apple research and developer docs | S61, S62 |

### Apple Intelligence is an architecture with a rented brain

On device, Apple runs a ~3B-parameter model optimised through KV-cache sharing and 2-bit quantisation-aware training; on its servers, a Parallel-Track Mixture-of-Experts model runs inside Private Cloud Compute, which enforces stateless processing, no privileged runtime access even for Apple staff, and verifiable software images with attestation. The binding constraint is memory bandwidth and power: phone-class memory caps practical on-device inference at single-digit billions of parameters, which is why harder queries are offloaded — a constraint visible in research needed to run 70B models at the edge. The ceiling is disclosed: a 32K-token context is small against frontier assistants, and Apple's own models were not frontier-quality, which is why the Google agreement exists. The unresolved question — the one that decides whether the privacy story holds — is where Gemini-derived inference physically runs. Apple says Apple Intelligence continues on Apple devices and Private Cloud Compute; trade reporting says Google's cloud performs the Gemini computation and puts the licence at ~$1bn a year, on top of a default-search payment of ~$20bn. Neither figure is Apple-confirmed [S8, S58, S60, S61, S86]. Apple's differentiation is orchestration, distribution and privacy, not model quality; an investor should underwrite the cash flow and the installed base, not the AI layer.

| Dimension | Apple 2024 (AFM v1) | Apple 2026 (Gemini-based AFM) | Google (supplier) | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Frontier model | Own ~3B on-device plus server model | Gemini-derived | Owns Gemini | S58, S61 |
| Cost structure | Fixed R&D and data-centre capex | Fixed R&D plus per-query licence | Licence revenue | S58, S86 |
| What Apple keeps | Silicon, OS, orchestration | Silicon, OS, interface, orchestration | Model, training, inference | S58, S60 |

### Products: a strong cycle, a late foldable, a spatial computer that never became a platform

The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max launched on 2026-09-09 at $1,199 and $1,299; the foldable iPhone Duo at $1,999 went on sale on 2026-10-23. iPhone net sales rose 22% to $196.5bn in the nine months to 2026-06-27, with Greater China up 30%. The C2 modem supports US mmWave and uses 15% less energy than the C1X, but the larger iPhone 18 Pro Max appears to keep a Qualcomm modem, so Qualcomm retains leverage over the highest-ASP SKU. Vision Pro is the counter-example to Apple's category-creation record: ~390,000 units in 2024, ~45,000 in the December 2025 quarter despite the M5 refresh, ~600,000 lifetime, and an IDC forecast of ~290,000 units in 2026 [S59, S13, S87].

### What is enforceable is regulatory, not patent

Apple publishes no patent count; the FY2025 10-K says only that it is "pursuing thousands of applications around the world" and that no single right protects its products. Patent counts and peer comparison were not obtainable — the registries could not be searched — so the patent moat is unquantified. What is documented feature by feature is a regulatory estate: hypertension and sleep-apnoea notifications, a hearing-aid De Novo grant and a medical imaging calibration feature, each cleared after its own clinical file. That is a slower, more durable barrier than a patent family, and the filings below date each clearance.

### The moat is wide at the bottom of the stack and thin at the top

|---|---|---|---|---|
| Custom SoC and modem | 9 | Top design team plus priority TSMC N2 access; a decade and an Intel acquisition | 4-5 years | S59, S64 |
| Hardware-OS integration | 8 | Six operating systems co-designed with custom silicon | 3-5 years | S5 |
| On-device model efficiency | 5 | Quantisation and KV-cache techniques are published | 1-2 years | S61 |
| Frontier model | 3 | Available to licence, as Apple has shown | 1-2 years, by cheque | S58 |
| FDA-cleared health features | 7 | Each feature needs its own trial and clearance | 3-4 years | S30, S33 |
| Installed base and developers | 10 | A decade of switching costs, record active base | 10+ years | S13, S87 |
| **Composite** | **8/10 hardware, 4/10 AI** | The stack is hard to copy; the intelligence is not | **4-5 years for hardware** | S58, S64 |

The replication test answers the question directly: 50 senior silicon and operating-system engineers with Apple's published patents could match a phone-class SoC and OS in four to five years, and could rent a competitive model next quarter. The moat protects the cash-generating layer, not the differentiating one. The counter-evidence is Apple's own record: Siri needed a Google licence, the car was cancelled, Vision Pro has not reached platform volumes. The advantage holds only if on-device AI lifts upgrade rates and regulators leave the App Store economics that fund the silicon intact. Two diligence questions settle it: whether the Google agreement allows fine-tuning for on-device use, and whether the 2027 Pro Max moves fully to the C2 [S58, S59, S87].

::: evidence
**Apple's integration advantage is durable in silicon and distribution, but it no longer extends to the model layer.**

The A20 Pro's 2nm node and 32-core Neural Engine keep Apple at the leading edge of phone silicon, and twelve FDA device records since 2020 give it a regulated feature estate rivals must replicate trial by trial. But basing the next Apple Foundation Models on Gemini concedes that the frontier layer is bought, and the reported ~$1bn annual licence turns a fixed R&D advantage into a variable cost paid to a competitor [S58, S64, S86].
:::

arguments.markdown:
Apple's policy exposure is not a licence-to-operate threat but a slow, legislated tax on Services gross profit: the €500 million DMA fine of 2025-04-23 and the April 2025 US contempt finding show a company that litigates first and complies later, while the three remedies that matter — Google's default-search payment, the US link-out commission and the EU fee structure — have so far been reshaped rather than removed [S7]. The question for a long-only holder is how much Services gross margin the next five years of enforcement takes, and whether the multiple already discounts it.

### The DMA fine is small; the cost structure is not

The Commission fined Apple €500 million on 2025-04-23 for breaching the anti-steering obligation and ordered it to remove restrictions on steering users outside the App Store. The same day it closed the user-choice investigation — a real concession — but issued preliminary findings in the Article 6(4) file on Apple's terms for alternative app marketplaces, where an adverse finding carries fines of up to 10% of annual worldwide net sales and further penalties for breaching a cease-and-desist order [S5]. Apple has appealed and says it complies. The record bounds the risk on both sides: on 2026-02-05 the Commission found Apple Ads and Apple Maps should not be designated, and no further Apple decision appears in its DMA record between the fine and 2026-09-28. Peer severity is modest — Meta paid €200 million in the same package, Google €890 million on 2026-07-23, Alphabet's Android fine of €4.1 billion only reached a final ECJ ruling in July 2026 — so repeated fines, not break-up, are the base rate.

The material part is the fee, not the penalty. Europe booked $111.0 billion of net sales in FY2025, up 10%, led by Services, and App Store commission is the highest-margin revenue Apple records, so a mandated fee cut in Brussels is worth more to the equity than any fine. Apple also warns that interoperability obligations force it to open technologies to third parties without charge and have in the past, and may in future, caused it not to launch or maintain features "such as Siri AI" in some jurisdictions — a product-availability risk, not only a revenue leak.

### A contempt finding, then a slow antitrust case

On 2025-04-30 the Northern District of California found Apple in violation of the 2021 Epic injunction, barred any commission on purchases made outside an app, and referred the company to the US Attorney on criminal contempt. The Ninth Circuit modified that on 2025-12-11 to allow parity rules and some commission on link-out purchases; Apple petitioned the Supreme Court on 2026-05-21, obtained certiorari on 2026-06-30 limited to the civil-contempt standard, and seeks a stay below [S6, S122]. Read narrowly this is a pricing dispute; read properly it is evidence that Apple's compliance function tested a court order rather than obeyed it, which raises the severity of the next remedy. That remedy is the DOJ case, filed 2024-03-21 with 16 states and the District of Columbia, seeking equitable relief only; it survived dismissal on 2025-06-30 and is in discovery on a schedule pointing to a 2027 trial. With no damages claimed, the risk is conduct-based — defaults, messaging, app distribution — and lands on the 2027-2029 Services line rather than the balance sheet.

### Google's payment survives, on worse terms

The search-distribution remedy is the largest dollar item, and the 2025-09-02 decision went Apple's way on the point that mattered: the court refused to ban Google's payments to distributors, citing harm to device makers and browser developers, and instead barred exclusive contracts while permitting default-placement payments not conditioned on exclusivity and running one year or less [S118, S42]. A final judgment followed in December 2025; Google appealed in January 2026 and the Department of Justice cross-appealed in February 2026, both pending at 2026-10-29. Apple does not disclose the payment, so the $20 billion-a-year figure in circulation is unverified in its filings. What the record establishes is that the revenue survives with annual renewal risk and mandatory choice screens, shifting pricing power to Apple at renewal and to rivals in the default setting.

### Two bear-case triggers did not fire in 2026

The Section 232 semiconductor investigation's initial results on 2026-01-14 imposed no additional tariff on Apple's products, and on 2026-02-20 the Supreme Court struck down certain IEEPA tariffs, with Apple claiming refunds it recognised as a reduction of products cost of sales; Section 301 tariffs were then imposed and further Section 232 action remains open. In China the opposite of closure happened: the CAC registered Apple Intelligence on 2026-07-15 with Alibaba's Qwen and Baidu, and Greater China net sales rose 22% to $18,816 million in the June 2026 quarter and 30% to $64,839 million for the nine months, from $49,884 million [S6, S121]. The binding constraint is the calendar: the Busan truce that suppresses tariff and rare-earth escalation was extended on 2026-09-23 from 2026-11-10 to 2027-01-10, making 2027 the next policy cliff.

### Tax is settled; the ESG tail is elsewhere

The Irish state-aid case ended against Apple: the ECJ confirmed the 2016 decision on 2024-09-10, producing a $10.2 billion net one-time charge and $15.8 billion payable to Ireland. The FY2025 effective tax rate of 15.6%, against 24.1% in FY2024, now sits just above the OECD Pillar Two 15% floor, so incremental Pillar Two cost is small and the live tax risk is the $23.2 billion of gross unrecognised benefits, $10.6 billion of which would move the rate if recognised [S5]. Tax is a settled cost, not a source of future earnings upside.

On environmental and social issues the record is stronger than the sector's: full third-party audit coverage of identified 3TG smelters for a tenth consecutive year, no finding of armed-group financing, a June 2024 instruction to suppliers to stop sourcing 3TG from the DRC and Rwanda, and recycled-content commitments for cobalt, tin, gold and rare earths. Those claims are company-prepared and not independently verified in this record, and the carbon-neutral-2030 commitment and its Scope 3 progress could not be verified from a published source in this run; that gap is stated, not filled. Governance offsets the conduct record: one class of common stock, an independent Chair separated from the CEO, an Audit Committee that owns privacy, cybersecurity, tax and enterprise risk, and related-party disclosure limited to one family-member employment. Control is not the issue; compliance culture is.

The tables below collect the exposure. They support a judgement that policy is a 100-300 basis point tax on Services gross margin plus a low-probability structural remedy in the United States, not a threat to the franchise: at Apple's scale, 100 basis points of Services gross margin is material annual gross profit, so the watchlist question is whether the multiple leaves room for that dilution. Three questions decide it: what fee Apple now charges on US link-out purchases after the December 2025 remand and how much spending has moved off in-app purchase; what Apple actually receives from Google at the first one-year renewal; and whether Article 6(4) produces a second EU fine before the General Court rules. None is a reason to avoid Apple; each is a reason to demand a price that assumes some of the loss.

arguments.markdown:
Apple's markets are contracting in units and expanding in value, and Apple is taking value share inside that contraction: the case for FY2026-FY2028 rests on premiumisation and Services attach rather than device volume, is strongest in the United States, is adequate in Europe, and in China depends on a domestic champion's pricing discipline.

### The pool is shrinking in units and growing in value

IDC's August 2026 forecast has worldwide smartphone shipments at just over 1.0 billion units in 2026, down 16.7% and the steepest annual contraction on record, while total market value rises 6.3% to $613 billion and the average selling price reaches a record $581, up 27.6% in a year and revised up from the $550 IDC published one quarter earlier. The cause is cost, not demand: DRAM and NAND prices are up more than 300% year on year as capacity is redirected to AI servers, memory is more than 65% of bill of materials at the low end, and the sub-$100 tier that shipped 173 million units in 2025 fell close to 60% in the second quarter of 2026. This is a supply shock with a dated end, so 2026-2027 flatters Apple's unit share while genuinely lifting its price, and 2028 is the test of whether either survives. [S39]

Two sizing methods agree closely: 1.0 billion units at the $581 average price gives $581 billion, within 5% of IDC's $613 billion, so the unit and price series can be read together rather than as rival estimates. On that base Apple's serviceable market is the premium tier it addresses — an iOS share of 23.6% of 2026 shipments, a record — while the revenue it can obtain is what it already books: $466.8 billion trailing twelve months to 2026-06-27, which at the 16.2% growth rate of the first nine months of FY2026 implies $483 billion for FY2026. IDC's PC-plus-tablet pool compounds at 1.5% a year from 2026 to 2030, so device pools are not growth markets at any price. [S6]

| Measure | Method | Figure | Year | Publisher | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| TAM, smartphone value (top-down) | Industry value estimate | $613bn, +6.3% | 2026 | IDC | S66 |
| TAM, smartphone value (bottom-up) | 1.0bn units x $581 ASP | ~$581bn | 2026 | Calculation on IDC inputs | S66 |
| TAM, personal computing devices | Units published, value not disclosed | ~398m units, -11.3%; 1.5% CAGR to 2030 | 2026 | IDC | S103 |
| SAM, premium smartphone tier | iOS share of shipments | 23.6% of units, record | 2026 | IDC | S66 |
| SOM, Apple revenue | Reported | $466.8bn TTM | TTM to 2026-06-27 | Apple 10-Q | S6 |
| Near-term obtainable revenue | FY2025 $416.2bn grown at the 9M FY2026 rate | ~$483bn | FY2026E | Calculation on Apple filings | S5, S13 |
| Adjacent services pool | Alphabet revenue | $471.1bn TTM | TTM to 2026-09-30 | Alphabet 10-Q | S42 |

### China is the swing factor, and India sits in the wrong line

Apple's revenue is moving toward the faster-growing regions, but the swing is China. In the first nine months of FY2026 Greater China produced $64.8 billion, up 30.0% on a base of $49.9 billion, after falling from $72.6 billion in FY2023 to $64.4 billion in FY2025; the Americas grew 11.4% to $149.4 billion, Europe 16.1% to $95.6 billion, Japan 10.4% and Rest of Asia Pacific 19.4%. Greater China's $14.9 billion increase contributes 4.1 percentage points of the group's 16.2% growth, more than any other segment, and part of it is currency: a favourable renminbi effect in Greater China, an unfavourable yen effect in Japan. One reporting artefact matters: the Europe segment includes India, the Middle East and Africa, so the fastest-growing large smartphone market is invisible in the line labelled Europe and India is not a segment an investor can track. [S13]

| Region | Market size (year) | Growth | Apple's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| United States / North America | 60% of Q1 2026 shipments above $800; US is 24.9% of global PC-plus-tablet units | Smartphone -6.3% in 2026; PC -14.6% in 2026 | Entered, leads the premium tier; 41.0% of Apple revenue is the Americas | Tariffs, carrier financing, antitrust suits | Samsung, Lenovo, HP, Dell | S39, S103, S13 |
| Greater China | ~66m units a quarter, 264m a year | -4.3% in Q2 2026, fifth straight decline; H2 2026 could be -20% | 18.1% of units, second behind Huawei; revenue +30.0% | Domestic operating system, subsidy withdrawal, data rules | Huawei 22.6%, OPPO 16.0%, vivo 16.0%, Xiaomi 12.4% | S40, S6 |
| Europe (segment includes India, Middle East, Africa) | India 31.0m units in Q1 2026 at a record $302 ASP | India units -4.1% but value +5.8%; Europe revenue +16.1% | Entered; fourth by units in India | DMA, price sensitivity, distribution | Samsung, Xiaomi, vivo, Lenovo, HP | S105, S103, S13 |
| Japan | Revenue $24.4bn in 9M FY2026 | Revenue +10.4%; units -25.6% in 2026 | Entered, premium strong; weak yen cuts revenue | Yen, saturated device base | Local Android vendors, Samsung | S13, S103, S6 |
| Rest of Asia Pacific | Revenue $30.2bn in 9M FY2026 | Revenue +19.4%; units -14% in 2026 | Entered, premium-led | Price-sensitive mass market, currency | Samsung, Xiaomi, OPPO, vivo | S13, S39, S103 |

### Services carries the margin and has no published pool size

The fastest-growing pool Apple actually monetises is Services: $109.2 billion, 26.2% of FY2025 revenue, at a 75.4% gross margin against 36.8% for products, growing 14.1% to $91.7 billion in the first nine months of FY2026. The adjacent pools are larger and largely not Apple's — Alphabet's trailing-twelve-month revenue is $471.1 billion — but the app economy itself has no published size in the sources retrieved: neither Apple nor the platform owners disclose app-store gross billings or mobile-advertising revenue in a sizeable form, so Apple's own Services line is the measured pool. The installed base behind it has the same gap: Apple states only that its active-device base reached an all-time high in the June 2026 quarter across every category and region, and publishes no device count in its FY2025 10-K or FY2026 results, so the figure of 2.3 billion devices often quoted alongside the business is unverified here and should carry none of the valuation. [S5]

### Who pays, and how much demand is policy

The budget owner is the consumer, in a discretionary purchase that is increasingly financed. In the United States and United Kingdom long-term interest-free financing is more prevalent, so IDC expects the premium end to hold while emerging markets fall more than 20%; in India brands lean on financing after the sub-$100 tier fell 59% and the $600-800 band grew 32%; in China the government subsidy that supported earlier quarters faded in the second quarter of 2026, so demand there is being withdrawn by policy rather than created by it. Apple's exposure to policy runs both ways: after the February 20, 2026 Supreme Court ruling struck down certain IEEPA tariffs, Apple recognised refunds as a reduction of product cost of sales, and those refunds contributed 2.0 percentage points of the June 2026 quarter's 50.1% gross margin — tariff policy moves Apple's margin by more than a product cycle does. [S105, S40, S13]

The counter-evidence is threefold, each strand dated. If memory prices normalise in 2028 as IDC expects, the entry tier rebuilds and Apple's 2026 share gain is contestable again. If China's June-quarter demand was pulled forward ahead of expected second-half price increases, as IDC's China team reports, the 30% growth line is a launch and currency effect. And if courts and the European Commission remove the App Store take rate, the 75%-margin layer that offsets hardware cyclicality stops compounding at its present rate. The investor implication is narrow: in a 1-billion-unit market Apple can grow revenue only if price rises faster than units fall, making average selling price, China durability and the Services take rate the variables worth monitoring. Sizing confidence is high, because two independent methods agree within 5%; confidence that the mix shift holds to 2028 is medium, because it rests on China and a legally contested commission. Three questions would close the gap: what share of Services revenue is commission-based rather than subscription, advertising or licensing; how much of the Greater China increase is currency; and what the current average replacement cycle is, measured rather than asserted. [S66, S40]

::: evidence
**Apple's addressable device market fell 16.7% in units in 2026 while growing 6.3% in value, and Apple's revenue grew 16.2% over nine months — the gap is premiumisation and China, not market growth (S66, S13).**

IDC forecasts 2026 shipments at just over 1.0 billion units against a market value of $613 billion and an ASP of $581 (S66, S39). Apple's nine-month FY2026 revenue was $364.4 billion, up 16.2%, with Greater China up 30.0% on a $49.9 billion base (S13, S6). The bottom-up check of 1.0 billion units at $581 gives $581 billion, within 5% of IDC's value estimate (S66).
:::

arguments.markdown:
Apple runs a hardware annuity with a services margin layered on top — 73 cents of services gross profit for every dollar of product gross profit — but the mix shift the multiple pays for stalled in fiscal 2026, when hardware margins, helped by tariff refunds, grew gross profit faster than Services. Apple sells through two routes, and the split is the least-discussed fact in the model: in fiscal 2025, 40% of net sales went through its own stores, online store and direct sales force and 60% through carriers, resellers and distributors. The carrier finances or subsidises the handset to win a contract, so the carrier bears the acquisition cost and Apple's selling expense stays at $27,601M, or 6.6% of revenue. There is little contracted backlog: deferred revenue was $13.7bn at 2025-09-27, 3.3% of revenue, two thirds of it recognised within a year. Apple is a repeat-purchase business recognised as it bills, not a subscription business with a book of contracted revenue [S5].

### The mix shift, and its reversal

The arithmetic of the mix shift is the strongest part of the case. In fiscal 2025 Services produced $109,158M of revenue at a 75.4% gross margin against $307,003M of Products at 36.8%: 26.2% of revenue but 42.2% of gross profit ($82,314M of $195,201M), up from 35.7% two years earlier, with services gross profit per dollar of product gross profit rising from $0.55 in fiscal 2023 to $0.73. Then the mechanism ran backwards. In the nine months to 2026-06-27 product gross profit rose 26.3% to $108,819M while services gross profit rose 15.3% to $69,963M, and Services fell to 39.1% of gross profit; product gross margin reached 39.9% against 36.9% a year earlier, taking total gross margin to 49.1% and to 50.1% in the June quarter against 46.5%. Apple attributes the gain to "a different mix of products and tariff refunds, partially offset by higher costs, including memory", the most consequential disclosure in this section: it makes fiscal 2026's margin hardware-led and partly a refund rather than a trading gain [S5, S6].

### Unit economics per revenue dollar, because there are no units

Apple discloses no unit volumes, average selling price or installed-base figure, so a per-device waterfall cannot be built from primary evidence. The economics of each revenue dollar can be.

| Unit-economics line | FY2025 | 9M FY2026 | Evidence and status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Product cost of sales, per $1,000 of product revenue | $632 | $601 | Bill of materials, assembly and warranty provision combined, not split | S5, S6 |
| Product gross profit | $368 | $399 | 36.8% to 39.9%; includes tariff refunds in fiscal 2026 | S5, S6 |
| Services cost of sales, per $1,000 of services revenue | $246 | $237 | Content, hosting and payment processing | S5, S6 |
| Services gross profit | $754 | $763 | 75.4% to 76.3% | S5, S6 |
| Services gross profit per $1 of product gross profit | $0.73 | $0.64 | Closest disclosed proxy for lifetime value against acquisition cost | S5, S6 |
| Customer acquisition cost, support and warranty | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Carriers bear acquisition; warranty sits inside cost of sales | S5 |
| LTV, LTV:CAC, CAC payback in months | Not computable | Not computable | Requires units, ASP and installed base, none of which Apple reports | S5 |

Apple therefore has no payback period to wait out: a device is gross-profit-positive on delivery at a 36.8% product margin, and the services stream that follows is nearly all incremental, since services cost of sales is $26,844M on $109,158M of revenue. The nearest disclosed proxy for lifetime value against acquisition cost is the $0.73 of services gross profit per dollar of product gross profit, and its fall to $0.64 is the number to watch — the annuity still grows, but no longer faster than the hardware that creates it [S5, S6].

### Pricing power shows up as mix, not as price

| Line | FY2025 net sales | Year on year | What the filing discloses about price and mix | Gross margin | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone | $209,586M | +4% | Growth "due to higher net sales of Pro models", i.e. mix rather than units | 36.8% products blended | S5 |
| Services | $109,158M | +14% | "advertising, the App Store and cloud services" | 75.4% | S5 |
| Mac | $33,708M | +12% | "laptops and desktops" | 36.8% products blended | S5 |
| iPad and Wearables | $63,709M | 0% | iPad Air and mini higher, Accessories and Wearables lower | 36.8% products blended | S5 |

Pricing power shows up as mix: iPhone revenue rose 22% to $196,515M in the nine months to 2026-06-27, attributed again to higher sales of Pro models rather than to units. The same disclosure prevents separating price from volume, and therefore prevents estimating elasticity — a 22% increase could be volume, price, or any combination. Apple publishes list prices on its own store but not in its filings, and this report did not retrieve a verified 2026 price list, so the table uses disclosed mix effects rather than price points; third-party unit data would settle it [S6].

### The highest-margin layer is also the most litigated

App Store economics are recognised net — Apple books "only the commission it retains" on third-party app sales — so a take-rate cut passes straight to revenue and gross profit with no offsetting cost. Apple is subject to a US court order barring it from charging a commission on certain consumer purchases, though the Ninth Circuit has instructed the district court to amend the injunction to permit one, and in the EU the Digital Markets Act forces alternative distribution, alternative payment processing and new fee structures, a plan the European Commission has challenged. A second concentration sits in the same line: Apple earns licensing revenue from Google for search distribution inside Services advertising, which Apple names as a primary driver of Services growth in both fiscal 2025 and the first nine months of fiscal 2026. The payment was $20bn in 2022 per unsealed court documents, 18.3% of fiscal 2025 Services revenue, and Apple does not disclose the current figure; the District of Columbia court order of 2025-09-02 preserved the ability to pay partners while banning exclusive agreements, but Apple states a reversal on appeal could impose remedies "prohibiting Google from offering the Company commercial terms for search distribution", and both the Department of Justice and Google appealed [S6, S82].

### Cost structure, and what would break the durability

The cost base is bought, not built: product cost of sales of $194,116M goes to TSMC for wafers, to memory suppliers for DRAM and NAND, and to Foxconn and its peers for assembly. Research and development reached $34,035M in the nine months to 2026-06-27, up 33% and 9.3% of revenue against 8.3% in fiscal 2025, on "infrastructure-related costs, including investments in artificial intelligence"; capital expenditure is 2.2% of trailing-twelve-month revenue against 34.9% at Microsoft in fiscal 2026. Apple rents its manufacturing and buys much of its AI capability through the income statement, so that bill reaches the operating margin immediately rather than through depreciation. For investors the implication is that the annuity is intact, but the margin expansion of the last four quarters is not the mix shift it is commonly described as: it is product mix, a tariff refund and memory cost timing, on top of a services base whose most profitable components face an appeal, a court order and a European regulatory process. Three facts would settle the durability question and none is disclosed — the current size of the search payment, the share of Services that is App Store commission, and the refund-versus-mix split; the fiscal 2026 annual report, not on EDGAR as of 2026-10-31, may settle them [S6, S27].

::: evidence
**The service mix still drives Apple's margin, but in fiscal 2026 it stopped being the marginal driver — hardware did, and part of that gain is a refund.**

In the nine months to June 2026 product gross profit grew faster than services gross profit for the first time in three years, and Apple attributes the higher product margin to product mix and tariff refunds rather than to trading gains, in the June 2026 quarterly report.
:::

arguments.markdown:
Apple's policy exposure is not a licence-to-operate threat but a slow, legislated tax on Services gross profit: the €500 million DMA fine of 2025-04-23 and the April 2025 US contempt finding show a company that litigates first and complies later, while the three remedies that matter — Google's default-search payment, the US link-out commission and the EU fee structure — have so far been reshaped rather than removed [S7]. The question for a long-only holder is how much Services gross margin the next five years of enforcement takes, and whether the multiple already discounts it.

### The DMA fine is small; the cost structure is not

The Commission fined Apple €500 million on 2025-04-23 for breaching the anti-steering obligation and ordered it to remove restrictions on steering users outside the App Store. The same day it closed the user-choice investigation — a real concession — but issued preliminary findings in the Article 6(4) file on Apple's terms for alternative app marketplaces, where an adverse finding carries fines of up to 10% of annual worldwide net sales and further penalties for breaching a cease-and-desist order [S5]. The record bounds the risk on both sides: on 2026-02-05 the Commission found Apple Ads and Apple Maps should not be designated, and no further Apple decision appears in its DMA record between the fine and 2026-09-28. Peer severity is modest — Meta paid €200 million in the same package, Google €890 million on 2026-07-23, Alphabet's Android fine of €4.1 billion only reached a final ECJ ruling in July 2026 — so repeated fines, not break-up, are the base rate.

The material part is the fee, not the penalty. Europe booked $111.0 billion of net sales in FY2025, up 10%, led by Services, and App Store commission is the highest-margin revenue Apple records, so a mandated fee cut in Brussels is worth more to the equity than any fine. Apple also warns that interoperability obligations force it to open technologies to third parties without charge and have in the past, and may in future, caused it not to launch or maintain features "such as Siri AI" in some jurisdictions — a product-availability risk, not only a revenue leak.

### A contempt finding, then a slow antitrust case

On 2025-04-30 the Northern District of California found Apple in violation of the 2021 Epic injunction, barred any commission on purchases made outside an app, and referred the company to the US Attorney on criminal contempt. The Ninth Circuit modified that on 2025-12-11 to allow parity rules and some commission on link-out purchases; Apple petitioned the Supreme Court on 2026-05-21, obtained certiorari on 2026-06-30 limited to the civil-contempt standard, and seeks a stay below [S6, S122]. Read narrowly this is a pricing dispute; read properly it is evidence that Apple's compliance function tested a court order rather than obeyed it, which raises the severity of the next remedy. That remedy is the DOJ case, filed 2024-03-21 with 16 states and the District of Columbia, seeking equitable relief only; it survived dismissal on 2025-06-30 and is in discovery on a schedule pointing to a 2027 trial. With no damages claimed, the risk is conduct-based — defaults, messaging, app distribution — and lands on the 2027-2029 Services line rather than the balance sheet.

### Google's payment survives, on worse terms

The search-distribution remedy is the largest dollar item, and the 2025-09-02 decision went Apple's way on the point that mattered: the court refused to ban Google's payments to distributors, citing harm to device makers and browser developers, and instead barred exclusive contracts while permitting default-placement payments not conditioned on exclusivity and running one year or less [S118, S42]. A final judgment followed in December 2025; Google appealed in January 2026 and the Department of Justice cross-appealed in February 2026, both pending at 2026-10-29. Apple does not disclose the payment, so the $20 billion-a-year figure in circulation is unverified in its filings. The revenue survives with annual renewal risk and mandatory choice screens.

### Two bear-case triggers did not fire in 2026

The Section 232 semiconductor investigation's initial results on 2026-01-14 imposed no additional tariff on Apple's products, and on 2026-02-20 the Supreme Court struck down certain IEEPA tariffs, with Apple claiming refunds it recognised as a reduction of products cost of sales; Section 301 tariffs were then imposed and further Section 232 action remains open. In China the opposite of closure happened: the CAC registered Apple Intelligence on 2026-07-15 with Alibaba's Qwen and Baidu, and Greater China net sales rose 22% to $18,816 million in the June 2026 quarter and 30% to $64,839 million for the nine months, from $49,884 million [S6, S121]. The binding constraint is the calendar: the Busan truce that suppresses tariff and rare-earth escalation was extended on 2026-09-23 from 2026-11-10 to 2027-01-10, making 2027 the next policy cliff.

### Tax is settled; the ESG tail is elsewhere

The Irish state-aid case ended against Apple: the ECJ confirmed the 2016 decision on 2024-09-10, producing a $10.2 billion net one-time charge and $15.8 billion payable to Ireland. The FY2025 effective tax rate of 15.6%, against 24.1% in FY2024, now sits just above the OECD Pillar Two 15% floor, so incremental Pillar Two cost is small and the live tax risk is the $23.2 billion of gross unrecognised benefits, $10.6 billion of which would move the rate if recognised [S5]. Tax is a settled cost, not a source of future earnings upside.

On environmental and social issues the record is stronger than the sector's: full third-party audit coverage of identified 3TG smelters for a tenth consecutive year, no finding of armed-group financing, a June 2024 instruction to suppliers to stop sourcing 3TG from the DRC and Rwanda, and recycled-content commitments for cobalt, tin, gold and rare earths. Those claims are company-prepared and not independently verified, and the carbon-neutral-2030 commitment and its Scope 3 progress could not be verified from a published source in this run; that gap is stated, not filled. Governance offsets the conduct record: one class of common stock, an independent Chair separated from the CEO, an Audit Committee that owns privacy, cybersecurity, tax and enterprise risk, and related-party disclosure limited to one family-member employment. Control is not the issue; compliance culture is.

The tables below collect the exposure. They support a judgement that policy is a 100-300 basis point tax on Services gross margin plus a low-probability structural remedy in the United States, not a threat to the franchise. Three questions decide the watchlist price: what fee Apple now charges on US link-out purchases after the December 2025 remand and how much spending has moved off in-app purchase; what Apple actually receives from Google at the first one-year renewal; and whether Article 6(4) produces a second EU fine before the General Court rules. None is a reason to avoid Apple; each is a reason to demand a price that assumes some of the loss.

arguments.markdown:
Apple's route to FY2028 growth is services mix, a richer iPhone cycle and India, with artificial intelligence as a retention feature and a possible iCloud+ upsell rather than a revenue line of its own; the plan is credible on cash generation and per-share compounding, but not yet on AI monetisation or on creating a new product category. The base is large and still growing: revenue reached $416.2bn in FY2025, and the nine months to 2026-06-27 produced $364.4bn, up 16%, with Services at $91.7bn, up 14% [S77, S6].

### Services carry the margin, and they are the part regulators can reach

Services were 26% of FY2025 revenue but 39% of gross profit in the nine months to June 2026, because they earn a 76.3% gross margin against 39.9% for products. Growth in that period came from advertising and cloud services, not from a new subscription. Mechanically, every services dollar adds about 76 cents of gross profit, so mix alone lifts group gross margin — 49.1% versus 46.8% a year earlier — even while memory and 2nm wafer costs squeeze hardware. That is the engine that funds the buyback and the silicon. It is also the engine the regulators are targeting: the European Commission fined Apple €500m on 2025-04-23 for anti-steering non-compliance, and the General Court dismissed Apple's challenge to its gatekeeper designation on 2026-07-08 [S85, S84, S6]. An investor should value the services annuity on gross profit that compounds in the low-to-mid teens, and apply a discount for the probability that a remedy compresses commission or default-search income rather than a one-off fine.

### AI is funded as cost and monetised, if at all, through storage

Apple introduced Siri AI with the iOS 27 cycle announced in the third quarter of FY2026, and R&D rose 33% to $34.0bn in the nine months to June 2026, driven by infrastructure including AI investments and headcount. No AI revenue line exists. The reported plan — that high-frequency, compute-intensive Siri use will be gated behind iCloud+ — is plausible because it reuses a price ladder already in place, but Apple has published no tier and no price, so it is unverified [S13, S6, S107]. The mechanism matters more than the price: AI raises the cost of serving every device while its clearest commercial effect is to protect upgrade rates and services attach. If Apple charges, the increment is bounded by storage-subscription willingness to pay, not by the value of the model; if it does not, AI is a permanent tax on gross margin. Either way, 2027 is the test of whether AI spend converts into units or ARPU.

### India lowers tariff risk, not unit cost

iPhone production in India rose 53% in 2025 to ~55 million units, ~25% of global output, and is projected at 28% in 2026; Tata Electronics overtook Foxconn in iPhone export assembly over the FY2022-FY2026 incentive period [S89, S91]. The strategy is rational given the tariff record in the filings: Section 232 semiconductor investigation results in January 2026, the Supreme Court striking down certain IEEPA tariffs in February 2026, and new Section 301 tariffs, with manufacturing purchase obligations of $57.0bn at 2026-06-27 [S6]. The limit is that assembly captures little of the value: components, displays and silicon still come from East Asia, so India is an insurance policy on tariffs and single-country concentration, not a margin lever. The signpost to watch is the share of US-bound iPhones assembled in India, which Apple has never disclosed.

### Capital allocation is disciplined and has become slightly bolder

R&D rose from $29.9bn in FY2023 to $34.6bn in FY2025 and is running at ~$45bn annualised in FY2026. Buybacks remain the primary use of cash: $25.8bn of stock was repurchased in the quarter to 2026-06-27 alone, alongside $4.0bn of dividends at $0.27 per share, which cut the share count to 14.61bn from 14.77bn at FY2025 year-end and helped EPS grow 29% against 27% net-income growth [S77, S6, S13]. M&A posture has shifted from tuck-ins: Apple confirmed the acquisition of the AI-audio start-up Q.ai on 2026-01-29, reported by the Financial Times at close to $2bn, and acquired the AI data-engineering company Ascend.io, notified to the European Commission on 2026-06-30; intangible assets rose from $11.1bn to $20.3bn between 2025-09-27 and 2026-06-27 [S88, S6]. Against ~$146bn of cash and marketable securities, that is affordable experimentation rather than a change of strategy — and it is the right test of whether Apple's AI gap can be bought in pieces.
