arguments.markdown:
Apple's competitive position strengthened in 2026 in every hardware line except smartwatches, but the gain is crisis-specific — bought with memory supply and price discipline rather than product superiority — and it is being offset where profit is made, because the App Store commission that funds the premium position is being dismantled by courts and regulators rather than by a rival's product. Apple leads no hardware category outright except detachable tablets, and its own annual report concedes a minority share in smartphones, personal computers, tablets and wearables. [S102]

### The lead is in integration, not in units

Apple's 20.2% of global smartphone shipments in Q2 2026 was a record for that quarter and a 3.9 percentage point gain, but Samsung's 22.7% was larger and Xiaomi's 26.4% collapse explains much of the redistribution. In personal computing devices Apple is second at 18.2% behind Lenovo's 20.1%, yet macOS shipments grew 17.4% while Windows fell 6.7% and Android 19.6%, and macOS is the only major operating system IDC expects to grow in 2026. The clearest structural lead is detachable tablets at 55.3%; the weakest spot is smartwatches, where Huawei leads 18.8% to 17.2%, so Apple's 15.5% of all wearables rests on earwear, where it holds 17.2%. [S104]

| Product | Apple share | Leader and challengers | Technology basis | Price position | Switching cost | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone, global units | 20.2% in Q2 2026, +3.9pp | Samsung 22.7% (+3.2pp); Xiaomi 11.3%, OPPO 10.5%, vivo 7.7% | iOS integration and secured memory supply | Premium; industry ASP $581, Apple above it | High: iCloud, iMessage, purchased apps | S102, S66 |
| iPhone, China units | 18.1%, +4.2pp | Huawei 22.6% (+4.5pp); OPPO 16.0%, vivo 16.0%, Xiaomi 12.4% | iOS against domestic HarmonyOS | Apple held prices while Android raised them | Medium: leaving iOS loses Apple services | S40 |
| PCs and tablets | 18.2%, -0.4% | Lenovo 20.1%; HP 12.7%, Dell 9.1%, Samsung 6.2% | macOS against Windows | MacBook Neo attacks entry pricing | Medium | S103, S106 |
| Services and App Store | $109.2bn in FY2025 at 75.4% gross margin | Alphabet $471.1bn TTM revenue; Netflix $49.7bn TTM | iOS distribution against Google Play | 15-30% commission, under challenge | High for consumers, falling for developers | S5, S42, S80 |

### Samsung is the dangerous one, and the reason is memory

Samsung is the most dangerous competitor, and not because of the Galaxy S26 Ultra. When memory is more than 65% of bill of materials at the low end, the binding constraint is supply access, and Samsung is the only top-five handset vendor that also sells memory: it grew shipments 8.1% and took 3.2 points of share in Q2 2026 while Xiaomi fell 26.4% and vivo 19.6%. Apple's answer was to secure memory early, which is why its units fell only 1.3% in 2026 against Android's 24.3% and why IDC puts iOS at a record 23.6% of shipments — a sourcing feat rather than a structural advantage, and it lapses when memory normalises while Samsung keeps its cost position. Samsung also holds the foldable franchise Apple attacks: IDC expects more than 17 million foldable iPhones by 2027 at an average price above $2,550, about 40% of a category growing 12.6% to 22.9 million units this year and more than half its $45.7 billion of value. [S66]

### In China the competitor and the rules are different

Huawei held 22.6% of a Chinese market that fell 4.3% in Q2 2026 and grew 19.9% by holding prices while Android rivals raised theirs, leaning on HarmonyOS, which IDC expects to reach 51 million units in 2026; Apple grew 24.4% and gained 4.2 points to 18.1%, so both premium ends expanded while OPPO, vivo and Xiaomi contracted. The mechanism is a domestic operating system plus price discipline, and neither is a feature Apple can copy. HarmonyOS draws on the same national preference that makes Apple's China revenue politically exposed, so the 30% China revenue growth belongs behind a competition risk: the revenue line can grow while the strategic position narrows. [S40]

### The profit pool is being taken by courts, not by rivals

Apple's FY2025 annual report discloses that it is subject to a U.S. court order preventing it from imposing any commission on certain purchases consumers make, that its compliance plan under the Digital Markets Act has been challenged by the European Commission, and that it faces U.S. monopolization suits over smartphones; separately, the September 2, 2025 remedies order against Google, if upheld on appeal, could remove the search-distribution payments that sit inside Services. No competitor needs to win a device sale for the 75.4% services gross margin to compress: a developer that routes a subscriber to the web converts a 15-30% commission into a payment-processing fee, and Services growth of 14.1% then arrives at a lower margin. The asymmetry is stark: the hardware position improved while the pricing power that monetises it was reduced by a court in the United States and a regulator in Europe. [S5]

### AI and the phone already in the buyer's pocket

Where Apple is not ahead is AI: the all-new Siri AI arrived at WWDC26 in June 2026, while Samsung's AI-equipped Galaxy S26 Ultra is credited by IDC with returning Samsung to first place in the first quarter of 2026, and research and development rose 32.5% to $34.0 billion in the first nine months of FY2026 — the cost of catching up, not the reward for leading. Unit position and profit per unit are moving in opposite directions, so the question worth paying for is not who sells more phones but what share of the transaction Apple still controls in 2027. Confidence is high in the shares and the legal facts and medium beyond 2028, when memory normalises and the crisis-specific advantage lapses. arguments.markdown:
Apple's route to FY2028 growth is services mix, a richer iPhone cycle and India, with artificial intelligence as a retention feature and a possible iCloud+ upsell rather than a revenue line of its own; the plan is credible on cash generation and per-share compounding, but not yet on AI monetisation or on creating a new product category. The base is large and still growing: revenue reached $416.2bn in FY2025, and the nine months to 2026-06-27 produced $364.4bn, up 16%, with Services at $91.7bn, up 14% [S77, S6].

### Services carry the margin, but the mix engine stalled in FY2026

Services were 26% of FY2025 revenue but 39% of gross profit in the nine months to June 2026, because they earn a 76.3% gross margin against 39.9% for products. The mix engine, however, stopped being the marginal driver: product gross profit grew 26% against 15% for services, so the rise in total gross margin to 49.1% from 46.8% came from hardware mix and tariff refunds, not from services, while memory costs kept rising. Services growth itself came from advertising and cloud services, with the Google search-distribution payment named as a primary driver. That is the engine that funds the buyback and the silicon, and it is also the engine regulators are targeting: the European Commission fined Apple €500m on 2025-04-23 for anti-steering non-compliance, and the General Court dismissed Apple's challenge to its gatekeeper designation on 2026-07-08 [S85, S84, S6]. An investor should value the services annuity on gross profit that compounds in the low-to-mid teens, and apply a discount for the probability that a remedy compresses commission or search income rather than a one-off fine.

### AI is funded as cost and monetised, if at all, through storage

Apple introduced Siri AI with the iOS 27 cycle announced in the third quarter of FY2026, and R&D rose 33% to $34.0bn in the nine months to June 2026, driven by infrastructure including AI investments and headcount. No AI revenue line exists. The reported plan — that high-frequency, compute-intensive Siri use will be gated behind iCloud+ — is plausible because it reuses a price ladder already in place, but Apple has published no tier and no price, so it is unverified [S13, S6, S107]. The mechanism matters more than the price: AI raises the cost of serving every device while its clearest commercial effect is to protect upgrade rates and services attach. If Apple charges, the increment is bounded by storage-subscription willingness to pay, not by the value of the model; if it does not, AI is a permanent tax on gross margin. Either way, 2027 is the test of whether AI spend converts into units or ARPU.

### India lowers tariff risk, not unit cost

iPhone production in India rose 53% in 2025 to ~55 million units, ~25% of global output, and is projected at 28% in 2026; Tata Electronics overtook Foxconn in iPhone export assembly over the FY2022-FY2026 incentive period. The strategy is rational given the tariff record in the filings — Section 232 semiconductor investigation results in January 2026, the Supreme Court striking down certain IEEPA tariffs in February 2026, and new Section 301 tariffs, with manufacturing purchase obligations of $57.0bn at 2026-06-27 [S89, S91, S6]. The limit is that assembly captures little of the value: components, displays and silicon still come from East Asia, so India is an insurance policy on tariffs and single-country concentration, not a margin lever. The signpost to watch is the share of US-bound iPhones assembled in India, which Apple has never disclosed.

### Capital allocation is disciplined and slightly bolder

R&D rose from $29.9bn in FY2023 to $34.6bn in FY2025 and is running at ~$45bn annualised in FY2026. Buybacks remain the primary use of cash: $25.8bn of stock was repurchased in the quarter to 2026-06-27 alone, alongside $4.0bn of dividends at $0.27 per share, which cut the share count to 14.61bn from 14.77bn at FY2025 year-end and helped EPS grow 29% against 27% net-income growth. M&A posture has shifted from tuck-ins: Apple confirmed the acquisition of the AI-audio start-up Q.ai on 2026-01-29, reported by the Financial Times at close to $2bn, and acquired the AI data-engineering company Ascend.io, notified to the European Commission on 2026-06-30; intangible assets rose from $11.1bn to $20.3bn between 2025-09-27 and 2026-06-27 [S77, S88, S6, S13]. Against ~$146bn of cash and marketable securities, that is affordable experimentation rather than a change of strategy — and it is the right test of whether Apple's AI gap can be bought in pieces.

|---|---|---|---|---|
| FY2026 results and 10-K | by 2026-11 | Pending | Whether 16% growth holds into the holiday quarter | S77, S6 |
| Siri AI full release (iOS 27) | 2026-09 | Launched at WWDC26 | Gemini-based assistant ships on schedule | S13, S86 |
| iPhone Duo ramp | 2026-10-23 on sale | Launched | Apple can create a $1,999 tier | S59 |
| AI subscription (iCloud+ gating) | Not announced | Reported only | AI becomes revenue rather than cost | S107 |
| Lower-cost Vision Pro | Late 2026 | Unconfirmed by Apple | Spatial computing can reach volume | S87 |
| DOJ settlement | 2026 talks | Unresolved | Size of the App Store remedy | S90 |
| India assembly share | FY2026 | ~28% projected | Tariff hedge is real | S91 |

| Partner | Scope | Signed | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Google | Next-generation Apple Foundation Models based on Gemini, multi-year, non-exclusive | 2026-01-12 | Active | S58 |
| Qualcomm | 5G modems, including the iPhone 18 Pro Max | Ongoing | Narrowing | S59 |
| TSMC | N3P and N2 wafer manufacturing | Ongoing | Active; wafer prices rising | S64 |
| Tata Electronics | India iPhone assembly and exports | Ongoing | Scaling; overtook Foxconn on exports | S91 |
| Foxconn | China and India assembly | Ongoing | Active | S89 |

### What must be true in twelve months, and the case against

Four things must happen for the strategy to be credible. First, the FY2026 holiday quarter has to show that the iPhone 18 and Duo cycle sustains double-digit growth without tariff refunds, which flattered the June quarter by ~2 percentage points of gross margin. Second, Apple must put a price on AI or show that it lifts upgrade rates, because a 33% R&D increase with no revenue attached is a margin problem. Third, a DOJ settlement or DMA remedy must leave the App Store commission and default-search payment substantially intact; both cases attack the services profit pool directly. Fourth, India must reach the projected share of output without a quality or logistics incident. The counter-case is strong and largely Apple's own record: AI features arrived well after they were demonstrated, Siri needed a Google licence, the car programme was cancelled, and Vision Pro shipped ~45,000 units in the December 2025 quarter, while Alphabet, Microsoft and Huawei set a faster cadence in models, cloud AI and, for Huawei, folding hardware and domestic silicon. Apple's answer is that it does not need to be first — it needs to be best integrated, and it monetises the installed base rather than the model. That is a defensible strategy for a cash-flow investor and a weak one for anyone buying AI optionality [S59, S87, S84, S90, S89].

::: evidence
**The strategy is credible as a cash-compounding plan and unproven as a growth plan.**

Services earn a structurally higher gross margin than hardware, and buybacks are large enough that earnings per share can compound faster than net income even with flat hardware; but AI is a large R&D increase with no disclosed price, Vision Pro has not become a platform, and the two antitrust cases target precisely the services lines that fund the plan.
:::

arguments.markdown:
Apple's policy exposure is not a licence-to-operate threat but a slow, legislated tax on Services gross profit: the €500 million DMA fine of 2025-04-23 and the April 2025 US contempt finding show a company that litigates first and complies later, while the three remedies that matter — Google's default-search payment, the US link-out commission and the EU fee structure — have so far been reshaped rather than removed [S7]. The question for a long-only holder is how much Services gross margin five more years of enforcement takes, and whether the multiple already discounts it.

### The DMA fine is small; the cost structure is not

The Commission fined Apple €500 million on 2025-04-23 for breaching the anti-steering obligation and ordered it to remove restrictions on steering users outside the App Store. The same day it closed the user-choice investigation — a real concession — but issued preliminary findings in the Article 6(4) file on Apple's terms for alternative app marketplaces, where an adverse finding carries fines of up to 10% of annual worldwide net sales [S5]. Two facts bound the risk: on 2026-02-05 the Commission found Apple Ads and Apple Maps should not be designated, and no further Apple decision appears in its DMA record between the fine and 2026-09-28. Peer fines are serial but modest — Meta €200 million in the same package, Google €890 million on 2026-07-23, Alphabet's €4.1 billion Android fine final only in July 2026 — so repeated fines, not break-up, are the base rate. The mechanism that matters is a transfer of pricing power from Apple's toll to developers and consumers: each mandated fee cut reaches Services gross margin before it reaches revenue.

The material part is the fee, not the penalty. Europe is Apple's second-largest reporting region and Services drove its FY2025 growth; App Store commission is the highest-margin revenue Apple records, so a mandated fee cut in Brussels is worth more to the equity than any fine. Apple also warns that interoperability obligations force it to open technologies to third parties without charge and have in the past, and may in future, caused it not to launch or maintain features "such as Siri AI" — a product-availability risk, not only a revenue leak.

### A contempt finding, then a slow antitrust case

On 2025-04-30 the Northern District of California found Apple in violation of the 2021 Epic injunction, barred any commission on purchases made outside an app, and referred the company to the US Attorney on criminal contempt. The Ninth Circuit modified that on 2025-12-11 to allow parity rules and some commission on link-out purchases; Apple petitioned the Supreme Court on 2026-05-21, obtained certiorari on 2026-06-30 limited to the civil-contempt standard, and seeks a stay below [S6, S122]. Apple's compliance function tested a court order rather than obeyed it, which raises the severity of the next remedy. That remedy is the DOJ case, filed 2024-03-21 with 16 states and the District of Columbia, seeking equitable relief only; it survived dismissal on 2025-06-30 and is in discovery on a schedule pointing to a 2027 trial. With no damages claimed, the risk is conduct-based — defaults, messaging, app distribution — and lands on the 2027-2029 Services line rather than the balance sheet.

### Google's payment survives, on worse terms

The search-distribution remedy went Apple's way on the point that mattered: the 2025-09-02 decision refused to ban Google's payments to distributors, citing harm to device makers and browser developers, and instead barred exclusive contracts while permitting default-placement payments not conditioned on exclusivity and running one year or less [S118, S42]. A final judgment followed in December 2025; both sides appealed in early 2026 and the appeals were pending at 2026-10-29. Apple does not disclose the payment; the $20 billion-a-year figure is unverified. The revenue survives with annual renewal risk and mandatory choice screens.

### Two bear-case triggers did not fire in 2026

The Section 232 semiconductor investigation's initial results on 2026-01-14 imposed no additional tariff on Apple's products, and on 2026-02-20 the Supreme Court struck down certain IEEPA tariffs, with Apple claiming refunds it recognised as a reduction of products cost of sales; Section 301 tariffs were then imposed. In China the opposite of closure happened: the CAC registered Apple Intelligence on 2026-07-15 with Alibaba's Qwen and Baidu, and Greater China net sales rose 22% to $18,816 million in the June 2026 quarter and 30% to $64,839 million for the nine months, from $49,884 million [S6, S121]. The binding constraint is the calendar: the Busan truce that suppresses tariff and rare-earth escalation was extended on 2026-09-23 from 2026-11-10 to 2027-01-10, making 2027 the next policy cliff.

### Tax is settled; the ESG tail is elsewhere

The Irish state-aid case ended against Apple: the ECJ confirmed the 2016 decision on 2024-09-10, producing a $10.2 billion net one-time charge and $15.8 billion payable to Ireland. The FY2025 effective tax rate of 15.6%, against 24.1% in FY2024, now sits just above the OECD Pillar Two 15% floor, so incremental Pillar Two cost is small and the live tax risk is the $23.2 billion of gross unrecognised benefits, $10.6 billion of which would move the rate if recognised [S5].

On environmental and social issues the record is stronger than the sector's: full third-party audit coverage of identified 3TG smelters for a tenth consecutive year, no finding of armed-group financing, a June 2024 instruction to suppliers to stop sourcing 3TG from the DRC and Rwanda, and recycled-content commitments for cobalt, tin, gold and rare earths. Those claims are company-prepared and unverified here, and the carbon-neutral-2030 target and its Scope 3 progress could not be checked against a published source; that gap is stated, not filled. Governance offsets the conduct record: one class of common stock, an independent Chair separated from the CEO, and an Audit Committee that owns privacy, cybersecurity, tax and enterprise risk. Control is not the issue; compliance culture is.

They support a judgement that policy is a recurring cost to Services gross margin, not a threat to the franchise. Three questions decide the watchlist price: what fee Apple now charges on US link-out purchases after the December 2025 remand and how much spending has moved off in-app purchase; what Apple actually receives from Google at the first one-year renewal; and whether Article 6(4) produces a second EU fine before the General Court rules. None is a reason to avoid Apple; each is a reason to demand a price that assumes some of the loss.

arguments.markdown:
Apple's cash conversion and balance sheet are as good as the multiple implies, but the earnings growth is not: fiscal 2025's 22.7% EPS growth becomes roughly 10% once the $10.2bn Irish State Aid tax charge in the prior year is normalised out, and fiscal 2026's margin is being flattered by a tariff refund Apple does not quantify.

The three-year record is one of slowing revenue and rising margin: revenue fell 2.8% in fiscal 2023, grew 2.0% in fiscal 2024 and 6.4% to $416,161M in fiscal 2025, while gross margin rose from 44.1% to 46.9% and operating margin from 29.8% to 32.0%. The latest filed period is the quarter ended 2026-06-27, where revenue rose 16.4% to $109,417M on gross margin of 50.1% and operating margin of 32.6%. No fourth-quarter fiscal 2026 earnings release and no fiscal 2026 annual report were on EDGAR as of 2026-10-31; Apple's fiscal 2025 equivalents were filed on 2025-10-30 and 2025-10-31, so the annual report is due imminently and the figures here are trailing twelve months to 2026-06-27 [S5, S6].

| Line item | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 | Q3 FY2026 | TTM to 2026-06-27 | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | $383,285M | $391,035M | $416,161M | $109,417M | $466,823M | S5, S6 |
| Gross margin | 44.1% | 46.2% | 46.9% | 50.1% | 48.7% | S5, S6 |
| Operating margin | 29.8% | 31.5% | 32.0% | 32.6% | 33.2% | S5, S6 |
| Net income | $96,995M | $93,736M | $112,010M | $29,789M | $128,930M | S5, S6 |
| Diluted EPS | $6.13 | $6.08 | $7.46 | $2.02 | $8.72 | S5, S6 |
| Effective tax rate | 14.7% | 24.1% | 15.6% | 17.9% | 17.3% | S5, S6 |
| Operating cash flow | $110,543M | $118,254M | $111,482M | n/a | $146,724M | S5, S6 |
| Capital expenditure | $10,959M | $9,447M | $12,715M | n/a | $10,041M | S5, S6 |
| Free cash flow | $99,584M | $108,807M | $98,767M | n/a | $136,683M | S5, S6 |
| Free cash flow / net income | 1.03x | 1.16x | 0.88x | n/a | 1.06x | S5, S6 |

### The growth is half tax base effect, and a quarter buyback

Fiscal 2025's net income rose 19.5%, but pretax income rose 7.5% ($132,729M against $123,485M) and the tax provision fell 30.3% to $20,719M because fiscal 2024 carried the one-time $10.2bn Irish charge — $15.8bn payable to Ireland, offset by a $4.8bn US foreign tax credit and $823M of released unrecognised benefits. Normalising fiscal 2024 at fiscal 2025's 15.6% effective rate gives $104,222M of net income, so underlying growth was 7.5%, not 19.5%. The EPS gap above that is the buyback: from fiscal 2023 to fiscal 2025, net income grew 15.5% while diluted EPS grew 21.7% and diluted shares fell 5.1%, so about 5.4 points of the EPS growth was a smaller denominator. That contribution is already fading — in the trailing twelve months EPS grew 16.9% against 15.1% for net income, about 1.9 points — because repurchases slowed to $62,094M in the nine months to 2026-06-27 from $70,579M while operating cash flow rose 43% [S5, S6].

Capital return has therefore stopped outrunning cash generation. Combined buybacks and dividends were $97,866M in the trailing twelve months against free cash flow of $136,683M, or 72%, against 107% in fiscal 2025, and net cash rose by $28,410M in nine months. At $344.63 on 2026-10-30 and 14,715M diluted shares the equity is worth about $5.07trn, which is 39.5x trailing EPS and a 2.70% free cash flow yield, while the ten-year Treasury yielded 4.93%. Repurchasing at that spread is accretive to EPS and not obviously accretive to value per share, and management has already cut the pace [S9].

### Cash is real; the working-capital cushion is not

Cash generation is the strongest part of the record and the hardest to fake: operating cash flow of $146,724M against capital expenditure of $10,041M, with free cash flow at 1.06x net income. The anomaly is fiscal 2025, when free cash flow fell to 0.88x of net income despite $111,482M of operating cash flow; cash paid for income taxes that year was $43,369M, or 32.7% of pretax income against a 15.6% book rate and 21.1% in fiscal 2024 — a gap consistent with settlement payments on the Irish case and the TCJA repatriation tax, the final $8.8bn of which was paid in the nine months to 2026-06-27. That supports reading the gap as timing, and the recovery to 1.06x is consistent with it. The working-capital change runs the other way: inventory reached $11,092M at 2026-06-27 from $5,925M a year earlier, an 87% increase against 16.2% revenue growth, lifting days inventory to 16.9 from 9.4 and pulling the cash conversion cycle to −56.8 days from −71.1 at the fiscal 2025 year-end [S5, S6].

The balance sheet carries no leverage risk. At 2026-06-27 Apple held $146,517M of cash and marketable securities against $84,344M of debt, for net cash of $62,173M, up from $33,763M at 2025-09-27, with commercial paper cut to $1,997M from $7,979M. Interest is not a coverage question: other income and expense netted to −$321M in fiscal 2025 because interest earned on the securities book offsets interest paid. The commitments that matter are forward purchases — $57.0bn of manufacturing purchase obligations, $56.2bn due within twelve months, and $29.3bn of other purchase obligations — which fix component supply and, with it, the cost base when memory prices move. Two details deserve attention: gross intangible assets rose $13,270M to $38,220M in nine months with no goodwill recognised, which points to purchased intellectual property or content rather than acquisitions and is not explained in the quarterly filing; and gross unrecognised tax benefits were $23.2bn at 2025-09-27, of which $10.6bn would affect the effective rate and up to $6bn may move within twelve months [S6].

### Returns are distorted by the buyback, not flattered by the business

Reported returns are not usable as quality scores. Return on equity was 148.8% and return on invested capital 320.6% in the trailing twelve months, but invested capital is only about $45,347M — $107,520M of equity plus $84,344M of debt less $146,517M of cash and securities — because $258,212M of cumulative buybacks have shrunk the equity base. The honest comparison is return on assets of 36.1% and an operating margin of 33.2%, against Microsoft's 35.9% return on invested capital in fiscal 2026 and Alphabet's 37.0% in fiscal 2025, both computed on real invested capital. The geographic picture also cuts against the standard bear case: Greater China revenue rose 30% to $64,839M in the nine months to 2026-06-27 and 22% in the June quarter, so nine months already exceed the whole of fiscal 2025's $64,377M after two years of decline [S6, S27].

### What moves the outcome, and by how much

Gross margin dominates. On trailing-twelve-month revenue of $466,823M, one point of gross margin is $4,668M of pretax profit, or 3.0% of net income, while one point of revenue growth at the current margin is $1,878M, or 1.5%. Three cases, all on the trailing twelve months and none a forecast: a two-point margin gain takes EPS to about $9.24; a two-point give-back to about $8.20; and a two-point give-back combined with the loss of the $20bn search licence, which sits in Services at near-100% incremental margin, takes it to about $7.11, 18.8% below the base. The single variable that moves the outcome most is therefore gross margin, not revenue growth, and it is the one Apple controls least while memory and NAND costs rise and a tariff refund unwinds [S6].

::: info warning
**The fiscal 2026 gross margin is not yet a clean number.** Apple attributes part of the product-margin gain to tariff refunds it does not quantify, while inventory nearly doubled year on year; both should be adjusted before 50.1% is treated as the new baseline, as the June 2026 quarterly report discloses [S5, S6].
:::

| Returns and working capital | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 | TTM to 2026-06-27 | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Return on equity | 171.9% | 157.4% | 171.4% | 148.8% | S5, S6 |
| Return on assets | 27.5% | 26.1% | 30.9% | 36.1% | S5, S6 |
| Days sales outstanding | 28.1 | 31.2 | 34.9 | 24.5 | S5, S6 |
| Days inventory outstanding | 10.8 | 12.6 | 9.4 | 16.9 | S5, S6 |
| Days payables outstanding | 106.7 | 119.7 | 115.4 | 98.3 | S5, S6 |
| Cash conversion cycle, days | −67.8 | −75.8 | −71.1 | −56.8 | S5, S6 |
| Net cash | $51,011M | $50,021M | $33,763M | $62,173M | S5, S6 |

The quality question resolves into three parts. The cash is real — 1.06x of net income at 2.2% capital intensity — and the balance sheet is net cash by $62,173M. The growth is weaker than reported, because tax normalisation and the buyback together account for most of the gap between 7.5% pretax growth and 22.7% EPS growth in fiscal 2025. And the margin sits at a cyclical high with one unquantified refund inside it. An investor paying 39.5x trailing earnings is paying for the first and third to persist while the second is already reversing.

arguments.markdown:
Apple's competitive position strengthened in 2026 in every hardware line except smartwatches, but the gain is crisis-specific — bought with memory supply and price discipline rather than product superiority — and it is being offset where profit is made, because the App Store commission that funds the premium position is being dismantled by courts and regulators rather than by a rival's product. Apple leads no hardware category outright except detachable tablets, and its annual report concedes a minority share in smartphones, personal computers, tablets and wearables. [S102]

### The lead is in integration, not in units

Apple's 20.2% of global smartphone shipments in Q2 2026 was a record for that quarter and a 3.9 percentage point gain, but Samsung's 22.7% was larger and Xiaomi's 26.4% collapse explains much of the redistribution. In personal computing devices Apple is second at 18.2% behind Lenovo's 20.1%, yet macOS shipments grew 17.4% while Windows fell 6.7% and Android 19.6%, and macOS is the only major operating system IDC expects to grow in 2026. The clearest structural lead is detachable tablets at 55.3%; the weakest spot is smartwatches, where Huawei leads 18.8% to 17.2%, so Apple's 15.5% of all wearables rests on earwear, where it holds 17.2%. [S104]

| Product | Apple share | Leader and challengers | Technology basis | Price position | Switching cost | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone, global units | 20.2% in Q2 2026, +3.9pp | Samsung 22.7% (+3.2pp); Xiaomi 11.3%, OPPO 10.5%, vivo 7.7% | iOS integration and secured memory supply | Premium; industry ASP $581, Apple above it | High: iCloud, iMessage, purchased apps | S102, S66 |
| iPhone, China units | 18.1%, +4.2pp | Huawei 22.6% (+4.5pp); OPPO 16.0%, vivo 16.0%, Xiaomi 12.4% | iOS against domestic HarmonyOS | Apple held prices while Android raised them | Medium: leaving iOS loses Apple services | S40 |
| PCs and tablets | 18.2%, -0.4% | Lenovo 20.1%; HP 12.7%, Dell 9.1%, Samsung 6.2% | macOS against Windows | MacBook Neo attacks entry pricing | Medium | S103, S106 |
| Services and App Store | $109.2bn in FY2025 at 75.4% gross margin | Alphabet $471.1bn TTM revenue; Netflix $49.7bn TTM | iOS distribution against Google Play | 15-30% commission, under challenge | High for consumers, falling for developers | S5, S42, S80 |

### Samsung is the dangerous one, and the reason is memory

Samsung is the most dangerous competitor, and not because of the Galaxy S26 Ultra. When memory is more than 65% of bill of materials at the low end, the binding constraint is supply access, and Samsung is the only top-five handset vendor that also sells memory: it grew shipments 8.1% and took 3.2 points of share in Q2 2026 while Xiaomi fell 26.4% and vivo 19.6%. Apple's answer was to secure memory early, which is why its units fell only 1.3% in 2026 against Android's 24.3% and why IDC puts iOS at a record 23.6% of shipments — a sourcing feat rather than a structural advantage, and it lapses when memory normalises while Samsung keeps its cost position. Samsung also holds the foldable franchise Apple attacks: IDC expects more than 17 million foldable iPhones by 2027 at an average price above $2,550, about 40% of a category growing 12.6% to 22.9 million units this year and more than half its $45.7 billion of value. [S66]

### In China the competitor and the rules are different

Huawei held 22.6% of a Chinese market that fell 4.3% in Q2 2026 and grew 19.9% by holding prices while Android rivals raised theirs, leaning on HarmonyOS, which IDC expects to reach 51 million units in 2026; Apple grew 24.4% and gained 4.2 points to 18.1%, so both premium ends expanded while OPPO, vivo and Xiaomi contracted. The mechanism is a domestic operating system plus price discipline, and neither is a feature Apple can copy. HarmonyOS draws on the same national preference that makes Apple's China revenue politically exposed, so the 30% China revenue growth belongs behind a competition risk: the revenue line can grow while the strategic position narrows. [S40]

### The profit pool is being taken by courts, not by rivals

Apple's FY2025 annual report discloses that it is subject to a U.S. court order preventing it from imposing any commission on certain purchases consumers make, that its compliance plan under the Digital Markets Act has been challenged by the European Commission, and that it faces U.S. monopolization suits over smartphones; separately, the September 2, 2025 remedies order against Google, if upheld on appeal, could remove the search-distribution payments that sit inside Services. No competitor needs to win a device sale for the 75.4% services gross margin to compress: a developer that routes a subscriber to the web converts a 15-30% commission into a payment-processing fee, and Services growth of 14.1% then arrives at a lower margin. The asymmetry is: the hardware position improved while the pricing power that monetises it was reduced by a court in the United States and a regulator in Europe. [S5]

| Product | Leader | Challenger | Niche | Emerging threat | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone | Samsung, 22.7% of units | Apple, 20.2% and gaining | Huawei in China, 22.6% | HarmonyOS at 51m units; AI-first Android flagships | S102, S40, S66 |
| PCs and tablets | Lenovo, 20.1% | Apple, 18.2%, with the only growing OS | Dell in workstations, 40.0% | HarmonyOS NEXT at 1.6%; Windows-on-ARM | S103, S106 |
| Smartwatches | Huawei, 18.8% | Apple, 17.2% | Garmin, 27.9% | Smart rings: Oura at 67.0% | S104 |
| Services | Apple, $109.2bn | Alphabet through Google Play | Netflix, Spotify, Epic | Web payments and alternative marketplaces | S5, S42, S80 |

### AI and the phone already in the buyer's pocket

Where Apple is not ahead is AI: the all-new Siri AI arrived at WWDC26 in June 2026, while Samsung's AI-equipped Galaxy S26 Ultra is credited by IDC with returning Samsung to first place in Q1 2026, and research and development rose 32.5% to $34.0 billion in the first nine months of FY2026 — the cost of catching up, not the reward for leading. The strongest competitor is the handset already in the buyer's pocket: replacement cycles are lengthening, IDC describes Chinese buyers as postponing rather than abandoning upgrades, and the 173 million sub-$100 units shipped in 2025 are leaving the market, which supports Services attach while suppressing units. Three risks follow: if AI becomes the reason a buyer upgrades, Apple competes on integration rather than capability; if HarmonyOS reaches first-time buyers in lower-tier cities, they never enter iOS; and if the U.S. injunction spreads to other storefronts, the take rate falls further. Unit position and profit per unit are moving in opposite directions, so the question worth paying for is not who sells more phones but what share of the transaction Apple controls in 2027. Confidence is high in the shares and the legal facts and medium beyond 2028, when memory normalises and the crisis-specific advantage lapses. Three questions would settle it: what proportion of Services revenue is commission; what margin the foldable carries at $2,550; and whether Siri AI runs on-device or through a partner, at what cost per query. [S13, S66, S40]

|---|---|---|
| Strengths | Record 23.6% iOS share of 2026 shipments; 20.2% of second-quarter units, up 3.9 points; 55.3% of detachable tablets; 15.5% of wearables and 17.2% of earwear; Services of $109.2bn at a 75.4% gross margin | S66, S102, S103, S104, S5, S6 |
| Weaknesses | Minority share in every hardware category by Apple's own description; second to Samsung in phones, Lenovo in PCs and Huawei in smartwatches; no disclosed active-device count; no published app-economy size | S5, S102, S103, S104 |
| Opportunities | More than 17m foldable iPhones and about 40% of a category at an average price above $2,550 by 2027, worth $45.7bn; macOS the only major operating system forecast to grow in 2026; India's $600-800 band growing 32% | S66, S103, S105 |
| Threats | Huawei at 22.6% of China with HarmonyOS at 51m units; a U.S. court order barring commission on certain external purchases; a DMA plan challenged by the European Commission; memory costs up more than 300% from a supplier that competes in handsets | S40, S5, S66, S102 |

Apple's FY2025 annual report discloses a U.S. court order barring commission on certain external purchases and a DMA plan challenged by the European Commission (S5).

arguments.markdown:
Apple's policy exposure is not a licence-to-operate threat but a slow, legislated tax on Services gross profit: the €500 million DMA fine of 2025-04-23 and the April 2025 US contempt finding show a company that litigates first and complies later, while the three remedies that matter — Google's default-search payment, the US link-out commission and the EU fee structure — have so far been reshaped rather than removed [S7]. The question for a long-only holder is how much Services gross margin five more years of enforcement takes, and whether the multiple already discounts it.

### The DMA fine is small; the cost structure is not

The Commission fined Apple €500 million on 2025-04-23 for breaching the anti-steering obligation and ordered it to remove restrictions on steering users outside the App Store. The same day it closed the user-choice investigation — a real concession — but issued preliminary findings in the Article 6(4) file on Apple's terms for alternative app marketplaces, where an adverse finding carries fines of up to 10% of annual worldwide net sales [S5]. Two facts bound it: on 2026-02-05 the Commission found Apple Ads and Apple Maps should not be designated, and no further Apple decision appears in its DMA record between the fine and 2026-09-28. Peer fines are serial but modest — Meta €200 million in the same package, Google €890 million on 2026-07-23, Alphabet's €4.1 billion Android fine final only in July 2026 — so repeated fines, not break-up, are the base rate. The implication is a transfer of pricing power from Apple's toll to developers and consumers: because each mandated fee cut reaches Services gross margin before it reaches revenue, fee orders should move the multiple and fine headlines should not.

Europe is Apple's second-largest region and Services drove its FY2025 growth; App Store commission is the highest-margin revenue Apple records, so a mandated fee cut in Brussels is worth more to the equity than any fine. Apple also warns that interoperability obligations force it to open technologies to third parties without charge and have in the past, and may in future, caused it not to launch or maintain features "such as Siri AI" — a product-availability risk, not only a revenue leak.

### A contempt finding, then a slow antitrust case

On 2025-04-30 the Northern District of California found Apple in violation of the 2021 Epic injunction, barred any commission on purchases made outside an app, and referred the company to the US Attorney on criminal contempt. The Ninth Circuit modified that on 2025-12-11 to allow parity rules and some commission on link-out purchases; Apple petitioned the Supreme Court on 2026-05-21, obtained certiorari on 2026-06-30 limited to the civil-contempt standard, and seeks a stay below [S6, S122]. Apple's compliance function tested a court order rather than obeyed it, which raises the severity of the next remedy. That remedy is the DOJ case, filed 2024-03-21 with 16 states and the District of Columbia, seeking equitable relief only; it survived dismissal on 2025-06-30 and is in discovery on a schedule pointing to a 2027 trial. With no damages claimed, the risk is conduct-based — defaults, messaging, app distribution — and lands on the 2027-2029 Services line rather than the balance sheet.

### Google's payment survives, on worse terms

The search-distribution remedy went Apple's way on the point that mattered: the 2025-09-02 decision refused to ban Google's payments to distributors, citing harm to device makers and browser developers, and instead barred exclusive contracts while permitting default-placement payments not conditioned on exclusivity and running one year or less [S118, S42]. A final judgment followed in December 2025; both sides appealed in early 2026 and the appeals were pending at 2026-10-29. Apple does not disclose the payment; the $20 billion-a-year figure is unverified. The revenue survives with annual renewal risk and mandatory choice screens.

### Two bear-case triggers did not fire in 2026

The Section 232 semiconductor investigation's initial results on 2026-01-14 imposed no additional tariff on Apple's products, and on 2026-02-20 the Supreme Court struck down certain IEEPA tariffs, with Apple claiming refunds it recognised as a reduction of products cost of sales; Section 301 tariffs were then imposed. In China the opposite of closure happened: the CAC registered Apple Intelligence on 2026-07-15 with Alibaba's Qwen and Baidu, and Greater China net sales rose 22% to $18,816 million in the June 2026 quarter and 30% to $64,839 million for the nine months, from $49,884 million [S6, S121]. The binding constraint is the calendar: the Busan truce that suppresses tariff and rare-earth escalation was extended on 2026-09-23 from 2026-11-10 to 2027-01-10, making 2027 the next policy cliff.

### Tax is settled; the ESG tail is elsewhere

The Irish state-aid case ended against Apple: the ECJ confirmed the 2016 decision on 2024-09-10, producing a $10.2 billion net one-time charge and $15.8 billion payable to Ireland. arguments.markdown:
Apple's competitive position strengthened in 2026 in every hardware line except smartwatches, but the gain is crisis-specific — bought with memory supply and price discipline rather than product superiority — and it is being offset where profit is made, because the App Store commission that funds the premium position is being dismantled by courts and regulators rather than by a rival's product. Apple leads no hardware category outright except detachable tablets, and its annual report concedes a minority share in smartphones, personal computers, tablets and wearables. Head to head, Samsung shipped 62.7 million handsets in the second quarter of 2026 to Apple's 55.7 million. [S102]

### The lead is in integration, not in units

Apple's 20.2% of global smartphone shipments in Q2 2026 was a record for that quarter and a 3.9 percentage point gain, but Samsung's 22.7% was larger and Xiaomi's 26.4% collapse explains much of the redistribution. In personal computing devices Apple is second at 18.2% against Lenovo's 20.1%, yet macOS shipments grew 17.4% while Windows fell 6.7% and Android 19.6%, and macOS is the only major operating system IDC expects to grow in 2026. The clearest structural lead is detachable tablets at 55.3%; the weakest spot is smartwatches, where Huawei leads 18.8% to 17.2%, so Apple's 15.5% of all wearables rests on earwear, where it holds 17.2%. [S104]

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone, global | Samsung | 22.7%, +3.2pp | 20.2%, +3.9pp | iOS integration and secured memory supply | Industry ASP $581; Apple above it | High: iCloud, iMessage, purchased apps | S102, S66 |
| iPhone, China | Huawei | 22.6%, +4.5pp | 18.1%, +4.2pp | iOS against domestic HarmonyOS | Apple held prices while Android raised them | Medium: leaving iOS loses Apple services | S40 |
| PCs and tablets | Lenovo | 20.1%, +2.5pp | 18.2%, -0.4% | macOS against Windows | MacBook Neo attacks entry pricing | Medium | S103, S106 |
| Services and App Store | Alphabet, Google Play | $471.1bn TTM revenue | $109.2bn Services at 75.4% gross margin | iOS distribution against Google Play | 15-30% commission, under challenge | High for consumers, falling for developers | S5, S42, S80 |

### Samsung is the dangerous one, and the reason is memory

Samsung is the most dangerous competitor, and not because of the Galaxy S26 Ultra. When memory is more than 65% of bill of materials at the low end, the binding constraint is supply access, and Samsung is the only top-five handset vendor that also sells memory: it grew shipments 8.1% and took 3.2 points of share in Q2 2026 while Xiaomi fell 26.4% and vivo 19.6%. Apple's answer was to secure memory early, which is why its units fell only 1.3% in 2026 against Android's 24.3% and why IDC puts iOS at a record 23.6% of shipments — a sourcing feat rather than a structural advantage, and it lapses when memory normalises while Samsung keeps its cost position. Samsung also holds the foldable franchise Apple attacks: IDC expects more than 17 million foldable iPhones by 2027 at an average price above $2,550, about 40% of a category growing 12.6% to 22.9 million units this year and more than half its $45.7 billion of value. [S66]

### In China the competitor and the rules are different

Huawei held 22.6% of a Chinese market that fell 4.3% in Q2 2026 and grew 19.9% by holding prices while Android rivals raised theirs, leaning on HarmonyOS, which IDC expects to reach 51 million units in 2026; Apple grew 24.4% and gained 4.2 points to 18.1%, so both premium ends expanded while OPPO, vivo and Xiaomi contracted. The mechanism is a domestic operating system plus price discipline, and neither is a feature Apple can copy. HarmonyOS draws on the national preference that makes Apple's China revenue politically exposed, so the 30% China revenue growth belongs behind a competition risk. [S40]

### The profit pool is being taken by courts, not by rivals

Apple's FY2025 annual report discloses that it is subject to a U.S. court order preventing it from imposing any commission on certain purchases consumers make, that its compliance plan under the Digital Markets Act has been challenged by the European Commission, and that it faces U.S. monopolization suits over smartphones; separately, the September 2, 2025 remedies order against Google, if upheld on appeal, could remove the search-distribution payments that sit inside Services. No competitor needs to win a device sale for the 75.4% services gross margin to compress: a developer that routes a subscriber to the web converts a 15-30% commission into a payment-processing fee, and Services growth of 14.1% then arrives at a lower margin. The hardware position improved while the pricing power behind it was cut by a court in the United States and a regulator in Europe. [S5]

| PCs and tablets | Lenovo, 20.1% | Apple, 18.2%, with the only growing OS | Dell in workstations, 40.0% | HarmonyOS NEXT at 1.6%; Windows-on-ARM | S103, S106 |
| Services | Apple, $109.2bn | Alphabet through Google Play | Netflix, Spotify, Epic | Web payments and alternative marketplaces | S5, S42, S80 |

### AI and the phone already in the buyer's pocket

Where Apple is not ahead is AI: the all-new Siri AI arrived at WWDC26 in June 2026, while Samsung's AI-equipped Galaxy S26 Ultra is credited by IDC with returning Samsung to first place in Q1 2026, and research and development rose 32.5% to $34.0 billion in the first nine months of FY2026 — the cost of catching up, not the reward for leading. The strongest competitor is the handset already in the buyer's pocket: replacement cycles are lengthening, IDC describes Chinese buyers as postponing rather than abandoning upgrades, and the 173 million sub-$100 units shipped in 2025 are leaving the market, which supports Services attach while suppressing units. Three risks follow: if AI becomes the reason a buyer upgrades, Apple competes on integration rather than capability; if HarmonyOS reaches first-time buyers in lower-tier cities, they never enter iOS; and if the U.S. injunction spreads to other storefronts, the take rate falls further. Unit position and profit per unit are moving in opposite directions, so the question worth paying for is not who sells more phones but what share of the transaction Apple controls in 2027. Confidence is high in the shares and the legal facts and medium beyond 2028, when memory normalises and the crisis-specific advantage lapses. Open diligence questions: what proportion of Services revenue is commission rather than subscription or advertising? What margin does the foldable carry at $2,550? Apple's silicon-plus-OS stack is still the widest integrated consumer technology stack in the industry, but in 2026 the company rented the one layer it could not build — the frontier model — so what remains defensible is distribution, custom silicon and regulated health sensing, not leadership in artificial intelligence. In two years: the A19 Pro shipped in September 2025 on TSMC N3P; the A20 Pro moved the iPhone to TSMC N2 in September 2026; the C2 modem reached the flagship; the first foldable iPhone shipped at $1,999; and on 2026-01-12 Apple and Google announced that the next generation of Apple Foundation Models would be based on Gemini [S58, S59, S63, S64].

### The silicon lead is real, costly, and rented from TSMC

The A19 Pro used TSMC N3P with two performance cores at up to 4.26 GHz; a year later the A20 Pro moved to TSMC N2 with a dual 16-core Neural Engine — 32 neural cores — and ~52 TOPS, about double the prior generation's AI throughput. N2 wafers are reported at ~$30,000 against $18,000-20,000 for 3nm, so each capability step arrives with higher silicon cost. Product gross margin was 39.9% in the nine months to 2026-06-27 versus 36.9% a year earlier, but only with tariff refunds and mix offsetting "higher costs, including memory", and the 10-Q warns that advanced-semiconductor, NAND and DRAM constraints are expected to intensify [S6, S64].

| Product gross margin | 39.9% vs 36.9% (9M FY2025) | Reported financials | S6 |
| On-device model / PCC context | ~3B parameters / 32K tokens | Apple research and developer docs | S61, S62 |

### Apple Intelligence is an architecture with a rented brain

On device, Apple runs a ~3B-parameter model optimised through KV-cache sharing and 2-bit quantisation-aware training; on its servers, a Parallel-Track Mixture-of-Experts model runs inside Private Cloud Compute, which enforces stateless processing, no privileged runtime access even for Apple staff, and verifiable software images with attestation. The binding constraint is memory bandwidth and power: phone-class memory caps practical on-device inference at single-digit billions of parameters, which is why harder queries are offloaded — a constraint visible in research needed to run 70B models at the edge. The ceiling is disclosed: a 32K-token context is small against frontier assistants, and Apple's own models were not frontier-quality, which is why the Google agreement exists. The unresolved question — the one that decides whether the privacy story holds — is where Gemini-derived inference physically runs. Apple says Apple Intelligence continues on Apple devices and Private Cloud Compute; trade reporting says Google's cloud performs the Gemini computation and puts the licence at ~$1bn a year, on top of a default-search payment of ~$20bn. Neither figure is Apple-confirmed [S8, S58, S60, S61, S86]. Apple's differentiation is orchestration, distribution and privacy, not model quality; an investor should underwrite the cash flow and the installed base, not the AI layer.

### Products: a strong cycle, a late foldable, a spatial computer that never became a platform

The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max launched on 2026-09-09 at $1,199 and $1,299; the foldable iPhone Duo at $1,999 went on sale on 2026-10-23. iPhone net sales rose 22% to $196.5bn in the nine months to 2026-06-27, with Greater China up 30%. The C2 modem supports US mmWave and uses 15% less energy than the C1X, but the larger iPhone 18 Pro Max appears to keep a Qualcomm modem, so Qualcomm retains leverage over the highest-ASP SKU. Vision Pro is the counter-example to Apple's category-creation record: ~390,000 units in 2024, ~45,000 in the December 2025 quarter despite the M5 refresh, ~600,000 lifetime, and an IDC forecast of ~290,000 units in 2026 [S59, S13, S87].

Apple's cash conversion and balance sheet are as good as the multiple implies, but the earnings growth is not: fiscal 2025's 22.7% EPS growth becomes roughly 10% once the $10.2bn Irish State Aid tax charge in the prior year is normalised out, and fiscal 2026's margin is being flattered by a tariff refund Apple does not quantify.

The three-year record is one of slowing revenue and rising margin: revenue fell 2.8% in fiscal 2023, grew 2.0% in fiscal 2024 and 6.4% to $416,161M in fiscal 2025, while gross margin rose from 44.1% to 46.9% and operating margin from 29.8% to 32.0%. ### The growth is half tax base effect, and a quarter buyback

Fiscal 2025's net income rose 19.5%, but pretax income rose 7.5% ($132,729M against $123,485M) and the tax provision fell 30.3% to $20,719M because fiscal 2024 carried the one-time $10.2bn Irish charge — $15.8bn payable to Ireland, offset by a $4.8bn US foreign tax credit and $823M of released unrecognised benefits. Normalising fiscal 2024 at fiscal 2025's 15.6% effective rate gives $104,222M of net income, so underlying growth was 7.5%, not 19.5%. The EPS gap above that is the buyback: from fiscal 2023 to fiscal 2025, net income grew 15.5% while diluted EPS grew 21.7% and diluted shares fell 5.1%, so about 5.4 points of the EPS growth was a smaller denominator. That contribution is already fading — in the trailing twelve months EPS grew 16.9% against 15.1% for net income, about 1.9 points — because repurchases slowed to $62,094M in the nine months to 2026-06-27 from $70,579M while operating cash flow rose 43% [S5, S6].

Capital return has therefore stopped outrunning cash generation. Combined buybacks and dividends were $97,866M in the trailing twelve months against free cash flow of $136,683M, or 72%, against 107% in fiscal 2025, and net cash rose by $28,410M in nine months. At $344.63 on 2026-10-30 and 14,715M diluted shares the equity is worth about $5.07trn, which is 39.5x trailing EPS and a 2.70% free cash flow yield, while the ten-year Treasury yielded 4.93%. Repurchasing at that spread is accretive to EPS and not obviously accretive to value per share, and management has already cut the pace [S9].

### Cash is real; the working-capital cushion is not

Cash generation is the strongest part of the record and the hardest to fake: operating cash flow of $146,724M against capital expenditure of $10,041M, with free cash flow at 1.06x net income. The anomaly is fiscal 2025, when free cash flow fell to 0.88x of net income despite $111,482M of operating cash flow; cash paid for income taxes that year was $43,369M, or 32.7% of pretax income against a 15.6% book rate and 21.1% in fiscal 2024 — a gap consistent with settlement payments on the Irish case and the TCJA repatriation tax, the final $8.8bn of which was paid in the nine months to 2026-06-27. That supports reading the gap as timing, and the recovery to 1.06x is consistent with it. The working-capital change runs the other way: inventory reached $11,092M at 2026-06-27 from $5,925M a year earlier, an 87% increase against 16.2% revenue growth, lifting days inventory to 16.9 from 9.4 and pulling the cash conversion cycle to −56.8 days from −71.1 at the fiscal 2025 year-end [S5, S6].

The balance sheet carries no leverage risk. At 2026-06-27 Apple held $146,517M of cash and marketable securities against $84,344M of debt, for net cash of $62,173M, up from $33,763M at 2025-09-27, with commercial paper cut to $1,997M from $7,979M. Interest is not a coverage question: other income and expense netted to −$321M in fiscal 2025 because interest earned on the securities book offsets interest paid. The commitments that matter are forward purchases — $57.0bn of manufacturing purchase obligations, $56.2bn due within twelve months, and $29.3bn of other purchase obligations — which fix component supply and, with it, the cost base when memory prices move. Two details deserve attention: gross intangible assets rose $13,270M to $38,220M in nine months with no goodwill recognised, which points to purchased intellectual property or content rather than acquisitions and is not explained in the quarterly filing; and gross unrecognised tax benefits were $23.2bn at 2025-09-27, of which $10.6bn would affect the effective rate and up to $6bn may move within twelve months [S6].

### Returns are distorted by the buyback, not flattered by the business

Reported returns are not usable as quality scores. Return on equity was 148.8% and return on invested capital 320.6% in the trailing twelve months, but invested capital is only about $45,347M — $107,520M of equity plus $84,344M of debt less $146,517M of cash and securities — because $258,212M of cumulative buybacks have shrunk the equity base. The honest comparison is return on assets of 36.1% and an operating margin of 33.2%, against Microsoft's 35.9% return on invested capital in fiscal 2026 and Alphabet's 37.0% in fiscal 2025, both computed on real invested capital. The geographic picture also cuts against the standard bear case: Greater China revenue rose 30% to $64,839M in the nine months to 2026-06-27 and 22% in the June quarter, so nine months already exceed the whole of fiscal 2025's $64,377M after two years of decline [S6, S27].

### What moves the outcome, and by how much

Gross margin dominates. On trailing-twelve-month revenue of $466,823M, one point of gross margin is $4,668M of pretax profit, or 3.0% of net income, while one point of revenue growth at the current margin is $1,878M, or 1.5%. Three cases, all on the trailing twelve months and none a forecast: a two-point margin gain takes EPS to about $9.24; a two-point give-back to about $8.20; and a two-point give-back combined with the loss of the $20bn search licence, which sits in Services at near-100% incremental margin, takes it to about $7.11, 18.8% below the base. The single variable that moves the outcome most is therefore gross margin, not revenue growth, and it is the one Apple controls least while memory and NAND costs rise and a tariff refund unwinds [S6].

**The fiscal 2026 gross margin is not yet a clean number.** Apple attributes part of the product-margin gain to tariff refunds it does not quantify, while inventory nearly doubled year on year; both should be adjusted before 50.1% is treated as the new baseline, as the June 2026 quarterly report discloses [S5, S6].
:::

## Section 1: Company Overview — Forensic Identity

### 1.1 Legal Entity Map

Map every legal entity in the corporate structure. This is not optional — investors must know exactly which entity they are investing in.

| Entity | Jurisdiction | Entity Type | Role | Ownership % | Ultimate Controller |
|--------|-------------|-------------|------|-------------|---------------------|
| [Holding Co] | Cayman/BVI | Ltd | IPO vehicle / top holding | 100% (top) | Founder(s) |
| [HK Co] | Hong Kong | Ltd | Intermediate holding | 100% by Holding Co | — |
| [WFOE] | Shanghai, China | Wholly foreign-owned enterprise | VIE anchor / operating license holder | 100% by HK Co | — |
| [VIE OpCo] | Beijing, China | Domestic limited company | Operating entity (holds ICP, licenses) | VIE controlled | Nominee shareholders |
| [Subsidiary 1] | [Location] | [Type] | R&D center | X% | — |
| [Subsidiary 2] | [Location] | [Type] | Sales entity | X% | — |

**Mandatory:**
- Distinguish VIE vs. non-VIE vs. red-chip architecture
- Identify which entity holds key licenses/assets/IP
- Flag nominee shareholder arrangements, contractual control gaps, and enforceability risk
- For public companies: specify listing venue, ticker, exchange, currency, shares outstanding, free float %

**If VIE architecture:**
- Who are the nominee shareholders? What is their relationship to the founder?
- What contracts bind the VIE (exclusive option, proxy, equity pledge, exclusive business cooperation)?
- Has any PRC court or arbitrator ruled on the enforceability of these specific VIE contracts?
- What happens to the VIE if the nominee shareholder dies, divorces, or goes bankrupt?

### 1.2 Complete Timeline

Build a timeline with **specific dates** (YYYY-MM or YYYY-MM-DD when available). Do not use "recently," "currently," or "soon."

| Date | Event | Significance | Source |
|------|-------|-------------|--------|
| YYYY-MM | Company founded by [Founder] at [Location] | Origin | [SX] |
| YYYY-MM | First product launched: [Product Name] | Product proof | [SX] |
| YYYY-MM | Series A: $X million at $Y valuation, led by [Investor] | Financing milestone | [SX] |
| YYYY-MM | Key hire: [Name] joined as [Role] from [Prior Company] | Team building | [SX] |
| YYYY-MM | FDA/CE/NMPA submission: [Product/Indication] | Regulatory milestone | [SX] |
| YYYY-MM | First paying customer / pilot launch | Commercial validation | [SX] |
| ... | ... | ... | ... |

**Minimum:** 8-15 dated milestones covering founding, product, financing, team, regulatory, commercial, and strategic events.

### 1.3 Equity & Cap Table

Build the most accurate cap table possible. Differentiate between **confirmed** (from filings, company disclosures) and **estimated** (from media, industry inference).

| Shareholder | Class | Shares | % Ownership | % Voting Rights | Investment Cost | Current Value (at latest round) | Return Multiple |
|-------------|-------|--------|-------------|-----------------|-----------------|--------------------------------|-----------------|
| Founder A | Ordinary / B-class (10:1) | X | ~45% | ~71% | $X | $X | Xx |
| Founder B | Ordinary | X | ~15% | ~12% | $X | $X | Xx |
| Investor 1 (Sequoia) | Preferred A | X | ~20% | ~8% | $X | $X | Xx |

| ESOP (undistributed) | — | X | ~10% | 0% | — | $X | — |
| **Total** | | | **100%** | **100%** | | | |

**Mandatory:**
- **Share class breakdown**: ordinary vs. preferred, voting vs. non-voting, vested vs. unvested
- **Super-voting rights**: any founder with >50% voting power despite minority equity? Detail the mechanism.
- **Liquidation preferences**: multiple (1x, 1.5x, 2x), participating vs. non-participating, seniority stack
- **Anti-dilution**: full ratchet vs. weighted average
- **ESOP**: total pool size, allocated vs. unallocated, annual refresh rate

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Playbook: analysis_core.md > Mandatory Evidence Gate

## Mandatory Evidence Gate

Do not draft the final report until every material section has an evidence packet in `_work/evidence_matrix.md`. Evidence may include public web sources, user-provided files, filings, databases, industry reports, patents, job posts, media interviews, customer/procurement records, or clearly labelled analyst estimates.

Minimum evidence packet per section:

| Required item | Minimum standard |
| --- | --- |
| Search work | 3-6 targeted queries unless user-provided materials are sufficient. |
| Sources opened | At least 2 independent sources; 3+ for market, competition, team, funding, financials, and risk when public data exists. |
| Source IDs | At least 2 distinct source IDs per section in `_work/evidence_matrix.md`; the final HTML should usually show 3+ distinct source IDs per major section. |
| Primary/source-of-truth check | At least 1 primary or near-primary source where available: filing, company page, registry, patent, investor announcement, regulatory record, official report, customer/procurement record. |
| Mechanism | Explain how the evidence changes economics, adoption, pricing power, risk, financing need, valuation, or exit probability. A fact without mechanism is not analysis. |
| Public-equity source-of-truth | For listed companies, use primary filings or company IR for financial statements and record market data timestamp, exchange, currency, latest price, market cap, and enterprise value if available. |
| Public-equity financial analysis | For listed companies, analyze income statement, balance sheet, cash flow statement, notes/accounting quality, valuation, peer comparison, and stock-price context before making a recommendation. |
| Company-claim verification | Mark material pitch-deck claims as verified, partially verified, unverified, contradicted, or not publicly disclosed. |
| Quantification | At least 2 numbers, ranges, or proxies for measurable sections; if unavailable, state what evidence is missing. |
| Comparison | At least 1 competitor, benchmark, base rate, industry norm, or historical comparable. |
| Counter-evidence | At least 1 contradicting source, weakness, adverse case, or reason the thesis may fail. |
| Investor implication | A decision-relevant conclusion: invest, pass, wait, lower valuation, add condition, or request diligence. |

The `_work/evidence_matrix.md` table is a hard gate. Each section's `Deep Evidence Table` must contain source IDs, source type, finding/fact, mechanism, benchmark or peer context, weakening evidence, investor implication, confidence, and follow-up. Do not mark a section complete by checking boxes unless those cells contain section-specific content.

Evidence gate failure rules:

- If a section has only company-provided material, write it as low-confidence and do not make a strong positive claim.

The latest filed period is the quarter ended 2026-06-27, where revenue rose 16.4% to $109,417M on gross margin of 50.1% and operating margin of 32.6%. No fourth-quarter fiscal 2026 earnings release and no fiscal 2026 annual report were on EDGAR as of 2026-10-31; Apple's fiscal 2025 equivalents were filed on 2025-10-30 and 2025-10-31, so the annual report is due imminently and the figures here are trailing twelve months to 2026-06-27 [S5, S6].

### The growth is half tax base effect, and a quarter buyback

Fiscal 2025's net income rose 19.5%, but pretax income rose 7.5% ($132,729M against $123,485M) and the tax provision fell 30.3% to $20,719M because fiscal 2024 carried the one-time $10.2bn Irish charge — $15.8bn payable to Ireland, offset by a $4.8bn US foreign tax credit and $823M of released unrecognised benefits. At $344.63 on 2026-10-30 and 14,715M diluted shares the equity is worth $5.07trn, 39.5x trailing EPS and a 2.70% free cash flow yield, while the ten-year Treasury yielded 4.93%; repurchasing at that spread is accretive to EPS and not obviously accretive to value per share [S5, S6, S9].

### Cash is real; the working-capital cushion is not

Cash generation is the strongest part of the record and the hardest to fake: operating cash flow of $146,724M against capital expenditure of $10,041M, with free cash flow at 1.06x net income. The anomaly is fiscal 2025, when free cash flow fell to 0.88x of net income despite $111,482M of operating cash flow; cash paid for income taxes that year was $43,369M, 32.7% of pretax income against a 15.6% book rate and 21.1% in fiscal 2024 — a gap consistent with settlement payments on the Irish case and the TCJA repatriation tax, the final $8.8bn of which was paid in the nine months to 2026-06-27. That supports reading the gap as timing, and the recovery to 1.06x is consistent with it. The working-capital change runs the other way: inventory reached $11,092M at 2026-06-27 from $5,925M a year earlier, an 87% increase against 16.2% revenue growth, lifting days inventory to 16.9 from 9.4 and pulling the cash conversion cycle to −56.8 days from −71.1 at the fiscal 2025 year-end [S5, S6].

The balance sheet carries no leverage risk: at 2026-06-27 Apple held $146,517M of cash and marketable securities against $84,344M of debt, for net cash of $62,173M, up from $33,763M, with commercial paper cut to $1,997M from $7,979M, and other income and expense netted to −$321M in fiscal 2025 because interest earned on the securities book offsets interest paid. The commitments that matter are forward purchases — $57.0bn of manufacturing purchase obligations, $56.2bn due within twelve months, and $29.3bn of other purchase obligations — which fix component supply and, with it, the cost base when memory prices move. Two accounting details deserve attention: gross intangible assets rose $13,270M to $38,220M in nine months with no goodwill recognised, which points to purchased intellectual property or content rather than acquisitions and is not explained in the quarterly filing; and gross unrecognised tax benefits were $23.2bn at 2025-09-27, of which $10.6bn would affect the effective rate and up to $6bn may move within twelve months. Reported returns are not usable as quality scores: return on equity was 148.8% and return on invested capital 320.6% on invested capital of $45,347M — $107,520M of equity plus $84,344M of debt less $146,517M of securities — because $258,212M of cumulative buybacks shrank the equity base. The honest comparison is return on assets of 36.1% against Microsoft's 35.9% return on invested capital in fiscal 2026 and Alphabet's 37.0% in fiscal 2025 [S6, S27, S41].

### What moves the outcome, and by how much

The geographic picture also cuts against the standard bear case: Greater China revenue rose 30% to $64,839M in the nine months to 2026-06-27 and 22% in the June quarter, so nine months already exceed the whole of fiscal 2025's $64,377M after two years of decline. What moves the outcome most is gross margin. On trailing-twelve-month revenue of $466,823M one point of gross margin is $4,668M of pretax profit, or 3.0% of net income, while one point of revenue growth at the current margin is $1,878M, or 1.5%. The cash is real and the balance sheet is net cash; the growth is weaker than reported; and the margin sits at a cyclical high with an unquantified refund inside it. An investor paying 39.5x trailing earnings is paying for the first and third to persist while the second is already reversing. The diligence question that matters most is what the fiscal 2026 annual report says about inventory composition and the size of the tariff refund, neither of which the quarterly filings quantify [S6, S82].

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Playbook: analysis_core.md > Mandatory Evidence Gate

## Mandatory Evidence Gate

Do not draft the final report until every material section has an evidence packet in `_work/evidence_matrix.md`. Evidence may include public web sources, user-provided files, filings, databases, industry reports, patents, job posts, media interviews, customer/procurement records, or clearly labelled analyst estimates.

Minimum evidence packet per section:

| Required item | Minimum standard |
| --- | --- |
| Search work | 3-6 targeted queries unless user-provided materials are sufficient. |
| Sources opened | At least 2 independent sources; 3+ for market, competition, team, funding, financials, and risk when public data exists. |
| Source IDs | At least 2 distinct source IDs per section in `_work/evidence_matrix.md`; the final HTML should usually show 3+ distinct source IDs per major section. |
| Primary/source-of-truth check | At least 1 primary or near-primary source where available: filing, company page, registry, patent, investor announcement, regulatory record, official report, customer/procurement record. |
| Mechanism | Explain how the evidence changes economics, adoption, pricing power, risk, financing need, valuation, or exit probability. A fact without mechanism is not analysis. |
| Public-equity source-of-truth | For listed companies, use primary filings or company IR for financial statements and record market data timestamp, exchange, currency, latest price, market cap, and enterprise value if available. |
| Public-equity financial analysis | For listed companies, analyze income statement, balance sheet, cash flow statement, notes/accounting quality, valuation, peer comparison, and stock-price context before making a recommendation. |
| Company-claim verification | Mark material pitch-deck claims as verified, partially verified, unverified, contradicted, or not publicly disclosed. |
| Quantification | At least 2 numbers, ranges, or proxies for measurable sections; if unavailable, state what evidence is missing. |
| Comparison | At least 1 competitor, benchmark, base rate, industry norm, or historical comparable. |
| Counter-evidence | At least 1 contradicting source, weakness, adverse case, or reason the thesis may fail. |
| Investor implication | A decision-relevant conclusion: invest, pass, wait, lower valuation, add condition, or request diligence. |

The `_work/evidence_matrix.md` table is a hard gate. Each section's `Deep Evidence Table` must contain source IDs, source type, finding/fact, mechanism, benchmark or peer context, weakening evidence, investor implication, confidence, and follow-up. Do not mark a section complete by checking boxes unless those cells contain section-specific content.

Evidence gate failure rules:

- If a section has only company-provided material, write it as low-confidence and do not make a strong positive claim.
- If no independent source can verify a claim, explicitly say `not independently verified`.
- If a section lacks counter-evidence, add a red-team paragraph with the most plausible failure mode.
- If a section lacks quantification, state which metric is missing and how it affects investment confidence.
- If a section lacks peer/benchmark context, do not score it above 7/10.
- For a public-equity report, do not issue Buy/Add/Sell/Reduce before analyzing latest price/valuation, income statement quality, margin drivers, cash flow conversion, working capital, capex, balance-sheet health, accounting notes, debt/liquidity, capital allocation, and downside risk. If financial statements or price data cannot be obtained, make that the central limitation and use Watchlist/Hold off unless the user only asked for a preliminary screen.

European Commission State Aid Decision
On August 30, 2016, the Commission announced its decision that Ireland granted state aid to the Company by providing tax opinions in 1991 and 2007 concerning the tax allocation of profits of the Irish branches of two subsidiaries of the Company (“State Aid Decision”). The State Aid Decision ordered Ireland to calculate and recover additional taxes from the Company for the period June 2003 through December 2014. Irish legislative changes, effective as of January 2015, eliminated the application of the tax opinions from that date forward.
The Company and Ireland appealed the State Aid Decision to the General Court of the Court of Justice of the European Union (“General Court”). On July 15, 2020, the General Court annulled the State Aid Decision. On September 25, 2020, the Commission appealed the General Court’s decision to the European Court of Justice (“ECJ”). On September 10, 2024, the ECJ announced that it had set aside the 2020 judgment of the General Court and confirmed the Commission’s 2016 State Aid Decision. As a result, during the fourth quarter of 2024 the Company recorded a one-time income tax charge of $ 10.2 billion, net, which represented $ 15.8 billion payable to Ireland via release of amounts held in escrow, partially offset by a U.S. foreign tax credit of $ 4.8 billion and a decrease in unrecognized tax benefits of $ 823 million.
