arguments.markdown:
Apple's competitive position strengthened in 2026 in every hardware line except smartwatches, but the gain is crisis-specific — bought with memory supply and price discipline rather than product superiority — and it is being offset where profit is made, because the App Store commission that funds the premium position is being dismantled by courts and regulators rather than by a rival's product. Apple leads no hardware category outright except detachable tablets, and its annual report concedes minority share in smartphones, PCs, tablets and wearables. Head to head, Samsung shipped 62.7 million handsets in the second quarter of 2026 versus Apple's 55.7 million. [S102]

### The lead is in integration, not in units

Apple's 20.2% of global smartphone shipments in Q2 2026 was a record for that quarter and a 3.9 percentage point gain, but Samsung's 22.7% was larger and Xiaomi's 26.4% collapse explains much of the redistribution. In personal computing Apple is second at 18.2% against Lenovo's 20.1%, yet macOS shipments grew 17.4% while Windows fell 6.7% and Android 19.6%, and macOS is the only major operating system IDC expects to grow in 2026. The clearest structural lead is detachable tablets at 55.3%; the weakest spot is smartwatches, where Huawei leads 18.8% to 17.2%, so Apple's 15.5% of all wearables rests on earwear, where it holds 17.2%. [S104]

| Product | Competitor | Competitor share, Q2 2026 | Apple share | Technology basis | Price position | Switching cost | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone, global | Samsung | 22.7%, +3.2pp | 20.2%, +3.9pp | iOS integration and secured memory supply | Industry ASP $581; Apple above it | High: iCloud, iMessage, purchased apps | S102, S66 |
| iPhone, China | Huawei | 22.6%, +4.5pp | 18.1%, +4.2pp | iOS against domestic HarmonyOS | Apple held prices while Android raised them | Medium: leaving iOS loses Apple services | S40 |
| PCs and tablets | Lenovo | 20.1%, +2.5pp | 18.2%, -0.4% | macOS against Windows | MacBook Neo attacks entry pricing | Medium | S103, S106 |
| Services and App Store | Alphabet, Google Play | $471.1bn TTM revenue | $109.2bn Services at 75.4% gross margin | iOS distribution against Google Play | 15-30% commission, under challenge | High for consumers, falling for developers | S5, S42, S80 |

### Samsung is the dangerous one, and the reason is memory

Samsung is the most dangerous competitor, and not because of the Galaxy S26 Ultra. When memory is more than 65% of bill of materials at the low end, the binding constraint is supply access, and Samsung is the only top-five handset vendor that also sells memory: it grew shipments 8.1% and took 3.2 points of share in Q2 2026 while Xiaomi fell 26.4% and vivo 19.6%. Apple's answer was to secure memory early, which is why its units fell only 1.3% in 2026 against Android's 24.3% and why IDC puts iOS at a record 23.6% of shipments — a sourcing feat rather than a structural advantage, and it lapses when memory normalises while Samsung keeps its cost position. Samsung also holds the foldable franchise Apple now attacks: the iPhone Duo went on sale on 2026-10-23 at a reported $1,999, below the $2,550 average price IDC assumes, against a forecast of more than 17 million foldable iPhones by 2027 and 40% of a category growing 12.6% to 22.9 million units this year. [S66, S59]

### In China the competitor and the rules are different

Huawei held 22.6% of a Chinese market that fell 4.3% in Q2 2026 and grew 19.9% by holding prices while Android rivals raised theirs, leaning on HarmonyOS, which IDC expects to reach 51 million units in 2026; Apple grew 24.4% and gained 4.2 points to 18.1%, so both premium ends expanded while OPPO, vivo and Xiaomi contracted. The mechanism is a domestic operating system plus price discipline, and neither is a feature Apple can copy. HarmonyOS draws on the national preference that makes Apple's China revenue politically exposed, so the 30% China revenue growth belongs behind a competition risk; Apple Intelligence was registered with the Chinese internet regulator on 2026-07-15 alongside Alibaba's Qwen and Baidu, which narrows the AI gap in the one market where it mattered most but does not settle it. [S40, S120]

### The profit pool is being taken by courts, not by rivals

Apple's FY2025 annual report discloses that it is subject to a U.S. court order preventing it from imposing any commission on certain purchases consumers make, that its compliance plan under the Digital Markets Act has been challenged by the European Commission, and that it faces U.S. monopolization suits over smartphones; separately, the September 2, 2025 remedies order against Google, if upheld, could remove the search-distribution payments inside Services. No competitor needs to win a device sale for the 75.4% services gross margin to compress: a developer that routes a subscriber to the web converts a 15-30% commission into a payment-processing fee, and Services growth of 14.1% then arrives at a lower margin. The hardware position improved while the pricing power behind it was cut by a court in the United States and a regulator in Europe. [S5]

| Product | Leader | Challenger | Niche | Emerging threat | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone | Samsung, 22.7% of units | Apple, 20.2% and gaining | Huawei in China, 22.6% | HarmonyOS at 51m units; AI-first Android flagships | S102, S40, S66 |
| PCs and tablets | Lenovo, 20.1% | Apple, 18.2%, with the only growing OS | Dell in workstations, 40.0% | HarmonyOS NEXT at 1.6%; Windows-on-ARM | S103, S106 |
| Services | Apple, $109.2bn | Alphabet through Google Play | Netflix, Spotify, Epic | Web payments and alternative marketplaces | S5, S42, S80 |

### AI and the phone already in the buyer's pocket

Where Apple is not ahead is AI: the all-new Siri AI arrived at WWDC26 in June 2026, while Samsung's AI-equipped Galaxy S26 Ultra is credited by IDC with returning Samsung to first place in Q1 2026, and research and development rose 32.5% to $34.0 billion in nine months of FY2026 — the cost of catching up, not the reward for leading. The strongest competitor is the handset already in the buyer's pocket: replacement cycles are lengthening, IDC describes Chinese buyers as postponing rather than abandoning upgrades, and the 173 million sub-$100 units shipped in 2025 are leaving the market, which supports Services attach while suppressing units. Three risks follow: if AI becomes the reason a buyer upgrades, Apple competes on integration rather than capability; if HarmonyOS reaches first-time buyers in lower-tier cities, they never enter iOS; and if the U.S. injunction spreads to other storefronts, the take rate falls further. Unit position and profit per unit are moving in opposite directions, so the question worth paying for is not who sells more phones but what share of the transaction Apple controls in 2027. Confidence is high in the shares and the legal facts and medium beyond 2028, when memory normalises and the crisis-specific advantage lapses. Open diligence questions: what proportion of Services revenue is commission rather than subscription or advertising? What margin does the foldable carry at $1,999? Does Siri AI run on-device or through a partner, and at what cost per query? [S13, S66, S40]

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Technology & Product (technology_product, revision 3 by Product Analyst, 8,960 characters)
Apple's silicon-plus-OS stack is still the widest integrated consumer technology stack in the industry, but in 2026 the company rented the one layer it could not build — the frontier model — so what remains defensible is distribution, custom silicon and regulated health sensing, not leadership in artificial intelligence. In two years: the A19 Pro shipped in September 2025 on TSMC N3P; the A20 Pro moved the iPhone to TSMC N2 in September 2026; the C2 modem reached the flagship; the first foldable iPhone shipped at $1,999; and on 2026-01-12 Apple and Google announced that the next generation of Apple Foundation Models would be based on Gemini [S58, S59, S63, S64].

### The silicon lead is real, costly, and rented from TSMC

The A19 Pro used TSMC N3P with two performance cores at up to 4.26 GHz; a year later the A20 Pro moved to TSMC N2 with a dual 16-core Neural Engine — 32 neural cores — and ~52 TOPS, about double the prior generation's AI throughput. N2 wafers are reported at ~$30,000 against $18,000-20,000 for 3nm, so each capability step arrives with higher silicon cost. Product gross margin was 39.9% in the nine months to 2026-06-27 versus 36.9% a year earlier, but only with tariff refunds and mix offsetting "higher costs, including memory", and the 10-Q warns that advanced-semiconductor, NAND and DRAM constraints are expected to intensify [S6, S64].

| Metric | Value | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Node, A19 Pro / A20 Pro | TSMC N3P (2025) / N2 (2026) | Teardown and trade reporting | S63, S64 |
| CPU clock, A19 Pro | up to 4.26 GHz, 6 cores | Published specification | S63 |
| Neural Engine, A20 Pro | 32 cores, ~52 TOPS, ~2x A19 Pro | Trade-press estimate | S64 |
| N2 wafer price | ~$30,000 vs $18,000-20,000 at 3nm | Trade-press estimate | S64 |
| Product gross margin | 39.9% vs 36.9% (9M FY2025) | Reported financials | S6 |
| On-device model / PCC context | ~3B parameters / 32K tokens | Apple research and developer docs | S61, S62 |

### Apple Intelligence is an architecture with a rented brain

On device, Apple runs a ~3B-parameter model optimised through KV-cache sharing and 2-bit quantisation-aware training; on its servers, a Parallel-Track Mixture-of-Experts model runs inside Private Cloud Compute, which enforces stateless processing, no privileged runtime access even for Apple staff, and verifiable software images with attestation. The binding constraint is memory bandwidth and power: phone-class memory caps practical on-device inference at single-digit billions of parameters, which is why harder queries are offloaded — a constraint visible in research needed to run 70B models at the edge. The ceiling is disclosed: a 32K-token context is small against frontier assistants, and Apple's own models were not frontier-quality, which is why the Google agreement exists. The unresolved question — the one that decides whether the privacy story holds — is where Gemini-derived inference physically runs. Apple says Apple Intelligence continues on Apple devices and Private Cloud Compute; trade reporting says Google's cloud performs the Gemini computation and puts the licence at ~$1bn a year, on top of a default-search payment of ~$20bn. Neither figure is Apple-confirmed [S8, S58, S60, S61, S86]. Apple's differentiation is orchestration, distribution and privacy, not model quality; an investor should underwrite the cash flow and the installed base, not the AI layer.

| Dimension | Apple 2024 (AFM v1) | Apple 2026 (Gemini-based AFM) | Google (supplier) | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Frontier model | Own ~3B on-device plus server model | Gemini-derived | Owns Gemini | S58, S61 |
| Cost structure | Fixed R&D and data-centre capex | Fixed R&D plus per-query licence | Licence revenue | S58, S86 |
| What Apple keeps | Silicon, OS, orchestration | Silicon, OS, interface, orchestration | Model, training, inference | S58, S60 |

### Products: a strong cycle, a late foldable, a spatial computer that never became a platform

The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max launched on 2026-09-09 at $1,199 and $1,299; the foldable iPhone Duo at $1,999 went on sale on 2026-10-23. iPhone net sales rose 22% to $196.5bn in the nine months to 2026-06-27, with Greater China up 30%. The C2 modem supports US mmWave and uses 15% less energy than the C1X, but the larger iPhone 18 Pro Max appears to keep a Qualcomm modem, so Qualcomm retains leverage over the highest-ASP SKU. Vision Pro is the counter-example to Apple's category-creation record: ~390,000 units in 2024, ~45,000 in the December 2025 quarter despite the M5 refresh, ~600,000 lifetime, and an IDC forecast of ~290,000 units in 2026 [S59, S13, S87].

| iPhone 18 Pro / Pro Max | Commercial | 2026-09 | $196.5bn, 54% of 9M | Products 39.9% | C2 in Pro Max, 2027 | S59, S6 |
| iPhone Duo (foldable) | Commercial | 2026-10-23 | Inside iPhone; undisclosed | Not disclosed | First-quarter volume | S59 |
| Watch Series 11 / Ultra 3 | Commercial | 2025-09 | Wearables $27.3bn, +2% | Not disclosed | Hypertension roll-out | S5, S6 |
| Vision Pro (M5) | Commercial | 2025-10 | ~45k units Q4 2025 | Not disclosed | Lower-cost model, late 2026 | S87 |
| Services | Commercial | — | $91.7bn, +14% | 76.3% | AI tier / iCloud+ gating | S6, S107 |

### What is enforceable is regulatory, not patent

Apple publishes no patent count; the FY2025 10-K says only that it is "pursuing thousands of applications around the world" and that no single right protects its products. Patent counts and peer comparison were not obtainable — the registries could not be searched — so the patent moat is unquantified. What is documented feature by feature is a regulatory estate: hypertension and sleep-apnoea notifications, a hearing-aid De Novo grant and a medical imaging calibration feature, each cleared after its own clinical file. That is a slower, more durable barrier than a patent family, and the filings below date each clearance.

| Sleep Apnea Notification | K240929 | US FDA | 2024-09-13 | Cleared 510(k) | Watch sensing | S33 |
| Hearing Aid Feature | DEN230081 | US FDA | 2024-09-12 | De Novo granted | AirPods | S34 |
| Medical Imaging Calibration | K253582 | US FDA | 2026-04-01 | Cleared 510(k) | Display calibration | S29 |

### The moat is wide at the bottom of the stack and thin at the top

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Custom SoC and modem | 9 | Top design team plus priority TSMC N2 access; a decade and an Intel acquisition | 4-5 years | S59, S64 |
| Hardware-OS integration | 8 | Six operating systems co-designed with custom silicon | 3-5 years | S5 |
| On-device model efficiency | 5 | Quantisation and KV-cache techniques are published | 1-2 years | S61 |
| Frontier model | 3 | Available to licence, as Apple has shown | 1-2 years, by cheque | S58 |
| FDA-cleared health features | 7 | Each feature needs its own trial and clearance | 3-4 years | S30, S33 |
| Installed base and developers | 10 | A decade of switching costs, record active base | 10+ years | S13, S87 |
| **Composite** | **8/10 hardware, 4/10 AI** | The stack is hard to copy; the intelligence is not | **4-5 years for hardware** | S58, S64 |

The replication test answers the question directly: 50 senior silicon and operating-system engineers with Apple's published patents could match a phone-class SoC and OS in four to five years, and could rent a competitive model next quarter. The moat protects the cash-generating layer, not the differentiating one. The counter-evidence is Apple's own record: Siri needed a Google licence, the car was cancelled, Vision Pro has not reached platform volumes. The advantage holds only if on-device AI lifts upgrade rates and regulators leave the App Store economics that fund the silicon intact. Two diligence questions settle it: whether the Google agreement allows fine-tuning for on-device use, and whether the 2027 Pro Max moves fully to the C2 [S58, S59, S87].

::: evidence
**Apple's integration advantage is durable in silicon and distribution, but it no longer extends to the model layer.**

The A20 Pro's 2nm node and 32-core Neural Engine keep Apple at the leading edge of phone silicon, and twelve FDA device records since 2020 give it a regulated feature estate rivals must replicate trial by trial. But basing the next Apple Foundation Models on Gemini concedes that the frontier layer is bought, and the reported ~$1bn annual licence turns a fixed R&D advantage into a variable cost paid to a competitor [S58, S64, S86].

arguments.markdown:
Apple's cash conversion and balance sheet are as good as the multiple implies, but the earnings growth is not: fiscal 2025's 22.7% EPS growth becomes 10.4% once the $10.2bn Irish State Aid tax charge in the prior year is normalised out, and fiscal 2026's margin is being flattered by a tariff refund Apple does not quantify. The three-year record is slowing revenue and rising margin: revenue fell 2.8% in fiscal 2023, grew 2.0% in fiscal 2024 and 6.4% to $416,161M in fiscal 2025, while gross margin rose from 44.1% to 46.9% and operating margin from 29.8% to 32.0%. The latest filed period is the quarter ended 2026-06-27, where revenue rose 16.4% to $109,417M on gross margin of 50.1% and operating margin of 32.6%. No fourth-quarter fiscal 2026 earnings release and no fiscal 2026 annual report were on EDGAR as of 2026-10-31; Apple's fiscal 2025 equivalents were filed on 2025-10-30 and 2025-10-31, so the annual report is due imminently and the figures here are trailing twelve months to 2026-06-27 [S5, S6].

| Free cash flow | $99,584M | $108,807M | $98,767M | n/a | $136,683M | S5, S6 |
| Free cash flow / net income | 1.03x | 1.16x | 0.88x | n/a | 1.06x | S5, S6 |

### The growth is half tax base effect, and a quarter buyback

Fiscal 2025's net income rose 19.5%, but pretax income rose 7.5% ($132,729M against $123,485M) and the tax provision fell 30.3% to $20,719M because fiscal 2024 carried the one-time $10.2bn Irish charge — $15.8bn payable to Ireland, offset by a $4.8bn US foreign tax credit and $823M of released unrecognised benefits. Normalising fiscal 2024 at fiscal 2025's 15.6% rate gives $104,222M and underlying growth of 7.5%, not 19.5%. The EPS gap above that is the buyback: from fiscal 2023 to fiscal 2025 net income grew 15.5% while diluted EPS grew 21.7% and diluted shares fell 5.1%, so 5.4 percentage points of EPS growth was a smaller denominator — and that contribution is fading, at 1.9 percentage points in the trailing twelve months (EPS +16.9% against net income +15.1%), because repurchases slowed to $62,094M in the nine months to 2026-06-27 from $70,579M while operating cash flow rose 43%. Capital return has stopped outrunning cash: buybacks and dividends were $97,866M against free cash flow of $136,683M, or 72%, against 107% in fiscal 2025, and net cash rose by $28,410M in nine months. At $344.63 on 2026-10-30 and 14,715M diluted shares the equity is worth $5.07trn, 39.5x trailing EPS and a 2.70% free cash flow yield, while the ten-year Treasury yielded 4.93%; repurchasing at that spread is accretive to EPS and not obviously accretive to value per share [S5, S6, S9].

### Cash is real; the working-capital cushion is not

Cash generation is the strongest part of the record and the hardest to fake: operating cash flow of $146,724M against capital expenditure of $10,041M, with free cash flow at 1.06x net income. The anomaly is fiscal 2025, when free cash flow fell to 0.88x of net income despite $111,482M of operating cash flow; cash paid for income taxes that year was $43,369M, 32.7% of pretax income against a 15.6% book rate and 21.1% in fiscal 2024 — a gap consistent with settlement payments on the Irish case and the TCJA repatriation tax, the final $8.8bn of which was paid in the nine months to 2026-06-27. That supports reading the gap as timing, and the recovery to 1.06x is consistent with it. The working-capital change runs the other way: inventory reached $11,092M at 2026-06-27 from $5,925M a year earlier, an 87% increase against 16.2% revenue growth, lifting days inventory to 16.9 from 9.4 and pulling the cash conversion cycle to −56.8 days from −71.1 at the fiscal 2025 year-end [S5, S6].

The balance sheet carries no leverage risk: at 2026-06-27 Apple held $146,517M of cash and marketable securities against $84,344M of debt, for net cash of $62,173M, up from $33,763M, with commercial paper cut to $1,997M from $7,979M, and other income and expense netted to −$321M in fiscal 2025 because interest earned on the securities book offsets interest paid. The commitments that matter are forward purchases — $57.0bn of manufacturing purchase obligations, $56.2bn due within twelve months, and $29.3bn of other purchase obligations — which fix component supply and, with it, the cost base when memory prices move. Two accounting details deserve attention: gross intangible assets rose $13,270M to $38,220M in nine months with no goodwill recognised, which indicates purchased intellectual property, content or asset acquisitions rather than share purchases, and is not explained in the quarterly filing; and gross unrecognised tax benefits were $23.2bn at 2025-09-27, of which $10.6bn would affect the effective rate and up to $6bn may move within twelve months [S6].

### Returns are distorted by the buyback, not flattered by the business

Reported returns are not usable as quality scores: return on equity was 148.8% and return on invested capital 320.6% on invested capital of $45,347M — $107,520M of equity plus $84,344M of debt less $146,517M of securities — because $258,212M of cumulative buybacks shrank the equity base. The honest comparison is return on assets of 36.1% against Microsoft's 35.9% return on invested capital in fiscal 2026 and Alphabet's 37.0% in fiscal 2025 [S6, S27, S41].

### What moves the outcome, and by how much

The geographic picture also cuts against the standard bear case: Greater China revenue rose 30% to $64,839M in the nine months to 2026-06-27 and 22% in the June quarter, so nine months already exceed the whole of fiscal 2025's $64,377M after two years of decline. What moves the outcome most is gross margin. On trailing-twelve-month revenue of $466,823M one point of gross margin is $4,668M of pretax profit, or 3.0% of net income, while one point of revenue growth at the current margin is $1,878M, or 1.5%. Three cases, all on the trailing twelve months and none a forecast: a two-point margin gain takes EPS to $9.24, a two-point give-back to $8.20, and a two-point give-back with the loss of the search licence to $7.11, 18.8% below the base — and the licence should be modelled as intact but repriced annually, because the September 2025 order permitted non-exclusive placement payments of one year or less rather than ending them, while the $20bn figure is a 2022 court-record number Apple has never confirmed. The cash is real and the balance sheet is net cash; the growth is weaker than reported; and the margin sits at a cyclical high with an unquantified refund inside it. An investor paying 39.5x trailing earnings is paying for the first and third to persist while the second is already reversing. The diligence question that matters most is what the fiscal 2026 annual report says about inventory composition and the size of the tariff refund, neither of which the quarterly filings quantify [S6, S82, S118].

::: info warning
**The fiscal 2026 gross margin is not yet a clean number.** Apple attributes an unquantified portion of the product-margin gain to tariff refunds and does not separate the refund from product mix; until the annual report does, the June quarter's margin should be treated as a peak rather than a baseline.
:::

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Market & Industry Analysis (market, revision 2 by Market Analyst, 8,997 characters)
Apple's markets are contracting in units and expanding in value, and Apple is taking value share inside that contraction: the case for FY2026-FY2028 rests on premiumisation and Services attach rather than device volume, is strongest in the United States, is adequate in Europe, and in China depends on a domestic champion's pricing discipline.

### The pool is shrinking in units and growing in value

IDC's August 2026 forecast has worldwide smartphone shipments at just over 1.0 billion units in 2026, down 16.7% and the steepest annual contraction on record, while total market value rises 6.3% to $613 billion and the average selling price reaches a record $581, up 27.6% in a year and revised up from the $550 IDC published one quarter earlier. The cause is cost, not demand: DRAM and NAND prices are up more than 300% year on year as capacity is redirected to AI servers, memory is more than 65% of bill of materials at the low end, and the sub-$100 tier that shipped 173 million units in 2025 fell close to 60% in the second quarter of 2026. This is a supply shock with a dated end, so 2026-2027 flatters Apple's unit share while genuinely lifting its price, and 2028 is the test of whether either survives. [S39]

Two sizing methods agree closely: 1.0 billion units at the $581 average price gives $581 billion, within 5% of IDC's $613 billion, so the unit and price series can be read together rather than as rival estimates. On that base Apple's serviceable market is the premium tier it addresses — an iOS share of 23.6% of 2026 shipments, a record — while the revenue it can obtain is what it already books: $466.8 billion trailing twelve months to 2026-06-27, which at the 16.2% growth rate of the first nine months of FY2026 implies $483 billion for FY2026. IDC's PC-plus-tablet pool compounds at 1.5% a year from 2026 to 2030, so device pools are not growth markets at any price. [S6]

| TAM, smartphone value (top-down) | Industry value estimate | $613bn, +6.3% | 2026 | IDC | S66 |
| TAM, smartphone value (bottom-up) | 1.0bn units x $581 ASP | ~$581bn | 2026 | Calculation on IDC inputs | S66 |
| TAM, personal computing devices | Units published, value not disclosed | ~398m units, -11.3%; 1.5% CAGR to 2030 | 2026 | IDC | S103 |

| SOM, Apple revenue | Reported | $466.8bn TTM | TTM to 2026-06-27 | Apple 10-Q | S6 |
| Near-term obtainable revenue | FY2025 $416.2bn grown at the 9M FY2026 rate | ~$483bn | FY2026E | Calculation on Apple filings | S5, S13 |
| Adjacent services pool | Alphabet revenue | $471.1bn TTM | TTM to 2026-09-30 | Alphabet 10-Q | S42 |

### China is the swing factor, and India sits in the wrong line

Apple's revenue is moving toward the faster-growing regions, but the swing is China. In the first nine months of FY2026 Greater China produced $64.8 billion, up 30.0% on a base of $49.9 billion, after falling from $72.6 billion in FY2023 to $64.4 billion in FY2025; the Americas grew 11.4% to $149.4 billion, Europe 16.1% to $95.6 billion, Japan 10.4% and Rest of Asia Pacific 19.4%. Greater China's $14.9 billion increase contributes 4.1 percentage points of the group's 16.2% growth, more than any other segment, and part of it is currency: a favourable renminbi effect in Greater China, an unfavourable yen effect in Japan. One reporting artefact matters: the Europe segment includes India, the Middle East and Africa, so the fastest-growing large smartphone market is invisible in the line labelled Europe and India is not a segment an investor can track. [S13]

| Greater China | ~66m units a quarter, 264m a year | -4.3% in Q2 2026, fifth straight decline; H2 2026 could be -20% | 18.1% of units, second behind Huawei; revenue +30.0% | Domestic operating system, subsidy withdrawal, data rules | Huawei 22.6%, OPPO 16.0%, vivo 16.0%, Xiaomi 12.4% | S40, S6 |
| Europe (segment includes India, Middle East, Africa) | India 31.0m units in Q1 2026 at a record $302 ASP | India units -4.1% but value +5.8%; Europe revenue +16.1% | Entered; fourth by units in India | DMA, price sensitivity, distribution | Samsung, Xiaomi, vivo, Lenovo, HP | S105, S103, S13 |
| Japan | Revenue $24.4bn in 9M FY2026 | Revenue +10.4%; units -25.6% in 2026 | Entered, premium strong; weak yen cuts revenue | Yen, saturated device base | Local Android vendors, Samsung | S13, S103, S6 |

### Services carries the margin and has no published pool size

The fastest-growing pool Apple actually monetises is Services: $109.2 billion, 26.2% of FY2025 revenue, at a 75.4% gross margin against 36.8% for products, growing 14.1% to $91.7 billion in the first nine months of FY2026. The adjacent pools are larger and largely not Apple's — Alphabet's trailing-twelve-month revenue is $471.1 billion — but the app economy itself has no published size in the sources retrieved: neither Apple nor the platform owners disclose app-store gross billings or mobile-advertising revenue in a sizeable form, so Apple's own Services line is the measured pool. The installed base behind it has the same gap: Apple states only that its active-device base reached an all-time high in the June 2026 quarter across every category and region, and publishes no device count in its FY2025 10-K or FY2026 results, so the figure of 2.3 billion devices often quoted alongside the business is unverified here and should carry none of the valuation. [S5]

### Who pays, and how much demand is policy

The budget owner is the consumer, in a discretionary purchase that is increasingly financed. In the United States and United Kingdom long-term interest-free financing is more prevalent, so IDC expects the premium end to hold while emerging markets fall more than 20%; in India brands lean on financing after the sub-$100 tier fell 59% and the $600-800 band grew 32%; in China the government subsidy that supported earlier quarters faded in the second quarter of 2026, so demand there is being withdrawn by policy rather than created by it. Apple's exposure to policy runs both ways: after the February 20, 2026 Supreme Court ruling struck down certain IEEPA tariffs, Apple recognised refunds as a reduction of product cost of sales, and those refunds contributed 2.0 percentage points of the June 2026 quarter's 50.1% gross margin — tariff policy moves Apple's margin by more than a product cycle does. [S105, S40, S13]

The counter-evidence is threefold, each strand dated. If memory prices normalise in 2028 as IDC expects, the entry tier rebuilds and Apple's 2026 share gain is contestable again. If China's June-quarter demand was pulled forward ahead of expected second-half price increases, as IDC's China team reports, the 30% growth line is a launch and currency effect. And if courts and the European Commission remove the App Store take rate, the 75%-margin layer that offsets hardware cyclicality stops compounding at its present rate. The investor implication is narrow: in a 1-billion-unit market Apple can grow revenue only if price rises faster than units fall, making average selling price, China durability and the Services take rate the variables worth monitoring. Sizing confidence is high, because two independent methods agree within 5%; confidence that the mix shift holds to 2028 is medium, because it rests on China and a legally contested commission. Three questions would close the gap: what share of Services revenue is commission-based rather than subscription, advertising or licensing; how much of the Greater China increase is currency; and what the current average replacement cycle is, measured rather than asserted. [S66, S40]

**Apple's addressable device market fell 16.7% in units in 2026 while growing 6.3% in value, and Apple's revenue grew 16.2% over nine months — the gap is premiumisation and China, not market growth (S66, S13).**

arguments.markdown:
Apple's competitive position strengthened in 2026 in every hardware line except smartwatches, but the gain is crisis-specific — bought with memory supply and price discipline rather than product superiority — and it is being offset where profit is made, because the App Store commission that funds the premium position is being dismantled by courts and regulators rather than by a rival's product. Apple leads no hardware category outright except detachable tablets, and its annual report concedes minority share in smartphones, PCs, tablets and wearables. Head to head, Samsung shipped 62.7 million handsets in the second quarter of 2026 versus Apple's 55.7 million. [S102]

### The lead is in integration, not in units

Apple's 20.2% of global smartphone shipments in Q2 2026 was a record for that quarter and a 3.9 percentage point gain, but Samsung's 22.7% was larger and Xiaomi's 26.4% collapse explains much of the redistribution. In personal computing Apple is second at 18.2% against Lenovo's 20.1%, yet macOS shipments grew 17.4% while Windows fell 6.7% and Android 19.6%, and macOS is the only major operating system IDC expects to grow in 2026. The clearest structural lead is detachable tablets at 55.3%; the weakest spot is smartwatches, where Huawei leads 18.8% to 17.2%, so Apple's 15.5% of all wearables rests on earwear, where it holds 17.2%. [S104]

| Product | Competitor | Competitor share, Q2 2026 | Apple share | Technology basis | Price position | Switching cost | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone, global | Samsung | 22.7%, +3.2pp | 20.2%, +3.9pp | iOS integration and secured memory supply | Industry ASP $581; Apple above it | High: iCloud, iMessage, purchased apps | S102, S66 |
| iPhone, China | Huawei | 22.6%, +4.5pp | 18.1%, +4.2pp | iOS against domestic HarmonyOS | Apple held prices while Android raised them | Medium: leaving iOS loses Apple services | S40 |
| PCs and tablets | Lenovo | 20.1%, +2.5pp | 18.2%, -0.4% | macOS against Windows | MacBook Neo attacks entry pricing | Medium | S103, S106 |
| Services and App Store | Alphabet, Google Play | $471.1bn TTM revenue | $109.2bn Services at 75.4% gross margin | iOS distribution against Google Play | 15-30% commission, under challenge | High for consumers, falling for developers | S5, S42, S80 |

### Samsung is the dangerous one, and the reason is memory

Samsung is the most dangerous competitor, and not because of the Galaxy S26 Ultra. When memory is more than 65% of bill of materials at the low end, the binding constraint is supply access, and Samsung is the only top-five handset vendor that also sells memory: it grew shipments 8.1% and took 3.2 points of share in Q2 2026 while Xiaomi fell 26.4% and vivo 19.6%. Apple's answer was to secure memory early, which is why its units fell only 1.3% in 2026 against Android's 24.3% and why IDC puts iOS at a record 23.6% of shipments — a sourcing feat rather than a structural advantage, and it lapses when memory normalises while Samsung keeps its cost position. Samsung also holds the foldable franchise Apple now attacks: the iPhone Duo went on sale on 2026-10-23 at a reported $1,999, below the $2,550 average price IDC assumes, against a forecast of more than 17 million foldable iPhones by 2027 and 40% of a category growing 12.6% to 22.9 million units this year. [S66, S59]

### In China the competitor and the rules are different

Huawei held 22.6% of a Chinese market that fell 4.3% in Q2 2026 and grew 19.9% by holding prices while Android rivals raised theirs, leaning on HarmonyOS, which IDC expects to reach 51 million units in 2026; Apple grew 24.4% and gained 4.2 points to 18.1%, so both premium ends expanded while OPPO, vivo and Xiaomi contracted. The mechanism is a domestic operating system plus price discipline, and neither is a feature Apple can copy. HarmonyOS draws on the national preference that makes Apple's China revenue politically exposed, so the 30% China revenue growth belongs behind a competition risk; Apple Intelligence was registered with the Chinese internet regulator on 2026-07-15 alongside Alibaba's Qwen and Baidu, which narrows the AI gap in the one market where it mattered most but does not settle it. [S40, S120]

### The profit pool is being taken by courts, not by rivals

Apple's FY2025 annual report discloses that it is subject to a U.S. court order preventing it from imposing any commission on certain purchases consumers make, that its compliance plan under the Digital Markets Act has been challenged by the European Commission, and that it faces U.S. monopolization suits over smartphones; separately, the September 2, 2025 remedies order against Google, if upheld, could remove the search-distribution payments inside Services. No competitor needs to win a device sale for the 75.4% services gross margin to compress: a developer that routes a subscriber to the web converts a 15-30% commission into a payment-processing fee, and Services growth of 14.1% then arrives at a lower margin. The hardware position improved while the pricing power behind it was cut by U.S. courts and European regulators. [S5]

| Product | Leader | Challenger | Niche | Emerging threat | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone | Samsung, 22.7% of units | Apple, 20.2% and gaining | Huawei in China, 22.6% | HarmonyOS at 51m units; AI-first Android flagships | S102, S40, S66 |
| PCs and tablets | Lenovo, 20.1% | Apple, 18.2%, with the only growing OS | Dell in workstations, 40.0% | HarmonyOS NEXT at 1.6%; Windows-on-ARM | S103, S106 |
| Services | Apple, $109.2bn | Alphabet through Google Play | Netflix, Spotify, Epic | Web payments and alternative marketplaces | S5, S42, S80 |

### AI and the phone already in the buyer's pocket

Where Apple is not ahead is AI: the all-new Siri AI arrived at WWDC26 in June 2026 on foundation models licensed from Google under their 2026-01-12 agreement, so its assistant now depends on the same company whose Play store it competes with. Samsung's AI-equipped Galaxy S26 Ultra is credited by IDC with returning Samsung to first place in Q1 2026, and research and development rose 32.5% to $34.0 billion in nine months of FY2026 — the cost of catching up, not the reward for leading. arguments.markdown:
Apple's competitive position strengthened in 2026 in every hardware line except smartwatches, but the gain is crisis-specific — bought with memory supply and price discipline rather than product superiority — and it is being offset where profit is made, because the App Store commission that funds the premium position is being dismantled by courts and regulators rather than by a rival's product. Apple leads no hardware category outright except detachable tablets, and its annual report concedes minority share in smartphones, PCs, tablets and wearables. Head to head, Samsung shipped 62.7 million handsets in Q2 2026 versus Apple's 55.7 million. [S102]

### The lead is in integration, not in units

Apple's 20.2% of global smartphone shipments in Q2 2026 was a record for that quarter and a 3.9 percentage point gain, but Samsung's 22.7% was larger and Xiaomi's 26.4% collapse explains much of the redistribution. In personal computing Apple is second at 18.2% to Lenovo's 20.1%, yet macOS shipments grew 17.4% while Windows fell 6.7% and Android 19.6%, and macOS is the only major operating system IDC expects to grow in 2026. The clearest structural lead is detachable tablets at 55.3%; the weakest spot is smartwatches, where Huawei leads 18.8% to 17.2%, so Apple's 15.5% of all wearables rests on earwear, where it holds 17.2%. [S104]

| Product | Competitor | Competitor share, Q2 2026 | Apple share | Technology basis | Price position | Switching cost | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone, global | Samsung | 22.7%, +3.2pp | 20.2%, +3.9pp | iOS integration and secured memory supply | Industry ASP $581; Apple above it | High: iCloud, iMessage, purchased apps | S102, S66 |
| iPhone, China | Huawei | 22.6%, +4.5pp | 18.1%, +4.2pp | iOS against domestic HarmonyOS | Apple held prices while Android raised them | Medium: leaving iOS loses Apple services | S40 |
| PCs and tablets | Lenovo | 20.1%, +2.5pp | 18.2%, -0.4% | macOS against Windows | MacBook Neo attacks entry pricing | Medium | S103, S106 |
| Services and App Store | Alphabet, Google Play | $471.1bn TTM revenue | $109.2bn Services at 75.4% gross margin | iOS distribution against Google Play | 15-30% commission, under challenge | High for consumers, falling for developers | S5, S42, S80 |

### Samsung is the dangerous one, and the reason is memory

Samsung is the most dangerous competitor, and not because of the Galaxy S26 Ultra. When memory is more than 65% of bill of materials at the low end, the binding constraint is supply access, and Samsung is the only top-five handset vendor that also sells memory: it grew shipments 8.1% and took 3.2 points of share in Q2 2026 while Xiaomi fell 26.4% and vivo 19.6%. Apple's answer was to secure memory early, which is why its units fell only 1.3% in 2026 against Android's 24.3% and why IDC puts iOS at a record 23.6% of shipments — a sourcing feat rather than a structural advantage, and it lapses when memory normalises while Samsung keeps its costs. Samsung also holds the foldable franchise Apple now attacks: the iPhone Duo went on sale on 2026-10-23 at a reported $1,999, below the $2,550 average price IDC assumes, against a forecast of more than 17 million foldable iPhones by 2027 and 40% of a category growing 12.6% to 22.9 million units this year. [S66, S59]

### In China the competitor and the rules are different

Huawei held 22.6% of a Chinese market that fell 4.3% in Q2 2026 and grew 19.9% by holding prices while Android rivals raised theirs, leaning on HarmonyOS, which IDC expects to reach 51 million units in 2026; Apple grew 24.4% and gained 4.2 points to 18.1%, so both premium ends expanded while OPPO, vivo and Xiaomi contracted. The mechanism is a domestic operating system plus price discipline, and neither is a feature Apple can copy. HarmonyOS draws on the national preference that makes Apple's China revenue politically exposed, so the 30% China revenue growth belongs behind a competition risk; Apple Intelligence was registered with China's internet regulator on 2026-07-15 alongside Alibaba's Qwen and Baidu, which narrows the AI gap in the one market where it mattered most but does not settle it. [S40, S120]

### The profit pool is being taken by courts, not by rivals

Apple's FY2025 annual report discloses that it is subject to a U.S. court order preventing it from imposing any commission on certain purchases consumers make, that its Digital Markets Act compliance plan has been challenged by the European Commission, and that it faces U.S. monopolization suits over smartphones; separately, the September 2, 2025 remedies order against Google, if upheld, could remove the search-distribution payments inside Services. No competitor needs to win a device sale for the 75.4% services margin to compress: a developer that routes a subscriber to the web converts a 15-30% commission into a payment-processing fee, and Services growth of 14.1% then arrives at a lower margin. The hardware position improved while the pricing power behind it was cut by U.S. courts and European regulators. [S5]

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Financial Analysis (financials, revision 3 by Fundamentals Analyst, 8,475 characters)
Apple's cash conversion and balance sheet are as good as the multiple implies, but the earnings growth is not: fiscal 2025's 22.7% EPS growth becomes 10.4% once the $10.2bn Irish State Aid tax charge in the prior year is normalised out, and fiscal 2026's margin is being flattered by a tariff refund Apple does not quantify. The three-year record is slowing revenue and rising margin: revenue fell 2.8% in fiscal 2023, grew 2.0% in fiscal 2024 and 6.4% to $416,161M in fiscal 2025, while gross margin rose from 44.1% to 46.9% and operating margin from 29.8% to 32.0%. The latest filed period is the quarter ended 2026-06-27, where revenue rose 16.4% to $109,417M on gross margin of 50.1% and operating margin of 32.6%. No fourth-quarter fiscal 2026 earnings release and no fiscal 2026 annual report were on EDGAR as of 2026-10-31; Apple's fiscal 2025 equivalents were filed on 2025-10-30 and 2025-10-31, so the annual report is due imminently and the figures here are trailing twelve months to 2026-06-27 [S5, S6].

| Line item | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 | Q3 FY2026 | TTM to 2026-06-27 | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | $383,285M | $391,035M | $416,161M | $109,417M | $466,823M | S5, S6 |
| Gross margin | 44.1% | 46.2% | 46.9% | 50.1% | 48.7% | S5, S6 |
| Operating margin | 29.8% | 31.5% | 32.0% | 32.6% | 33.2% | S5, S6 |
| Net income | $96,995M | $93,736M | $112,010M | $29,789M | $128,930M | S5, S6 |
| Diluted EPS | $6.13 | $6.08 | $7.46 | $2.02 | $8.72 | S5, S6 |
| Effective tax rate | 14.7% | 24.1% | 15.6% | 17.9% | 17.3% | S5, S6 |
| Operating cash flow | $110,543M | $118,254M | $111,482M | n/a | $146,724M | S5, S6 |
| Capital expenditure | $10,959M | $9,447M | $12,715M | n/a | $10,041M | S5, S6 |
| Free cash flow | $99,584M | $108,807M | $98,767M | n/a | $136,683M | S5, S6 |
| Free cash flow / net income | 1.03x | 1.16x | 0.88x | n/a | 1.06x | S5, S6 |

### The growth is half tax base effect, and a quarter buyback

Fiscal 2025's net income rose 19.5%, but pretax income rose 7.5% ($132,729M against $123,485M) and the tax provision fell 30.3% to $20,719M because fiscal 2024 carried the one-time $10.2bn Irish charge — $15.8bn payable to Ireland, offset by a $4.8bn US foreign tax credit and $823M of released unrecognised benefits. Normalising fiscal 2024 at fiscal 2025's 15.6% rate gives $104,222M and underlying growth of 7.5%, not 19.5%. The EPS gap above that is the buyback: from fiscal 2023 to fiscal 2025 net income grew 15.5% while diluted EPS grew 21.7% and diluted shares fell 5.1%, so 5.4 percentage points of EPS growth was a smaller denominator — and that contribution is fading, at 1.9 percentage points in the trailing twelve months (EPS +16.9% against net income +15.1%), because repurchases slowed to $62,094M in the nine months to 2026-06-27 from $70,579M while operating cash flow rose 43%. Capital return has stopped outrunning cash: buybacks and dividends were $97,866M against free cash flow of $136,683M, or 72%, against 107% in fiscal 2025, and net cash rose by $28,410M in nine months. At $344.63 on 2026-10-30 and 14,715M diluted shares the equity is worth $5.07trn, 39.5x trailing EPS and a 2.70% free cash flow yield, while the ten-year Treasury yielded 4.93%; repurchasing at that spread is accretive to EPS and not obviously accretive to value per share [S5, S6, S9].

### Cash is real; the working-capital cushion is not

Cash generation is the strongest part of the record and the hardest to fake: operating cash flow of $146,724M against capital expenditure of $10,041M, with free cash flow at 1.06x net income. The anomaly is fiscal 2025, when free cash flow fell to 0.88x of net income despite $111,482M of operating cash flow; cash paid for income taxes that year was $43,369M, 32.7% of pretax income against a 15.6% book rate and 21.1% in fiscal 2024 — a gap consistent with settlement payments on the Irish case and the TCJA repatriation tax, the final $8.8bn of which was paid in the nine months to 2026-06-27. That supports reading the gap as timing, and the recovery to 1.06x is consistent with it. The working-capital change runs the other way: inventory reached $11,092M at 2026-06-27 from $5,925M a year earlier, an 87% increase against 16.2% revenue growth, lifting days inventory to 16.9 from 9.4 and pulling the cash conversion cycle to −56.8 days from −71.1 at the fiscal 2025 year-end [S5, S6].

The balance sheet carries no leverage risk: at 2026-06-27 Apple held $146,517M of cash and marketable securities against $84,344M of debt, for net cash of $62,173M, up from $33,763M, with commercial paper cut to $1,997M from $7,979M, and other income and expense netted to −$321M in fiscal 2025 because interest earned on the securities book offsets interest paid. The commitments that matter are forward purchases — $57.0bn of manufacturing purchase obligations, $56.2bn due within twelve months, and $29.3bn of other purchase obligations — which fix component supply and, with it, the cost base when memory prices move. Two accounting details deserve attention: gross intangible assets rose $13,270M to $38,220M in nine months with no goodwill recognised, which indicates purchased intellectual property, content or asset acquisitions rather than share purchases, and is not explained in the quarterly filing; and gross unrecognised tax benefits were $23.2bn at 2025-09-27, of which $10.6bn would affect the effective rate and up to $6bn may move within twelve months [S6].

### Returns are distorted by the buyback, not flattered by the business

Reported returns are not usable as quality scores: return on equity was 148.8% and return on invested capital 320.6% on invested capital of $45,347M — $107,520M of equity plus $84,344M of debt less $146,517M of securities — because $258,212M of cumulative buybacks shrank the equity base. The honest comparison is return on assets of 36.1% against Microsoft's 35.9% return on invested capital in fiscal 2026 and Alphabet's 37.0% in fiscal 2025 [S6, S27, S41].

### What moves the outcome, and by how much

The geographic picture also cuts against the standard bear case: Greater China revenue rose 30% to $64,839M in the nine months to 2026-06-27 and 22% in the June quarter, so nine months already exceed the whole of fiscal 2025's $64,377M after two years of decline. What moves the outcome most is gross margin. On trailing-twelve-month revenue of $466,823M one point of gross margin is $4,668M of pretax profit, or 3.0% of net income, while one point of revenue growth at the current margin is $1,878M, or 1.5%. Three cases, all on the trailing twelve months and none a forecast: a two-point margin gain takes EPS to $9.24, a two-point give-back to $8.20, and a two-point give-back with the loss of the search licence to $7.11, 18.8% below the base — and the licence should be modelled as intact but repriced annually, because the September 2025 order permitted non-exclusive placement payments of one year or less rather than ending them, while the $20bn figure is a 2022 court-record number Apple has never confirmed. The cash is real and the balance sheet is net cash; the growth is weaker than reported; and the margin sits at a cyclical high with an unquantified refund inside it. An investor paying 39.5x trailing earnings is paying for the first and third to persist while the second is already reversing. The diligence question that matters most is what the fiscal 2026 annual report says about inventory composition and the size of the tariff refund, neither of which the quarterly filings quantify [S6, S82, S118].

::: info warning
**The fiscal 2026 gross margin is not yet a clean number.** Apple attributes an unquantified portion of the product-margin gain to tariff refunds and does not separate the refund from product mix; until the annual report does, the June quarter's margin should be treated as a peak rather than a baseline.
:::

arguments.markdown:
Apple's cash conversion and balance sheet are as good as the multiple implies, but the earnings growth is not: fiscal 2025's 22.7% EPS growth becomes 10.4% once the $10.2bn Irish State Aid tax charge in the prior year is normalised out, and 2.0 points of the June 2026 quarter's 50.1% gross margin came from tariff refunds rather than trading. The three-year record is slowing revenue and rising margin: revenue fell 2.8% in fiscal 2023, grew 2.0% in fiscal 2024 and 6.4% to $416,161M in fiscal 2025, while gross margin rose from 44.1% to 46.9% and operating margin from 29.8% to 32.0%. The latest filed period is the quarter ended 2026-06-27, where revenue rose 16.4% to $109,417M on gross margin of 50.1% and operating margin of 32.6%. No fourth-quarter fiscal 2026 earnings release and no fiscal 2026 annual report were on EDGAR as of 2026-10-31; Apple's fiscal 2025 equivalents were filed on 2025-10-30 and 2025-10-31, so the annual report is due imminently and the figures here are trailing twelve months to 2026-06-27 [S5, S6, S13].

| Line item | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 | Q3 FY2026 | TTM to 2026-06-27 | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | $383,285M | $391,035M | $416,161M | $109,417M | $466,823M | S5, S6 |
| Gross margin | 44.1% | 46.2% | 46.9% | 50.1% | 48.7% | S5, S6 |
| Operating margin | 29.8% | 31.5% | 32.0% | 32.6% | 33.2% | S5, S6 |
| Net income | $96,995M | $93,736M | $112,010M | $29,789M | $128,930M | S5, S6 |
| Diluted EPS | $6.13 | $6.08 | $7.46 | $2.02 | $8.72 | S5, S6 |
| Effective tax rate | 14.7% | 24.1% | 15.6% | 17.9% | 17.3% | S5, S6 |
| Operating cash flow | $110,543M | $118,254M | $111,482M | n/a | $146,724M | S5, S6 |
| Capital expenditure | $10,959M | $9,447M | $12,715M | n/a | $10,041M | S5, S6 |
| Free cash flow | $99,584M | $108,807M | $98,767M | n/a | $136,683M | S5, S6 |
| Free cash flow / net income | 1.03x | 1.16x | 0.88x | n/a | 1.06x | S5, S6 |

### The growth is half tax base effect, and a quarter buyback

Fiscal 2025's net income rose 19.5%, but pretax income rose 7.5% ($132,729M against $123,485M) and the tax provision fell 30.3% to $20,719M because fiscal 2024 carried the one-time $10.2bn Irish charge — $15.8bn payable to Ireland, offset by a $4.8bn US foreign tax credit and $823M of released unrecognised benefits. Normalising fiscal 2024 at fiscal 2025's 15.6% rate gives $104,222M and underlying growth of 7.5%, not 19.5%. The EPS gap above that is the buyback: from fiscal 2023 to fiscal 2025 net income grew 15.5% while diluted EPS grew 21.7% and diluted shares fell 5.1%, so 5.4 percentage points of EPS growth was a smaller denominator — and that contribution is fading, at 1.9 percentage points in the trailing twelve months (EPS +16.9% against net income +15.1%), because repurchases slowed to $62,094M in the nine months to 2026-06-27 from $70,579M while operating cash flow rose 43%. Capital return has stopped outrunning cash: buybacks and dividends were $97,866M against free cash flow of $136,683M, or 72%, against 107% in fiscal 2025, and net cash rose by $28,410M in nine months. At $344.63 on 2026-10-30 and 14,715M diluted shares the equity is worth $5.07trn, 39.5x trailing EPS and a 2.70% free cash flow yield, while the ten-year Treasury yielded 4.93%; repurchasing at that spread is accretive to EPS and not obviously accretive to value per share [S5, S6, S9].

### Cash is real; the working-capital cushion is not

Cash generation is the strongest part of the record and the hardest to fake: operating cash flow of $146,724M against capital expenditure of $10,041M, with free cash flow at 1.06x net income. The anomaly is fiscal 2025, when free cash flow fell to 0.88x of net income despite $111,482M of operating cash flow; cash paid for income taxes that year was $43,369M, 32.7% of pretax income against a 15.6% book rate and 21.1% in fiscal 2024 — a gap consistent with settlement payments on the Irish case and the TCJA repatriation tax, the final $8.8bn of which was paid in the nine months to 2026-06-27. That supports reading the gap as timing, and the recovery to 1.06x is consistent with it. The working-capital change runs the other way: inventory reached $11,092M at 2026-06-27 from $5,925M a year earlier, an 87% increase against 16.2% revenue growth, lifting days inventory to 16.9 from 9.4 and pulling the cash conversion cycle to −56.8 days from −71.1 at the fiscal 2025 year-end [S5, S6].

The balance sheet carries no leverage risk: at 2026-06-27 Apple held $146,517M of cash and marketable securities against $84,344M of debt, for net cash of $62,173M, up from $33,763M, with commercial paper cut to $1,997M from $7,979M, and other income and expense netted to −$321M in fiscal 2025 because interest earned on the securities book offsets interest paid. The commitments that matter are forward purchases — $57.0bn of manufacturing purchase obligations, $56.2bn due within twelve months, and $29.3bn of other purchase obligations — which fix component supply and, with it, the cost base when memory prices move. Two accounting details deserve attention: gross intangible assets rose $13,270M to $38,220M in nine months with no goodwill recognised, which indicates purchased intellectual property, content or asset acquisitions rather than share purchases, and is not explained in the quarterly filing; and gross unrecognised tax benefits were $23.2bn at 2025-09-27, of which $10.6bn would affect the effective rate and up to $6bn may move within twelve months [S6].

### Returns are distorted by the buyback, not flattered by the business

Reported returns are not usable as quality scores: return on equity was 148.8% and return on invested capital 320.6% on invested capital of $45,347M — $107,520M of equity plus $84,344M of debt less $146,517M of securities — because $258,212M of cumulative buybacks shrank the equity base. The honest comparison is return on assets of 36.1% against Microsoft's 35.9% return on invested capital in fiscal 2026 and Alphabet's 37.0% in fiscal 2025 [S6, S27, S41].

### What moves the outcome, and by how much

The geographic picture also cuts against the standard bear case: Greater China revenue rose 30% to $64,839M in the nine months to 2026-06-27 and 22% in the June quarter, so nine months already exceed the whole of fiscal 2025's $64,377M after two years of decline. What moves the outcome most is gross margin. On trailing-twelve-month revenue of $466,823M one point of gross margin is $4,668M of pretax profit, or 3.0% of net income, while one point of revenue growth at the current margin is $1,878M, or 1.5%. Three cases, all on the trailing twelve months and none a forecast: a two-point margin gain takes EPS to $9.24, a two-point give-back to $8.20, and a two-point give-back with the loss of the search licence to $7.11, 18.8% below the base — and the licence should be modelled as intact but repriced annually, because the September 2025 order permitted non-exclusive placement payments of one year or less rather than ending them, while the $20bn figure is a 2022 court-record number Apple has never confirmed. The cash is real and the balance sheet is net cash; the growth is weaker than reported; and the margin sits at a cyclical high with a tariff-refund component inside it. An investor paying 39.5x trailing earnings is paying for the first and third to persist while the second is already reversing. The diligence question that matters most is what the fiscal 2026 annual report says about inventory composition and the split between refund and product mix, neither of which the quarterly filings settle [S6, S82, S118].

::: info warning
**The fiscal 2026 gross margin is not yet a clean number.** Strip out the tariff refund Apple attributes to the June quarter and the margin is still above any full year in this record, but a smaller step-change than the reported figure implies; against an inventory build growing faster than revenue, the annual report carries the burden of proof.
:::

On March 21, 2024, the DOJ and a number of state and district attorneys general filed a civil antitrust lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey against the Company alleging monopolization or attempted monopolization in the markets for “performance smartphones” and “smartphones” in violation of U.S. antitrust laws. In addition, various civil litigation matters have been filed in state and federal courts in the U.S. alleging similar violations of U.S. antitrust laws and seeking monetary damages and other nonmonetary relief. The California District Court found that certain provisions of the Company’s App Review Guidelines violate California’s unfair competition law and issued an injunction (the “2021 Injunction”) enjoining the Company from prohibiting developers from including in their apps buttons, external links, or other calls to action that direct customers to purchasing mechanisms other than the Company’s in-app purchase system. The 2021 Injunction applies to apps on the U.S. storefronts of the iOS and iPadOS App Stores. On January 16, 2024, the Company implemented a plan to comply with the 2021 Injunction and filed a statement of compliance with the California District Court. On September 30, 2024, the Company filed a motion with the California District Court to narrow or vacate the 2021 Injunction. The Company will continue to vigorously defend its actions and employees, and has appealed the California District Court’s most recent decision to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit (“Ninth Circuit Court”). {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Technology & Product (technology_product, revision 3 by Product Analyst, 8,960 characters)
Apple's silicon-plus-OS stack is still the widest integrated consumer technology stack in the industry, but in 2026 the company rented the one layer it could not build — the frontier model — so what remains defensible is distribution, custom silicon and regulated health sensing, not leadership in artificial intelligence. In two years: the A19 Pro shipped in September 2025 on TSMC N3P; the A20 Pro moved the iPhone to TSMC N2 in September 2026; the C2 modem reached the flagship; the first foldable iPhone shipped at $1,999; and on 2026-01-12 Apple and Google announced that the next generation of Apple Foundation Models would be based on Gemini [S58, S59, S63, S64].

### The silicon lead is real, costly, and rented from TSMC

The A19 Pro used TSMC N3P with two performance cores at up to 4.26 GHz; a year later the A20 Pro moved to TSMC N2 with a dual 16-core Neural Engine — 32 neural cores — and ~52 TOPS, about double the prior generation's AI throughput. N2 wafers are reported at ~$30,000 against $18,000-20,000 for 3nm, so each capability step arrives with higher silicon cost. Product gross margin was 39.9% in the nine months to 2026-06-27 versus 36.9% a year earlier, but only with tariff refunds and mix offsetting "higher costs, including memory", and the 10-Q warns that advanced-semiconductor, NAND and DRAM constraints are expected to intensify [S6, S64].

| Metric | Value | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Node, A19 Pro / A20 Pro | TSMC N3P (2025) / N2 (2026) | Teardown and trade reporting | S63, S64 |
| CPU clock, A19 Pro | up to 4.26 GHz, 6 cores | Published specification | S63 |
| Neural Engine, A20 Pro | 32 cores, ~52 TOPS, ~2x A19 Pro | Trade-press estimate | S64 |
| N2 wafer price | ~$30,000 vs $18,000-20,000 at 3nm | Trade-press estimate | S64 |
| Product gross margin | 39.9% vs 36.9% (9M FY2025) | Reported financials | S6 |
| On-device model / PCC context | ~3B parameters / 32K tokens | Apple research and developer docs | S61, S62 |

### Apple Intelligence is an architecture with a rented brain

On device, Apple runs a ~3B-parameter model optimised through KV-cache sharing and 2-bit quantisation-aware training; on its servers, a Parallel-Track Mixture-of-Experts model runs inside Private Cloud Compute, which enforces stateless processing, no privileged runtime access even for Apple staff, and verifiable software images with attestation. The binding constraint is memory bandwidth and power: phone-class memory caps practical on-device inference at single-digit billions of parameters, which is why harder queries are offloaded — a constraint visible in research needed to run 70B models at the edge. The ceiling is disclosed: a 32K-token context is small against frontier assistants, and Apple's own models were not frontier-quality, which is why the Google agreement exists. The unresolved question — the one that decides whether the privacy story holds — is where Gemini-derived inference physically runs. Apple says Apple Intelligence continues on Apple devices and Private Cloud Compute; trade reporting says Google's cloud performs the Gemini computation and puts the licence at ~$1bn a year, on top of a default-search payment of ~$20bn. Neither figure is Apple-confirmed [S8, S58, S60, S61, S86]. Apple's differentiation is orchestration, distribution and privacy, not model quality; an investor should underwrite the cash flow and the installed base, not the AI layer.

| Dimension | Apple 2024 (AFM v1) | Apple 2026 (Gemini-based AFM) | Google (supplier) | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Frontier model | Own ~3B on-device plus server model | Gemini-derived | Owns Gemini | S58, S61 |
| Cost structure | Fixed R&D and data-centre capex | Fixed R&D plus per-query licence | Licence revenue | S58, S86 |
| What Apple keeps | Silicon, OS, orchestration | Silicon, OS, interface, orchestration | Model, training, inference | S58, S60 |

### Products: a strong cycle, a late foldable, a spatial computer that never became a platform

The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max launched on 2026-09-09 at $1,199 and $1,299; the foldable iPhone Duo at $1,999 went on sale on 2026-10-23. iPhone net sales rose 22% to $196.5bn in the nine months to 2026-06-27, with Greater China up 30%. The C2 modem supports US mmWave and uses 15% less energy than the C1X, but the larger iPhone 18 Pro Max appears to keep a Qualcomm modem, so Qualcomm retains leverage over the highest-ASP SKU. Vision Pro is the counter-example to Apple's category-creation record: ~390,000 units in 2024, ~45,000 in the December 2025 quarter despite the M5 refresh, ~600,000 lifetime, and an IDC forecast of ~290,000 units in 2026 [S59, S13, S87].

| Product | Stage | Launch | Revenue or share | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone 18 Pro / Pro Max | Commercial | 2026-09 | $196.5bn, 54% of 9M | Products 39.9% | C2 in Pro Max, 2027 | S59, S6 |
| iPhone Duo (foldable) | Commercial | 2026-10-23 | Inside iPhone; undisclosed | Not disclosed | First-quarter volume | S59 |
| Watch Series 11 / Ultra 3 | Commercial | 2025-09 | Wearables $27.3bn, +2% | Not disclosed | Hypertension roll-out | S5, S6 |
| Vision Pro (M5) | Commercial | 2025-10 | ~45k units Q4 2025 | Not disclosed | Lower-cost model, late 2026 | S87 |
| Services | Commercial | — | $91.7bn, +14% | 76.3% | AI tier / iCloud+ gating | S6, S107 |

### What is enforceable is regulatory, not patent

Apple publishes no patent count; the FY2025 10-K says only that it is "pursuing thousands of applications around the world" and that no single right protects its products. Patent counts and peer comparison were not obtainable — the registries could not be searched — so the patent moat is unquantified. What is documented feature by feature is a regulatory estate: hypertension and sleep-apnoea notifications, a hearing-aid De Novo grant and a medical imaging calibration feature, each cleared after its own clinical file. That is a slower, more durable barrier than a patent family, and the filings below date each clearance.

| Asset | Identifier | Jurisdiction | Date | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Patent portfolio | Count not disclosed | US and foreign | Ongoing | "Thousands of applications" | Unquantified | S5 |
| Hypertension Notification | K250507 | US FDA | 2025-09-11 | Cleared 510(k) | Watch sensing | S30 |
| Sleep Apnea Notification | K240929 | US FDA | 2024-09-13 | Cleared 510(k) | Watch sensing | S33 |
| Hearing Aid Feature | DEN230081 | US FDA | 2024-09-12 | De Novo granted | AirPods | S34 |
| Medical Imaging Calibration | K253582 | US FDA | 2026-04-01 | Cleared 510(k) | Display calibration | S29 |

### The moat is wide at the bottom of the stack and thin at the top

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Custom SoC and modem | 9 | Top design team plus priority TSMC N2 access; a decade and an Intel acquisition | 4-5 years | S59, S64 |
| Hardware-OS integration | 8 | Six operating systems co-designed with custom silicon | 3-5 years | S5 |
| On-device model efficiency | 5 | Quantisation and KV-cache techniques are published | 1-2 years | S61 |
| Frontier model | 3 | Available to licence, as Apple has shown | 1-2 years, by cheque | S58 |
| FDA-cleared health features | 7 | Each feature needs its own trial and clearance | 3-4 years | S30, S33 |
| Installed base and developers | 10 | A decade of switching costs, record active base | 10+ years | S13, S87 |
| **Composite** | **8/10 hardware, 4/10 AI** | The stack is hard to copy; the intelligence is not | **4-5 years for hardware** | S58, S64 |

The replication test answers the question directly: 50 senior silicon and operating-system engineers with Apple's published patents could match a phone-class SoC and OS in four to five years, and could rent a competitive model next quarter. The moat protects the cash-generating layer, not the differentiating one. The counter-evidence is Apple's own record: Siri needed a Google licence, the car was cancelled, Vision Pro has not reached platform volumes. The advantage holds only if on-device AI lifts upgrade rates and regulators leave the App Store economics that fund the silicon intact. Two diligence questions settle it: whether the Google agreement allows fine-tuning for on-device use, and whether the 2027 Pro Max moves fully to the C2 [S58, S59, S87].

::: evidence
**Apple's integration advantage is durable in silicon and distribution, but it no longer extends to the model layer.**

The A20 Pro's 2nm node and 32-core Neural Engine keep Apple at the leading edge of phone silicon, and twelve FDA device records since 2020 give it a regulated feature estate rivals must replicate trial by trial. But basing the next Apple Foundation Models on Gemini concedes that the frontier layer is bought, and the reported ~$1bn annual licence turns a fixed R&D advantage into a variable cost paid to a competitor [S58, S64, S86].

Globally, several jurisdictions have adopted, or may in the future adopt, competition-related laws and regulations imposing wide-ranging obligations on technology companies and significant limitations on businesses, including the Company. For example, the Company has implemented changes to iOS, iPadOS, the App Store and Safari ® in the EU as it seeks to comply with the DMA, including new business terms and alternative fee structures for iOS and iPadOS apps, alternative methods of distribution for iOS and iPadOS apps, alternative payment processing for apps across the Company’s operating systems, and additional tools and application programming interfaces for developers. In addition, the DMA imposes interoperability obligations on the Company requiring it to make certain of its technologies and features available to third-party products and services for free, which increases security and privacy risks, requires significant engineering resources, and can adversely affect the functionality, competitiveness, and user experience of the Company’s products. Interoperability and other requirements have in the past, and may in the future, cause the Company to not launch or maintain products, services and features, such as Siri AI, in certain jurisdictions. Any of these outcomes can have a negative impact on the Company’s competitive advantage and materially adversely affect its business, results of operations, financial condition and stock price.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Development Strategy (strategy, revision 4 by Product Analyst, 7,775 characters)
Apple's route to FY2028 growth is services mix, a richer iPhone cycle and India, with artificial intelligence as a retention feature and a possible iCloud+ upsell rather than a revenue line of its own; the plan is credible on cash generation and per-share compounding, but not yet on AI monetisation or on creating a new product category. The base is large and still growing: revenue reached $416.2bn in FY2025, and the nine months to 2026-06-27 produced $364.4bn, up 16%, with Services at $91.7bn, up 14% [S77, S6].

### Services carry the margin, but the mix engine stalled in FY2026

Services were 26% of FY2025 revenue but 39% of gross profit in the nine months to June 2026, because they earn a 76.3% gross margin against 39.9% for products. The mix engine, however, stopped being the marginal driver: product gross profit grew 26% against 15% for services, so the rise in total gross margin to 49.1% from 46.8% came from hardware mix and tariff refunds, not from services, while memory costs kept rising. Services growth itself came from advertising and cloud services, with the Google search-distribution payment named as a primary driver. That is the engine that funds the buyback and the silicon, and it is also the engine regulators are targeting: the European Commission fined Apple €500m on 2025-04-23 for anti-steering non-compliance, and the General Court dismissed Apple's challenge to its gatekeeper designation on 2026-07-08 [S85, S84, S6]. An investor should value the services annuity on gross profit that compounds in the low-to-mid teens, and apply a discount for the probability that a remedy compresses commission or search income rather than a one-off fine.

### AI is funded as cost and monetised, if at all, through storage

Apple introduced Siri AI with the iOS 27 cycle announced in the third quarter of FY2026, and R&D rose 33% to $34.0bn in the nine months to June 2026, driven by infrastructure including AI investments and headcount. No AI revenue line exists. The reported plan — that high-frequency, compute-intensive Siri use will be gated behind iCloud+ — is plausible because it reuses a price ladder already in place, but Apple has published no tier and no price, so it is unverified [S13, S6, S107]. The mechanism matters more than the price: AI raises the cost of serving every device while its clearest commercial effect is to protect upgrade rates and services attach. If Apple charges, the increment is bounded by storage-subscription willingness to pay, not by the value of the model; if it does not, AI is a permanent tax on gross margin. Either way, 2027 is the test of whether AI spend converts into units or ARPU.

### India lowers tariff risk, not unit cost

iPhone production in India rose 53% in 2025 to ~55 million units, ~25% of global output, and is projected at 28% in 2026; Tata Electronics overtook Foxconn in iPhone export assembly over the FY2022-FY2026 incentive period. The strategy is rational given the tariff record in the filings — Section 232 semiconductor investigation results in January 2026, the Supreme Court striking down certain IEEPA tariffs in February 2026, and new Section 301 tariffs, with manufacturing purchase obligations of $57.0bn at 2026-06-27 [S89, S91, S6]. The limit is that assembly captures little of the value: components, displays and silicon still come from East Asia, so India is an insurance policy on tariffs and single-country concentration, not a margin lever. The signpost to watch is the share of US-bound iPhones assembled in India, which Apple has never disclosed.

### Capital allocation is disciplined and slightly bolder

R&D rose from $29.9bn in FY2023 to $34.6bn in FY2025 and is running at ~$45bn annualised in FY2026. Buybacks remain the primary use of cash: $25.8bn of stock was repurchased in the quarter to 2026-06-27 alone, alongside $4.0bn of dividends at $0.27 per share, which cut the share count to 14.61bn from 14.77bn at FY2025 year-end and helped EPS grow 29% against 27% net-income growth. M&A posture has shifted from tuck-ins: Apple confirmed the acquisition of the AI-audio start-up Q.ai on 2026-01-29, reported by the Financial Times at close to $2bn, and acquired the AI data-engineering company Ascend.io, notified to the European Commission on 2026-06-30; intangible assets rose from $11.1bn to $20.3bn between 2025-09-27 and 2026-06-27 [S77, S88, S6, S13]. Against ~$146bn of cash and marketable securities, that is affordable experimentation rather than a change of strategy — and it is the right test of whether Apple's AI gap can be bought in pieces.

| Milestone | Target date | Status | What it proves | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FY2026 results and 10-K | by 2026-11 | Pending | Whether 16% growth holds into the holiday quarter | S77, S6 |
| Siri AI full release (iOS 27) | 2026-09 | Launched at WWDC26 | Gemini-based assistant ships on schedule | S13, S86 |
| iPhone Duo ramp | 2026-10-23 on sale | Launched | Apple can create a $1,999 tier | S59 |
| AI subscription (iCloud+ gating) | Not announced | Reported only | AI becomes revenue rather than cost | S107 |
| Lower-cost Vision Pro | Late 2026 | Unconfirmed by Apple | Spatial computing can reach volume | S87 |
| DOJ settlement | 2026 talks | Unresolved | Size of the App Store remedy | S90 |
| India assembly share | FY2026 | ~28% projected | Tariff hedge is real | S91 |

| Partner | Scope | Signed | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Google | Next-generation Apple Foundation Models based on Gemini, multi-year, non-exclusive | 2026-01-12 | Active | S58 |
| Qualcomm | 5G modems, including the iPhone 18 Pro Max | Ongoing | Narrowing | S59 |
| TSMC | N3P and N2 wafer manufacturing | Ongoing | Active; wafer prices rising | S64 |
| Tata Electronics | India iPhone assembly and exports | Ongoing | Scaling; overtook Foxconn on exports | S91 |
| Foxconn | China and India assembly | Ongoing | Active | S89 |

### What must be true in twelve months, and the case against

Four things must happen for the strategy to be credible. First, the FY2026 holiday quarter has to show that the iPhone 18 and Duo cycle sustains double-digit growth without tariff refunds, which flattered the June quarter by ~2 percentage points of gross margin. Second, Apple must put a price on AI or show that it lifts upgrade rates, because a 33% R&D increase with no revenue attached is a margin problem. Third, a DOJ settlement or DMA remedy must leave the App Store commission and default-search payment substantially intact; both cases attack the services profit pool directly. Fourth, India must reach the projected share of output without a quality or logistics incident. The counter-case is strong and largely Apple's own record: AI features arrived well after they were demonstrated, Siri needed a Google licence, the car programme was cancelled, and Vision Pro shipped ~45,000 units in the December 2025 quarter, while Alphabet, Microsoft and Huawei set a faster cadence in models, cloud AI and, for Huawei, folding hardware and domestic silicon. Apple's answer is that it does not need to be first — it needs to be best integrated, and it monetises the installed base rather than the model. That is a defensible strategy for a cash-flow investor and a weak one for anyone buying AI optionality [S59, S87, S84, S90, S89].

::: evidence
**The strategy is credible as a cash-compounding plan and unproven as a growth plan.**

Services earn a structurally higher gross margin than hardware, and buybacks are large enough that earnings per share can compound faster than net income even with flat hardware; but AI is a large R&D increase with no disclosed price, Vision Pro has not become a platform, and the two antitrust cases target precisely the services lines that fund the plan.
:::"}],"isError":false}
