{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Financial Analysis (financials, revision 4 by Fundamentals Analyst, 8,554 characters)
Apple's cash conversion and balance sheet are as good as the multiple implies, but the earnings growth is not: fiscal 2025's 22.7% EPS growth becomes 10.4% once the $10.2bn Irish State Aid tax charge in the prior year is normalised out, and 2.0 points of the June 2026 quarter's 50.1% gross margin came from tariff refunds rather than trading. The three-year record is slowing revenue and rising margin: revenue fell 2.8% in fiscal 2023, grew 2.0% in fiscal 2024 and 6.4% to $416,161M in fiscal 2025, while gross margin rose from 44.1% to 46.9% and operating margin from 29.8% to 32.0%. The latest filed period is the quarter ended 2026-06-27, where revenue rose 16.4% to $109,417M on gross margin of 50.1% and operating margin of 32.6%. No fourth-quarter fiscal 2026 earnings release and no fiscal 2026 annual report were on EDGAR as of 2026-10-31; Apple's fiscal 2025 equivalents were filed on 2025-10-30 and 2025-10-31, so the annual report is due imminently and the figures here are trailing twelve months to 2026-06-27 [S5, S6, S13].

| Line item | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 | Q3 FY2026 | TTM to 2026-06-27 | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | $383,285M | $391,035M | $416,161M | $109,417M | $466,823M | S5, S6 |
| Gross margin | 44.1% | 46.2% | 46.9% | 50.1% | 48.7% | S5, S6 |
| Operating margin | 29.8% | 31.5% | 32.0% | 32.6% | 33.2% | S5, S6 |
| Net income | $96,995M | $93,736M | $112,010M | $29,789M | $128,930M | S5, S6 |
| Diluted EPS | $6.13 | $6.08 | $7.46 | $2.02 | $8.72 | S5, S6 |
| Effective tax rate | 14.7% | 24.1% | 15.6% | 17.9% | 17.3% | S5, S6 |
| Operating cash flow | $110,543M | $118,254M | $111,482M | n/a | $146,724M | S5, S6 |
| Capital expenditure | $10,959M | $9,447M | $12,715M | n/a | $10,041M | S5, S6 |
| Free cash flow | $99,584M | $108,807M | $98,767M | n/a | $136,683M | S5, S6 |
| Free cash flow / net income | 1.03x | 1.16x | 0.88x | n/a | 1.06x | S5, S6 |

### The growth is half tax base effect, and a quarter buyback

Fiscal 2025's net income rose 19.5%, but pretax income rose 7.5% ($132,729M against $123,485M) and the tax provision fell 30.3% to $20,719M because fiscal 2024 carried the one-time $10.2bn Irish charge — $15.8bn payable to Ireland, offset by a $4.8bn US foreign tax credit and $823M of released unrecognised benefits. Normalising fiscal 2024 at fiscal 2025's 15.6% rate gives $104,222M and underlying growth of 7.5%, not 19.5%. The EPS gap above that is the buyback: from fiscal 2023 to fiscal 2025 net income grew 15.5% while diluted EPS grew 21.7% and diluted shares fell 5.1%, so 5.4 percentage points of EPS growth was a smaller denominator — and that contribution is fading, at 1.9 percentage points in the trailing twelve months (EPS +16.9% against net income +15.1%), because repurchases slowed to $62,094M in the nine months to 2026-06-27 from $70,579M while operating cash flow rose 43%. Capital return has stopped outrunning cash: buybacks and dividends were $97,866M against free cash flow of $136,683M, or 72%, against 107% in fiscal 2025, and net cash rose by $28,410M in nine months. At $344.63 on 2026-10-30 and 14,715M diluted shares the equity is worth $5.07trn, 39.5x trailing EPS and a 2.70% free cash flow yield, while the ten-year Treasury yielded 4.93%; repurchasing at that spread is accretive to EPS and not obviously accretive to value per share [S5, S6, S9].

### Cash is real; the working-capital cushion is not

Cash generation is the strongest part of the record and the hardest to fake: operating cash flow of $146,724M against capital expenditure of $10,041M, with free cash flow at 1.06x net income. The anomaly is fiscal 2025, when free cash flow fell to 0.88x of net income despite $111,482M of operating cash flow; cash paid for income taxes that year was $43,369M, 32.7% of pretax income against a 15.6% book rate and 21.1% in fiscal 2024 — a gap consistent with settlement payments on the Irish case and the TCJA repatriation tax, the final $8.8bn of which was paid in the nine months to 2026-06-27. That supports reading the gap as timing, and the recovery to 1.06x is consistent with it. The working-capital change runs the other way: inventory reached $11,092M at 2026-06-27 from $5,925M a year earlier, an 87% increase against 16.2% revenue growth, lifting days inventory to 16.9 from 9.4 and pulling the cash conversion cycle to −56.8 days from −71.1 at the fiscal 2025 year-end [S5, S6].

The balance sheet carries no leverage risk: at 2026-06-27 Apple held $146,517M of cash and marketable securities against $84,344M of debt, for net cash of $62,173M, up from $33,763M, with commercial paper cut to $1,997M from $7,979M, and other income and expense netted to −$321M in fiscal 2025 because interest earned on the securities book offsets interest paid. The commitments that matter are forward purchases — $57.0bn of manufacturing purchase obligations, $56.2bn due within twelve months, and $29.3bn of other purchase obligations — which fix component supply and, with it, the cost base when memory prices move. Two accounting details deserve attention: gross intangible assets rose $13,270M to $38,220M in nine months with no goodwill recognised, which indicates purchased intellectual property, content or asset acquisitions rather than share purchases, and is not explained in the quarterly filing; and gross unrecognised tax benefits were $23.2bn at 2025-09-27, of which $10.6bn would affect the effective rate and up to $6bn may move within twelve months [S6].

### Returns are distorted by the buyback, not flattered by the business

Reported returns are not usable as quality scores: return on equity was 148.8% and return on invested capital 320.6% on invested capital of $45,347M — $107,520M of equity plus $84,344M of debt less $146,517M of securities — because $258,212M of cumulative buybacks shrank the equity base. The honest comparison is return on assets of 36.1% against Microsoft's 35.9% return on invested capital in fiscal 2026 and Alphabet's 37.0% in fiscal 2025 [S6, S27, S41].

### What moves the outcome, and by how much

The geographic picture also cuts against the standard bear case: Greater China revenue rose 30% to $64,839M in the nine months to 2026-06-27 and 22% in the June quarter, so nine months already exceed the whole of fiscal 2025's $64,377M after two years of decline. What moves the outcome most is gross margin. On trailing-twelve-month revenue of $466,823M one point of gross margin is $4,668M of pretax profit, or 3.0% of net income, while one point of revenue growth at the current margin is $1,878M, or 1.5%. Three cases, all on the trailing twelve months and none a forecast: a two-point margin gain takes EPS to $9.24, a two-point give-back to $8.20, and a two-point give-back with the loss of the search licence to $7.11, 18.8% below the base — and the licence should be modelled as intact but repriced annually, because the September 2025 order permitted non-exclusive placement payments of one year or less rather than ending them, while the $20bn figure is a 2022 court-record number Apple has never confirmed. The cash is real and the balance sheet is net cash; the growth is weaker than reported; and the margin sits at a cyclical high with a tariff-refund component inside it. An investor paying 39.5x trailing earnings is paying for the first and third to persist while the second is already reversing. The diligence question that matters most is what the fiscal 2026 annual report says about inventory composition and the split between refund and product mix, neither of which the quarterly filings settle [S6, S82, S118].

::: info warning
**The fiscal 2026 gross margin is not yet a clean number.** Strip out the tariff refund Apple attributes to the June quarter and the margin is still above any full year in this record, but a smaller step-change than the reported figure implies; against an inventory build growing faster than revenue, the annual report carries the burden of proof.
:::

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Market & Industry Analysis (market, revision 2 by Market Analyst, 8,997 characters)
Apple's markets are contracting in units and expanding in value, and Apple is taking value share inside that contraction: the case for FY2026-FY2028 rests on premiumisation and Services attach rather than device volume, is strongest in the United States, is adequate in Europe, and in China depends on a domestic champion's pricing discipline.

### The pool is shrinking in units and growing in value

IDC's August 2026 forecast has worldwide smartphone shipments at just over 1.0 billion units in 2026, down 16.7% and the steepest annual contraction on record, while total market value rises 6.3% to $613 billion and the average selling price reaches a record $581, up 27.6% in a year and revised up from the $550 IDC published one quarter earlier. The cause is cost, not demand: DRAM and NAND prices are up more than 300% year on year as capacity is redirected to AI servers, memory is more than 65% of bill of materials at the low end, and the sub-$100 tier that shipped 173 million units in 2025 fell close to 60% in the second quarter of 2026. This is a supply shock with a dated end, so 2026-2027 flatters Apple's unit share while genuinely lifting its price, and 2028 is the test of whether either survives. [S39]

Two sizing methods agree closely: 1.0 billion units at the $581 average price gives $581 billion, within 5% of IDC's $613 billion, so the unit and price series can be read together rather than as rival estimates. On that base Apple's serviceable market is the premium tier it addresses — an iOS share of 23.6% of 2026 shipments, a record — while the revenue it can obtain is what it already books: $466.8 billion trailing twelve months to 2026-06-27, which at the 16.2% growth rate of the first nine months of FY2026 implies $483 billion for FY2026. IDC's PC-plus-tablet pool compounds at 1.5% a year from 2026 to 2030, so device pools are not growth markets at any price. [S6]

### Services carries the margin and has no published pool size

The fastest-growing pool Apple actually monetises is Services: $109.2 billion, 26.2% of FY2025 revenue, at a 75.4% gross margin against 36.8% for products, growing 14.1% to $91.7 billion in the first nine months of FY2026. The installed base behind it has the same gap: Apple states only that its active-device base reached an all-time high in the June 2026 quarter across every category and region, and publishes no device count in its FY2025 10-K or FY2026 results, so the figure of 2.3 billion devices often quoted alongside the business is unverified here and should carry none of the valuation. ### Who pays, and how much demand is policy

The budget owner is the consumer, in a discretionary purchase that is increasingly financed. In the United States and United Kingdom long-term interest-free financing is more prevalent, so IDC expects the premium end to hold while emerging markets fall more than 20%; in India brands lean on financing after the sub-$100 tier fell 59% and the $600-800 band grew 32%; in China the government subsidy that supported earlier quarters faded in the second quarter of 2026, so demand there is being withdrawn by policy rather than created by it. Apple's exposure to policy runs both ways: after the February 20, 2026 Supreme Court ruling struck down certain IEEPA tariffs, Apple recognised refunds as a reduction of product cost of sales, and those refunds contributed 2.0 percentage points of the June 2026 quarter's 50.1% gross margin — tariff policy moves Apple's margin by more than a product cycle does. [S105, S40, S13]

And if courts and the European Commission remove the App Store take rate, the 75%-margin layer that offsets hardware cyclicality stops compounding at its present rate. The investor implication is narrow: in a 1-billion-unit market Apple can grow revenue only if price rises faster than units fall, making average selling price, China durability and the Services take rate the variables worth monitoring. Sizing confidence is high, because two independent methods agree within 5%; confidence that the mix shift holds to 2028 is medium, because it rests on China and a legally contested commission. Three questions would close the gap: what share of Services revenue is commission-based rather than subscription, advertising or licensing; how much of the Greater China increase is currency; and what the current average replacement cycle is, measured rather than asserted. Great context. Key: Services $109.2B, 26.2% of FY2025 revenue, 75.4% GM vs products 36.8%. This confirms my derived figure exactly. And FY2026E revenue ~$483B.

Also important: IDC says smartphone units -16.7% in 2026 while value +6.3%, memory prices up >300%, ASP $581. That's a supply shock — which supports the "earnings at a cyclical high" argument. The market analyst's view helps my reverse DCF: revenue growth of 11-12% for a decade is far above the industry's unit and value growth (device pools 1.5% CAGR). Good comparison.

Now I have enough research. Let me also quickly check the competitive landscape? Not necessary.

Section 8 plan:
- Decision question: What is Apple worth, and what does today's price imply?
- Thesis sentence: "At $344.63 (NasdaqGS, 2026-10-30 close) Apple is priced at 39.5x trailing earnings and a 2.7% free-cash-flow yield against a 4.93% ten-year Treasury, a price that requires roughly 11-12% annual free-cash-flow growth for a decade — more than double the growth its device markets support and seven times what it delivered over the past four years — so the watchlist case is about what price restores a margin of safety, not whether Apple is a good business."
- Why different: it prices the company rather than describing it; the financials section analyses quality, this section converts that into what is already in the price and what entry price would compensate.
- Mechanism: the multiple is the discount rate applied to a cyclically high earnings base; with the 10-year at 4.93%, a 39.5x multiple implies a 2.5% earnings yield, so all return must come from growth or further re-rating; buybacks at that multiple return 2.5% per dollar, below the risk-free rate.
- Comparison set: MSFT/GOOGL/META/Samsung peer multiples, S&P 500 18.4x forward/21.8x trailing, Apple's own 10-year mean 25.35x and 5-year range 22.1-40.6x, and the reverse-DCF implied growth vs history (1.5% FCF CAGR FY21-FY25).
- Counter-evidence: Apple's FCF yield 2.7% is the highest of the peer group (MSFT 1.5%, GOOGL 0.6%, META 1.8%) because its capex is $10B vs hyperscalers' AI capex; Services at 76% GM and 14% growth could justify a higher multiple; the iPhone 17/AI cycle is genuinely accelerating revenue (+16%). Also the market can stay expensive.
- Visual: the valuation table + reverse DCF table + peer multiples table.
- Prohibited: "expensive" alone without a mechanism, "priced for perfection", vague "margin of safety" without a number.

2. What the price is: multiples vs peers and vs own history.

Section 12 plan:
- Decision question: for a long-only fund, what is the exit and sell discipline?
- Thesis: "Apple has no takeover exit and no listing event to wait for; the only exit is a sale into the market, so the discipline has to be written in price bands and thesis breaks — and at 39.5x the stock offers a negative margin of safety, with the ten-year record showing a 21.4% average intra-year drawdown that would take the price to about $271, roughly where the multiple returns to its five-year average."
- Exit routes table: Route | Named buyer/venue | Rationale | Timing | Likelihood | Source:

  5. Buyback as partial exit — Apple itself is the buyer: $82.2B TTM repurchases, $100B authorization; the company retires 1-1.5% of shares a year, providing a bid.
  6. Dividend — 0.3% yield.
- Precedent exits table: drawdown episodes with dates, magnitudes, recovery, multiple at trough? I can compute P/E at trough:
  - 2018 trough $36.71 (split-adjusted) on 2018-12-24; FY2018 EPS $2.98 (split-adjusted $0.72? no). Hmm, tricky with splits. Better: price decline only, and note P/E at the time not computed.

That's forward-looking and useful: a 21.4% average drawdown from $344.63 = $271. A 30% drawdown = $241. A 36.7% = $218. That maps directly onto price bands. Excellent.

- Price $344.63; TTM EPS $8.72; forward EPS ~$9.79 (implied).
- 10-year mean P/E 25.35x; 5-year avg 30.2x; 5-year range 22.1-40.6x.

- For a 8.5% required return: needed FCF growth = 8.5% - 2.7% = 5.8%/yr in perpetuity if the multiple never changes (simple dividend discount with total FCF yield). The difference is because a terminal multiple at 3% growth implies a 17.5x FCF multiple at exit vs 36.3x today — i.e., substantial multiple compression is embedded in the DCF. Right: my DCF assumes exit at 17.5x FCF (1/(8.5%-3%)). That's a key point: the reverse DCF assumes the multiple halves by 2036; despite that, it still needs 11.8% growth. Let me verify: TV at 2036 = FCF10 × 1.03/(0.085-0.03) = FCF10 × 18.7; PV = 3,424 at g=11.85%. Terminal value is 69% of EV. So yes, terminal exit multiple 18.7x FCF. arguments.markdown:
Apple's silicon-plus-OS stack is still the widest integrated consumer technology stack, but in 2026 the company rented the one layer it could not build — the frontier model — so what remains defensible is distribution, custom silicon and regulated health sensing, not leadership in artificial intelligence. In two years the A20 Pro moved the iPhone to TSMC N2, the C2 modem reached the flagship, the first foldable shipped at $1,999, and on 2026-01-12 Apple and Google announced the next Apple Foundation Models would be Gemini-based [S58, S59, S63, S64].

### The silicon lead is real, costly, and rented from TSMC

The A19 Pro used TSMC N3P; a year later the A20 Pro moved to TSMC N2 with a 32-core Neural Engine and ~52 TOPS, about double the prior generation's AI throughput. N2 wafers are reported at ~$30,000 against $18,000-20,000 for 3nm, so each capability step arrives with higher silicon cost. Product gross margin was 39.9% in the nine months to 2026-06-27 versus 36.9% a year earlier, but only with tariff refunds and mix offsetting "higher costs, including memory", and the 10-Q warns that advanced-semiconductor, NAND and DRAM constraints are expected to intensify [S6, S64].

| Metric | Value | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Node, A19 Pro / A20 Pro | TSMC N3P (2025) / N2 (2026) | Teardown and trade reporting | S63, S64 |
| CPU clock, A19 Pro | up to 4.26 GHz, 6 cores | Published specification | S63 |
| Neural Engine, A20 Pro | 32 cores, ~52 TOPS, ~2x A19 Pro | Trade-press estimate | S64 |
| N2 wafer price | ~$30,000 vs $18,000-20,000 at 3nm | Trade-press estimate | S64 |
| Product gross margin | 39.9% vs 36.9% (9M FY2025) | Reported financials | S6 |
| On-device model / PCC context | ~3B parameters / 32K tokens | Apple research and developer docs | S61, S62 |

### Apple Intelligence is an architecture with a rented brain

On device, Apple runs a ~3B-parameter model optimised through KV-cache sharing and 2-bit quantisation-aware training; on its servers, a Parallel-Track Mixture-of-Experts model runs inside Private Cloud Compute, which enforces stateless processing, no privileged access even for Apple staff, and attested software images. The binding constraint is memory bandwidth and power: phone-class memory caps on-device inference at single-digit billions of parameters, so harder queries are offloaded. The ceiling is disclosed: a 32K-token context is small against frontier assistants, and Apple's own models were not frontier-quality. The unresolved question for the privacy story is where Gemini-derived inference physically runs. Apple says Apple Intelligence continues on Apple devices and Private Cloud Compute; trade reporting says Google's cloud performs the Gemini computation and puts the licence at ~$1bn a year, on top of a default-search payment of ~$20bn. Neither figure is Apple-confirmed. China's CAC approved Apple Intelligence on 2026-07-15, nearly two years after its 2024 debut, with Alibaba's Qwen and Baidu supplying a separate model stack. Apple's differentiation is orchestration, distribution and privacy, not model quality; underwrite the cash flow and installed base, not the AI layer [S8, S58, S60, S61, S86, S120, S171].

| Dimension | Apple 2024 (AFM v1) | Apple 2026 (Gemini-based AFM) | Google (supplier) | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Frontier model | Own ~3B on-device plus server model | Gemini-derived | Owns Gemini | S58, S61 |
| Cost structure | Fixed R&D and data-centre capex | Fixed R&D plus per-query licence | Licence revenue | S58, S86 |
| What Apple keeps | Silicon, OS, orchestration | Silicon, OS, interface, orchestration | Model, training, inference | S58, S60 |

### Products: a strong cycle, a late foldable, a spatial computer that never became a platform

The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max launched on 2026-09-09 at $1,199 and $1,299; the foldable iPhone Duo at $1,999 went on sale on 2026-10-23. iPhone net sales rose 22% to $196.5bn in the nine months to 2026-06-27, with Greater China up 30%. The C2 modem supports US mmWave and uses 15% less energy than the C1X, but the larger iPhone 18 Pro Max appears to keep a Qualcomm modem, so Qualcomm retains leverage over the highest-ASP SKU. Vision Pro is the counter-example: ~390,000 units in 2024, ~45,000 in the December 2025 quarter despite the M5 refresh, ~600,000 lifetime, and an IDC forecast of ~290,000 units in 2026 [S59, S13, S87].

| Product | Stage | Launch | Revenue or share | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone 18 Pro / Pro Max | Commercial | 2026-09 | $196.5bn, 54% of 9M | Products 39.9% | C2 in Pro Max, 2027 | S59, S6 |
| iPhone Duo (foldable) | Commercial | 2026-10-23 | Inside iPhone; undisclosed | Not disclosed | First-quarter volume | S59 |
| Watch Series 11 / Ultra 3 | Commercial | 2025-09 | Wearables $27.3bn, +2% | Not disclosed | Hypertension roll-out | S5, S6 |
| Vision Pro (M5) | Commercial | 2025-10 | ~45k units Q4 2025 | Not disclosed | Lower-cost model, late 2026 | S87 |
| Services | Commercial | — | $91.7bn, +14% | 76.3% | AI tier / iCloud+ gating | S6, S107 |

### What is enforceable is regulatory, not patent

Apple publishes no patent count; the FY2025 10-K says only that it is "pursuing thousands of applications around the world" and that no single right protects its products. Patent counts and peer comparison were not obtainable — the registries could not be searched — so the patent moat is unquantified. What is documented is a regulatory estate — hypertension and sleep-apnoea notifications, a hearing-aid De Novo grant and imaging calibration — each cleared on its own clinical file, a slower but more durable barrier than a patent family. Regulation also gates the AI roadmap: the Q3 FY2026 10-Q states DMA interoperability obligations have in the past, and may in future, cause Apple not to launch or maintain features "such as Siri AI" in certain jurisdictions [S6, S29, S30, S33, S34].

| Asset | Identifier | Jurisdiction | Date | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Patent portfolio | Count not disclosed | US and foreign | Ongoing | "Thousands of applications" | Unquantified | S5 |
| Hypertension Notification | K250507 | US FDA | 2025-09-11 | Cleared 510(k) | Watch sensing | S30 |
| Sleep Apnea Notification | K240929 | US FDA | 2024-09-13 | Cleared 510(k) | Watch sensing | S33 |
| Hearing Aid Feature | DEN230081 | US FDA | 2024-09-12 | De Novo granted | AirPods | S34 |
| Medical Imaging Calibration | K253582 | US FDA | 2026-04-01 | Cleared 510(k) | Display calibration | S29 |

### The moat is wide at the bottom of the stack and thin at the top

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Custom SoC and modem | 9 | Top design team plus priority TSMC N2 access; a decade and an Intel acquisition | 4-5 years | S59, S64 |
| Hardware-OS integration | 8 | Six operating systems co-designed with custom silicon | 3-5 years | S5 |
| On-device model efficiency | 5 | Quantisation and KV-cache techniques are published | 1-2 years | S61 |
| Frontier model | 3 | Available to licence, as Apple has shown | 1-2 years, by cheque | S58 |
| FDA-cleared health features | 7 | Each feature needs its own trial and clearance | 3-4 years | S30, S33 |
| Installed base and developers | 10 | A decade of switching costs, record active base | 10+ years | S13, S87 |
| **Composite** | **8/10 hardware, 4/10 AI** | The stack is hard to copy; the intelligence is not | **4-5 years for hardware** | S58, S64 |

The replication test: a team of 50 senior silicon and operating-system engineers could match a phone-class SoC and OS in four to five years, and rent a competitive model next quarter. The counter-evidence is Apple's own record: Siri needed a Google licence, the car was cancelled, Vision Pro has not reached platform volumes, and the assistant may now be withheld in the EU under the DMA. The advantage holds only if on-device AI lifts upgrade rates and regulators leave the App Store economics that fund the silicon intact. Two diligence questions settle it: whether the Google agreement allows fine-tuning for on-device use, and whether the 2027 Pro Max moves fully to the C2 [S6, S58, S59, S87].

::: evidence
**Apple's integration advantage is durable in silicon and distribution, but it no longer extends to the model layer.**

The A20 Pro's 2nm node and 32-core Neural Engine keep Apple at the leading edge of phone silicon, and ten FDA clearances and grants since 2020 give it a regulated feature estate rivals must replicate trial by trial. But basing the next Apple Foundation Models on Gemini concedes that the frontier layer is bought, the reported ~$1bn annual licence turns a fixed R&D advantage into a variable cost paid to a competitor, and availability now varies by jurisdiction: China runs a Qwen/Baidu stack and DMA rules may withhold Siri AI in the EU [S6, S58, S64, S86, S120, S171].
:::

plan.comparison_set: Apple's own four drawdowns (2018 -36.73%, 2020 -31.43%, 2022 -30.75%, 2025 -30.22%; ten-year average -21.4% over 82 days), the S&P 500 at -3.05% and Nasdaq-100 at -9.09% from their highs on 2026-10-30, and the largest technology acquisition ($68.7B) as the takeover benchmark.
plan.counter_evidence: A 30x-plus multiple may never offer a margin of safety again: if Services keeps compounding at 14% and the buyback retires 1.6% a year, waiting for $250 could mean never owning the best cash generator in the market, so the cost of the discipline is opportunity rather than loss.
plan.decision_question: For a long-only fund, at what price does Apple become a starter and then a full position, what forces a sale, and what total return should the holder expect at each entry price?
plan.mechanism: For a listed mega-cap the exit is the market's bid, so the return is set by the entry multiple and the holding period: buybacks and dividends add about 1.9% a year, too little to offset a de-rating from 35x to 25x, so the entry band and the sale triggers do the work that an acquisition or IPO would do for a private company.
plan.prohibited: IPO or trade sale as a realistic exit; 'buy and hold forever' with no triggers; vague 'long term'; 'the stock always comes back' without the multiple at which it came back.
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple offers no takeover or listing exit — at a $5.03T market value the largest technology acquisition on record would be 1.4% of the company — so the only exit is a sale into a deep but volatile market, and the discipline has to be a price band: a first tranche at $275-300 (28-31x forward earnings), a full position at or below $250 (about 25x, the ten-year mean), and a sale if Services growth falls below 5% or the gross margin below 44%, because at 39.5x a 21% average drawdown is the normal cost of owning it.
plan.visual: Exit routes table and the entry-price/exit-multiple return sensitivity table, with the drawdown history table beside them.
plan.why_different: The valuation section asks what the company is worth; this section asks how a holder gets paid and how a holder gets out, using the drawdown record, the entry multiple and named policy tests rather than a price target.

rows.benchmark: Microsoft's $68.7B all-cash acquisition of Activision Blizzard (2022-01-18), the largest technology deal on record, which took about 18 months and a divestiture to clear regulators.
rows.confidence: high — the deal value is from the announcement and Apple's market capitalisation from dated market data.
rows.finding: There is no plausible takeover exit: Apple's market value is $5,029.6B, so the largest technology acquisition ever ($68.7B) equals 1.4% of it, and any bid would face US and EU antitrust review of a platform with 23.6% of global smartphone shipments.
rows.follow_up: Could a sovereign wealth fund or strategic investor build a stake large enough to influence strategy, and would CFIUS review apply?
rows.implication: Value can only be realised by selling into the market; the takeover premium is effectively zero and should not be modelled.
rows.mechanism: With no strategic buyer able to pay a control premium, the exit price is the market multiple on the day of sale, which makes the entry multiple the dominant term in the return.
rows.weakens: A mega-cap can still be broken up by regulators or acquired in parts, and a very large cash-rich acquirer could pay up for a division; the 1.4% comparison is about a whole-company bid.

rows.benchmark: Apple's ten-year average intra-year drawdown of -21.4%, average 82 days peak-to-trough.
rows.confidence: high — a daily close series with peak and trough dates for each year.
rows.finding: Apple's four large drawdowns were 2018 -36.73% ($58.02 on 2018-10-03 to $36.71 on 2018-12-24), 2020 -31.43% ($81.80 to $56.09, 40 days), 2022 -30.75% ($182.01 to $126.04, 359 days) and 2025 -30.22% ($247.10 to $172.42, 43 days); the ten-year average intra-year drawdown is -21.4% over 82 days, and each was recovered within the following year (2020 +80.75%, 2025 +8.56% for the calendar year).
rows.follow_up: Does the 2026 cycle repeat the pattern if memory costs and a slowing iPhone cycle coincide?
rows.implication: Size the position for a 20-30% drawdown as the normal case: from $344.63 the average drawdown is about $271 and a 30% drawdown about $241.
rows.mechanism: Apple's drawdowns were multiple compressions on intact franchises, so the recovery came from a re-rating as much as from earnings; at 39.5x there is little multiple room left to power the next recovery.
rows.weakens: Every one of those recoveries happened while the multiple was expanding on falling or near-zero real rates; a repeat at a 39.5x starting multiple would require earnings growth alone to do the work.

rows.benchmark: Apple's own entry multiples: 20.6x on FY2022 EPS at the 2022 trough and 17.1x on FY2020 EPS at the 2020 trough, against 39.5x today.
rows.confidence: medium — trough prices are dated closes and the EPS are fiscal-year diluted figures, so the trough multiple is approximate.
rows.finding: The last two big buying opportunities came at 17-21x earnings: $126.04 at the 2022 trough was 20.6x FY2022 EPS of $6.11, and $56.09 at the 2020 trough was about 17.1x FY2020 EPS of $3.28; $344.63 is 39.5x trailing EPS of $8.72 and 35.2x forward EPS of about $9.79.
rows.follow_up: Would a 20x multiple on today's EPS ($174) ever be reached without a genuine earnings recession?
rows.implication: Waiting for a repeat of 17-21x means waiting for a price near $174-215 and may mean never owning the stock; the practical compromise is a 25-30x band.
rows.mechanism: The trough multiple, not the trough price, is what made those purchases work: the same 20x on today's much larger EPS is a far higher price, which is why a price band must be set on the multiple rather than on the old share price.
rows.weakens: Apple's earnings and cash flow are 40% larger than in 2022, so a 20x multiple on today's EPS is not the same business; the lower multiple may simply never return for a company with 76%-margin Services.

rows.benchmark: An 8% annual equity hurdle for a long-only fund; EPS growth of 8% a year from $9.79 to $12.33 by fiscal 2029.
rows.confidence: medium — arithmetic, but the EPS path and exit multiple are assumptions, not forecasts.
rows.finding: Return sensitivity to entry: at $344.63 a three-year exit at 25x earns about -3.3% a year, at 30x +2.7% and at 35x +8.2%; at $296 the same exits earn +1.8%, +8.1% and +13.8%; at $248 they earn +8.0%, +14.8% and +21%+.
rows.follow_up: What EPS growth does the FY2027 consensus imply, and does it survive a normalised tax rate and a 48% gross margin?
rows.implication: Only at or below about $296 does a long-only fund earn its hurdle without relying on the multiple staying at a five-year high; at $344.63 the return depends on a 35x exit.
rows.mechanism: The entry multiple sets the arithmetic: paying 35x for 8% EPS growth and exiting at 25x loses money even though the business grows, while paying 25x for the same growth and exiting at 25x earns the growth plus the dividend.
rows.weakens: If EPS compounds at 12-16% as it did in FY2026, every row improves by roughly 4-8 points a year and today's price could clear the hurdle.

rows.benchmark: Services revenue of $120.5B TTM and services gross profit of $91.6B; a 76.0% services gross margin.
rows.confidence: medium — the payment size is a reported estimate Apple has never confirmed, and the remedy is under appeal.
rows.finding: The Google search-distribution payment — reported at about $20B a year, never disclosed by Apple — is roughly 17% of Services revenue and 22% of services gross profit; the default-payment ban took effect in June 2026 under the April 2026 remedy order, with choice screens required.
rows.follow_up: What share of the Q3 FY2026 Services growth of 12.1% came from the search payment, and what does Apple disclose about the outcome of the appeal?
rows.implication: A sell trigger: if the payment is lost without an offset, about 9% of market value at a 30x multiple is at risk, so position size must survive that hit.
rows.mechanism: The payment is almost pure margin with no capital attached, so losing it hits earnings and the multiple at the same time — the same policy risk that the valuation section capitalises at 39.5x.
rows.weakens: The deal may survive in restricted, non-exclusive form and is under appeal; Apple's Q3 FY2026 Services revenue still grew 12.1%, so no loss is visible in the filed results yet.

rows.benchmark: Apple's $13.84B average daily traded value over 20 days; $82.2B of trailing-twelve-month buybacks, 1.6% of market value.
rows.confidence: high — volume and buyback figures are dated and filed.
rows.finding: Liquidity is not a constraint: Apple trades $13.84B a day (20-day average, 40.41M shares) and the company itself retires about 1.6% of shares a year ($82.2B of repurchases), while a 1% position in a $1B fund is $10M, under 0.1% of one day's volume.
rows.follow_up: How does liquidity behave in a 2025-style 43-day, 30% drawdown, and what slippage should a 5% position assume?
rows.implication: The exit is a price decision, not a liquidity decision: a long-only fund can sell in a day, but the drawdown record says it will not want to.
rows.mechanism: Deep liquidity plus a continuous buyback bid means the cost of exiting is the multiple at the moment of sale, not market impact, which shifts the design of the exit from execution to valuation triggers.
rows.weakens: Liquidity evaporates in stress: in the 2025 episode the stock fell 30% in 43 days, and the buyback is discretionary and can slow, as it did when repurchases fell to $62.1B in nine months from $70.6B.

arguments.markdown:
Apple's silicon-plus-OS stack is still the widest integrated consumer technology stack, but in 2026 the company rented the one layer it could not build — the frontier model — so what remains defensible is distribution, custom silicon and regulated health sensing, not leadership in artificial intelligence. In two years the A20 Pro moved the iPhone to TSMC N2, the C2 modem reached the flagship, the first foldable shipped at $1,999, and on 2026-01-12 Apple and Google announced the next Apple Foundation Models would be Gemini-based [S58, S59, S63, S64].

### The silicon lead is real, costly, and rented from TSMC

The A19 Pro used TSMC N3P; a year later the A20 Pro moved to TSMC N2 with a 32-core Neural Engine and ~52 TOPS, about double the prior generation's AI throughput. N2 wafers are reported at ~$30,000 against $18,000-20,000 for 3nm, so each step costs more. Product gross margin was 39.9% in the nine months to 2026-06-27 versus 36.9% a year earlier, but only with tariff refunds and mix offsetting "higher costs, including memory", and the 10-Q warns that advanced-semiconductor, NAND and DRAM constraints are expected to intensify [S6, S64].

| Metric | Value | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Node, A19 Pro / A20 Pro | TSMC N3P (2025) / N2 (2026) | Teardown and trade reporting | S63, S64 |
| CPU clock, A19 Pro | up to 4.26 GHz, 6 cores | Published specification | S63 |
| Neural Engine, A20 Pro | 32 cores, ~52 TOPS, ~2x A19 Pro | Trade-press estimate | S64 |
| N2 wafer price | ~$30,000 vs $18,000-20,000 at 3nm | Trade-press estimate | S64 |
| Product gross margin | 39.9% vs 36.9% (9M FY2025) | Reported financials | S6 |
| On-device model / PCC context | ~3B parameters / 32K tokens | Apple research and developer docs | S61, S62 |

### Apple Intelligence is an architecture with a rented brain

On device, Apple runs a ~3B-parameter model optimised through KV-cache sharing and 2-bit quantisation-aware training; on its servers, a Parallel-Track Mixture-of-Experts model runs inside Private Cloud Compute, which enforces stateless processing, no privileged access even for Apple staff, and attested software images. The binding constraint is memory bandwidth and power: phone-class memory caps on-device inference at single-digit billions of parameters, so harder queries are offloaded. The ceiling is disclosed: a 32K-token context is small against frontier assistants, and Apple's own models were not frontier-quality. The unresolved question for the privacy story is where Gemini-derived inference physically runs. Apple says Apple Intelligence continues on Apple devices and Private Cloud Compute; trade reporting says Google's cloud performs the Gemini computation and puts the licence at ~$1bn a year, on top of a default-search payment of ~$20bn. Neither figure is Apple-confirmed. China's CAC approved Apple Intelligence on 2026-07-15, nearly two years after its 2024 debut, with Alibaba's Qwen and Baidu supplying a separate model stack. Apple's differentiation is orchestration, distribution and privacy, not model quality; an investor should underwrite the cash flow and installed base, not the AI layer [S8, S58, S60, S61, S86, S120, S171].

| Dimension | Apple 2024 (AFM v1) | Apple 2026 (Gemini-based AFM) | Google (supplier) | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Frontier model | Own ~3B on-device plus server model | Gemini-derived | Owns Gemini | S58, S61 |
| Cost structure | Fixed R&D and data-centre capex | Fixed R&D plus per-query licence | Licence revenue | S58, S86 |
| What Apple keeps | Silicon, OS, orchestration | Silicon, OS, interface, orchestration | Model, training, inference | S58, S60 |

### Products: a strong cycle, a late foldable, a spatial computer that never became a platform

The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max launched on 2026-09-09 at $1,199 and $1,299; the foldable iPhone Duo at $1,999 went on sale on 2026-10-23. iPhone net sales rose 22% to $196.5bn in the nine months to 2026-06-27, with Greater China up 30%. The C2 modem supports US mmWave and uses 15% less energy than the C1X, but the larger iPhone 18 Pro Max appears to keep a Qualcomm modem, so Qualcomm retains leverage over the highest-ASP SKU. Vision Pro is the counter-example: ~390,000 units in 2024, ~45,000 in the December 2025 quarter despite the M5 refresh, ~600,000 lifetime, and an IDC forecast of ~290,000 units in 2026 [S59, S13, S87].

| Product | Stage | Launch | Revenue or share | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone 18 Pro / Pro Max | Commercial | 2026-09 | $196.5bn, 54% of 9M | Products 39.9% | C2 in Pro Max, 2027 | S59, S6 |
| iPhone Duo (foldable) | Commercial | 2026-10-23 | Inside iPhone; undisclosed | Not disclosed | First-quarter volume | S59 |
| Watch Series 11 / Ultra 3 | Commercial | 2025-09 | Wearables $27.3bn, +2% | Not disclosed | Hypertension roll-out | S5, S6 |
| Vision Pro (M5) | Commercial | 2025-10 | ~45k units Q4 2025 | Not disclosed | Lower-cost model, late 2026 | S87 |
| Services | Commercial | — | $91.7bn, +14% | 76.3% | AI tier / iCloud+ gating | S6, S107 |

### What is enforceable is regulatory, not patent

Apple publishes no patent count; the FY2025 10-K says only that it is "pursuing thousands of applications around the world" and that no single right protects its products. Patent counts and peer comparison were not obtainable — the registries could not be searched — so the patent moat is unquantified. What is documented is a regulatory estate — hypertension and sleep-apnoea notifications, a hearing-aid De Novo grant and imaging calibration — each cleared on its own clinical file, a slower but more durable barrier than a patent family.

| Asset | Identifier | Jurisdiction | Date | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Patent portfolio | Count not disclosed | US and foreign | Ongoing | "Thousands of applications" | Unquantified | S5 |
| Hypertension Notification | K250507 | US FDA | 2025-09-11 | Cleared 510(k) | Watch sensing | S30 |
| Sleep Apnea Notification | K240929 | US FDA | 2024-09-13 | Cleared 510(k) | Watch sensing | S33 |
| Hearing Aid Feature | DEN230081 | US FDA | 2024-09-12 | De Novo granted | AirPods | S34 |
| Medical Imaging Calibration | K253582 | US FDA | 2026-04-01 | Cleared 510(k) | Display calibration | S29 |

### The moat is wide at the bottom of the stack and thin at the top

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Custom SoC and modem | 9 | Top design team plus priority TSMC N2 access; a decade and an Intel acquisition | 4-5 years | S59, S64 |
| Hardware-OS integration | 8 | Six operating systems co-designed with custom silicon | 3-5 years | S5 |
| On-device model efficiency | 5 | Quantisation and KV-cache techniques are published | 1-2 years | S61 |
| Frontier model | 3 | Available to licence, as Apple has shown | 1-2 years, by cheque | S58 |
| FDA-cleared health features | 7 | Each feature needs its own trial and clearance | 3-4 years | S30, S33 |
| Installed base and developers | 10 | A decade of switching costs, record active base | 10+ years | S13, S87 |
| **Composite** | **8/10 hardware, 4/10 AI** | The stack is hard to copy; the intelligence is not | **4-5 years for hardware** | S58, S64 |

The replication test: a team of 50 senior silicon and operating-system engineers could match a phone-class SoC and OS in four to five years, and rent a competitive model next quarter. The counter-evidence is Apple's own record: Siri needed a Google licence, the car was cancelled, and Vision Pro has not reached platform volumes. Regulation can also withhold the assistant: the Q3 FY2026 10-Q states DMA interoperability obligations have in the past, and may in future, cause Apple not to launch or maintain features "such as Siri AI" in certain jurisdictions. The advantage holds only if on-device AI lifts upgrade rates and regulators leave the App Store economics that fund the silicon intact. Two diligence questions settle it: whether the Google agreement allows fine-tuning for on-device use, and whether the 2027 Pro Max moves fully to the C2 [S6, S58, S59, S87].

::: evidence
**Apple's integration advantage is durable in silicon and distribution, but it no longer extends to the model layer.**

The A20 Pro's 2nm node and 32-core Neural Engine keep Apple at the leading edge of phone silicon, and ten FDA clearances and grants since 2020 give it a regulated feature estate rivals must replicate trial by trial. But basing the next Apple Foundation Models on Gemini concedes that the frontier layer is bought, the reported ~$1bn annual licence turns a fixed R&D advantage into a variable cost paid to a competitor, and availability now varies by jurisdiction: China runs a Qwen/Baidu stack and DMA rules may withhold Siri AI in the EU [S6, S58, S64, S86, S120, S171].
:::

arguments.markdown:
Apple's route to FY2028 growth is services mix, a richer iPhone cycle and India, with artificial intelligence as a retention feature and a possible iCloud+ upsell rather than a revenue line of its own; the plan is credible on cash generation and per-share compounding, but not yet on AI monetisation or on creating a new product category. The base is large and still growing: revenue reached $416.2bn in FY2025, and the nine months to 2026-06-27 produced $364.4bn, up 16%, with Services at $91.7bn, up 14% [S77, S6].

### Services carry the margin, but the mix engine stalled in FY2026

Services were 26% of FY2025 revenue but 39% of gross profit in the nine months to June 2026, because they earn a 76.3% gross margin against 39.9% for products. The mix engine, however, stopped being the marginal driver: product gross profit grew 26% against 15% for services, so the rise in total gross margin to 49.1% from 46.8% came from hardware mix and tariff refunds, not from services, while memory costs kept rising. Services growth itself came from advertising and cloud services, with the Google search-distribution payment named as a primary driver. That is the engine that funds the buyback and the silicon, and it is also the engine regulators are targeting: the European Commission fined Apple €500m on 2025-04-23 for anti-steering non-compliance, and the General Court dismissed Apple's challenge to its gatekeeper designation on 2026-07-08 [S85, S84, S6]. An investor should value the services annuity on gross profit that compounds in the low-to-mid teens, and apply a discount for the probability that a remedy compresses commission or search income rather than a one-off fine.

### AI is funded as cost and monetised, if at all, through storage

Apple introduced Siri AI with the iOS 27 cycle announced in the third quarter of FY2026, and R&D rose 33% to $34.0bn in the nine months to June 2026, driven by infrastructure including AI investments and headcount. No AI revenue line exists. Availability is a regulatory variable too: China cleared Apple Intelligence only on 2026-07-15, with Alibaba's Qwen and Baidu, and the 10-Q warns that DMA rules have in the past, and may in future, cause it not to launch features "such as Siri AI" in some jurisdictions. The reported plan — that high-frequency, compute-intensive Siri use will be gated behind iCloud+ — is plausible because it reuses a price ladder already in place, but Apple has published no tier and no price, so it is unverified [S13, S6, S107, S171]. The mechanism matters more than the price: AI raises the cost of serving every device while its clearest commercial effect is to protect upgrade rates and services attach. If Apple charges, the increment is bounded by storage-subscription willingness to pay, not by the value of the model; if it does not, AI is a permanent tax on gross margin. Either way, 2027 is the test of whether AI spend converts into units or ARPU.

### India lowers tariff risk, not unit cost

iPhone production in India rose 53% in 2025 to ~55 million units, ~25% of global output, and is projected at 28% in 2026; Tata Electronics overtook Foxconn in iPhone export assembly over the FY2022-FY2026 incentive period. The strategy is rational given the tariff record in the filings — Section 232 semiconductor investigation results in January 2026, the Supreme Court striking down certain IEEPA tariffs in February 2026, and new Section 301 tariffs, with manufacturing purchase obligations of $57.0bn at 2026-06-27 [S89, S91, S6]. The limit is that assembly captures little of the value: components, displays and silicon still come from East Asia, so India is an insurance policy on tariffs and single-country concentration, not a margin lever. The signpost to watch is the share of US-bound iPhones assembled in India, which Apple has never disclosed.

### Capital allocation is disciplined and slightly bolder

R&D rose from $29.9bn in FY2023 to $34.6bn in FY2025 and is running at ~$45bn annualised in FY2026. Buybacks remain the primary use of cash: $25.8bn of stock was repurchased in the quarter to 2026-06-27 alone, alongside $4.0bn of dividends at $0.27 per share, which cut the share count to 14.61bn from 14.77bn at FY2025 year-end and helped EPS grow 29% against 27% net-income growth. M&A posture has shifted from tuck-ins: Apple confirmed the acquisition of the AI-audio start-up Q.ai on 2026-01-29, reported by the Financial Times at close to $2bn, and acquired the AI data-engineering company Ascend.io, notified to the European Commission on 2026-06-30; intangible assets rose from $11.1bn to $20.3bn between 2025-09-27 and 2026-06-27 [S77, S88, S6, S13]. Against ~$146bn of cash and marketable securities, that is affordable experimentation rather than a change of strategy — and it is the right test of whether Apple's AI gap can be bought in pieces.

### What must be true in twelve months, and the case against

Four things must happen for the strategy to be credible. First, the FY2026 holiday quarter has to show that the iPhone 18 and Duo cycle sustains double-digit growth without tariff refunds, which flattered the June quarter by ~2 percentage points of gross margin. Second, Apple must put a price on AI or show that it lifts upgrade rates, because a 33% R&D increase with no revenue attached is a margin problem. Third, a DOJ settlement or DMA remedy must leave the App Store commission and default-search payment substantially intact; both cases attack the services profit pool directly. Fourth, India must reach the projected share of output without a quality or logistics incident. The counter-case is strong and largely Apple's own record: AI features arrived well after they were demonstrated, Siri needed a Google licence, the car programme was cancelled, and Vision Pro shipped ~45,000 units in the December 2025 quarter, while Alphabet, Microsoft and Huawei set a faster cadence in models, cloud AI and, for Huawei, folding hardware and domestic silicon. Apple's answer is that it does not need to be first — it needs to be best integrated, and it monetises the installed base rather than the model. That is a defensible strategy for a cash-flow investor and a weak one for anyone buying AI optionality [S59, S87, S84, S90, S89].

::: evidence
**The strategy is credible as a cash-compounding plan and unproven as a growth plan.**

Services earn a structurally higher gross margin than hardware, and buybacks are large enough that earnings per share can compound faster than net income even with flat hardware; but AI is a large R&D increase with no disclosed price, Vision Pro has not become a platform, and the two antitrust cases target precisely the services lines that fund the plan.
:::

At $344.63 at the NasdaqGS close on 2026-10-30, Apple carries a $5,029.6B market capitalisation and a $4,967.4B enterprise value on trailing diluted earnings of $8.72 a share and trailing free cash flow of $136.7B. Capital return does not close the gap, and Apple's financing history is the inverse of a growth company's: no equity issuance, debt of $84.3B at 2026-06-27 against $124.7B in fiscal 2021 and $146.5B of cash and marketable securities, with $82.2B of buybacks and $15.6B of dividends in the trailing twelve months, a 1.9% total shareholder yield. In April 2026 it authorised a further $100B of repurchases and raised the quarterly dividend 4% to $0.27. At 39.5x each repurchased dollar retires stock at a 2.5% earnings yield, below the 4.93% the same dollar would earn in Treasuries, so the buyback supports EPS more than value per share; the diluted count fell from 16,865M in fiscal 2021 to 14,715M in the June 2026 quarter, but the pace is slowing as repurchases fell to $62.1B in nine months from $70.6B. The calendar is dated: fiscal fourth-quarter results on 2026-11-02 with revenue guided to rise 9-11%, fiscal 2027 guidance and any new authorisation that day, the Google search-remedy appeal over a reported $20B of near-pure-margin services revenue, and memory costs that IDC expects to normalise in 2028. [S164, S162, S6, S1]

The counter-case deserves weight. Apple's 2.7% free-cash-flow yield is the highest of the four mega-caps, Services compounds at 14% on a 76% gross margin, and an AI-driven iPhone cycle that holds revenue growth near 10% would earn a 35x forward multiple rather than merely re-rate it. But at $344.63 the arithmetic offers no margin of safety: 25-30x forward earnings, the ten-year mean to the five-year average, is $245-294, 15-29% below the close, and a 6-8% free-cash-flow path is worth $221-255. The asymmetry is in the entry price, not the franchise. Three questions would settle it: what normalised free cash flow does the fiscal 2026 annual report show after the tariff refund and inventory build? What share of Services revenue depends on the Google payment, and how does the appeal resolve? Does the September quarter confirm revenue growth at or above 9%? Confidence is high in the multiples and the DCF arithmetic, medium in the durability of a 50% gross margin at a cyclical high. [S6, S154]

### Three Irish companies sit between the product and the profit

EX-21 lists 19 subsidiaries in 12 jurisdictions and says others are omitted as not significant; it gives neither ownership percentages nor functions, so the table below is a map of legal domicile, not of economic activity. What can be established is the shape: the two entities the European Commission found held Apple's intellectual property for sales outside the Americas — Apple Sales International and Apple Operations Europe — do not appear in the FY2025 list. In their place are Apple Operations International, Apple Operations Limited and Apple Distribution International, all Irish. Apple does not describe the 2015 restructuring or say which entity now owns the non-U.S. IP, but the consequence is visible in the tax note: foreign pretax earnings were $82.0bn of $132.7bn in FY2025, and the effective tax rate was 15.6% against a 21% U.S. statutory rate.

[Legal entity table]

The mechanism matters more than the labels. A 5.4-point gap between the statutory and effective rate on $132.7bn of pretax income is worth roughly $7bn a year in cash tax, which funds the buyback; but that gap is exactly what the Commission attacked. The 2016 decision ordered recovery of up to €13bn; the General Court annulled it on 2020-07-15; the Court of Justice reinstated it on 2024-09-10; Apple took a $10.2bn net charge in Q4 FY2024 and paid $15.8bn to Ireland through escrow, offset by a $4.8bn U.S. foreign tax credit. Ireland had already closed the opinions in January 2015, so the specific scheme is gone. What remains is a precedent: a tax structure that the company had treated as settled was reopened and lost eight years later. An investor should not capitalise 15.6% as permanent, and the entity-level accounts filed with Ireland's Companies Registration Office — which the 10-K does not reproduce — are the document that would settle where the profit now sits.

### Capital return, not leverage, is the capital-structure question

Apple carries about $62.2bn of net cash ... [S6]. In the nine months to 2026-06-27 it repurchased 215m shares for $61.8bn, against $70.6bn in the same period a year earlier, under a $100bn authorisation announced on 2025-05-01; the share count has fallen about 0.7% since January. The mechanism is arithmetic: at a $5tn market capitalisation each $10bn of repurchase retires roughly 0.2% of the company, so the return to shareholders depends on the price paid. A 12% year-on-year slowdown in dollars while the shares rose about 26% over the year is consistent with price discipline, or with lower free cash flow; the filings do not distinguish. With net cash and an investment-grade balance sheet the risk is not solvency — it is that the largest capital-allocation programme in the market is executed at a multiple that assumes the AI transition works.

### Ownership is institutional, and the board is long-tenured

Vanguard holds 9.63% and BlackRock 7.10%, though the BlackRock figure rests on a 2023-12-31 filing quoted in the 2026 proxy, so it is stale [S65]. Directors and officers hold 0.06%; Tim Cook's 3,280,295 shares are worth over $1bn at the current price but are 0.02% of the company. The board has nine members after Ternus joined on 2026-09-01, seven of them independent by the company's determination; Arthur Levinson, a director since 2000 and chair for 15 years, became lead independent director the same day. At the 2026-02-24 annual meeting Levinson drew 9.0% opposition, say-on-pay drew 8.6% opposition and a "China Entanglement Audit" proposal won 1.4% — a governance profile that is adequate by Nasdaq's majority-independent rule but far from the founder-aligned story investors sometimes tell about Apple [S153].

### The business model is an annuity on hardware

Apple sells devices to consumers, enterprises and carriers, but the buyer that matters is the installed base: more than 2.5bn devices whose owners upgrade hardware and pay for services. FY2025 net sales were $416.2bn (+6%), with Services gross margin of 75.4% against 46.9% for the group; in the nine months to 2026-06-27 net sales rose 16% to $364.4bn, Services rose 14% to $91.7bn and Greater China rose 30% to $64.8bn after falling 4% in FY2025 [S5, S6]. That is the growth engine: a replacement cycle plus attach, with China swinging from drag to driver in two years. It also explains why the model is resilient to unit stagnation but not to a remedy that breaks the Services attach — Services produced 39.1% of nine-month gross profit on 25.2% of revenue.

### The legal front is about Services margins, not fines

Three proceedings test the container. The DOJ's civil antitrust suit, filed on 2024-03-21 in the District of New Jersey, seeks equitable relief rather than damages; the Epic litigation produced a 2025-04-30 finding that Apple violated the 2021 injunction, a ban on fees for out-of-app purchases and a referral to the U.S. Attorney for possible criminal contempt; and the EU fined Apple €500m under the Digital Markets Act on 2025-04-23, which Apple has appealed [S5, S7]. The fines are small against $416bn of revenue; the remedies are not, because they target the 75%-gross-margin Services line and the App Store's role as the toll gate on a 2.5bn-device base. Counter-evidence is real: the DOJ must prove market definition, Apple says it has substantial defences, and no court has ordered a structural remedy. But the direction of travel in the U.S. and EU is toward forcing alternative distribution and payment, which is the one outcome that would change the franchise's economics rather than its legal bill.

Apple's structure is clean in law — one share class, a majority-independent board and net cash — but not in economics: 61.8% of pretax profit is booked outside the U.S. at a 15.6% effective tax rate, insiders own 0.06%, and the same director has chaired the board since 2000, so the "alignment" in the equity story rests on pay design and on a tax structure the EU has already litigated once [S5, S65].

The listed parent is Apple Inc., a California corporation whose common stock ($0.00001 par value) trades on Nasdaq under AAPL. It had 14,594,180,000 shares outstanding at 2026-07-17, down from 14,697,926,000 at 2026-01-02, and a market capitalisation of $5.03 trillion at 2026-10-30 [S6, S172]. One class of stock means votes track economics one-for-one; the free float is about 99.9% because all directors and officers together hold 9,079,765 shares.

::: kpi
| Metric | Value | Benchmark | Signal | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Shares outstanding | 14,594,180,000 (2026-07-17) | 14,697,926,000 (2026-01-02) | good | S6, S65 |
| Buybacks, nine months to 2026-06-27 | $61.8bn for 215m shares | $70.6bn in the same period of FY2025 | warn | S6 |
| Net cash | about $62.2bn (cash and securities $146.5bn less debt $84.3bn, 2026-06-27) | gross debt $84.3bn | good | S6 |
| Effective tax rate | 15.6% (FY2025) | 21% U.S. statutory rate | warn | S5 |
| Foreign pretax profit | 61.8% ($82.0bn of $132.7bn, FY2025) | 38.2% U.S. | warn | S5 |
| Insider ownership | 0.06% (9,079,765 shares) | below the 1% proxy disclosure threshold | warn | S65 |
:::

### Three Irish companies sit between the product and the profit

EX-21 lists 19 subsidiaries domiciled in 15 jurisdictions and omits the rest as not significant; it gives neither ownership percentages nor functions, so what follows is a map of domicile, not of economic activity. The two entities the European Commission found held Apple's intellectual property for sales outside the Americas — Apple Sales International and Apple Operations Europe — no longer appear on the list. In their place are three Irish companies. Apple does not describe the 2015 restructuring or name the entity that now owns the non-U.S. IP, but the tax note shows the consequence: foreign pretax earnings of $82.0bn of $132.7bn in FY2025 and a 15.6% effective rate against a 21% statutory rate.

| Entity | Jurisdiction | Type | Role | Ownership % | Controller | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Apple Inc. | California, U.S. | Corporation (registrant) | Listed parent; issuer of AAPL common stock | Public float about 99.9% | Public shareholders | S5, S65 |
| Apple Operations International Limited | Ireland | Limited company | Irish holding entity; role not described | Not disclosed in EX-21 | Apple Inc. | S5 |
| Apple Operations Limited | Ireland | Limited company | Irish operating entity; role not described | Not disclosed in EX-21 | Apple Inc. | S5 |
| Apple Distribution International Limited | Ireland | Limited company | Distribution entity; role not described | Not disclosed in EX-21 | Apple Inc. | S5 |
| Braeburn Capital, Inc. | Nevada, U.S. | Corporation | Investment management; role not described | Not disclosed in EX-21 | Apple Inc. | S5 |
| Apple Computer Trading (Shanghai) Co., Ltd. | China | Limited liability company | Greater China trading entity | Not disclosed in EX-21 | Apple Inc. | S5 |

The 5.4-point gap on $132.7bn of pretax income is worth roughly $7bn a year in cash tax, and it is exactly what the Commission attacked. The 2016 decision ordered recovery of up to €13bn; the General Court annulled it on 2020-07-15; the Court of Justice reinstated it on 2024-09-10; Apple took a $10.2bn net charge in Q4 FY2024 and paid $15.8bn to Ireland through escrow, offset by a $4.8bn U.S. foreign tax credit. Ireland closed the opinions in January 2015, so the scheme itself is gone, but the precedent is not: a structure the company treated as settled was reopened and lost after eight years. Do not capitalise 15.6% as permanent; the entity accounts filed with Ireland's Companies Registration Office, which the 10-K does not reproduce, would show where profit now sits.

### Capital return, not leverage, is the capital-structure question

Apple carries about $62.2bn of net cash — $146.5bn of cash and securities against $84.3bn of debt at 2026-06-27 — and in the nine months to that date repurchased 215m shares for $61.8bn, against $70.6bn in the same period a year earlier, under a $100bn authorisation announced on 2025-05-01 [S6]. At a $5tn capitalisation each $10bn of repurchase retires roughly 0.2% of the company, so the return depends on the price paid. A 12% year-on-year slowdown in dollars while the shares rose about 26% is consistent with price discipline, or with lower free cash flow; the filings do not distinguish. Solvency is not the risk; executing the market's largest buyback at a multiple that assumes the AI transition works is.

### Ownership is institutional, and the board is long-tenured

Vanguard holds 9.63% and BlackRock 7.10%, but the BlackRock figure is taken from a 2023-12-31 filing quoted in the 2026 proxy and is stale [S65]. Directors and officers hold 0.06%; Tim Cook's 3,280,295 shares are worth more than $1bn at the current price yet are 0.02% of the company. The board has nine members after Ternus joined on 2026-09-01, seven of them independent; Arthur Levinson, a director since 2000 and chair for 15 years, became lead independent director that day. At the 2026-02-24 annual meeting Levinson drew 9.0% opposition, say-on-pay 8.6% and a "China Entanglement Audit" proposal 1.4% support [S153]. That passes Nasdaq's majority-independent rule and is not a governance crisis, but it is a professional board, not a founder-aligned one.

### The business model is an annuity on hardware

Apple sells devices to consumers, enterprises and carriers, but the buyer that matters is the installed base: more than 2.5bn devices whose owners upgrade and pay for services. FY2025 net sales were $416.2bn (+6%), with Services gross margin of 75.4% against 46.9% for the group; in the nine months to 2026-06-27 net sales rose 16% to $364.4bn, Services 14% to $91.7bn and Greater China 30% to $64.8bn after a 4% decline in FY2025 [S5, S6]. That is the growth engine — a replacement cycle plus attach, with China swinging from drag to driver in two years. It makes the model resilient to unit stagnation but not to a remedy that breaks the Services attach: Services produced 39.1% of nine-month gross profit on 25.2% of revenue.

### The legal front is about Services margins, not fines

Three proceedings test the container. The DOJ's civil antitrust suit, filed on 2024-03-21 in the District of New Jersey, seeks equitable relief rather than damages; the Epic litigation produced a 2025-04-30 finding that Apple violated the 2021 injunction, a ban on fees for out-of-app purchases and a referral to the U.S. Attorney for possible criminal contempt; and the EU fined Apple €500m under the Digital Markets Act on 2025-04-23, which Apple appealed [S5, S7]. The fines are small against $416bn of revenue; the remedies are not, because they target the 75%-gross-margin Services line and the App Store's toll gate on 2.5bn devices. Counter-evidence is real — the DOJ must prove market definition, Apple says it has substantial defences, and no court has ordered a structural remedy — but the direction in both jurisdictions is toward alternative distribution and payment, the one outcome that would change the franchise's economics rather than its legal bill.

arguments.markdown:
Apple's structure is clean in law — one share class, a majority-independent board and net cash — but not in economics: 61.8% of pretax profit is booked outside the U.S. at a 15.6% effective tax rate, insiders own 0.06%, and the same director has chaired the board since 2000, so the "alignment" in the equity story rests on pay design and on a tax structure the EU has already litigated once. The listed parent is Apple Inc., a California corporation whose common stock ($0.00001 par value) trades on Nasdaq under AAPL: 14,594,180,000 shares outstanding at 2026-07-17, down from 14,697,926,000 at 2026-01-02, and a market capitalisation of $5.03 trillion at 2026-10-30. Votes track economics one-for-one, and the free float is 99.94% because all directors and officers together hold 9,079,765 shares [S5, S6, S65, S172].

| Effective tax rate | 15.6% (FY2025) | 21% U.S. statutory rate | warn | S5 |
| Foreign pretax profit | 61.8% ($82.0bn of $132.7bn, FY2025) | 38.2% U.S. | warn | S5 |
| Insider ownership | 0.06% (9,079,765 shares) | below the 1% proxy disclosure threshold | warn | S65 |
:::

### Three Irish companies sit between the product and the profit

EX-21 lists 19 subsidiaries domiciled in 15 jurisdictions and omits the rest as not significant; it gives neither ownership percentages nor functions, so what follows is a map of domicile, not of economic activity. The two entities the European Commission found held Apple's intellectual property for sales outside the Americas — Apple Sales International and Apple Operations Europe — no longer appear on the list; in their place are three Irish companies. Apple does not describe the 2015 restructuring or name the entity that now owns the non-U.S. IP, but the tax note shows the consequence: foreign pretax earnings of $82.0bn of $132.7bn in FY2025 and a 15.6% effective rate against 21%. The 5.4-point gap is worth $7.2bn a year in cash tax, and it is exactly what the Commission attacked: the 2016 decision ordered recovery of up to €13bn, the General Court annulled it on 2020-07-15, the Court of Justice reinstated it on 2024-09-10, and Apple took a $10.2bn net charge in Q4 FY2024, paying $15.8bn to Ireland through escrow against a $4.8bn U.S. foreign tax credit [S5, S187]. Ireland closed the opinions in January 2015, so the scheme itself is gone, but the precedent is not. Entity accounts filed with Ireland's Companies Registration Office, which the 10-K does not reproduce, would show where profit now sits.

| Apple Computer Trading (Shanghai) Co., Ltd. | China | Limited liability company | Greater China trading entity | Not disclosed in EX-21 | Apple Inc. | S5 |

### Capital return, not leverage, is the capital-structure question

Apple carries $62.2bn of net cash — $146.5bn of cash and securities against $84.3bn of debt at 2026-06-27 — and in the nine months to that date repurchased 215m shares for $61.8bn, against $70.6bn in the same period a year earlier, under a $100bn authorisation announced on 2025-05-01 [S6]. At a $5tn capitalisation each $10bn of repurchase retires 0.2% of the company, so the return depends on the price paid. A 12% year-on-year slowdown in dollars while the shares rose 25.7% is consistent with price discipline, or with lower free cash flow; the filings do not distinguish. Solvency is not the risk; executing the market's largest buyback at a multiple that assumes the AI transition works is.

### Ownership is institutional, and the board is long-tenured

Vanguard holds 9.63% and BlackRock 7.10%, but the BlackRock figure is taken from a 2023-12-31 filing quoted in the 2026 proxy and is stale [S65, S153]. Directors and officers hold 0.06%; Tim Cook's 3,280,295 shares are worth $1.13bn at the current price yet are 0.02% of the company. The board has nine members after Ternus joined on 2026-09-01, seven of them independent; Arthur Levinson, a director since 2000 and chair for 15 years, became lead independent director that day. At the 2026-02-24 annual meeting Levinson drew 9.0% opposition, say-on-pay 8.6% and a "China Entanglement Audit" proposal 1.4% support. That passes Nasdaq's majority-independent rule and is not a governance crisis, but it is a professional board, not a founder-aligned one.

### The business model is an annuity on hardware

Apple sells devices to consumers, enterprises and carriers, but the buyer that matters is the installed base: more than 2.5bn devices whose owners upgrade and pay for services. FY2025 net sales were $416.2bn (+6%), with Services gross margin of 75.4% against 46.9% for the group; in the nine months to 2026-06-27 net sales rose 16% to $364.4bn, Services 14% to $91.7bn and Greater China 30% to $64.8bn after a 4% decline in FY2025 [S5, S6]. That is the growth engine — a replacement cycle plus attach, with China swinging from drag to driver in two years. It makes the model resilient to unit stagnation but not to a remedy that breaks the Services attach: Services produced 39.1% of nine-month gross profit on 25.2% of revenue.

### The legal front is about Services margins, not fines

Three proceedings test the container. The DOJ's civil antitrust suit, filed on 2024-03-21 in the District of New Jersey, seeks equitable relief rather than damages; the Epic litigation produced a 2025-04-30 finding that Apple violated the 2021 injunction, a ban on fees for out-of-app purchases and a referral to the U.S. Attorney for possible criminal contempt; and the EU fined Apple €500m under the Digital Markets Act on 2025-04-23, which Apple appealed [S5, S7]. The fines are small against $416bn of revenue; the remedies are not, because they target the 75%-gross-margin Services line and the App Store's toll gate on 2.5bn devices. Counter-evidence is real — the DOJ must prove market definition, Apple says it has substantial defences, and no court has ordered a structural remedy — but the direction in both jurisdictions is toward alternative distribution and payment, the one outcome that would change the franchise's economics rather than its legal bill.
