arguments.markdown:
Apple has no takeover exit and no listing event ahead of it. At a $5,029.6B market value the largest technology acquisition on record, Microsoft's $68.7B all-cash purchase of Activision Blizzard agreed on 2022-01-18, equals 1.4% of the company, and any bid would face the US and EU review that took that deal roughly 18 months and a divestiture to clear; a leveraged buyout of a $4.97T enterprise value is arithmetically impossible. The exit is a sale into the market, at a $13.84B average daily traded value where a 1% position in a $1B fund is $10M, 0.07% of one day's volume. The exit question is therefore not whether a holder can sell but at what multiple, which makes the sell discipline a set of price bands and thesis breaks rather than an event to wait for. [S9, S169]

| Exit route | Named buyer or venue | Rationale | Timing | Likelihood | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Open-market sale | NasdaqGS, $13.84B average daily traded value | The only route that absorbs a position without a discount | Any trading day | The route actually used | S9 |
| Strategic acquisition | No named buyer; largest tech deal $68.7B vs $5,029.6B market value | Size, antitrust, no strategic gap Apple fills | Not foreseeable | Very low | S169 |
| Leveraged buyout | None | $4.97T enterprise value and $84.3B of debt cannot be financed | Not foreseeable | Negligible | S6 |
| Company buyback (partial exit) | Apple Inc. | $82.2B repurchased in twelve months; $100B authorised April 2026; 1.6% of shares a year | Ongoing | High but discretionary | S164, S6 |
| Dividend | Apple Inc. | $0.27 a quarter, 0.31% yield, raised annually | Quarterly | Certain while declared | S13 |
| Index and passive flows | S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 constituent | Structural bid, not an exit route | Ongoing | Structural | S163 |

Apple's own record sets the cost of ownership. Over the last ten completed years the average intra-year peak-to-trough drawdown was 21.4%, lasting 82 days, and four episodes exceeded 30%: 2018 fell 36.73%, 2020 31.43%, 2022 30.75% and 2025 30.22%. Each was recovered, with 2020 returning 80.75% for the calendar year and 2025 8.56%, but each recovery came with a re-rating as well as earnings growth, and a holder buying at 39.5x cannot count on the re-rating half. From $344.63 the average drawdown is $271 and a 30% drawdown is $240. On 2026-10-30 Apple was 1.23% below its all-time-high close while the Nasdaq-100 was 9.09% below its own and the S&P 500 3.05%, so the stock enters any correction from relative strength rather than weakness. [S163, S168]

| Precedent episode | Peak | Trough | Drawdown | Days | Equivalent price from $344.63 | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2018 | $58.02 (2018-10-03) | $36.71 (2018-12-24) | -36.73% | 82 | $218 | S163 |
| 2020 | $81.80 (2020-02-12) | $56.09 (2020-03-23) | -31.43% | 40 | $236 | S163 |
| 2022 | $182.01 (2022-01-03) | $126.04 (2022-12-28) | -30.75% | 359 | $239 | S163 |
| 2025 | $247.10 (2025-02-24) | $172.42 (2025-04-08) | -30.22% | 43 | $240 | S163 |
| Ten-year average | - | - | -21.39% | 82 | $271 | S163 |

The multiple, not the remembered share price, is what made past entries work. The 2022 trough of $126.04 on 2022-12-28 was 20.6x fiscal 2022 diluted EPS of $6.11; today's 39.5x is nearly double that, and a repeat of 20x on today's trailing $8.72 would be $174 or $196 on forward $9.79, levels last seen in 2023 and not reached without an earnings recession. That is why the band is set on the forward multiple: 25-30x, the ten-year mean of 25.35x to the five-year average of 30.2x, is $248-296, and the bear case of a two-point gross-margin give-back on $8.20 of EPS at 25x is $205. The fair value in the middle case is not today's price; it is the price at which the multiple stops assuming the re-rating continues. [S163, S2]

| Scenario | EPS assumption | Multiple | Fair value | Versus $344.63 | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bear: gross margin falls two points, tax normalised | $8.20 | 25.0x | $205 | -41% | S6, S154 |
| Base: consensus forward EPS, five-year average multiple | $9.79 | 30.2x | $296 | -14% | S157 |
| Bull: AI cycle holds, multiple at five-year high | $10.50 | 38.0x | $399 | +16% | S157, S156 |

A long-only fund should underwrite a three-to-five-year hold, because that is the period over which the Services annuity and the installed base can compound enough to absorb a de-rating. On forward EPS of $9.79 growing 8% a year to $12.33 by fiscal 2029 and $3.37 of cumulative dividends, the annual total return depends almost entirely on the exit multiple, and the entry price decides whether the fund is paid for waiting. At $344.63 a 25x exit loses 3.3% a year and a 35x exit earns 8.2%; at $296 the same exits earn 1.8% and 13.8%; at $248 they earn 8.0% and 20.6%. The hurdle of 8% a year is met at today's price only if the multiple stays at 35x, which is the top of the five-year range, not its middle. [S157, S154]

| Entry price | Forward P/E | 3-year annual return at exit 25x | At exit 30x | At exit 35x | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $344.63 | 35.2x | -3.3% | +2.7% | +8.2% | S9, S157 |
| $296 | 30.2x | +1.8% | +8.1% | +13.8% | S157, S154 |
| $248 | 25.3x | +8.0% | +14.8% | +20.6% | S154, S6 |

| Sell trigger | Threshold | Action | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Valuation | Forward P/E above 40x (over $395) with no EPS upgrade | Trim to half | S157, S156 |
| Valuation | Forward P/E at or below 25.5x (at or below $250) | Add to full position | S154 |
| Thesis break: Services | Services revenue growth below 5% year on year for two quarters | Sell | S13 |
| Thesis break: margin | Gross margin below 44%, the fiscal 2023 level | Sell | S5 |
| Thesis break: search payment | Google payment removed without an offsetting services gain | Sell or halve | S165 |
| Thesis break: China | Greater China revenue down 10% year on year | Reassess, then sell | S13 |

The policy tests are narrow for a US holder: no foreign-buyer limit applies to a sale of shares, there is no lock-up, and the listing venue is not in question at NasdaqGS, the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq-100. The binding policy risk sits in the asset, not the exit. The Google search payment, reported at $20B a year, is 17% of Services revenue and 22% of services gross profit, and the default-payment ban took effect in June 2026 under the April 2026 remedy order; at a 30x multiple its loss is $450B, 9% of market value. That is the one event that would force a sale regardless of price. The slower ones are App Store commission rules under the DMA and the DOJ case, and China, where revenue was $64.8B in nine months of fiscal 2026 and can turn on subsidy or geopolitical policy rather than on Apple's execution. [S165, S13]

The strongest case against this discipline is that a 30x-plus multiple never offers a margin of safety again. If Services compounds at 14% on a 76% gross margin and the buyback retires 1.6% of the shares a year, a fund that waits for $250 may simply never own the best cash generator in the market, and the cost of the discipline is opportunity rather than loss. The answer is a time rule rather than a permanent price target: if Apple trades above $296 for four consecutive quarters while Services growth stays above 10%, reassess the band against the then-current multiple instead of waiting for a level the business has outgrown. Until then, watchlist above $300, a first tranche at $275-296, and a full position at or below $250. Confidence is high in the drawdown record and the return arithmetic, medium in the multiple at which a future buyer will pay, because that depends on the ten-year yield, which was 4.93% on 2026-10-30. The diligence questions are the exit terms of the Google payment, the durability of the 50.1% June-quarter gross margin without the tariff refund, and whether the buyback is re-authorised at $100B in 2027. [S154, S157]

arguments.markdown:
The succession is done and internal — Ternus, Srouji, Federighi and Parekh are all Apple lifers — which lowers cultural and execution risk but concentrates the AI transition in a software chief who has outsourced the frontier model to Google and a first-time CEO who has never run a P&L, so the team offers continuity rather than evidence of renewal. The board appointed John Ternus CEO effective 2026-09-01, with Tim Cook as executive chair and Arthur Levinson, chair for the previous 15 years, as lead independent director. Ternus, 50, joined Apple's product design team in 2001, became VP Hardware Engineering in 2013 and SVP in 2021; his record includes iPad, AirPods, the iPhone 17 line and the MacBook Neo, but no disclosed CEO, P&L or capital-allocation role before 2026 [S152, S177].

::: evidence
**The board has already executed the succession, and the bench is internal: Ternus, Srouji, Federighi, Parekh, Cue and O'Brien have each spent more than 20 years at Apple, and the appointment was unanimous.**

The 8-K of 2026-04-20 records the board's appointment of Ternus as CEO effective 2026-09-01, Cook's move to executive chair and Levinson's to lead independent director [S152]. Ternus joined Apple in 2001 and has led hardware engineering since 2021 [S177]. The doubt sits one level down: the AI organisation was rebuilt on 2025-12-01 around an external hire reporting to Federighi, and the rebuilt Siri will run on Google's Gemini models [S183, S186].
:::

The division of labour is unusually clear for a company of this size. Ternus integrates and decides; Johny Srouji became chief hardware officer on 2026-04-20, adding hardware engineering to silicon and becoming the single owner of Apple's deepest technical moat; Craig Federighi owns software and, since December 2025, AI; Eddy Cue runs services and now health; Kevan Parekh funds the company; Sabih Khan runs operations; Deirdre O'Brien runs retail and people [S179, S184]. That design fits a business whose advantage is integration across silicon, software and services, but it places the two capabilities that matter most in the next cycle — silicon and AI/software — in two individuals with no disclosed deputies.

### AI leadership failed once and has been rebuilt around an outside hire and an outside model

John Giannandrea stepped down as AI chief on 2025-12-01 after the Siri delay; Amar Subramanya, formerly corporate VP of AI at Microsoft and head of engineering for Google's Gemini Assistant, joined as VP of AI reporting to Federighi, while the rest of the AI organisation was split between Khan and Cue [S183, S186]. On 2026-01-12 Apple and Google announced a multiyear deal to power Apple's AI features, including the Siri upgrade due in 2026, with Gemini. The mechanism is speed for dependency: Apple gets a competitive assistant without building a frontier model, but it hands a competitor the most valuable interface in consumer technology and caps the differentiation it can charge for. Underwrite AI as a feature that protects the hardware replacement cycle, not as a new profit pool, until Apple discloses model economics.

### Pay is high and equity-heavy, but it is not the binding constraint

Cook's 2025 total target compensation was $59m: a $3m base unchanged since 2016, a cash incentive at 200% of base and a $50m equity target, positioned in the 80th-90th percentile of the primary peer group; the other named executives target $1m base, 200% cash and $20m equity, and Parekh's target was $16.75m [S65, S153]. The CEO ownership guideline is 10 times salary and other executives three times. The design retains executives through the transition rather than rewarding new AI outcomes: 8.6% of votes cast opposed say-on-pay at the 2026-02-24 annual meeting, a protest worth noting but not a rejection. Pay is therefore a weak signal for the investment case; who stays is more important than what they are paid.

### Five senior roles changed in 24 months, all through planned transitions

The CFO moved from Luca Maestri to Parekh on 2025-01-01, the COO from Jeff Williams to Khan in July 2025, the general counsel from Kate Adams to Jennifer Newstead on 2026-03-01, the AI chief from Giannandrea to Subramanya on 2025-12-01 and the CEO from Cook to Ternus on 2026-09-01 [S170, S166]. Against Apple's near-static 2011-2023 executive team that is a large amount of institutional change at once. The mitigating evidence is that none was a resignation under pressure and two brought external experience; the unmitigated risk is coordination — a first-time CEO, a new CFO, a new general counsel and a rebuilt AI organisation learning each other while antitrust remedies and a China reset land.

### The missing capability is frontier AI at the top, not finance or operations

No board member has operating AI-lab experience — Wanda Austin ran Aerospace, Alex Gorsky ran Johnson & Johnson — and the AI leader sits at VP level, outside the executive team [S179, S173]. That is the reference check a diligence team should run: who inside Apple can credibly challenge Google's model roadmap, and what retention packages hold Srouji and Federighi, the two people whose departure would impair the franchise. Counter-evidence is genuine: internal succession worked in 2011 when Cook replaced Steve Jobs, Ternus's product record is strong, and the Gemini deal buys time. The judgement is not that the team is weak; it is that the team is unproven at exactly the task the next three years demand.

arguments.markdown:
The succession is done and internal — Ternus, Srouji, Federighi and Parekh are all Apple lifers — which lowers cultural and execution risk but concentrates the AI transition in a software chief who has outsourced the frontier model to Google and a first-time CEO who has never run a P&L, so the team offers continuity rather than evidence of renewal. The board appointed John Ternus CEO effective 2026-09-01, with Tim Cook as executive chair and Arthur Levinson, chair for the previous 15 years, as lead independent director. Ternus, 50, joined Apple's product design team in 2001, became VP Hardware Engineering in 2013 and SVP in 2021; his record includes iPad, AirPods, the iPhone 17 line and the MacBook Neo, but no disclosed CEO, P&L or capital-allocation role before 2026 [S152, S177].

::: evidence
**The board has already executed the succession, and the bench is internal: Ternus, Srouji, Federighi, Parekh, Cue and O'Brien have each spent more than 20 years at Apple, and the appointment was unanimous.**

The 8-K of 2026-04-20 records the board's appointment of Ternus as CEO effective 2026-09-01, Cook's move to executive chair and Levinson's to lead independent director [S152]. Ternus joined Apple in 2001 and has led hardware engineering since 2021 [S177]. The doubt sits one level down: the AI organisation was rebuilt on 2025-12-01 around an external hire reporting to Federighi, and the rebuilt Siri will run on Google's Gemini models [S183, S186].
:::

The division of labour is unusually clear for a company of this size. Ternus integrates and decides; Johny Srouji became chief hardware officer on 2026-04-20, adding hardware engineering to silicon and becoming the single owner of Apple's deepest technical moat; Craig Federighi owns software and, since December 2025, AI; Eddy Cue runs services and now health; Kevan Parekh funds the company; Sabih Khan runs operations; Deirdre O'Brien runs retail and people [S179, S184]. That design fits a business whose advantage is integration across silicon, software and services, but it places the two capabilities that matter most in the next cycle — silicon and AI/software — in two individuals with no disclosed deputies.

### AI leadership failed once and has been rebuilt around an outside hire and an outside model

John Giannandrea stepped down as AI chief on 2025-12-01 after the Siri delay; Amar Subramanya, formerly corporate VP of AI at Microsoft and head of engineering for Google's Gemini Assistant, joined as VP of AI reporting to Federighi, while the rest of the AI organisation was split between Khan and Cue [S183, S186]. On 2026-01-12 Apple and Google announced a multiyear deal to power Apple's AI features, including the Siri upgrade due in 2026, with Gemini. The mechanism is speed for dependency: Apple gets a competitive assistant without building a frontier model, but it hands a competitor the most valuable interface in consumer technology and caps the differentiation it can charge for. Underwrite AI as a feature that protects the hardware replacement cycle, not as a new profit pool, until Apple discloses model economics.

### Pay is high and equity-heavy, but it is not the binding constraint

Cook's 2025 total target compensation was $59m: a $3m base unchanged since 2016, a cash incentive at 200% of base and a $50m equity target, positioned in the 80th-90th percentile of the primary peer group; the other named executives target $1m base, 200% cash and $20m equity, and Parekh's target was $16.75m [S65, S153]. The CEO ownership guideline is 10 times salary and other executives three times. The design retains executives through the transition rather than rewarding new AI outcomes: 8.6% of votes cast opposed say-on-pay at the 2026-02-24 annual meeting, a protest worth noting but not a rejection. Pay is therefore a weak signal for the investment case; who stays is more important than what they are paid.

### Five senior roles changed in 24 months, all through planned transitions

The CFO moved from Luca Maestri to Parekh on 2025-01-01, the COO from Jeff Williams to Khan in July 2025, the general counsel from Kate Adams to Jennifer Newstead on 2026-03-01, the AI chief from Giannandrea to Subramanya on 2025-12-01 and the CEO from Cook to Ternus on 2026-09-01 [S170, S166]. Against Apple's near-static 2011-2023 executive team that is a large amount of institutional change at once. None was a resignation under pressure, and two brought external experience; the risk is coordination — a first-time CEO, a new CFO, a new general counsel and a rebuilt AI organisation learning each other while antitrust remedies and a China reset land.

Apple's cash conversion and balance sheet are as good as the multiple implies, but the earnings growth is not: fiscal 2025's 22.7% EPS growth becomes 10.4% once the $10.2bn Irish State Aid tax charge in the prior year is normalised out, and 2.0 points of the June 2026 quarter's 50.1% gross margin came from tariff refunds rather than trading. The three-year record is slowing revenue and rising margin: revenue fell 2.8% in fiscal 2023, grew 2.0% in fiscal 2024 and 6.4% to $416,161M in fiscal 2025, while gross margin rose from 44.1% to 46.9% and operating margin from 29.8% to 32.0%. The latest filed period is the quarter ended 2026-06-27, where revenue rose 16.4% to $109,417M on gross margin of 50.1% and operating margin of 32.6%. No fourth-quarter fiscal 2026 earnings release and no fiscal 2026 annual report were on EDGAR as of 2026-10-31; Apple's fiscal 2025 equivalents were filed on 2025-10-30 and 2025-10-31, so the annual report is due imminently and the figures here are trailing twelve months to 2026-06-27 [S5, S6, S13].

### The growth is half tax base effect, and a quarter buyback

Fiscal 2025's net income rose 19.5%, but pretax income rose 7.5% ($132,729M against $123,485M) and the tax provision fell 30.3% to $20,719M because fiscal 2024 carried the one-time $10.2bn Irish charge — $15.8bn payable to Ireland, offset by a $4.8bn US foreign tax credit and $823M of released unrecognised benefits. Normalising fiscal 2024 at fiscal 2025's 15.6% rate gives $104,222M and underlying growth of 7.5%, not 19.5%. The EPS gap above that is the buyback: from fiscal 2023 to fiscal 2025 net income grew 15.5% while diluted EPS grew 21.7% and diluted shares fell 5.1%, so 5.4 percentage points of EPS growth was a smaller denominator — and that contribution is fading, at 1.9 percentage points in the trailing twelve months (EPS +16.9% against net income +15.1%), because repurchases slowed to $62,094M in the nine months to 2026-06-27 from $70,579M while operating cash flow rose 43%. Capital return has stopped outrunning cash: buybacks and dividends were $97,866M against free cash flow of $136,683M, or 72%, against 107% in fiscal 2025, and net cash rose by $28,410M in nine months. At $344.63 on 2026-10-30 and 14,715M diluted shares the equity is worth $5.07trn, 39.5x trailing EPS and a 2.70% free cash flow yield, while the ten-year Treasury yielded 4.93%; repurchasing at that spread is accretive to EPS and not obviously accretive to value per share [S5, S6, S9].

### Cash is real; the working-capital cushion is not

Cash generation is the strongest part of the record and the hardest to fake: operating cash flow of $146,724M against capital expenditure of $10,041M, with free cash flow at 1.06x net income. The anomaly is fiscal 2025, when free cash flow fell to 0.88x of net income despite $111,482M of operating cash flow; cash paid for income taxes that year was $43,369M, 32.7% of pretax income against a 15.6% book rate and 21.1% in fiscal 2024 — a gap consistent with settlement payments on the Irish case and the TCJA repatriation tax, the final $8.8bn of which was paid in the nine months to 2026-06-27. That supports reading the gap as timing, and the recovery to 1.06x is consistent with it. The working-capital change runs the other way: inventory reached $11,092M at 2026-06-27 from $5,925M a year earlier, an 87% increase against 16.2% revenue growth, lifting days inventory to 16.9 from 9.4 and pulling the cash conversion cycle to −56.8 days from −71.1 at the fiscal 2025 year-end [S5, S6].

The balance sheet carries no leverage risk: at 2026-06-27 Apple held $146,517M of cash and marketable securities against $84,344M of debt, for net cash of $62,173M, up from $33,763M, with commercial paper cut to $1,997M from $7,979M, and other income and expense netted to −$321M in fiscal 2025 because interest earned on the securities book offsets interest paid. The commitments that matter are forward purchases — $57.0bn of manufacturing purchase obligations, $56.2bn due within twelve months, and $29.3bn of other purchase obligations — which fix component supply and, with it, the cost base when memory prices move. Two accounting details deserve attention: gross intangible assets rose $13,270M to $38,220M in nine months with no goodwill recognised, which indicates purchased intellectual property, content or asset acquisitions rather than share purchases, and is not explained in the quarterly filing; and gross unrecognised tax benefits were $23.2bn at 2025-09-27, of which $10.6bn would affect the effective rate and up to $6bn may move within twelve months [S6].

### Returns are distorted by the buyback, not flattered by the business

Reported returns are not usable as quality scores: return on equity was 148.8% and return on invested capital 320.6% on invested capital of $45,347M — $107,520M of equity plus $84,344M of debt less $146,517M of securities — because $258,212M of cumulative buybacks shrank the equity base. The honest comparison is return on assets of 36.1% against Microsoft's 35.9% return on invested capital in fiscal 2026 and Alphabet's 37.0% in fiscal 2025 [S6, S27, S41].

### What moves the outcome, and by how much

The geographic picture also cuts against the standard bear case: Greater China revenue rose 30% to $64,839M in the nine months to 2026-06-27 and 22% in the June quarter, so nine months already exceed the whole of fiscal 2025's $64,377M after two years of decline. What moves the outcome most is gross margin. On trailing-twelve-month revenue of $466,823M one point of gross margin is $4,668M of pretax profit, or 3.0% of net income, while one point of revenue growth at the current margin is $1,878M, or 1.5%. Three cases, all on the trailing twelve months and none a forecast: a two-point margin gain takes EPS to $9.24, a two-point give-back to $8.20, and a two-point give-back with the loss of the search licence to $7.11, 18.8% below the base — and the licence should be modelled as intact but repriced annually, because the September 2025 order permitted non-exclusive placement payments of one year or less rather than ending them, while the $20bn figure is a 2022 court-record number Apple has never confirmed. The cash is real and the balance sheet is net cash; the growth is weaker than reported; and the margin sits at a cyclical high with a tariff-refund component inside it. An investor paying 39.5x trailing earnings is paying for the first and third to persist while the second is already reversing. The diligence question that matters most is what the fiscal 2026 annual report says about inventory composition and the split between refund and product mix, neither of which the quarterly filings settle [S6, S82, S118].

::: info warning
**The fiscal 2026 gross margin is not yet a clean number.** Strip out the tariff refund Apple attributes to the June quarter and the margin is still above any full year in this record, but a smaller step-change than the reported figure implies; against an inventory build growing faster than revenue, the annual report carries the burden of proof.
:::

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Market & Industry Analysis (market, revision 2 by Market Analyst, 8,997 characters)
Apple's markets are contracting in units and expanding in value, and Apple is taking value share inside that contraction: the case for FY2026-FY2028 rests on premiumisation and Services attach rather than device volume, is strongest in the United States, is adequate in Europe, and in China depends on a domestic champion's pricing discipline.

### The pool is shrinking in units and growing in value

IDC's August 2026 forecast has worldwide smartphone shipments at just over 1.0 billion units in 2026, down 16.7% and the steepest annual contraction on record, while total market value rises 6.3% to $613 billion and the average selling price reaches a record $581, up 27.6% in a year and revised up from the $550 IDC published one quarter earlier. The cause is cost, not demand: DRAM and NAND prices are up more than 300% year on year as capacity is redirected to AI servers, memory is more than 65% of bill of materials at the low end, and the sub-$100 tier that shipped 173 million units in 2025 fell close to 60% in the second quarter of 2026. This is a supply shock with a dated end, so 2026-2027 flatters Apple's unit share while genuinely lifting its price, and 2028 is the test of whether either survives. [S39]

Two sizing methods agree closely: 1.0 billion units at the $581 average price gives $581 billion, within 5% of IDC's $613 billion, so the unit and price series can be read together rather than as rival estimates. On that base Apple's serviceable market is the premium tier it addresses — an iOS share of 23.6% of 2026 shipments, a record — while the revenue it can obtain is what it already books: $466.8 billion trailing twelve months to 2026-06-27, which at the 16.2% growth rate of the first nine months of FY2026 implies $483 billion for FY2026. IDC's PC-plus-tablet pool compounds at 1.5% a year from 2026 to 2030, so device pools are not growth markets at any price. [S6]

| TAM, smartphone value (bottom-up) | 1.0bn units x $581 ASP | ~$581bn | 2026 | Calculation on IDC inputs | S66 |
| TAM, personal computing devices | Units published, value not disclosed | ~398m units, -11.3%; 1.5% CAGR to 2030 | 2026 | IDC | S103 |
| SAM, premium smartphone tier | iOS share of shipments | 23.6% of units, record | 2026 | IDC | S66 |
| SOM, Apple revenue | Reported | $466.8bn TTM | TTM to 2026-06-27 | Apple 10-Q | S6 |

| Adjacent services pool | Alphabet revenue | $471.1bn TTM | TTM to 2026-09-30 | Alphabet 10-Q | S42 |

### China is the swing factor, and India sits in the wrong line

Apple's revenue is moving toward the faster-growing regions, but the swing is China. In the first nine months of FY2026 Greater China produced $64.8 billion, up 30.0% on a base of $49.9 billion, after falling from $72.6 billion in FY2023 to $64.4 billion in FY2025; the Americas grew 11.4% to $149.4 billion, Europe 16.1% to $95.6 billion, Japan 10.4% and Rest of Asia Pacific 19.4%. Greater China's $14.9 billion increase contributes 4.1 percentage points of the group's 16.2% growth, more than any other segment, and part of it is currency: a favourable renminbi effect in Greater China, an unfavourable yen effect in Japan. One reporting artefact matters: the Europe segment includes India, the Middle East and Africa, so the fastest-growing large smartphone market is invisible in the line labelled Europe and India is not a segment an investor can track. [S13]

### Services carries the margin and has no published pool size

The fastest-growing pool Apple actually monetises is Services: $109.2 billion, 26.2% of FY2025 revenue, at a 75.4% gross margin against 36.8% for products, growing 14.1% to $91.7 billion in the first nine months of FY2026. The adjacent pools are larger and largely not Apple's — Alphabet's trailing-twelve-month revenue is $471.1 billion — but the app economy itself has no published size in the sources retrieved: neither Apple nor the platform owners disclose app-store gross billings or mobile-advertising revenue in a sizeable form, so Apple's own Services line is the measured pool. The installed base behind it has the same gap: Apple states only that its active-device base reached an all-time high in the June 2026 quarter across every category and region, and publishes no device count in its FY2025 10-K or FY2026 results, so the figure of 2.3 billion devices often quoted alongside the business is unverified here and should carry none of the valuation. [S5]

### Who pays, and how much demand is policy

The budget owner is the consumer, in a discretionary purchase that is increasingly financed. In the United States and United Kingdom long-term interest-free financing is more prevalent, so IDC expects the premium end to hold while emerging markets fall more than 20%; in India brands lean on financing after the sub-$100 tier fell 59% and the $600-800 band grew 32%; in China the government subsidy that supported earlier quarters faded in the second quarter of 2026, so demand there is being withdrawn by policy rather than created by it. Apple's exposure to policy runs both ways: after the February 20, 2026 Supreme Court ruling struck down certain IEEPA tariffs, Apple recognised refunds as a reduction of product cost of sales, and those refunds contributed 2.0 percentage points of the June 2026 quarter's 50.1% gross margin — tariff policy moves Apple's margin by more than a product cycle does. [S105, S40, S13]

The counter-evidence is threefold, each strand dated. If memory prices normalise in 2028 as IDC expects, the entry tier rebuilds and Apple's 2026 share gain is contestable again. If China's June-quarter demand was pulled forward ahead of expected second-half price increases, as IDC's China team reports, the 30% growth line is a launch and currency effect. And if courts and the European Commission remove the App Store take rate, the 75%-margin layer that offsets hardware cyclicality stops compounding at its present rate. The investor implication is narrow: in a 1-billion-unit market Apple can grow revenue only if price rises faster than units fall, making average selling price, China durability and the Services take rate the variables worth monitoring. Sizing confidence is high, because two independent methods agree within 5%; confidence that the mix shift holds to 2028 is medium, because it rests on China and a legally contested commission. Three questions would close the gap: what share of Services revenue is commission-based rather than subscription, advertising or licensing; how much of the Greater China increase is currency; and what the current average replacement cycle is, measured rather than asserted. [S66, S40]

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Technology & Product (technology_product, revision 5 by Product Analyst, 8,835 characters)
Apple's silicon-plus-OS stack is still the widest integrated consumer technology stack, but in 2026 the company rented the one layer it could not build — the frontier model — so what remains defensible is distribution, custom silicon and regulated health sensing, not leadership in artificial intelligence. In two years the A20 Pro moved the iPhone to TSMC N2, the C2 modem reached the flagship, the first foldable shipped at $1,999, and on 2026-01-12 Apple and Google announced the next Apple Foundation Models would be Gemini-based [S58, S59, S63, S64].

### The silicon lead is real, costly, and rented from TSMC

The A19 Pro used TSMC N3P; a year later the A20 Pro moved to TSMC N2 with a 32-core Neural Engine and ~52 TOPS, about double the prior generation's AI throughput. N2 wafers are reported at ~$30,000 against $18,000-20,000 for 3nm, so each step costs more. Product gross margin was 39.9% in the nine months to 2026-06-27 versus 36.9% a year earlier, but only with tariff refunds and mix offsetting "higher costs, including memory", and the 10-Q warns that advanced-semiconductor, NAND and DRAM constraints are expected to intensify [S6, S64].

| Node, A19 Pro / A20 Pro | TSMC N3P (2025) / N2 (2026) | Teardown and trade reporting | S63, S64 |
| CPU clock, A19 Pro | up to 4.26 GHz, 6 cores | Published specification | S63 |
| Neural Engine, A20 Pro | 32 cores, ~52 TOPS, ~2x A19 Pro | Trade-press estimate | S64 |
| N2 wafer price | ~$30,000 vs $18,000-20,000 at 3nm | Trade-press estimate | S64 |
| Product gross margin | 39.9% vs 36.9% (9M FY2025) | Reported financials | S6 |
| On-device model / PCC context | ~3B parameters / 32K tokens | Apple research and developer docs | S61, S62 |

### Apple Intelligence is an architecture with a rented brain

On device, Apple runs a ~3B-parameter model optimised through KV-cache sharing and 2-bit quantisation-aware training; on its servers, a Parallel-Track Mixture-of-Experts model runs inside Private Cloud Compute, which enforces stateless processing, no privileged access even for Apple staff, and attested software images. The binding constraint is memory bandwidth and power: phone-class memory caps on-device inference at single-digit billions of parameters, so harder queries are offloaded. The ceiling is disclosed: a 32K-token context is small against frontier assistants, and Apple's own models were not frontier-quality. The unresolved question for the privacy story is where Gemini-derived inference physically runs. Apple says Apple Intelligence continues on Apple devices and Private Cloud Compute; trade reporting says Google's cloud performs the Gemini computation and puts the licence at ~$1bn a year, on top of a default-search payment of ~$20bn. Neither figure is Apple-confirmed. China's CAC approved Apple Intelligence on 2026-07-15, nearly two years after its 2024 debut, with Alibaba's Qwen and Baidu supplying a separate model stack. Apple's differentiation is orchestration, distribution and privacy, not model quality; an investor should underwrite the cash flow and installed base, not the AI layer [S8, S58, S60, S61, S86, S120, S171].

| What Apple keeps | Silicon, OS, orchestration | Silicon, OS, interface, orchestration | Model, training, inference | S58, S60 |

### Products: a strong cycle, a late foldable, a spatial computer that never became a platform

The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max launched on 2026-09-09 at $1,199 and $1,299; the foldable iPhone Duo at $1,999 went on sale on 2026-10-23. iPhone net sales rose 22% to $196.5bn in the nine months to 2026-06-27, with Greater China up 30%. The C2 modem supports US mmWave and uses 15% less energy than the C1X, but the larger iPhone 18 Pro Max appears to keep a Qualcomm modem, so Qualcomm retains leverage over the highest-ASP SKU. Vision Pro is the counter-example: ~390,000 units in 2024, ~45,000 in the December 2025 quarter despite the M5 refresh, ~600,000 lifetime, and an IDC forecast of ~290,000 units in 2026 [S59, S13, S87].

### What is enforceable is regulatory, not patent

Apple publishes no patent count; the FY2025 10-K says only that it is "pursuing thousands of applications around the world" and that no single right protects its products. Patent counts and peer comparison were not obtainable — the registries could not be searched — so the patent moat is unquantified. What is documented is a regulatory estate — hypertension and sleep-apnoea notifications, a hearing-aid De Novo grant and imaging calibration — each cleared on its own clinical file, a slower but more durable barrier than a patent family.

At $344.63 at the NasdaqGS close on 2026-10-30, Apple carries a $5,029.6B market capitalisation and a $4,967.4B enterprise value on trailing diluted earnings of $8.72 a share and trailing free cash flow of $136.7B. That is 39.5x trailing earnings, 35.2x forward earnings of $9.79 and a 2.7% free-cash-flow yield, against a 4.93% ten-year Treasury yield on the same day: the buyer accepts 2.2 points less cash yield than the risk-free asset and is paid only if the cash flow compounds. The shares sit 1.2% below their all-time closing high of $348.91 on 2026-10-29, have returned 27.5% over twelve months against 10.8% for the S&P 500 and 19.4% for the technology sector ETF, and trade at or above the average analyst target. Apple is a high-quality business at a price that already capitalises several good years; the actionable question is the entry band, not the quality. [S9, S6]

The one metric on which Apple is cheap is cash: its 36.8x price-to-free-cash-flow is 43% below the peer median of 64.6x, because capital expenditure is $10.0B a year while the hyperscalers fund AI capacity. The comparison therefore splits: on earnings Apple is the most expensive large technology company in the set, on free cash flow the least expensive. Its own record points the same way. Sum of the parts makes the premium explicit. On trailing twelve months, Products produced $346.3B of revenue and $135.5B of gross profit, and Services $120.5B and $91.6B at a 76.0% gross margin. At 3-5x sales for hardware and 10-14x for Services the two parts are worth $2.25-3.42T, 31-55% below the $4.97T enterprise value; to reach today's value with hardware at 5x sales, Services would have to be capitalised at 27x revenue, 2.5 times Microsoft's 11.1x. That premium is what the ecosystem and the buyback are worth to the market, and it may be rational, but the buyer is not getting hardware and services at peer prices. Apple discloses no segment operating income, so the split of $72.3B of trailing operating expenses (65% to Products) is an assumption; at 12-16x segment EBIT the parts are worth $2.39-3.28T, a similar answer. Capital return does not close the gap, and Apple's financing history is the inverse of a growth company's: no equity issuance, debt of $84.3B at 2026-06-27 against $124.7B in fiscal 2021 and $146.5B of cash and marketable securities, with $82.2B of buybacks and $15.6B of dividends in the trailing twelve months, a 1.9% total shareholder yield. In April 2026 it authorised a further $100B of repurchases and raised the quarterly dividend 4% to $0.27. At 39.5x each repurchased dollar retires stock at a 2.5% earnings yield, below the 4.93% the same dollar would earn in Treasuries, so the buyback supports EPS more than value per share; the diluted count fell from 16,865M in fiscal 2021 to 14,715M in the June 2026 quarter, but the pace is slowing as repurchases fell to $62.1B in nine months from $70.6B. The calendar is dated: fiscal fourth-quarter results on 2026-11-02 with revenue guided to rise 9-11%, fiscal 2027 guidance and any new authorisation that day, the Google search-remedy appeal over a reported $20B of near-pure-margin services revenue, and memory costs that IDC expects to normalise in 2028. [S164, S162, S6, S1]

The counter-case deserves weight. Apple's 2.7% free-cash-flow yield is the highest of the four mega-caps, Services compounds at 14% on a 76% gross margin, and an AI-driven iPhone cycle that holds revenue growth near 10% would earn a 35x forward multiple rather than merely re-rate it. But at $344.63 the arithmetic offers no margin of safety: 25-30x forward earnings, the ten-year mean to the five-year average, is $245-294, 15-29% below the close, and a 6-8% free-cash-flow path is worth $221-255. The asymmetry is in the entry price, not the franchise. Three diligence questions would settle it: what normalised free cash flow does the fiscal 2026 annual report show after the tariff refund and inventory build? What share of Services revenue depends on the Google payment, and how does the appeal resolve? Does the September quarter confirm revenue growth at or above 9%? Confidence is high in the multiples and the DCF arithmetic, medium in the durability of a 50% gross margin at a cyclical high. [S6, S154]

arguments.markdown:
Apple's structure is clean in law — one share class, a majority-independent board and net cash — but not in economics: 61.8% of pretax profit is booked outside the U.S. at a 15.6% effective tax rate, insiders own 0.06%, and the same director has chaired the board since 2000, so the "alignment" in the equity story rests on pay design and on a tax structure the EU has already litigated once. The listed parent is Apple Inc., a California corporation whose common stock ($0.00001 par value) trades on Nasdaq under AAPL: 14,594,180,000 shares outstanding at 2026-07-17, down from 14,697,926,000 at 2026-01-02, and a market capitalisation of $5.03 trillion at 2026-10-30. Votes track economics one-for-one, and the free float is 99.94% because all directors and officers together hold 9,079,765 shares [S5, S6, S65, S172].

::: kpi
| Metric | Value | Benchmark | Signal | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Shares outstanding | 14,594,180,000 (2026-07-17) | 14,697,926,000 (2026-01-02) | good | S6, S65 |
| Buybacks, nine months to 2026-06-27 | $61.8bn for 215m shares | $70.6bn in the same period of FY2025 | warn | S6 |
| Net cash | $62.2bn (cash and securities $146.5bn less debt $84.3bn, 2026-06-27) | gross debt $84.3bn | good | S6 |
| Effective tax rate | 15.6% (FY2025) | 21% U.S. statutory rate | warn | S5 |
| Foreign pretax profit | 61.8% ($82.0bn of $132.7bn, FY2025) | 38.2% U.S. | warn | S5 |
| Insider ownership | 0.06% (9,079,765 shares) | below the 1% proxy disclosure threshold | warn | S65 |
:::

### Three Irish companies sit between the product and the profit

EX-21 lists 19 subsidiaries domiciled in 15 jurisdictions and omits the rest as not significant; it gives neither ownership percentages nor functions, so what follows is a map of domicile, not of economic activity. The two entities the European Commission found held Apple's intellectual property for sales outside the Americas — Apple Sales International and Apple Operations Europe — no longer appear on the list; in their place are three Irish companies. Apple does not describe the 2015 restructuring or name the entity that now owns the non-U.S. IP, but the tax note shows the consequence: foreign pretax earnings of $82.0bn of $132.7bn in FY2025 and a 15.6% effective rate against 21%. The 5.4-point gap is worth $7.2bn a year in cash tax, and it is exactly what the Commission attacked: the 2016 decision ordered recovery of up to €13bn, the General Court annulled it on 2020-07-15, the Court of Justice reinstated it on 2024-09-10, and Apple took a $10.2bn net charge in Q4 FY2024, paying $15.8bn to Ireland through escrow against a $4.8bn U.S. foreign tax credit [S5, S187]. Ireland closed the opinions in January 2015, so the scheme itself is gone, but the precedent is not. Entity accounts filed with Ireland's Companies Registration Office, which the 10-K does not reproduce, would show where profit now sits.

| Apple Inc. | California, U.S. | Corporation (registrant) | Listed parent; issuer of AAPL common stock | Public float 99.94% | Public shareholders | S5, S65 |
| Apple Operations International Limited | Ireland | Limited company | Irish holding entity; role not described | Not disclosed in EX-21 | Apple Inc. | S5 |
| Apple Operations Limited | Ireland | Limited company | Irish operating entity; role not described | Not disclosed in EX-21 | Apple Inc. | S5 |

| Apple Computer Trading (Shanghai) Co., Ltd. | China | Limited liability company | Greater China trading entity | Not disclosed in EX-21 | Apple Inc. | S5 |

### Capital return, not leverage, is the capital-structure question

Apple carries $62.2bn of net cash — $146.5bn of cash and securities against $84.3bn of debt at 2026-06-27 — and in the nine months to that date repurchased 215m shares for $61.8bn, against $70.6bn in the same period a year earlier, under a $100bn authorisation announced on 2025-05-01 [S6]. At a $5tn capitalisation each $10bn of repurchase retires 0.2% of the company, so the return depends on the price paid. A 12% year-on-year slowdown in dollars while the shares rose 25.7% is consistent with price discipline, or with lower free cash flow; the filings do not distinguish. Solvency is not the risk; executing the market's largest buyback at a multiple that assumes the AI transition works is.

### Ownership is institutional, and the board is long-tenured

Vanguard holds 9.63% and BlackRock 7.10%, but the BlackRock figure is taken from a 2023-12-31 filing quoted in the 2026 proxy and is stale [S65, S153]. Directors and officers hold 0.06%; Tim Cook's 3,280,295 shares are worth $1.13bn at the current price yet are 0.02% of the company. The board has nine members after Ternus joined on 2026-09-01, seven of them independent; Arthur Levinson, a director since 2000 and chair for 15 years, became lead independent director that day. At the 2026-02-24 annual meeting Levinson drew 9.0% opposition, say-on-pay 8.6% and a "China Entanglement Audit" proposal 1.4% support. That passes Nasdaq's majority-independent rule and is not a governance crisis, but it is a professional board, not a founder-aligned one.

### The business model is an annuity on hardware

Apple sells devices to consumers, enterprises and carriers, but the buyer that matters is the installed base: more than 2.5bn devices whose owners upgrade and pay for services. FY2025 net sales were $416.2bn (+6%), with Services gross margin of 75.4% against 46.9% for the group; in the nine months to 2026-06-27 net sales rose 16% to $364.4bn, Services 14% to $91.7bn and Greater China 30% to $64.8bn after a 4% decline in FY2025 [S5, S6]. That is the growth engine — a replacement cycle plus attach, with China swinging from drag to driver in two years. It makes the model resilient to unit stagnation but not to a remedy that breaks the Services attach: Services produced 39.1% of nine-month gross profit on 25.2% of revenue.

### The legal front is about Services margins, not fines

Three proceedings test the container. The DOJ's civil antitrust suit, filed on 2024-03-21 in the District of New Jersey, seeks equitable relief rather than damages; the Epic litigation produced a 2025-04-30 finding that Apple violated the 2021 injunction, a ban on fees for out-of-app purchases and a referral to the U.S. Attorney for possible criminal contempt; and the EU fined Apple €500m under the Digital Markets Act on 2025-04-23, which Apple appealed [S5, S7]. The fines are small against $416bn of revenue; the remedies are not, because they target the 75%-gross-margin Services line and the App Store's toll gate on 2.5bn devices. Counter-evidence is real — the DOJ must prove market definition, Apple says it has substantial defences, and no court has ordered a structural remedy — but the direction in both jurisdictions is toward alternative distribution and payment, the one outcome that would change the franchise's economics rather than its legal bill.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Exit Strategy Analysis (exit, revision 3 by Valuation Analyst, 7,847 characters)
Apple has no takeover exit and no listing event ahead of it. At a $5,029.6B market value the largest technology acquisition on record, Microsoft's $68.7B all-cash purchase of Activision Blizzard agreed on 2022-01-18, equals 1.4% of the company, and any bid would face the US and EU antitrust review that Microsoft's own deal attracted; a leveraged buyout of a $4.97T enterprise value is arithmetically impossible. The exit is a sale into the market, at a $13.84B average daily traded value where a 1% position in a $1B fund is $10M, 0.07% of one day's volume. The exit question is therefore not whether a holder can sell but at what multiple, which makes the sell discipline a set of price bands and thesis breaks rather than an event to wait for. [S9, S169]

| Exit route | Named buyer or venue | Rationale | Timing | Likelihood | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Open-market sale | NasdaqGS, $13.84B average daily traded value | The only route that absorbs a position without a discount | Any trading day | The route actually used | S9 |
| Strategic acquisition | No named buyer; largest tech deal $68.7B vs $5,029.6B market value | Size, antitrust, no strategic gap Apple fills | Not foreseeable | Very low | S169 |
| Leveraged buyout | None | $4.97T enterprise value and $84.3B of debt cannot be financed | Not foreseeable | Negligible | S6 |
| Company buyback (partial exit) | Apple Inc. | $82.2B repurchased in twelve months; $100B authorised April 2026; 1.6% of shares a year | Ongoing | High but discretionary | S164, S6 |

| Index and passive flows | S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 constituent | Structural bid, not an exit route | Ongoing | Structural | S163 |

Apple's own record sets the cost of ownership. Over the last ten completed years the average intra-year peak-to-trough drawdown was 21.4%, lasting 82 days, and four episodes exceeded 30%: 2018 fell 36.73%, 2020 31.43%, 2022 30.75% and 2025 30.22%. Each was recovered, with 2020 returning 80.75% for the calendar year and 2025 8.56%, but each recovery came with a re-rating as well as earnings growth, and a holder buying at 39.5x cannot count on the re-rating half. From $344.63 the average drawdown is $271 and a 30% drawdown is $240. On 2026-10-30 Apple was 1.23% below its all-time-high close while the Nasdaq-100 was 9.09% below its own and the S&P 500 3.05%, so the stock enters any correction from relative strength rather than weakness. The multiple, not the remembered share price, is what made past entries work. The 2022 trough of $126.04 on 2022-12-28 was 20.6x fiscal 2022 diluted EPS of $6.11; today's 39.5x is nearly double that, and a repeat of 20x on today's trailing $8.72 would be $174 or $196 on forward $9.79, levels last seen in 2023 and not reached without an earnings recession. That is why the band is set on the forward multiple: 25-30x, the ten-year mean of 25.35x to the five-year average of 30.2x, is $248-296, and the bear case of a two-point gross-margin give-back on $8.20 of EPS at 25x is $205. The fair value in the middle case is not today's price; it is the price at which the multiple stops assuming the re-rating continues. [S163, S2]

The binding policy risk sits in the asset, not the exit. The Google search payment, reported at $20B a year, is 17% of Services revenue and 22% of services gross profit, and the default-payment ban took effect in June 2026 under the April 2026 remedy order; at a 30x multiple its loss is $450B, 9% of market value. That is the one event that would force a sale regardless of price. The slower ones are App Store commission rules under the DMA and the DOJ case, and China, where revenue was $64.8B in nine months of fiscal 2026 and can turn on subsidy or geopolitical policy rather than on Apple's execution. [S165, S13]

The strongest case against this discipline is that a 30x-plus multiple never offers a margin of safety again. If Services compounds at 14% on a 76% gross margin and the buyback retires 1.6% of the shares a year, a fund that waits for $250 may simply never own the best cash generator in the market, and the cost of the discipline is opportunity rather than loss. The answer is a time rule rather than a permanent price target: if Apple trades above $296 for four consecutive quarters while Services growth stays above 10%, reassess the band against the then-current multiple instead of waiting for a level the business has outgrown. Until then, watchlist above $300, a first tranche at $275-296, and a full position at or below $250. Confidence is high in the drawdown record and the return arithmetic, medium in the multiple at which a future buyer will pay, because that depends on the ten-year yield, which was 4.93% on 2026-10-30. The three-year record is slowing revenue and rising margin: revenue fell 2.8% in fiscal 2023, grew 2.0% in fiscal 2024 and 6.4% to $416,161M in fiscal 2025, while gross margin rose from 44.1% to 46.9% and operating margin from 29.8% to 32.0%. ### The growth is half tax base effect, and a quarter buyback

Fiscal 2025's net income rose 19.5%, but pretax income rose 7.5% ($132,729M against $123,485M) and the tax provision fell 30.3% to $20,719M because fiscal 2024 carried the one-time $10.2bn Irish charge — $15.8bn payable to Ireland, offset by a $4.8bn US foreign tax credit and $823M of released unrecognised benefits. Normalising fiscal 2024 at fiscal 2025's 15.6% rate gives $104,222M and underlying growth of 7.5%, not 19.5%. The EPS gap above that is the buyback: from fiscal 2023 to fiscal 2025 net income grew 15.5% while diluted EPS grew 21.7% and diluted shares fell 5.1%, so 5.4 percentage points of EPS growth was a smaller denominator — and that contribution is fading, at 1.9 percentage points in the trailing twelve months (EPS +16.9% against net income +15.1%), because repurchases slowed to $62,094M in the nine months to 2026-06-27 from $70,579M while operating cash flow rose 43%. Capital return has stopped outrunning cash: buybacks and dividends were $97,866M against free cash flow of $136,683M, or 72%, against 107% in fiscal 2025, and net cash rose by $28,410M in nine months. At $344.63 on 2026-10-30 and 14,715M diluted shares the equity is worth $5.07trn, 39.5x trailing EPS and a 2.70% free cash flow yield, while the ten-year Treasury yielded 4.93%; repurchasing at that spread is accretive to EPS and not obviously accretive to value per share [S5, S6, S9].

### Cash is real; the working-capital cushion is not

Cash generation is the strongest part of the record and the hardest to fake: operating cash flow of $146,724M against capital expenditure of $10,041M, with free cash flow at 1.06x net income. The anomaly is fiscal 2025, when free cash flow fell to 0.88x of net income despite $111,482M of operating cash flow; cash paid for income taxes that year was $43,369M, 32.7% of pretax income against a 15.6% book rate and 21.1% in fiscal 2024 — a gap consistent with settlement payments on the Irish case and the TCJA repatriation tax, the final $8.8bn of which was paid in the nine months to 2026-06-27. That supports reading the gap as timing, and the recovery to 1.06x is consistent with it. The working-capital change runs the other way: inventory reached $11,092M at 2026-06-27 from $5,925M a year earlier, an 87% increase against 16.2% revenue growth, lifting days inventory to 16.9 from 9.4 and pulling the cash conversion cycle to −56.8 days from −71.1 at the fiscal 2025 year-end [S5, S6].

The balance sheet carries no leverage risk: at 2026-06-27 Apple held $146,517M of cash and marketable securities against $84,344M of debt, for net cash of $62,173M, up from $33,763M, with commercial paper cut to $1,997M from $7,979M, and other income and expense netted to −$321M in fiscal 2025 because interest earned on the securities book offsets interest paid. The commitments that matter are forward purchases — $57.0bn of manufacturing purchase obligations, $56.2bn due within twelve months, and $29.3bn of other purchase obligations — which fix component supply and, with it, the cost base when memory prices move. Two accounting details deserve attention: gross intangible assets rose $13,270M to $38,220M in nine months with no goodwill recognised, which indicates purchased intellectual property, content or asset acquisitions rather than share purchases, and is not explained in the quarterly filing; and gross unrecognised tax benefits were $23.2bn at 2025-09-27, of which $10.6bn would affect the effective rate and up to $6bn may move within twelve months [S6].

### Returns are distorted by the buyback, not flattered by the business

Reported returns are not usable as quality scores: return on equity was 148.8% and return on invested capital 320.6% on invested capital of $45,347M — $107,520M of equity plus $84,344M of debt less $146,517M of securities — because $258,212M of cumulative buybacks shrank the equity base. The honest comparison is return on assets of 36.1% against Microsoft's 35.9% return on invested capital in fiscal 2026 and Alphabet's 37.0% in fiscal 2025 [S6, S27, S41].

### What moves the outcome, and by how much

The geographic picture also cuts against the standard bear case: Greater China revenue rose 30% to $64,839M in the nine months to 2026-06-27 and 22% in the June quarter, so nine months already exceed the whole of fiscal 2025's $64,377M after two years of decline. What moves the outcome most is gross margin. On trailing-twelve-month revenue of $466,823M one point of gross margin is $4,668M of pretax profit, or 3.0% of net income, while one point of revenue growth at the current margin is $1,878M, or 1.5%. Three cases, all on the trailing twelve months and none a forecast: a two-point margin gain takes EPS to $9.24, a two-point give-back to $8.20, and a two-point give-back with the loss of the search licence to $7.11, 18.8% below the base — and the licence should be modelled as intact but repriced annually, because the September 2025 order permitted non-exclusive placement payments of one year or less rather than ending them, while the $20bn figure is a 2022 court-record number Apple has never confirmed. The cash is real and the balance sheet is net cash; the growth is weaker than reported; and the margin sits at a cyclical high with a tariff-refund component inside it. An investor paying 39.5x trailing earnings is paying for the first and third to persist while the second is already reversing. The diligence question that matters most is what the fiscal 2026 annual report says about inventory composition and the split between refund and product mix, neither of which the quarterly filings settle [S6, S82, S118].

::: info warning
**The fiscal 2026 gross margin is not yet a clean number.** Strip out the tariff refund Apple attributes to the June quarter and the margin is still above any full year in this record, but a smaller step-change than the reported figure implies; against an inventory build growing faster than revenue, the annual report carries the burden of proof.
:::

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Market & Industry Analysis (market, revision 2 by Market Analyst, 8,997 characters)
Apple's markets are contracting in units and expanding in value, and Apple is taking value share inside that contraction: the case for FY2026-FY2028 rests on premiumisation and Services attach rather than device volume, is strongest in the United States, is adequate in Europe, and in China depends on a domestic champion's pricing discipline.

### The pool is shrinking in units and growing in value

IDC's August 2026 forecast has worldwide smartphone shipments at just over 1.0 billion units in 2026, down 16.7% and the steepest annual contraction on record, while total market value rises 6.3% to $613 billion and the average selling price reaches a record $581, up 27.6% in a year and revised up from the $550 IDC published one quarter earlier. The cause is cost, not demand: DRAM and NAND prices are up more than 300% year on year as capacity is redirected to AI servers, memory is more than 65% of bill of materials at the low end, and the sub-$100 tier that shipped 173 million units in 2025 fell close to 60% in the second quarter of 2026. This is a supply shock with a dated end, so 2026-2027 flatters Apple's unit share while genuinely lifting its price, and 2028 is the test of whether either survives. [S39]

Two sizing methods agree closely: 1.0 billion units at the $581 average price gives $581 billion, within 5% of IDC's $613 billion, so the unit and price series can be read together rather than as rival estimates. On that base Apple's serviceable market is the premium tier it addresses — an iOS share of 23.6% of 2026 shipments, a record — while the revenue it can obtain is what it already books: $466.8 billion trailing twelve months to 2026-06-27, which at the 16.2% growth rate of the first nine months of FY2026 implies $483 billion for FY2026. IDC's PC-plus-tablet pool compounds at 1.5% a year from 2026 to 2030, so device pools are not growth markets at any price. [S6]

### China is the swing factor, and India sits in the wrong line

Apple's revenue is moving toward the faster-growing regions, but the swing is China. In the first nine months of FY2026 Greater China produced $64.8 billion, up 30.0% on a base of $49.9 billion, after falling from $72.6 billion in FY2023 to $64.4 billion in FY2025; the Americas grew 11.4% to $149.4 billion, Europe 16.1% to $95.6 billion, Japan 10.4% and Rest of Asia Pacific 19.4%. Greater China's $14.9 billion increase contributes 4.1 percentage points of the group's 16.2% growth, more than any other segment, and part of it is currency: a favourable renminbi effect in Greater China, an unfavourable yen effect in Japan. One reporting artefact matters: the Europe segment includes India, the Middle East and Africa, so the fastest-growing large smartphone market is invisible in the line labelled Europe and India is not a segment an investor can track. [S13]

### Services carries the margin and has no published pool size

The fastest-growing pool Apple actually monetises is Services: $109.2 billion, 26.2% of FY2025 revenue, at a 75.4% gross margin against 36.8% for products, growing 14.1% to $91.7 billion in the first nine months of FY2026. The adjacent pools are larger and largely not Apple's — Alphabet's trailing-twelve-month revenue is $471.1 billion — but the app economy itself has no published size in the sources retrieved: neither Apple nor the platform owners disclose app-store gross billings or mobile-advertising revenue in a sizeable form, so Apple's own Services line is the measured pool. The installed base behind it has the same gap: Apple states only that its active-device base reached an all-time high in the June 2026 quarter across every category and region, and publishes no device count in its FY2025 10-K or FY2026 results, so the figure of 2.3 billion devices often quoted alongside the business is unverified here and should carry none of the valuation. [S5]

### Who pays, and how much demand is policy

The budget owner is the consumer, in a discretionary purchase that is increasingly financed. In the United States and United Kingdom long-term interest-free financing is more prevalent, so IDC expects the premium end to hold while emerging markets fall more than 20%; in India brands lean on financing after the sub-$100 tier fell 59% and the $600-800 band grew 32%; in China the government subsidy that supported earlier quarters faded in the second quarter of 2026, so demand there is being withdrawn by policy rather than created by it. Apple's exposure to policy runs both ways: after the February 20, 2026 Supreme Court ruling struck down certain IEEPA tariffs, Apple recognised refunds as a reduction of product cost of sales, and those refunds contributed 2.0 percentage points of the June 2026 quarter's 50.1% gross margin — tariff policy moves Apple's margin by more than a product cycle does. [S105, S40, S13]

The counter-evidence is threefold, each strand dated. If memory prices normalise in 2028 as IDC expects, the entry tier rebuilds and Apple's 2026 share gain is contestable again. If China's June-quarter demand was pulled forward ahead of expected second-half price increases, as IDC's China team reports, the 30% growth line is a launch and currency effect. And if courts and the European Commission remove the App Store take rate, the 75%-margin layer that offsets hardware cyclicality stops compounding at its present rate. The investor implication is narrow: in a 1-billion-unit market Apple can grow revenue only if price rises faster than units fall, making average selling price, China durability and the Services take rate the variables worth monitoring. Sizing confidence is high, because two independent methods agree within 5%; confidence that the mix shift holds to 2028 is medium, because it rests on China and a legally contested commission. Three questions would close the gap: what share of Services revenue is commission-based rather than subscription, advertising or licensing; how much of the Greater China increase is currency; and what the current average replacement cycle is, measured rather than asserted. [S66, S40]

::: evidence
**Apple's addressable device market fell 16.7% in units in 2026 while growing 6.3% in value, and Apple's revenue grew 16.2% over nine months — the gap is premiumisation and China, not market growth (S66, S13).**

IDC forecasts 2026 shipments at just over 1.0 billion units against a market value of $613 billion and an ASP of $581 (S66, S39). Apple's nine-month FY2026 revenue was $364.4 billion, up 16.2%, with Greater China up 30.0% on a $49.9 billion base (S13, S6). The bottom-up check of 1.0 billion units at $581 gives $581 billion, within 5% of IDC's value estimate (S66).
:::"}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Company Overview (company_overview, revision 3 by Company Analyst, 8,885 characters)
Apple's structure is clean in law — one share class, a majority-independent board and net cash — but not in economics: 61.8% of pretax profit is booked outside the U.S. at a 15.6% effective tax rate, insiders own 0.06%, and the same director has chaired the board since 2000, so the "alignment" in the equity story rests on pay design and on a tax structure the EU has already litigated once. The listed parent is Apple Inc., a California corporation whose common stock ($0.00001 par value) trades on Nasdaq under AAPL: 14,594,180,000 shares outstanding at 2026-07-17, down from 14,697,926,000 at 2026-01-02, and a market capitalisation of $5.03 trillion at 2026-10-30. Votes track economics one-for-one, and the free float is 99.94% because all directors and officers together hold 9,079,765 shares [S5, S6, S65, S172].

### Three Irish companies sit between the product and the profit

EX-21 lists 19 subsidiaries domiciled in 15 jurisdictions and omits the rest as not significant; it gives neither ownership percentages nor functions, so what follows is a map of domicile, not of economic activity. The two entities the European Commission found held Apple's intellectual property for sales outside the Americas — Apple Sales International and Apple Operations Europe — no longer appear on the list; in their place are three Irish companies. Apple does not describe the 2015 restructuring or name the entity that now owns the non-U.S. IP, but the tax note shows the consequence: foreign pretax earnings of $82.0bn of $132.7bn in FY2025 and a 15.6% effective rate against 21%. The 5.4-point gap is worth $7.2bn a year in cash tax, and it is exactly what the Commission attacked: the 2016 decision ordered recovery of up to €13bn, the General Court annulled it on 2020-07-15, the Court of Justice reinstated it on 2024-09-10, and Apple took a $10.2bn net charge in Q4 FY2024, paying $15.8bn to Ireland through escrow against a $4.8bn U.S. foreign tax credit [S5, S187]. Ireland closed the opinions in January 2015, so the scheme itself is gone, but the precedent is not. Entity accounts filed with Ireland's Companies Registration Office, which the 10-K does not reproduce, would show where profit now sits.

### Capital return, not leverage, is the capital-structure question

Apple carries $62.2bn of net cash — $146.5bn of cash and securities against $84.3bn of debt at 2026-06-27 — and in the nine months to that date repurchased 215m shares for $61.8bn, against $70.6bn in the same period a year earlier, under a $100bn authorisation announced on 2025-05-01 [S6]. At a $5tn capitalisation each $10bn of repurchase retires 0.2% of the company, so the return depends on the price paid. A 12% year-on-year slowdown in dollars while the shares rose 25.7% is consistent with price discipline, or with lower free cash flow; the filings do not distinguish. Solvency is not the risk; executing the market's largest buyback at a multiple that assumes the AI transition works is.

### Ownership is institutional, and the board is long-tenured

Vanguard holds 9.63% and BlackRock 7.10%, but the BlackRock figure is taken from a 2023-12-31 filing quoted in the 2026 proxy and is stale [S65, S153]. Directors and officers hold 0.06%; Tim Cook's 3,280,295 shares are worth $1.13bn at the current price yet are 0.02% of the company. The board has nine members after Ternus joined on 2026-09-01, seven of them independent; Arthur Levinson, a director since 2000 and chair for 15 years, became lead independent director that day. At the 2026-02-24 annual meeting Levinson drew 9.0% opposition, say-on-pay 8.6% and a "China Entanglement Audit" proposal 1.4% support. That passes Nasdaq's majority-independent rule and is not a governance crisis, but it is a professional board, not a founder-aligned one.

### The business model is an annuity on hardware

Apple sells devices to consumers, enterprises and carriers, but the buyer that matters is the installed base: more than 2.5bn devices whose owners upgrade and pay for services. FY2025 net sales were $416.2bn (+6%), with Services gross margin of 75.4% against 46.9% for the group; in the nine months to 2026-06-27 net sales rose 16% to $364.4bn, Services 14% to $91.7bn and Greater China 30% to $64.8bn after a 4% decline in FY2025 [S5, S6]. That is the growth engine — a replacement cycle plus attach, with China swinging from drag to driver in two years. It makes the model resilient to unit stagnation but not to a remedy that breaks the Services attach: Services produced 39.1% of nine-month gross profit on 25.2% of revenue.

### The legal front is about Services margins, not fines

Three proceedings test the container. The DOJ's civil antitrust suit, filed on 2024-03-21 in the District of New Jersey, seeks equitable relief rather than damages; the Epic litigation produced a 2025-04-30 finding that Apple violated the 2021 injunction, a ban on fees for out-of-app purchases and a referral to the U.S. Attorney for possible criminal contempt; and the EU fined Apple €500m under the Digital Markets Act on 2025-04-23, which Apple appealed [S5, S7]. The fines are small against $416bn of revenue; the remedies are not, because they target the 75%-gross-margin Services line and the App Store's toll gate on 2.5bn devices. Counter-evidence is real — the DOJ must prove market definition, Apple says it has substantial defences, and no court has ordered a structural remedy — but the direction in both jurisdictions is toward alternative distribution and payment, the one outcome that would change the franchise's economics rather than its legal bill.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Founding Team & Key Personnel (team, revision 2 by Company Analyst, 8,571 characters)
The succession is done and internal — Ternus, Srouji, Federighi and Parekh are all Apple lifers — which lowers cultural and execution risk but concentrates the AI transition in a software chief who has outsourced the frontier model to Google and a first-time CEO who has never run a P&L, so the team offers continuity rather than evidence of renewal. The board appointed John Ternus CEO effective 2026-09-01, with Tim Cook as executive chair and Arthur Levinson, chair for the previous 15 years, as lead independent director. Ternus, 50, joined Apple's product design team in 2001, became VP Hardware Engineering in 2013 and SVP in 2021; his record includes iPad, AirPods, the iPhone 17 line and the MacBook Neo, but no disclosed CEO, P&L or capital-allocation role before 2026 [S152, S177].

::: evidence
**The board has already executed the succession by promoting an internal hardware engineer, and the appointment was unanimous.**

The 8-K of 2026-04-20 records the board's appointment of Ternus as CEO effective 2026-09-01, Cook's move to executive chair and Levinson's to lead independent director. Ternus joined Apple in 2001 and has led hardware engineering since 2021. The doubt sits one level down: the AI organisation was rebuilt on 2025-12-01 around an external hire reporting to Federighi, and the rebuilt Siri will run on Google's Gemini models [S152, S177, S183, S186].
:::

The division of labour is unusually clear for a company of this size. Ternus integrates and decides; Johny Srouji became chief hardware officer on 2026-04-20, adding hardware engineering to silicon and becoming the single owner of Apple's deepest technical moat; Craig Federighi owns software and, since December 2025, AI; Eddy Cue runs services and now health; Kevan Parekh funds the company; Sabih Khan runs operations; Deirdre O'Brien runs retail and people [S179, S184]. That design fits a business whose advantage is integration across silicon, software and services, but it places the two capabilities that matter most in the next cycle — silicon and AI/software — in two individuals with no disclosed deputies.

### AI leadership failed once and has been rebuilt around an outside hire and an outside model

John Giannandrea stepped down as AI chief on 2025-12-01 after the Siri delay; Amar Subramanya, formerly corporate VP of AI at Microsoft and head of engineering for Google's Gemini Assistant, joined as VP of AI reporting to Federighi, while the rest of the AI organisation was split between Khan and Cue. On 2026-01-12 Apple and Google announced a multiyear deal to power Apple's AI features, including the Siri upgrade due in 2026, with Gemini [S183, S186]. The mechanism is speed for dependency: Apple gets a competitive assistant without building a frontier model, but it hands a competitor the most valuable interface in consumer technology and caps the differentiation it can charge for. Underwrite AI as a feature that protects the hardware replacement cycle, not as a new profit pool, until Apple discloses model economics.

### Pay and turnover: equity retains, but the C-suite is new

Cook's 2025 total target compensation was $59m: a $3m base unchanged since 2016, a cash incentive at 200% of base and a $50m equity target, positioned in the 80th-90th percentile of the primary peer group; the other named executives target $1m base, 200% cash and $20m equity, and Parekh's target was $16.75m. The CEO ownership guideline is 10 times salary. The design retains executives through the transition rather than rewarding new AI outcomes: 8.6% of votes cast opposed say-on-pay at the 2026-02-24 annual meeting, a protest worth noting but not a rejection. Retention is being tested at the same time. The CFO moved from Luca Maestri to Parekh on 2025-01-01, the COO from Jeff Williams to Khan in July 2025, the general counsel from Kate Adams to Jennifer Newstead on 2026-03-01, the AI chief from Giannandrea to Subramanya on 2025-12-01 and the CEO from Cook to Ternus on 2026-09-01. Against Apple's near-static 2011-2023 executive team that is a large amount of institutional change at once; none was a resignation under pressure, and the risk is coordination while antitrust remedies and a China reset land [S65, S153, S170, S166].

### The missing capability is frontier AI at the top, not finance or operations

No board member has operating AI-lab experience — Wanda Austin ran Aerospace, Alex Gorsky ran Johnson & Johnson — and the AI leader sits at VP level, outside the executive team [S179, S173]. That is the reference check a diligence team should run: who inside Apple can credibly challenge Google's model roadmap, and what retention packages hold Srouji and Federighi, the two people whose departure would impair the franchise. Counter-evidence is genuine: internal succession worked in 2011 when Cook replaced Steve Jobs, Ternus's product record is strong, and the Gemini deal buys time. The judgement is not that the team is weak; it is that the team is unproven at exactly the task the next three years demand.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Technology & Product (technology_product, revision 5 by Product Analyst, 8,835 characters)
Apple's silicon-plus-OS stack is still the widest integrated consumer technology stack, but in 2026 the company rented the one layer it could not build — the frontier model — so what remains defensible is distribution, custom silicon and regulated health sensing, not leadership in artificial intelligence. In two years the A20 Pro moved the iPhone to TSMC N2, the C2 modem reached the flagship, the first foldable shipped at $1,999, and on 2026-01-12 Apple and Google announced the next Apple Foundation Models would be Gemini-based [S58, S59, S63, S64].

### The silicon lead is real, costly, and rented from TSMC

The A19 Pro used TSMC N3P; a year later the A20 Pro moved to TSMC N2 with a 32-core Neural Engine and ~52 TOPS, about double the prior generation's AI throughput. N2 wafers are reported at ~$30,000 against $18,000-20,000 for 3nm, so each step costs more. Product gross margin was 39.9% in the nine months to 2026-06-27 versus 36.9% a year earlier, but only with tariff refunds and mix offsetting "higher costs, including memory", and the 10-Q warns that advanced-semiconductor, NAND and DRAM constraints are expected to intensify [S6, S64].

| Metric | Value | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Node, A19 Pro / A20 Pro | TSMC N3P (2025) / N2 (2026) | Teardown and trade reporting | S63, S64 |
| CPU clock, A19 Pro | up to 4.26 GHz, 6 cores | Published specification | S63 |
| Neural Engine, A20 Pro | 32 cores, ~52 TOPS, ~2x A19 Pro | Trade-press estimate | S64 |
| N2 wafer price | ~$30,000 vs $18,000-20,000 at 3nm | Trade-press estimate | S64 |
| Product gross margin | 39.9% vs 36.9% (9M FY2025) | Reported financials | S6 |
| On-device model / PCC context | ~3B parameters / 32K tokens | Apple research and developer docs | S61, S62 |

### Apple Intelligence is an architecture with a rented brain

On device, Apple runs a ~3B-parameter model optimised through KV-cache sharing and 2-bit quantisation-aware training; on its servers, a Parallel-Track Mixture-of-Experts model runs inside Private Cloud Compute, which enforces stateless processing, no privileged access even for Apple staff, and attested software images. The binding constraint is memory bandwidth and power: phone-class memory caps on-device inference at single-digit billions of parameters, so harder queries are offloaded. The ceiling is disclosed: a 32K-token context is small against frontier assistants, and Apple's own models were not frontier-quality. The unresolved question for the privacy story is where Gemini-derived inference physically runs. Apple says Apple Intelligence continues on Apple devices and Private Cloud Compute; trade reporting says Google's cloud performs the Gemini computation and puts the licence at ~$1bn a year, on top of a default-search payment of ~$20bn. Neither figure is Apple-confirmed. China's CAC approved Apple Intelligence on 2026-07-15, nearly two years after its 2024 debut, with Alibaba's Qwen and Baidu supplying a separate model stack. Apple's differentiation is orchestration, distribution and privacy, not model quality; an investor should underwrite the cash flow and installed base, not the AI layer [S8, S58, S60, S61, S86, S120, S171].
