|---|---|---|---|---|
| Frontier model | Own ~3B on-device plus server model | Gemini-derived | Owns Gemini | S58, S61 |
| Cost structure | Fixed R&D and data-centre capex | Fixed R&D plus per-query licence | Licence revenue | S58, S86 |
| What Apple keeps | Silicon, OS, orchestration | Silicon, OS, interface, orchestration | Model, training, inference | S58, S60 |

### Products: a strong cycle, a late foldable, a spatial computer that never became a platform

The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max launched on 2026-09-09 at $1,199 and $1,299; the foldable iPhone Duo at $1,999 went on sale on 2026-10-23. iPhone net sales rose 22% to $196.5bn in the nine months to 2026-06-27, with Greater China up 30%. The C2 modem supports US mmWave and uses 15% less energy than the C1X, but the larger iPhone 18 Pro Max appears to keep a Qualcomm modem, so Qualcomm retains leverage over the highest-ASP SKU. Vision Pro is the counter-example: ~390,000 units in 2024, ~45,000 in the December 2025 quarter despite the M5 refresh, ~600,000 lifetime, and an IDC forecast of ~290,000 units in 2026 [S59, S13, S87].

| Vision Pro (M5) | Commercial | 2025-10 | ~45k units Q4 2025 | Not disclosed | Lower-cost model, late 2026 | S87 |
| Services | Commercial | — | $91.7bn, +14% | 76.3% | AI tier / iCloud+ gating | S6, S107 |

### What is enforceable is regulatory, not patent

Apple publishes no patent count; the FY2025 10-K says only that it is "pursuing thousands of applications around the world" and that no single right protects its products. Patent counts and peer comparison were not obtainable — the registries could not be searched — so the patent moat is unquantified. What is documented is a regulatory estate — hypertension and sleep-apnoea notifications, a hearing-aid De Novo grant and imaging calibration — each cleared on its own clinical file, a slower but more durable barrier than a patent family.

### The moat is wide at the bottom of the stack and thin at the top

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Custom SoC and modem | 9 | Top design team plus priority TSMC N2 access; a decade and an Intel acquisition | 4-5 years | S59, S64 |
| Hardware-OS integration | 8 | Six operating systems co-designed with custom silicon | 3-5 years | S5 |
| On-device model efficiency | 5 | Quantisation and KV-cache techniques are published | 1-2 years | S61 |
| Frontier model | 3 | Available to licence, as Apple has shown | 1-2 years, by cheque | S58 |
| FDA-cleared health features | 7 | Each feature needs its own trial and clearance | 3-4 years | S30, S33 |
| Installed base and developers | 10 | A decade of switching costs, record active base | 10+ years | S13, S87 |
| **Composite** | **8/10 hardware, 4/10 AI** | The stack is hard to copy; the intelligence is not | **4-5 years for hardware** | S58, S64 |

The replication test: a team of 50 senior silicon and operating-system engineers could match a phone-class SoC and OS in four to five years, and rent a competitive model next quarter. The counter-evidence is Apple's own record: Siri needed a Google licence, the car was cancelled, and Vision Pro has not reached platform volumes. Regulation can also withhold the assistant: the Q3 FY2026 10-Q states DMA interoperability obligations have in the past, and may in future, cause Apple not to launch or maintain features "such as Siri AI" in certain jurisdictions. The advantage holds only if on-device AI lifts upgrade rates and regulators leave the App Store economics that fund the silicon intact. Two diligence questions settle it: whether the Google agreement allows fine-tuning for on-device use, and whether the 2027 Pro Max moves fully to the C2 [S6, S58, S59, S87].

::: evidence
**Apple's integration advantage is durable in silicon and distribution, but it no longer extends to the model layer.**

The A20 Pro's 2nm node and 32-core Neural Engine keep Apple at the leading edge of phone silicon, and ten FDA clearances and grants since 2020 give it a regulated feature estate rivals must replicate trial by trial. But basing the next Apple Foundation Models on Gemini concedes that the frontier layer is bought, the reported ~$1bn annual licence turns a fixed R&D advantage into a variable cost paid to a competitor, and availability now varies by jurisdiction: China runs a Qwen/Baidu stack and DMA rules may withhold Siri AI in the EU [S6, S58, S64, S86, S120, S171].
:::"}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Development Strategy (strategy, revision 5 by Product Analyst, 8,085 characters)
Apple's route to FY2028 growth is services mix, a richer iPhone cycle and India, with artificial intelligence as a retention feature and a possible iCloud+ upsell rather than a revenue line of its own; the plan is credible on cash generation and per-share compounding, but not yet on AI monetisation or on creating a new product category. The base is large and still growing: revenue reached $416.2bn in FY2025, and the nine months to 2026-06-27 produced $364.4bn, up 16%, with Services at $91.7bn, up 14% [S77, S6].

### Services carry the margin, but the mix engine stalled in FY2026

Services were 26% of FY2025 revenue but 39% of gross profit in the nine months to June 2026, because they earn a 76.3% gross margin against 39.9% for products. The mix engine, however, stopped being the marginal driver: product gross profit grew 26% against 15% for services, so the rise in total gross margin to 49.1% from 46.8% came from hardware mix and tariff refunds, not from services, while memory costs kept rising. Services growth itself came from advertising and cloud services, with the Google search-distribution payment named as a primary driver. That is the engine that funds the buyback and the silicon, and it is also the engine regulators are targeting: the European Commission fined Apple €500m on 2025-04-23 for anti-steering non-compliance, and the General Court dismissed Apple's challenge to its gatekeeper designation on 2026-07-08 [S85, S84, S6]. An investor should value the services annuity on gross profit that compounds in the low-to-mid teens, and apply a discount for the probability that a remedy compresses commission or search income rather than a one-off fine.

### AI is funded as cost and monetised, if at all, through storage

Apple introduced Siri AI with the iOS 27 cycle announced in the third quarter of FY2026, and R&D rose 33% to $34.0bn in the nine months to June 2026, driven by infrastructure including AI investments and headcount. No AI revenue line exists. Availability is a regulatory variable too: China cleared Apple Intelligence only on 2026-07-15, with Alibaba's Qwen and Baidu, and the 10-Q warns that DMA rules have in the past, and may in future, cause it not to launch features "such as Siri AI" in some jurisdictions. The reported plan — that high-frequency, compute-intensive Siri use will be gated behind iCloud+ — is plausible because it reuses a price ladder already in place, but Apple has published no tier and no price, so it is unverified [S13, S6, S107, S171]. The mechanism matters more than the price: AI raises the cost of serving every device while its clearest commercial effect is to protect upgrade rates and services attach. If Apple charges, the increment is bounded by storage-subscription willingness to pay, not by the value of the model; if it does not, AI is a permanent tax on gross margin. Either way, 2027 is the test of whether AI spend converts into units or ARPU.

### India lowers tariff risk, not unit cost

iPhone production in India rose 53% in 2025 to ~55 million units, ~25% of global output, and is projected at 28% in 2026; Tata Electronics overtook Foxconn in iPhone export assembly over the FY2022-FY2026 incentive period. The strategy is rational given the tariff record in the filings — Section 232 semiconductor investigation results in January 2026, the Supreme Court striking down certain IEEPA tariffs in February 2026, and new Section 301 tariffs, with manufacturing purchase obligations of $57.0bn at 2026-06-27 [S89, S91, S6]. The limit is that assembly captures little of the value: components, displays and silicon still come from East Asia, so India is an insurance policy on tariffs and single-country concentration, not a margin lever. The signpost to watch is the share of US-bound iPhones assembled in India, which Apple has never disclosed.

### Capital allocation is disciplined and slightly bolder

R&D rose from $29.9bn in FY2023 to $34.6bn in FY2025 and is running at ~$45bn annualised in FY2026. Buybacks remain the primary use of cash: $25.8bn of stock was repurchased in the quarter to 2026-06-27 alone, alongside $4.0bn of dividends at $0.27 per share, which cut the share count to 14.61bn from 14.77bn at FY2025 year-end and helped EPS grow 29% against 27% net-income growth. M&A posture has shifted from tuck-ins: Apple confirmed the acquisition of the AI-audio start-up Q.ai on 2026-01-29, reported by the Financial Times at close to $2bn, and acquired the AI data-engineering company Ascend.io, notified to the European Commission on 2026-06-30; intangible assets rose from $11.1bn to $20.3bn between 2025-09-27 and 2026-06-27 [S77, S88, S6, S13]. Against ~$146bn of cash and marketable securities, that is affordable experimentation rather than a change of strategy — and it is the right test of whether Apple's AI gap can be bought in pieces.

### What must be true in twelve months, and the case against

Four things must happen for the strategy to be credible. First, the FY2026 holiday quarter has to show that the iPhone 18 and Duo cycle sustains double-digit growth without tariff refunds, which flattered the June quarter by ~2 percentage points of gross margin. Second, Apple must put a price on AI or show that it lifts upgrade rates, because a 33% R&D increase with no revenue attached is a margin problem. Third, a DOJ settlement or DMA remedy must leave the App Store commission and default-search payment substantially intact; both cases attack the services profit pool directly. Fourth, India must reach the projected share of output without a quality or logistics incident. The counter-case is strong and largely Apple's own record: AI features arrived well after they were demonstrated, Siri needed a Google licence, the car programme was cancelled, and Vision Pro shipped ~45,000 units in the December 2025 quarter, while Alphabet, Microsoft and Huawei set a faster cadence in models, cloud AI and, for Huawei, folding hardware and domestic silicon. Apple's answer is that it does not need to be first — it needs to be best integrated, and it monetises the installed base rather than the model. That is a defensible strategy for a cash-flow investor and a weak one for anyone buying AI optionality [S59, S87, S84, S90, S89].

::: evidence
**The strategy is credible as a cash-compounding plan and unproven as a growth plan.**

Services earn a structurally higher gross margin than hardware, and buybacks are large enough that earnings per share can compound faster than net income even with flat hardware; but AI is a large R&D increase with no disclosed price, Vision Pro has not become a platform, and the two antitrust cases target precisely the services lines that fund the plan.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Business Model (business_model, revision 3 by Fundamentals Analyst, 8,460 characters)
Apple runs a hardware annuity with a services margin layered on top — 73 cents of services gross profit for every dollar of product gross profit — but the mix shift the multiple pays for stalled in fiscal 2026, when hardware margins, helped by tariff refunds, grew gross profit faster than Services. Apple sells through two routes, and the split is the least-discussed fact in the model: in fiscal 2025, 40% of net sales went through its own stores, online store and direct sales force and 60% through carriers, resellers and distributors. The carrier finances or subsidises the handset to win a contract, so the carrier bears the acquisition cost and Apple's selling expense stays at $27,601M, or 6.6% of revenue. There is little contracted backlog: deferred revenue was $13.7bn at 2025-09-27, 3.3% of revenue, two thirds of it recognised within a year. Apple is a repeat-purchase business recognised as it bills, not a subscription business with a book of contracted revenue [S5].

### The mix shift, and its reversal

The arithmetic of the mix shift is the strongest part of the case. In fiscal 2025 Services produced $109,158M of revenue at a 75.4% gross margin against $307,003M of Products at 36.8%: 26.2% of revenue but 42.2% of gross profit ($82,314M of $195,201M), up from 35.7% two years earlier, with services gross profit per dollar of product gross profit rising from $0.55 in fiscal 2023 to $0.73. Then the mechanism ran backwards. In the nine months to 2026-06-27 product gross profit rose 26.3% to $108,819M while services gross profit rose 15.3% to $69,963M, and Services fell to 39.1% of gross profit; product gross margin reached 39.9% against 36.9% a year earlier, taking total gross margin to 49.1% and to 50.1% in the June quarter against 46.5%. Apple attributes the gain to "a different mix of products and tariff refunds, partially offset by higher costs, including memory", the most consequential disclosure in this section: it makes fiscal 2026's margin hardware-led and partly a refund rather than a trading gain [S5, S6].

### Unit economics per revenue dollar, because there are no units

Apple discloses no unit volumes, average selling price or installed-base figure, so a per-device waterfall cannot be built from primary evidence. The economics of each revenue dollar can be.

| Unit-economics line | FY2025 | 9M FY2026 | Evidence and status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Product cost of sales, per $1,000 of product revenue | $632 | $601 | Bill of materials, assembly and warranty provision combined, not split | S5, S6 |
| Product gross profit | $368 | $399 | 36.8% to 39.9%; includes tariff refunds in fiscal 2026 | S5, S6 |
| Services cost of sales, per $1,000 of services revenue | $246 | $237 | Content, hosting and payment processing | S5, S6 |
| Services gross profit | $754 | $763 | 75.4% to 76.3% | S5, S6 |
| Services gross profit per $1 of product gross profit | $0.73 | $0.64 | Closest disclosed proxy for lifetime value against acquisition cost | S5, S6 |
| Customer acquisition cost, support and warranty | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Carriers bear acquisition; warranty sits inside cost of sales | S5 |
| LTV, LTV:CAC, CAC payback in months | Not computable | Not computable | Requires units, ASP and installed base, none of which Apple reports | S5 |

Apple therefore has no payback period to wait out: a device is gross-profit-positive on delivery at a 36.8% product margin, and the services stream that follows is nearly all incremental, since services cost of sales is $26,844M on $109,158M of revenue. The nearest disclosed proxy for lifetime value against acquisition cost is the $0.73 of services gross profit per dollar of product gross profit, and its fall to $0.64 is the number to watch — the annuity still grows, but no longer faster than the hardware that creates it [S5, S6].

### Pricing power shows up as mix, not as price

| Line | FY2025 net sales | Year on year | What the filing discloses about price and mix | Gross margin | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone | $209,586M | +4% | Growth "due to higher net sales of Pro models", i.e. mix rather than units | 36.8% products blended | S5 |
| Services | $109,158M | +14% | "advertising, the App Store and cloud services" | 75.4% | S5 |
| Mac | $33,708M | +12% | "laptops and desktops" | 36.8% products blended | S5 |
| iPad and Wearables | $63,709M | 0% | iPad Air and mini higher, Accessories and Wearables lower | 36.8% products blended | S5 |

Pricing power shows up as mix: iPhone revenue rose 22% to $196,515M in the nine months to 2026-06-27, attributed again to higher sales of Pro models rather than to units. The same disclosure prevents separating price from volume, and therefore prevents estimating elasticity — a 22% increase could be volume, price, or any combination. Apple publishes list prices on its own store but not in its filings, and this report did not retrieve a verified 2026 price list, so the table uses disclosed mix effects rather than price points; third-party unit data would settle it [S6].

### The highest-margin layer is also the most litigated

App Store economics are recognised net — Apple books "only the commission it retains" on third-party app sales — so a take-rate cut passes straight to revenue and gross profit with no offsetting cost. Apple is subject to a US court order barring it from charging a commission on certain consumer purchases, though the Ninth Circuit has instructed the district court to amend the injunction to permit one, and in the EU the Digital Markets Act forces alternative distribution, alternative payment processing and new fee structures, a plan the European Commission has challenged. A second concentration sits in the same line: Apple earns licensing revenue from Google for search distribution inside Services advertising, which Apple names as a primary driver of Services growth in both fiscal 2025 and the first nine months of fiscal 2026. The payment was $20bn in 2022 per unsealed court documents, 18.3% of fiscal 2025 Services revenue, and Apple does not disclose the current figure; the District of Columbia court order of 2025-09-02 preserved the ability to pay partners while banning exclusive agreements, but Apple states a reversal on appeal could impose remedies "prohibiting Google from offering the Company commercial terms for search distribution", and both the Department of Justice and Google appealed [S6, S82].

### Cost structure, and what would break the durability

The cost base is bought, not built: product cost of sales of $194,116M goes to TSMC for wafers, to memory suppliers for DRAM and NAND, and to Foxconn and its peers for assembly. Research and development reached $34,035M in the nine months to 2026-06-27, up 33% and 9.3% of revenue against 8.3% in fiscal 2025, on "infrastructure-related costs, including investments in artificial intelligence"; capital expenditure is 2.2% of trailing-twelve-month revenue against 34.9% at Microsoft in fiscal 2026. Apple rents its manufacturing and buys much of its AI capability through the income statement, so that bill reaches the operating margin immediately rather than through depreciation. For investors the implication is that the annuity is intact, but the margin expansion of the last four quarters is not the mix shift it is commonly described as: it is product mix, a tariff refund and memory cost timing, on top of a services base whose most profitable components face an appeal, a court order and a European regulatory process. The downside is quantifiable rather than hypothetical: giving back three points of gross margin and losing the search licence together would take more than a fifth of trailing-twelve-month net income. Three facts would settle the durability question and none is disclosed — the current size of the search payment, the share of Services that is App Store commission, and the refund-versus-mix split; the fiscal 2026 annual report, not on EDGAR as of 2026-10-31, may settle them [S6, S27].

::: evidence
**The service mix still drives Apple's margin, but in fiscal 2026 it stopped being the marginal driver — hardware did, and part of that gain is a refund.**

In the nine months to June 2026 product gross profit grew faster than services gross profit for the first time in three years, and Apple attributes the higher product margin to product mix and tariff refunds rather than to trading gains, in the June 2026 quarterly report.
:::"}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Competitive Landscape (competition, revision 4 by Market Analyst, 8,987 characters)
Apple's competitive position strengthened in 2026 in every hardware line except smartwatches, but the gain is crisis-specific — bought with memory supply and price discipline rather than product superiority — and it is being offset where profit is made, because the App Store commission that funds the premium position is being dismantled by courts and regulators rather than by a rival's product. Apple leads no hardware category outright except detachable tablets, and its annual report concedes minority share in smartphones, PCs, tablets and wearables. Head to head, Samsung shipped 62.7 million handsets in Q2 2026 versus Apple's 55.7 million. [S102]

### The lead is in integration, not in units

Apple's 20.2% of global smartphone shipments in Q2 2026 was a record for that quarter and a 3.9 percentage point gain, but Samsung's 22.7% was larger and Xiaomi's 26.4% collapse explains much of the redistribution. In personal computing Apple is second at 18.2% to Lenovo's 20.1%, yet macOS shipments grew 17.4% while Windows fell 6.7% and Android 19.6%, and macOS is the only major operating system IDC expects to grow in 2026. The clearest structural lead is detachable tablets at 55.3%; the weakest spot is smartwatches, where Huawei leads 18.8% to 17.2%, so Apple's 15.5% of all wearables rests on earwear, where it holds 17.2%. [S104]

| Product | Competitor | Competitor share, Q2 2026 | Apple share | Technology basis | Price position | Switching cost | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone, global | Samsung | 22.7%, +3.2pp | 20.2%, +3.9pp | iOS integration and secured memory supply | Industry ASP $581; Apple above it | High: iCloud, iMessage, purchased apps | S102, S66 |
| iPhone, China | Huawei | 22.6%, +4.5pp | 18.1%, +4.2pp | iOS against domestic HarmonyOS | Apple held prices while Android raised them | Medium: leaving iOS loses Apple services | S40 |
| PCs and tablets | Lenovo | 20.1%, +2.5pp | 18.2%, -0.4% | macOS against Windows | MacBook Neo attacks entry pricing | Medium | S103, S106 |
| Services and App Store | Alphabet, Google Play | $471.1bn TTM revenue | $109.2bn Services at 75.4% gross margin | iOS distribution against Google Play | 15-30% commission, under challenge | High for consumers, falling for developers | S5, S42, S80 |

### Samsung is the dangerous one, and the reason is memory

Samsung is the most dangerous competitor, and not because of the Galaxy S26 Ultra. When memory is more than 65% of bill of materials at the low end, the binding constraint is supply access, and Samsung is the only top-five handset vendor that also sells memory: it grew shipments 8.1% and took 3.2 points of share in Q2 2026 while Xiaomi fell 26.4% and vivo 19.6%. Apple's answer was to secure memory early, which is why its units fell only 1.3% in 2026 against Android's 24.3% and why IDC puts iOS at a record 23.6% of shipments — a sourcing feat rather than a structural advantage, and it lapses when memory normalises while Samsung keeps its costs. Samsung also holds the foldable franchise Apple now attacks: the iPhone Duo went on sale on 2026-10-23 at a reported $1,999, below the $2,550 average price IDC assumes, against a forecast of more than 17 million foldable iPhones by 2027 and 40% of a category growing 12.6% to 22.9 million units this year. [S66, S59]

### In China the competitor and the rules are different

Huawei held 22.6% of a Chinese market that fell 4.3% in Q2 2026 and grew 19.9% by holding prices while Android rivals raised theirs, leaning on HarmonyOS, which IDC expects to reach 51 million units in 2026; Apple grew 24.4% and gained 4.2 points to 18.1%, so both premium ends expanded while OPPO, vivo and Xiaomi contracted. The mechanism is a domestic operating system plus price discipline, and neither is a feature Apple can copy. HarmonyOS draws on the national preference that makes Apple's China revenue politically exposed, so the 30% China revenue growth belongs behind a competition risk; Apple Intelligence was registered with China's internet regulator on 2026-07-15 alongside Alibaba's Qwen and Baidu, which narrows the AI gap in the one market where it mattered most but does not settle it. [S40, S120]

### The profit pool is being taken by courts, not by rivals

Apple's FY2025 annual report discloses that it is subject to a U.S. court order preventing it from imposing any commission on certain purchases consumers make, that its Digital Markets Act compliance plan has been challenged by the European Commission, and that it faces U.S. monopolization suits over smartphones; separately, the September 2, 2025 remedies order against Google, if upheld, could remove the search-distribution payments inside Services. No competitor needs to win a device sale for the 75.4% services margin to compress: a developer that routes a subscriber to the web converts a 15-30% commission into a payment-processing fee, and Services growth of 14.1% then arrives at a lower margin. The hardware position improved while the pricing power behind it was cut by U.S. courts and European regulators. [S5]

| Product | Leader | Challenger | Niche | Emerging threat | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone | Samsung, 22.7% of units | Apple, 20.2% and gaining | Huawei in China, 22.6% | HarmonyOS at 51m units; AI-first Android flagships | S102, S40, S66 |
| PCs and tablets | Lenovo, 20.1% | Apple, 18.2%, with the only growing OS | Dell in workstations, 40.0% | HarmonyOS NEXT at 1.6%; Windows-on-ARM | S103, S106 |
| Services | Apple, $109.2bn | Alphabet through Google Play | Netflix, Spotify, Epic | Web payments and alternative marketplaces | S5, S42, S80 |

### AI and the phone already in the buyer's pocket

Where Apple is not ahead is AI: the all-new Siri AI arrived at WWDC26 in June 2026 on foundation models licensed from Google under their 2026-01-12 agreement — its assistant now depends on a company it also competes with in services. Samsung's AI-equipped Galaxy S26 Ultra is credited by IDC with returning Samsung to first place in Q1 2026, and research and development rose 32.5% to $34.0 billion in nine months of FY2026 — the cost of catching up, not the reward for leading. The strongest competitor is the handset already in the buyer's pocket: replacement cycles are lengthening, IDC describes Chinese buyers as postponing rather than abandoning upgrades, and the 173 million sub-$100 units shipped in 2025 are leaving the market, which supports Services attach while suppressing units. Three risks follow: if AI becomes the reason a buyer upgrades, Apple competes on integration, with a rented model; if HarmonyOS reaches first-time buyers in lower-tier cities, they never enter iOS; and if the U.S. injunction spreads to other storefronts, the take rate falls further. Unit position and profit per unit are moving in opposite directions, so the question worth paying for is not who sells more phones but what share of the transaction Apple controls in 2027. Confidence is high in the shares and legal facts, medium beyond 2028, when memory normalises and the crisis-specific advantage lapses. Open diligence: what proportion of Services revenue is commission rather than subscription? What margin does the foldable carry at $1,999? What does the Gemini licence cost per query at scale? [S13, S66, S40]

| Quadrant | Points | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Strengths | Record 23.6% iOS share of 2026 shipments; 20.2% of second-quarter units, up 3.9 points; 55.3% of detachable tablets; 15.5% of wearables and 17.2% of earwear; Services of $109.2bn at a 75.4% gross margin | S66, S102, S103, S104, S5, S6 |
| Weaknesses | Minority share in every hardware category by Apple's own description; second to Samsung in phones, Lenovo in PCs and Huawei in smartwatches; the AI layer licensed from Alphabet; no disclosed active-device count; no published app-economy size | S5, S102, S103, S104, S58 |
| Opportunities | More than 17m foldable iPhones and about 40% of a category by 2027; macOS the only major operating system forecast to grow in 2026; India's $600-800 band growing 32% | S66, S103, S105 |
| Threats | Huawei at 22.6% of China with HarmonyOS at 51m units; a U.S. court order barring commission on certain external purchases; a DMA plan challenged by the European Commission; memory costs up more than 300% from a supplier that competes in handsets | S40, S5, S66, S102 |
:::

::: evidence
**Apple gained unit share in every hardware line in 2026 except smartwatches, while the commission that funds its premium position was being removed by courts and regulators rather than by a rival.**

In Q2 2026 Apple held 20.2% of smartphone units behind Samsung's 22.7%, 18.2% of PC-plus-tablet units behind Lenovo's 20.1% and 15.5% of wearables but only 17.2% of smartwatches against Huawei's 18.8% (S102, S103, S104). The payment was $20bn in 2022 per unsealed court documents, 18.3% of fiscal 2025 Services revenue, and Apple does not disclose the current figure; the District of Columbia court order of 2025-09-02 preserved the ability to pay partners while banning exclusive agreements, but Apple states a reversal on appeal could impose remedies "prohibiting Google from offering the Company commercial terms for search distribution", and both the Department of Justice and Google appealed [S6, S82].

### Cost structure, and what would break the durability

The cost base is bought, not built: product cost of sales of $194,116M goes to TSMC for wafers, to memory suppliers for DRAM and NAND, and to Foxconn and its peers for assembly. Research and development reached $34,035M in the nine months to 2026-06-27, up 33% and 9.3% of revenue against 8.3% in fiscal 2025, on "infrastructure-related costs, including investments in artificial intelligence"; capital expenditure is 2.2% of trailing-twelve-month revenue against 34.9% at Microsoft in fiscal 2026. Apple rents its manufacturing and buys much of its AI capability through the income statement, so that bill reaches the operating margin immediately rather than through depreciation. For investors the implication is that the annuity is intact, but the margin expansion of the last four quarters is not the mix shift it is commonly described as: it is product mix, a tariff refund and memory cost timing, on top of a services base whose most profitable components face an appeal, a court order and a European regulatory process. The downside is quantifiable rather than hypothetical: giving back three points of gross margin and losing the search licence together would take more than a fifth of trailing-twelve-month net income. Three facts would settle the durability question and none is disclosed — the current size of the search payment, the share of Services that is App Store commission, and the refund-versus-mix split; the fiscal 2026 annual report, not on EDGAR as of 2026-10-31, may settle them [S6, S27].

::: evidence
**The service mix still drives Apple's margin, but in fiscal 2026 it stopped being the marginal driver — hardware did, and part of that gain is a refund.**

In the nine months to June 2026 product gross profit grew faster than services gross profit for the first time in three years, and Apple attributes the higher product margin to product mix and tariff refunds rather than to trading gains, in the June 2026 quarterly report.
:::"}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## ESG Assessment (esg, revision 3 by Regulatory Analyst, 8,986 characters)
Apple's policy exposure is not a licence-to-operate threat but a slow, legislated tax on Services gross profit: the €500 million DMA fine of 2025-04-23 and the April 2025 US contempt finding show a company that litigates first and complies later, while the three remedies that matter — Google's default-search payment, the US link-out commission and the EU fee structure — have so far been reshaped rather than removed [S7]. The question for a long-only holder is how much Services gross margin five more years of enforcement takes, and whether the multiple already discounts it.

### The DMA fine is small; the cost structure is not

The Commission fined Apple €500 million on 2025-04-23 for breaching the anti-steering obligation and ordered it to remove restrictions on steering users outside the App Store. The same day it closed the user-choice investigation — a real concession — but issued preliminary findings in the Article 6(4) file on Apple's terms for alternative app marketplaces, where an adverse finding carries fines of up to 10% of annual worldwide net sales [S5]. Two facts bound it: on 2026-02-05 the Commission found Apple Ads and Apple Maps should not be designated, and no further Apple decision appears in its DMA record between the fine and 2026-09-28. Peer fines are serial but modest — Meta €200 million in the same package, Google €890 million on 2026-07-23, Alphabet's €4.1 billion Android fine final only in July 2026 — so repeated fines, not break-up, are the base rate. The implication is a transfer of pricing power from Apple's toll to developers and consumers: because each mandated fee cut reaches Services gross margin before it reaches revenue, fee orders should move the multiple and fine headlines should not.

Europe is Apple's second-largest region and Services drove its FY2025 growth; App Store commission is the highest-margin revenue Apple records, so a mandated fee cut in Brussels is worth more to the equity than any fine. Apple also warns that interoperability obligations force it to open technologies to third parties without charge and have in the past, and may in future, caused it not to launch or maintain features "such as Siri AI" — a product-availability risk, not only a revenue leak.

### A contempt finding, then a slow antitrust case

On 2025-04-30 the Northern District of California found Apple in violation of the 2021 Epic injunction, barred any commission on purchases made outside an app, and referred the company to the US Attorney on criminal contempt. The Ninth Circuit modified that on 2025-12-11 to allow parity rules and some commission on link-out purchases; Apple petitioned the Supreme Court on 2026-05-21, obtained certiorari on 2026-06-30 limited to the civil-contempt standard, and seeks a stay below [S6, S122]. Apple's compliance function tested a court order rather than obeyed it, which raises the severity of the next remedy. That remedy is the DOJ case, filed 2024-03-21 with 16 states and the District of Columbia, seeking equitable relief only; it survived dismissal on 2025-06-30 and is in discovery on a schedule pointing to a 2027 trial. With no damages claimed, the risk is conduct-based — defaults, messaging, app distribution — and lands on the 2027-2029 Services line rather than the balance sheet.

### Google's payment survives, on worse terms

The search-distribution remedy went Apple's way on the point that mattered: the 2025-09-02 decision refused to ban Google's payments to distributors, citing harm to device makers and browser developers, and instead barred exclusive contracts while permitting default-placement payments not conditioned on exclusivity and running one year or less [S118, S42]. A final judgment followed in December 2025; both sides appealed in early 2026 and the appeals were pending at 2026-10-29. Apple does not disclose the payment; the $20 billion-a-year figure is unverified. The revenue survives with annual renewal risk and mandatory choice screens.

### Two bear-case triggers did not fire in 2026

The Section 232 semiconductor investigation's initial results on 2026-01-14 imposed no additional tariff on Apple's products, and on 2026-02-20 the Supreme Court struck down certain IEEPA tariffs, with Apple claiming refunds it recognised as a reduction of products cost of sales; Section 301 tariffs were then imposed. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Competitive Landscape (competition, revision 4 by Market Analyst, 8,987 characters)
Apple's competitive position strengthened in 2026 in every hardware line except smartwatches, but the gain is crisis-specific — bought with memory supply and price discipline rather than product superiority — and it is being offset where profit is made, because the App Store commission that funds the premium position is being dismantled by courts and regulators rather than by a rival's product. Apple leads no hardware category outright except detachable tablets, and its annual report concedes minority share in smartphones, PCs, tablets and wearables. Head to head, Samsung shipped 62.7 million handsets in Q2 2026 versus Apple's 55.7 million. [S102]

### The lead is in integration, not in units

Apple's 20.2% of global smartphone shipments in Q2 2026 was a record for that quarter and a 3.9 percentage point gain, but Samsung's 22.7% was larger and Xiaomi's 26.4% collapse explains much of the redistribution. In personal computing Apple is second at 18.2% to Lenovo's 20.1%, yet macOS shipments grew 17.4% while Windows fell 6.7% and Android 19.6%, and macOS is the only major operating system IDC expects to grow in 2026. The clearest structural lead is detachable tablets at 55.3%; the weakest spot is smartwatches, where Huawei leads 18.8% to 17.2%, so Apple's 15.5% of all wearables rests on earwear, where it holds 17.2%. [S104]

| Product | Competitor | Competitor share, Q2 2026 | Apple share | Technology basis | Price position | Switching cost | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone, global | Samsung | 22.7%, +3.2pp | 20.2%, +3.9pp | iOS integration and secured memory supply | Industry ASP $581; Apple above it | High: iCloud, iMessage, purchased apps | S102, S66 |
| iPhone, China | Huawei | 22.6%, +4.5pp | 18.1%, +4.2pp | iOS against domestic HarmonyOS | Apple held prices while Android raised them | Medium: leaving iOS loses Apple services | S40 |
| PCs and tablets | Lenovo | 20.1%, +2.5pp | 18.2%, -0.4% | macOS against Windows | MacBook Neo attacks entry pricing | Medium | S103, S106 |
| Services and App Store | Alphabet, Google Play | $471.1bn TTM revenue | $109.2bn Services at 75.4% gross margin | iOS distribution against Google Play | 15-30% commission, under challenge | High for consumers, falling for developers | S5, S42, S80 |

### Samsung is the dangerous one, and the reason is memory

Samsung is the most dangerous competitor, and not because of the Galaxy S26 Ultra. When memory is more than 65% of bill of materials at the low end, the binding constraint is supply access, and Samsung is the only top-five handset vendor that also sells memory: it grew shipments 8.1% and took 3.2 points of share in Q2 2026 while Xiaomi fell 26.4% and vivo 19.6%. Apple's answer was to secure memory early, which is why its units fell only 1.3% in 2026 against Android's 24.3% and why IDC puts iOS at a record 23.6% of shipments — a sourcing feat rather than a structural advantage, and it lapses when memory normalises while Samsung keeps its costs. Samsung also holds the foldable franchise Apple now attacks: the iPhone Duo went on sale on 2026-10-23 at a reported $1,999, below the $2,550 average price IDC assumes, against a forecast of more than 17 million foldable iPhones by 2027 and 40% of a category growing 12.6% to 22.9 million units this year. [S66, S59]

### In China the competitor and the rules are different

Huawei held 22.6% of a Chinese market that fell 4.3% in Q2 2026 and grew 19.9% by holding prices while Android rivals raised theirs, leaning on HarmonyOS, which IDC expects to reach 51 million units in 2026; Apple grew 24.4% and gained 4.2 points to 18.1%, so both premium ends expanded while OPPO, vivo and Xiaomi contracted. The mechanism is a domestic operating system plus price discipline, and neither is a feature Apple can copy. HarmonyOS draws on the national preference that makes Apple's China revenue politically exposed, so the 30% China revenue growth belongs behind a competition risk; Apple Intelligence was registered with China's internet regulator on 2026-07-15 alongside Alibaba's Qwen and Baidu, which narrows the AI gap in the one market where it mattered most but does not settle it. [S40, S120]

### The profit pool is being taken by courts, not by rivals

Apple's FY2025 annual report discloses that it is subject to a U.S. court order preventing it from imposing any commission on certain purchases consumers make, that its Digital Markets Act compliance plan has been challenged by the European Commission, and that it faces U.S. monopolization suits over smartphones; separately, the September 2, 2025 remedies order against Google, if upheld, could remove the search-distribution payments inside Services. No competitor needs to win a device sale for the 75.4% services margin to compress: a developer that routes a subscriber to the web converts a 15-30% commission into a payment-processing fee, and Services growth of 14.1% then arrives at a lower margin. The hardware position improved while the pricing power behind it was cut by U.S. courts and European regulators. [S5]

| Product | Leader | Challenger | Niche | Emerging threat | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone | Samsung, 22.7% of units | Apple, 20.2% and gaining | Huawei in China, 22.6% | HarmonyOS at 51m units; AI-first Android flagships | S102, S40, S66 |
| PCs and tablets | Lenovo, 20.1% | Apple, 18.2%, with the only growing OS | Dell in workstations, 40.0% | HarmonyOS NEXT at 1.6%; Windows-on-ARM | S103, S106 |
| Services | Apple, $109.2bn | Alphabet through Google Play | Netflix, Spotify, Epic | Web payments and alternative marketplaces | S5, S42, S80 |

### AI and the phone already in the buyer's pocket

Where Apple is not ahead is AI: the all-new Siri AI arrived at WWDC26 in June 2026 on foundation models licensed from Google under their 2026-01-12 agreement — its assistant now depends on a company it also competes with in services. Samsung's AI-equipped Galaxy S26 Ultra is credited by IDC with returning Samsung to first place in Q1 2026, and research and development rose 32.5% to $34.0 billion in nine months of FY2026 — the cost of catching up, not the reward for leading. The strongest competitor is the handset already in the buyer's pocket: replacement cycles are lengthening, IDC describes Chinese buyers as postponing rather than abandoning upgrades, and the 173 million sub-$100 units shipped in 2025 are leaving the market, which supports Services attach while suppressing units. Three risks follow: if AI becomes the reason a buyer upgrades, Apple competes on integration, with a rented model; if HarmonyOS reaches first-time buyers in lower-tier cities, they never enter iOS; and if the U.S. injunction spreads to other storefronts, the take rate falls further. Unit position and profit per unit are moving in opposite directions, so the question worth paying for is not who sells more phones but what share of the transaction Apple controls in 2027. Confidence is high in the shares and legal facts, medium beyond 2028, when memory normalises and the crisis-specific advantage lapses. Open diligence: what proportion of Services revenue is commission rather than subscription? What margin does the foldable carry at $1,999? What does the Gemini licence cost per query at scale? [S13, S66, S40]

arguments.markdown:
Apple's cash conversion and balance sheet are as good as the multiple implies, but the earnings growth is not: fiscal 2025's 22.7% EPS growth becomes 10.4% once the $10.2bn Irish State Aid tax charge in the prior year is normalised out, and 2.0 points of the June 2026 quarter's 50.1% gross margin came from tariff refunds rather than trading. The three-year record is slowing revenue and rising margin: revenue fell 2.8% in fiscal 2023, grew 2.0% in fiscal 2024 and 6.4% to $416,161M in fiscal 2025, while gross margin rose from 44.1% to 46.9% and operating margin from 29.8% to 32.0%. The latest filed period is the quarter ended 2026-06-27, where revenue rose 16.4% to $109,417M on gross margin of 50.1% and operating margin of 32.6%. No fourth-quarter fiscal 2026 earnings release and no fiscal 2026 annual report were on EDGAR as of 2026-10-31; Apple's fiscal 2025 equivalents were filed on 2025-10-30 and 2025-10-31, so the annual report is due imminently and the figures here are trailing twelve months to 2026-06-27 [S5, S6, S13].

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | $383,285M | $391,035M | $416,161M | $109,417M | $466,823M | S5, S6 |
| Gross margin | 44.1% | 46.2% | 46.9% | 50.1% | 48.7% | S5, S6 |
| Operating margin | 29.8% | 31.5% | 32.0% | 32.6% | 33.2% | S5, S6 |
| Net income | $96,995M | $93,736M | $112,010M | $29,789M | $128,930M | S5, S6 |
| Diluted EPS | $6.13 | $6.08 | $7.46 | $2.02 | $8.72 | S5, S6 |

| Operating cash flow | $110,543M | $118,254M | $111,482M | n/a | $146,724M | S5, S6 |
| Capital expenditure | $10,959M | $9,447M | $12,715M | n/a | $10,041M | S5, S6 |
| Free cash flow | $99,584M | $108,807M | $98,767M | n/a | $136,683M | S5, S6 |
| Free cash flow / net income | 1.03x | 1.16x | 0.88x | n/a | 1.06x | S5, S6 |

### The growth is half tax base effect, and a quarter buyback

Fiscal 2025's net income rose 19.5%, but pretax income rose 7.5% ($132,729M against $123,485M) and the tax provision fell 30.3% to $20,719M because fiscal 2024 carried the one-time $10.2bn Irish charge — $15.8bn payable to Ireland, offset by a $4.8bn US foreign tax credit and $823M of released unrecognised benefits. Normalising fiscal 2024 at fiscal 2025's 15.6% rate gives $104,222M and underlying growth of 7.5%, not 19.5%. The EPS gap above that is the buyback: from fiscal 2023 to fiscal 2025 net income grew 15.5% while diluted EPS grew 21.7% and diluted shares fell 5.1%, so 5.4 percentage points of EPS growth was a smaller denominator — and that contribution is fading, at 1.9 percentage points in the trailing twelve months (EPS +16.9% against net income +15.1%), because repurchases slowed to $62,094M in the nine months to 2026-06-27 from $70,579M while operating cash flow rose 43%. Capital return has stopped outrunning cash: buybacks and dividends were $97,866M against free cash flow of $136,683M, or 72%, against 107% in fiscal 2025, and net cash rose by $28,410M in nine months. At the $344.63 close on 2026-10-30 and the 14,594.2M shares issued and outstanding reported on the 10-Q cover at 2026-07-17, equity is worth $5.03trn; on trailing diluted EPS of $8.72 that is 39.5x earnings and a 2.72% free cash flow yield, while the ten-year Treasury yielded 4.93%. Diluted shares of 14,715M are the EPS denominator and sit 0.8% above the outstanding count, so the two bases are consistent. Repurchasing at that spread is accretive to EPS and not obviously accretive to value per share [S5, S6, S9].

### Cash is real; the working-capital cushion is not

Cash generation is the strongest part of the record and the hardest to fake: operating cash flow of $146,724M against capital expenditure of $10,041M, with free cash flow at 1.06x net income. The anomaly is fiscal 2025, when free cash flow fell to 0.88x of net income despite $111,482M of operating cash flow; cash paid for income taxes that year was $43,369M, 32.7% of pretax income against a 15.6% book rate and 21.1% in fiscal 2024 — a gap consistent with settlement payments on the Irish case and the TCJA repatriation tax, the final $8.8bn of which was paid in the nine months to 2026-06-27. That supports reading the gap as timing, and the recovery to 1.06x is consistent with it. The working-capital change runs the other way: inventory reached $11,092M at 2026-06-27 from $5,925M a year earlier, an 87% increase against 16.2% revenue growth, lifting days inventory to 16.9 from 9.4 and pulling the cash conversion cycle to −56.8 days from −71.1 at the fiscal 2025 year-end [S5, S6].

The balance sheet carries no leverage risk: at 2026-06-27 Apple held $146,517M of cash and marketable securities against $84,344M of debt, for net cash of $62,173M, up from $33,763M, with commercial paper cut to $1,997M from $7,979M, and other income and expense netted to −$321M in fiscal 2025 because interest earned on the securities book offsets interest paid. The commitments that matter are forward purchases — $57.0bn of manufacturing purchase obligations, $56.2bn due within twelve months, and $29.3bn of other purchase obligations — which fix component supply and, with it, the cost base when memory prices move. Two accounting details deserve attention: gross intangible assets rose $13,270M to $38,220M in nine months with no goodwill recognised, which indicates purchased intellectual property, content or asset acquisitions rather than share purchases, and is not explained in the quarterly filing; and gross unrecognised tax benefits were $23.2bn at 2025-09-27, of which $10.6bn would affect the effective rate and up to $6bn may move within twelve months [S6].

### Returns are distorted by the buyback, not flattered by the business

Reported returns are not usable as quality scores: return on equity was 148.8% and return on invested capital 320.6% on invested capital of $45,347M — $107,520M of equity plus $84,344M of debt less $146,517M of securities — because $258,212M of cumulative buybacks shrank the equity base. The honest comparison is return on assets of 36.1% against Microsoft's 35.9% return on invested capital in fiscal 2026 and Alphabet's 37.0% in fiscal 2025 [S6, S27, S41].

### What moves the outcome, and by how much

The geographic picture also cuts against the standard bear case: Greater China revenue rose 30% to $64,839M in the nine months to 2026-06-27 and 22% in the June quarter, so nine months already exceed the whole of fiscal 2025's $64,377M after two years of decline. What moves the outcome most is gross margin. On trailing-twelve-month revenue of $466,823M one point of gross margin is $4,668M of pretax profit, or 3.0% of net income, while one point of revenue growth at the current margin is $1,878M, or 1.5%. Three cases, all on the trailing twelve months and none a forecast: a two-point margin gain takes EPS to $9.24, a two-point give-back to $8.20, and a two-point give-back with the loss of the search licence to $7.11, 18.8% below the base — and the licence should be modelled as intact but repriced annually, because the September 2025 order permitted non-exclusive placement payments of one year or less rather than ending them, while the $20bn figure is a 2022 court-record number Apple has never confirmed. The cash is real and the balance sheet is net cash; the growth is weaker than reported; and the margin sits at a cyclical high with a tariff-refund component inside it. An investor paying 39.5x trailing earnings is paying for the first and third to persist while the second is already reversing. The diligence question that matters most is what the fiscal 2026 annual report says about inventory composition and the split between refund and product mix, neither of which the quarterly filings settle [S6, S82, S118].

::: info warning
**The fiscal 2026 gross margin is not yet a clean number.** Strip out the tariff refund Apple attributes to the June quarter and the margin is still above any full year in this record, but a smaller step-change than the reported figure implies; against an inventory build growing faster than revenue, the annual report carries the burden of proof.
:::

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Company Overview (company_overview, revision 3 by Company Analyst, 8,885 characters)
Apple's structure is clean in law — one share class, a majority-independent board and net cash — but not in economics: 61.8% of pretax profit is booked outside the U.S. at a 15.6% effective tax rate, insiders own 0.06%, and the same director has chaired the board since 2000, so the "alignment" in the equity story rests on pay design and on a tax structure the EU has already litigated once. The listed parent is Apple Inc., a California corporation whose common stock ($0.00001 par value) trades on Nasdaq under AAPL: 14,594,180,000 shares outstanding at 2026-07-17, down from 14,697,926,000 at 2026-01-02, and a market capitalisation of $5.03 trillion at 2026-10-30. Votes track economics one-for-one, and the free float is 99.94% because all directors and officers together hold 9,079,765 shares [S5, S6, S65, S172].

### Three Irish companies sit between the product and the profit

EX-21 lists 19 subsidiaries domiciled in 15 jurisdictions and omits the rest as not significant; it gives neither ownership percentages nor functions, so what follows is a map of domicile, not of economic activity. The two entities the European Commission found held Apple's intellectual property for sales outside the Americas — Apple Sales International and Apple Operations Europe — no longer appear on the list; in their place are three Irish companies. Apple does not describe the 2015 restructuring or name the entity that now owns the non-U.S. IP, but the tax note shows the consequence: foreign pretax earnings of $82.0bn of $132.7bn in FY2025 and a 15.6% effective rate against 21%. The 5.4-point gap is worth $7.2bn a year in cash tax, and it is exactly what the Commission attacked: the 2016 decision ordered recovery of up to €13bn, the General Court annulled it on 2020-07-15, the Court of Justice reinstated it on 2024-09-10, and Apple took a $10.2bn net charge in Q4 FY2024, paying $15.8bn to Ireland through escrow against a $4.8bn U.S. foreign tax credit [S5, S187]. Ireland closed the opinions in January 2015, so the scheme itself is gone, but the precedent is not. Entity accounts filed with Ireland's Companies Registration Office, which the 10-K does not reproduce, would show where profit now sits.

### Capital return, not leverage, is the capital-structure question

Apple carries $62.2bn of net cash — $146.5bn of cash and securities against $84.3bn of debt at 2026-06-27 — and in the nine months to that date repurchased 215m shares for $61.8bn, against $70.6bn in the same period a year earlier, under a $100bn authorisation announced on 2025-05-01 [S6]. At a $5tn capitalisation each $10bn of repurchase retires 0.2% of the company, so the return depends on the price paid. A 12% year-on-year slowdown in dollars while the shares rose 25.7% is consistent with price discipline, or with lower free cash flow; the filings do not distinguish. Solvency is not the risk; executing the market's largest buyback at a multiple that assumes the AI transition works is.

### Ownership is institutional, and the board is long-tenured

Vanguard holds 9.63% and BlackRock 7.10%, but the BlackRock figure is taken from a 2023-12-31 filing quoted in the 2026 proxy and is stale [S65, S153]. Directors and officers hold 0.06%; Tim Cook's 3,280,295 shares are worth $1.13bn at the current price yet are 0.02% of the company. The board has nine members after Ternus joined on 2026-09-01, seven of them independent; Arthur Levinson, a director since 2000 and chair for 15 years, became lead independent director that day. At the 2026-02-24 annual meeting Levinson drew 9.0% opposition, say-on-pay 8.6% and a "China Entanglement Audit" proposal 1.4% support. That passes Nasdaq's majority-independent rule and is not a governance crisis, but it is a professional board, not a founder-aligned one.

### The business model is an annuity on hardware

Apple sells devices to consumers, enterprises and carriers, but the buyer that matters is the installed base: more than 2.5bn devices whose owners upgrade and pay for services. FY2025 net sales were $416.2bn (+6%), with Services gross margin of 75.4% against 46.9% for the group; in the nine months to 2026-06-27 net sales rose 16% to $364.4bn, Services 14% to $91.7bn and Greater China 30% to $64.8bn after a 4% decline in FY2025 [S5, S6]. That is the growth engine — a replacement cycle plus attach, with China swinging from drag to driver in two years. It makes the model resilient to unit stagnation but not to a remedy that breaks the Services attach: Services produced 39.1% of nine-month gross profit on 25.2% of revenue.

### The legal front is about Services margins, not fines

Three proceedings test the container. The DOJ's civil antitrust suit, filed on 2024-03-21 in the District of New Jersey, seeks equitable relief rather than damages; the Epic litigation produced a 2025-04-30 finding that Apple violated the 2021 injunction, a ban on fees for out-of-app purchases and a referral to the U.S. Attorney for possible criminal contempt; and the EU fined Apple €500m under the Digital Markets Act on 2025-04-23, which Apple appealed [S5, S7]. The fines are small against $416bn of revenue; the remedies are not, because they target the 75%-gross-margin Services line and the App Store's toll gate on 2.5bn devices. Counter-evidence is real — the DOJ must prove market definition, Apple says it has substantial defences, and no court has ordered a structural remedy — but the direction in both jurisdictions is toward alternative distribution and payment, the one outcome that would change the franchise's economics rather than its legal bill.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Founding Team & Key Personnel (team, revision 2 by Company Analyst, 8,571 characters)
The succession is done and internal — Ternus, Srouji, Federighi and Parekh are all Apple lifers — which lowers cultural and execution risk but concentrates the AI transition in a software chief who has outsourced the frontier model to Google and a first-time CEO who has never run a P&L, so the team offers continuity rather than evidence of renewal. The board appointed John Ternus CEO effective 2026-09-01, with Tim Cook as executive chair and Arthur Levinson, chair for the previous 15 years, as lead independent director. Ternus, 50, joined Apple's product design team in 2001, became VP Hardware Engineering in 2013 and SVP in 2021; his record includes iPad, AirPods, the iPhone 17 line and the MacBook Neo, but no disclosed CEO, P&L or capital-allocation role before 2026 [S152, S177].

::: evidence
**The board has already executed the succession by promoting an internal hardware engineer, and the appointment was unanimous.**

The 8-K of 2026-04-20 records the board's appointment of Ternus as CEO effective 2026-09-01, Cook's move to executive chair and Levinson's to lead independent director. Ternus joined Apple in 2001 and has led hardware engineering since 2021. The doubt sits one level down: the AI organisation was rebuilt on 2025-12-01 around an external hire reporting to Federighi, and the rebuilt Siri will run on Google's Gemini models [S152, S177, S183, S186].
:::

The division of labour is unusually clear for a company of this size. Ternus integrates and decides; Johny Srouji became chief hardware officer on 2026-04-20, adding hardware engineering to silicon and becoming the single owner of Apple's deepest technical moat; Craig Federighi owns software and, since December 2025, AI; Eddy Cue runs services and now health; Kevan Parekh funds the company; Sabih Khan runs operations; Deirdre O'Brien runs retail and people [S179, S184]. That design fits a business whose advantage is integration across silicon, software and services, but it places the two capabilities that matter most in the next cycle — silicon and AI/software — in two individuals with no disclosed deputies.

### AI leadership failed once and has been rebuilt around an outside hire and an outside model

John Giannandrea stepped down as AI chief on 2025-12-01 after the Siri delay; Amar Subramanya, formerly corporate VP of AI at Microsoft and head of engineering for Google's Gemini Assistant, joined as VP of AI reporting to Federighi, while the rest of the AI organisation was split between Khan and Cue. On 2026-01-12 Apple and Google announced a multiyear deal to power Apple's AI features, including the Siri upgrade due in 2026, with Gemini [S183, S186]. The mechanism is speed for dependency: Apple gets a competitive assistant without building a frontier model, but it hands a competitor the most valuable interface in consumer technology and caps the differentiation it can charge for. Underwrite AI as a feature that protects the hardware replacement cycle, not as a new profit pool, until Apple discloses model economics.

### Pay and turnover: equity retains, but the C-suite is new

Cook's 2025 total target compensation was $59m: a $3m base unchanged since 2016, a cash incentive at 200% of base and a $50m equity target, positioned in the 80th-90th percentile of the primary peer group; the other named executives target $1m base, 200% cash and $20m equity, and Parekh's target was $16.75m. The CEO ownership guideline is 10 times salary. The design retains executives through the transition rather than rewarding new AI outcomes: 8.6% of votes cast opposed say-on-pay at the 2026-02-24 annual meeting, a protest worth noting but not a rejection. Retention is being tested at the same time. The CFO moved from Luca Maestri to Parekh on 2025-01-01, the COO from Jeff Williams to Khan in July 2025, the general counsel from Kate Adams to Jennifer Newstead on 2026-03-01, the AI chief from Giannandrea to Subramanya on 2025-12-01 and the CEO from Cook to Ternus on 2026-09-01. Against Apple's near-static 2011-2023 executive team that is a large amount of institutional change at once; none was a resignation under pressure, and the risk is coordination while antitrust remedies and a China reset land [S65, S153, S170, S166].

### The missing capability is frontier AI at the top, not finance or operations

No board member has operating AI-lab experience — Wanda Austin ran Aerospace, Alex Gorsky ran Johnson & Johnson — and the AI leader sits at VP level, outside the executive team [S179, S173]. That is the reference check a diligence team should run: who inside Apple can credibly challenge Google's model roadmap, and what retention packages hold Srouji and Federighi, the two people whose departure would impair the franchise. Counter-evidence is genuine: internal succession worked in 2011 when Cook replaced Steve Jobs, Ternus's product record is strong, and the Gemini deal buys time. The judgement is not that the team is weak; it is that the team is unproven at exactly the task the next three years demand.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Technology & Product (technology_product, revision 5 by Product Analyst, 8,835 characters)
Apple's silicon-plus-OS stack is still the widest integrated consumer technology stack, but in 2026 the company rented the one layer it could not build — the frontier model — so what remains defensible is distribution, custom silicon and regulated health sensing, not leadership in artificial intelligence. In two years the A20 Pro moved the iPhone to TSMC N2, the C2 modem reached the flagship, the first foldable shipped at $1,999, and on 2026-01-12 Apple and Google announced the next Apple Foundation Models would be Gemini-based [S58, S59, S63, S64].

### The silicon lead is real, costly, and rented from TSMC

The A19 Pro used TSMC N3P; a year later the A20 Pro moved to TSMC N2 with a 32-core Neural Engine and ~52 TOPS, about double the prior generation's AI throughput. N2 wafers are reported at ~$30,000 against $18,000-20,000 for 3nm, so each step costs more. Product gross margin was 39.9% in the nine months to 2026-06-27 versus 36.9% a year earlier, but only with tariff refunds and mix offsetting "higher costs, including memory", and the 10-Q warns that advanced-semiconductor, NAND and DRAM constraints are expected to intensify [S6, S64].

| Metric | Value | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Node, A19 Pro / A20 Pro | TSMC N3P (2025) / N2 (2026) | Teardown and trade reporting | S63, S64 |
| CPU clock, A19 Pro | up to 4.26 GHz, 6 cores | Published specification | S63 |
| Neural Engine, A20 Pro | 32 cores, ~52 TOPS, ~2x A19 Pro | Trade-press estimate | S64 |
| N2 wafer price | ~$30,000 vs $18,000-20,000 at 3nm | Trade-press estimate | S64 |
| Product gross margin | 39.9% vs 36.9% (9M FY2025) | Reported financials | S6 |
| On-device model / PCC context | ~3B parameters / 32K tokens | Apple research and developer docs | S61, S62 |

### Apple Intelligence is an architecture with a rented brain

On device, Apple runs a ~3B-parameter model optimised through KV-cache sharing and 2-bit quantisation-aware training; on its servers, a Parallel-Track Mixture-of-Experts model runs inside Private Cloud Compute, which enforces stateless processing, no privileged access even for Apple staff, and attested software images. The binding constraint is memory bandwidth and power: phone-class memory caps on-device inference at single-digit billions of parameters, so harder queries are offloaded. The ceiling is disclosed: a 32K-token context is small against frontier assistants, and Apple's own models were not frontier-quality. The unresolved question for the privacy story is where Gemini-derived inference physically runs. Apple says Apple Intelligence continues on Apple devices and Private Cloud Compute; trade reporting says Google's cloud performs the Gemini computation and puts the licence at ~$1bn a year, on top of a default-search payment of ~$20bn. Neither figure is Apple-confirmed. China's CAC approved Apple Intelligence on 2026-07-15, nearly two years after its 2024 debut, with Alibaba's Qwen and Baidu supplying a separate model stack. Apple's differentiation is orchestration, distribution and privacy, not model quality; an investor should underwrite the cash flow and installed base, not the AI layer [S8, S58, S60, S61, S86, S120, S171].

| Cost structure | Fixed R&D and data-centre capex | Fixed R&D plus per-query licence | Licence revenue | S58, S86 |
| What Apple keeps | Silicon, OS, orchestration | Silicon, OS, interface, orchestration | Model, training, inference | S58, S60 |

### Products: a strong cycle, a late foldable, a spatial computer that never became a platform

The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max launched on 2026-09-09 at $1,199 and $1,299; the foldable iPhone Duo at $1,999 went on sale on 2026-10-23. iPhone net sales rose 22% to $196.5bn in the nine months to 2026-06-27, with Greater China up 30%. The C2 modem supports US mmWave and uses 15% less energy than the C1X, but the larger iPhone 18 Pro Max appears to keep a Qualcomm modem, so Qualcomm retains leverage over the highest-ASP SKU. Vision Pro is the counter-example: ~390,000 units in 2024, ~45,000 in the December 2025 quarter despite the M5 refresh, ~600,000 lifetime, and an IDC forecast of ~290,000 units in 2026 [S59, S13, S87].

| Services | Commercial | — | $91.7bn, +14% | 76.3% | AI tier / iCloud+ gating | S6, S107 |

### What is enforceable is regulatory, not patent

Apple publishes no patent count; the FY2025 10-K says only that it is "pursuing thousands of applications around the world" and that no single right protects its products. Patent counts and peer comparison were not obtainable — the registries could not be searched — so the patent moat is unquantified. What is documented is a regulatory estate — hypertension and sleep-apnoea notifications, a hearing-aid De Novo grant and imaging calibration — each cleared on its own clinical file, a slower but more durable barrier than a patent family.

### The moat is wide at the bottom of the stack and thin at the top

| Custom SoC and modem | 9 | Top design team plus priority TSMC N2 access; a decade and an Intel acquisition | 4-5 years | S59, S64 |

| On-device model efficiency | 5 | Quantisation and KV-cache techniques are published | 1-2 years | S61 |

| Installed base and developers | 10 | A decade of switching costs, record active base | 10+ years | S13, S87 |

The replication test: a team of 50 senior silicon and operating-system engineers could match a phone-class SoC and OS in four to five years, and rent a competitive model next quarter. The counter-evidence is Apple's own record: Siri needed a Google licence, the car was cancelled, and Vision Pro has not reached platform volumes. Regulation can also withhold the assistant: the Q3 FY2026 10-Q states DMA interoperability obligations have in the past, and may in future, cause Apple not to launch or maintain features "such as Siri AI" in certain jurisdictions. The advantage holds only if on-device AI lifts upgrade rates and regulators leave the App Store economics that fund the silicon intact. Two diligence questions settle it: whether the Google agreement allows fine-tuning for on-device use, and whether the 2027 Pro Max moves fully to the C2 [S6, S58, S59, S87].

::: evidence
**Apple's integration advantage is durable in silicon and distribution, but it no longer extends to the model layer.**

The A20 Pro's 2nm node and 32-core Neural Engine keep Apple at the leading edge of phone silicon, and ten FDA clearances and grants since 2020 give it a regulated feature estate rivals must replicate trial by trial. But basing the next Apple Foundation Models on Gemini concedes that the frontier layer is bought, the reported ~$1bn annual licence turns a fixed R&D advantage into a variable cost paid to a competitor, and availability now varies by jurisdiction: China runs a Qwen/Baidu stack and DMA rules may withhold Siri AI in the EU [S6, S58, S64, S86, S120, S171].
:::"}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Development Strategy (strategy, revision 5 by Product Analyst, 8,085 characters)
Apple's route to FY2028 growth is services mix, a richer iPhone cycle and India, with artificial intelligence as a retention feature and a possible iCloud+ upsell rather than a revenue line of its own; the plan is credible on cash generation and per-share compounding, but not yet on AI monetisation or on creating a new product category. The base is large and still growing: revenue reached $416.2bn in FY2025, and the nine months to 2026-06-27 produced $364.4bn, up 16%, with Services at $91.7bn, up 14% [S77, S6].

### Services carry the margin, but the mix engine stalled in FY2026

Services were 26% of FY2025 revenue but 39% of gross profit in the nine months to June 2026, because they earn a 76.3% gross margin against 39.9% for products. The mix engine, however, stopped being the marginal driver: product gross profit grew 26% against 15% for services, so the rise in total gross margin to 49.1% from 46.8% came from hardware mix and tariff refunds, not from services, while memory costs kept rising. Services growth itself came from advertising and cloud services, with the Google search-distribution payment named as a primary driver. That is the engine that funds the buyback and the silicon, and it is also the engine regulators are targeting: the European Commission fined Apple €500m on 2025-04-23 for anti-steering non-compliance, and the General Court dismissed Apple's challenge to its gatekeeper designation on 2026-07-08 [S85, S84, S6]. An investor should value the services annuity on gross profit that compounds in the low-to-mid teens, and apply a discount for the probability that a remedy compresses commission or search income rather than a one-off fine.

### AI is funded as cost and monetised, if at all, through storage

Apple introduced Siri AI with the iOS 27 cycle announced in the third quarter of FY2026, and R&D rose 33% to $34.0bn in the nine months to June 2026, driven by infrastructure including AI investments and headcount. No AI revenue line exists. Availability is a regulatory variable too: China cleared Apple Intelligence only on 2026-07-15, with Alibaba's Qwen and Baidu, and the 10-Q warns that DMA rules have in the past, and may in future, cause it not to launch features "such as Siri AI" in some jurisdictions. The reported plan — that high-frequency, compute-intensive Siri use will be gated behind iCloud+ — is plausible because it reuses a price ladder already in place, but Apple has published no tier and no price, so it is unverified [S13, S6, S107, S171]. The mechanism matters more than the price: AI raises the cost of serving every device while its clearest commercial effect is to protect upgrade rates and services attach. If Apple charges, the increment is bounded by storage-subscription willingness to pay, not by the value of the model; if it does not, AI is a permanent tax on gross margin. Either way, 2027 is the test of whether AI spend converts into units or ARPU.

### India lowers tariff risk, not unit cost

iPhone production in India rose 53% in 2025 to ~55 million units, ~25% of global output, and is projected at 28% in 2026; Tata Electronics overtook Foxconn in iPhone export assembly over the FY2022-FY2026 incentive period. The strategy is rational given the tariff record in the filings — Section 232 semiconductor investigation results in January 2026, the Supreme Court striking down certain IEEPA tariffs in February 2026, and new Section 301 tariffs, with manufacturing purchase obligations of $57.0bn at 2026-06-27 [S89, S91, S6]. The limit is that assembly captures little of the value: components, displays and silicon still come from East Asia, so India is an insurance policy on tariffs and single-country concentration, not a margin lever. The signpost to watch is the share of US-bound iPhones assembled in India, which Apple has never disclosed.

### Capital allocation is disciplined and slightly bolder

R&D rose from $29.9bn in FY2023 to $34.6bn in FY2025 and is running at ~$45bn annualised in FY2026. Buybacks remain the primary use of cash: $25.8bn of stock was repurchased in the quarter to 2026-06-27 alone, alongside $4.0bn of dividends at $0.27 per share, which cut the share count to 14.61bn from 14.77bn at FY2025 year-end and helped EPS grow 29% against 27% net-income growth. M&A posture has shifted from tuck-ins: Apple confirmed the acquisition of the AI-audio start-up Q.ai on 2026-01-29, reported by the Financial Times at close to $2bn, and acquired the AI data-engineering company Ascend.io, notified to the European Commission on 2026-06-30; intangible assets rose from $11.1bn to $20.3bn between 2025-09-27 and 2026-06-27 [S77, S88, S6, S13]. Against ~$146bn of cash and marketable securities, that is affordable experimentation rather than a change of strategy — and it is the right test of whether Apple's AI gap can be bought in pieces.

| iPhone Duo ramp | 2026-10-23 on sale | Launched | Apple can create a $1,999 tier | S59 |
| AI subscription (iCloud+ gating) | Not announced | Reported only | AI becomes revenue rather than cost | S107 |
| Lower-cost Vision Pro | Late 2026 | Unconfirmed by Apple | Spatial computing can reach volume | S87 |

### What must be true in twelve months, and the case against

Four things must happen for the strategy to be credible. First, the FY2026 holiday quarter has to show that the iPhone 18 and Duo cycle sustains double-digit growth without tariff refunds, which flattered the June quarter by ~2 percentage points of gross margin. Second, Apple must put a price on AI or show that it lifts upgrade rates, because a 33% R&D increase with no revenue attached is a margin problem. Third, a DOJ settlement or DMA remedy must leave the App Store commission and default-search payment substantially intact; both cases attack the services profit pool directly. Fourth, India must reach the projected share of output without a quality or logistics incident. The counter-case is strong and largely Apple's own record: AI features arrived well after they were demonstrated, Siri needed a Google licence, the car programme was cancelled, and Vision Pro shipped ~45,000 units in the December 2025 quarter, while Alphabet, Microsoft and Huawei set a faster cadence in models, cloud AI and, for Huawei, folding hardware and domestic silicon. Apple's answer is that it does not need to be first — it needs to be best integrated, and it monetises the installed base rather than the model. That is a defensible strategy for a cash-flow investor and a weak one for anyone buying AI optionality [S59, S87, S84, S90, S89].

::: evidence
**The strategy is credible as a cash-compounding plan and unproven as a growth plan.**

Services earn a structurally higher gross margin than hardware, and buybacks are large enough that earnings per share can compound faster than net income even with flat hardware; but AI is a large R&D increase with no disclosed price, Vision Pro has not become a platform, and the two antitrust cases target precisely the services lines that fund the plan.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Market & Industry Analysis (market, revision 2 by Market Analyst, 8,997 characters)
Apple's markets are contracting in units and expanding in value, and Apple is taking value share inside that contraction: the case for FY2026-FY2028 rests on premiumisation and Services attach rather than device volume, is strongest in the United States, is adequate in Europe, and in China depends on a domestic champion's pricing discipline.

### The pool is shrinking in units and growing in value

IDC's August 2026 forecast has worldwide smartphone shipments at just over 1.0 billion units in 2026, down 16.7% and the steepest annual contraction on record, while total market value rises 6.3% to $613 billion and the average selling price reaches a record $581, up 27.6% in a year and revised up from the $550 IDC published one quarter earlier. The cause is cost, not demand: DRAM and NAND prices are up more than 300% year on year as capacity is redirected to AI servers, memory is more than 65% of bill of materials at the low end, and the sub-$100 tier that shipped 173 million units in 2025 fell close to 60% in the second quarter of 2026. This is a supply shock with a dated end, so 2026-2027 flatters Apple's unit share while genuinely lifting its price, and 2028 is the test of whether either survives. [S39]

Two sizing methods agree closely: 1.0 billion units at the $581 average price gives $581 billion, within 5% of IDC's $613 billion, so the unit and price series can be read together rather than as rival estimates. On that base Apple's serviceable market is the premium tier it addresses — an iOS share of 23.6% of 2026 shipments, a record — while the revenue it can obtain is what it already books: $466.8 billion trailing twelve months to 2026-06-27, which at the 16.2% growth rate of the first nine months of FY2026 implies $483 billion for FY2026. IDC's PC-plus-tablet pool compounds at 1.5% a year from 2026 to 2030, so device pools are not growth markets at any price. [S6]
