| TAM, smartphone value (bottom-up) | 1.0bn units x $581 ASP | ~$581bn | 2026 | Calculation on IDC inputs | S66 |
| TAM, personal computing devices | Units published, value not disclosed | ~398m units, -11.3%; 1.5% CAGR to 2030 | 2026 | IDC | S103 |
| SAM, premium smartphone tier | iOS share of shipments | 23.6% of units, record | 2026 | IDC | S66 |
| SOM, Apple revenue | Reported | $466.8bn TTM | TTM to 2026-06-27 | Apple 10-Q | S6 |
| Near-term obtainable revenue | FY2025 $416.2bn grown at the 9M FY2026 rate | ~$483bn | FY2026E | Calculation on Apple filings | S5, S13 |
| Adjacent services pool | Alphabet revenue | $471.1bn TTM | TTM to 2026-09-30 | Alphabet 10-Q | S42 |

### China is the swing factor, and India sits in the wrong line

Apple's revenue is moving toward the faster-growing regions, but the swing is China. In the first nine months of FY2026 Greater China produced $64.8 billion, up 30.0% on a base of $49.9 billion, after falling from $72.6 billion in FY2023 to $64.4 billion in FY2025; the Americas grew 11.4% to $149.4 billion, Europe 16.1% to $95.6 billion, Japan 10.4% and Rest of Asia Pacific 19.4%. Greater China's $14.9 billion increase contributes 4.1 percentage points of the group's 16.2% growth, more than any other segment, and part of it is currency: a favourable renminbi effect in Greater China, an unfavourable yen effect in Japan. One reporting artefact matters: the Europe segment includes India, the Middle East and Africa, so the fastest-growing large smartphone market is invisible in the line labelled Europe and India is not a segment an investor can track. [S13]

| Region | Market size (year) | Growth | Apple's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| United States / North America | 60% of Q1 2026 shipments above $800; US is 24.9% of global PC-plus-tablet units | Smartphone -6.3% in 2026; PC -14.6% in 2026 | Entered, leads the premium tier; 41.0% of Apple revenue is the Americas | Tariffs, carrier financing, antitrust suits | Samsung, Lenovo, HP, Dell | S39, S103, S13 |
| Greater China | ~66m units a quarter, 264m a year | -4.3% in Q2 2026, fifth straight decline; H2 2026 could be -20% | 18.1% of units, second behind Huawei; revenue +30.0% | Domestic operating system, subsidy withdrawal, data rules | Huawei 22.6%, OPPO 16.0%, vivo 16.0%, Xiaomi 12.4% | S40, S6 |
| Europe (segment includes India, Middle East, Africa) | India 31.0m units in Q1 2026 at a record $302 ASP | India units -4.1% but value +5.8%; Europe revenue +16.1% | Entered; fourth by units in India | DMA, price sensitivity, distribution | Samsung, Xiaomi, vivo, Lenovo, HP | S105, S103, S13 |
| Japan | Revenue $24.4bn in 9M FY2026 | Revenue +10.4%; units -25.6% in 2026 | Entered, premium strong; weak yen cuts revenue | Yen, saturated device base | Local Android vendors, Samsung | S13, S103, S6 |
| Rest of Asia Pacific | Revenue $30.2bn in 9M FY2026 | Revenue +19.4%; units -14% in 2026 | Entered, premium-led | Price-sensitive mass market, currency | Samsung, Xiaomi, OPPO, vivo | S13, S39, S103 |

### Services carries the margin and has no published pool size

The fastest-growing pool Apple actually monetises is Services: $109.2 billion, 26.2% of FY2025 revenue, at a 75.4% gross margin against 36.8% for products, growing 14.1% to $91.7 billion in the first nine months of FY2026. The adjacent pools are larger and largely not Apple's — Alphabet's trailing-twelve-month revenue is $471.1 billion — but the app economy itself has no published size in the sources retrieved: neither Apple nor the platform owners disclose app-store gross billings or mobile-advertising revenue in a sizeable form, so Apple's own Services line is the measured pool. The installed base behind it has the same gap: Apple states only that its active-device base reached an all-time high in the June 2026 quarter across every category and region, and publishes no device count in its FY2025 10-K or FY2026 results, so the figure of 2.3 billion devices often quoted alongside the business is unverified here and should carry none of the valuation. [S5]

### Who pays, and how much demand is policy

The budget owner is the consumer, in a discretionary purchase that is increasingly financed. In the United States and United Kingdom long-term interest-free financing is more prevalent, so IDC expects the premium end to hold while emerging markets fall more than 20%; in India brands lean on financing after the sub-$100 tier fell 59% and the $600-800 band grew 32%; in China the government subsidy that supported earlier quarters faded in the second quarter of 2026, so demand there is being withdrawn by policy rather than created by it. Apple's exposure to policy runs both ways: after the February 20, 2026 Supreme Court ruling struck down certain IEEPA tariffs, Apple recognised refunds as a reduction of product cost of sales, and those refunds contributed 2.0 percentage points of the June 2026 quarter's 50.1% gross margin — tariff policy moves Apple's margin by more than a product cycle does. [S105, S40, S13]

The counter-evidence is threefold, each strand dated. If memory prices normalise in 2028 as IDC expects, the entry tier rebuilds and Apple's 2026 share gain is contestable again. If China's June-quarter demand was pulled forward ahead of expected second-half price increases, as IDC's China team reports, the 30% growth line is a launch and currency effect. And if courts and the European Commission remove the App Store take rate, the 75%-margin layer that offsets hardware cyclicality stops compounding at its present rate. The investor implication is narrow: in a 1-billion-unit market Apple can grow revenue only if price rises faster than units fall, making average selling price, China durability and the Services take rate the variables worth monitoring. Sizing confidence is high, because two independent methods agree within 5%; confidence that the mix shift holds to 2028 is medium, because it rests on China and a legally contested commission. Three questions would close the gap: what share of Services revenue is commission-based rather than subscription, advertising or licensing; how much of the Greater China increase is currency; and what the current average replacement cycle is, measured rather than asserted. [S66, S40]

::: evidence
**Apple's addressable device market fell 16.7% in units in 2026 while growing 6.3% in value, and Apple's revenue grew 16.2% over nine months — the gap is premiumisation and China, not market growth (S66, S13).**

IDC forecasts 2026 shipments at just over 1.0 billion units against a market value of $613 billion and an ASP of $581 (S66, S39). Apple's nine-month FY2026 revenue was $364.4 billion, up 16.2%, with Greater China up 30.0% on a $49.9 billion base (S13, S6). The bottom-up check of 1.0 billion units at $581 gives $581 billion, within 5% of IDC's value estimate (S66).
:::"}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Competitive Landscape (competition, revision 4 by Market Analyst, 8,987 characters)
Apple's competitive position strengthened in 2026 in every hardware line except smartwatches, but the gain is crisis-specific — bought with memory supply and price discipline rather than product superiority — and it is being offset where profit is made, because the App Store commission that funds the premium position is being dismantled by courts and regulators rather than by a rival's product. Apple leads no hardware category outright except detachable tablets, and its annual report concedes minority share in smartphones, PCs, tablets and wearables. Head to head, Samsung shipped 62.7 million handsets in Q2 2026 versus Apple's 55.7 million. [S102]

### The lead is in integration, not in units

Apple's 20.2% of global smartphone shipments in Q2 2026 was a record for that quarter and a 3.9 percentage point gain, but Samsung's 22.7% was larger and Xiaomi's 26.4% collapse explains much of the redistribution. In personal computing Apple is second at 18.2% to Lenovo's 20.1%, yet macOS shipments grew 17.4% while Windows fell 6.7% and Android 19.6%, and macOS is the only major operating system IDC expects to grow in 2026. The clearest structural lead is detachable tablets at 55.3%; the weakest spot is smartwatches, where Huawei leads 18.8% to 17.2%, so Apple's 15.5% of all wearables rests on earwear, where it holds 17.2%. [S104]

| iPhone, global | Samsung | 22.7%, +3.2pp | 20.2%, +3.9pp | iOS integration and secured memory supply | Industry ASP $581; Apple above it | High: iCloud, iMessage, purchased apps | S102, S66 |
| iPhone, China | Huawei | 22.6%, +4.5pp | 18.1%, +4.2pp | iOS against domestic HarmonyOS | Apple held prices while Android raised them | Medium: leaving iOS loses Apple services | S40 |
| PCs and tablets | Lenovo | 20.1%, +2.5pp | 18.2%, -0.4% | macOS against Windows | MacBook Neo attacks entry pricing | Medium | S103, S106 |
| Services and App Store | Alphabet, Google Play | $471.1bn TTM revenue | $109.2bn Services at 75.4% gross margin | iOS distribution against Google Play | 15-30% commission, under challenge | High for consumers, falling for developers | S5, S42, S80 |

### Samsung is the dangerous one, and the reason is memory

Samsung is the most dangerous competitor, and not because of the Galaxy S26 Ultra. When memory is more than 65% of bill of materials at the low end, the binding constraint is supply access, and Samsung is the only top-five handset vendor that also sells memory: it grew shipments 8.1% and took 3.2 points of share in Q2 2026 while Xiaomi fell 26.4% and vivo 19.6%. Apple's answer was to secure memory early, which is why its units fell only 1.3% in 2026 against Android's 24.3% and why IDC puts iOS at a record 23.6% of shipments — a sourcing feat rather than a structural advantage, and it lapses when memory normalises while Samsung keeps its costs. Samsung also holds the foldable franchise Apple now attacks: the iPhone Duo went on sale on 2026-10-23 at a reported $1,999, below the $2,550 average price IDC assumes, against a forecast of more than 17 million foldable iPhones by 2027 and 40% of a category growing 12.6% to 22.9 million units this year. [S66, S59]

### In China the competitor and the rules are different

Huawei held 22.6% of a Chinese market that fell 4.3% in Q2 2026 and grew 19.9% by holding prices while Android rivals raised theirs, leaning on HarmonyOS, which IDC expects to reach 51 million units in 2026; Apple grew 24.4% and gained 4.2 points to 18.1%, so both premium ends expanded while OPPO, vivo and Xiaomi contracted. The mechanism is a domestic operating system plus price discipline, and neither is a feature Apple can copy. HarmonyOS draws on the national preference that makes Apple's China revenue politically exposed, so the 30% China revenue growth belongs behind a competition risk; Apple Intelligence was registered with China's internet regulator on 2026-07-15 alongside Alibaba's Qwen and Baidu, which narrows the AI gap in the one market where it mattered most but does not settle it. [S40, S120]

### The profit pool is being taken by courts, not by rivals

Apple's FY2025 annual report discloses that it is subject to a U.S. court order preventing it from imposing any commission on certain purchases consumers make, that its Digital Markets Act compliance plan has been challenged by the European Commission, and that it faces U.S. monopolization suits over smartphones; separately, the September 2, 2025 remedies order against Google, if upheld, could remove the search-distribution payments inside Services. No competitor needs to win a device sale for the 75.4% services margin to compress: a developer that routes a subscriber to the web converts a 15-30% commission into a payment-processing fee, and Services growth of 14.1% then arrives at a lower margin. The hardware position improved while the pricing power behind it was cut by U.S. courts and European regulators. [S5]

| Product | Leader | Challenger | Niche | Emerging threat | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone | Samsung, 22.7% of units | Apple, 20.2% and gaining | Huawei in China, 22.6% | HarmonyOS at 51m units; AI-first Android flagships | S102, S40, S66 |
| PCs and tablets | Lenovo, 20.1% | Apple, 18.2%, with the only growing OS | Dell in workstations, 40.0% | HarmonyOS NEXT at 1.6%; Windows-on-ARM | S103, S106 |
| Services | Apple, $109.2bn | Alphabet through Google Play | Netflix, Spotify, Epic | Web payments and alternative marketplaces | S5, S42, S80 |

### AI and the phone already in the buyer's pocket

Where Apple is not ahead is AI: the all-new Siri AI arrived at WWDC26 in June 2026 on foundation models licensed from Google under their 2026-01-12 agreement — its assistant now depends on a company it also competes with in services. Samsung's AI-equipped Galaxy S26 Ultra is credited by IDC with returning Samsung to first place in Q1 2026, and research and development rose 32.5% to $34.0 billion in nine months of FY2026 — the cost of catching up, not the reward for leading. The strongest competitor is the handset already in the buyer's pocket: replacement cycles are lengthening, IDC describes Chinese buyers as postponing rather than abandoning upgrades, and the 173 million sub-$100 units shipped in 2025 are leaving the market, which supports Services attach while suppressing units. Three risks follow: if AI becomes the reason a buyer upgrades, Apple competes on integration, with a rented model; if HarmonyOS reaches first-time buyers in lower-tier cities, they never enter iOS; and if the U.S. injunction spreads to other storefronts, the take rate falls further. Unit position and profit per unit are moving in opposite directions, so the question worth paying for is not who sells more phones but what share of the transaction Apple controls in 2027. Confidence is high in the shares and legal facts, medium beyond 2028, when memory normalises and the crisis-specific advantage lapses. Open diligence: what proportion of Services revenue is commission rather than subscription? What margin does the foldable carry at $1,999? What does the Gemini licence cost per query at scale? {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Business Model (business_model, revision 3 by Fundamentals Analyst, 8,460 characters)
Apple runs a hardware annuity with a services margin layered on top — 73 cents of services gross profit for every dollar of product gross profit — but the mix shift the multiple pays for stalled in fiscal 2026, when hardware margins, helped by tariff refunds, grew gross profit faster than Services. Apple sells through two routes, and the split is the least-discussed fact in the model: in fiscal 2025, 40% of net sales went through its own stores, online store and direct sales force and 60% through carriers, resellers and distributors. The carrier finances or subsidises the handset to win a contract, so the carrier bears the acquisition cost and Apple's selling expense stays at $27,601M, or 6.6% of revenue. There is little contracted backlog: deferred revenue was $13.7bn at 2025-09-27, 3.3% of revenue, two thirds of it recognised within a year. Apple is a repeat-purchase business recognised as it bills, not a subscription business with a book of contracted revenue [S5].

### The mix shift, and its reversal

The arithmetic of the mix shift is the strongest part of the case. In fiscal 2025 Services produced $109,158M of revenue at a 75.4% gross margin against $307,003M of Products at 36.8%: 26.2% of revenue but 42.2% of gross profit ($82,314M of $195,201M), up from 35.7% two years earlier, with services gross profit per dollar of product gross profit rising from $0.55 in fiscal 2023 to $0.73. Then the mechanism ran backwards. In the nine months to 2026-06-27 product gross profit rose 26.3% to $108,819M while services gross profit rose 15.3% to $69,963M, and Services fell to 39.1% of gross profit; product gross margin reached 39.9% against 36.9% a year earlier, taking total gross margin to 49.1% and to 50.1% in the June quarter against 46.5%. Apple attributes the gain to "a different mix of products and tariff refunds, partially offset by higher costs, including memory", the most consequential disclosure in this section: it makes fiscal 2026's margin hardware-led and partly a refund rather than a trading gain [S5, S6].

### Unit economics per revenue dollar, because there are no units

Apple discloses no unit volumes, average selling price or installed-base figure, so a per-device waterfall cannot be built from primary evidence. The economics of each revenue dollar can be.

| Unit-economics line | FY2025 | 9M FY2026 | Evidence and status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Product cost of sales, per $1,000 of product revenue | $632 | $601 | Bill of materials, assembly and warranty provision combined, not split | S5, S6 |
| Product gross profit | $368 | $399 | 36.8% to 39.9%; includes tariff refunds in fiscal 2026 | S5, S6 |
| Services cost of sales, per $1,000 of services revenue | $246 | $237 | Content, hosting and payment processing | S5, S6 |
| Services gross profit | $754 | $763 | 75.4% to 76.3% | S5, S6 |
| Services gross profit per $1 of product gross profit | $0.73 | $0.64 | Closest disclosed proxy for lifetime value against acquisition cost | S5, S6 |
| Customer acquisition cost, support and warranty | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Carriers bear acquisition; warranty sits inside cost of sales | S5 |
| LTV, LTV:CAC, CAC payback in months | Not computable | Not computable | Requires units, ASP and installed base, none of which Apple reports | S5 |

Apple therefore has no payback period to wait out: a device is gross-profit-positive on delivery at a 36.8% product margin, and the services stream that follows is nearly all incremental, since services cost of sales is $26,844M on $109,158M of revenue. The nearest disclosed proxy for lifetime value against acquisition cost is the $0.73 of services gross profit per dollar of product gross profit, and its fall to $0.64 is the number to watch — the annuity still grows, but no longer faster than the hardware that creates it [S5, S6].

### Pricing power shows up as mix, not as price

| Line | FY2025 net sales | Year on year | What the filing discloses about price and mix | Gross margin | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone | $209,586M | +4% | Growth "due to higher net sales of Pro models", i.e. mix rather than units | 36.8% products blended | S5 |
| Services | $109,158M | +14% | "advertising, the App Store and cloud services" | 75.4% | S5 |
| Mac | $33,708M | +12% | "laptops and desktops" | 36.8% products blended | S5 |
| iPad and Wearables | $63,709M | 0% | iPad Air and mini higher, Accessories and Wearables lower | 36.8% products blended | S5 |

Pricing power shows up as mix: iPhone revenue rose 22% to $196,515M in the nine months to 2026-06-27, attributed again to higher sales of Pro models rather than to units. The same disclosure prevents separating price from volume, and therefore prevents estimating elasticity — a 22% increase could be volume, price, or any combination. Apple publishes list prices on its own store but not in its filings, and this report did not retrieve a verified 2026 price list, so the table uses disclosed mix effects rather than price points; third-party unit data would settle it [S6].

### The highest-margin layer is also the most litigated

App Store economics are recognised net — Apple books "only the commission it retains" on third-party app sales — so a take-rate cut passes straight to revenue and gross profit with no offsetting cost. Apple is subject to a US court order barring it from charging a commission on certain consumer purchases, though the Ninth Circuit has instructed the district court to amend the injunction to permit one, and in the EU the Digital Markets Act forces alternative distribution, alternative payment processing and new fee structures, a plan the European Commission has challenged. A second concentration sits in the same line: Apple earns licensing revenue from Google for search distribution inside Services advertising, which Apple names as a primary driver of Services growth in both fiscal 2025 and the first nine months of fiscal 2026. The payment was $20bn in 2022 per unsealed court documents, 18.3% of fiscal 2025 Services revenue, and Apple does not disclose the current figure; the District of Columbia court order of 2025-09-02 preserved the ability to pay partners while banning exclusive agreements, but Apple states a reversal on appeal could impose remedies "prohibiting Google from offering the Company commercial terms for search distribution", and both the Department of Justice and Google appealed [S6, S82].

### Cost structure, and what would break the durability

The cost base is bought, not built: product cost of sales of $194,116M goes to TSMC for wafers, to memory suppliers for DRAM and NAND, and to Foxconn and its peers for assembly. Research and development reached $34,035M in the nine months to 2026-06-27, up 33% and 9.3% of revenue against 8.3% in fiscal 2025, on "infrastructure-related costs, including investments in artificial intelligence"; capital expenditure is 2.2% of trailing-twelve-month revenue against 34.9% at Microsoft in fiscal 2026. Apple rents its manufacturing and buys much of its AI capability through the income statement, so that bill reaches the operating margin immediately rather than through depreciation. For investors the implication is that the annuity is intact, but the margin expansion of the last four quarters is not the mix shift it is commonly described as: it is product mix, a tariff refund and memory cost timing, on top of a services base whose most profitable components face an appeal, a court order and a European regulatory process. The downside is quantifiable rather than hypothetical: giving back three points of gross margin and losing the search licence together would take more than a fifth of trailing-twelve-month net income. Three facts would settle the durability question and none is disclosed — the current size of the search payment, the share of Services that is App Store commission, and the refund-versus-mix split; the fiscal 2026 annual report, not on EDGAR as of 2026-10-31, may settle them [S6, S27].

::: evidence
**The service mix still drives Apple's margin, but in fiscal 2026 it stopped being the marginal driver — hardware did, and part of that gain is a refund.**

In the nine months to June 2026 product gross profit grew faster than services gross profit for the first time in three years, and Apple attributes the higher product margin to product mix and tariff refunds rather than to trading gains, in the June 2026 quarterly report.
:::"}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Financial Analysis (financials, revision 5 by Fundamentals Analyst, 8,785 characters)
Apple's cash conversion and balance sheet are as good as the multiple implies, but the earnings growth is not: fiscal 2025's 22.7% EPS growth becomes 10.4% once the $10.2bn Irish State Aid tax charge in the prior year is normalised out, and 2.0 points of the June 2026 quarter's 50.1% gross margin came from tariff refunds rather than trading. The three-year record is slowing revenue and rising margin: revenue fell 2.8% in fiscal 2023, grew 2.0% in fiscal 2024 and 6.4% to $416,161M in fiscal 2025, while gross margin rose from 44.1% to 46.9% and operating margin from 29.8% to 32.0%. The latest filed period is the quarter ended 2026-06-27, where revenue rose 16.4% to $109,417M on gross margin of 50.1% and operating margin of 32.6%. No fourth-quarter fiscal 2026 earnings release and no fiscal 2026 annual report were on EDGAR as of 2026-10-31; Apple's fiscal 2025 equivalents were filed on 2025-10-30 and 2025-10-31, so the annual report is due imminently and the figures here are trailing twelve months to 2026-06-27 [S5, S6, S13].

### The growth is half tax base effect, and a quarter buyback

Fiscal 2025's net income rose 19.5%, but pretax income rose 7.5% ($132,729M against $123,485M) and the tax provision fell 30.3% to $20,719M because fiscal 2024 carried the one-time $10.2bn Irish charge — $15.8bn payable to Ireland, offset by a $4.8bn US foreign tax credit and $823M of released unrecognised benefits. Normalising fiscal 2024 at fiscal 2025's 15.6% rate gives $104,222M and underlying growth of 7.5%, not 19.5%. The EPS gap above that is the buyback: from fiscal 2023 to fiscal 2025 net income grew 15.5% while diluted EPS grew 21.7% and diluted shares fell 5.1%, so 5.4 percentage points of EPS growth was a smaller denominator — and that contribution is fading, at 1.9 percentage points in the trailing twelve months (EPS +16.9% against net income +15.1%), because repurchases slowed to $62,094M in the nine months to 2026-06-27 from $70,579M while operating cash flow rose 43%. Capital return has stopped outrunning cash: buybacks and dividends were $97,866M against free cash flow of $136,683M, or 72%, against 107% in fiscal 2025, and net cash rose by $28,410M in nine months. At the $344.63 close on 2026-10-30 and the 14,594.2M shares issued and outstanding reported on the 10-Q cover at 2026-07-17, equity is worth $5.03trn; on trailing diluted EPS of $8.72 that is 39.5x earnings and a 2.72% free cash flow yield, while the ten-year Treasury yielded 4.93%. Diluted shares of 14,715M are the EPS denominator and sit 0.8% above the outstanding count, so the two bases are consistent. Repurchasing at that spread is accretive to EPS and not obviously accretive to value per share [S5, S6, S9].

### Cash is real; the working-capital cushion is not

Cash generation is the strongest part of the record and the hardest to fake: operating cash flow of $146,724M against capital expenditure of $10,041M, with free cash flow at 1.06x net income. The anomaly is fiscal 2025, when free cash flow fell to 0.88x of net income despite $111,482M of operating cash flow; cash paid for income taxes that year was $43,369M, 32.7% of pretax income against a 15.6% book rate and 21.1% in fiscal 2024 — a gap consistent with settlement payments on the Irish case and the TCJA repatriation tax, the final $8.8bn of which was paid in the nine months to 2026-06-27. That supports reading the gap as timing, and the recovery to 1.06x is consistent with it. The working-capital change runs the other way: inventory reached $11,092M at 2026-06-27 from $5,925M a year earlier, an 87% increase against 16.2% revenue growth, lifting days inventory to 16.9 from 9.4 and pulling the cash conversion cycle to −56.8 days from −71.1 at the fiscal 2025 year-end [S5, S6].

The balance sheet carries no leverage risk: at 2026-06-27 Apple held $146,517M of cash and marketable securities against $84,344M of debt, for net cash of $62,173M, up from $33,763M, with commercial paper cut to $1,997M from $7,979M, and other income and expense netted to −$321M in fiscal 2025 because interest earned on the securities book offsets interest paid. The commitments that matter are forward purchases — $57.0bn of manufacturing purchase obligations, $56.2bn due within twelve months, and $29.3bn of other purchase obligations — which fix component supply and, with it, the cost base when memory prices move. Two accounting details deserve attention: gross intangible assets rose $13,270M to $38,220M in nine months with no goodwill recognised, which indicates purchased intellectual property, content or asset acquisitions rather than share purchases, and is not explained in the quarterly filing; and gross unrecognised tax benefits were $23.2bn at 2025-09-27, of which $10.6bn would affect the effective rate and up to $6bn may move within twelve months [S6].

### Returns are distorted by the buyback, not flattered by the business

Reported returns are not usable as quality scores: return on equity was 148.8% and return on invested capital 320.6% on invested capital of $45,347M — $107,520M of equity plus $84,344M of debt less $146,517M of securities — because $258,212M of cumulative buybacks shrank the equity base. The honest comparison is return on assets of 36.1% against Microsoft's 35.9% return on invested capital in fiscal 2026 and Alphabet's 37.0% in fiscal 2025 [S6, S27, S41].

### What moves the outcome, and by how much

The geographic picture also cuts against the standard bear case: Greater China revenue rose 30% to $64,839M in the nine months to 2026-06-27 and 22% in the June quarter, so nine months already exceed the whole of fiscal 2025's $64,377M after two years of decline. What moves the outcome most is gross margin. On trailing-twelve-month revenue of $466,823M one point of gross margin is $4,668M of pretax profit, or 3.0% of net income, while one point of revenue growth at the current margin is $1,878M, or 1.5%. Three cases, all on the trailing twelve months and none a forecast: a two-point margin gain takes EPS to $9.24, a two-point give-back to $8.20, and a two-point give-back with the loss of the search licence to $7.11, 18.8% below the base — and the licence should be modelled as intact but repriced annually, because the September 2025 order permitted non-exclusive placement payments of one year or less rather than ending them, while the $20bn figure is a 2022 court-record number Apple has never confirmed. The cash is real and the balance sheet is net cash; the growth is weaker than reported; and the margin sits at a cyclical high with a tariff-refund component inside it. An investor paying 39.5x trailing earnings is paying for the first and third to persist while the second is already reversing. The diligence question that matters most is what the fiscal 2026 annual report says about inventory composition and the split between refund and product mix, neither of which the quarterly filings settle [S6, S82, S118].

::: info warning
**The fiscal 2026 gross margin is not yet a clean number.** Strip out the tariff refund Apple attributes to the June quarter and the margin is still above any full year in this record, but a smaller step-change than the reported figure implies; against an inventory build growing faster than revenue, the annual report carries the burden of proof.
:::

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Exit Strategy Analysis (exit, revision 3 by Valuation Analyst, 7,847 characters)
Apple has no takeover exit and no listing event ahead of it. At a $5,029.6B market value the largest technology acquisition on record, Microsoft's $68.7B all-cash purchase of Activision Blizzard agreed on 2022-01-18, equals 1.4% of the company, and any bid would face the US and EU antitrust review that Microsoft's own deal attracted; a leveraged buyout of a $4.97T enterprise value is arithmetically impossible. The exit is a sale into the market, at a $13.84B average daily traded value where a 1% position in a $1B fund is $10M, 0.07% of one day's volume. The exit question is therefore not whether a holder can sell but at what multiple, which makes the sell discipline a set of price bands and thesis breaks rather than an event to wait for. [S9, S169]

Over the last ten completed years the average intra-year peak-to-trough drawdown was 21.4%, lasting 82 days, and four episodes exceeded 30%: 2018 fell 36.73%, 2020 31.43%, 2022 30.75% and 2025 30.22%. Each was recovered, with 2020 returning 80.75% for the calendar year and 2025 8.56%, but each recovery came with a re-rating as well as earnings growth, and a holder buying at 39.5x cannot count on the re-rating half. Apple's policy exposure is not a licence-to-operate threat but a slow, legislated tax on Services gross profit: the €500 million DMA fine of 2025-04-23 and the April 2025 US contempt finding show a company that litigates first and complies later, while the three remedies that matter — Google's default-search payment, the US link-out commission and the EU fee structure — have so far been reshaped rather than removed [S7]. The question for a long-only holder is how much Services gross margin five more years of enforcement takes, and whether the multiple already discounts it.

### The DMA fine is small; the cost structure is not

The Commission fined Apple €500 million on 2025-04-23 for breaching the anti-steering obligation and ordered it to remove restrictions on steering users outside the App Store. The same day it closed the user-choice investigation — a real concession — but issued preliminary findings in the Article 6(4) file on Apple's terms for alternative app marketplaces, where an adverse finding carries fines of up to 10% of annual worldwide net sales [S5]. Two facts bound it: on 2026-02-05 the Commission found Apple Ads and Apple Maps should not be designated, and no further Apple decision appears in its DMA record between the fine and 2026-09-28. Peer fines are serial but modest — Meta €200 million in the same package, Google €890 million on 2026-07-23, Alphabet's €4.1 billion Android fine final only in July 2026 — so repeated fines, not break-up, are the base rate. The implication is a transfer of pricing power from Apple's toll to developers and consumers: because each mandated fee cut reaches Services gross margin before it reaches revenue, fee orders should move the multiple and fine headlines should not.

Europe is Apple's second-largest region and Services drove its FY2025 growth; App Store commission is the highest-margin revenue Apple records, so a mandated fee cut in Brussels is worth more to the equity than any fine. Apple also warns that interoperability obligations force it to open technologies to third parties without charge and have in the past, and may in future, caused it not to launch or maintain features "such as Siri AI" — a product-availability risk, not only a revenue leak.

### A contempt finding, then a slow antitrust case

On 2025-04-30 the Northern District of California found Apple in violation of the 2021 Epic injunction, barred any commission on purchases made outside an app, and referred the company to the US Attorney on criminal contempt. The Ninth Circuit modified that on 2025-12-11 to allow parity rules and some commission on link-out purchases; Apple petitioned the Supreme Court on 2026-05-21, obtained certiorari on 2026-06-30 limited to the civil-contempt standard, and seeks a stay below [S6, S122]. Apple's compliance function tested a court order rather than obeyed it, which raises the severity of the next remedy. That remedy is the DOJ case, filed 2024-03-21 with 16 states and the District of Columbia, seeking equitable relief only; it survived dismissal on 2025-06-30 and is in discovery on a schedule pointing to a 2027 trial. With no damages claimed, the risk is conduct-based — defaults, messaging, app distribution — and lands on the 2027-2029 Services line rather than the balance sheet.

### Google's payment survives, on worse terms

The search-distribution remedy went Apple's way on the point that mattered: the 2025-09-02 decision refused to ban Google's payments to distributors, citing harm to device makers and browser developers, and instead barred exclusive contracts while permitting default-placement payments not conditioned on exclusivity and running one year or less [S118, S42]. A final judgment followed in December 2025; both sides appealed in early 2026 and the appeals were pending at 2026-10-29. Apple does not disclose the payment; the $20 billion-a-year figure is unverified. The revenue survives with annual renewal risk and mandatory choice screens.

### Two bear-case triggers did not fire in 2026

The Section 232 semiconductor investigation's initial results on 2026-01-14 imposed no additional tariff on Apple's products, and on 2026-02-20 the Supreme Court struck down certain IEEPA tariffs, with Apple claiming refunds it recognised as a reduction of products cost of sales; Section 301 tariffs were then imposed. In China the opposite of closure happened: the CAC registered Apple Intelligence on 2026-07-15 with Alibaba's Qwen and Baidu, and Greater China net sales rose 22% to $18,816 million in the June 2026 quarter and 30% to $64,839 million for the nine months, from $49,884 million [S6, S121]. The binding constraint is the calendar: the Busan truce that suppresses tariff and rare-earth escalation was extended on 2026-09-23 from 2026-11-10 to 2027-01-10, making 2027 the next policy cliff.

### Tax is settled; the ESG tail is elsewhere

The Irish state-aid case ended against Apple: the ECJ confirmed the 2016 decision on 2024-09-10, producing a $10.2 billion net one-time charge and $15.8 billion payable to Ireland. The FY2025 effective tax rate of 15.6%, against 24.1% in FY2024, now sits just above the OECD Pillar Two 15% floor, so incremental Pillar Two cost is small and the live tax risk is the $23.2 billion of gross unrecognised benefits, $10.6 billion of which would move the rate if recognised [S5].

On environmental and social issues the record is stronger than the sector's: full third-party audit coverage of identified 3TG smelters for a tenth consecutive year, no finding of armed-group financing, a June 2024 instruction to suppliers to stop sourcing 3TG from the DRC and Rwanda, and recycled-content commitments for cobalt, tin, gold and rare earths. Those claims are company-prepared and unverified here, and the carbon-neutral-2030 target and its Scope 3 progress could not be checked against a published source; that gap is stated, not filled. Governance offsets the conduct record: one class of common stock, an independent Chair separated from the CEO, and an Audit Committee that owns privacy, cybersecurity, tax and enterprise risk. Control is not the issue; compliance culture is.

They support a judgement that policy is a recurring cost to Services gross margin, not a threat to the franchise. Three questions decide the watchlist price: what fee Apple now charges on US link-out purchases after the December 2025 remand and how much spending has moved off in-app purchase; what Apple actually receives from Google at the first one-year renewal; and whether Article 6(4) produces a second EU fine before the General Court rules. None is a reason to avoid Apple; each is a reason to demand a price that assumes some of the loss.

The Company has historically experienced higher net sales in its first quarter compared to other quarters in its fiscal year due in part to seasonal holiday demand. Additionally, new product and service introductions can significantly impact net sales, cost of sales and operating expenses. The timing of product introductions can also impact the Company’s net sales to its indirect distribution channels as these channels are filled with new inventory following a product launch, and channel inventory of an older product often declines as the launch of a newer product approaches. Net sales can also be affected when consumers and distributors anticipate a product introduction.
Beginning in the second quarter of 2025, new tariffs were announced on imports to the U.S., including additional tariffs on imports from China, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam and the European Union (“EU”), among others. In response, several countries have imposed, or threatened to impose, reciprocal tariffs on imports from the U.S. and other retaliatory measures. On January 14, 2026, initial results were published of the previously announced U.S. Department of Commerce investigation under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, as amended, into imports of semiconductors, semiconductor manufacturing equipment, and their derivative products, including downstream products that contain semiconductors. The announcement of the initial results of the investigation did not impose any additional tariffs affecting the Company’s products. Separately, on February 20, 2026, the U.S. Supreme Court (“Supreme Court”) issued a ruling striking down certain tariffs previously imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act of 1977. arguments.markdown:
Apple has no takeover exit and no listing event ahead of it. At a $5,029.6B market value the largest technology acquisition on record, Microsoft's $68.7B all-cash purchase of Activision Blizzard agreed on 2022-01-18, equals 1.4% of the company, and any bid would face the US and EU antitrust review that Microsoft's own deal attracted; a leveraged buyout of a $4.97T enterprise value is arithmetically impossible. The exit is a sale into the market, at a $13.84B average daily traded value where a 1% position in a $1B fund is $10M, 0.07% of one day's volume. The exit question is therefore not whether a holder can sell but at what multiple, which makes the sell discipline a set of price bands and thesis breaks rather than an event to wait for. [S9, S169]

| Exit route | Named buyer or venue | Rationale | Timing | Likelihood | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Open-market sale | NasdaqGS, $13.84B average daily traded value | The only route that absorbs a position without a discount | Any trading day | The route actually used | S9 |
| Strategic acquisition | No named buyer; largest tech deal $68.7B vs $5,029.6B market value | Size, antitrust, no strategic gap Apple fills | Not foreseeable | Very low | S169 |
| Leveraged buyout | None | $4.97T enterprise value and $84.3B of debt cannot be financed | Not foreseeable | Negligible | S6 |
| Company buyback (partial exit) | Apple Inc. | $82.2B repurchased in twelve months; $100B authorised April 2026; 1.6% of shares a year | Ongoing | High but discretionary | S164, S6 |
| Dividend | Apple Inc. | $0.27 a quarter, 0.31% yield, raised annually | Quarterly | Certain while declared | S13 |
| Index and passive flows | S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 constituent | Structural bid, not an exit route | Ongoing | Structural | S163 |

Apple's own record sets the cost of ownership. Over the last ten completed years the average intra-year peak-to-trough drawdown was 21.4%, lasting 82 days, and four episodes exceeded 30%: 2018 fell 36.73%, 2020 31.43%, 2022 30.75% and 2025 30.22%. Each was recovered, with 2020 returning 80.75% for the calendar year and 2025 8.56%, but each recovery came with a re-rating as well as earnings growth, and a holder buying at 39.5x cannot count on the re-rating half. From $344.63 the average drawdown is $271 and a 30% drawdown is $240. On 2026-10-30 Apple was 1.23% below its all-time-high close while the Nasdaq-100 was 9.09% below its own and the S&P 500 3.05%, so the stock enters any correction from relative strength rather than weakness. [S163, S168]

| Precedent episode | Peak | Trough | Drawdown | Days | Equivalent price from $344.63 | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2018 | $58.02 (2018-10-03) | $36.71 (2018-12-24) | -36.73% | 82 | $218 | S163 |
| 2020 | $81.80 (2020-02-12) | $56.09 (2020-03-23) | -31.43% | 40 | $236 | S163 |
| 2022 | $182.01 (2022-01-03) | $126.04 (2022-12-28) | -30.75% | 359 | $239 | S163 |
| 2025 | $247.10 (2025-02-24) | $172.42 (2025-04-08) | -30.22% | 43 | $240 | S163 |
| Ten-year average | - | - | -21.39% | 82 | $271 | S163 |

The multiple, not the remembered share price, is what made past entries work. The 2022 trough of $126.04 on 2022-12-28 was 20.6x fiscal 2022 diluted EPS of $6.11; today's 39.5x is nearly double that, and a repeat of 20x on today's trailing $8.72 would be $174 or $196 on forward $9.79, levels last seen in 2023 and not reached without an earnings recession. That is why the band is set on the forward multiple: 25-30x, the ten-year mean of 25.35x to the five-year average of 30.2x, is $248-296, and the bear case of a two-point gross-margin give-back on $8.20 of EPS at 25x is $205. The fair value in the middle case is not today's price; it is the price at which the multiple stops assuming the re-rating continues. [S163, S2]

| Scenario | EPS assumption | Multiple | Fair value | Versus $344.63 | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bear: gross margin falls two points, tax normalised | $8.20 | 25.0x | $205 | -41% | S6, S154 |
| Base: consensus forward EPS, five-year average multiple | $9.79 | 30.2x | $296 | -14% | S157 |
| Bull: AI cycle holds, multiple at five-year high | $10.50 | 38.0x | $399 | +16% | S157, S156 |

A long-only fund should underwrite a three-to-five-year hold, because that is the period over which the Services annuity and the installed base can compound enough to absorb a de-rating. On forward EPS of $9.79 growing 8% a year to $12.33 by fiscal 2029 and $3.37 of cumulative dividends, the annual total return depends almost entirely on the exit multiple, and the entry price decides whether the fund is paid for waiting. At $344.63 a 25x exit loses 3.3% a year and a 35x exit earns 8.1%; at $296 the same exits earn 1.7% and 13.8%; at $248 they earn 8.0% and 20.8%. The hurdle of 8% a year is met at today's price only if the multiple stays at 35x, which is the top of the five-year range, not its middle. [S157, S154]

| Entry price | Forward P/E | 3-year annual return at exit 25x | At exit 30x | At exit 35x | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $344.63 | 35.2x | -3.3% | +2.7% | +8.1% | S9, S157 |
| $296 | 30.2x | +1.7% | +8.1% | +13.8% | S157, S154 |
| $248 | 25.3x | +8.0% | +14.8% | +20.8% | S154, S6 |

| Sell trigger | Threshold | Action | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Valuation | Forward P/E above 40x (over $395) with no EPS upgrade | Trim to half | S157, S156 |
| Valuation | Forward P/E at or below 25.5x (at or below $250) | Add to full position | S154 |
| Thesis break: Services | Services revenue growth below 5% year on year for two quarters | Sell | S13 |
| Thesis break: margin | Gross margin below 44%, the fiscal 2023 level | Sell | S5 |
| Thesis break: search payment | Payment lost or materially cut at the one-year renewal, or on appeal, without an offsetting services gain | Sell or halve | S118, S42 |
| Thesis break: China | Greater China revenue down 10% year on year | Reassess, then sell | S13 |

The policy tests are narrow for a US holder: no foreign-buyer limit applies to a sale of shares, there is no lock-up, and the listing venue is not in question at NasdaqGS, the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq-100. The binding policy risk sits in the asset, not the exit. The Google search payment, reported at $20B in 2022 and never disclosed by Apple, is on today's base about 17% of trailing Services revenue of $120.5B and 22% of services gross profit of $91.6B, and it survived the D.D.C.'s remedies decision of 2025-09-02: the court refused the DOJ's proposed near-total ban on distribution payments, barring exclusive contracts but permitting default-placement payments not conditioned on exclusivity and running one year or less. Final judgment followed in December 2025, Google appealed in January 2026 and the DOJ and states cross-appealed in February 2026; the appeals were pending at 2026-10-29. The payment therefore continues on non-exclusive, annually renegotiated terms, and the event that would force a sale is its loss or material cut at a renewal or on appeal, not a ban already in force. [S118, S42, S82]

The arithmetic of that event is large enough to size the position around it. Twenty billion dollars of near-pure-margin revenue taxed at 21% is $15.8B of earnings, and capitalised at 30x that is $474B, 9.4% of the $5,029.6B market value; a holder needs that hit to be survivable at the position size chosen today. The slower policy risks are App Store commission rules under the DMA and the DOJ case, and China, where revenue was $64.8B in nine months of fiscal 2026 and can turn on subsidy or geopolitical policy rather than on Apple's execution. Each is a reason the entry multiple matters more than the policy calendar: at 39.5x there is no cushion for a Services margin shock. [S13]

The strongest case against this discipline is that a 30x-plus multiple never offers a margin of safety again. If Services compounds at 14% on a 76% gross margin and the buyback retires 1.6% of the shares a year, a fund that waits for $250 may simply never own the best cash generator in the market, and the cost of the discipline is opportunity rather than loss. The answer is a time rule rather than a permanent price target: if Apple trades above $296 for four consecutive quarters while Services growth stays above 10%, reassess the band against the then-current multiple instead of waiting for a level the business has outgrown. Until then, watchlist above $300, a first tranche at $275-296, and a full position at or below $250. Confidence is high in the drawdown record and the return arithmetic, medium in the multiple at which a future buyer will pay, because that depends on the ten-year yield, which was 4.93% on 2026-10-30. The diligence questions are the exit terms of the Google payment, the durability of the 50.1% June-quarter gross margin without the tariff refund, and whether the buyback is re-authorised at $100B in 2027. [S154, S157]

The fastest-growing pool Apple monetises is Services, but its share of revenue fell in FY2026: $91.7 billion in the first nine months, 25.2% of $364.4 billion and up 14%, at a 76.3% gross margin against 75.4% for FY2025, when Services was $109.2 billion, 26.2% of revenue. Hardware grew faster than Services, so the mix shifted toward premium handsets and China rather than toward the recurring pool — the opposite of what a Services-led thesis needs. The app economy itself has no published size in the sources retrieved: neither Apple nor the platform owners disclose app-store gross billings or mobile-advertising revenue, so Apple's Services line is the measured pool. The installed base is disclosed: Apple put it at more than 2.5 billion active devices on 2026-04-20, which is the stock behind Services and the upgrade pool, but Apple still does not publish a replacement rate, so upgrade timing cannot be sized from public data. [S5, S6, S174]

### Who pays, and how much demand is policy

The budget owner is the consumer, in a discretionary purchase that is increasingly financed. In the United States and United Kingdom interest-free financing is more prevalent, so IDC expects the premium end to hold while emerging markets fall more than 20%; in India brands lean on financing after the sub-$100 tier fell 59% and the $600-800 band grew 32%; in China the government subsidy that supported earlier quarters faded in the second quarter of 2026, so demand there is being withdrawn by policy rather than created by it. Policy moves Apple's margin more than a product cycle does: after the February 20, 2026 Supreme Court ruling struck down certain IEEPA tariffs, Apple recognised refunds as a reduction of product cost of sales, and those refunds contributed 2.0 percentage points of the June 2026 quarter's 50.1% gross margin. [S105, S40, S13]

### What would break the premiumisation case

Counter-evidence is fourfold. If memory prices normalise in 2028 as IDC expects, the entry tier rebuilds and Apple's 2026 share gain is contestable again. If China's June-quarter demand was pulled forward ahead of second-half price increases, as IDC's China team reports, the 30% growth line is a launch and currency effect. If courts and the European Commission remove the App Store take rate, the margin layer that offsets hardware cyclicality stops compounding. The investor implication is narrow: in a 1-billion-unit market Apple can grow revenue only if price rises faster than units fall, making average selling price, China durability and the Services take rate the variables worth monitoring. Sizing confidence is high, because two independent methods agree within 5%; confidence that the mix shift holds to 2028 is medium, because it rests on China and a legally contested commission. Three questions would close the gap: what share of Services revenue is commission-based rather than subscription, advertising or licensing; how much of the Greater China increase is currency; and what the current average replacement cycle is, measured rather than asserted. arguments.markdown:
Apple has no takeover exit and no listing event ahead of it. At a $5,029.6B market value the largest technology acquisition on record, Microsoft's $68.7B all-cash purchase of Activision Blizzard agreed on 2022-01-18, equals 1.4% of the company, and any bid would face the US and EU antitrust review that Microsoft's own deal attracted; a leveraged buyout of a $4.97T enterprise value is arithmetically impossible. The exit is a sale into the market, at a $13.84B average daily traded value where a 1% position in a $1B fund is $10M, 0.07% of one day's volume. The exit question is therefore not whether a holder can sell but at what multiple, which makes the sell discipline a set of price bands and thesis breaks rather than an event to wait for. [S9, S169]

| Exit route | Named buyer or venue | Rationale | Timing | Likelihood | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Open-market sale | NasdaqGS, $13.84B average daily traded value | The only route that absorbs a position without a discount | Any trading day | The route actually used | S9 |
| Strategic acquisition | No named buyer; largest tech deal $68.7B vs $5,029.6B market value | Size, antitrust, no strategic gap Apple fills | Not foreseeable | Very low | S169 |
| Leveraged buyout | None | $4.97T enterprise value and $84.3B of debt cannot be financed | Not foreseeable | Negligible | S6 |
| Company buyback (partial exit) | Apple Inc. | $82.2B repurchased in twelve months; $100B authorised April 2026; 1.6% of shares a year | Ongoing | High but discretionary | S164, S6 |
| Dividend | Apple Inc. | $0.27 a quarter, 0.31% yield, raised annually | Quarterly | Certain while declared | S13 |
| Index and passive flows | S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 constituent | Structural bid, not an exit route | Ongoing | Structural | S163 |

Apple's own record sets the cost of ownership. Over the last ten completed years the average intra-year peak-to-trough drawdown was 21.4%, lasting 82 days, and four episodes exceeded 30%: 2018 fell 36.73%, 2020 31.43%, 2022 30.75% and 2025 30.22%. Each was recovered, with 2020 returning 80.75% for the calendar year and 2025 8.56%, but each recovery came with a re-rating as well as earnings growth, and a holder buying at 39.5x cannot count on the re-rating half. From $344.63 the average drawdown is $271 and a 30% drawdown is $240. On 2026-10-30 Apple was 1.23% below its all-time-high close while the Nasdaq-100 was 9.09% below its own and the S&P 500 3.05%, so the stock enters any correction from relative strength rather than weakness. [S163, S168]

| Precedent episode | Peak | Trough | Drawdown | Days | Equivalent price from $344.63 | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2018 | $58.02 (2018-10-03) | $36.71 (2018-12-24) | -36.73% | 82 | $218 | S163 |
| 2020 | $81.80 (2020-02-12) | $56.09 (2020-03-23) | -31.43% | 40 | $236 | S163 |
| 2022 | $182.01 (2022-01-03) | $126.04 (2022-12-28) | -30.75% | 359 | $239 | S163 |
| 2025 | $247.10 (2025-02-24) | $172.42 (2025-04-08) | -30.22% | 43 | $240 | S163 |
| Ten-year average | - | - | -21.39% | 82 | $271 | S163 |

The multiple, not the remembered share price, is what made past entries work. The 2022 trough of $126.04 on 2022-12-28 was 20.6x fiscal 2022 diluted EPS of $6.11; today's 39.5x is nearly double that, and a repeat of 20x on today's trailing $8.72 would be $174 or $196 on forward $9.79, levels last seen in 2023 and not reached without an earnings recession. That is why the band is set on the forward multiple: 25-30x, the ten-year mean of 25.35x to the five-year average of 30.2x, is $248-296, and the bear case of a two-point gross-margin give-back on $8.20 of EPS at 25x is $205. The fair value in the middle case is not today's price; it is the price at which the multiple stops assuming the re-rating continues. [S163, S2]

| Scenario | EPS assumption | Multiple | Fair value | Versus $344.63 | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bear: gross margin falls two points, tax normalised | $8.20 | 25.0x | $205 | -41% | S6, S154 |
| Base: consensus forward EPS, five-year average multiple | $9.79 | 30.2x | $296 | -14% | S157 |
| Bull: AI cycle holds, multiple at five-year high | $10.50 | 38.0x | $399 | +16% | S157, S156 |

A long-only fund should underwrite a three-to-five-year hold, because that is the period over which the Services annuity and the installed base can compound enough to absorb a de-rating. On forward EPS of $9.79 growing 8% a year to $12.33 by fiscal 2029 and $3.37 of cumulative dividends, the annual total return depends almost entirely on the exit multiple, and the entry price decides whether the fund is paid for waiting. At $344.63 a 25x exit loses 3.3% a year and a 35x exit earns 8.1%; at $296 the same exits earn 1.7% and 13.8%; at $248 they earn 8.0% and 20.8%. The hurdle of 8% a year is met at today's price only if the multiple stays at 35x, which is the top of the five-year range, not its middle. [S157, S154]

| $344.63 | 35.2x | -3.3% | +2.7% | +8.1% | S9, S157 |

| $248 | 25.3x | +8.0% | +14.8% | +20.8% | S154, S6 |

| Valuation | Forward P/E at or below 25.5x (at or below $250) | Add to full position | S154 |
| Thesis break: Services | Services revenue growth below 5% year on year for two quarters | Sell | S13 |
| Thesis break: margin | Gross margin below 44%, the fiscal 2023 level | Sell | S5 |
| Thesis break: search payment | Payment lost or materially cut at the one-year renewal, or on appeal, without an offsetting services gain | Sell or halve | S118, S42 |
| Thesis break: China | Greater China revenue down 10% year on year | Reassess, then sell | S13 |

The policy tests are narrow for a US holder: no foreign-buyer limit applies to a sale of shares, there is no lock-up, and the listing venue is not in question at NasdaqGS, the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq-100. The binding policy risk sits in the asset, not the exit. The Google search payment, reported at $20B in 2022 and never disclosed by Apple, is on today's base about 17% of trailing Services revenue of $120.5B and 22% of services gross profit of $91.6B, and it survived the D.D.C.'s remedies decision of 2025-09-02: the court refused the DOJ's proposed near-total ban on distribution payments, barring exclusive contracts but permitting default-placement payments not conditioned on exclusivity and running one year or less. Final judgment followed in December 2025, Google appealed in January 2026 and the DOJ and states cross-appealed in February 2026; the appeals were pending at 2026-10-29. The payment therefore continues on non-exclusive, annually renegotiated terms, and the event that would force a sale is its loss or material cut at a renewal or on appeal, not a ban already in force. ### The growth is half tax base effect, and a quarter buyback

Fiscal 2025's net income rose 19.5%, but pretax income rose 7.5% ($132,729M against $123,485M) and the tax provision fell 30.3% to $20,719M because fiscal 2024 carried the one-time $10.2bn Irish charge — $15.8bn payable to Ireland, offset by a $4.8bn US foreign tax credit and $823M of released unrecognised benefits. Normalising fiscal 2024 at fiscal 2025's 15.6% rate gives $104,222M and underlying growth of 7.5%, not 19.5%. The EPS gap above that is the buyback: from fiscal 2023 to fiscal 2025 net income grew 15.5% while diluted EPS grew 21.7% and diluted shares fell 5.1%, so 5.4 percentage points of EPS growth was a smaller denominator — and that contribution is fading, at 1.9 percentage points in the trailing twelve months (EPS +16.9% against net income +15.1%), because repurchases slowed to $62,094M in the nine months to 2026-06-27 from $70,579M while operating cash flow rose 43%. Capital return has stopped outrunning cash: buybacks and dividends were $97,866M against free cash flow of $136,683M, or 72%, against 107% in fiscal 2025, and net cash rose by $28,410M in nine months. At the $344.63 close on 2026-10-30 and the 14,594.2M shares issued and outstanding reported on the 10-Q cover at 2026-07-17, equity is worth $5.03trn; on trailing diluted EPS of $8.72 that is 39.5x earnings and a 2.72% free cash flow yield, while the ten-year Treasury yielded 4.93%. Diluted shares of 14,715M are the EPS denominator and sit 0.8% above the outstanding count, so the two bases are consistent. Repurchasing at that spread is accretive to EPS and not obviously accretive to value per share [S5, S6, S9].

### Cash is real; the working-capital cushion is not

Cash generation is the strongest part of the record and the hardest to fake: operating cash flow of $146,724M against capital expenditure of $10,041M, with free cash flow at 1.06x net income. The anomaly is fiscal 2025, when free cash flow fell to 0.88x of net income despite $111,482M of operating cash flow; cash paid for income taxes that year was $43,369M, 32.7% of pretax income against a 15.6% book rate and 21.1% in fiscal 2024 — a gap consistent with settlement payments on the Irish case and the TCJA repatriation tax, the final $8.8bn of which was paid in the nine months to 2026-06-27. That supports reading the gap as timing, and the recovery to 1.06x is consistent with it. The working-capital change runs the other way: inventory reached $11,092M at 2026-06-27 from $5,925M a year earlier, an 87% increase against 16.2% revenue growth, lifting days inventory to 16.9 from 9.4 and pulling the cash conversion cycle to −56.8 days from −71.1 at the fiscal 2025 year-end [S5, S6].

The balance sheet carries no leverage risk: at 2026-06-27 Apple held $146,517M of cash and marketable securities against $84,344M of debt, for net cash of $62,173M, up from $33,763M, with commercial paper cut to $1,997M from $7,979M, and other income and expense netted to −$321M in fiscal 2025 because interest earned on the securities book offsets interest paid. The commitments that matter are forward purchases — $57.0bn of manufacturing purchase obligations, $56.2bn due within twelve months, and $29.3bn of other purchase obligations — which fix component supply and, with it, the cost base when memory prices move. Two accounting details deserve attention: gross intangible assets rose $13,270M to $38,220M in nine months with no goodwill recognised, which indicates purchased intellectual property, content or asset acquisitions rather than share purchases, and is not explained in the quarterly filing; and gross unrecognised tax benefits were $23.2bn at 2025-09-27, of which $10.6bn would affect the effective rate and up to $6bn may move within twelve months [S6].

Reported returns are not usable as quality scores: return on equity was 148.8% and return on invested capital 320.6% on invested capital of $45,347M — $107,520M of equity plus $84,344M of debt less $146,517M of securities — because $258,212M of cumulative buybacks shrank the equity base. The honest comparison is return on assets of 36.1% against Microsoft's 35.9% return on invested capital in fiscal 2026 and Alphabet's 37.0% in fiscal 2025 [S6, S27, S41].

### What moves the outcome, and by how much

The geographic picture also cuts against the standard bear case: Greater China revenue rose 30% to $64,839M in the nine months to 2026-06-27 and 22% in the June quarter, so nine months already exceed the whole of fiscal 2025's $64,377M after two years of decline. What moves the outcome most is gross margin. On trailing-twelve-month revenue of $466,823M one point of gross margin is $4,668M of pretax profit, or 3.0% of net income, while one point of revenue growth at the current margin is $1,878M, or 1.5%. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Business Model (business_model, revision 3 by Fundamentals Analyst, 8,460 characters)
Apple runs a hardware annuity with a services margin layered on top — 73 cents of services gross profit for every dollar of product gross profit — but the mix shift the multiple pays for stalled in fiscal 2026, when hardware margins, helped by tariff refunds, grew gross profit faster than Services. Apple sells through two routes, and the split is the least-discussed fact in the model: in fiscal 2025, 40% of net sales went through its own stores, online store and direct sales force and 60% through carriers, resellers and distributors. The carrier finances or subsidises the handset to win a contract, so the carrier bears the acquisition cost and Apple's selling expense stays at $27,601M, or 6.6% of revenue. There is little contracted backlog: deferred revenue was $13.7bn at 2025-09-27, 3.3% of revenue, two thirds of it recognised within a year. Apple is a repeat-purchase business recognised as it bills, not a subscription business with a book of contracted revenue [S5].

### The mix shift, and its reversal

The arithmetic of the mix shift is the strongest part of the case. In fiscal 2025 Services produced $109,158M of revenue at a 75.4% gross margin against $307,003M of Products at 36.8%: 26.2% of revenue but 42.2% of gross profit ($82,314M of $195,201M), up from 35.7% two years earlier, with services gross profit per dollar of product gross profit rising from $0.55 in fiscal 2023 to $0.73. Then the mechanism ran backwards. In the nine months to 2026-06-27 product gross profit rose 26.3% to $108,819M while services gross profit rose 15.3% to $69,963M, and Services fell to 39.1% of gross profit; product gross margin reached 39.9% against 36.9% a year earlier, taking total gross margin to 49.1% and to 50.1% in the June quarter against 46.5%. Apple attributes the gain to "a different mix of products and tariff refunds, partially offset by higher costs, including memory", the most consequential disclosure in this section: it makes fiscal 2026's margin hardware-led and partly a refund rather than a trading gain [S5, S6].

### Unit economics per revenue dollar, because there are no units

Apple discloses no unit volumes, average selling price or installed-base figure, so a per-device waterfall cannot be built from primary evidence. The economics of each revenue dollar can be.

| Unit-economics line | FY2025 | 9M FY2026 | Evidence and status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Product cost of sales, per $1,000 of product revenue | $632 | $601 | Bill of materials, assembly and warranty provision combined, not split | S5, S6 |
| Product gross profit | $368 | $399 | 36.8% to 39.9%; includes tariff refunds in fiscal 2026 | S5, S6 |
| Services cost of sales, per $1,000 of services revenue | $246 | $237 | Content, hosting and payment processing | S5, S6 |
| Services gross profit | $754 | $763 | 75.4% to 76.3% | S5, S6 |
| Services gross profit per $1 of product gross profit | $0.73 | $0.64 | Closest disclosed proxy for lifetime value against acquisition cost | S5, S6 |
| Customer acquisition cost, support and warranty | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Carriers bear acquisition; warranty sits inside cost of sales | S5 |
| LTV, LTV:CAC, CAC payback in months | Not computable | Not computable | Requires units, ASP and installed base, none of which Apple reports | S5 |

Apple therefore has no payback period to wait out: a device is gross-profit-positive on delivery at a 36.8% product margin, and the services stream that follows is nearly all incremental, since services cost of sales is $26,844M on $109,158M of revenue. The nearest disclosed proxy for lifetime value against acquisition cost is the $0.73 of services gross profit per dollar of product gross profit, and its fall to $0.64 is the number to watch — the annuity still grows, but no longer faster than the hardware that creates it [S5, S6].

### Pricing power shows up as mix, not as price

| Line | FY2025 net sales | Year on year | What the filing discloses about price and mix | Gross margin | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone | $209,586M | +4% | Growth "due to higher net sales of Pro models", i.e. mix rather than units | 36.8% products blended | S5 |
| Services | $109,158M | +14% | "advertising, the App Store and cloud services" | 75.4% | S5 |
| Mac | $33,708M | +12% | "laptops and desktops" | 36.8% products blended | S5 |
| iPad and Wearables | $63,709M | 0% | iPad Air and mini higher, Accessories and Wearables lower | 36.8% products blended | S5 |

Pricing power shows up as mix: iPhone revenue rose 22% to $196,515M in the nine months to 2026-06-27, attributed again to higher sales of Pro models rather than to units. The same disclosure prevents separating price from volume, and therefore prevents estimating elasticity — a 22% increase could be volume, price, or any combination. Apple publishes list prices on its own store but not in its filings, and this report did not retrieve a verified 2026 price list, so the table uses disclosed mix effects rather than price points; third-party unit data would settle it [S6].

### The highest-margin layer is also the most litigated

App Store economics are recognised net — Apple books "only the commission it retains" on third-party app sales — so a take-rate cut passes straight to revenue and gross profit with no offsetting cost. Apple is subject to a US court order barring it from charging a commission on certain consumer purchases, though the Ninth Circuit has instructed the district court to amend the injunction to permit one, and in the EU the Digital Markets Act forces alternative distribution, alternative payment processing and new fee structures, a plan the European Commission has challenged. A second concentration sits in the same line: Apple earns licensing revenue from Google for search distribution inside Services advertising, which Apple names as a primary driver of Services growth in both fiscal 2025 and the first nine months of fiscal 2026. The payment was $20bn in 2022 per unsealed court documents, 18.3% of fiscal 2025 Services revenue, and Apple does not disclose the current figure; the District of Columbia court order of 2025-09-02 preserved the ability to pay partners while banning exclusive agreements, but Apple states a reversal on appeal could impose remedies "prohibiting Google from offering the Company commercial terms for search distribution", and both the Department of Justice and Google appealed [S6, S82].

### Cost structure, and what would break the durability

The cost base is bought, not built: product cost of sales of $194,116M goes to TSMC for wafers, to memory suppliers for DRAM and NAND, and to Foxconn and its peers for assembly. Research and development reached $34,035M in the nine months to 2026-06-27, up 33% and 9.3% of revenue against 8.3% in fiscal 2025, on "infrastructure-related costs, including investments in artificial intelligence"; capital expenditure is 2.2% of trailing-twelve-month revenue against 34.9% at Microsoft in fiscal 2026. Apple rents its manufacturing and buys much of its AI capability through the income statement, so that bill reaches the operating margin immediately rather than through depreciation. For investors the implication is that the annuity is intact, but the margin expansion of the last four quarters is not the mix shift it is commonly described as: it is product mix, a tariff refund and memory cost timing, on top of a services base whose most profitable components face an appeal, a court order and a European regulatory process. The downside is quantifiable rather than hypothetical: giving back three points of gross margin and losing the search licence together would take more than a fifth of trailing-twelve-month net income. Three facts would settle the durability question and none is disclosed — the current size of the search payment, the share of Services that is App Store commission, and the refund-versus-mix split; the fiscal 2026 annual report, not on EDGAR as of 2026-10-31, may settle them [S6, S27].

::: evidence
**The service mix still drives Apple's margin, but in fiscal 2026 it stopped being the marginal driver — hardware did, and part of that gain is a refund.**

In the nine months to June 2026 product gross profit grew faster than services gross profit for the first time in three years, and Apple attributes the higher product margin to product mix and tariff refunds rather than to trading gains, in the June 2026 quarterly report.
:::"}],"isError":false}
