### Pricing power shows up as mix, not as price

| Line | FY2025 net sales | Year on year | What the filing discloses about price and mix | Gross margin | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone | $209,586M | +4% | Growth "due to higher net sales of Pro models", i.e. mix rather than units | 36.8% products blended | S5 |
| Services | $109,158M | +14% | "advertising, the App Store and cloud services" | 75.4% | S5 |
| Mac | $33,708M | +12% | "laptops and desktops" | 36.8% products blended | S5 |
| iPad and Wearables | $63,709M | 0% | iPad Air and mini higher, Accessories and Wearables lower | 36.8% products blended | S5 |

iPhone revenue rose 22% to $196,515M in the nine months to 2026-06-27, again "due to higher net sales of Pro models", so pricing power arrives as mix rather than as price. The same disclosure prevents separating price from volume and therefore prevents estimating elasticity: a 22% increase could be volume, price or any combination. Apple publishes list prices on its own store but not in its filings, and no verified 2026 price list was retrieved, so the table uses disclosed mix effects; third-party unit data would settle it [S6].

### The highest-margin layer is also the most litigated

App Store economics are recognised net — Apple books "only the commission it retains" on third-party app sales — so a take-rate cut passes straight to revenue and gross profit with no offsetting cost. Apple is subject to a US court order barring it from charging a commission on certain consumer purchases, though the Ninth Circuit has instructed the district court to amend the injunction to permit one, and in the EU the Digital Markets Act forces alternative distribution, alternative payment processing and new fee structures, a plan the European Commission has challenged. A second concentration sits in the same line: Apple earns licensing revenue from Google for search distribution inside Services advertising, which Apple names as a primary driver of Services growth in both fiscal 2025 and the first nine months of fiscal 2026. The payment was $20bn in 2022 per unsealed court documents, 18.3% of fiscal 2025 Services revenue, and Apple does not disclose the current figure; the District of Columbia court order of 2025-09-02 preserved the ability to pay partners while banning exclusive agreements, but Apple states a reversal on appeal could impose remedies "prohibiting Google from offering the Company commercial terms for search distribution", and both the Department of Justice and Google appealed [S6, S82].

### Cost structure, and what would break the durability

The cost base is bought, not built: product cost of sales of $194,116M goes to TSMC for wafers, to memory suppliers for DRAM and NAND, and to Foxconn and its peers for assembly. Research and development reached $34,035M in the nine months to 2026-06-27, up 33% and 9.3% of revenue against 8.3% in fiscal 2025, on "infrastructure-related costs, including investments in artificial intelligence"; capital expenditure is 2.2% of trailing-twelve-month revenue against 34.9% at Microsoft in fiscal 2026. Apple rents its manufacturing and buys much of its AI capability through the income statement, so that bill reaches the operating margin immediately rather than through depreciation. What remains is a disclosure gap rather than a modelled one: Apple reports the 60% indirect share, the carrier receivable and the fact that price protection and other incentive programmes reduce Products net sales, but not the carrier-only share of net sales, the wholesale discount, the subsidy per device or the reseller-support spend inside SG&A; carrier 10-K equipment-revenue and promotional lines, or paid channel sell-in data, would settle them, and one point of wholesale terms across the indirect channel is $2.5bn of revenue, 1.3% of fiscal 2025 gross profit. The annuity is intact, but the margin expansion of the last four quarters is not the mix shift it is commonly described as: it is product mix, a tariff refund and memory cost timing, on top of a services base whose most profitable components face an appeal, a court order and a European regulatory process. Giving back three points of gross margin and losing the search licence together would take more than a fifth of trailing-twelve-month net income. Three facts would settle durability and none is disclosed — the current size of the search payment, the share of Services that is App Store commission, and the refund-versus-mix split; the fiscal 2026 annual report, not on EDGAR as of 2026-10-31, may settle them [S6, S27].

::: evidence
**The service mix still drives Apple's margin, but in fiscal 2026 it stopped being the marginal driver — hardware did, and part of that gain is a refund.**

In the nine months to June 2026 product gross profit grew faster than services gross profit for the first time in three years, and Apple attributes the higher product margin to product mix and tariff refunds rather than to trading gains. The installed base the annuity rests on grew more slowly than revenue over the past year, so the next leg depends on revenue per device rather than on more devices.
:::

arguments.title: IFI CLAIMS: AI Patents Break 100,000 Grants Milestone (28 July 2026)
arguments.claims: Worldwide AI patent grants reached 107,279 in 2025, up 83% on three years earlier. 2025 AI filings: Samsung 2,162 worldwide (682 US), Huawei 1,822, Google 1,672; US filings Samsung 682, Google 671, Microsoft 585. Apple is absent from the cited top-three AI applicant rankings. Establishes a peer base rate for AI patenting against which Apple's portfolio can be benchmarked.
arguments.claims_weakened: Weakens any claim that Apple leads AI IP; does not measure granted families, only filings in AI, and does not report an Apple-specific count.

arguments.title: IFI Claims 2025 US patent grants ranking, reported by United Daily News / jcpatent (14 January 2026)
arguments.claims: 2025 US patent grants: Samsung Electronics 7,054 (first, fourth consecutive year), TSMC 4,194 (second), Qualcomm third, Huawei 3,052 (fourth), Apple 2,722 (sixth, down 11.6% from 3,082 in 2024). Total US grants 323,272 in 2025, down 0.2%; applications down 8.6% to 393,344.
arguments.claims_weakened: A secondary-language report of IFI data; counts granted US patents, not families, so it is a proxy for portfolio breadth only and says nothing about AI, health, foldable or AR sub-portfolios.

arguments.title: Intel to Acquire Infineon's Wireless Solutions Business (30 August 2010)
arguments.claims: Intel agreed to buy Infineon's Wireless Solutions (WLS) cellular business for approximately $1.4bn cash, expected to close in Q1 2011, to add 3G/LTE modem capability to its phone and tablet platforms. Dated start of Intel's phone-modem attempt.
arguments.claims_weakened: Shows a well-funded entrant entering baseband with an acquisition rather than a clean-sheet team, which is the relevant replication route.

arguments.title: Intel Completes Sale of Smartphone Modem Business to Apple (2 December 2019)
arguments.claims: Intel completed the sale of its smartphone modem business to Apple for $1bn, announced 2019-07-25, exiting phone modems roughly nine years after buying Infineon's WLS unit (closed Q1 2011).
arguments.claims_weakened: Undermines a four-to-five-year replication assumption for a phone-modem business by a well-capitalised new entrant.

arguments.title: Apple to acquire the majority of Intel's smartphone modem business (25 July 2019)
arguments.claims: Apple agreed to buy the majority of Intel's smartphone modem business, about 2,200 employees and IP that would take Apple's wireless patent portfolio to over 17,000 patents, for $1bn, closing Q4 2019.
arguments.claims_weakened: Establishes that Apple's in-house modem began from acquired staff and patents, not organic development, so the C1 timeline measures integration, not clean-sheet design.

arguments.title: Android Authority: Why is the entire Galaxy S25 series powered by the Snapdragon 8 Elite? (26 January 2025)
arguments.claims: Every Galaxy S25 model shipped on Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Elite in 2025, with no Exynos variant, after Samsung's 4nm yield problems; Galaxy S23 was also all-Snapdragon in 2023; Samsung retired its Mongoose custom CPU cores in 2020 after middling efficiency results. Base rate for how long a foundry-owning OEM takes to reach parity in phone silicon.
arguments.claims_weakened: Reduces the credibility of a four-to-five-year replication estimate for a phone-class SoC by a funded team, and shows that vertical integration alone does not close the gap.

rows.finding: FY2025 EX-21 lists 19 subsidiaries including three Irish entities (Apple Operations International, Apple Operations Limited, Apple Distribution International); Apple Sales International and Apple Operations Europe, the entities named in the 2016 Commission decision, are absent. Foreign pretax earnings were $82.0bn of $132.7bn (61.8%) in FY2025; the effective tax rate was 15.6%.
rows.mechanism: Profit booked outside the U.S. at 5.4pp below the 21% statutory rate raises after-tax cash flow, but entity-level profit is undisclosed, so the durability of the tax structure cannot be tested from the filings.
rows.benchmark: U.S. statutory rate 21%; Apple's own effective rate 14.7% FY2023, 24.1% FY2024 (state-aid charge), 15.6% FY2025.
rows.weakens: The 10-K gives no entity-level income, ownership percentages or transfer-pricing detail; EX-21 omits subsidiaries that are not significant.
rows.implication: Do not capitalise the 15.6% rate as permanent; require the Irish CRO accounts and transfer-pricing disclosure before underwriting it.
rows.confidence: medium: filing facts high, role of each Irish entity inferred from the pre-2015 structure.
rows.follow_up: Which entity books non-U.S. profit, and what effective rate applies under Pillar Two from FY2026?

rows.finding: EC state-aid decision 2016-08-30 (up to €13bn); General Court annulled it 2020-07-15; the ECJ set that aside and confirmed the decision 2024-09-10; Apple recorded a $10.2bn net Q4 FY2024 charge, paying $15.8bn to Ireland by releasing escrow, offset by a $4.8bn U.S. foreign tax credit and $823m of unrecognised tax benefits.
rows.mechanism: A retroactive liability equal to 11.9% of one year's pretax income shows tax rulings can be clawed back with interest, raising the discount rate applied to non-U.S. profit.
rows.benchmark: FY2025 pretax income $132.7bn; the $15.8bn recovery equals 11.9% of it.
rows.weakens: Ireland changed its law effective January 2015, eliminating the tax opinions; no comparable live case is disclosed.
rows.implication: Price a policy tail on the tax rate; the legal precedent is now settled against the company.
rows.confidence: high: dates and amounts from the 10-K.
rows.follow_up: Is any Pillar Two top-up tax or new EU transfer-pricing challenge outstanding?

rows.finding: 14,594,180,000 shares outstanding at 2026-07-17 versus 14,697,926,000 at 2026-01-02; 215m shares repurchased for $61.8bn in the nine months to 2026-06-27 versus $70.6bn in the prior-year period. Two successive $100bn repurchase programmes were authorised: 2025-05-01 (8-K filed that day) and 2026-04-30 (8-K filed that day, announced with Q2 FY2026 results), each described as an additional programme. Cash and securities of $146.5bn against $84.3bn of debt gives about $62.2bn net cash at 2026-06-27; market capitalisation $5.03tn on 2026-10-30.
rows.mechanism: Buybacks shrink the count about 0.7% in 6.5 months, but the dollar pace fell 12% year on year as the share price rose, so repurchase price discipline matters more at a $5tn capitalisation.
rows.benchmark: Nine-month FY2025 repurchases $70.6bn; 215m shares equal about 1.5% of the count in nine months.
rows.weakens: The company discloses no intrinsic-value estimate; buybacks can still be EPS-accretive even at high prices. The 10-Q does not state remaining capacity under either authorisation.
rows.implication: Treat capital allocation, not liquidity, as the balance-sheet risk at 2026 prices; track average repurchase price and remaining authority.
rows.confidence: high on figures and authorisation dates (8-K primary text); medium on the capital-allocation judgement.
rows.follow_up: What average price did Apple pay in FY2026, and how much of the two $100bn authorisations remains unspent?

plan.decision_question: Is Apple's corporate, ownership and capital structure as clean and shareholder-aligned as the equity story assumes?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple's structure is clean in law — one share class, a majority-independent board and net cash — but not in economics: 61.8% of pretax profit is booked outside the U.S. at a 15.6% effective rate, insiders own 0.06%, and the same director has chaired the board since 2000, so 'alignment' rests on pay design and a tax structure the EU has already litigated once.
plan.why_different: Other sections price the business, market and product; this one audits the container — which entities hold the profit, who controls the votes, and how capital is returned.
plan.mechanism: The legal and tax structure sets after-tax cash flow and policy tail risk; the ownership and board structure determines whose interests capital allocation serves.
plan.comparison_set: Apple's own 2023-2025 effective tax rates, FY2025 versus FY2026 buyback pace, and the Nasdaq majority-independent board rule.
plan.counter_evidence: The tax structure survived the ECJ in 2024; Cook's 3.28m shares make his alignment material; buybacks and services have compounded per-share value for a decade.
plan.visual: kpi table, 15-row timeline and legal-entity table
plan.prohibited: clean structure, shareholder-aligned without evidence, huge, strong, well positioned, many

arguments.markdown:
Apple runs a hardware annuity with a services margin on top — 73 cents of services gross profit per dollar of product gross profit — but the mix shift the multiple pays for stalled in fiscal 2026, when hardware margins, helped by tariff refunds, grew gross profit faster than Services. In fiscal 2025, 40% of net sales went through Apple's own stores and direct sales force and 60%, or $249,697M of $416,161M, through carriers, resellers and distributors. The carrier finances or subsidises the handset, so it bears the acquisition cost and Apple's selling expense stays at $27,601M, or 6.6% of revenue; the dependency is contractual, not permanent, because Apple's risk factor says resellers offer financing, installment plans or subsidies that "may be discontinued or modified any time." The balance-sheet footprint is smaller: carriers were 27% of trade receivables at 2026-06-27, $8,477M of $31,398M, down from 34% of $39,777M at 2025-09-27 [S5, S6].

### The installed base, and what $187 a device does not say

Apple reported more than 2.5 billion active devices on 2026-01-29, against more than 2.35 billion a year earlier, and repeated the figure in its 2026-04-20 succession release; the count is company-reported, not audited. Divided into $466,823M of trailing-twelve-month revenue to 2026-06-27 it gives at most $187 of revenue per active device a year, a ceiling because the denominator is a floor. On fiscal 2025 revenue and Services the same arithmetic gives $166 and $44, so Services are about a quarter of revenue per device, and the base grew roughly 6% while nine-month revenue grew 16.2%. The metric does not capture users rather than devices, the gap between a Pro iPhone and AirPods, first-time buyers, regional pricing or services attach, and it divides a trailing year by a count four months older [S150, S191, S5, S6].

### The mix shift, and its reversal

In fiscal 2025 Services produced $109,158M of revenue at a 75.4% gross margin against $307,003M of Products at 36.8%: 26.2% of revenue but 42.2% of gross profit ($82,314M of $195,201M), up from 35.7% two years earlier, with services gross profit per dollar of product gross profit rising from $0.55 in fiscal 2023 to $0.73. Then the mechanism ran backwards. In the nine months to 2026-06-27 product gross profit rose 26.3% to $108,819M and services gross profit 15.3% to $69,963M, so Services fell to 39.1% of gross profit; product gross margin reached 39.9% against 36.9%, taking total gross margin to 49.1% and to 50.1% in the June quarter against 46.5%. Apple attributes the gain to "a different mix of products and tariff refunds, partially offset by higher costs, including memory": fiscal 2026's margin is hardware-led and partly a refund, not a trading gain. A device is gross-profit-positive on delivery at 36.8% and the services that follow are nearly all incremental, services cost of sales being $26,844M on $109,158M of revenue; the $0.73 per dollar is therefore the closest disclosed proxy for lifetime value against acquisition cost, and its fall to $0.64 the number to watch [S5, S6].

### Unit economics per revenue dollar, because there are no units

| Unit-economics line | FY2025 | 9M FY2026 | Evidence and status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Product cost of sales, per $1,000 of product revenue | $632 | $601 | BOM, assembly and warranty, not split | S5, S6 |
| Product gross profit | $368 | $399 | 36.8% to 39.9%; includes tariff refunds | S5, S6 |
| Services cost of sales, per $1,000 of services revenue | $246 | $237 | Content, hosting and payment processing | S5, S6 |
| Services gross profit | $754 | $763 | 75.4% to 76.3% | S5, S6 |
| Services gross profit per $1 of product gross profit | $0.73 | $0.64 | Closest disclosed lifetime-value proxy | S5, S6 |
| Revenue per active device per year | $166 | $187 TTM | More than 2.5bn devices; average, not cohort | S5, S6, S150 |
| Carrier receivables, share of trade receivables | 34% | 27% | $13,524M of $39,777M; $8,477M of $31,398M; one customer 18% | S5, S6 |
| CAC, LTV, LTV:CAC, payback in months | Not disclosed | Not computable | Carriers bear acquisition; no units, ASP or retention disclosed | S5 |

### Pricing power shows up as mix, not as price

| Line | FY2025 net sales | Year on year | Disclosed price and mix driver | Gross margin | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone | $209,586M | +4% | "higher net sales of Pro models", mix not units | 36.8% blended | S5 |
| Services | $109,158M | +14% | "advertising, the App Store and cloud services" | 75.4% | S5 |
| Mac | $33,708M | +12% | "laptops and desktops" | 36.8% blended | S5 |
| iPad and Wearables | $63,709M | 0% | iPad Air and mini higher, Accessories and Wearables lower | 36.8% blended | S5 |

iPhone revenue rose 22% to $196,515M in the nine months to 2026-06-27, again "due to higher net sales of Pro models": pricing power arrives as mix, not price. The same disclosure prevents separating price from volume and therefore prevents estimating elasticity. Apple publishes list prices on its own store but not in its filings, and no verified 2026 price list was retrieved; third-party unit data would settle it [S6].

### The highest-margin layer is also the most litigated

App Store economics are recognised net — Apple books "only the commission it retains" on third-party app sales — so a take-rate cut passes straight to revenue and gross profit with no offsetting cost. Apple is subject to a US court order barring a commission on certain consumer purchases, though the Ninth Circuit has told the district court to amend the injunction to permit one, and in the EU the Digital Markets Act forces alternative distribution, payment processing and fee structures. A second concentration sits in the same line: licensing revenue from Google for search distribution inside Services advertising, which Apple names as a primary driver of Services growth in fiscal 2025 and the first nine months of fiscal 2026. The payment was $20bn in 2022 per unsealed court documents, 18.3% of fiscal 2025 Services revenue, and Apple does not disclose the current figure; the District of Columbia order of 2025-09-02 preserved payments while banning exclusive agreements, but Apple says a reversal could impose remedies "prohibiting Google from offering the Company commercial terms for search distribution" [S6, S82].

### Cost structure, and what would break the durability

The cost base is bought, not built: product cost of sales of $194,116M goes to TSMC for wafers, memory suppliers for DRAM and NAND, and Foxconn and its peers for assembly. Research and development reached $34,035M in the nine months to 2026-06-27, up 33% and 9.3% of revenue against 8.3% in fiscal 2025, on "infrastructure-related costs, including investments in artificial intelligence"; capital expenditure is 2.2% of trailing-twelve-month revenue against 34.9% at Microsoft in fiscal 2026. Apple rents its manufacturing and buys much of its AI through the income statement, so that bill reaches the operating margin immediately. What remains is a disclosure gap: Apple reports the 60% indirect share, the carrier receivable and that price protection and other incentives reduce Products net sales, but not the carrier-only share of sales, the wholesale discount, the subsidy per device or the reseller-support spend inside SG&A; carrier 10-K equipment-revenue and promotional lines, or paid channel sell-in data, would settle them, and one point of wholesale terms across the indirect channel is $2.5bn of revenue, 1.3% of fiscal 2025 gross profit. The annuity is intact, but the margin expansion of the last four quarters is not the mix shift it is described as: it is product mix, a tariff refund and memory cost timing, on a services base whose most profitable parts face an appeal, a court order and a European regulatory process. Giving back three points of gross margin and losing the search licence together would take more than a fifth of trailing-twelve-month net income. Three facts would settle durability and none is disclosed — the current search payment, the App Store share of Services and the refund-versus-mix split; the fiscal 2026 annual report, not on EDGAR as of 2026-10-31, may settle them [S6, S27].

::: evidence
**The service mix still drives Apple's margin, but in fiscal 2026 it stopped being the marginal driver — hardware did, and part of that gain is a refund.**

In the nine months to June 2026 product gross profit grew faster than services gross profit for the first time in three years, and Apple attributes the higher product margin to product mix and tariff refunds rather than to trading gains. The installed base grew more slowly than revenue, so the next leg depends on revenue per device rather than on more devices.
:::

Entity accounts filed with Ireland's Companies Registration Office, which the 10-K does not reproduce, would show where profit now sits.

### Capital return, not leverage, is the capital-structure question

Apple carries $62.2bn of net cash — $146.5bn of cash and securities against $84.3bn of debt at 2026-06-27 — and in the nine months to that date repurchased 215m shares for $61.8bn, against $70.6bn a year earlier, under successive $100bn authorisations approved on 2025-05-01 and 2026-04-30, the latest announced with Q2 FY2026 results [S6, S204, S205]. At a $5tn capitalisation each $10bn of repurchase retires 0.2% of the company, so the return depends on the price paid. A 12% year-on-year slowdown in dollars while the shares rose 25.7% is consistent with price discipline, or with lower free cash flow; the filings do not distinguish. Solvency is not the risk; executing the market's largest buyback at a multiple that assumes the AI transition works is.

### Ownership is institutional, and the board is long-tenured

Vanguard holds 9.63% and BlackRock 7.10%, but the BlackRock figure is taken from a 2023-12-31 filing quoted in the 2026 proxy and is stale [S65, S153]. Directors and officers hold 0.06%; Tim Cook's 3,280,295 shares are worth $1.13bn at the current price yet are 0.02% of the company. The board has nine members after Ternus joined on 2026-09-01, seven of them independent; Arthur Levinson, a director since 2000 and chair for 15 years, became lead independent director that day. At the 2026-02-24 annual meeting Levinson drew 9.0% opposition, say-on-pay 8.6% and a "China Entanglement Audit" proposal 1.4% support. That passes Nasdaq's majority-independent rule and is not a governance crisis, but it is a professional board, not a founder-aligned one.

### The business model is an annuity on hardware

Apple sells devices to consumers, enterprises and carriers, but the buyer that matters is the installed base: more than 2.5bn devices whose owners upgrade and pay for services. FY2025 net sales were $416.2bn (+6%), with Services gross margin of 75.4% against 46.9% for the group; in the nine months to 2026-06-27 net sales rose 16% to $364.4bn, Services 14% to $91.7bn and Greater China 30% to $64.8bn after a 4% decline in FY2025 [S5, S6]. That is the growth engine — a replacement cycle plus attach, with China swinging from drag to driver in two years. It makes the model resilient to unit stagnation but not to a remedy that breaks the Services attach: Services produced 39.1% of nine-month gross profit on 25.2% of revenue.

### The legal front is about Services margins, not fines

Three proceedings test the container. The DOJ's civil antitrust suit, filed on 2024-03-21 in the District of New Jersey, seeks equitable relief rather than damages; the Epic litigation produced a 2025-04-30 finding that Apple violated the 2021 injunction, a ban on fees for out-of-app purchases and a referral to the U.S. Attorney for possible criminal contempt; and the EU fined Apple €500m under the Digital Markets Act on 2025-04-23, which Apple appealed [S5, S7]. The fines are small against $416bn of revenue; the remedies are not, because they target the 75%-gross-margin Services line and the App Store's toll gate on 2.5bn devices. Counter-evidence is real — the DOJ must prove market definition, Apple says it has substantial defences, and no court has ordered a structural remedy — but the direction in both jurisdictions is toward alternative distribution and payment, the one outcome that would change the franchise's economics rather than its legal bill.

arguments.markdown:
Apple runs a hardware annuity with a services margin on top — 73 cents of services gross profit per dollar of product gross profit — but the mix shift the multiple pays for stalled in fiscal 2026, when hardware margins, helped by tariff refunds, grew gross profit faster than Services. In fiscal 2025, 40% of net sales went through Apple's own stores and direct sales force and 60%, or $249,697M of $416,161M, through carriers, resellers and distributors. The carrier finances or subsidises the handset, so it bears the acquisition cost and Apple's selling expense stays at $27,601M, or 6.6% of revenue; the dependency is contractual, not permanent, because Apple's risk factor says resellers offer financing, installment plans or subsidies that "may be discontinued or modified any time." The balance-sheet footprint is smaller: carriers were 27% of trade receivables at 2026-06-27, $8,477M of $31,398M, down from 34% of $39,777M at 2025-09-27 [S5, S6].

### The installed base, and what $187 a device does not say

Apple reported more than 2.5 billion active devices on 2026-01-29, against more than 2.35 billion a year earlier, and repeated the figure in its 2026-04-20 succession release; the count is company-reported, not audited. Divided into $466,823M of trailing-twelve-month revenue to 2026-06-27 it gives at most $187 of revenue per active device a year, a ceiling because the denominator is a floor. On fiscal 2025 revenue and Services the same arithmetic gives $166 and $44, so Services are about a quarter of revenue per device, and the base grew roughly 6% while nine-month revenue grew 16.2%. The metric does not capture users rather than devices, the gap between a Pro iPhone and AirPods, first-time buyers, regional pricing or services attach, and it divides a trailing year by a count four months older [S150, S191, S5, S6].

### The mix shift, and its reversal

In fiscal 2025 Services produced $109,158M of revenue at a 75.4% gross margin against $307,003M of Products at 36.8%: 26.2% of revenue but 42.2% of gross profit ($82,314M of $195,201M), up from 35.7% two years earlier, with services gross profit per dollar of product gross profit rising from $0.55 in fiscal 2023 to $0.73. Then the mechanism ran backwards. In the nine months to 2026-06-27 product gross profit rose 26.3% to $108,819M and services gross profit 15.3% to $69,963M, so Services fell to 39.1% of gross profit; product gross margin reached 39.9% against 36.9%, taking total gross margin to 49.1% and to 50.1% in the June quarter against 46.5%. Apple attributes the gain to "a different mix of products and tariff refunds, partially offset by higher costs, including memory": fiscal 2026's margin is hardware-led and partly a refund, not a trading gain. A device is gross-profit-positive on delivery at 36.8% and the services that follow are nearly all incremental, services cost of sales being $26,844M on $109,158M of revenue; the $0.73 per dollar is therefore the closest disclosed proxy for lifetime value against acquisition cost, and its fall to $0.64 the number to watch [S5, S6].

### Unit economics per revenue dollar, because there are no units

| Unit-economics line | FY2025 | 9M FY2026 | Evidence and status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Product cost of sales, per $1,000 of product revenue | $632 | $601 | BOM, assembly and warranty, not split | S5, S6 |
| Product gross profit | $368 | $399 | 36.8% to 39.9%; includes tariff refunds | S5, S6 |
| Services cost of sales, per $1,000 of services revenue | $246 | $237 | Content, hosting and payment processing | S5, S6 |
| Services gross profit | $754 | $763 | 75.4% to 76.3% | S5, S6 |
| Services gross profit per $1 of product gross profit | $0.73 | $0.64 | Closest disclosed lifetime-value proxy | S5, S6 |
| Revenue per active device per year | $166 | $187 TTM | More than 2.5bn devices; average, not cohort | S5, S6, S150 |
| Carrier receivables, share of trade receivables | 34% | 27% | $13,524M of $39,777M; $8,477M of $31,398M; one customer 18% | S5, S6 |
| CAC, LTV, LTV:CAC, payback in months | Not disclosed | Not computable | Carriers bear acquisition; no units, ASP or retention disclosed | S5 |

### Pricing power shows up as mix, not as price

| Line | FY2025 net sales | Year on year | Disclosed price and mix driver | Gross margin | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone | $209,586M | +4% | "higher net sales of Pro models", mix not units | 36.8% blended | S5 |
| Services | $109,158M | +14% | "advertising, the App Store and cloud services" | 75.4% | S5 |
| Mac | $33,708M | +12% | "laptops and desktops" | 36.8% blended | S5 |
| iPad and Wearables | $63,709M | 0% | iPad Air and mini higher, Accessories and Wearables lower | 36.8% blended | S5 |

iPhone revenue rose 22% to $196,515M in the nine months to 2026-06-27, again "due to higher net sales of Pro models": pricing power arrives as mix, not price. The same disclosure prevents separating price from volume and therefore prevents estimating elasticity. Apple publishes list prices on its own store but not in its filings, and no verified 2026 price list was retrieved; third-party unit data would settle it [S6].

### The highest-margin layer is also the most litigated

App Store economics are recognised net — Apple books "only the commission it retains" on third-party app sales — so a take-rate cut passes straight to revenue and gross profit with no offsetting cost. Apple is subject to a US court order barring a commission on certain consumer purchases, though the Ninth Circuit has told the district court to amend the injunction to permit one, and in the EU the Digital Markets Act forces alternative distribution, payment processing and fee structures. A second concentration sits in the same line: licensing revenue from Google for search distribution inside Services advertising, which Apple names as a primary driver of Services growth in fiscal 2025 and the first nine months of fiscal 2026. The payment was $20bn in 2022 per unsealed court documents, 18.3% of fiscal 2025 Services revenue, and Apple does not disclose the current figure; the District of Columbia order of 2025-09-02 preserved payments while banning exclusive agreements, but Apple says a reversal could impose remedies "prohibiting Google from offering the Company commercial terms for search distribution" [S6, S82].

### Cost structure, and what would break the durability

The cost base is bought, not built: product cost of sales of $194,116M goes to TSMC for wafers, memory suppliers for DRAM and NAND, and Foxconn and its peers for assembly. Research and development reached $34,035M in the nine months to 2026-06-27, up 33% and 9.3% of revenue against 8.3% in fiscal 2025, on "infrastructure-related costs, including investments in artificial intelligence"; capital expenditure is 2.2% of trailing-twelve-month revenue against 34.9% at Microsoft in fiscal 2026. Apple rents its manufacturing and buys much of its AI through the income statement, so that bill reaches the operating margin immediately. What remains is a disclosure gap: Apple reports the 60% indirect share, the carrier receivable and that price protection and other incentives reduce Products net sales, but not the carrier-only share of sales, the wholesale discount, the subsidy per device or the reseller-support spend inside SG&A; carrier 10-K equipment-revenue and promotional lines, or paid channel sell-in data, would settle them, and one point of wholesale terms across the indirect channel is $2.5bn of revenue, 1.3% of fiscal 2025 gross profit. For investors the durable asset is the installed base and the $44 of services revenue per device; the margin expansion of the last four quarters is not the mix shift it is described as, but product mix, a tariff refund and memory cost timing, on a services base whose most profitable parts face an appeal, a court order and a European regulatory process. Giving back three points of gross margin and losing the search licence together would take more than a fifth of trailing-twelve-month net income. Three facts would settle durability and none is disclosed — the current search payment, the App Store share of Services and the refund-versus-mix split; the fiscal 2026 annual report, not on EDGAR as of 2026-10-31, may settle them [S6, S27].

::: evidence
**The service mix still drives Apple's margin, but in fiscal 2026 it stopped being the marginal driver — hardware did, and part of that gain is a refund.**

In the nine months to June 2026 product gross profit grew faster than services gross profit for the first time in three years, and Apple attributes the higher product margin to product mix and tariff refunds rather than to trading gains. The installed base grew more slowly than revenue, so the next leg depends on revenue per device rather than on more devices.
:::

Apple's 20.2% of global smartphone shipments in Q2 2026 was a record for that quarter and a 3.9 percentage point gain, but Samsung's 22.7% was larger and Xiaomi's 26.4% collapse explains much of the redistribution. In personal computing Apple is second at 18.2% to Lenovo's 20.1%, yet macOS shipments grew 17.4% while Windows fell 6.7% and Android 19.6%, and macOS is the only major operating system IDC expects to grow in 2026. The clearest structural lead is detachable tablets at 55.3%; the weakest spot is smartwatches, where Huawei leads 18.8% to 17.2%, so Apple's 15.5% of all wearables rests on earwear, where it holds 17.2%. [S104]

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone, global | Samsung | 22.7%, +3.2pp | 20.2%, +3.9pp | iOS integration and secured memory supply | Industry ASP $581; Apple above it | High: iCloud, iMessage, purchased apps | S102, S66 |
| iPhone, China | Huawei | 22.6%, +4.5pp | 18.1%, +4.2pp | iOS against domestic HarmonyOS | Apple held prices while Android raised them | Medium: leaving iOS loses Apple services | S40 |
| PCs and tablets | Lenovo | 20.1%, +2.5pp | 18.2%, -0.4% | macOS against Windows | MacBook Neo attacks entry pricing | Medium | S103, S106 |
| Services and App Store | Alphabet, Google Play | $471.1bn TTM revenue | $91.7bn Services, 76.3% margin (9M FY2026) | iOS distribution against Google Play | 15-30% commission, under challenge | High for consumers, falling for developers | S5, S42, S80 |

### Samsung is the dangerous one, and the reason is memory

Samsung is the most dangerous competitor, and not because of the Galaxy S26 Ultra. When memory is more than 65% of bill of materials at the low end, the binding constraint is supply access, and Samsung is the only top-five handset vendor that also sells memory: it grew shipments 8.1% and took 3.2 points of share in Q2 2026 while Xiaomi fell 26.4% and vivo 19.6%. Apple's answer was to secure memory early, which is why its units fell only 1.3% in 2026 against Android's 24.3% and why IDC puts iOS at a record 23.6% of shipments — a sourcing feat rather than a structural advantage, and it lapses when memory normalises while Samsung keeps its costs. Samsung also holds the foldable franchise Apple now attacks: the iPhone Duo went on sale on 2026-10-23 at a reported $1,999, below the $2,550 average price IDC assumes, against a forecast of more than 17 million foldable iPhones by 2027 and 40% of a category growing 12.6% to 22.9 million units this year. [S66, S59]

### In China the competitor and the rules are different

Huawei held 22.6% of a Chinese market that fell 4.3% in Q2 2026 and grew 19.9% by holding prices while Android rivals raised theirs, leaning on HarmonyOS, which IDC expects to reach 51 million units in 2026; Apple grew 24.4% and gained 4.2 points to 18.1%, so both premium ends expanded while OPPO, vivo and Xiaomi contracted. The mechanism is a domestic operating system plus price discipline, and neither is a feature Apple can copy. HarmonyOS draws on the national preference that makes Apple's China revenue politically exposed, so the 30% China revenue growth belongs behind a competition risk; Apple Intelligence was registered with China's internet regulator on 2026-07-15 alongside Alibaba's Qwen and Baidu, which narrows the AI gap in the one market where it mattered most but does not settle it. [S40, S120]

### The profit pool is being taken by courts, not by rivals

Apple's FY2025 annual report discloses that it is subject to a U.S. court order preventing it from imposing any commission on certain purchases consumers make, that its Digital Markets Act compliance plan has been challenged by the European Commission, and that it faces U.S. monopolization suits over smartphones; separately, the September 2, 2025 remedies order against Google, if upheld, could remove the search-distribution payments inside Services. No competitor needs to win a device sale for the 76.3% services margin to compress: a developer that routes a subscriber to the web converts a 15-30% commission into a payment-processing fee, and Services growth of 14.1% then arrives at a lower margin. The hardware position improved while the pricing power behind it was cut by U.S. courts and European regulators. [S5]

|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone | Samsung, 22.7% of units | Apple, 20.2% and gaining | Huawei in China, 22.6% | HarmonyOS at 51m units; AI-first Android flagships | S102, S40, S66 |
| PCs and tablets | Lenovo, 20.1% | Apple, 18.2%, with the only growing OS | Dell in workstations, 40.0% | HarmonyOS NEXT at 1.6%; Windows-on-ARM | S103, S106 |
| Services | Apple, $91.7bn (9M) | Alphabet through Google Play | Netflix, Spotify, Epic | Web payments and alternative marketplaces | S5, S42, S80 |

### AI and the phone already in the buyer's pocket

Where Apple is not ahead is AI: the all-new Siri AI arrived at WWDC26 in June 2026 on foundation models licensed from Google under their 2026-01-12 agreement — its assistant now depends on a company it also competes with in services. Samsung's AI-equipped Galaxy S26 Ultra is credited by IDC with returning Samsung to first place in Q1 2026, and research and development rose 32.5% to $34.0 billion in nine months of FY2026 — the cost of catching up, not the reward for leading. The strongest competitor is the handset already in the buyer's pocket: replacement cycles are lengthening, IDC describes Chinese buyers as postponing rather than abandoning upgrades, and the 173 million sub-$100 units shipped in 2025 are leaving the market, which supports Services attach while suppressing units. Three risks follow: if AI becomes the reason a buyer upgrades, Apple competes on integration, with a rented model; if HarmonyOS reaches first-time buyers in lower-tier cities, they never enter iOS; and if the U.S. injunction spreads to other storefronts, the take rate falls further. Unit position and profit per unit are moving in opposite directions, so the question worth paying for is not who sells more phones but what share of the transaction Apple controls in 2027. Confidence is high in the shares and legal facts, medium beyond 2028, when memory normalises and the crisis-specific advantage lapses. Open diligence: what proportion of Services revenue is commission rather than subscription? What margin does the foldable carry at $1,999? What does the Gemini licence cost per query at scale? {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Market & Industry Analysis (market, revision 5 by Market Analyst, 8,990 characters)
Apple's markets are contracting in units and expanding in value, and Apple is taking value share inside that contraction: the case for FY2026-FY2028 rests on premiumisation and installed-base monetisation rather than unit volume or a Services mix shift, is strongest in the United States, is adequate in Europe, and in China depends on a domestic champion's pricing discipline.

### The pool is shrinking in units and growing in value

IDC's August 2026 forecast has worldwide smartphone shipments at just over 1.0 billion units in 2026, down 16.7%, while total market value rises 6.3% to $613 billion and the average selling price reaches a record $581, up 27.6% in a year. The cause is cost, not demand: DRAM and NAND prices are up more than 300% year on year as capacity is redirected to AI servers, memory is more than 65% of bill of materials at the low end, and the sub-$100 tier fell close to 60% in the second quarter of 2026. This is a supply shock with a dated end, so 2026-2027 flatters Apple's unit share while genuinely lifting its price, and 2028 is the test of whether either survives. [S66]

Two sizing methods agree closely: 1.0 billion units at the $581 average price gives $581 billion, within 5% of IDC's $613 billion, so the two series are consistent rather than rival estimates. On that base Apple's serviceable market is the premium tier it addresses — an iOS share of 23.6% of 2026 shipments, a record — while the revenue it can obtain is what it already books: $466.8 billion trailing twelve months to 2026-06-27, which at the 16.2% growth rate of the first nine months of FY2026 implies $483 billion for FY2026. [S6]

| Measure | Method | Figure | Year | Publisher | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| TAM, smartphone value (top-down) | Industry value estimate | $613bn, +6.3% | 2026 | IDC | S66 |
| TAM, smartphone value (bottom-up) | 1.0bn units x $581 ASP | ~$581bn | 2026 | Calculation on IDC inputs | S66 |
| TAM, personal computing devices | Units only | ~398m units, -11.3%; 1.5% CAGR to 2030 | 2026 | IDC | S103 |
| SAM, premium smartphone tier | iOS share of shipments | 23.6% of units, record | 2026 | IDC | S66 |
| SOM, Apple revenue | Reported | $466.8bn TTM | TTM to 2026-06-27 | Apple 10-Q | S6 |
| Near-term obtainable revenue | FY2025 $416.2bn grown at the 9M FY2026 rate | ~$483bn | FY2026E | Calculation on Apple filings | S5, S13 |

### China is the swing factor, and India sits in the wrong line

Apple's revenue is moving toward the faster-growing regions, but the swing is China. In the first nine months of FY2026 Greater China produced $64.8 billion, up 30.0% on a base of $49.9 billion, after falling from $72.6 billion in FY2023 to $64.4 billion in FY2025; the Americas grew 11.4% to $149.4 billion, Europe 16.1% to $95.6 billion, Japan 10.4% and Rest of Asia Pacific 19.4%. Greater China's $14.9 billion increase contributes 4.1 percentage points of the group's 16.2% growth, more than any other segment, and part of it is currency: a favourable renminbi effect in Greater China, an unfavourable yen effect in Japan. Europe includes India, the Middle East and Africa, so the fastest-growing large smartphone market is invisible in the segment line. [S13]

| Region | Market size (year) | Growth | Apple's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| United States / North America | 60% of Q1 2026 shipments above $800; 24.9% of global PC-plus-tablet units | Smartphone -6.3% in 2026; PC -14.6% in 2026 | Entered, leads the premium tier; 41.0% of Apple revenue is the Americas | Tariffs, carrier financing, antitrust suits | Samsung, Lenovo, HP, Dell | S39, S103, S13 |
| Greater China | ~66m units a quarter, 264m a year | -4.3% in Q2 2026, fifth straight decline; H2 2026 could be -20% | 18.1% of units, second behind Huawei; revenue +30.0% | Domestic operating system, subsidy withdrawal, data rules | Huawei 22.6%, OPPO 16.0%, vivo 16.0%, Xiaomi 12.4% | S40, S6 |
| Europe (includes India, Middle East, Africa) | India 31.0m units in Q1 2026 at a record $302 ASP | India units -4.1% but value +5.8%; Europe revenue +16.1% | Entered; fourth by units in India | DMA, price sensitivity, distribution | Samsung, Xiaomi, vivo, Lenovo, HP | S105, S103, S13 |
| Japan | Revenue $24.4bn in 9M FY2026 | Revenue +10.4%; units -25.6% in 2026 | Entered, premium strong; weak yen cuts revenue | Yen, saturated device base | Local Android vendors, Samsung | S13, S103, S6 |
| Rest of Asia Pacific | Revenue $30.2bn in 9M FY2026 | Revenue +19.4%; units -14% in 2026 | Entered, premium-led | Price-sensitive mass market, currency | Samsung, Xiaomi, OPPO, vivo | S13, S39, S103 |

### Services carries the profit, but the mix moved back to hardware

The fastest-growing pool Apple monetises is Services, but its share of revenue fell in FY2026: $91.7 billion in the first nine months, 25.2% of $364.4 billion and up 14%, at a 76.3% gross margin against 75.4% for FY2025, when Services was $109.2 billion, 26.2% of revenue. Hardware grew faster than Services, so the mix shifted toward premium handsets and China rather than toward the recurring pool — the opposite of what a Services-led thesis needs. The app economy itself has no published size in the sources retrieved: neither Apple nor the platform owners disclose app-store gross billings or mobile-advertising revenue, so Apple's Services line is the measured pool. The installed base is disclosed: Apple put it at more than 2.5 billion active devices on 2026-01-29, up from 2.35 billion a year earlier, which is the stock behind Services and the upgrade pool, but Apple still does not publish a replacement rate, so upgrade timing cannot be sized from public data. [S5, S6, S174, S191]

### Who pays, and how much demand is policy

The budget owner is the consumer, in a discretionary purchase that is increasingly financed. In the United States and United Kingdom interest-free financing is common, so IDC expects the premium end to hold while emerging markets fall more than 20%; in India brands lean on financing after the sub-$100 tier fell 59% and the $600-800 band grew 32%; in China the government subsidy that supported earlier quarters faded in the second quarter of 2026, so demand there is being withdrawn by policy rather than created by it. Policy moves Apple's margin more than a product cycle does: after the February 20, 2026 Supreme Court ruling struck down certain IEEPA tariffs, Apple recognised refunds as a reduction of product cost of sales, and those refunds contributed 2.0 percentage points of the June 2026 quarter's 50.1% gross margin. [S105, S40, S13]

### What would break the premiumisation case

Counter-evidence is fourfold. If memory prices normalise in 2028 as IDC expects, the entry tier rebuilds and Apple's 2026 share gain is contestable again. If China's June-quarter demand was pulled forward ahead of second-half price increases, as IDC's China team reports, the 30% growth line is a launch and currency effect. If courts and the European Commission remove the App Store take rate, the margin layer that offsets hardware cyclicality stops compounding. And the search-distribution payment — $20 billion in 2022, equal to 17% of trailing Services revenue of $120.5 billion and 22% of trailing Services gross profit of $91.6 billion — has not been banned: the September 2, 2025 remedies decision declined to ban distributor payments, and the December 2025 final judgment that restricts distribution is under appeal by Google and the Department of Justice, both pending at 2026-10-29. The investor implication is narrow: in a 1-billion-unit market Apple can grow device revenue only if price rises faster than units fall, making average selling price, China durability and the Services take rate the variables worth monitoring. Sizing confidence is high, because two independent methods agree within 5%; confidence that the mix shift holds to 2028 is medium, because it rests on China and a legally contested commission. Three diligence questions remain open: what share of Services revenue is commission-based rather than subscription, advertising or licensing? How much of the Greater China increase is currency? And what is the current average replacement cycle, measured rather than asserted? [S66, S40, S82, S118, S42, S5]

::: evidence
**Apple's addressable device market fell 16.7% in units in 2026 while growing 6.3% in value, and Apple's revenue grew 16.2% over nine months — the gap is premiumisation and China, not market growth, and Services is not gaining mix (S66, S13, S6).**

IDC forecasts 2026 shipments at just over 1.0 billion units against a market value of $613 billion and an ASP of $581 (S66, S39). Apple's nine-month FY2026 revenue was $364.4 billion, up 16.2%, with Greater China up 30.0% on a $49.9 billion base and Services at 25.2% of revenue against 26.2% in FY2025 (S13, S6). The bottom-up check of 1.0 billion units at $581 gives $581 billion, within 5% of IDC's value estimate (S66).
:::"}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Business Model (business_model, revision 5 by Fundamentals Analyst, 8,834 characters)
Apple runs a hardware annuity with a services margin on top — 73 cents of services gross profit per dollar of product gross profit — but the mix shift the multiple pays for stalled in fiscal 2026, when hardware margins, helped by tariff refunds, grew gross profit faster than Services. In fiscal 2025, 40% of net sales went through Apple's own stores and direct sales force and 60%, or $249,697M of $416,161M, through carriers, resellers and distributors. The carrier finances or subsidises the handset, so it bears the acquisition cost and Apple's selling expense stays at $27,601M, or 6.6% of revenue; the dependency is contractual, not permanent, because Apple's risk factor says resellers offer financing, installment plans or subsidies that "may be discontinued or modified any time." The balance-sheet footprint is smaller: carriers were 27% of trade receivables at 2026-06-27, $8,477M of $31,398M, down from 34% of $39,777M at 2025-09-27 [S5, S6].

### The installed base, and what $187 a device does not say

Apple reported more than 2.5 billion active devices on 2026-01-29, against more than 2.35 billion a year earlier, and repeated the figure in its 2026-04-20 succession release; the count is company-reported, not audited. Divided into $466,823M of trailing-twelve-month revenue to 2026-06-27 it gives at most $187 of revenue per active device a year, a ceiling because the denominator is a floor. On fiscal 2025 revenue and Services the same arithmetic gives $166 and $44, so Services are about a quarter of revenue per device, and the base grew roughly 6% while nine-month revenue grew 16.2%. The metric does not capture users rather than devices, the gap between a Pro iPhone and AirPods, first-time buyers, regional pricing or services attach, and it divides a trailing year by a count four months older [S150, S191, S5, S6].

### The mix shift, and its reversal

In fiscal 2025 Services produced $109,158M of revenue at a 75.4% gross margin against $307,003M of Products at 36.8%: 26.2% of revenue but 42.2% of gross profit ($82,314M of $195,201M), up from 35.7% two years earlier, with services gross profit per dollar of product gross profit rising from $0.55 in fiscal 2023 to $0.73. Then the mechanism ran backwards. In the nine months to 2026-06-27 product gross profit rose 26.3% to $108,819M and services gross profit 15.3% to $69,963M, so Services fell to 39.1% of gross profit; product gross margin reached 39.9% against 36.9%, taking total gross margin to 49.1% and to 50.1% in the June quarter against 46.5%. Apple attributes the gain to "a different mix of products and tariff refunds, partially offset by higher costs, including memory": fiscal 2026's margin is hardware-led and partly a refund, not a trading gain. A device is gross-profit-positive on delivery at 36.8% and the services that follow are nearly all incremental, services cost of sales being $26,844M on $109,158M of revenue; the $0.73 per dollar is therefore the closest disclosed proxy for lifetime value against acquisition cost, and its fall to $0.64 the number to watch [S5, S6].

### Unit economics per revenue dollar, because there are no units

| Unit-economics line | FY2025 | 9M FY2026 | Evidence and status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Product cost of sales, per $1,000 of product revenue | $632 | $601 | BOM, assembly and warranty, not split | S5, S6 |
| Product gross profit | $368 | $399 | 36.8% to 39.9%; includes tariff refunds | S5, S6 |
| Services cost of sales, per $1,000 of services revenue | $246 | $237 | Content, hosting and payment processing | S5, S6 |
| Services gross profit | $754 | $763 | 75.4% to 76.3% | S5, S6 |
| Services gross profit per $1 of product gross profit | $0.73 | $0.64 | Closest disclosed lifetime-value proxy | S5, S6 |
| Revenue per active device per year | $166 | $187 TTM | More than 2.5bn devices; average, not cohort | S5, S6, S150 |
| Carrier receivables, share of trade receivables | 34% | 27% | $13,524M of $39,777M; $8,477M of $31,398M; one customer 18% | S5, S6 |
| CAC, LTV, LTV:CAC, payback in months | Not disclosed | Not computable | Carriers bear acquisition; no units, ASP or retention disclosed | S5 |

### Pricing power shows up as mix, not as price

| Line | FY2025 net sales | Year on year | Disclosed price and mix driver | Gross margin | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone | $209,586M | +4% | "higher net sales of Pro models", mix not units | 36.8% blended | S5 |
| Services | $109,158M | +14% | "advertising, the App Store and cloud services" | 75.4% | S5 |
| Mac | $33,708M | +12% | "laptops and desktops" | 36.8% blended | S5 |
| iPad and Wearables | $63,709M | 0% | iPad Air and mini higher, Accessories and Wearables lower | 36.8% blended | S5 |

iPhone revenue rose 22% to $196,515M in the nine months to 2026-06-27, again "due to higher net sales of Pro models": pricing power arrives as mix, not price. The same disclosure prevents separating price from volume and therefore prevents estimating elasticity. Apple publishes list prices on its own store but not in its filings, and no verified 2026 price list was retrieved; third-party unit data would settle it [S6].

### The highest-margin layer is also the most litigated

App Store economics are recognised net — Apple books "only the commission it retains" on third-party app sales — so a take-rate cut passes straight to revenue and gross profit with no offsetting cost. Apple is subject to a US court order barring a commission on certain consumer purchases, though the Ninth Circuit has told the district court to amend the injunction to permit one, and in the EU the Digital Markets Act forces alternative distribution, payment processing and fee structures. A second concentration sits in the same line: licensing revenue from Google for search distribution inside Services advertising, which Apple names as a primary driver of Services growth in fiscal 2025 and the first nine months of fiscal 2026. The payment was $20bn in 2022 per unsealed court documents, 18.3% of fiscal 2025 Services revenue, and Apple does not disclose the current figure; the District of Columbia order of 2025-09-02 preserved payments while banning exclusive agreements, but Apple says a reversal could impose remedies "prohibiting Google from offering the Company commercial terms for search distribution" [S6, S82].

### Cost structure, and what would break the durability

The cost base is bought, not built: product cost of sales of $194,116M goes to TSMC for wafers, memory suppliers for DRAM and NAND, and Foxconn and its peers for assembly. Research and development reached $34,035M in the nine months to 2026-06-27, up 33% and 9.3% of revenue against 8.3% in fiscal 2025, on "infrastructure-related costs, including investments in artificial intelligence"; capital expenditure is 2.2% of trailing-twelve-month revenue against 34.9% at Microsoft in fiscal 2026. Apple rents its manufacturing and buys much of its AI through the income statement, so that bill reaches the operating margin immediately. What remains is a disclosure gap: Apple reports the 60% indirect share, the carrier receivable and that price protection and other incentives reduce Products net sales, but not the carrier-only share of sales, the wholesale discount, the subsidy per device or the reseller-support spend inside SG&A; carrier 10-K equipment-revenue and promotional lines, or paid channel sell-in data, would settle them, and one point of wholesale terms across the indirect channel is $2.5bn of revenue, 1.3% of fiscal 2025 gross profit. For investors the durable asset is the installed base and the $44 of services revenue per device; the margin expansion of the last four quarters is not the mix shift it is described as, but product mix, a tariff refund and memory cost timing, on a services base whose most profitable parts face an appeal, a court order and a European regulatory process. Giving back three points of gross margin and losing the search licence together would take more than a fifth of trailing-twelve-month net income. Three facts would settle durability and none is disclosed — the current search payment, the App Store share of Services and the refund-versus-mix split; the fiscal 2026 annual report, not on EDGAR as of 2026-10-31, may settle them [S6, S27].

::: evidence
**The service mix still drives Apple's margin, but in fiscal 2026 it stopped being the marginal driver — hardware did, and part of that gain is a refund.**

In the nine months to June 2026 product gross profit grew faster than services gross profit for the first time in three years, and Apple attributes the higher product margin to product mix and tariff refunds rather than to trading gains. The installed base grew more slowly than revenue, so the next leg depends on revenue per device rather than on more devices.

Apple's exit is the market, not a buyer, and at $344.63 the margin-adjusted 15/50/35 case is worth $266, 23% below the close, so the discipline is a $240-265 starter, a full position at or below $225 and a trim at $395. At a $5,029.6B market value the largest technology acquisition on record, Microsoft's $68.7B all-cash purchase of Activision Blizzard agreed on 2022-01-18, equals 1.4% of the company, and any bid would face the US and EU antitrust review that Microsoft's own deal attracted; a leveraged buyout of a $4.97T enterprise value is arithmetically impossible. The exit is a sale into the market, at a $13.84B average daily traded value where a 1% position in a $1B fund is $10M, 0.07% of one day's volume. The exit question is therefore not whether a holder can sell but at what multiple a holder should buy and when a holder should sell. [S9, S169, S154]

Over the last ten completed years the average intra-year peak-to-trough drawdown was 21.4%, lasting 82 days, and four episodes exceeded 30%: 2018 fell 36.73%, 2020 31.43%, 2022 30.75% and 2025 30.22%. Each was recovered, with 2020 returning 80.75% for the calendar year and 2025 8.56%, but each recovery came with a re-rating as well as earnings growth, and a holder buying at 38.9x margin-adjusted earnings cannot count on the re-rating half. From $344.63 the average drawdown is $271 and a 30% drawdown is $240. On 2026-10-30 Apple was 1.23% below its all-time-high close while the Nasdaq-100 was 9.09% below its own and the S&P 500 3.05%, so the stock enters any correction from relative strength rather than weakness. The policy tests are narrow for a US holder: no foreign-buyer limit applies to a sale of shares, there is no lock-up, and the listing venue is not in question at NasdaqGS, the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq-100. The binding policy risk sits in the asset, not the exit. The Google search payment, reported at $20B in 2022 and never disclosed by Apple, is on today's base about 17% of trailing Services revenue of $120.5B and 22% of services gross profit of $91.6B, and it survived the D.D.C.'s remedies decision of 2025-09-02: the court refused the DOJ's proposed near-total ban on distribution payments, barring exclusive contracts but permitting default-placement payments not conditioned on exclusivity and running one year or less. Final judgment followed in December 2025, Google appealed in January 2026 and the DOJ and states cross-appealed in February 2026; the appeals were pending at 2026-10-29. The payment therefore continues on non-exclusive, annually renegotiated terms, and the event that would force a sale is its loss or material cut at a renewal or on appeal, not a ban already in force. The arithmetic of that event is large enough to size the position around it: $20B of near-pure-margin revenue taxed at 21% is $15.8B of earnings, and capitalised at 30x that is $474B, 9.4% of the $5,029.6B market value. The slower policy risks are App Store commission rules under the DMA and the DOJ case, and China, where revenue was $64.8B in nine months of fiscal 2026 and can turn on subsidy or geopolitical policy rather than on Apple's execution. At 38.9x margin-adjusted earnings there is no cushion for a services margin shock. [S118, S42, S82, S13]

The strongest case against this discipline is that a 30x-plus multiple never offers a margin of safety again. The stock has averaged 30.2x over five years, and its five-year range of 22.1-40.6x shows a 25x entry is not exotic; if Services compounds at 14% on a 76% gross margin and the buyback retires 1.6% of the shares a year, a fund that waits for $225 may simply never own the best cash generator in the market, and the cost of the discipline is opportunity rather than loss. The answer is a time rule rather than a permanent price target: if Apple trades above $268 for four consecutive quarters while Services growth stays above 10%, reassess the band against the then-current multiple instead of waiting for a level the business has outgrown. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Investment Potential & Thesis (thesis, revision 3 by Lead Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,505 characters)
Apple at $344.63 is a great business at a price that assumes its best margin year is permanent. More than 2.5bn active devices, a record 23.6% of smartphone shipments and a quarter of revenue from Services make the need real; custom silicon, iOS and carrier distribution make the capability defensible, though the frontier model is licensed from Google. The economics scale: $466.8bn of trailing revenue, $136.7bn of free cash flow and capital expenditure at 2.2% of sales. The question is price. If a ~50% gross margin is a floor, the stock is fairly valued at 35x forward earnings; if it is a refund-and-memory peak, fair value is $268, 22% below the close. [S199]

Demand is replacement, not discovery. Global units fall 16.7% to 1.0bn in 2026 while market value rises 6.3% to $613bn, and Apple's nine-month revenue grew 16.2% on price and on share taken from a collapsing entry tier. Greater China supplied 4.1 points of that growth with revenue up 30.0%. The moat is real: the A20 Pro on TSMC N2, a 76.3% services gross margin, 60% of sales through carriers and selling expense at 6.6% of revenue. It protects the annuity, not the growth. Siri runs on a Google-built model, Vision Pro shipped 45,000 units in the December 2025 quarter, and interoperability rules may keep the rebuilt assistant out of the European Union. [S191, S66]

The economics turn at the line the multiple capitalises. Services produced 39.1% of gross profit in nine months, down from 42.2% in FY2025, because product gross profit grew 26.3% against 15.3%. The margin is not clean: 50.1% in June included 2.0 points of tariff refunds and the 47-48% September guide includes another point, leaving 46-47% underlying against 48.1% in June ex-refund, which management attributed to memory. Two points on $490bn of FY2027 revenue is $9.8bn of pretax profit, 6.3% of trailing net income, leaving EPS near $8.87 rather than the $9.79 consensus. Jefferies' $263.66 target of 2026-08-10 is within 2% of that arithmetic. [S201]

Consensus is right about the franchise and wrong about the price. The average target is $339.35, below the close. The stock trades at 39.5x trailing and 35.2x forward earnings against a 21.0x mega-cap peer median and 21.76x for the S&P 500 — 88% above peers and 1.8 times the index, at the 100th percentile of a five-year range whose average is 30.2x. A 2.7% free-cash-flow yield against a 4.93% ten-year Treasury demands 11.8% free-cash-flow growth for a decade; the company delivered 1.5% in fiscal 2021-2025. The asymmetry runs against the buyer: the bull case pays 16% before dividends and needs the margin question answered in Apple's favour, the base case loses 22% even though the franchise performs, and the bear loses 41%. Weighting the cases 20/50/30 gives an expected value of $275, a 20% negative return, which is why the position is zero rather than small. The bull case is not a fantasy — Apple has beaten estimates through the squeeze and raised iPad and Mac prices without visible demand destruction — but it is the minority case because the company's own September guide already carries the give-back the consensus EPS denies. [S9, S154]

Circuit argument from 2026-12-09; first renewal terms | S6, S82, S118 |
| 3 | Services compound in the low-to-mid teens without a mandated take-rate collapse | Medium | Two quarters below 5% growth; a remedy stripping commission on a material share | A three-point growth cut removes $3.6bn of revenue and 2.8% of net income | EU Article 6(4); US link-out migration; services growth decelerating | S6, S5, S122 |

Three transfers sit outside the operating story and each lands on the same high-margin layer. The reported $20bn search payment is 22% of services gross profit, and the D.D.C. remedies decision of 2025-09-02 preserved it only on non-exclusive, one-year-or-shorter terms, with appeals pending and argument sought from 2026-12-09. The Digital Markets Act produced a €500m fine on 2025-04-23 and an open Article 6(4) file; the US Department of Justice case is in discovery toward a 2027 trial. China is the third: revenue rose 30% in nine months, but Huawei holds 22.6% of units with HarmonyOS and price discipline, and IDC expects China shipments to fall 20% in the second half of 2026, so the region that supplied the most growth enters FY2027 against its hardest comparison. Capital allocation does not cushion any of it: $62.1bn of stock was repurchased in nine months at a 2.5% earnings yield against a 4.93% Treasury. The decision tree follows: invest now no, because expected value is below the price and the margin question is open; pass no, because the franchise, balance sheet and cash conversion are the best in the peer set and the AI risk is a cost rather than an existential break; wait for the 2026-11-02 guide; then invest with conditions at $240-265 for a 1-2% starter and at or below $225 for a 3-4% position capped at 4%, trimming above $395. Microsoft after 2014 shows that a legacy incumbent can re-rate through a platform shift — market value from $381bn to $3.0tn in a decade — but Microsoft began near 10-12x earnings, so much of its return came from re-rating; Apple starts at 39.5x and would have to earn the return. Nokia shows the failure mode: 40-50% of global handsets in 2007, under 5% by 2013, because the platform shift moved value to software it did not control. Apple owns its platform and rents the frontier model, closer to Microsoft's early cloud years than to Nokia's collapse; the difference is the price of admission. Two diligence questions decide the entry: what the December guide implies for gross margin ex-refund, and whether the first one-year renewal of the search payment holds near $20bn. Confidence is high in the arithmetic and the multiples, medium in the FY2027 margin path because Apple's pricing response to memory costs is undisclosed, and low in any forecast of AI revenue, which does not yet exist. At or above 48% ex-refund on 2026-11-02 the base moves toward $296 and the starter band toward $270; near 45% it converges on the bear case. [S198, S200]

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Comprehensive Scoring & Recommendation (scoring, revision 3 by Lead Analyst, changed since the previous version, 7,351 characters)
Apple scores 5.7 out of 10: a franchise in the top decile of its peer set, priced in the bottom decile of its own history. The score is not a verdict on the business. Business quality and financial strength score 9 each; valuation scores 2 and earnings durability 4, and the 25% weight on valuation is what turns the composite into a watchlist score rather than a buy. On a margin-adjusted base of $268 the stock is 22% above fair value, and the probability-weighted value of $275 is a 20% negative return from the $344.63 close of 2026-10-30. The recommendation is Watchlist, with no position, a starter band of $240-265 and a full position at or below $225. [S199, S9]

| Dimension | Weight | Score (1-10) | Rationale | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Business quality and moat | 20% | 9 | More than 2.5bn active devices, a record 23.6% iOS share of 2026 shipments, a 76.3% services gross margin and return on assets of 36.1% against Microsoft's 35.9% ROIC and Alphabet's 37.0% | S191, S66, S6, S27, S41 |
| Financial quality and balance sheet | 15% | 9 | Free cash flow 1.06x net income, capex 2.2% of revenue against 34.9% at Microsoft, net cash of $62.2bn and commercial paper cut to $2.0bn | S6, S27 |
| Growth and market runway | 15% | 5 | Revenue up 16.2% in nine months but on price and share taken from a collapsing entry tier; global units fall 16.7%, Services grow 14.1% and China enters a 20% unit decline | S6, S66, S195 |
| Earnings quality and durability | 10% | 4 | FY2025 EPS growth of 22.7% is 10.4% normalised; 2.0 points of the June gross margin are tariff refunds; inventory up 87% against revenue up 16.2% | S5, S6, S199 |
| Valuation | 25% | 2 | 39.5x trailing and 35.2x forward against a 21.0x peer median; 2.7% free-cash-flow yield against a 4.93% ten-year; reverse DCF needs 11.8% growth against 1.5% delivered | S9, S154, S155 |
| Policy and regulatory | 10% | 6 | DMA fine of €500m on 2025-04-23, US contempt finding, DOJ case toward a 2027 trial, search payment on one-year non-exclusive terms; China access intact | S7, S5, S118, S42 |
| Management and capital allocation | 5% | 6 | Succession complete with Ternus as CEO from 2026-09-01; $62.1bn repurchased in nine months at a 2.5% earnings yield against 4.93% | S152, S174, S6, S164 |
| **Composite** | **100%** | **5.7** | Weighted average of the seven dimensions, to one decimal | S9, S6, S154 |

The weighted average is the composite: business quality and financial strength keep the name on the watchlist, while valuation and earnings durability keep it out. Every dimension scoring 7 or above carries a peer or historical benchmark, and the two lowest scores are the ones the price depends on. The installed base, services margin, cash conversion and net cash position are at or above the mega-cap peer set; the multiple is being paid for an earnings base that contains a refund and a memory-cost tailwind the company has already guided away.

The recommendation changes with the margin, not with the narrative. If gross margin settles near 45%, EPS lands between $8.20 and $8.50; at the five-year average multiple of 30.2x that is $248-257, and at the bear multiple of 25x it is $205. If margin holds at 48% and the AI cycle lifts upgrades, EPS reaches $10.50 and 38x gives $399. The full-position entry at or below $225 is set so that the downside to the bear case is about 9%, while the base case pays 19% and the bull case 77%. The recommendation would move to Buy only with two consecutive quarters at or above 47% gross margin ex-refund and a price at or below $265; it would move to Reduce if the stock held above $395 without an EPS upgrade, and to Sell if two quarters of gross margin fell below 45% or services growth fell below 5% for two quarters. [S6, S118]

Position sizing follows the arithmetic rather than the enthusiasm. At $344.63 the probability-weighted return is negative, so the Kelly fraction is zero and the fund holds a watchlist slot, not stock. At $250, with a 70% chance of the base outcome (+10%) and a 30% chance of the bear (-18%), the full Kelly fraction is 16% and a quarter-Kelly is 4%, which becomes the cap because a single regulatory event, loss of the search payment, is worth 9.4% of market value. The plan is a 1-2% starter at $240-265, a 3-4% full position at or below $225, and a trim above $395. Maximum loss at the full-position entry is the $205 bear case, about 9%, against a $399 bull case. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Financial Analysis (financials, revision 5 by Fundamentals Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,785 characters)
Apple's cash conversion and balance sheet are as good as the multiple implies, but the earnings growth is not: fiscal 2025's 22.7% EPS growth becomes 10.4% once the $10.2bn Irish State Aid tax charge in the prior year is normalised out, and 2.0 points of the June 2026 quarter's 50.1% gross margin came from tariff refunds rather than trading. The three-year record is slowing revenue and rising margin: revenue fell 2.8% in fiscal 2023, grew 2.0% in fiscal 2024 and 6.4% to $416,161M in fiscal 2025, while gross margin rose from 44.1% to 46.9% and operating margin from 29.8% to 32.0%. The latest filed period is the quarter ended 2026-06-27, where revenue rose 16.4% to $109,417M on gross margin of 50.1% and operating margin of 32.6%. No fourth-quarter fiscal 2026 earnings release and no fiscal 2026 annual report were on EDGAR as of 2026-10-31; Apple's fiscal 2025 equivalents were filed on 2025-10-30 and 2025-10-31, so the annual report is due imminently and the figures here are trailing twelve months to 2026-06-27 [S5, S6, S13].

| Operating margin | 29.8% | 31.5% | 32.0% | 32.6% | 33.2% | S5, S6 |
| Net income | $96,995M | $93,736M | $112,010M | $29,789M | $128,930M | S5, S6 |
