{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Company Overview (company_overview, revision 4 by Company Analyst, 8,947 characters)
Apple's structure is clean in law — one share class, a majority-independent board and net cash — but not in economics: 61.8% of pretax profit is booked outside the U.S. at a 15.6% effective tax rate, insiders own 0.06%, and the same director has chaired the board since 2000, so the "alignment" in the equity story rests on pay design and on a tax structure the EU has already litigated once. The listed parent is Apple Inc., a California corporation whose common stock ($0.00001 par value) trades on Nasdaq under AAPL: 14,594,180,000 shares outstanding at 2026-07-17, down from 14,697,926,000 at 2026-01-02, and a market capitalisation of $5.03 trillion at 2026-10-30. Votes track economics one-for-one, and the free float is 99.94% because all directors and officers together hold 9,079,765 shares [S5, S6, S65, S172].

| Metric | Value | Benchmark | Signal | Source |

| Shares outstanding | 14,594,180,000 (2026-07-17) | 14,697,926,000 (2026-01-02) | good | S6, S65 |
| Buybacks, nine months to 2026-06-27 | $61.8bn for 215m shares | $70.6bn in the same period of FY2025 | warn | S6 |
| Net cash | $62.2bn (cash and securities $146.5bn less debt $84.3bn, 2026-06-27) | gross debt $84.3bn | good | S6 |
| Effective tax rate | 15.6% (FY2025) | 21% U.S. statutory rate | warn | S5 |
| Foreign pretax profit | 61.8% ($82.0bn of $132.7bn, FY2025) | 38.2% U.S. | warn | S5 |
| Insider ownership | 0.06% (9,079,765 shares) | below the 1% proxy disclosure threshold | warn | S65 |
:::

### Three Irish companies sit between the product and the profit

EX-21 lists 19 subsidiaries domiciled in 15 jurisdictions and omits the rest as not significant; it gives neither ownership percentages nor functions, so what follows is a map of domicile, not of economic activity. The two entities the European Commission found held Apple's intellectual property for sales outside the Americas — Apple Sales International and Apple Operations Europe — no longer appear on the list; in their place are three Irish companies. Apple does not describe the 2015 restructuring or name the entity that now owns the non-U.S. IP, but the tax note shows the consequence: foreign pretax earnings of $82.0bn of $132.7bn in FY2025 and a 15.6% effective rate against 21%. The 5.4-point gap is worth $7.2bn a year in cash tax, and it is exactly what the Commission attacked: the 2016 decision ordered recovery of up to €13bn, the General Court annulled it on 2020-07-15, the Court of Justice reinstated it on 2024-09-10, and Apple took a $10.2bn net charge in Q4 FY2024, paying $15.8bn to Ireland through escrow against a $4.8bn U.S. foreign tax credit [S5, S187]. Ireland closed the opinions in January 2015, so the scheme itself is gone, but the precedent is not. Entity accounts filed with Ireland's Companies Registration Office, which the 10-K does not reproduce, would show where profit now sits.

| Apple Operations International Limited | Ireland | Limited company | Irish holding entity; role not described | Not disclosed in EX-21 | Apple Inc. | S5 |
| Apple Operations Limited | Ireland | Limited company | Irish operating entity; role not described | Not disclosed in EX-21 | Apple Inc. | S5 |

| Braeburn Capital, Inc. | Nevada, U.S. | Corporation | Investment management; role not described | Not disclosed in EX-21 | Apple Inc. | S5 |
| Apple Computer Trading (Shanghai) Co., Ltd. | China | Limited liability company | Greater China trading entity | Not disclosed in EX-21 | Apple Inc. | S5 |

### Capital return, not leverage, is the capital-structure question

Apple carries $62.2bn of net cash — $146.5bn of cash and securities against $84.3bn of debt at 2026-06-27 — and in the nine months to that date repurchased 215m shares for $61.8bn, against $70.6bn a year earlier, under successive $100bn authorisations approved on 2025-05-01 and 2026-04-30, the latest announced with Q2 FY2026 results [S6, S204, S205]. At a $5tn capitalisation each $10bn of repurchase retires 0.2% of the company, so the return depends on the price paid. A 12% year-on-year slowdown in dollars while the shares rose 25.7% is consistent with price discipline, or with lower free cash flow; the filings do not distinguish. Solvency is not the risk; executing the market's largest buyback at a multiple that assumes the AI transition works is.

### Ownership is institutional, and the board is long-tenured

Vanguard holds 9.63% and BlackRock 7.10%, but the BlackRock figure is taken from a 2023-12-31 filing quoted in the 2026 proxy and is stale [S65, S153]. Directors and officers hold 0.06%; Tim Cook's 3,280,295 shares are worth $1.13bn at the current price yet are 0.02% of the company. The board has nine members after Ternus joined on 2026-09-01, seven of them independent; Arthur Levinson, a director since 2000 and chair for 15 years, became lead independent director that day. At the 2026-02-24 annual meeting Levinson drew 9.0% opposition, say-on-pay 8.6% and a "China Entanglement Audit" proposal 1.4% support. That passes Nasdaq's majority-independent rule and is not a governance crisis, but it is a professional board, not a founder-aligned one.

### The business model is an annuity on hardware

Apple sells devices to consumers, enterprises and carriers, but the buyer that matters is the installed base: more than 2.5bn devices whose owners upgrade and pay for services. FY2025 net sales were $416.2bn (+6%), with Services gross margin of 75.4% against 46.9% for the group; in the nine months to 2026-06-27 net sales rose 16% to $364.4bn, Services 14% to $91.7bn and Greater China 30% to $64.8bn after a 4% decline in FY2025 [S5, S6]. That is the growth engine — a replacement cycle plus attach, with China swinging from drag to driver in two years. It makes the model resilient to unit stagnation but not to a remedy that breaks the Services attach: Services produced 39.1% of nine-month gross profit on 25.2% of revenue.

### The legal front is about Services margins, not fines

Three proceedings test the container. The DOJ's civil antitrust suit, filed on 2024-03-21 in the District of New Jersey, seeks equitable relief rather than damages; the Epic litigation produced a 2025-04-30 finding that Apple violated the 2021 injunction, a ban on fees for out-of-app purchases and a referral to the U.S. Attorney for possible criminal contempt; and the EU fined Apple €500m under the Digital Markets Act on 2025-04-23, which Apple appealed [S5, S7]. The fines are small against $416bn of revenue; the remedies are not, because they target the 75%-gross-margin Services line and the App Store's toll gate on 2.5bn devices. Counter-evidence is real — the DOJ must prove market definition, Apple says it has substantial defences, and no court has ordered a structural remedy — but the direction in both jurisdictions is toward alternative distribution and payment, the one outcome that would change the franchise's economics rather than its legal bill.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Founding Team & Key Personnel (team, revision 2 by Company Analyst, 8,571 characters)
The succession is done and internal — Ternus, Srouji, Federighi and Parekh are all Apple lifers — which lowers cultural and execution risk but concentrates the AI transition in a software chief who has outsourced the frontier model to Google and a first-time CEO who has never run a P&L, so the team offers continuity rather than evidence of renewal. The board appointed John Ternus CEO effective 2026-09-01, with Tim Cook as executive chair and Arthur Levinson, chair for the previous 15 years, as lead independent director. Ternus, 50, joined Apple's product design team in 2001, became VP Hardware Engineering in 2013 and SVP in 2021; his record includes iPad, AirPods, the iPhone 17 line and the MacBook Neo, but no disclosed CEO, P&L or capital-allocation role before 2026 [S152, S177].

::: evidence
**The board has already executed the succession by promoting an internal hardware engineer, and the appointment was unanimous.**

The 8-K of 2026-04-20 records the board's appointment of Ternus as CEO effective 2026-09-01, Cook's move to executive chair and Levinson's to lead independent director. Ternus joined Apple in 2001 and has led hardware engineering since 2021. The doubt sits one level down: the AI organisation was rebuilt on 2025-12-01 around an external hire reporting to Federighi, and the rebuilt Siri will run on Google's Gemini models [S152, S177, S183, S186].
:::

The division of labour is unusually clear for a company of this size. Ternus integrates and decides; Johny Srouji became chief hardware officer on 2026-04-20, adding hardware engineering to silicon and becoming the single owner of Apple's deepest technical moat; Craig Federighi owns software and, since December 2025, AI; Eddy Cue runs services and now health; Kevan Parekh funds the company; Sabih Khan runs operations; Deirdre O'Brien runs retail and people [S179, S184]. That design fits a business whose advantage is integration across silicon, software and services, but it places the two capabilities that matter most in the next cycle — silicon and AI/software — in two individuals with no disclosed deputies.

### AI leadership failed once and has been rebuilt around an outside hire and an outside model

John Giannandrea stepped down as AI chief on 2025-12-01 after the Siri delay; Amar Subramanya, formerly corporate VP of AI at Microsoft and head of engineering for Google's Gemini Assistant, joined as VP of AI reporting to Federighi, while the rest of the AI organisation was split between Khan and Cue. On 2026-01-12 Apple and Google announced a multiyear deal to power Apple's AI features, including the Siri upgrade due in 2026, with Gemini [S183, S186]. The mechanism is speed for dependency: Apple gets a competitive assistant without building a frontier model, but it hands a competitor the most valuable interface in consumer technology and caps the differentiation it can charge for. Underwrite AI as a feature that protects the hardware replacement cycle, not as a new profit pool, until Apple discloses model economics.

### Pay and turnover: equity retains, but the C-suite is new

Cook's 2025 total target compensation was $59m: a $3m base unchanged since 2016, a cash incentive at 200% of base and a $50m equity target, positioned in the 80th-90th percentile of the primary peer group; the other named executives target $1m base, 200% cash and $20m equity, and Parekh's target was $16.75m. The CEO ownership guideline is 10 times salary. The design retains executives through the transition rather than rewarding new AI outcomes: 8.6% of votes cast opposed say-on-pay at the 2026-02-24 annual meeting, a protest worth noting but not a rejection. Retention is being tested at the same time. The CFO moved from Luca Maestri to Parekh on 2025-01-01, the COO from Jeff Williams to Khan in July 2025, the general counsel from Kate Adams to Jennifer Newstead on 2026-03-01, the AI chief from Giannandrea to Subramanya on 2025-12-01 and the CEO from Cook to Ternus on 2026-09-01. Against Apple's near-static 2011-2023 executive team that is a large amount of institutional change at once; none was a resignation under pressure, and the risk is coordination while antitrust remedies and a China reset land [S65, S153, S170, S166].

### The missing capability is frontier AI at the top, not finance or operations

No board member has operating AI-lab experience — Wanda Austin ran Aerospace, Alex Gorsky ran Johnson & Johnson — and the AI leader sits at VP level, outside the executive team [S179, S173]. That is the reference check a diligence team should run: who inside Apple can credibly challenge Google's model roadmap, and what retention packages hold Srouji and Federighi, the two people whose departure would impair the franchise. Counter-evidence is genuine: internal succession worked in 2011 when Cook replaced Steve Jobs, Ternus's product record is strong, and the Gemini deal buys time. The judgement is not that the team is weak; it is that the team is unproven at exactly the task the next three years demand.

At 39.5x each repurchased dollar retires stock at a 2.5% earnings yield, below the 4.93% the same dollar would earn in Treasuries, so the buyback supports EPS more than value per share; the diluted count fell from 16,865M in fiscal 2021 to 14,715M in the June 2026 quarter, but the pace is slowing as repurchases fell to $62.1B in nine months from $70.6B. The calendar is dated: fiscal fourth-quarter results on 2026-11-02 with revenue guided to rise 9-11%, fiscal 2027 guidance and any new authorisation that day, the Google search-remedy appeal over a reported $20B of near-pure-margin services revenue, and memory costs that IDC expects to normalise in 2028. [S164, S162, S6, S1]

The counter-case deserves weight. Apple's 2.7% free-cash-flow yield is the highest of the four mega-caps, Services compounds at 14% on a 76% gross margin, and an AI-driven iPhone cycle that holds revenue growth near 10% would earn a 35x forward multiple rather than merely re-rate it. But at $344.63 the arithmetic offers no margin of safety: 25-30x forward earnings, the ten-year mean to the five-year average, is $245-294, 15-29% below the close, and a 6-8% free-cash-flow path is worth $221-255. The asymmetry is in the entry price, not the franchise. Three diligence questions would settle it: what normalised free cash flow does the fiscal 2026 annual report show after the tariff refund and inventory build? What share of Services revenue depends on the Google payment, and how does the appeal resolve? Does the September quarter confirm revenue growth at or above 9%? rows.finding: Display-less smart glasses shipped about 2.25m units in Q1 2026 (+167% YoY); IDC forecasts 13.6m units and $5.1bn revenue in 2026, 27.3m units by 2030, and Meta held 68.7% of Q2 2026 units.
rows.mechanism: A new form factor is scaling fast off a small base and is controlled by one vendor's distribution (EssilorLuxottica retail, Meta's ad-funded subsidies), not by Apple.
rows.benchmark: 13.6m glasses against IDC's just over 1.0bn smartphones in 2026 is 1.3% of phone units; IDC's 2030 forecast is 2.7%.
rows.weakens: The category is growing 26-40% a year and Meta's 68.7% share is a platform-level position Apple does not hold in any new category.
rows.implication: No near-term substitution for the iPhone, but the option value of the next interface sits with a competitor; monitor 2027 launch cycle and cellular-independent display glasses.
rows.confidence: high on IDC figures, medium on the 2030 path because the forecast is three product cycles out
rows.follow_up: At what price and with what connectivity do display glasses stop being a phone accessory?

rows.finding: Meta Ray-Ban Display starts at $799 in the US (£749, €899, CA$1,149) and expanded to five markets on 2026-09-23; it remains phone-tethered and sold largely through eyewear retail.
rows.mechanism: Meta is buying distribution and habit at a premium price with an accessory model, not undercutting the phone.
rows.benchmark: $799 is 38% above the $581 smartphone ASP and 3.4x below Apple's reported $1,999 foldable.
rows.weakens: A $799 accessory that needs an iPhone or Android phone to work does not substitute for either; Meta's own launch material stresses navigation and calls, not phone replacement.
rows.implication: The threat is real only when price falls to the iPhone's own ASP and the phone tether is cut; today neither holds.
rows.confidence: high (company pricing), medium on uptake because no unit disclosure accompanies the expansion
rows.follow_up: What unit sell-through has the US launch achieved, and what share of buyers are iPhone users?

rows.finding: OpenAI's first hardware device is reported (2026-07-14) as a screenless, movable home speaker built with former Apple engineers; Apple sued OpenAI over trade secrets in July 2026.
rows.mechanism: The AI entrant attacks the assistant interface at home first, not the phone; Apple's response is litigation rather than a shipping product.
rows.benchmark: No form factor or launch date is confirmed, against Apple's 2.5bn-device installed base.
rows.weakens: A home speaker is not a phone competitor; the report is unconfirmed and based on anonymous sources.
rows.implication: Do not price an OpenAI phone threat into 2027; price the possibility that the assistant layer moves off the phone.
rows.confidence: medium: single reported account, company has not confirmed
rows.follow_up: Does OpenAI ship a phone or a wearable by 2028, and does it run on iOS?

rows.finding: Open-weight models are production-ready: Qwen3-32B runs on one H100 at about $0.82 per million tokens ($0.34 spot) and Llama 4 Scout at $0.87, with DeepSeek V3.2 needing eight H100s at about $13.89.
rows.mechanism: The assistant layer is commoditising, so a handset maker can self-host a competent model rather than license one, eroding any AI subscription premium and Apple's rented-Gemini differentiation.
rows.benchmark: Under $1 per million tokens is under a tenth of a cent for a 1,000-token query, against a Gemini licence of undisclosed cost.
rows.weakens: The source is a GPU-cloud vendor with an interest in self-hosting, and it flags its own benchmark figures as unverified; quality at the low end is not established.
rows.implication: Apple's AI position is not a moat and neither is a rival's; value stays in distribution and integration.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: What does Apple pay Google per query, and what share of Siri queries run on-device?

rows.finding: Transsion sits outside IDC's Q2 2026 global top five, whose 'Others' bucket is 27.7% of 276.3m units; HONOR also sits outside the top five but grew H1 2026 shipments 53% and holds more than 50% of foldables in Malaysia, Singapore and Hong Kong.
rows.mechanism: Memory costs concentrate share at the premium end and squeeze the sub-$200 tier where Transsion competes, while HONOR wins a foldable niche rather than scale.
rows.benchmark: Samsung 22.7% and Apple 20.2% against a combined 'Others' of 27.7% in Q2 2026.
rows.weakens: Neither challenger has scale; the HONOR figures come from a media summary of IDC data, and regional shares for both were not retrievable in this run.
rows.implication: The competitive threat in 2026 is consolidation at the top, not disruption from below; watch HONOR in foldables as the price umbrella Apple's $1,999 Duo creates.
rows.confidence: medium: IDC top-five table is primary-grade, HONOR growth is second-hand
rows.follow_up: What are Transsion's and HONOR's unit shares in Africa, India and Southeast Asia in 2026?

rows.finding: Apple's calendar-2026 gains are supply-driven: Apple units fell only 1.3% against Android's 24.3% because it secured memory early, and iOS reached a record 23.6% of shipments while Samsung, which sells memory, grew 8.1% and took 3.2 points.
rows.mechanism: When memory is over 65% of low-end bill of materials, supply access determines share; the advantage lapses when memory normalises and Samsung keeps its cost position.
rows.benchmark: Samsung 22.7% (+3.2pp) versus Apple 20.2% (+3.9pp) in Q2 2026; Xiaomi -26.4%, vivo -19.6%.
rows.weakens: Apple's gain is real and larger in percentage points than Samsung's; if memory stays tight beyond 2028 the advantage persists.
rows.implication: Do not capitalise the 2026 share gain as a permanent competitive improvement; it is a cyclical rent.
rows.confidence: high on the shares, medium on the timing of normalisation
rows.follow_up: How much memory inventory has Apple contracted, and at what price through 2027?

arguments.markdown:
Apple's silicon-plus-OS stack remains the widest integrated consumer stack, but in 2026 Apple rented the one layer it could not build — the frontier model — leaving distribution, custom silicon and regulated health sensing as the defensible assets, not leadership in artificial intelligence. In two years the A20 Pro moved to TSMC N2, the C2 reached the flagship, the first foldable shipped at $1,999, and on 2026-01-12 Apple and Google said the next Apple Foundation Models would be Gemini-based [S58, S59, S63, S64].

### The silicon lead is real, costly, and rented from TSMC

The A19 Pro used TSMC N3P; a year later the A20 Pro moved to N2 with a 32-core Neural Engine and ~52 TOPS. N2 wafers are reported at ~$30,000 against $18,000-20,000 for 3nm. Product gross margin was 39.9% in the nine months to 2026-06-27 versus 36.9%, but only with tariff refunds and mix offsetting "higher costs, including memory", and the 10-Q expects memory and node constraints to intensify [S6, S64].

| Metric | Value | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Node, A19 Pro / A20 Pro | TSMC N3P (2025) / N2 (2026) | Trade reporting | S63, S64 |
| Neural Engine, A20 Pro | 32 cores, ~52 TOPS, ~2x A19 Pro | Trade-press estimate | S64 |
| N2 wafer price | ~$30,000 vs $18,000-20,000 at 3nm | Trade-press estimate | S64 |
| On-device model / PCC context | ~3B parameters / 32K tokens | Apple research and docs | S61, S62 |

### Apple Intelligence is an architecture with a rented brain

On device Apple runs a ~3B-parameter model with KV-cache sharing and 2-bit quantisation-aware training; server queries go to a Parallel-Track Mixture-of-Experts model inside Private Cloud Compute, which enforces stateless processing, no privileged access and attested images. Memory bandwidth caps on-device inference at a few billion parameters, so harder queries are offloaded. Where Gemini-derived inference runs is unresolved: Apple says Apple Intelligence continues on its devices and PCC, while trade reporting puts the Gemini computation in Google's cloud at a reported ~$1bn a year; neither is Apple-confirmed. China's CAC approved Apple Intelligence on 2026-07-15, with Qwen and Baidu on a separate stack. Differentiation is orchestration, distribution and privacy, not model quality; the strategic consequence is that a fixed-R&D moat becomes a cost that scales with usage, so rented intelligence pays only if it lifts upgrades or carries a subscription [S8, S58, S60, S61, S86, S120, S171].

| Dimension | Apple 2024 (AFM v1) | Apple 2026 (Gemini-based) | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Model ownership | Own ~3B on-device plus server model | Gemini-derived | S58, S61 |
| Cost | Fixed R&D and capex | Fixed R&D plus per-query licence | S58, S86 |
| What Apple keeps | Silicon, OS, orchestration | Silicon, OS, interface, orchestration | S58, S60 |

### Products: a strong cycle, a late foldable, a spatial computer that never became a platform

The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max launched on 2026-09-09 at $1,199 and $1,299; the foldable iPhone Duo at $1,999 went on sale on 2026-10-23. iPhone net sales rose 22% to $196.5bn in the nine months to 2026-06-27, with Greater China up 30%. The C2 supports US mmWave and uses 15% less energy than the C1X, but the larger iPhone 18 Pro Max appears to keep a Qualcomm modem, so Qualcomm keeps leverage over the highest-ASP SKU. Vision Pro is the counter-example: ~45,000 units in the December 2025 quarter, ~600,000 lifetime, IDC forecasting ~290,000 in 2026 [S59, S13, S87].

| Product | Stage | Launch | Revenue or share | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone 18 Pro / Pro Max | Commercial | 2026-09 | $196.5bn, 54% of 9M | 39.9% products | C2 in Pro Max, 2027 | S59, S6 |
| iPhone Duo (foldable) | Commercial | 2026-10-23 | In iPhone; undisclosed | Not disclosed | First-quarter volume | S59 |
| Watch Series 11 / Ultra 3 | Commercial | 2025-09 | Wearables $27.3bn, +2% | Not disclosed | Hypertension roll-out | S5, S6 |
| Services | Commercial | — | $91.7bn, +14% | 76.3% | AI tier / iCloud+ gating | S6, S107 |

### What is enforceable is regulatory, not patent

Apple publishes no patent count; the FY2025 10-K says only that it is "pursuing thousands of applications around the world" and that no single right protects its products. Families and technology-specific grants remain unverified — no patent number could be checked, because USPTO Patent Center and EPO Espacenet could not be searched — and an export of 2024-2026 Apple-assigned families in on-device AI, health, foldable hinge and AR optics has been requested. arguments.markdown:
Apple's silicon-plus-OS stack is the widest integrated consumer stack, but in 2026 Apple rented the one layer it could not build — the frontier model — leaving distribution, custom silicon and regulated health sensing as the defensible assets, not leadership in artificial intelligence. In two years the A20 Pro moved to TSMC N2, the C2 reached the flagship, the first foldable shipped at $1,999, and on 2026-01-12 Apple and Google said the next Apple Foundation Models would be Gemini-based [S58, S59, S63, S64].

### The silicon lead is real, costly, and rented from TSMC

The A19 Pro used TSMC N3P; a year later the A20 Pro moved to N2 with a 32-core Neural Engine and ~52 TOPS. N2 wafers are reported at ~$30,000 against $18,000-20,000 for 3nm. Product gross margin was 39.9% in the nine months to 2026-06-27 versus 36.9%, but only with tariff refunds and mix offsetting "higher costs, including memory", and the 10-Q expects memory and node constraints to worsen [S6, S64].

| Metric | Value | Method | Source |

| Node, A19 Pro / A20 Pro | TSMC N3P (2025) / N2 (2026) | Trade reporting | S63, S64 |
| Neural Engine, A20 Pro | 32 cores, ~52 TOPS, ~2x A19 Pro | Trade-press estimate | S64 |
| N2 wafer price | ~$30,000 vs $18,000-20,000 at 3nm | Trade-press estimate | S64 |
| On-device model / PCC context | ~3B parameters / 32K tokens | Apple research and docs | S61, S62 |

### Apple Intelligence is an architecture with a rented brain

On device Apple runs a ~3B-parameter model with KV-cache sharing and 2-bit quantisation-aware training; server queries go to a Parallel-Track Mixture-of-Experts model inside Private Cloud Compute, with stateless processing, no privileged access and attested images. Memory bandwidth caps on-device inference at a few billion parameters, so harder queries are offloaded. Where Gemini-derived inference runs is unresolved: Apple says Apple Intelligence continues on its devices and PCC, while trade reporting puts the Gemini computation in Google's cloud at a reported ~$1bn a year; neither is Apple-confirmed. China's CAC approved Apple Intelligence on 2026-07-15, with Qwen and Baidu on a separate stack. Differentiation is orchestration, distribution and privacy, not model quality; the strategic consequence is that a fixed-R&D moat becomes a cost that scales with usage, so rented intelligence pays only if it lifts upgrades or carries a subscription [S8, S58, S60, S61, S86, S120, S171].

| Cost | Fixed R&D and capex | Fixed R&D plus per-query licence | S58, S86 |
| What Apple keeps | Silicon, OS, orchestration | Silicon, OS, interface, orchestration | S58, S60 |

### Products: a strong cycle, a late foldable, a spatial computer that never became a platform

The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max launched on 2026-09-09 at $1,199 and $1,299; the foldable iPhone Duo at $1,999 went on sale on 2026-10-23. iPhone net sales rose 22% to $196.5bn in the nine months to 2026-06-27, with Greater China up 30%. The C2 supports US mmWave and uses 15% less energy than the C1X, but the larger iPhone 18 Pro Max appears to keep a Qualcomm modem, so Qualcomm keeps leverage over the top SKU. Vision Pro is the counter-example: ~45,000 units in the December 2025 quarter, ~600,000 lifetime, IDC forecasting ~290,000 in 2026 [S59, S13, S87].

### What is enforceable is regulatory, not patent

Apple publishes no patent count; the FY2025 10-K says only that it is "pursuing thousands of applications around the world" and that no single right protects its products. Families and technology-specific grants remain unverified — no patent number could be checked, because USPTO Patent Center and EPO Espacenet could not be searched — and an export of 2024-2026 Apple-assigned families in on-device AI, health, foldable hinge and AR optics has been requested. | Frontier model | 3 | Available to licence, as Apple has shown | Gemini licence reported at ~$1bn a year | 1-2 years, by cheque | S58 |
| FDA-cleared health features | 7 | Each feature needs its own trial and clearance | Four Apple clearances since 2024; rivals must file separately | 3-4 years | S30, S33, S34 |
| Installed base and developers | 8 | Switching costs and services attach, but not exclusive | Every platform owner holds a multi-billion-device base; monetisation depth is the barrier | 10+ years | S5 |
| **Composite** | **8/10 hardware, 4/10 AI** | Hard to copy, easy to rent; IP adds no credit | 8+ years for a new entrant; Samsung still buys flagship silicon | — | S58, S64, S207 |

The replication test is a base rate. Intel bought Infineon's wireless unit for ~$1.4bn in 2011 and sold its modem business to Apple for $1bn in 2019 — nine years without a durable phone-modem position. Apple started from that purchase, 2,200 engineers and over 17,000 wireless patents, and shipped the C1 in the iPhone 16e in February 2025, just over five years later; in 2026 the largest iPhone still appears to carry Qualcomm. Samsung designs Exynos and owns a foundry, yet every Galaxy S25 shipped on Snapdragon 8 Elite in 2025. Parity takes eight to ten years, which is why the composite is capped at 8/10 with no IP credit. A granted-family count against Samsung and Alphabet would move it: parity in on-device AI, health, hinge and AR optics would restore the withheld point (9/10); fewer than half Samsung's families in foldables and AR optics would cut those sub-scores and add freedom-to-operate cost, holding 8/10 or below. Counter-evidence: Siri needed a Google licence, the car was cancelled, Vision Pro never reached platform volumes. The 10-Q warns DMA rules may stop Apple launching features "such as Siri AI" in some jurisdictions. Diligence: does the Google deal allow on-device fine-tuning, and does the 2027 Pro Max move fully to the C2? [S6, S58, S59, S87, S206, S207, S209, S210]

::: evidence
**Apple's integration advantage is durable in silicon and distribution, but it no longer extends to the model layer.**

The A20 Pro's 2nm node and 32-core Neural Engine keep Apple at the leading edge, and its FDA clearances give it a regulated feature estate. But basing the next Apple Foundation Models on Gemini concedes that the frontier layer is bought: the reported ~$1bn licence turns a fixed R&D advantage into a variable cost paid to a competitor, and availability varies by jurisdiction, with China on a Qwen/Baidu stack and DMA rules possibly withholding Siri AI in the EU [S6, S58, S64, S86, S120, S171].
:::

arguments.markdown:
Apple's silicon-plus-OS stack is the widest integrated consumer stack, but in 2026 Apple rented the one layer it could not build — the frontier model — leaving distribution, custom silicon and regulated health sensing as the defensible assets, not leadership in artificial intelligence. In two years the A20 Pro moved to TSMC N2, the C2 reached the flagship, the first foldable shipped at $1,999, and on 2026-01-12 Apple and Google said the next Apple Foundation Models would be Gemini-based [S58, S59, S63, S64].

### The silicon lead is real, costly, and rented from TSMC

The A19 Pro used TSMC N3P; a year later the A20 Pro moved to N2 with a 32-core Neural Engine and ~52 TOPS. N2 wafers are reported at ~$30,000 against $18,000-20,000 for 3nm. Product gross margin was 39.9% in the nine months to 2026-06-27 versus 36.9%, but only with tariff refunds and mix offsetting "higher costs, including memory", and the 10-Q expects memory and node constraints to worsen [S6, S64].

| Metric | Value | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Node, A19 Pro / A20 Pro | TSMC N3P (2025) / N2 (2026) | Trade reporting | S63, S64 |
| Neural Engine, A20 Pro | 32 cores, ~52 TOPS, ~2x A19 Pro | Trade-press estimate | S64 |
| N2 wafer price | ~$30,000 vs $18,000-20,000 at 3nm | Trade-press estimate | S64 |
| On-device model / PCC context | ~3B parameters / 32K tokens | Apple research and docs | S61, S62 |

### Apple Intelligence is an architecture with a rented brain

On device Apple runs a ~3B-parameter model with KV-cache sharing and 2-bit quantisation-aware training; server queries go to a Parallel-Track Mixture-of-Experts model inside Private Cloud Compute, with stateless processing, no privileged access and attested images. Memory bandwidth caps on-device inference at a few billion parameters, so harder queries are offloaded. Where Gemini-derived inference runs is unresolved: Apple says Apple Intelligence continues on its devices and PCC, while trade reporting puts the Gemini computation in Google's cloud at a reported ~$1bn a year; neither is Apple-confirmed. China's CAC approved Apple Intelligence on 2026-07-15, with Qwen and Baidu on a separate stack. Differentiation is orchestration, distribution and privacy, not model quality; so a fixed-R&D moat becomes a cost that scales with usage: rented intelligence pays only if it lifts upgrades or carries a subscription [S8, S58, S60, S61, S86, S120, S171].

| Dimension | Apple 2024 (AFM v1) | Apple 2026 (Gemini-based) | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Model ownership | Own ~3B on-device plus server model | Gemini-derived | S58, S61 |
| Cost | Fixed R&D and capex | Fixed R&D plus per-query licence | S58, S86 |
| What Apple keeps | Silicon, OS, orchestration | Silicon, OS, interface, orchestration | S58, S60 |

### Products: a strong cycle, a late foldable, a spatial computer that never became a platform

The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max launched on 2026-09-09 at $1,199 and $1,299; the foldable iPhone Duo at $1,999 went on sale on 2026-10-23. iPhone net sales rose 22% to $196.5bn in the nine months to 2026-06-27, with Greater China up 30%. The C2 supports US mmWave and uses 15% less energy than the C1X, but the larger iPhone 18 Pro Max appears to keep a Qualcomm modem, so Qualcomm keeps the top-SKU leverage. Vision Pro is the counter-example: ~45,000 units in the December 2025 quarter, ~600,000 lifetime, IDC forecasting ~290,000 in 2026 [S59, S13, S87].

| Product | Stage | Launch | Revenue or share | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone 18 Pro / Pro Max | Commercial | 2026-09 | $196.5bn, 54% of 9M | 39.9% products | C2 in Pro Max, 2027 | S59, S6 |
| iPhone Duo (foldable) | Commercial | 2026-10-23 | In iPhone; undisclosed | Not disclosed | First-quarter volume | S59 |
| Watch Series 11 / Ultra 3 | Commercial | 2025-09 | Wearables $27.3bn, +2% | Not disclosed | Hypertension roll-out | S5, S6 |
| Services | Commercial | — | $91.7bn, +14% | 76.3% | AI tier / iCloud+ gating | S6, S107 |

### What is enforceable is regulatory, not patent

Apple publishes no patent count; the FY2025 10-K says only that it is "pursuing thousands of applications around the world" and that no single right protects its products. Families and technology-specific grants remain unverified — no patent number could be checked, because USPTO Patent Center and EPO Espacenet could not be searched — and an export of 2024-2026 Apple-assigned families in on-device AI, health, foldable hinge and AR optics has been requested. The only cross-company measure retrieved is grants: Apple took 2,722 US patents in 2025, sixth and down 11.6%, against Samsung's 7,054, first; in AI filings Apple is absent from the top three, where Samsung filed 2,162, Huawei 1,822 and Google 1,672. The enforceable estate is regulatory: the four FDA clearances below [S5, S29, S30, S33, S34, S208, S211].

| Asset | Identifier | Jurisdiction | Date | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Patent portfolio | Count not disclosed | US and foreign | Ongoing | "Thousands of applications"; families and grants unverified | US grants 2,722 vs 7,054 Samsung; family count missing | S5, S208, S211 |
| Hypertension Notification | K250507 | US FDA | 2025-09-11 | Cleared 510(k) | Watch sensing | S30 |
| Sleep Apnea Notification | K240929 | US FDA | 2024-09-13 | Cleared 510(k) | Watch sensing | S33 |
| Hearing Aid Feature | DEN230081 | US FDA | 2024-09-12 | De Novo granted | AirPods | S34 |
| Medical Imaging Calibration | K253582 | US FDA | 2026-04-01 | Cleared 510(k) | Display calibration | S29 |

### The moat is wide at the bottom of the stack and thin at the top

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Benchmark or base rate | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Custom SoC and modem | 8 | Design team plus N2 access; no IP credit while family grants are unverified | Samsung designs Exynos and owns a foundry, yet every Galaxy S25 shipped on Snapdragon 8 Elite in 2025 | 8+ years to parity | S59, S64, S207 |
| Hardware-OS integration | 8 | Six operating systems co-designed with custom silicon | No peer ships a leading-edge phone SoC and its OS at scale | 5-7 years | S5 |
| On-device model efficiency | 5 | Quantisation and KV-cache methods are published | ~3B parameters and 32K context disclosed | 1-2 years | S61 |
| Frontier model | 3 | Available to licence, as Apple has shown | Gemini licence reported at ~$1bn a year | 1-2 years, by cheque | S58 |
| FDA-cleared health features | 7 | Each feature needs its own trial and clearance | Four Apple clearances since 2024; rivals must file separately | 3-4 years | S30, S33, S34 |
| Installed base and developers | 8 | Switching costs and services attach, but not exclusive | Every platform owner holds a multi-billion-device base; monetisation depth is the barrier | 10+ years | S5 |
| **Composite** | **8/10 hardware, 4/10 AI** | Hard to copy, easy to rent; IP adds no credit | 8+ years for a new entrant; Samsung still buys flagship silicon | — | S58, S64, S207 |

The replication test is a base rate. Intel bought Infineon's wireless unit for ~$1.4bn in 2011 and sold its modem business to Apple for $1bn in 2019 — nine years without a durable phone-modem position. Apple started from that purchase, 2,200 engineers and over 17,000 wireless patents, and shipped the C1 in the iPhone 16e in February 2025, just over five years later; in 2026 the largest iPhone still appears to carry Qualcomm. Samsung designs Exynos and owns a foundry, yet every Galaxy S25 shipped on Snapdragon 8 Elite in 2025. Parity takes eight to ten years, which is why the composite is capped at 8/10 with no IP credit. A granted-family count against Samsung and Alphabet would move it: parity in on-device AI, health, hinge and AR optics would restore the withheld point (9/10); fewer than half Samsung's families in foldables and AR optics would cut those sub-scores and add freedom-to-operate cost, holding 8/10 or below. Counter-evidence: Siri needed a Google licence, the car was cancelled, Vision Pro never reached platform volumes. The 10-Q warns DMA rules may stop Apple launching features "such as Siri AI" in some jurisdictions. Diligence: does the Google deal allow on-device fine-tuning, and does the 2027 Pro Max move fully to the C2? [S6, S58, S59, S87, S206, S207, S209, S210]

::: evidence
**Apple's integration advantage is durable in silicon and distribution, but it no longer extends to the model layer.**

The A20 Pro's 2nm node and 32-core Neural Engine keep Apple at the leading edge, and its FDA clearances give it a regulated feature estate. But basing the next Apple Foundation Models on Gemini concedes that the frontier layer is bought: the reported ~$1bn licence turns a fixed R&D advantage into a variable cost paid to a competitor, and availability varies by jurisdiction, with China on a Qwen/Baidu stack and DMA rules possibly withholding Siri AI in the EU [S6, S58, S64, S86, S120, S171].
:::

arguments.markdown:
Apple's markets are contracting in units and expanding in value, and Apple is taking value share inside that contraction: the case for FY2026-FY2028 rests on premiumisation and installed-base monetisation rather than unit volume or a Services mix shift, is strongest in the United States, is adequate in Europe, and in China depends on a domestic champion's pricing discipline.

### The pool is shrinking in units and growing in value

IDC's August 2026 forecast has worldwide smartphone shipments at just over 1.0 billion units in 2026, down 16.7%, while total market value rises 6.3% to $613 billion and the average selling price reaches a record $581, up 27.6% in a year. The cause is cost, not demand: DRAM and NAND prices are up more than 300% year on year, memory is more than 65% of bill of materials at the low end, and the sub-$100 tier fell close to 60% in the second quarter of 2026. This is a supply shock with a dated end — IDC expects memory prices to keep rising until at least 2028 — so 2026-2027 flatters Apple's unit share while genuinely lifting its price, and 2028 is the test of whether either survives. [S66]

Two sizing methods agree closely: 1.0 billion units at the $581 average price gives $581 billion, within 5% of IDC's $613 billion, so the two series are consistent rather than rival estimates. On that base Apple's serviceable market is the premium tier it addresses — an iOS share of 23.6% of 2026 shipments, a record — while the revenue it can obtain is what it already books: $466.8 billion trailing twelve months to 2026-06-27, which at the 16.2% growth rate of the first nine months of FY2026 implies $483 billion for FY2026. [S6]

| TAM, personal computing devices | Units only | ~398m units, -11.3%; 1.5% CAGR to 2030 | 2026 | IDC | S103 |

| SOM, Apple revenue | Reported | $466.8bn TTM | TTM to 2026-06-27 | Apple 10-Q | S6 |
| Near-term obtainable revenue | FY2025 $416.2bn grown at the 9M FY2026 rate | ~$483bn | FY2026E | Calculation on Apple filings | S5, S13 |

### China is the swing factor, and India sits in the wrong line

Apple's revenue is moving toward the faster-growing regions, but the swing is China. In the first nine months of FY2026 Greater China produced $64.8 billion, up 30.0% on a base of $49.9 billion, after two years of decline from $72.6 billion in FY2023; the Americas grew 11.4% to $149.4 billion, Europe 16.1% to $95.6 billion, Japan 10.4% and Rest of Asia Pacific 19.4%. Greater China's $14.9 billion increase contributes 4.1 percentage points of the group's 16.2% growth, more than any other segment, and part of it is currency. Europe includes India, the Middle East and Africa, so the fastest-growing large smartphone market is invisible in the segment line. [S13]

### Services carries the profit, but the mix moved back to hardware

The fastest-growing pool Apple monetises is Services, but its share of revenue fell in FY2026: $91.7 billion in the first nine months, 25.2% of $364.4 billion and up 14%, at a 76.3% gross margin against 75.4% and a 26.2% share in FY2025. Hardware grew faster than Services, so the mix shifted toward premium handsets and China rather than toward the recurring pool — the opposite of what a Services-led thesis needs. The app economy itself has no published size in the sources retrieved: neither Apple nor the platform owners disclose app-store gross billings or mobile-advertising revenue, so Apple's Services line is the measured pool. The installed base is disclosed at more than 2.5 billion active devices on 2026-01-29, up from 2.35 billion a year earlier, but Apple publishes no replacement rate. [S5, S6, S174, S191]

### Who pays, and how much demand is policy

The budget owner is the consumer, but the transaction is intermediated: 60% of FY2025 net sales, $249,697 million of $416,161 million, went through carriers, resellers and distributors. Apple does not disclose the carrier-only share or the subsidy per device, but it does disclose the risk transfer: resellers offer financing, instalment plans or subsidies that "may be discontinued or modified any time", and carriers were 27% of trade receivables at 2026-06-27, $8,477 million of $31,398 million, with one customer at 18%. Price protection and other customer incentives are deducted from Products net sales without an amount being given, so the channel's cost to Apple is a revenue deduction, not a disclosed expense; one point of wholesale terms across the indirect channel is $2.5 billion of revenue, 1.3% of FY2025 gross profit. The demand that channel finances is policy-sensitive: US and UK interest-free financing holds the premium end while emerging markets fall more than 20%, China's government subsidy faded in the second quarter of 2026, and India's $600-800 band grew 32% on financing after the sub-$100 tier fell 59%. Policy also moves margin: after the 2026-02-20 Supreme Court ruling struck down certain IEEPA tariffs, refunds contributed 2.0 points of the June quarter's 50.1% gross margin. Carrier 10-K equipment-revenue and promotional lines, or paid channel sell-in data, would settle the missing subsidy figure; Apple's fiscal 2026 annual report was not on EDGAR at 2026-10-31. [S5, S6, S105, S40, S13]

### What would break the premiumisation case

Counter-evidence is fourfold. If memory prices normalise from 2028, the entry tier rebuilds and the 2026 share gain is contestable. If China's June-quarter demand was pulled forward ahead of second-half price increases, as IDC's China team reports, the 30% growth line is a launch and currency effect. If courts and the European Commission remove the App Store take rate, the margin layer that offsets hardware cyclicality stops compounding. And the search-distribution payment — $20 billion in 2022, 17% of trailing Services revenue of $120.5 billion and 22% of trailing Services gross profit of $91.6 billion — has not been banned: the 2025-09-02 remedies decision declined to ban distributor payments, and the December 2025 final judgment is under appeal by Google and the Department of Justice, both pending at 2026-10-29. The investor implication is narrow: in a 1-billion-unit market Apple can grow device revenue only if price rises faster than units fall, making average selling price, China durability, the carrier channel and the Services take rate the variables worth monitoring. Sizing confidence is high, because two independent methods agree within 5%; confidence that the mix shift holds to 2028 is medium. Three diligence questions remain open: what share of Services revenue is commission rather than subscription, advertising or licensing? How much of the Greater China increase is currency? And what is the current average replacement cycle, measured rather than asserted? [S66, S40, S82, S118, S42]

IDC forecasts 2026 shipments at just over 1.0 billion units against a market value of $613 billion and an ASP of $581 (S66, S102). Apple's nine-month FY2026 revenue was $364.4 billion, up 16.2%, with Greater China up 30.0% on a $49.9 billion base and Services at 25.2% of revenue against 26.2% in FY2025 (S13, S6). In FY2025, 60% of net sales, $249,697 million, went through carriers, resellers and distributors, and carriers were 27% of trade receivables at 2026-06-27 (S5, S6).

Apple's exit is the market, not a buyer, and at $344.63 the margin-adjusted 15/50/35 case is worth $266, 23% below the close, which means the discipline is a $240-265 starter, a full position at or below $225 and a trim at $395. The exit is a sale into the market: a 1% position in a $1B fund is $10M, 0.07% of the $13.84B daily traded value. Slower policy risks are DMA and DOJ commission rules, and China, where revenue was $64.8B in nine months of fiscal 2026 and can turn on policy rather than execution. At 38.9x margin-adjusted earnings there is no cushion for a services margin shock. [S118, S42, S82, S13]

The strongest case against this discipline is that a 30x-plus multiple never offers a margin of safety again. Its five-year range of 22.1-40.6x shows a 25x entry is not exotic; if Services compounds at 14% on a 76% gross margin and the buyback retires 1.6% of the shares a year, a fund that waits for $225 may never own the best cash generator in the market, and the cost of the discipline is opportunity rather than loss. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Financial Analysis (financials, revision 5 by Fundamentals Analyst, 8,785 characters)
Apple's cash conversion and balance sheet are as good as the multiple implies, but the earnings growth is not: fiscal 2025's 22.7% EPS growth becomes 10.4% once the $10.2bn Irish State Aid tax charge in the prior year is normalised out, and 2.0 points of the June 2026 quarter's 50.1% gross margin came from tariff refunds rather than trading. The three-year record is slowing revenue and rising margin: revenue fell 2.8% in fiscal 2023, grew 2.0% in fiscal 2024 and 6.4% to $416,161M in fiscal 2025, while gross margin rose from 44.1% to 46.9% and operating margin from 29.8% to 32.0%. The latest filed period is the quarter ended 2026-06-27, where revenue rose 16.4% to $109,417M on gross margin of 50.1% and operating margin of 32.6%. No fourth-quarter fiscal 2026 earnings release and no fiscal 2026 annual report were on EDGAR as of 2026-10-31; Apple's fiscal 2025 equivalents were filed on 2025-10-30 and 2025-10-31, so the annual report is due imminently and the figures here are trailing twelve months to 2026-06-27 [S5, S6, S13].

### The growth is half tax base effect, and a quarter buyback

Fiscal 2025's net income rose 19.5%, but pretax income rose 7.5% ($132,729M against $123,485M) and the tax provision fell 30.3% to $20,719M because fiscal 2024 carried the one-time $10.2bn Irish charge — $15.8bn payable to Ireland, offset by a $4.8bn US foreign tax credit and $823M of released unrecognised benefits. Normalising fiscal 2024 at fiscal 2025's 15.6% rate gives $104,222M and underlying growth of 7.5%, not 19.5%. The EPS gap above that is the buyback: from fiscal 2023 to fiscal 2025 net income grew 15.5% while diluted EPS grew 21.7% and diluted shares fell 5.1%, so 5.4 percentage points of EPS growth was a smaller denominator — and that contribution is fading, at 1.9 percentage points in the trailing twelve months (EPS +16.9% against net income +15.1%), because repurchases slowed to $62,094M in the nine months to 2026-06-27 from $70,579M while operating cash flow rose 43%. Capital return has stopped outrunning cash: buybacks and dividends were $97,866M against free cash flow of $136,683M, or 72%, against 107% in fiscal 2025, and net cash rose by $28,410M in nine months. At the $344.63 close on 2026-10-30 and the 14,594.2M shares issued and outstanding reported on the 10-Q cover at 2026-07-17, equity is worth $5.03trn; on trailing diluted EPS of $8.72 that is 39.5x earnings and a 2.72% free cash flow yield, while the ten-year Treasury yielded 4.93%. Diluted shares of 14,715M are the EPS denominator and sit 0.8% above the outstanding count, so the two bases are consistent. Repurchasing at that spread is accretive to EPS and not obviously accretive to value per share [S5, S6, S9].

### Cash is real; the working-capital cushion is not

Cash generation is the strongest part of the record and the hardest to fake: operating cash flow of $146,724M against capital expenditure of $10,041M, with free cash flow at 1.06x net income. The anomaly is fiscal 2025, when free cash flow fell to 0.88x of net income despite $111,482M of operating cash flow; cash paid for income taxes that year was $43,369M, 32.7% of pretax income against a 15.6% book rate and 21.1% in fiscal 2024 — a gap consistent with settlement payments on the Irish case and the TCJA repatriation tax, the final $8.8bn of which was paid in the nine months to 2026-06-27. That supports reading the gap as timing, and the recovery to 1.06x is consistent with it. The working-capital change runs the other way: inventory reached $11,092M at 2026-06-27 from $5,925M a year earlier, an 87% increase against 16.2% revenue growth, lifting days inventory to 16.9 from 9.4 and pulling the cash conversion cycle to −56.8 days from −71.1 at the fiscal 2025 year-end [S5, S6].

The balance sheet carries no leverage risk: at 2026-06-27 Apple held $146,517M of cash and marketable securities against $84,344M of debt, for net cash of $62,173M, up from $33,763M, with commercial paper cut to $1,997M from $7,979M, and other income and expense netted to −$321M in fiscal 2025 because interest earned on the securities book offsets interest paid. The commitments that matter are forward purchases — $57.0bn of manufacturing purchase obligations, $56.2bn due within twelve months, and $29.3bn of other purchase obligations — which fix component supply and, with it, the cost base when memory prices move. Two accounting details deserve attention: gross intangible assets rose $13,270M to $38,220M in nine months with no goodwill recognised, which indicates purchased intellectual property, content or asset acquisitions rather than share purchases, and is not explained in the quarterly filing; and gross unrecognised tax benefits were $23.2bn at 2025-09-27, of which $10.6bn would affect the effective rate and up to $6bn may move within twelve months [S6].

### Returns are distorted by the buyback, not flattered by the business

Reported returns are not usable as quality scores: return on equity was 148.8% and return on invested capital 320.6% on invested capital of $45,347M — $107,520M of equity plus $84,344M of debt less $146,517M of securities — because $258,212M of cumulative buybacks shrank the equity base. The honest comparison is return on assets of 36.1% against Microsoft's 35.9% return on invested capital in fiscal 2026 and Alphabet's 37.0% in fiscal 2025 [S6, S27, S41].

### What moves the outcome, and by how much

The geographic picture also cuts against the standard bear case: Greater China revenue rose 30% to $64,839M in the nine months to 2026-06-27 and 22% in the June quarter, so nine months already exceed the whole of fiscal 2025's $64,377M after two years of decline. What moves the outcome most is gross margin. On trailing-twelve-month revenue of $466,823M one point of gross margin is $4,668M of pretax profit, or 3.0% of net income, while one point of revenue growth at the current margin is $1,878M, or 1.5%. Three cases, all on the trailing twelve months and none a forecast: a two-point margin gain takes EPS to $9.24, a two-point give-back to $8.20, and a two-point give-back with the loss of the search licence to $7.11, 18.8% below the base — and the licence should be modelled as intact but repriced annually, because the September 2025 order permitted non-exclusive placement payments of one year or less rather than ending them, while the $20bn figure is a 2022 court-record number Apple has never confirmed. The cash is real and the balance sheet is net cash; the growth is weaker than reported; and the margin sits at a cyclical high with a tariff-refund component inside it. An investor paying 39.5x trailing earnings is paying for the first and third to persist while the second is already reversing. The diligence question that matters most is what the fiscal 2026 annual report says about inventory composition and the split between refund and product mix, neither of which the quarterly filings settle [S6, S82, S118].

::: info warning
**The fiscal 2026 gross margin is not yet a clean number.** Strip out the tariff refund Apple attributes to the June quarter and the margin is still above any full year in this record, but a smaller step-change than the reported figure implies; against an inventory build growing faster than revenue, the annual report carries the burden of proof.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Market & Industry Analysis (market, revision 5 by Market Analyst, 8,990 characters)
Apple's markets are contracting in units and expanding in value, and Apple is taking value share inside that contraction: the case for FY2026-FY2028 rests on premiumisation and installed-base monetisation rather than unit volume or a Services mix shift, is strongest in the United States, is adequate in Europe, and in China depends on a domestic champion's pricing discipline.

### The pool is shrinking in units and growing in value

IDC's August 2026 forecast has worldwide smartphone shipments at just over 1.0 billion units in 2026, down 16.7%, while total market value rises 6.3% to $613 billion and the average selling price reaches a record $581, up 27.6% in a year. The cause is cost, not demand: DRAM and NAND prices are up more than 300% year on year as capacity is redirected to AI servers, memory is more than 65% of bill of materials at the low end, and the sub-$100 tier fell close to 60% in the second quarter of 2026. This is a supply shock with a dated end, so 2026-2027 flatters Apple's unit share while genuinely lifting its price, and 2028 is the test of whether either survives. [S66]

Two sizing methods agree closely: 1.0 billion units at the $581 average price gives $581 billion, within 5% of IDC's $613 billion, so the two series are consistent rather than rival estimates. On that base Apple's serviceable market is the premium tier it addresses — an iOS share of 23.6% of 2026 shipments, a record — while the revenue it can obtain is what it already books: $466.8 billion trailing twelve months to 2026-06-27, which at the 16.2% growth rate of the first nine months of FY2026 implies $483 billion for FY2026. [S6]

| Measure | Method | Figure | Year | Publisher | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| TAM, smartphone value (top-down) | Industry value estimate | $613bn, +6.3% | 2026 | IDC | S66 |
| TAM, smartphone value (bottom-up) | 1.0bn units x $581 ASP | ~$581bn | 2026 | Calculation on IDC inputs | S66 |
| TAM, personal computing devices | Units only | ~398m units, -11.3%; 1.5% CAGR to 2030 | 2026 | IDC | S103 |
| SAM, premium smartphone tier | iOS share of shipments | 23.6% of units, record | 2026 | IDC | S66 |
| SOM, Apple revenue | Reported | $466.8bn TTM | TTM to 2026-06-27 | Apple 10-Q | S6 |
| Near-term obtainable revenue | FY2025 $416.2bn grown at the 9M FY2026 rate | ~$483bn | FY2026E | Calculation on Apple filings | S5, S13 |

### China is the swing factor, and India sits in the wrong line

Apple's revenue is moving toward the faster-growing regions, but the swing is China. In the first nine months of FY2026 Greater China produced $64.8 billion, up 30.0% on a base of $49.9 billion, after falling from $72.6 billion in FY2023 to $64.4 billion in FY2025; the Americas grew 11.4% to $149.4 billion, Europe 16.1% to $95.6 billion, Japan 10.4% and Rest of Asia Pacific 19.4%. Greater China's $14.9 billion increase contributes 4.1 percentage points of the group's 16.2% growth, more than any other segment, and part of it is currency: a favourable renminbi effect in Greater China, an unfavourable yen effect in Japan. Europe includes India, the Middle East and Africa, so the fastest-growing large smartphone market is invisible in the segment line. [S13]

| Region | Market size (year) | Growth | Apple's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| United States / North America | 60% of Q1 2026 shipments above $800; 24.9% of global PC-plus-tablet units | Smartphone -6.3% in 2026; PC -14.6% in 2026 | Entered, leads the premium tier; 41.0% of Apple revenue is the Americas | Tariffs, carrier financing, antitrust suits | Samsung, Lenovo, HP, Dell | S39, S103, S13 |
| Greater China | ~66m units a quarter, 264m a year | -4.3% in Q2 2026, fifth straight decline; H2 2026 could be -20% | 18.1% of units, second behind Huawei; revenue +30.0% | Domestic operating system, subsidy withdrawal, data rules | Huawei 22.6%, OPPO 16.0%, vivo 16.0%, Xiaomi 12.4% | S40, S6 |
| Europe (includes India, Middle East, Africa) | India 31.0m units in Q1 2026 at a record $302 ASP | India units -4.1% but value +5.8%; Europe revenue +16.1% | Entered; fourth by units in India | DMA, price sensitivity, distribution | Samsung, Xiaomi, vivo, Lenovo, HP | S105, S103, S13 |
| Japan | Revenue $24.4bn in 9M FY2026 | Revenue +10.4%; units -25.6% in 2026 | Entered, premium strong; weak yen cuts revenue | Yen, saturated device base | Local Android vendors, Samsung | S13, S103, S6 |
| Rest of Asia Pacific | Revenue $30.2bn in 9M FY2026 | Revenue +19.4%; units -14% in 2026 | Entered, premium-led | Price-sensitive mass market, currency | Samsung, Xiaomi, OPPO, vivo | S13, S39, S103 |

### Services carries the profit, but the mix moved back to hardware

The fastest-growing pool Apple monetises is Services, but its share of revenue fell in FY2026: $91.7 billion in the first nine months, 25.2% of $364.4 billion and up 14%, at a 76.3% gross margin against 75.4% for FY2025, when Services was $109.2 billion, 26.2% of revenue. Hardware grew faster than Services, so the mix shifted toward premium handsets and China rather than toward the recurring pool — the opposite of what a Services-led thesis needs. The app economy itself has no published size in the sources retrieved: neither Apple nor the platform owners disclose app-store gross billings or mobile-advertising revenue, so Apple's Services line is the measured pool. The installed base is disclosed: Apple put it at more than 2.5 billion active devices on 2026-01-29, up from 2.35 billion a year earlier, which is the stock behind Services and the upgrade pool, but Apple still does not publish a replacement rate, so upgrade timing cannot be sized from public data. [S5, S6, S174, S191]

### Who pays, and how much demand is policy

The budget owner is the consumer, in a discretionary purchase that is increasingly financed. In the United States and United Kingdom interest-free financing is common, so IDC expects the premium end to hold while emerging markets fall more than 20%; in India brands lean on financing after the sub-$100 tier fell 59% and the $600-800 band grew 32%; in China the government subsidy that supported earlier quarters faded in the second quarter of 2026, so demand there is being withdrawn by policy rather than created by it. Policy moves Apple's margin more than a product cycle does: after the February 20, 2026 Supreme Court ruling struck down certain IEEPA tariffs, Apple recognised refunds as a reduction of product cost of sales, and those refunds contributed 2.0 percentage points of the June 2026 quarter's 50.1% gross margin. [S105, S40, S13]

### What would break the premiumisation case

Counter-evidence is fourfold. If memory prices normalise in 2028 as IDC expects, the entry tier rebuilds and Apple's 2026 share gain is contestable again. If China's June-quarter demand was pulled forward ahead of second-half price increases, as IDC's China team reports, the 30% growth line is a launch and currency effect. If courts and the European Commission remove the App Store take rate, the margin layer that offsets hardware cyclicality stops compounding. And the search-distribution payment — $20 billion in 2022, equal to 17% of trailing Services revenue of $120.5 billion and 22% of trailing Services gross profit of $91.6 billion — has not been banned: the September 2, 2025 remedies decision declined to ban distributor payments, and the December 2025 final judgment that restricts distribution is under appeal by Google and the Department of Justice, both pending at 2026-10-29. The investor implication is narrow: in a 1-billion-unit market Apple can grow device revenue only if price rises faster than units fall, making average selling price, China durability and the Services take rate the variables worth monitoring. Sizing confidence is high, because two independent methods agree within 5%; confidence that the mix shift holds to 2028 is medium, because it rests on China and a legally contested commission. Three diligence questions remain open: what share of Services revenue is commission-based rather than subscription, advertising or licensing? How much of the Greater China increase is currency? And what is the current average replacement cycle, measured rather than asserted? [S66, S40, S82, S118, S42, S5]

::: evidence
**Apple's addressable device market fell 16.7% in units in 2026 while growing 6.3% in value, and Apple's revenue grew 16.2% over nine months — the gap is premiumisation and China, not market growth, and Services is not gaining mix (S66, S13, S6).**

IDC forecasts 2026 shipments at just over 1.0 billion units against a market value of $613 billion and an ASP of $581 (S66, S39). Apple's nine-month FY2026 revenue was $364.4 billion, up 16.2%, with Greater China up 30.0% on a $49.9 billion base and Services at 25.2% of revenue against 26.2% in FY2025 (S13, S6). The bottom-up check of 1.0 billion units at $581 gives $581 billion, within 5% of IDC's value estimate (S66).
:::"}],"isError":false}

arguments.markdown:
Apple's silicon-plus-OS stack is the widest integrated consumer stack, but in 2026 Apple rented the one layer it could not build — the frontier model — leaving distribution, custom silicon and regulated health sensing as the defensible assets, not leadership in artificial intelligence. In two years the A20 Pro moved to TSMC N2, the C2 reached the flagship, the first foldable shipped at $1,999, and on 2026-01-12 Apple and Google said the next Apple Foundation Models would be Gemini-based [S58, S59, S63, S64].

### The silicon lead is real, costly, and rented from TSMC

The A19 Pro used TSMC N3P; a year later the A20 Pro moved to N2 with a 32-core Neural Engine and ~52 TOPS. N2 wafers are reported at ~$30,000 against $18,000-20,000 for 3nm. Product gross margin was 39.9% in the nine months to 2026-06-27 versus 36.9%, but only with tariff refunds and mix offsetting "higher costs, including memory", and the 10-Q expects memory and node constraints to worsen [S6, S64].

| Metric | Value | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Node, A19 Pro / A20 Pro | TSMC N3P (2025) / N2 (2026) | Trade reporting | S63, S64 |
| Neural Engine, A20 Pro | 32 cores, ~52 TOPS, ~2x A19 Pro | Trade-press estimate | S64 |
| N2 wafer price | ~$30,000 vs $18,000-20,000 at 3nm | Trade-press estimate | S64 |
| On-device model / PCC context | ~3B parameters / 32K tokens | Apple research and docs | S61, S62 |

### Apple Intelligence is an architecture with a rented brain

On device Apple runs a ~3B-parameter model with KV-cache sharing and 2-bit quantisation-aware training; server queries go to a Parallel-Track Mixture-of-Experts model inside Private Cloud Compute, with stateless processing, no privileged access and attested images. Memory bandwidth caps on-device inference at a few billion parameters; harder queries are offloaded. Where Gemini-derived inference runs is unresolved: Apple says Apple Intelligence continues on its devices and PCC, while trade reporting puts the Gemini computation in Google's cloud at a reported ~$1bn a year; neither is Apple-confirmed. China's CAC approved Apple Intelligence on 2026-07-15, with Qwen and Baidu on a separate stack. Differentiation is orchestration, distribution and privacy, not model quality; so a fixed-R&D moat becomes a cost that scales with usage: rented intelligence pays only if it lifts upgrades or carries a subscription [S8, S58, S60, S61, S86, S120, S171].

| Dimension | Apple 2024 (AFM v1) | Apple 2026 (Gemini-based) | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Model ownership | Own ~3B on-device plus server model | Gemini-derived | S58, S61 |
| Cost | Fixed R&D and capex | Fixed R&D plus per-query licence | S58, S86 |
| What Apple keeps | Silicon, OS, orchestration | Silicon, OS, interface, orchestration | S58, S60 |

### Products: a strong cycle, a late foldable, a spatial computer that never became a platform

The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max launched on 2026-09-09 at $1,199 and $1,299; the foldable iPhone Duo at $1,999 went on sale on 2026-10-23. iPhone net sales rose 22% to $196.5bn in the nine months to 2026-06-27, with Greater China up 30%. The C2 supports US mmWave and uses 15% less energy than the C1X, but the larger iPhone 18 Pro Max appears to keep a Qualcomm modem, so Qualcomm keeps the top-SKU leverage. Vision Pro is the counter-example: ~45,000 units in the December 2025 quarter, ~600,000 lifetime, IDC forecasting ~290,000 in 2026 [S59, S13, S87].

| Product | Stage | Launch | Revenue or share | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone 18 Pro / Pro Max | Commercial | 2026-09 | $196.5bn, 54% of 9M | 39.9% products | C2 in Pro Max, 2027 | S59, S6 |
| iPhone Duo (foldable) | Commercial | 2026-10-23 | In iPhone; undisclosed | Not disclosed | First-quarter volume | S59 |
| Watch Series 11 / Ultra 3 | Commercial | 2025-09 | Wearables $27.3bn, +2% | Not disclosed | Hypertension roll-out | S5, S6 |
| Services | Commercial | — | $91.7bn, +14% | 76.3% | AI tier / iCloud+ gating | S6, S107 |

### What is enforceable is regulatory, not patent

Apple publishes no patent count; the FY2025 10-K says only that it is "pursuing thousands of applications around the world" and that no single right protects its products. Families and technology-specific grants remain unverified — no patent number could be checked, because USPTO Patent Center and EPO Espacenet could not be searched — and an export of 2024-2026 Apple-assigned families in on-device AI, health, foldable hinge and AR optics has been requested. The only cross-company measure retrieved is grants: Apple took 2,722 US patents in 2025, sixth and down 11.6%, against Samsung's 7,054, first. The enforceable estate is regulatory: the four FDA clearances below.

| Asset | Identifier | Jurisdiction | Date | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Patent portfolio | Count not disclosed | US and foreign | Ongoing | "Thousands of applications"; families and grants unverified | US grants 2,722 vs 7,054 Samsung; AI filings 2,162 Samsung, 1,822 Huawei, 1,672 Google; family count missing | S5, S208, S211 |
| Hypertension Notification | K250507 | US FDA | 2025-09-11 | Cleared 510(k) | Watch sensing | S30 |
| Sleep Apnea Notification | K240929 | US FDA | 2024-09-13 | Cleared 510(k) | Watch sensing | S33 |
| Hearing Aid Feature | DEN230081 | US FDA | 2024-09-12 | De Novo granted | AirPods | S34 |
| Medical Imaging Calibration | K253582 | US FDA | 2026-04-01 | Cleared 510(k) | Display calibration | S29 |

### The moat is wide at the bottom of the stack and thin at the top

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Benchmark or base rate | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Custom SoC and modem | 8 | Design team plus N2 access; no IP credit while family grants are unverified | Samsung designs Exynos and owns a foundry, yet every Galaxy S25 shipped on Snapdragon 8 Elite in 2025 | 8+ years to parity | S59, S64, S207 |
| Hardware-OS integration | 8 | Six operating systems co-designed with custom silicon | No peer ships a leading-edge phone SoC and its OS at scale | 5-7 years | S5 |
| On-device model efficiency | 5 | Quantisation and KV-cache methods are published | ~3B parameters and 32K context disclosed | 1-2 years | S61 |
| Frontier model | 3 | Available to licence, as Apple has shown | Gemini licence reported at ~$1bn a year | 1-2 years, by cheque | S58 |
| FDA-cleared health features | 7 | Each feature needs its own trial and clearance | Four Apple clearances since 2024; rivals must file separately | 3-4 years | S30, S33, S34 |
| Installed base and developers | 8 | Switching costs and services attach, but not exclusive | Every platform owner holds a multi-billion-device base; monetisation depth is the barrier | 10+ years | S5 |
| **Composite** | **8/10 hardware, 4/10 AI** | Hard to copy, easy to rent; IP adds no credit | 8+ years for a new entrant; Samsung still buys flagship silicon | — | S58, S64, S207 |

The replication test is a base rate. Intel bought Infineon's wireless unit for ~$1.4bn in 2011 and sold its modem business to Apple for $1bn in 2019 — nine years without a durable phone-modem position. Apple started from that purchase, 2,200 engineers and over 17,000 wireless patents, and shipped the C1 in the iPhone 16e in February 2025, just over five years later; in 2026 the largest iPhone still appears to carry Qualcomm. Samsung designs Exynos and owns a foundry, yet every Galaxy S25 shipped on Snapdragon 8 Elite in 2025. Parity takes eight to ten years, which is why the composite is capped at 8/10 with no IP credit. A granted-family count against Samsung and Alphabet would move it: parity in on-device AI, health, hinge and AR optics would restore the withheld point (9/10); fewer than half Samsung's families in foldables and AR optics would cut those sub-scores and add freedom-to-operate cost, holding 8/10 or below. Counter-evidence: Siri needed a Google licence, the car was cancelled, Vision Pro never reached platform volumes. The 10-Q warns DMA rules may stop Apple launching features "such as Siri AI" in some jurisdictions. Diligence: does the Google deal allow on-device fine-tuning, and does the 2027 Pro Max move fully to the C2? [S6, S58, S59, S87, S206, S207, S209, S210]

::: evidence
**Apple's integration advantage is durable in silicon and distribution, but it no longer extends to the model layer.**

The A20 Pro's 2nm node and 32-core Neural Engine keep Apple at the leading edge, and its FDA clearances give it a regulated estate. But basing the next Apple Foundation Models on Gemini concedes that the frontier layer is bought: the reported ~$1bn licence turns a fixed R&D advantage into a variable cost paid to a competitor, and availability varies by jurisdiction, with China on a Qwen/Baidu stack and DMA rules possibly withholding Siri AI in the EU [S6, S58, S64, S86, S120, S171].
:::

arguments.markdown:
Apple's markets are contracting in units and expanding in value, and Apple is taking value share inside that contraction: the case for FY2026-FY2028 rests on premiumisation and installed-base monetisation rather than unit volume or a Services mix shift, is strongest in the United States, adequate in Europe, and in China depends on a domestic champion's pricing discipline.

### The pool is shrinking in units and growing in value

IDC's August 2026 forecast has worldwide smartphone shipments at just over 1.0 billion units in 2026, down 16.7%, while total market value rises 6.3% to $613 billion and the average selling price reaches a record $581, up 27.6% in a year. The cause is cost, not demand: DRAM and NAND prices are up more than 300% year on year, memory is more than 65% of bill of materials at the low end, and the sub-$100 tier fell close to 60% in the second quarter of 2026. This supply shock has a dated end — IDC expects memory prices to rise until at least 2028 — so 2026-2027 flatters Apple's unit share while lifting its price; 2028 tests whether either survives. [S66]

Two sizing methods agree closely: 1.0 billion units at the $581 average price gives $581 billion, within 5% of IDC's $613 billion, so the two series are consistent rather than rival estimates. On that base Apple's serviceable market is the premium tier it addresses — an iOS share of 23.6% of 2026 shipments, a record — while the revenue it can obtain is what it already books: $466.8 billion trailing twelve months to 2026-06-27, or about $483 billion for FY2026 at the nine-month growth rate. [S6]

### China is the swing factor, and India sits in the wrong line

Apple's revenue is moving toward the faster-growing regions, but the swing is China. ### Services carries the profit, but the mix moved back to hardware

The fastest-growing pool Apple monetises is Services, but its share of revenue fell in FY2026: $91.7 billion in the first nine months, 25.2% of $364.4 billion and up 14%, at a 76.3% gross margin against 75.4% and a 26.2% share in FY2025. Hardware grew faster than Services, so the mix shifted toward premium handsets and China rather than toward the recurring pool — the opposite of what a Services-led thesis needs. The app economy has no published size in the sources retrieved — no platform owner discloses app-store billings or mobile-advertising revenue — so Apple's Services line is the measured pool. The installed base is disclosed at more than 2.5 billion active devices on 2026-01-29, up from 2.35 billion a year earlier, but Apple publishes no replacement rate. [S5, S6, S174, S191]

### Who pays, and how much demand is policy

The budget owner is the consumer, but the transaction is intermediated: 60% of FY2025 net sales, $249,697 million of $416,161 million, went through carriers, resellers and distributors. Apple does not disclose the carrier-only share or the subsidy per device, but it does disclose the risk transfer: resellers offer financing, instalment plans or subsidies that "may be discontinued or modified any time", and carriers were 27% of trade receivables at 2026-06-27, $8,477 million of $31,398 million, with one customer at 18%. Price protection and other customer incentives are deducted from Products net sales without an amount being given, so the channel's cost to Apple is a revenue deduction, not a disclosed expense; one point of wholesale terms across the indirect channel is $2.5 billion of revenue, 1.3% of FY2025 gross profit. The demand that channel finances is policy-sensitive: US and UK interest-free financing holds the premium end while emerging markets fall more than 20%, China's government subsidy faded in the second quarter of 2026, and India's $600-800 band grew 32% after the sub-$100 tier fell 59%. Policy also moves margin: after the 2026-02-20 Supreme Court ruling struck down certain IEEPA tariffs, refunds contributed 2.0 points of the June quarter's 50.1% gross margin. Carrier 10-K equipment-revenue and promotional lines, or paid channel sell-in data, would settle the missing subsidy figure; Apple's fiscal 2026 annual report was not on EDGAR at 2026-10-31. [S5, S6, S105, S40, S13]

### What would break the premiumisation case

Counter-evidence is fourfold. If memory prices normalise from 2028, the entry tier rebuilds and the 2026 share gain is contestable. If China's June-quarter demand was pulled forward ahead of second-half price increases, as IDC's China team reports, the 30% growth line is a launch and currency effect. If courts and the European Commission remove the App Store take rate, the margin layer that offsets hardware cyclicality stops compounding. And the search-distribution payment — $20 billion in 2022, 17% of trailing Services revenue of $120.5 billion and 22% of trailing Services gross profit of $91.6 billion — has not been banned: the 2025-09-02 remedies decision declined to ban distributor payments, and the December 2025 final judgment is under appeal by Google and the Department of Justice, both pending at 2026-10-29. The investor implication is narrow: in a 1-billion-unit market Apple can grow device revenue only if price rises faster than units fall, so average selling price, China durability, the carrier channel and the Services take rate are the variables to monitor. Sizing confidence is high, because two independent methods agree within 5%; confidence that the mix shift holds to 2028 is medium. Three diligence questions remain open: what share of Services revenue is commission rather than subscription, advertising or licensing? How much of the Greater China increase is currency? And what is the current average replacement cycle, measured rather than asserted? [S66, S40, S82, S118, S42]

::: evidence
**Apple's addressable device market fell 16.7% in units in 2026 while growing 6.3% in value, and revenue grew 16.2% over nine months — the gap is premiumisation and China, not market growth, and 60% of sales run through a channel whose subsidy Apple does not disclose (S66, S13, S6, S5).**
