rows.finding: In FY2025 Services produced $82,314M of gross profit on $109,158M of revenue (75.4% margin), 42.2% of Apple's $195,201M total gross profit from 26.2% of revenue; Services gross profit per $1 of Products gross profit rose from $0.55 in FY2023 to $0.73 in FY2025.
rows.mechanism: The installed base is an annuity: a device sold at a 36-38% product margin carries a stream of services at 71-76% margin whose incremental cost is close to nil, so each hardware dollar underwrites a growing high-margin attach.
rows.benchmark: Apple's own FY2023 mix (Services 22.2% of revenue, 35.7% of gross profit) and Microsoft's 67.9% FY2026 gross margin, which is a pure software mix rather than a hardware-plus-attach mix.
rows.weakens: Services gross margin is flat year on year at 75.6% in Q3 FY2026, so the attach is not itself becoming more profitable; the mix gain comes from revenue share, not margin rate.
rows.implication: The mix-shift thesis is real at the gross-profit level and is the single best explanation for the re-rating; it argues for paying for durability of attach rather than for device growth.
rows.confidence: high - audited segment and category data in the FY2025 10-K
rows.follow_up: What share of Services gross profit comes from third-party licensing (Google) versus Apple's own subscriptions, and does Apple disclose App Store revenue?

rows.finding: The mix shift reversed in FY2026: over the nine months to 2026-06-27 Products gross profit grew 26.3% ($108,819M vs $86,190M) while Services gross profit grew 15.3% ($69,963M vs $60,670M), so Services fell to 39.1% of gross profit from 42.2% in FY2025.
rows.mechanism: Products gross margin jumped to 39.9% in 9M FY2026 and 40.1% in Q3 from 34.5% a year earlier, which Apple attributes to 'a different mix of products and tariff refunds, partially offset by higher costs, including memory'. Hardware margin expansion, not services mix, drove FY2026 gross profit.
rows.benchmark: FY2025 Products gross margin of 36.8% and FY2024's 37.2%; the 3.1-point nine-month gain is the largest in the three-year record and part of it is a tariff-refund credit rather than trading.
rows.weakens: The prevailing narrative that Apple's margin expansion is services-led. In FY2026 it was hardware-led and partly one-off, so the durability of the current 50.1% total gross margin is weaker than the Services share implies.
rows.implication: Do not capitalise the FY2026 gross margin as structural; normalise products gross margin toward the high 30s before valuing, and treat the refund as non-recurring.
rows.confidence: high on the arithmetic; medium on how much of the margin gain is refund versus mix, which Apple does not split
rows.follow_up: How large was the tariff refund recognised in products cost of sales, and when does the Section 232 semiconductor investigation resolve?

rows.finding: Apple earns licensing revenue from Google for search distribution and concedes in its FY2025 10-K that a reversal of the 2025-09-02 D.C. District Court remedies order on appeal 'could result in imposition of certain remedies initially proposed by the DOJ, such as those prohibiting Google from offering the Company commercial terms for search distribution'; the payment was $20bn in 2022 per unsealed court documents. Apple does not disclose the current amount.
rows.mechanism: Google pays for default placement because Apple's base produces high-value search queries; the payment is booked inside Services advertising at near-100% incremental margin, so its loss would hit Services gross profit disproportionately to revenue.
rows.benchmark: $20bn in 2022 equals 18.3% of Apple's FY2025 Services revenue of $109,158M and 24.3% of FY2025 Services gross profit of $82,314M, on a two-year-old figure that Apple has never confirmed.
rows.weakens: Apple's Services revenue is often described as diversified; on these figures a single counterparty's litigation outcome sits inside the fastest-growing line, and Eddy Cue testified that Google queries on Apple devices fell for the first time in April 2025.
rows.implication: A regulatory hit to services profit is a live, priced risk rather than a tail; it argues for a discount to the multiple, and for asking what the replacement economics are in an AI-search world.
rows.confidence: high on the legal timetable and Apple's own risk language; medium on the dollar amount, which is a 2022 court-record figure and not a company disclosure
rows.follow_up: What is the current annual payment, what is its term, and has Apple disclosed any replacement search partner or AI-answer deal?

rows.finding: App Store revenue is recognised net: Apple records 'only the commission it retains' for third-party app sales, and it is currently subject to a US court order 'preventing it from imposing any commission or fee on certain purchases that consumers make', although the Ninth Circuit has instructed the district court to amend the injunction to allow a commission.
rows.mechanism: Because the commission is recognised gross in Services revenue at close to zero cost, any take-rate compression passes straight to revenue and gross profit with no offsetting cost reduction; the same is true of every euro of DMA-driven alternative distribution in the EU.
rows.benchmark: The DMA already forces alternative distribution, alternative payment processing and new fee structures in the EU; Apple states its compliance plan 'has been challenged by the Commission' and that non-compliance carries significant fines.
rows.weakens: Apple does not disclose App Store revenue, the commission rate, or the EU share of it, so the size of the exposure cannot be calculated from filings - it can only be bounded by the Services line.
rows.implication: Treat a structural take-rate cut as a permanent margin haircut to Services rather than a one-off; size it from total Services gross profit of $82,314M in FY2025.
rows.confidence: high - Apple's own risk-factor language
rows.follow_up: What proportion of Services revenue is App Store commission, and how much of that is EU-billed? Apple's Developer Program fee schedule would settle the current rate.

rows.finding: During 2025, 60% of Apple's net sales went through indirect channels (carriers and resellers) and 40% through its own retail and online stores, while SG&A was $27,601M, or 6.6% of revenue.
rows.mechanism: Carriers carry a large part of device acquisition cost through subsidies and instalment plans, so Apple's own selling cost stays near 7% of revenue while a competitor selling direct would carry retail, marketing and channel margin itself - a structural CAC advantage that is not visible in a unit-economics waterfall.
rows.benchmark: SG&A at 6.6% of revenue versus R&D at 8.3%; and versus a telecom-carrier distribution model in which the carrier subsidises the handset to sell a contract.
rows.weakens: Unit economics per device, LTV and LTV:CAC cannot be computed from Apple's disclosure at all, so any per-device table in this report is an approximation and is labelled as such.
rows.implication: The 40/60 direct/indirect split is the reason Apple's margins survive at scale; it also means a carrier-driven demand shock (subsidy withdrawal, eSIM-led direct sales) moves volumes faster than Apple's cost base.
rows.confidence: high on the split; low on translating it into a per-customer CAC, because Apple discloses no unit volumes, no ASP and no marketing line
rows.follow_up: What share of iPhone sales in the US is carrier-financed, and how is the shift to eSIM-only devices changing the carrier/Apple revenue split?

rows.finding: Apple states that future gross margins 'will be subject to volatility and downward pressure', and its Q3 FY2026 10-Q warns of 'a period of supply constraints and increasing costs for components ... including advanced semiconductors, storage (NAND) and memory (DRAM)' and that it 'expects these trends to intensify' and 'may materially negatively impact' gross margin.
rows.mechanism: Apple's hardware gross margin is a residual of component pricing against a fixed price ladder; when DRAM and NAND inflate, Apple either absorbs the cost or raises prices into a price-sensitive consumer, so the 39.9% products margin is the peak of a cycle rather than a floor.
rows.benchmark: Products gross margin of 36.8% in FY2025, 37.2% in FY2024 and 36.5% in FY2023 - a three-year band of 0.7 points that the FY2026 39.9% now sits 3.1 points above.
rows.weakens: Any valuation that holds the FY2026 gross margin or operating margin constant; also weakens the case that Apple's pricing power fully offsets input inflation.
rows.implication: Model a gross margin give-back of 1.5-3 points in FY2027 as the memory cycle bites, which on FY2026 TTM revenue of $466,823M is $7-14bn of gross profit before any offset.
rows.confidence: high - the company itself names the mechanism
rows.follow_up: How much of FY2026 memory cost inflation has already been passed through in price, and what is the contract length on DRAM/NAND supply?

rows.finding: Apple converted 1.06x of trailing-twelve-month net income into free cash flow to 2026-06-27 ($136,683M free cash flow on $128,930M net income) with capex at 2.2% of revenue, against Microsoft at 0.50x and 34.9% capex/revenue in FY2026, Alphabet at 0.55x and 22.7% in FY2025 and Meta at 0.76x and 34.7% in FY2025.
rows.mechanism: Apple outsources wafer fabrication and final assembly to TSMC and Foxconn, so the industry's capital intensity sits on suppliers' balance sheets; Microsoft, Alphabet and Meta own their datacentres and are now spending a third of revenue on AI compute, which is why their cash conversion has fallen.
rows.benchmark: Microsoft FY2026 capex $115,948M on $331,839M revenue; Alphabet FY2025 capex $91,447M on $402,836M; Meta FY2025 capex $69,691M on $200,966M.
rows.weakens: The assumption that Apple's capital-light model is unambiguously superior: it also means Apple is buying AI capability through R&D expense (up 32% year on year to $11,729M in Q3 FY2026) rather than owning compute, and may be under-invested relative to peers if AI inference becomes the core platform.
rows.implication: Apple's cash conversion is the best in the peer set and supports the multiple; the offsetting risk is that the peers' capex is building a capability Apple is renting.
rows.confidence: high - all four from their own filings
rows.follow_up: What is Apple's own AI compute arrangement and cost, given R&D is up 33% in nine months to $34,035M?

plan.decision_question: How does Apple convert a hardware installed base into services profit, and how durable is that mix shift through the Google remedies, the DMA and Epic, and a memory-cost cycle?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple runs a hardware annuity with a services margin on top - every dollar of product gross profit now carries 73 cents of services gross profit - but the mix shift that the multiple pays for stalled in FY2026, when hardware margins helped by tariff refunds grew gross profit twice as fast as Services.
plan.why_different: This section owns the revenue model and the per-unit economics - who pays, for what, and at what margin; the financial statements and their quality sit in the financials section, and share and competitor behaviour sit in the competitive landscape.
plan.mechanism: A device sold at a 37-40% product gross margin carries a stream of services at 71-76% gross margin whose incremental cost is near zero; the attach is funded by 60% indirect distribution in which carriers absorb acquisition cost, and the highest-margin layer of Services is a single counterparty's licensing payment.
plan.comparison_set: Apple's own FY2023-FY2025 progression, and Microsoft, Alphabet and Meta on gross margin, capex intensity and cash conversion; telecom-carrier distribution as the channel benchmark.
plan.counter_evidence: FY2026 products gross profit grew 26.3% versus Services at 15.3%, so the mix shift reversed; the Google payment depends on an appeal Apple says could remove it; the App Store commission is under a court order and DMA-mandated alternative fees; and memory and NAND costs are rising with the company warning margins face downward pressure.
plan.visual: The unit-economics waterfall per $1,000 of revenue by line, plus a pricing-and-mix table showing what each line earns and the disclosed price/mix driver.
plan.prohibited: banned_empty_phrases: 'strong ecosystem', 'sticky ecosystem', 'seamless ecosystem', 'high barriers to entry', 'wide moat', 'strong brand', 'well positioned', 'huge installed base', 'services flywheel', 'clear business model'; banned_vagueness: 'many users', 'billions of devices' without a date and a source, 'about $20bn' without a period; no unlabelled per-device figures.

queries: Apple 10-K FY2025 Item 1 - direct vs indirect distribution: 40% direct, 60% indirect net sales

rows.finding: Apple reported more than 2.5 billion active devices on 2026-01-29, against more than 2.35 billion a year earlier. Against $466,823M of TTM revenue to 2026-06-27 that is at most $187 of revenue per active device a year; on FY2025 figures the same arithmetic gives $166 of revenue and $44 of Services per device.
rows.mechanism: The installed base is the annuity denominator: revenue per device can rise only through services attach, mix or price, because device count grows slowly.
rows.benchmark: Installed base grew roughly 6% (2.35bn to 2.5bn) while nine-month FY2026 revenue grew 16.2%, so revenue per device rose; no peer discloses a comparable active-device base.
rows.weakens: Company-reported and unaudited; devices are not users; the denominator is a floor and four months older than the trailing revenue.
rows.implication: The next leg of growth must come from monetising existing devices, making services attach and Pro-model mix the variables to underwrite rather than unit growth.
rows.confidence: high on the arithmetic, medium on the interpretation
rows.follow_up: What is services revenue per active device and the paid-subscription attach rate by category?

rows.finding: 60% of FY2025 net sales, $249,697M of $416,161M, went through carriers, resellers and distributors; Apple's risk factor states that resellers offer financing, installment plans or subsidies that 'may be discontinued or modified any time'.
rows.mechanism: Carriers underwrite handset demand, which lowers Apple's acquisition cost but transfers pricing and promotion decisions to third parties.
rows.benchmark: SG&A was $27,601M, 6.6% of FY2025 revenue, below R&D at 8.3%; the indirect channel carries demand generation that a direct model would put in Apple's own cost base.
rows.weakens: Apple does not disclose the carrier-only share of sales or the wholesale discount, so the revenue at risk cannot be isolated.
rows.implication: A carrier promotion cut hits units before it hits Apple's cost line, so hardware revenue is more cyclical than the services mix implies.
rows.confidence: high on the disclosure, medium on materiality
rows.follow_up: What share of iPhone units is sold through carriers in the US, Europe and Japan?

rows.finding: Carriers were 27% of trade receivables at 2026-06-27, $8,477M of $31,398M, down from 34%, $13,524M of $39,777M, at 2025-09-27; one customer was 18% of receivables at 2026-06-27 against 12% a year earlier.
rows.mechanism: The channel's balance-sheet exposure is shrinking even as its revenue share holds, so the risk sits in demand and pricing, not in collectibility.
rows.benchmark: Carrier receivables were 1.8% of TTM revenue at 2026-06-27 against 3.2% of FY2025 revenue at 2025-09-27; Apple requires credit support or collateral from certain customers.
rows.weakens: Receivables measure billing, not subsidy depth or channel margin.
rows.implication: Channel credit is not the exposure; the 60% revenue dependence is, and it belongs in the hardware sensitivity rather than the balance-sheet risk.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Which customer is the 18% of receivables, and what credit support covers it?

rows.finding: Apple reduces Products net sales for future returns, price protection and other customer incentive programmes based on expectations and history, without disclosing the amount.
rows.mechanism: Channel margin and price protection are contra-revenue, so a deeper wholesale discount cuts product revenue and product gross margin rather than raising SG&A.
rows.benchmark: One point of wholesale terms across the $249,697M indirect channel equals $2.5bn of revenue, 1.3% of FY2025 gross profit.
rows.weakens: No split between returns, price protection and incentives, and the wholesale-discount sensitivity is modelled, not disclosed.
rows.implication: Model product gross margin as the channel-term shock absorber; a services-only margin model misses where carrier terms land.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: What are the return, price-protection and incentive accruals by period?

rows.finding: Services produced 42.2% of FY2025 gross profit, but product gross profit grew 26.3% in the nine months to 2026-06-27 against 15.3% for Services, taking Services to 39.1% of gross profit.
rows.mechanism: Handset margin, product mix and tariff refunds drove FY2026 gross profit, so the mix-shift mechanism did not operate in the year.
rows.benchmark: Services gross profit per dollar of product gross profit fell from $0.73 to $0.64; Services gross margin was 76.3% against 39.9% for products.
rows.weakens: One year is not a trend, and the services base still grew 15.3%.
rows.implication: The multiple's services-mix premise needs reacceleration in services gross profit or a lower entry price.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: What split of the FY2026 product margin gain is tariff refund versus mix?

plan.decision_question: How does Apple convert a hardware installed base into services profit, and how durable is that mix shift?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple runs a hardware annuity with a services margin layered on top, but the mix shift the multiple pays for stalled in fiscal 2026, when hardware margins, helped by tariff refunds, grew gross profit faster than Services.

rows.finding: Services reached $109.2bn in FY2025 (26% of $416.2bn revenue) and $91.7bn in the nine months to 2026-06-27, up 14%, with growth attributed to advertising and cloud services; services gross margin was 76.3% against 39.9% for products.
rows.mechanism: Each incremental services dollar carries about 76 cents of gross profit, so a services-led mix shift lifts total gross margin even while memory and N2 wafer costs push product gross margin down; services revenue depends on installed-base monetisation rather than unit growth.
rows.benchmark: FY2025: Services 26% of revenue and 36% of gross profit; 9M FY2026: 25% of revenue and 39% of gross profit; total gross margin 49.1% versus 46.8%.
rows.weakens: Services growth has slowed from 14% (9M FY2026) versus the prior year's pace, and the largest components are exposed to DMA and DOJ remedies.
rows.implication: Services mix, not AI, is the reliable margin engine; value the company on services gross profit compounding at low-to-mid teens and treat any acceleration as upside, not base case.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: What share of services growth is advertising versus App Store commission, and how much of advertising is Apple's own inventory versus the Google default-search payment?

rows.finding: R&D rose 33% to $34.0bn in the nine months to 2026-06-27 from $25.7bn, driven by infrastructure costs including AI investments and headcount, while Siri AI shipped in the iOS 27 cycle announced in Q3 FY2026 and Apple has disclosed no AI-specific revenue.
rows.mechanism: Apple funds AI as R&D and data-centre infrastructure rather than as a separate product, so its return appears only indirectly through upgrade rates and services attach; the absence of a price point means the investment is a defensive cost until monetised.
rows.benchmark: R&D $34.6bn in FY2025 (8.3% of sales), $31.4bn in FY2024 and $29.9bn in FY2023; Q3 FY2026 R&D was 11% of sales.
rows.weakens: The iCloud+ gating plan is reported, not announced: Apple has published no AI subscription price, so the monetisation route is unverified.
rows.implication: AI is currently a cost line: the burden is to show it lifts iPhone upgrade rates or services ARPU within two cycles, or it dilutes operating margin.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Does Apple disclose the split of AI infrastructure spend between capex, opex and payments to Google, and does the FY2026 10-K quantify the Gemini licence?

rows.finding: iPhone production in India rose 53% in 2025 to about 55 million units, roughly a quarter of global output, with India's share projected at 28% in 2026 and Tata Electronics overtaking Foxconn in export assembly.
rows.mechanism: Moving final assembly to India reduces exposure to US tariffs on China and diversifies single-country risk, but assembly captures a small share of value, so the benefit shows up as avoided cost rather than higher revenue.
rows.benchmark: India about 25% of global iPhone output in 2025 and a projected 28% in 2026, versus a negligible share in 2020.
rows.weakens: Assembly share is not value share; component localisation remains low and the figures are third-party estimates that Apple does not confirm.
rows.implication: India is a tariff-risk hedge rather than a margin driver; it supports the hardware gross-margin floor but does not change the growth algorithm.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: What is India's share of iPhone value added and of US-bound units, and what tariff rate applies to Indian-assembled iPhones after the 2026 Section 301 and Section 232 actions?

rows.finding: Apple acquired Q.ai, an Israeli AI-audio start-up, confirmed 2026-01-29 and reported by the Financial Times at close to $2bn, plus the AI data-engineering company Ascend.io, listed by the European Commission with a 2026-06-30 notification.
rows.mechanism: Buying small AI teams converts cash into capability without the integration risk of a large deal; the intangible increase shows the accounting footprint but not yet a product.
rows.benchmark: Prior M&A ceiling: Beats at $3bn (2014); Apple's disclosed intangible assets rose from $11.1bn at 2025-09-27 to $20.3bn at 2026-06-27.
rows.weakens: Q.ai's price is press-reported and its technology is undisclosed; a $2bn deal against $416bn of revenue cannot move the group's growth rate.
rows.implication: M&A posture has shifted from tuck-ins to $2bn-class AI deals, but remains small relative to $146bn of cash and securities: it signals intent, not a change in strategy.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: What did Apple actually buy in Q.ai (silent speech, audio AI), and how much of the $9.2bn increase in intangibles is acquisition versus capitalised licences?

rows.finding: The European Commission fined Apple EUR 500m on 2025-04-23 for anti-steering non-compliance, and the EU General Court dismissed Apple's challenge to its gatekeeper designation for the App Store and iOS on 2026-07-08; Apple and the DOJ were reported in 2026 to be in early settlement talks over the 2024 US antitrust case.
rows.mechanism: Both cases attack the rent extracted between developers and users — App Store commission and default-search placement — so a remedy compresses services gross margin directly rather than through a one-off fine.
rows.benchmark: DMA fines can reach 10% of global annual turnover; the EUR 500m fine equals about 0.12% of FY2025 revenue but the remedy, not the fine, is the risk.
rows.weakens: Neither case has produced a final remedy: the DMA fine was for steering, and a DOJ settlement could preserve most of the economics.
rows.implication: Regulatory remedies target the highest-margin services lines; a structural or behavioural remedy should lower the multiple on services rather than on hardware.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: What are the terms of any DOJ settlement, and does the DMA interoperability specification extend to the App Store commission structure rather than only to steering?

rows.finding: Vision Pro shipped about 390,000 units in 2024 and about 45,000 in Q4 2025, with IDC forecasting about 290,000 units and $636m of revenue in 2026; Wearables, Home and Accessories grew 2% to $27.3bn in the nine months to 2026-06-27.
rows.mechanism: A platform needs unit volumes to attract developers; at 45,000 units a quarter Vision Pro cannot sustain a developer economy, so its costs stay in R&D while its revenue rounds to nothing at group level.
rows.benchmark: Vision Pro about 600,000 units lifetime versus roughly 55 million iPhones assembled in India alone in 2025; the segment grew only 2% in 9M FY2026.
rows.weakens: Apple does not report Vision Pro units, so all figures are IDC estimates; a cheaper model could change the trajectory.
rows.implication: Spatial computing and home remain option value, not a growth driver; a valuation that capitalises a new-category optionality should discount it heavily.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: Is there a lower-cost Vision product in the FY2027 plan, and does Apple report any smart-home device revenue inside the Wearables, Home and Accessories line?

plan.decision_question: Where does Apple's revenue growth come from by FY2028, and is the strategy credible?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple's route to FY2028 growth is services mix, a richer iPhone cycle and India, with AI as a retention feature and a possible iCloud+ upsell rather than a revenue line of its own; the plan is credible on cash generation and per-share compounding, but not yet on AI monetisation or on creating a new category.
plan.why_different: This section tests stated and revealed strategy against resources and dates: which milestones must land, which partners carry them, and what the next twelve months must prove. The financial statements themselves and the valuation belong to other sections.
plan.mechanism: Services grow off an installed base that reached a new record, and each incremental services dollar carries about 76 cents of gross profit, so mix shift lifts group margin even when hardware costs rise; AI is funded as R&D and capital expenditure and monetised, if at all, through iCloud+ rather than a new product line; India lowers tariff and concentration risk but captures assembly rather than component value; buybacks convert that cash into per-share growth.
plan.comparison_set: Apple's own mix in FY2025 (Services 26% of revenue, 36% of gross profit) versus 9M FY2026 (25% of revenue, 39% of gross profit); R&D intensity 8.3% of FY2025 sales versus 11% in Q3 FY2026; the Beats $3bn deal (2014) as the prior M&A ceiling; the €500m DMA fine as the base rate for regulatory cost; Vision Pro as the base rate for a new-category launch.
plan.counter_evidence: AI features arrived roughly two years after they were first demonstrated, and Siri required a Google licence; the car programme was cancelled and Vision Pro shipped only ~45,000 units in Q4 2025; R&D is up 33% with no disclosed AI revenue; a DOJ settlement or DMA remedy could cut App Store commission and default-search income, which are the highest-margin services lines; and the 2026 growth rate leans on a weak FY2025 comparison, tariff refunds and currency.
plan.visual: Milestone table (Milestone | Target date | Status | What it proves | Source) and partner table (Partner | Scope | Signed | Status | Source); the services-mix and capital-return figures carry the thesis.
plan.prohibited: huge market, strong team, high barriers to entry, clear business model, fierce competition, risks are manageable, well positioned, world-class, best-in-class, about 5, many patents, recently, industry-leading (as an assertion), secular growth story

rows.finding: Worldwide smartphone shipments fall 16.7% in 2026 to just over 1bn units while market value rises 6.3% to $613bn and ASP reaches a record $581 (+27.6%), revised up from $550 one quarter earlier; memory costs are up over 300% YoY and rise until at least 2028.
rows.mechanism: AI-server demand diverts NAND/DRAM capacity, raising bill-of-materials for every handset maker; OEMs pass the cost to consumers and cut entry tiers, so the value pool survives while unit volume contracts, and only vendors with early memory contracts and premium mix can hold price.
rows.benchmark: IDC's own prior vintage (13.9% decline, 1.09bn units, $550 ASP) was superseded within one quarter; 173m sub-$100 units shipped in 2025, a segment down almost 60% in Q2 2026.
rows.weakens: Any unit-volume growth model for Apple, and the assumption that the smartphone market grows with global GDP; also weakens Apple's entry-level reach and emerging-market expansion case.
rows.implication: Judge Apple on value share, ASP and Services attach rather than unit growth; a 1bn-unit market at $581 ASP is a $581bn pool that Apple monetises at roughly twice the industry ASP, so the near-term revenue case does not need market growth.
rows.confidence: high - one primary statistical agency, two vintages, internally consistent (1bn units x $581 = $581bn versus the stated $613bn value, a 5% gap)
rows.follow_up: Does Apple's ASP rise fast enough in FY2027 to offset the unit decline implied by a -16.7% 2026 and a flat-to-down 2027?

rows.finding: Apple gained 3.9 percentage points of global smartphone share in Q2 2026 to 20.2% on record Q2 shipments (+14.9%) and is on track for a record 22% annual share; iOS reaches 23.6% of 2026 shipments while Apple's own units fall 1.3%; Samsung leads at 22.7% (+3.2pp) and Xiaomi fell 26.4%.
rows.mechanism: Share gains come from supply security and price discipline in a cost shock, not from product innovation: Apple and Samsung held prices while Android peers raised them, so demand migrated up the price ladder.
rows.benchmark: Q1 2026 Samsung 21.2% versus Apple 21.0% (a statistical tie); Q2 2026 Samsung 22.7% versus Apple 20.2%; Xiaomi -26.4% and vivo -19.6% in Q2 2026.
rows.weakens: The claim that Apple's share gains are structural: they coincide with a one-off memory shock, and IDC expects normalisation only in 2028, after which price-led Android vendors can rebuild.
rows.implication: Underwrite Apple on margin and services rather than on a permanent share gain; the share number to watch is whether iOS holds 22-24% once memory costs normalise in 2028.
rows.confidence: high - IDC final historical data for two consecutive quarters, consistent with Apple's own +22.4% iPhone revenue growth in the first nine months of FY2026
rows.follow_up: What share does iOS hold in 2028 when IDC expects memory supply to normalise?

rows.finding: Apple's nine-month FY2026 segment revenue: Americas $149.4bn (+11.4%), Europe $95.6bn (+16.1%), Greater China $64.8bn (+30.0%), Japan $24.4bn (+10.4%), Rest of Asia Pacific $30.2bn (+19.4%) on total revenue of $364.4bn (+16.2%); Greater China had fallen from $72.6bn in FY2023 to $64.4bn in FY2025 before this rebound.
rows.mechanism: Greater China's swing is the largest single driver of group growth: a $14.9bn increase on a $49.9bn base adds 4.1 percentage points to group growth, and renminbi strength plus iPhone 17 demand did the work; Europe's segment definition includes India, the Middle East and Africa, so the fastest-growing geography is inside a line item labelled Europe.
rows.benchmark: FY2023 Greater China $72.6bn, FY2024 $67.0bn, FY2025 $64.4bn (a two-year decline of 11.3%), then +30.0% in the first nine months of FY2026.
rows.weakens: The 2025-era narrative that Apple is losing China permanently; but it also weakens any reading of the regional table as a clean guide to where growth happens, because India is not a separate line.
rows.implication: The revenue mix is shifting toward the faster-growing regions in FY2026, but the swing factor is China, a market where policy and a domestic champion set the terms; an investor should size China at a discount to its 17.8% of revenue.
rows.confidence: high on the figures (audited 10-K plus filed 10-Q), medium on durability of the China rebound
rows.follow_up: How much of the Greater China increase is currency and how much is unit growth, and what happens when the renminbi tailwind reverses?

rows.finding: Services produced $109.2bn (26.2% of FY2025 revenue) at a 75.4% gross margin, grew 14.1% to $91.7bn in the first nine months of FY2026, and is the only large pool where Apple's margin is not capped by hardware competition.
rows.mechanism: Services monetise an installed base that Apple says reached an all-time high in the June 2026 quarter, at near-zero marginal cost, so each incremental dollar of services revenue carries about twice the gross margin of hardware; the adjacent pools are larger than Apple's: Alphabet's trailing-twelve-month revenue is $471.1bn and Netflix's $49.7bn.
rows.benchmark: Products gross margin 36.8% versus Services 75.4% in FY2025; Services grew 14% in FY2025 and 14.1% in the first nine months of FY2026, versus total revenue growth of 6.4% and 16.2%.
rows.weakens: The durability of the take rate: Apple discloses a U.S. court order barring commission on certain external purchases and a DMA compliance plan the European Commission has challenged.
rows.implication: Services is the valuation support, but its growth must be priced net of a lower take rate; the app-economy pool size is not disclosed by any source retrieved, so the section states that gap rather than estimating it.
rows.confidence: high on reported figures, low on the size of the app-economy pool (not disclosed)
rows.follow_up: What share of Services revenue is commission-based and therefore exposed to the U.S. injunction and the DMA?

rows.finding: China is a share fight in a shrinking market: 66m units in Q2 2026 (-4.3%), the fifth consecutive quarterly decline, with Huawei at 22.6% (+19.4%) and Apple at 18.1% (+24.4%); first-half 2026 shipments were 134m units (-4.2%) and IDC expects the decline to widen to about 20% in the second half before a recovery around 2028-2029.
rows.mechanism: Huawei held prices while other Android vendors raised theirs, widened its line-up and leaned on domestic brand loyalty, so it captured the entry and mid tiers; Apple captured the premium tier, which is why Apple's China revenue (+30%) outran its China unit share (18.1%).
rows.benchmark: Huawei 22.6% versus Apple 18.1% in units, but Apple's Greater China revenue per unit is higher: $64.8bn of nine-month revenue against an 18.1% share of a market running at roughly 264m units a year.
rows.weakens: The claim that China revenue follows China unit share; the two diverge by a factor that reflects Apple's price premium, and both can move in opposite directions.
rows.implication: China can grow Apple's revenue while Apple stays second in units, but the Huawei-led price discipline is the mechanism that decides whether that holds; size China exposure with a policy and competition discount.
rows.confidence: high - IDC preliminary quarterly data with vendor-level shares and a stated outlook
rows.follow_up: Does Huawei's HarmonyOS expansion into the entry tier pull first-time buyers away from iOS permanently, or only delay them?

rows.finding: India ships 31.0m smartphones a quarter (-4.1% in Q1 2026) at a record $302 ASP, with the $600-800 band up 32% and Apple fourth by units behind vivo, Samsung and OPPO; the sub-$100 segment fell 59% and its share halved.
rows.mechanism: Memory cost inflation forces Indian buyers up the price ladder faster than incomes rise, which mechanically expands Apple's addressable slice of the market without Apple having to cut price; but the same inflation cuts the number of first-time smartphone buyers who would later upgrade.
rows.benchmark: India ASP $302 versus a global ASP of $581; Apple fourth by units in a market where the $800-plus band is only 7% of shipments.
rows.weakens: The claim that India is Apple's next volume market within the forecast horizon; at a 7% share for the $800-plus band, the near-term revenue contribution is small.
rows.implication: Treat India as a five-year option priced mainly through Services and premium share, not as a driver of FY2027 revenue; the segment table should show it as a planned expansion market inside Europe.
rows.confidence: medium-high - IDC quarterly data for one quarter, with the price-band detail that supports the mechanism
rows.follow_up: What is Apple's unit share and revenue share in India for a full year, and how much of it is manufacturing-linked local content?

plan.decision_question: How large and how fast-growing are the markets Apple serves, and is its revenue mix shifting toward the faster-growing ones?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple's markets are contracting in units and expanding in value, and Apple is taking value share inside that contraction — so the market case rests on premiumisation and Services attach rather than device volume, is strongest in the United States and weakest in China, where a domestic champion and a fading subsidy set the terms.
plan.why_different: This section sizes the pools and their growth; it does not explain the product (technology_product), the accounting (financials) or the rivals' strategies as such (competition). It answers whether the demand exists and where, not whether Apple wins it.
plan.mechanism: Memory scarcity raises handset bill-of-materials, entry tiers become unviable, demand migrates up the price ladder, and value concentrates in vendors with supply contracts and premium mix; Apple monetises that migration through a higher ASP and a 75%-gross-margin Services layer on an installed base that keeps growing even when units do not.
plan.comparison_set: Apple's own FY2023-FY2025 regional history (Greater China $72.6bn to $64.4bn then +30%), IDC's prior forecast vintages, Samsung and Xiaomi share moves in the same quarters, and Alphabet and Netflix as scale references for the services pool.
plan.counter_evidence: If memory prices normalise in 2028, price-led Android vendors rebuild the entry tier and Apple's share gain reverses; if the App Store take rate is removed by courts and the DMA, Services growth no longer carries the margin mix; and if China's subsidy-driven premium demand fades as it did in Q2 2026, the +30% China line is a one-year currency-and-launch effect rather than a trend.
plan.visual: Two tables: a market-size table (TAM/SAM/SOM with method, publisher and year) and a regional table (Region | market size and year | growth | Apple's position | barriers | key competitors | source).
plan.prohibited: huge market, strong growth, well positioned, clear runway, fierce competition, robust demand, secular tailwind, TAM of $X trillion without a publisher and year, 'about 2.3 billion devices' presented as fact without a source

rows.benchmark: The valuation work capitalises it at about $450bn at 30x, near 9% of market value; that is a multiple-based estimate, not a disclosed value.
rows.weakens: The numerator is a 2022 figure, Apple does not disclose the current amount, and the ratios mix a 2022 numerator with 2026 denominators.
rows.implication: Price the payment as a live policy risk, but not as a loss already incurred.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: What is the current annual payment and its renewal terms?

rows.finding: No default-payment ban is in force: the 2025-09-02 remedies decision declined to ban distributor payments, the December 2025 final judgment restricting distribution is under appeal by Google (2026-01) and the DOJ (2026-02), pending at 2026-10-29.
rows.mechanism: Remedies litigation runs slower than headline risk; the revenue remains until a final, non-appealed order.
rows.benchmark: The secondary claim of an April 2026 order and June 2026 ban (S165) against the court record summarised in S118 and Alphabet's 10-Q (S42).
rows.weakens: S165 asserts a ban that a material fact in Alphabet's October 2026 filing would have disclosed; the claim is unsupported and not used.
rows.implication: Do not price an immediate loss; price the appeal outcome and the 2027-2028 timing.
rows.confidence: high that the ban claim is unsupported; medium on the ultimate outcome
rows.follow_up: What does the final judgment say about default payments, and when will the D.C. Circuit rule?

rows.finding: Worldwide smartphone shipments fall 16.7% to just over 1.0bn units in 2026 while value rises 6.3% to $613bn and ASP reaches $581, up 27.6%.
rows.mechanism: Memory costs remove the entry tier and lift ASP; unit-share gains bought with early memory supply flatter Apple through 2027.
rows.benchmark: IDC's prior $550 ASP; bottom-up 1.0bn units x $581 = $581bn, within 5% of $613bn.
rows.weakens: The figures are third-party estimates, and a 2028 entry-tier recovery could reverse Apple's share gain.
rows.implication: Revenue growth must come from price and mix, not volume; 2028 is the test when memory normalises.
rows.confidence: high for 2026; medium for 2027-2028
rows.follow_up: When does IDC expect memory prices to normalise, and what unit recovery follows?

rows.finding: Greater China revenue was $64.8bn in nine months of FY2026, up 30.0% on $49.9bn, while Apple held 18.1% of Q2 2026 units behind Huawei's 22.6%.
rows.mechanism: China growth is a price, currency and launch effect while unit share remains second, so the mix shifts toward the most politically exposed region.
rows.benchmark: Greater China revenue of $72.6bn in FY2023 and $64.4bn in FY2025; Americas grew 11.4%.
rows.weakens: Renminbi strength and pull-forward ahead of second-half price increases; IDC sees China down as much as 20% in H2 2026.
rows.implication: China durability is the swing factor for the FY2026 growth rate and for the premiumisation case beyond 2027.
rows.confidence: high on the figures; medium on durability
rows.follow_up: How much of the 30% increase is currency, and what was the June-quarter unit trend?

plan.decision_question: How large and how fast-growing are the markets Apple serves, and is its revenue mix shifting toward the faster-growing ones?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple's markets are contracting in units and expanding in value, and Apple is taking value share inside that contraction: the case for FY2026-FY2028 rests on premiumisation and installed-base monetisation rather than unit volume or a Services mix shift, is strongest in the United States, is adequate in Europe, and in China depends on a domestic champion's pricing discipline.
plan.why_different: This section sizes the pool from the outside and tests Apple's mix against it; it does not map rivals (competition) or model the P&L (financials). Its distinctive finding is that unit and value move in opposite directions and that Services lost mix in FY2026.
plan.mechanism: A memory supply shock removes the entry tier, cuts units 16.7% and lifts ASP 27.6%; Apple's early memory supply turns that into record unit share and revenue growth, while Greater China's price and currency effect supplies 4.1 points of group growth. Services grows 14% but slower than hardware, so mix shifts toward China and premium handsets, not toward the recurring pool; the Google search payment and the App Store take rate are the policy variables that decide whether the high-margin layer survives.
plan.comparison_set: Top-down IDC market value against bottom-up units x ASP; Apple revenue growth against market unit and value growth; FY2025 Services mix against nine-month FY2026; China revenue against China unit share; Apple's ASP against the $581 industry ASP.
plan.counter_evidence: Memory normalisation in 2028 rebuilds the entry tier and contests Apple's share gain; China demand may be pulled forward ahead of second-half price increases; courts and the DMA may remove the App Store take rate; the Google search payment is concentrated and legally exposed, though no ban is in force.
plan.visual: The market-size table (TAM/SAM/SOM, top-down and bottom-up) plus the regional table with Apple's position and competitors in each geography.
plan.prohibited: huge market, strong growth, well positioned, fierce competition, clear market leader, robust demand, recently, about 5, many

rows.finding: In FY2025, 60% of Apple's net sales ($249,697M of $416,161M) went through carriers, resellers and distributors and 40% through Apple's own stores and sales force.
rows.mechanism: Third-party channels carry the customer acquisition and financing cost, which is why Apple's selling expense is 6.6% of revenue while its products reach subsidised price points.
rows.benchmark: Direct-to-consumer peers such as Microsoft report a different channel mix; Apple's own 40/60 split is the only disclosed anchor.
rows.weakens: Apple does not split carriers from resellers, so the share exposed to carrier subsidy changes is unknown and could be well below 60%.
rows.implication: Any carrier de-emphasis of premium handsets would hit more than half of revenue; this is a structural exposure the Services narrative hides.
rows.confidence: high: audited 10-K disclosure
rows.follow_up: What share of the 60% is carrier versus open-channel retail?

rows.finding: Carriers were 27% of trade receivables at 2026-06-27 ($8,477M of $31,398M) against 34% at 2025-09-27; one customer was 18% of trade receivables; reseller financing, instalment plans and subsidies 'may be discontinued or modified any time'; price protection and customer incentives are netted against Products net sales without a disclosed amount.
rows.mechanism: The subsidy is a third-party balance sheet, not an Apple cost line; Apple's exposure is credit concentration plus a revenue deduction it does not quantify, so a subsidy cut passes through volume and price rather than a disclosed expense.
rows.benchmark: One point of wholesale terms across the indirect channel equals $2.5bn of revenue, 1.3% of FY2025 gross profit; selling expense was $27,601M or 6.6% of revenue.
rows.weakens: Receivables concentration fell, which suggests improving carrier credit, not rising subsidy dependence.
rows.implication: The missing number is the subsidy per device; carrier 10-K equipment-revenue and promotional lines or paid channel sell-in data would settle it, and until then channel risk is unquantified.
rows.confidence: high on disclosures, low on the size of the subsidy because it is not disclosed
rows.follow_up: What do Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile disclose for device promotional expense and Apple mix?

rows.finding: Worldwide smartphone shipments fall 16.7% to just over 1.0bn units in 2026 while market value rises 6.3% to $613bn and ASP reaches a record $581 (+27.6%); the sub-$100 tier fell close to 60% in Q2 2026.
rows.mechanism: Memory at over 65% of low-end bill of materials removes the entry tier and pushes buyers up the price ladder, so value grows while units shrink.
rows.benchmark: Bottom-up 1.0bn units x $581 = $581bn, within 5% of IDC's $613bn.
rows.weakens: A supply shock is not demand growth; when memory normalises the entry tier can rebuild and ASP growth stalls.
rows.implication: Apple can grow revenue only by price and mix faster than units fall; the TAM is not the constraint, price is.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: When does IDC expect memory to normalise, and what ASP does it model for 2027-2028?

rows.finding: Nine-month FY2026 revenue: Greater China $64.8bn (+30.0%), Americas $149.4bn (+11.4%), Europe $95.6bn (+16.1%), Japan $24.4bn (+10.4%), Rest of Asia Pacific $30.2bn (+19.4%); Greater China contributes 4.1 points of the 16.2% group growth.
rows.mechanism: China's growth is a launch, currency and price-discipline effect after two years of decline, so the fastest-growing region is also the most politically exposed.
rows.benchmark: Greater China fell from $72.6bn in FY2023 to $64.4bn in FY2025 before the 2026 rebound.
rows.weakens: Europe includes India, so the fastest-growing large phone market is invisible in the segment line and the regional read is incomplete.
rows.implication: The mix shift toward faster-growing markets is real but narrow and partly currency; India cannot be sized from Apple's reported segments.
rows.confidence: high on the revenue figures, medium on the currency split because Apple does not disclose it
rows.follow_up: How much of Greater China's 30% is currency, and what is India's revenue contribution?

rows.finding: Services were $91.7bn, 25.2% of $364.4bn nine-month FY2026 revenue, up 14% at a 76.3% gross margin; in FY2025 Services were $109.2bn, 26.2% of revenue at 75.4%.
rows.mechanism: Hardware grew 16.2% against Services' 14%, so the mix moved back toward hardware even as the services margin improved.
rows.benchmark: Services were 26.2% of revenue in FY2025; the direction of the mix shift reversed in FY2026.
rows.weakens: The Services margin rose, so profit mix may still favour Services even as revenue mix does not.
rows.implication: The case cannot rest on a Services mix shift in FY2026; it rests on premium hardware and installed-base monetisation.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: What is the Services gross-profit share in the nine months, and how much of Services is commission?

rows.finding: Apple reported more than 2.5bn active devices on 2026-01-29, up from 2.35bn a year earlier; no replacement rate is published.
rows.mechanism: A growing installed base supports Services attach and the upgrade pool even when unit shipments fall.
rows.benchmark: About 6% device growth against 16.2% revenue growth: revenue per device is rising.
rows.weakens: The count is company-reported and unaudited, and it counts devices rather than users or iPhone owners.
rows.implication: Installed-base monetisation is the durable asset; replacement timing is the missing input for unit forecasts.
rows.confidence: medium: company-reported, repeated in two releases
rows.follow_up: What is the average iPhone replacement cycle in 2026, by region?

rows.finding: The nearest adjacent device pool, smart glasses, is forecast at 13.6m units and $5.1bn revenue in 2026, about 0.8% of the $613bn phone market, with Meta at 68.7% of units.
rows.mechanism: Adjacent pools are too small to replace phone revenue this decade but are where the next interface is being contested.
rows.benchmark: $5.1bn glasses revenue against $613bn smartphones and $91.7bn nine-month Services.
rows.weakens: The category is growing 26-40% a year and could compound faster than a linear forecast.
rows.implication: Do not add glasses to Apple's TAM now; treat them as an option the company does not control.
rows.confidence: high on 2026, medium on 2030
rows.follow_up: What unit share would glasses need to take 5% of phone value?

IDC wearables market 2026 shipments Apple Watch share Garmin Samsung
IDC worldwide PC shipments 2026 forecast Apple Mac share
European Commission Apple fine Digital Markets Act App Store anti-steering 2025 2026
SEC: Apple FY2025 10-K Item 1 (competition, distribution) and Item 1A (DMA, court order, Google remedies)
SEC: Apple 8-K 2026-07-30 exhibit 99.1 (Siri AI, category revenue)
SEC filings: Alphabet 10-K FY2025 and 10-Q 2026-09-30; Netflix 10-K FY2025
IDC: global smartphone shipments Q2 2026 (idc.com/promo/smartphone-market-share)

rows.finding: Apple leads no hardware category outright except detachable tablets: it is second in global smartphones (20.2% in Q2 2026 behind Samsung's 22.7%), second in PCs and tablets combined (18.2% behind Lenovo's 20.1%), holds 55.3% of detachables, is first in total wearables (15.5%) but second in smartwatches (17.2% to Huawei's 18.8%).
rows.mechanism: Apple wins where tight hardware-software integration is the buyer's deciding attribute (detachables, earwear) and loses where scale and price set the market (smartphones, notebooks, smartwatches), so its economics depend on holding a premium price on a minority unit share rather than on converting the market.
rows.benchmark: Apple's own 10-K states it has a minority share in global smartphones, PCs, tablets and wearables; Samsung at 22.7%, Lenovo at 20.1%, Huawei at 18.8% of smartwatches.
rows.weakens: Any framing of Apple as the market leader in phones or PCs; the 10-K's own language contradicts it.
rows.implication: Do not underwrite an Apple share story; underwrite a margin story. The premium position is a price position, and price positions erode when a lower-cost rival reaches parity on the features buyers check.
rows.confidence: high - IDC quarterly tracker data for a single quarter plus Apple's primary filing
rows.follow_up: What is Apple's value share, as opposed to unit share, in each category, and is there a published revenue-share series?

rows.finding: Samsung grew shipments 8.1% and gained 3.2 percentage points in Q2 2026 while every Chinese Android vendor in the top five fell by double digits; IDC attributes the split to secured memory supply, and Apple's 1.3% unit decline in 2026 against Android's 24.3% comes from the same mechanism.
rows.mechanism: In a component shortage the binding constraint is supply access, not product design: a vendor that makes its own memory can hold handset prices and take share while rivals pass cost through, so Samsung profits on both sides of Apple's bill of materials.
rows.benchmark: Xiaomi fell 26.4% and vivo 19.6% in the same quarter; the sub-$100 segment fell almost 60% in Q2 2026.
rows.weakens: The reading that Apple's 2026 share gain is a verdict on product quality, and the assumption that Apple's supply chain is a durable moat rather than a one-year sourcing feat.
rows.implication: Samsung is the most dangerous competitor, and the threat is vertical integration in memory rather than a better phone; that is a cost-of-goods threat Apple can only answer with long-term supply contracts and price, which is exactly what it did in 2026.
rows.confidence: high on the share data, medium on the attribution cause
rows.follow_up: How much of Samsung's handset cost advantage comes from internal memory supply, and would a Korean won or memory-price reversal remove it?

rows.finding: Apple enters foldables in the second half of 2026 and IDC expects it to ship more than 17m foldable iPhones by 2027, about 40% of a category growing 12.6% in 2026 to 22.9m units and 18% in 2027, at an ASP above $2,550 generating over $45.7bn of value, more than half the category.
rows.mechanism: A late entrant with a much higher price can still capture the category's value if its brand carries the premium: Apple converts a declining niche into the only growing smartphone segment, which raises blended ASP without needing volume.
rows.benchmark: Apple's foldable ASP above $2,550 against a global smartphone ASP of $581; category size 22.9m units in 2026 against a market of about 1bn.
rows.weakens: The claim that Apple's innovation cycle has stalled; but it also caps the upside, because 22.9m units is roughly 2% of the smartphone market.
rows.implication: Foldables support the average-selling-price and margin line rather than unit growth, and they open a direct challenge to Samsung and Huawei in the one premium segment those two had held alone.
rows.confidence: medium - a forecast from a single agency, with Apple's own product not yet through a full cycle
rows.follow_up: What is the gross margin on the foldable, and does the hinge and display supply chain give Apple a cost advantage or a cost penalty?

rows.finding: The App Store's commission is being removed by courts and regulators rather than by a competing store: Apple's FY2025 10-K discloses that it is subject to a U.S. court order preventing it from imposing any commission on certain external purchases, that its DMA compliance plan has been challenged by the European Commission, and that it faces U.S. monopolization suits over smartphones.
rows.mechanism: A regulated platform loses pricing power at the point of payment: if developers can route buyers to the web, Apple's commission falls toward a payment-processing fee, and the profit pool that funds the premium hardware position shrinks without any rival winning a single device sale.
rows.benchmark: Epic Games' litigation against the App Store; the European Commission's DMA enforcement against Apple's compliance plan; Google's own search-distribution remedies order of 2025-09-02.
rows.weakens: The claim that Apple's ecosystem lock-in protects Services pricing indefinitely, and any valuation that capitalises the 2026 Services margin as permanent.
rows.implication: Services growth should be valued at a lower multiple than its 14% growth and 75% gross margin imply, and the take rate, not store share, is the metric to underwrite.
rows.confidence: high on the legal facts, low on the revenue at risk (not disclosed)
rows.follow_up: What proportion of Services revenue is commission-based rather than subscription or advertising, and what take rate survives in the United States and the EU in 2027?

rows.finding: AI is the one product dimension where Apple is not ahead: Samsung shipped the Galaxy S26 Ultra with AI features that IDC credits for its return to first place in Q1 2026, Huawei scales a domestic operating system to 51m units, and Apple's answer, the all-new Siri AI, arrived at WWDC26 with research and development spending up 32.5% to $34.0bn in the first nine months of FY2026.
rows.mechanism: When a feature becomes the reason a buyer upgrades, the vendor that ships it first sets the comparison; Apple's late launch means it competes on integration and privacy rather than on capability, which protects loyalty but not price.
rows.benchmark: Huawei's HarmonyOS at 51m units in 2026 against 22.6% China share, and Apple's own Siri AI launched at WWDC26 in June 2026.
rows.weakens: The assumption that Apple's integration advantage converts into an AI advantage; IDC's China commentary names AI competition as a factor in the premium tier.
rows.implication: Watch AI-driven share loss in China in 2027 as the leading indicator; if it appears, the premium price that funds the model is exposed before unit share moves.
rows.confidence: medium - direction supported, but no measured share effect of AI features on purchases in the sources retrieved
rows.follow_up: Do AI features change purchase intent in China and the United States, and does Apple's Siri AI run on-device or through a partner model, with what cost per query?

rows.finding: The largest competitor is the phone already in the buyer's hand: replacement cycles are lengthening, entry-level buyers are leaving the market rather than trading up, and IDC expects demand to return only when a replacement cycle comes due in 2028-2029.
rows.mechanism: A working device is a substitute for a new one at any price above zero, so the elasticity of upgrade timing, not the features of a rival phone, sets the volume; Apple's installed base grows slowly while its revenue per device rises.
rows.benchmark: China's 66m units a quarter, of which Apple takes 18.1%; 173m sub-$100 units shipped globally in 2025 now becoming unviable; IDC's statement that consumers are postponing rather than abandoning upgrades.
rows.weakens: Forecasts that treat a 2026 share gain as a demand inflection; IDC's China note explicitly describes demand as deferred, not destroyed, and Apple's rise as partly pull-forward.
rows.implication: Longer cycles support Services revenue and suppress hardware units, which is consistent with Apple's reported mix; but it also means the FY2026 iPhone growth rate is not a base for FY2027.
rows.confidence: high - three independent IDC datasets agree on the direction
rows.follow_up: What is the measured average replacement cycle now, and how much of Apple's FY2026 iPhone growth is pull-forward ahead of expected price increases rather than new demand?

plan.decision_question: Is Apple's competitive position strengthening or eroding, product by product and region by region?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple's competitive position strengthened in 2026 in every hardware line except smartwatches, but the strengthening is crisis-specific — bought with memory supply and price discipline rather than product superiority — and it is being offset where it matters most for profit, because the App Store commission that funds the premium position is being dismantled by courts and the DMA rather than by a rival's product.
plan.why_different: This section identifies who takes the buyer and the profit pool, product by product and region by region; the market section sizes the pool and the financial section explains the accounting. Only here are rivals' shares, prices and legal constraints compared directly with Apple's.
plan.mechanism: Apple's 2026 gains come from secured memory supply, price discipline and premium mix rather than from product superiority, so the advantage is strongest where buyers can finance an $800-plus device and weakest where a domestic champion prices in local currency under a domestic operating system; meanwhile the profit pool that funds the position, the App Store commission, is being removed by courts and the DMA rather than by a competitor's product.
plan.comparison_set: Samsung (22.7% global units, 8.1% growth), Xiaomi (-26.4%), Huawei (22.6% in China, +19.9%), Lenovo (20.1% of PCs), HP and Dell, and for Services Alphabet (trailing-twelve-month revenue $471.1bn) and Netflix ($49.7bn) as scale references, against Apple's own 10-K admission of minority share in smartphones, PCs, tablets and wearables.
plan.counter_evidence: Huawei's 22.6% China share with a domestic operating system; a U.S. court order that already bars Apple from charging commission on certain external purchases; a DMA compliance plan the European Commission has challenged; and the fact that Apple's own 10-K concedes minority share in every hardware category, so the premium position is a margin position, not a unit market position.
plan.visual: Per-product competitor table with share, technology, price position and source; plus a positioning table (product by leader, challenger, niche, emerging threat) and a SWOT component.
plan.prohibited: fierce competition, strong moat, well positioned, clearly winning, best-in-class, 'Apple dominates' without a product and a share figure, unqualified '2.3 billion installed base'

rows.finding: Display-less smart glasses shipped about 2.25m units in Q1 2026 (+167% YoY); IDC forecasts 13.6m units and $5.1bn revenue in 2026, 27.3m units by 2030, and Meta held 68.7% of Q2 2026 units.
rows.mechanism: A new form factor is scaling fast off a small base and is controlled by one vendor's distribution (EssilorLuxottica retail, Meta's ad-funded subsidies), not by Apple.
rows.benchmark: 13.6m glasses against IDC's just over 1.0bn smartphones in 2026 is 1.3% of phone units; IDC's 2030 forecast is 2.7%.
rows.weakens: The category is growing 26-40% a year and Meta's 68.7% share is a platform-level position Apple does not hold in any new category.
rows.implication: No near-term substitution for the iPhone, but the option value of the next interface sits with a competitor; monitor 2027 launch cycle and cellular-independent display glasses.
rows.confidence: high on IDC figures, medium on the 2030 path because the forecast is three product cycles out
rows.follow_up: At what price and with what connectivity do display glasses stop being a phone accessory?

rows.finding: Meta Ray-Ban Display starts at $799 in the US (£749, €899, CA$1,149) and expanded to five markets on 2026-09-23; it remains phone-tethered and sold largely through eyewear retail.
rows.mechanism: Meta is buying distribution and habit at a premium price with an accessory model, not undercutting the phone.
rows.benchmark: $799 is 38% above the $581 smartphone ASP and 3.4x below Apple's reported $1,999 foldable.
rows.weakens: A $799 accessory that needs an iPhone or Android phone to work does not substitute for either; Meta's own launch material stresses navigation and calls, not phone replacement.
rows.implication: The threat is real only when price falls to the iPhone's own ASP and the phone tether is cut; today neither holds.
rows.confidence: high (company pricing), medium on uptake because no unit disclosure accompanies the expansion
rows.follow_up: What unit sell-through has the US launch achieved, and what share of buyers are iPhone users?

rows.finding: OpenAI's first hardware device is reported (2026-07-14) as a screenless, movable home speaker built with former Apple engineers; Apple sued OpenAI over trade secrets in July 2026.
rows.mechanism: The AI entrant attacks the assistant interface at home first, not the phone; Apple's response is litigation rather than a shipping product.
rows.benchmark: No form factor or launch date is confirmed, against Apple's 2.5bn-device installed base.
rows.weakens: A home speaker is not a phone competitor; the report is unconfirmed and based on anonymous sources.
rows.implication: Do not price an OpenAI phone threat into 2027; price the possibility that the assistant layer moves off the phone.
rows.confidence: medium: single reported account, company has not confirmed
rows.follow_up: Does OpenAI ship a phone or a wearable by 2028, and does it run on iOS?

rows.finding: Open-weight models are production-ready: Qwen3-32B runs on one H100 at about $0.82 per million tokens ($0.34 spot) and Llama 4 Scout at $0.87, with DeepSeek V3.2 needing eight H100s at about $13.89.
rows.mechanism: The assistant layer is commoditising, so a handset maker can self-host a competent model rather than license one, eroding any AI subscription premium and Apple's rented-Gemini differentiation.
rows.benchmark: Under $1 per million tokens is under a tenth of a cent for a 1,000-token query, against a Gemini licence of undisclosed cost.
rows.weakens: The source is a GPU-cloud vendor with an interest in self-hosting, and it flags its own benchmark figures as unverified; quality at the low end is not established.
rows.implication: Apple's AI position is not a moat and neither is a rival's; value stays in distribution and integration.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: What does Apple pay Google per query, and what share of Siri queries run on-device?

rows.finding: Transsion sits outside IDC's Q2 2026 global top five, whose 'Others' bucket is 27.7% of 276.3m units; HONOR also sits outside the top five but grew H1 2026 shipments 53% and holds more than 50% of foldables in Malaysia, Singapore and Hong Kong.
rows.mechanism: Memory costs concentrate share at the premium end and squeeze the sub-$200 tier where Transsion competes, while HONOR wins a foldable niche rather than scale.
rows.benchmark: Samsung 22.7% and Apple 20.2% against a combined 'Others' of 27.7% in Q2 2026.
rows.weakens: Neither challenger has scale; the HONOR figures come from a media summary of IDC data, and regional shares for both were not retrievable in this run.
rows.implication: The competitive threat in 2026 is consolidation at the top, not disruption from below; watch HONOR in foldables as the price umbrella Apple's $1,999 Duo creates.
rows.confidence: medium: IDC top-five table is primary-grade, HONOR growth is second-hand
rows.follow_up: What are Transsion's and HONOR's unit shares in Africa, India and Southeast Asia in 2026?

rows.finding: Apple's calendar-2026 gains are supply-driven: Apple units fell only 1.3% against Android's 24.3% because it secured memory early, and iOS reached a record 23.6% of shipments while Samsung, which sells memory, grew 8.1% and took 3.2 points.
rows.mechanism: When memory is over 65% of low-end bill of materials, supply access determines share; the advantage lapses when memory normalises and Samsung keeps its cost position.
rows.benchmark: Samsung 22.7% (+3.2pp) versus Apple 20.2% (+3.9pp) in Q2 2026; Xiaomi -26.4%, vivo -19.6%.
rows.weakens: Apple's gain is real and larger in percentage points than Samsung's; if memory stays tight beyond 2028 the advantage persists.
rows.implication: Do not capitalise the 2026 share gain as a permanent competitive improvement; it is a cyclical rent.
rows.confidence: high on the shares, medium on the timing of normalisation
rows.follow_up: How much memory inventory has Apple contracted, and at what price through 2027?

rows.finding: FY2025 net income rose 19.5% to $112,010M, but pretax income rose only 7.5% ($132,729M vs $123,485M) while the tax provision fell 30.3% to $20,719M from $29,749M; FY2024 carried the one-time $10.2bn Irish State Aid charge (a $15.8bn payment to Ireland less a $4.8bn US foreign tax credit and $823M of released unrecognised benefits). Normalising FY2024 at FY2025's 15.6% effective rate gives $104,222M, so underlying net income growth was 7.5%.
rows.mechanism: A one-off tax charge in the base year, not a change in trading, produced half of the following year's net income growth - the classic base-effect distortion in a two-year comparison.
rows.benchmark: Reported FY2025 net income growth of +19.5% and diluted EPS growth of +22.7% ($6.08 to $7.46).
rows.weakens: The reading that Apple's FY2025 was an acceleration year; on a normalised tax rate the company grew earnings at roughly the rate of revenue.
rows.implication: Halve the growth rate you extrapolate. The 22.7% EPS growth of FY2025 is a tax-base artefact as much as an operating result, and the FY2026 comparison is against a clean base, so any FY2026 deceleration is not a deterioration.
rows.confidence: high - both the provision and the charge are audited and disclosed
rows.follow_up: What is the sustainable effective tax rate under OECD Pillar Two, and how much of the $23.2bn of gross unrecognised tax benefits (up to $6bn of which may move within 12 months) is a cash exposure?

rows.finding: Buybacks contributed about 5.4 points of the 21.7% EPS growth from FY2023 to FY2025, so roughly a quarter of EPS growth was a smaller denominator; in the trailing twelve months to 2026-06-27 the contribution fell to about 1.9 points (EPS +16.9%, net income +15.1%) because repurchases slowed to $62,094M in the nine months from $70,579M a year earlier while free cash flow rose 43% to $116,996M from $81,754M.
rows.mechanism: At a constant net income, a 5% smaller share count adds 5% to EPS with no operating improvement; the mechanism reverses when the repurchase pace slows, which is what happened in FY2026.
rows.benchmark: FY2023-FY2025: net income +15.5%, diluted EPS +21.7%, diluted shares -5.1% (15,813M to 15,005M), on $258,212M of cumulative buybacks.
rows.weakens: The view that Apple's EPS growth is understated by buybacks and that management will keep shrinking the count at the same rate.
rows.implication: The buyback is a real but shrinking contributor; do not model EPS growth the way FY2023-FY2025 delivered it, because the pace of repurchase has already slowed and net cash is building instead.
rows.confidence: high - share counts and repurchase cash flows are disclosed
rows.follow_up: Why did Apple cut the repurchase pace by 12% while free cash flow rose 43%, building $28bn of net cash - is it tariff or AI investment, or price discipline at 39.5x earnings?

rows.finding: Cash paid for income taxes was $43,369M in FY2025, or 32.7% of pretax income, against a $20,719M tax provision and a 15.6% book rate - the widest gap in the three years - and free cash flow fell to 0.88x of net income from 1.16x, despite operating cash flow of $111,482M; by the trailing twelve months to 2026-06-27 the ratio had recovered to 1.06x on $146,724M of operating cash flow and $10,041M of capex.
rows.mechanism: Deferred and settlement payments decouple cash tax from book tax; when the cash rate exceeds the book rate the accounting profit overstates distributable cash for that period, and free cash flow per share - not EPS - is the better measure of what funds the buyback.
rows.benchmark: FY2024 FCF/net income of 1.16x and FY2023 of 1.03x; FY2023 cash taxes were 16.4% of pretax income and FY2024 were 21.1%.
rows.weakens: Simple FCF-to-net-income ratios and any valuation that capitalises net income without checking the cash tax line.
rows.implication: The 15.6% book tax rate is not the cash tax rate; on FY2025 evidence, a third of pretax income left as cash tax, which matters for anyone valuing Apple on net income rather than on cash.
rows.confidence: high on the figures; medium on the driver, because Apple does not reconcile the cash tax figure to the Irish settlement line by line
rows.follow_up: Which payments drove the $43.4bn of FY2025 cash taxes, and does the FY2026 profile normalise once the final $8.8bn of TCJA repatriation tax was paid in the nine months to 2026-06-27?

rows.finding: Inventory rose to $11,092M at 2026-06-27 from $5,925M a year earlier, an 87% increase against 16.2% revenue growth, lifting days inventory to 16.9 from 9.4 and pulling the cash conversion cycle to -56.8 days from -71.1; receivables fell to $31,398M from $39,777M at the FY2025 year-end and payables to $64,525M from $69,860M.
rows.mechanism: Negative working capital is a funding source only while payables and deferred revenue grow faster than inventory and receivables; when inventory nearly doubles, the supplier-funded float shrinks and the cash goes into stock.
rows.benchmark: FY2025 days inventory of 9.4 and cash conversion cycle of -71.1 days at the September year-end; Q3 FY2025 inventory of $5,925M at the same seasonal point.
rows.weakens: The claim that Apple's negative working capital is a permanent, stable source of cash.
rows.implication: Ask for the inventory composition before accepting the 50.1% gross margin: a build of this size either finances a strong December quarter or precedes a write-down, and the answer is not in the filings yet.
rows.confidence: high on the balance-sheet change; medium on the cause, which Apple describes only as component cost and supply pressure
rows.follow_up: Is the $5.2bn inventory build pre-tariff and pre-launch stock, or unsold units - and what does the FY2026 10-K show about inventory valuation and any write-down?

rows.finding: At 2026-06-27 Apple held $39,544M of cash plus $106,973M of marketable securities against $84,344M of debt, for net cash of $62,173M, up from $33,763M nine months earlier; commercial paper fell to $1,997M from $7,979M, and off-balance-sheet commitments included $57.0bn of manufacturing purchase obligations ($56.2bn due within twelve months) and $29.3bn of other purchase obligations.
rows.mechanism: Apple funds itself from operations and holds more securities than debt, so the interest line nets to near zero; the meaningful financial commitment is the forward purchase book that fixes component supply and, with it, the cost base.
rows.benchmark: Net cash of $33,763M at 2025-09-27, total debt of $98,657M, and interest expense not separately tagged because other income absorbs it (net other expense of $321M in FY2025).
rows.weakens: Any concern framed as leverage or interest cover; equally, it weakens the use of net cash as a valuation add-on, since most of it is working capital and tax reserve rather than surplus.
rows.implication: Balance-sheet risk is not the issue - refinancing, interest cover and liquidity are all comfortable; the real commitment is the $57bn purchase obligation, which is a cost risk rather than a solvency risk.
rows.confidence: high - all balances are on the face of the statements
rows.follow_up: How much of the $57.0bn manufacturing commitment is priced on memory and NAND at current spot, and what happens to the gross margin if those prices stay elevated for four quarters?

rows.finding: Apple's trailing-twelve-month return on equity was 148.8% and return on invested capital 320.6% on invested capital of about $45,347M (equity of $107,520M plus debt of $84,344M less $146,517M of cash and securities), against a return on assets of 36.1% and an operating margin of 33.2%.
rows.mechanism: Buybacks and large cash balances shrink invested capital, so ROIC mechanically rises with financial policy rather than operating performance; ROE is distorted the same way when equity is $107,520M on $128,930M of net income.
rows.benchmark: Microsoft FY2026 ROIC 35.9% and Alphabet FY2025 ROIC 37.0%, both computed on invested capital in the hundreds of billions.
rows.weakens: Cross-company ROIC comparisons that put Apple's triple-digit figure beside Microsoft's 35.9% as if the denominators were alike.
rows.implication: Do not read 320% ROIC as a quality score; the denominator has been shrunk by $258bn of buybacks and by holding cash. ROA of 36.1% is the honest number, and it is still the best in the peer set.
rows.confidence: high on the figures; the comparison is limited by how differently the four companies are capitalised
rows.follow_up: What is Apple's return on gross capital employed including the supplier and contract-manufacturing assets it does not own, and is that the right denominator to compare with Microsoft's 35.9%?

rows.finding: Greater China revenue rose 30% to $64,839M in the nine months to 2026-06-27 and 22% to $18,816M in the June quarter, so nine months already exceed the whole of FY2025's $64,377M after two years of decline; on sensitivity, three points of gross margin on TTM revenue of $466,823M is $14,005M of pretax profit, or 9.0% of TTM net income, and losing the $20bn search payment at near-100% incremental margin would remove about $16,540M after tax, or 12.8%.
rows.mechanism: Gross margin and a single licensing line are both high-margin and both politically or cyclically exposed, so they dominate the variance; revenue growth at a 49% margin matters less per point than a margin change at constant revenue.
rows.benchmark: Greater China revenue of $72,559M in FY2023, $66,952M in FY2024 (-8%) and $64,377M in FY2025 (-4%); TTM net income of $128,930M and TTM EPS of $8.72.
rows.weakens: The bear case built mainly on China share loss - on the latest three quarters, Greater China is the fastest-growing large segment, not the weakest.
rows.implication: The two variables that move the outcome most are gross margin and the search payment, not revenue growth - a 3-point margin give-back and the loss of the search deal together would cut TTM net income by about 22%.
rows.confidence: high on the segment and sensitivity arithmetic; medium on the Google amount, which is a 2022 court figure
rows.follow_up: Is the Greater China rebound volume or price, and how much of it is the iPhone 17 cycle rather than a durable share recovery against Huawei?
