plan.decision_question: Are Apple's earnings and cash flow as high-quality as the multiple implies, and what would break the quality?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple's cash conversion and balance sheet are as good as the multiple implies, but the earnings growth is not: FY2025's 22.7% EPS growth becomes roughly 10% once the $10.2bn Irish tax charge in the prior year is normalised out, and FY2026's margin is being flattered by a tariff refund Apple does not quantify.
plan.why_different: This section tests the statements and their notes for quality - what the tax line, the buyback, working capital and the non-cash items do to reported growth; the business model section explains where the revenue comes from, and the valuation section decides what multiple to pay for it.
plan.mechanism: Buybacks shrink the share count against a rising net income, so EPS outgrows net income; the tax line, not operations, drove half of FY2025's net income growth after the Irish charge; and negative working capital plus a capital-light model let Apple convert net income into free cash at close to 1x, which peers spending a third of revenue on capex cannot.
plan.comparison_set: Apple's own FY2023-FY2025 and TTM record; Microsoft FY2026, Alphabet FY2025 and Meta FY2025 on margin, capex intensity, cash conversion, ROIC and stock-based compensation; the 10-year Treasury yield of 4.93% as the cost of the buyback.
plan.counter_evidence: FY2025's 22.7% EPS growth is roughly half tax-base effect from the $10.2bn Irish State Aid charge in FY2024; cash taxes paid were $43,369M against a $20,719M provision; inventory rose 87% year on year to $11,092M; the FY2026 gross margin carries an unquantified tariff refund; and $20bn of search licensing sits with one counterparty under appeal.
plan.visual: A three-year plus TTM statement table and a returns and working-capital table, with a warning box on the tariff refund, the inventory build and the cash-versus-book tax gap.
plan.prohibited: banned_empty_phrases: 'fortress balance sheet', 'high-quality earnings' without definition, 'risks are manageable', 'well positioned', 'strong cash generation'; banned_patterns: quoting EPS growth without the tax normalisation in the same sentence, quoting ROE or ROIC without noting the buyback and net-cash distortion, any full-year FY2026 figure that the filings do not contain.

rows.finding: The European Commission fined Apple €500m on 2025-04-23 for breaching the DMA anti-steering obligation and issued a cease and desist order; the parallel Article 6(4) investigation into alternative-app terms remains open with a statutory ceiling of 10% of annual worldwide net sales, and Apple has appealed the Article 5(4) decision.
rows.mechanism: A regulator sets the price of the App Store toll in its jurisdiction and can escalate to a revenue-based fine, so the compliance cost is a recurring operating expense rather than a one-off legal charge.
rows.benchmark: Meta was fined €200m in the same 2025-04-23 package; Google was fined €890m on 2026-07-23 for Play steering and search self-preferencing; Alphabet's Android case produced a €4.1bn fine affirmed in 2022 and finally upheld by the ECJ in July 2026.
rows.weakens: The Commission closed its separate Apple user-choice investigation on the same day and found on 2026-02-05 that Apple Ads and Apple Maps should not be designated, so the DMA's reach over Apple is narrower than headlines imply; no further Apple DMA fine appears through 2026-09-28.
rows.implication: Price the DMA as a permanent 100-200bp drag on EU App Store take rate plus a tail fine, not as a solvency event.
rows.confidence: high - primary regulator release plus two Apple filings
rows.follow_up: Does the Article 6(4) file end in a second fine before the 2027 appeal ruling, and what fee structure does Apple's EU compliance plan now carry?

rows.finding: The N.D. Cal. found Apple in civil contempt on 2025-04-30 and barred any commission on out-of-app purchases; the Ninth Circuit modified that on 2025-12-11 to allow parity requirements and some commission on link-outs, and the Supreme Court granted cert on 2026-06-30 limited to the civil-contempt standard.
rows.mechanism: Judicial remedies reset the US App Store commission on digital goods bought through external links, the highest-margin revenue line Apple has; a contempt finding also shifts the default in later disputes toward stricter remedies.
rows.benchmark: Apple's US storefront historically charged 15-30% on in-app digital purchases; the 2025 injunction took that to zero on out-of-app purchases before the Ninth Circuit reinstated a partial fee.
rows.weakens: The Ninth Circuit expressly held Apple can charge some commission and the Supreme Court review is about the contempt standard, not the injunction's antitrust merits, so a total loss of US commission is not the base case.
rows.implication: Assume a permanent step-down in US link-out commission; this is the single most concrete Services gross-profit leak in the file.
rows.confidence: high - company disclosure of court orders, dated to the day
rows.follow_up: What fee has Apple actually set on US link-out purchases since the December 2025 remand, and what share of US digital-goods spend has moved off in-app purchase?

rows.finding: The Google search remedies decision of 2025-09-02 rejected Chrome and Android divestiture, barred exclusive distribution deals for six years but expressly permitted Google to keep paying distributors such as Apple for default placement if the deals are non-exclusive and run one year or less; a final judgment was entered in December 2025 and both sides' appeals were pending at 2026-10-29.
rows.mechanism: The court protected the payment stream to avoid harming device makers, so Apple's search-distribution revenue survives but loses its exclusivity and multi-year lock-in, which transfers pricing power to Apple at each annual renewal.
rows.benchmark: The plaintiffs sought a near-total ban on search-related payments to distribution partners; the court rejected it, citing the harm to device makers, carriers and browser developers.
rows.weakens: Apple does not disclose the payment; the roughly $20bn-a-year figure used in press coverage is unverified in Apple's filings, and a one-year term cap plus mandatory choice screens could erode it at the next renewal.
rows.implication: Treat the search payment as intact through 2027 with renegotiation risk each year, not as an expiring asset.
rows.confidence: high on the legal terms, low on the dollar amount
rows.follow_up: What does Apple's next Safari default agreement look like after the one-year term cap, and has Apple begun surfacing alternative search or AI assistants?

rows.finding: US tariff exposure was re-priced twice in 2026: the Section 232 semiconductor investigation's initial results on 2026-01-14 imposed no additional tariff on Apple products, and on 2026-02-20 the Supreme Court struck down certain IEEPA tariffs, with Apple claiming refunds recognised as a reduction of products cost of sales; Section 301 tariffs were then imposed.
rows.mechanism: Tariffs hit products gross margin directly and are only partly offset by shifting assembly to India and Vietnam, so the risk is a margin level shift rather than a demand shock.
rows.benchmark: Section 232 semiconductor tariffs were widely expected to capture downstream devices containing chips; the initial results spared them, against a base case of a mid-single-digit percentage tariff on China-assembled iPhones.
rows.weakens: Apple warns that further Section 232 or Section 301 measures remain possible and that rare-earth and component availability could still bite; the truce that underpins the calm expires 2027-01-10.
rows.implication: Remove the 2025-style tariff cliff from the near-term model but keep a standing margin haircut for Section 301 and future sector actions.
rows.confidence: high - company disclosure in the Q3 FY2026 10-Q
rows.follow_up: What net tariff cost is embedded in the FY2027 products gross-margin guide, and how much China assembly remains for US-bound units?

rows.finding: The opposite of the China-closure case happened: China's CAC registered Apple Intelligence for the mainland market on 2026-07-15 with Alibaba's Qwen and Baidu, and Greater China net sales rose to $18,816m in Q3 FY2026 from $15,369m a year earlier, up 22%, and to $64,839m for the nine months from $49,884m, up 30%.
rows.mechanism: Data and AI rules act as a market-access gate: once a foreign model is registered with a domestic partner, the gate becomes a toll and a localisation requirement rather than a prohibition.
rows.benchmark: Apple Intelligence had been unavailable in China since its 2024 debut, a 21-22 month gap that fed the share-loss narrative to Huawei.
rows.weakens: Registration is not the same as launch at scale, and the truce that covers rare-earth and tariff escalation expires 2027-01-10, so a political reversal would re-open the gate.
rows.implication: The China regulatory tail is smaller than the bear case assumes; the demand question is competitive, not regulatory.
rows.confidence: medium - secondary reporting on the CAC registration, primary on the revenue
rows.follow_up: Has Apple Intelligence shipped to mainstream Chinese users, and what data-localisation obligations attach to the Alibaba and Baidu arrangements?

rows.finding: The Irish state-aid case closed against Apple: the ECJ set aside the General Court on 2024-09-10 and confirmed the 2016 decision, producing a $10.2bn net one-time tax charge and $15.8bn payable to Ireland in Q4 FY2024; the FY2025 effective tax rate was 15.6% against 24.1% in FY2024, with $23.2bn of gross unrecognised tax benefits outstanding.
rows.mechanism: Tax is a jurisdiction-allocation negotiation: the one-off is sunk, but the structural risk is that Pillar Two's 15% floor and EU state-aid precedent remove the gap between Apple's foreign rate and the US rate.
rows.benchmark: A 15.6% FY2025 effective rate sits just above the OECD Pillar Two 15% minimum, leaving little room for further erosion but also little incremental Pillar Two cost.
rows.weakens: Apple's 10-K does not quantify a Pillar Two charge and the $23.2bn of unrecognised benefits ($10.6bn rate-relevant) is a two-way risk that could swing the rate either way.
rows.implication: Treat tax as a settled cost, not a lever; do not underwrite future EPS growth from a lower tax rate.
rows.confidence: high on the historical figures, medium on forward Pillar Two exposure
rows.follow_up: What Pillar Two top-up tax did Apple accrue in FY2026, and how much of the $23.2bn of unrecognised benefits relates to transfer pricing rather than the Irish case?

rows.finding: Supply-chain ESG is Apple's strongest record in this file: 100% of identified 3TG smelters and refiners in its supply chain participated in independent third-party conflict-minerals audits for the tenth consecutive year at 2024-12-31, no smelter was found to have financed armed groups, and in June 2024 Apple told suppliers to stop sourcing 3TG from DRC and Rwanda.
rows.mechanism: Audited downstream traceability converts a reputational tail into a procurement cost, which is why Apple can keep selling into regulated Western markets without a forced-labour delisting event.
rows.benchmark: The 3TG audit standard (OECD due diligence, independent third-party audit) is the base rate for large hardware OEMs; ten consecutive years at 100% is at the top of the range.
rows.weakens: The report covers minerals, not assembly labour or Uyghur forced-labour allegations in components, and it is the company's own filing with no independent verification of the underlying audits.
rows.implication: No ESG discount on sourcing; the residual risk is assembly labour in China and India, which these audits do not cover.
rows.confidence: medium-high - primary filing, company-prepared audit summary
rows.follow_up: What third-party audit evidence covers assembly labour in China and India, and has any supplier been terminated over labour findings in the past three years?

rows.finding: Governance is clean on control but not on compliance conduct: Apple has a single class of common stock, an independent Chair separated from the CEO, an Audit Committee that met nine times in 2025 and oversees privacy, cybersecurity, tax and enterprise risk, and related-party disclosures limited to one family-member employment; yet a federal court found it in civil contempt in April 2025 and referred it to the U.S. Attorney for a criminal-contempt determination.
rows.mechanism: A one-share-one-vote board aligned with shareholders reduces extraction risk; a contempt finding shows management chose litigation over compliance in a core profit pool, which raises the probability of stricter remedies in the next case.
rows.benchmark: Peers: Alphabet and Meta both operate dual-class structures; Apple does not, so control risk is lower even though its enforcement record is worse.
rows.weakens: The contempt finding is on appeal and the Supreme Court took the case on the legal standard, so it may not survive as a finding of wrongdoing.
rows.implication: Governance is an asset; compliance culture is the liability. Price a higher probability of adverse remedies, not a discount for control.
rows.confidence: high - proxy and 10-K disclosure
rows.follow_up: Did the U.S. Attorney decline or open a criminal-contempt inquiry, and how has Apple changed its App Review compliance function since April 2025?

plan.decision_question: Which policy, legal and ESG exposures can impair Apple's cash flow, margin or licence to operate, and how much of that is already priced?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple's policy exposure is not a licence-to-operate threat but a slow, legislated tax on Services gross profit: the €500m DMA fine and the 2025 US contempt finding show a company that litigates rather than complies, while the three remedies that actually matter - Google's default payment, the US link-out commission and the EU fee structure - have so far been reshaped rather than removed.
plan.why_different: The other sections price demand, mix and multiples; this one prices the legal and policy claim on a slice of Services gross profit and the compliance-culture discount that belongs in the required return, not in the revenue line.
plan.mechanism: Remedies move pricing power from Apple's App Store toll to developers and consumers; each basis point of Services gross margin is worth roughly a tenth of a billion dollars on Apple's scale, so a 100-200bp take-rate cut is an earnings event, not an existential one. Compliance-culture findings raise the probability of stricter remedies next time.
plan.comparison_set: DMA and antitrust enforcement against Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta and Samsung: Meta €200m (2025-04-23), Google €890m (2026-07-23), Alphabet Android €4.1bn affirmed 2022 and finally upheld July 2026, Amazon and Microsoft cloud designation proceedings opened 2026-06-25; Samsung has no DMA gatekeeper designation. Base rate: fines are frequent, structural break-ups are not.
plan.counter_evidence: Greater China net sales up 30% for the nine months to 2026-06-27 and CAC registration of Apple Intelligence on 2026-07-15 undercut the China-closure case; the Ninth Circuit restored a commission on link-outs; the Commission closed the user-choice probe and declined to designate Apple Ads and Maps; Section 232 initial results imposed no tariff; no further Apple DMA fine appears through 2026-09-28.
plan.visual: Policy impact matrix (Factor | Exposure | Probability | Impact | Mitigant | Source) plus the regulatory record table
plan.prohibited: risks are manageable; well positioned; high barriers to entry; huge market; fierce competition; about/roughly counts without a source; any sentence about how the section is written

rows.finding: A ten-year reverse DCF on enterprise value of $4,967.4B, TTM free cash flow of $136.7B, 3.0% terminal growth and an 8.5% WACC implies 11.8% annual FCF growth for ten years; the implied growth is 10.5% at an 8.0% WACC and 13.4% at 9.0%. Apple's FCF grew from $93.0B in FY2021 to $98.8B in FY2025, a 1.5% compound rate.
rows.mechanism: The terminal value is capitalised at 18.7x FCF against today's 36.3x EV/FCF, so the model already assumes the multiple halves by 2036 and still needs double-digit FCF growth to justify today's price; the growth has to come from the business, not from re-rating.
rows.benchmark: Apple's own FY2021-FY2025 FCF CAGR of 1.5% and revenue CAGR of 3.3%; IDC's device pools compound at about 1.5% a year to 2030, so 11.8% must come from price, Services and mix.
rows.weakens: TTM FCF of $136.7B is a working-capital and margin high against FY2025's $98.8B; on the lower base the same enterprise value implies about 16% growth, so the result is sensitive to which FCF base is normal.
rows.implication: No margin of safety at $344.63; at a 6% FCF growth path the same DCF gives about $221 a share, at 8% about $255 and at 10% about $298.
rows.confidence: medium-high — the arithmetic is reproducible, but the FCF base and the 65/35 opex assumptions are analyst judgements.
rows.follow_up: What normalised FCF does the FY2026 10-K support once inventory and the tariff refund are stripped out?

rows.finding: Sum of the parts: products revenue $346.3B and gross profit $135.5B, Services revenue $120.5B and gross profit $91.6B on trailing twelve months; at 3-5x EV/Sales for products and 10-14x for Services the parts are worth $2.25-3.42T, against an enterprise value of $4.97T. To reach $4.97T with products at 5x sales, Services must be capitalised at about 27x revenue.
rows.mechanism: The market is paying for the ecosystem and the buyback as a single cash-flow stream, not for what hardware and services would fetch as separate peer-valued businesses; the premium is 31-55% above the parts.
rows.benchmark: MSFT 11.1x EV/Sales, GOOGL 7.1x, META 6.6x, Samsung 12.5x P/E for hardware.
rows.weakens: Apple does not report segment operating income, so the 65/35 opex split is an assumption; Apple's 39.1% product gross margin is far above Samsung or PC hardware peers, so a pure peer multiple understates the hardware franchise.
rows.implication: The SOTP is a downside anchor ($2.3-3.4T, or $157-234 a share before net cash), not a price target: it shows the size of the ecosystem premium an investor is buying.
rows.confidence: medium — segment revenue and gross profit are derived from filed data, but the opex allocation and multiple choice are assumptions.
rows.follow_up: What would Services be worth at 20x EV/Sales if 20% of its revenue is a Google payment that a court could remove?

rows.finding: Apple's P/E was 24.6x at FY2022 year-end, 27.9x at FY2023, 37.5x at FY2024, 34.2x at FY2025 and 39.5x on 2026-10-30; the ten-year mean is 25.35x, the five-year average 30.2x, the five-year range 22.1-40.6x and the current multiple sits at the 100th percentile of it. From 2022-09-24 to 2026-10-30 the share price rose 129% while diluted EPS rose 43%, so about half the return came from the multiple.
rows.mechanism: Re-rating against a rising discount rate did the work: the ten-year Treasury yield rose 84bp in the last twelve months to 4.93%, yet Apple's multiple expanded, which cannot be repeated indefinitely because the earnings yield is already below the Treasury.
rows.benchmark: Its own ten-year mean of 25.35x and five-year range of 22.1-40.6x; S&P 500 trailing 21.76x.
rows.weakens: The EPS base is flattered: FY2025's 22.7% EPS growth becomes 10.4% normalising the Irish tax charge, and the June 2026 gross margin contained about two points of tariff refunds.
rows.implication: Future returns must come from earnings, not from multiple expansion; a return to the five-year average multiple alone would put the shares near $296.
rows.confidence: high — fiscal-year multiples are computed from filed EPS and closing prices, and the history is corroborated by two independent trackers.
rows.follow_up: How much of the 2024-2026 re-rating survives if the ten-year yield stays near 5%?

rows.finding: The last filed results are Q3 FY2026 (2026-06-27): revenue $109.4B, +16.4%, gross margin 50.1% including about two points of tariff refunds, EPS $2.02 +29%; fiscal Q4 revenue is guided to +9-11% with results due 2026-11-02. The sell-side consensus target is $339.35 across 50 analysts and the 43-analyst range is $245-$405, so the 2026-10-30 price is at or above the average target.
rows.mechanism: The price has run past the average analyst target, so the Q4 event carries asymmetric risk: a beat is already partly priced, while a guide below +9% would remove the growth the reverse DCF requires.
rows.benchmark: Consensus $339.35 versus $344.63 price; the low target of $245 is within 1% of the 52-week low of $243.42.
rows.weakens: Consensus targets lag price in momentum cycles and the dispersion is wide ($245-$405, a 65% spread), so the average target is a sentiment read, not a valuation.
rows.implication: No analyst cushion into 2026-11-02; a long-only fund should let the print pass before establishing a position.
rows.confidence: medium — two independent trackers, but they disagree on sample size and median, and Apple's guidance is an analyst aggregation rather than a company point guide.
rows.follow_up: Does the Q4 release confirm the +9-11% revenue guide and a gross margin above 48% ex-refunds?

rows.finding: Capital return: quarterly dividend $0.27 (0.31% yield), a new $100B buyback authorised in April 2026, $82.2B of repurchases and $15.6B of dividends in the trailing twelve months, a total shareholder yield of 1.9% against a peer median of 0.5%, and diluted shares down from 16,865M in FY2021 to 14,715M in Q3 FY2026 (-12.7%).

rows.benchmark: Peer median total shareholder yield 0.5%; Apple 1.9%; ten-year Treasury 4.93%.
rows.weakens: The buyback still retires about 1.6% of the shares a year and the $100B authorisation is about 2% of market value, so capital return is a real bid under the stock; the dividend has been raised annually.
rows.implication: Capital return is a floor under EPS and a partial exit route for holders, not a source of return at today's multiple.
rows.confidence: high — buyback and dividend cash flows are from the filed cash-flow statement and the authorisation from the April 2026 release.

plan.decision_question: What is Apple worth on 2026-10-30, and what revenue growth, margin and terminal assumptions does the $344.63 close already discount?
plan.thesis_sentence: At $344.63 on NasdaqGS (2026-10-30 close) Apple is priced at 39.5x trailing earnings, 35.2x forward earnings and a 2.7% free-cash-flow yield against a 4.93% ten-year Treasury, a price that requires roughly 11-12% annual free-cash-flow growth for a decade — several times what its device markets or its own last four years delivered — so the watchlist case turns on the entry price that restores a margin of safety, not on whether Apple is a good business.
plan.why_different: The financial analysis measures the quality of the earnings; this section converts those same statements and prices into what the buyer is paying for them: implied growth, peer-relative premium, sum-of-the-parts discount and the entry band that follows.
plan.mechanism: At 39.5x the earnings yield is 2.5% versus 4.93% on the ten-year Treasury, and the reverse DCF already assumes the FCF multiple halves to 18.7x by 2036, so the price can only be earned through double-digit FCF growth from the Services mix and an iPhone cycle, not from further re-rating; each buyback dollar retires stock at 2.5%, below the risk-free yield.
plan.comparison_set: MSFT 27.3x, GOOGL 14.6x, META 21.0x (peer median 21.0x), Samsung 12.5x; S&P 500 18.40x forward and 21.76x trailing; Apple's own ten-year mean P/E of 25.35x, five-year range 22.1-40.6x, and FY2021-FY2025 FCF CAGR of 1.5%.
plan.counter_evidence: Apple's 2.7% FCF yield is the highest of the four mega-caps because capital expenditure is $10B against hyperscaler AI budgets, and if the AI iPhone cycle lifts revenue 10%+ for several years while Services compounds at 14% on a 76% gross margin, a 35x forward multiple can be earned rather than merely re-rated.
plan.visual: Valuation methods table (reverse DCF at four growth rates plus sum of the parts) with the peer multiples table beside it.
plan.prohibited: cheap or expensive with no mechanism; 'priced for perfection'; 'margin of safety' without a number; 'the market is always right'; any statement about how the section is written.

rows.finding: There is no plausible takeover exit: Apple's market value is $5,029.6B, so the largest technology acquisition ever ($68.7B) equals 1.4% of it, and any bid would face US and EU antitrust review of a platform with 23.6% of global smartphone shipments.
rows.mechanism: With no strategic buyer able to pay a control premium, the exit price is the market multiple on the day of sale, which makes the entry multiple the dominant term in the return.
rows.benchmark: Microsoft's $68.7B all-cash acquisition of Activision Blizzard (2022-01-18), the largest technology deal on record, which took about 18 months and a divestiture to clear regulators.
rows.weakens: A mega-cap can still be broken up by regulators or acquired in parts, and a very large cash-rich acquirer could pay up for a division; the 1.4% comparison is about a whole-company bid.
rows.implication: Value can only be realised by selling into the market; the takeover premium is effectively zero and should not be modelled.
rows.confidence: high — the deal value is from the announcement and Apple's market capitalisation from dated market data.
rows.follow_up: Could a sovereign wealth fund or strategic investor build a stake large enough to influence strategy, and would CFIUS review apply?

rows.finding: Apple's four large drawdowns were 2018 -36.73% ($58.02 on 2018-10-03 to $36.71 on 2018-12-24), 2020 -31.43% ($81.80 to $56.09, 40 days), 2022 -30.75% ($182.01 to $126.04, 359 days) and 2025 -30.22% ($247.10 to $172.42, 43 days); the ten-year average intra-year drawdown is -21.4% over 82 days, and each was recovered within the following year (2020 +80.75%, 2025 +8.56% for the calendar year).
rows.mechanism: Apple's drawdowns were multiple compressions on intact franchises, so the recovery came from a re-rating as much as from earnings; at 39.5x there is little multiple room left to power the next recovery.
rows.benchmark: Apple's ten-year average intra-year drawdown of -21.4%, average 82 days peak-to-trough.
rows.weakens: Every one of those recoveries happened while the multiple was expanding on falling or near-zero real rates; a repeat at a 39.5x starting multiple would require earnings growth alone to do the work.
rows.implication: Size the position for a 20-30% drawdown as the normal case: from $344.63 the average drawdown is about $271 and a 30% drawdown about $241.
rows.confidence: high — a daily close series with peak and trough dates for each year.
rows.follow_up: Does the 2026 cycle repeat the pattern if memory costs and a slowing iPhone cycle coincide?

rows.finding: The last two big buying opportunities came at 17-21x earnings: $126.04 at the 2022 trough was 20.6x FY2022 EPS of $6.11, and $56.09 at the 2020 trough was about 17.1x FY2020 EPS of $3.28; $344.63 is 39.5x trailing EPS of $8.72 and 35.2x forward EPS of about $9.79.
rows.mechanism: The trough multiple, not the trough price, is what made those purchases work: the same 20x on today's much larger EPS is a far higher price, which is why a price band must be set on the multiple rather than on the old share price.
rows.benchmark: Apple's own entry multiples: 20.6x on FY2022 EPS at the 2022 trough and 17.1x on FY2020 EPS at the 2020 trough, against 39.5x today.
rows.weakens: Apple's earnings and cash flow are 40% larger than in 2022, so a 20x multiple on today's EPS is not the same business; the lower multiple may simply never return for a company with 76%-margin Services.
rows.implication: Waiting for a repeat of 17-21x means waiting for a price near $174-215 and may mean never owning the stock; the practical compromise is a 25-30x band.
rows.confidence: medium — trough prices are dated closes and the EPS are fiscal-year diluted figures, so the trough multiple is approximate.
rows.follow_up: Would a 20x multiple on today's EPS ($174) ever be reached without a genuine earnings recession?

rows.finding: Return sensitivity to entry: at $344.63 a three-year exit at 25x earns about -3.3% a year, at 30x +2.7% and at 35x +8.2%; at $296 the same exits earn +1.8%, +8.1% and +13.8%; at $248 they earn +8.0%, +14.8% and +21%+.
rows.mechanism: The entry multiple sets the arithmetic: paying 35x for 8% EPS growth and exiting at 25x loses money even though the business grows, while paying 25x for the same growth and exiting at 25x earns the growth plus the dividend.
rows.benchmark: An 8% annual equity hurdle for a long-only fund; EPS growth of 8% a year from $9.79 to $12.33 by fiscal 2029.
rows.weakens: If EPS compounds at 12-16% as it did in FY2026, every row improves by roughly 4-8 points a year and today's price could clear the hurdle.
rows.implication: Only at or below about $296 does a long-only fund earn its hurdle without relying on the multiple staying at a five-year high; at $344.63 the return depends on a 35x exit.
rows.confidence: medium — arithmetic, but the EPS path and exit multiple are assumptions, not forecasts.
rows.follow_up: What EPS growth does the FY2027 consensus imply, and does it survive a normalised tax rate and a 48% gross margin?

rows.finding: The Google search-distribution payment — reported at about $20B a year, never disclosed by Apple — is roughly 17% of Services revenue and 22% of services gross profit; the default-payment ban took effect in June 2026 under the April 2026 remedy order, with choice screens required.
rows.mechanism: The payment is almost pure margin with no capital attached, so losing it hits earnings and the multiple at the same time — the same policy risk that the valuation section capitalises at 39.5x.
rows.benchmark: Services revenue of $120.5B TTM and services gross profit of $91.6B; a 76.0% services gross margin.
rows.weakens: The deal may survive in restricted, non-exclusive form and is under appeal; Apple's Q3 FY2026 Services revenue still grew 12.1%, so no loss is visible in the filed results yet.
rows.implication: A sell trigger: if the payment is lost without an offset, about 9% of market value at a 30x multiple is at risk, so position size must survive that hit.
rows.confidence: medium — the payment size is a reported estimate Apple has never confirmed, and the remedy is under appeal.
rows.follow_up: What share of the Q3 FY2026 Services growth of 12.1% came from the search payment, and what does Apple disclose about the outcome of the appeal?

rows.finding: Liquidity is not a constraint: Apple trades $13.84B a day (20-day average, 40.41M shares) and the company itself retires about 1.6% of shares a year ($82.2B of repurchases), while a 1% position in a $1B fund is $10M, under 0.1% of one day's volume.
rows.mechanism: Deep liquidity plus a continuous buyback bid means the cost of exiting is the multiple at the moment of sale, not market impact, which shifts the design of the exit from execution to valuation triggers.
rows.benchmark: Apple's $13.84B average daily traded value over 20 days; $82.2B of trailing-twelve-month buybacks, 1.6% of market value.
rows.weakens: Liquidity evaporates in stress: in the 2025 episode the stock fell 30% in 43 days, and the buyback is discretionary and can slow, as it did when repurchases fell to $62.1B in nine months from $70.6B.
rows.implication: The exit is a price decision, not a liquidity decision: a long-only fund can sell in a day, but the drawdown record says it will not want to.
rows.confidence: high — volume and buyback figures are dated and filed.
rows.follow_up: How does liquidity behave in a 2025-style 43-day, 30% drawdown, and what slippage should a 5% position assume?

plan.thesis_sentence: Apple offers no takeover or listing exit — at a $5.03T market value the largest technology acquisition on record would be 1.4% of the company — so the only exit is a sale into a deep but volatile market, and the discipline has to be a price band: a first tranche at $275-300 (28-31x forward earnings), a full position at or below $250 (about 25x, the ten-year mean), and a sale if Services growth falls below 5% or the gross margin below 44%, because at 39.5x a 21% average drawdown is the normal cost of owning it.

plan.comparison_set: Apple's own four drawdowns (2018 -36.73%, 2020 -31.43%, 2022 -30.75%, 2025 -30.22%; ten-year average -21.4% over 82 days), the S&P 500 at -3.05% and Nasdaq-100 at -9.09% from their highs on 2026-10-30, and the largest technology acquisition ($68.7B) as the takeover benchmark.

rows.finding: There is no plausible takeover exit: Apple's market value is $5,029.6B, so the largest technology acquisition ever ($68.7B) equals 1.4% of it, and any bid would face US and EU antitrust review of a platform with 23.6% of global smartphone shipments.
rows.mechanism: With no strategic buyer able to pay a control premium, the exit price is the market multiple on the day of sale, which makes the entry multiple the dominant term in the return.
rows.benchmark: Microsoft's $68.7B all-cash acquisition of Activision Blizzard (2022-01-18), the largest technology deal on record, which took about 18 months and a divestiture to clear regulators.
rows.weakens: A mega-cap can still be broken up by regulators or acquired in parts, and a very large cash-rich acquirer could pay up for a division; the 1.4% comparison is about a whole-company bid.
rows.implication: Value can only be realised by selling into the market; the takeover premium is effectively zero and should not be modelled.
rows.confidence: high — the deal value is from the announcement and Apple's market capitalisation from dated market data.
rows.follow_up: Could a sovereign wealth fund or strategic investor build a stake large enough to influence strategy, and would CFIUS review apply?

rows.finding: Apple's four large drawdowns were 2018 -36.73% ($58.02 on 2018-10-03 to $36.71 on 2018-12-24), 2020 -31.43% ($81.80 to $56.09, 40 days), 2022 -30.75% ($182.01 to $126.04, 359 days) and 2025 -30.22% ($247.10 to $172.42, 43 days); the ten-year average intra-year drawdown is -21.4% over 82 days, and each was recovered within the following year (2020 +80.75%, 2025 +8.56% for the calendar year).
rows.mechanism: Apple's drawdowns were multiple compressions on intact franchises, so the recovery came from a re-rating as much as from earnings; at 39.5x there is little multiple room left to power the next recovery.
rows.benchmark: Apple's ten-year average intra-year drawdown of -21.4%, average 82 days peak-to-trough.
rows.weakens: Every one of those recoveries happened while the multiple was expanding on falling or near-zero real rates; a repeat at a 39.5x starting multiple would require earnings growth alone to do the work.
rows.implication: Size the position for a 20-30% drawdown as the normal case: from $344.63 the average drawdown is about $271 and a 30% drawdown about $241.
rows.confidence: high — a daily close series with peak and trough dates for each year.
rows.follow_up: Does the 2026 cycle repeat the pattern if memory costs and a slowing iPhone cycle coincide?

rows.finding: The last two big buying opportunities came at 17-21x earnings: $126.04 at the 2022 trough was 20.6x FY2022 EPS of $6.11, and $56.09 at the 2020 trough was about 17.1x FY2020 EPS of $3.28; $344.63 is 39.5x trailing EPS of $8.72 and 35.2x forward EPS of about $9.79.
rows.mechanism: The trough multiple, not the trough price, is what made those purchases work: the same 20x on today's much larger EPS is a far higher price, which is why a price band must be set on the multiple rather than on the old share price.
rows.benchmark: Apple's own entry multiples: 20.6x on FY2022 EPS at the 2022 trough and 17.1x on FY2020 EPS at the 2020 trough, against 39.5x today.
rows.weakens: Apple's earnings and cash flow are 40% larger than in 2022, so a 20x multiple on today's EPS is not the same business; the lower multiple may simply never return for a company with 76%-margin Services.
rows.implication: Waiting for a repeat of 17-21x means waiting for a price near $174-215 and may mean never owning the stock; the practical compromise is a 25-30x band.
rows.confidence: medium — trough prices are dated closes and the EPS are fiscal-year diluted figures, so the trough multiple is approximate.
rows.follow_up: Would a 20x multiple on today's EPS ($174) ever be reached without a genuine earnings recession?

rows.finding: Return sensitivity to entry: at $344.63 a three-year exit at 25x earns about -3.3% a year, at 30x +2.7% and at 35x +8.2%; at $296 the same exits earn +1.8%, +8.1% and +13.8%; at $248 they earn +8.0%, +14.8% and +21%+.
rows.mechanism: The entry multiple sets the arithmetic: paying 35x for 8% EPS growth and exiting at 25x loses money even though the business grows, while paying 25x for the same growth and exiting at 25x earns the growth plus the dividend.
rows.benchmark: An 8% annual equity hurdle for a long-only fund; EPS growth of 8% a year from $9.79 to $12.33 by fiscal 2029.
rows.weakens: If EPS compounds at 12-16% as it did in FY2026, every row improves by roughly 4-8 points a year and today's price could clear the hurdle.
rows.implication: Only at or below about $296 does a long-only fund earn its hurdle without relying on the multiple staying at a five-year high; at $344.63 the return depends on a 35x exit.
rows.confidence: medium — arithmetic, but the EPS path and exit multiple are assumptions, not forecasts.
rows.follow_up: What EPS growth does the FY2027 consensus imply, and does it survive a normalised tax rate and a 48% gross margin?

rows.finding: The Google search payment, reported at $20B in 2022 (the latest figure in testimony) and never disclosed by Apple, is about 17% of trailing Services revenue of $120.5B and 22% of services gross profit of $91.6B. The D.D.C.'s 2025-09-02 remedies decision refused the DOJ's proposed near-total ban on distribution payments and instead barred exclusive contracts while permitting default-placement payments not conditioned on exclusivity and running one year or less; final judgment was entered in December 2025, Google appealed in January 2026, the DOJ and states cross-appealed in February 2026, and the appeals were pending at 2026-10-29.
rows.mechanism: The payment survives on annually renegotiable, non-exclusive terms, so its value depends on renewal economics and the appeal rather than on a ban already in force; because it is almost pure margin, a cut hits earnings and the multiple together.
rows.benchmark: Services revenue $120.5B TTM; services gross profit $91.6B at a 76.0% gross margin.
rows.weakens: A competing independent report claimed an April 2026 order banned the payment from June 2026; the CRS analysis of the September 2025 decision and Alphabet's 10-Q legal note contradict it, and no primary record shows such a ban.
rows.implication: Sell trigger: loss or material cut of the payment at the one-year renewal or on appeal without an offsetting services gain; about 9% of market value at 30x is at risk.
rows.confidence: high on the remedy status and appeal timeline (primary court analysis and Alphabet's filed legal proceedings); medium on the $20B payment size, which Apple has never disclosed.
rows.follow_up: What does Apple receive at the first one-year renewal, and how much of Services growth does it explain?

rows.finding: Liquidity is not a constraint: Apple trades $13.84B a day (20-day average, 40.41M shares) and the company itself retires about 1.6% of shares a year ($82.2B of repurchases), while a 1% position in a $1B fund is $10M, under 0.1% of one day's volume.
rows.mechanism: Deep liquidity plus a continuous buyback bid means the cost of exiting is the multiple at the moment of sale, not market impact, which shifts the design of the exit from execution to valuation triggers.
rows.benchmark: Apple's $13.84B average daily traded value over 20 days; $82.2B of trailing-twelve-month buybacks, 1.6% of market value.
rows.weakens: Liquidity evaporates in stress: in the 2025 episode the stock fell 30% in 43 days, and the buyback is discretionary and can slow, as it did when repurchases fell to $62.1B in nine months from $70.6B.
rows.implication: The exit is a price decision, not a liquidity decision: a long-only fund can sell in a day, but the drawdown record says it will not want to.
rows.confidence: high — volume and buyback figures are dated and filed.
rows.follow_up: How does liquidity behave in a 2025-style 43-day, 30% drawdown, and what slippage should a 5% position assume?

rows.finding: June-quarter gross margin 50.1% included about 2 points of tariff refunds and diluted EPS $2.02 included $0.11 of refunds; the team's margin-adjusted EPS is $8.87, and 30.2x gives the $268 base case.
rows.mechanism: A refund-inflated margin, not underlying pricing power, is what the trailing multiple capitalises; removing it and adding the memory give-back cuts forward EPS from the $9.79 consensus to $8.87.
rows.benchmark: Consensus forward EPS $9.79; trailing P/E 39.5x versus 38.9x on the margin-adjusted figure.
rows.weakens: If the refunds persist or memory costs ease, EPS stays nearer $9.79 and the base case rises toward $296.
rows.implication: At $344.63 the stock is 29% above the base case; the starter band belongs at $240-265, not at today's price.

rows.finding: The $100B repurchase programme was announced on 2025-05-01, not April 2026; $221M was used by 2025-09-27 and $61.8B in the nine months to 2026-06-27, leaving about $38B.
rows.mechanism: Capital return retires about 1.6% of shares a year, so a holder's exit can be partial and continuous rather than a single sale.
rows.benchmark: Trailing repurchase payments of $82.2B and dividends of $15.6B, a 1.9% total shareholder yield against a 4.93% ten-year Treasury.
rows.weakens: At 39.5x each repurchased dollar earns a 2.5% earnings yield, below the Treasury, so buybacks support EPS more than value.
rows.implication: The buyback is a real but slow exit route; the sell discipline must still rest on price.
rows.confidence: high: the 10-K item 5 and the 10-Q equity note state the dates and amounts.

rows.finding: The scenario case is $399 bull (15%, 38x on $10.50), $268 base (50%, 30.2x on $8.87) and $205 bear (35%, 25x on $8.20), an expected value of $266, 23% below the $344.63 close.

rows.weakens: If the multiple holds above 35x, the expected value rises toward $350 and the discipline never buys.

rows.confidence: medium: the EPS paths are the team's calculation; the multiple anchors are observed.

rows.finding: There is no takeover exit: the largest technology acquisition on record, Microsoft's $68.7B deal for Activision Blizzard, equals 1.4% of Apple's $5,029.6B market value; average daily traded value is $13.84B.

rows.weakens: A break-up or a large spin-off is not contemplated; nothing in the record suggests a buyer.

rows.finding: Apple's 2026-07-30 release contains no September-quarter outlook; the 9-11% revenue growth and 47-48% gross margin figures are management's call guidance as reported by third parties.
rows.mechanism: The base case depends on a guide the filing does not state, so the evidence is one grade weaker than a filed number.
rows.benchmark: The release's own text, which stops at the cash-flow statement and the dividend declaration.
rows.weakens: If the guide is wrong or withdrawn, the $8.87 base moves; consensus of $9.79 implies a smaller give-back.
rows.implication: Size the starter tranche only after the 2026-11-02 release confirms the margin path.
rows.confidence: medium: the call guidance is trade-reported, not verified in the release.

rows.finding: The board appointed John Ternus CEO effective 2026-09-01, with Tim Cook as executive chair and Arthur Levinson as lead independent director; Ternus, 50, joined Apple in 2001, became VP Hardware Engineering in 2013 and SVP in 2021, and has no disclosed CEO or P&L role before 2026.
rows.mechanism: An internal hardware engineer preserves product-integration culture, but value is migrating to software, AI and services at the moment he takes over.
rows.benchmark: Apple's 2011 Jobs-to-Cook transition, also an internal promotion; Ternus is Apple's eighth CEO.
rows.weakens: Ternus's product record (iPad, AirPods, iPhone 17/Air, MacBook Neo), a unanimous board and a five-month handover argue for continuity.
rows.implication: Succession risk is lower than feared but renewal risk is higher: the new CEO has never allocated capital or answered to public markets.
rows.confidence: high: appointment, date and biography from the 8-K and company release.
rows.follow_up: What operating authority does Cook retain as executive chair, and what is Ternus's CEO compensation?

rows.finding: John Giannandrea stepped down as AI chief on 2025-12-01 after Siri's delay; Amar Subramanya (ex-Microsoft corporate VP of AI, 16 years at Google and head of engineering for Gemini Assistant) became VP of AI reporting to Craig Federighi; Apple announced a multiyear deal on 2026-01-12 to use Google Gemini for the Siri upgrade due in 2026.
rows.mechanism: Apple is buying frontier capability from a competitor while rebuilding internal leadership: faster than building, but it weakens differentiation and gives Google leverage.
rows.benchmark: Microsoft-OpenAI and Google DeepMind own frontier models; Apple had pursued in-house AI since 2018.
rows.weakens: Federighi's software record, Subramanya's Gemini experience and Apple's distribution still give it the fastest route to mass-market AI.
rows.implication: Underwrite AI as a feature that protects hardware replacement, not as a new profit pool, until Apple discloses model economics.
rows.confidence: high on facts; medium on competitive consequence.
rows.follow_up: What are the Gemini deal terms, and is Apple training a frontier model in parallel?

rows.finding: Srouji became chief hardware officer combining silicon and hardware engineering; Federighi holds software plus AI; Cue added health to services; Parekh has been CFO since 2025-01-01; Khan COO since 2025-07; Newstead GC from 2026-03-01; O'Brien runs retail and people. Most of the executive team has spent 20+ years at Apple, and two people carry the silicon and AI remits.
rows.mechanism: Concentrating silicon in Srouji and software/AI in Federighi creates key-person risk in exactly the two capabilities the transition depends on.
rows.benchmark: The 2011-2023 team was near-static; four senior roles (CFO, COO, GC, AI) changed in 2025-2026.
rows.weakens: Deep internal pipeline and Srouji's expanded remit give one accountable owner for hardware.
rows.implication: Diligence should ask for named deputies in silicon and AI; key-person risk is the team's main discount.
rows.confidence: high on roles; medium on the key-person judgement.
rows.follow_up: Who are Srouji's and Federighi's deputies, and are retention packages in place?

rows.finding: Cook's 2025 total target compensation was $59m (base $3m unchanged since 2016, cash incentive at 200% of base, $50m equity target), positioned in the 80th-90th percentile of peer CEO pay; other named executives target $1m base, 200% cash and $20m equity; Parekh's target was $16.75m; the CEO ownership guideline is 10x salary; say-on-pay drew 8.6% opposition on 2026-02-24.
rows.mechanism: Pay is peer-benchmarked high but equity-heavy, which retains executives through a multiyear transition; the 8.6% protest signals some shareholder discomfort.
rows.benchmark: 80th-90th percentile of the primary peer group, as disclosed by the company.
rows.weakens: 8.6% opposition is not a crisis but is above routine approval; CEO pay is immaterial to a $5tn market value.
rows.implication: Pay is a weak signal for the investment case; retaining Srouji and Federighi matters more than the level.
rows.confidence: high.
rows.follow_up: How is Ternus's CEO pay structured, and does it carry AI and China metrics?

rows.finding: Planned transitions replaced the CFO (Maestri to Parekh, effective 2025-01-01), COO (Williams to Khan, 2025-07), general counsel (Adams to Newstead, effective 2026-03-01), AI chief (Giannandrea to Subramanya, 2025-12-01) and CEO (Cook to Ternus, 2026-09-01) within 24 months.
rows.mechanism: Staggered, pre-announced transitions preserve continuity, but the whole C-suite turned over while AI and antitrust pressure intensified.
rows.benchmark: Apple's prior decade had almost no C-suite turnover.
rows.weakens: All were planned successions rather than resignations; Newstead and Subramanya bring external experience.
rows.implication: Execution risk lies in coordination, not departures; the first 12 months of Ternus's team are the test.
rows.confidence: high.
rows.follow_up: Has any 2026 departure not been pre-announced, particularly in design after Williams retired?

rows.finding: Cook (Auburn 1982, Duke MBA 1988; 12 years at IBM, then Compaq) is the operator and policy face; Ternus the product engineer; Srouji the silicon builder; Federighi the software and AI owner; Cue the services monetiser; Parekh the finance disciplinarian. No board member has operating frontier-AI experience.
rows.mechanism: Apple's model rewards integration across silicon, software and services; the division of labour matches that model but leaves no frontier-AI owner at CEO or board level.
rows.benchmark: Microsoft's Satya Nadella (engineering and cloud) and Google's Sundar Pichai (product) versus a hardware engineer as Apple CEO.
rows.weakens: The board's aerospace (Austin) and pharmaceutical (Gorsky) experience may be more relevant to manufacturing and health than to AI.
rows.implication: The missing hire is not a CFO but a credible AI product leader with executive authority; Subramanya is VP-level and not on the executive team.
rows.confidence: medium.
rows.follow_up: Will Subramanya be elevated to the executive team, and will the board add AI expertise?

rows.finding: Apple guided fiscal Q4 2026 gross margin to 47-48% including about 1 point of tariff refunds, i.e. roughly 46-47% ex-refunds against 48.1% ex-refund in the June quarter, with consensus revenue of about $113.3bn and EPS of about $1.99.
rows.mechanism: The company itself prices the memory cost transfer into the next quarter's margin: a 2.1-3.1 point sequential decline, and a lower underlying margin than a year earlier once the refund is stripped out, which is the opposite of a new 50% floor.
rows.benchmark: June 2026 quarter 50.1% reported and 48.1% ex-refund; fiscal 2025 full-year 46.9%; fiscal 2023 44.1%.
rows.weakens: The thesis-table reading that FY2027 consensus EPS of $9.79 is a reasonable base case unadjusted.
rows.implication: Trailing EPS of $8.72 is a margin peak, not a run-rate; the base-case forward EPS of $9.79 needs margin to stabilise before FY2027 begins. Price the entry band lower.
rows.confidence: medium - company guidance confirmed by a specialist preview; the ex-refund split is a calculation on Apple's own disclosure
rows.follow_up: Does the December-quarter guide on 2026-11-02 imply gross margin below 46% ex-refund?

rows.finding: DRAM sufficiency ratio of -1% to -2% in 2026, a widening supply-demand gap in 2027, meaningful new capacity only in the second half of 2027 and substantial output not before 2028; consumer device shipments fall again in 2027.
rows.mechanism: HBM and AI-server demand crowd out commodity DRAM, so the three suppliers keep pricing power over handset makers for another eighteen months; that fixes Apple's cost base while its service annuity price is fixed, compressing the blended margin.
rows.benchmark: IDC's 2028 normalisation for device pools; Apple's own 10-Q statement that component constraints and costs are expected to intensify.
rows.weakens: The base-case driver that margin gives back about a point and then settles.
rows.implication: A one-point give-back is optimistic; model two to four points through FY2027 and test the buy band against $8.20-8.90 of EPS.
rows.confidence: high for 2027 DRAM tightness; medium for the size of the margin hit, which depends on price pass-through not disclosed
rows.follow_up: What iPhone 18 Pro price increase does Apple announce for 2027, and does volume hold?

rows.finding: China smartphone shipments fell 15.4% to 57.9m units in Q3 2026, a sixth straight decline; Apple's own units fell 4.3% while its share rose to 17.8% from 15.8%; Huawei shipped 12.2m units for about 21% share and grew 17.3%.
rows.mechanism: In a shrinking market share gains come from rivals' exits, not from demand: Apple's 30% Greater China revenue growth in nine months of FY2026 was price, mix and currency on falling units, so the line mean-reverts once the price comparison laps.
rows.benchmark: Greater China revenue $64.8bn in nine months of FY2026 against $49.9bn a year earlier; Apple share 18.1% in Q2 2026 and 17.8% in Q3 2026; Huawei 22.6% in Q2.
rows.weakens: The market section's framing of China growth as a competitive win rather than a price and mix effect.
rows.implication: China is a 17.8% revenue line with declining volume; a 20% revenue fall removes about 4% of net income, and the FY2027 comparison is against a +30% base.
rows.confidence: high on the IDC data, medium on the revenue elasticity
rows.follow_up: What does the December-quarter China revenue line show against the +22% June comparison?

rows.finding: The D.C. Circuit was asked by both the DOJ and Google to prioritise the search cross-appeals so argument could be scheduled as early as 2026-12-09, against a payment reported at $20bn in 2022 that is 16.6% of trailing services revenue and about 22% of services gross profit.
rows.mechanism: A near-pure-margin payment capitalised at 30x is $474bn, 9.4% of market value; the remedy on appeal could restore an outright ban, so a legal event inside the twelve-month window carries a discrete, quantifiable EV hit.
rows.benchmark: The 2025-09-02 remedies decision refused a ban and permitted non-exclusive one-year payments; DOJ seeks to vacate that refusal; Apple's own 10-Q warns a reversal could prohibit commercial terms for search distribution.
rows.weakens: The exit section's treatment of the payment as a slow policy risk rather than a dated December 2026 catalyst.
rows.implication: Price a 30% chance of a 50% cut and a 10% chance of loss at about $13 a share, 3.8% of the price; the base case as written assumes the payment renews near current terms with no discount.
rows.confidence: medium - the argument date comes from a paywalled legal report; the payment size is a 2022 court figure Apple has never confirmed
rows.follow_up: Is oral argument held on 2026-12-09, and does the D.C. Circuit rule before the first one-year renewal?

rows.finding: Tariff refunds are not one-off: they were about 2 points of the June 2026 quarter and about 1 point of the September guide, so roughly 1.5 points across the second half of FY2026, worth $0.11 of June-quarter EPS on $2.02.
rows.mechanism: A cash refund from struck-down IEEPA tariffs is recognised as a reduction of products cost of sales, so it raises reported margin without changing price or unit economics and disappears when the refund cycle closes.
rows.benchmark: June-quarter EPS $2.02 including $0.11 of refund; products gross margin 39.9% against 36.9%.
rows.weakens: The characterisation of the refund as a single-quarter item in the earnings-quality discussion.
rows.implication: Normalised FY2026 EPS is closer to $8.70 than $8.87 on a clean margin, and the reported 49.1% nine-month margin overstates the trading margin by about a point.
rows.confidence: high - both figures are in Apple's own release and guidance
rows.follow_up: Does the FY2026 annual report quantify the full-year refund?

rows.finding: Apple repurchased $62.1bn of stock in nine months of FY2026 at a 39.5x trailing multiple, a 2.5% earnings yield against a 4.93% ten-year Treasury, while total shareholder yield is 1.9%.
rows.mechanism: Buying stock above intrinsic value transfers wealth from continuing to selling holders; the EPS benefit (+1.9 points of growth) is real and the value benefit is negative while the multiple exceeds fair value.
rows.benchmark: Ten-year Treasury 4.93%; five-year average P/E 30.2x; $100bn authorisation of April 2026.
rows.weakens: The capital-return pillar of the bull case at today's multiple.
rows.implication: The buyback supports the EPS line and not the value per share, so a de-rating is not cushioned by capital return at this price.
rows.confidence: high on the numbers, medium on the average repurchase price which is not disclosed
rows.follow_up: Does Apple slow the pace of repurchases in FY2027 or re-authorise at $100bn?

plan.decision_question: Given that the company's own September guide implies a lower underlying gross margin than a year earlier and the DRAM market offers no relief before 2028, is FY2027 EPS of $9.79 (and therefore the $296 base value) achievable, or does the starter band belong near $250?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple's franchise risk is small and its price risk is large, and the price risk runs through one number: the gross margin, which Apple itself guides down two to three points in the September 2026 quarter while DRAM stays tight through 2027, so the entry band of $275-296 is set 10-15% too high and the bear case is nearer one in three than one in four.
plan.why_different: Prices every risk against the valuation it damages (EV percentage, dollars per share, points of net income) instead of listing it, separates the one thesis-breaking risk from six manageable ones, and dates each signpost.
plan.mechanism: Memory inflation is a cost transfer from Apple to its suppliers: HBM and server DRAM crowd out consumer DRAM, the three DRAM makers earn more per wafer, and Apple pays more per device while its fixed-price services annuity cannot absorb the hit. Each point of gross margin is 3.0% of net income, so a two-point further decline cancels roughly a year of revenue growth and breaks the forward-EPS base of the valuation.
plan.comparison_set: Peer multiples Microsoft 27.3x, Alphabet 14.6x, Meta 21.0x, Samsung 12.5x against Apple 39.5x; Apple's own five-year average 30.2x and ten-year mean 25.35x; the ten-year average intra-year drawdown of 21.4%; the 2025 tariff episode (-30.2% peak to trough) as the closest recent stress.
plan.counter_evidence: Apple has beaten EPS consensus in eight straight reports, passed memory costs through on iPad and Mac prices in 2026, holds net cash of $62.2bn so no financing risk exists, and a 47-48% gross margin is still above any full year before 2025; the bear case could be the consensus already, in which case the risk is being early rather than wrong.
plan.visual: risk-matrix with eight ranked risks plus a danger info card for the gross-margin risk
plan.prohibited: risks are manageable; huge market; well positioned; clear business model; fierce competition; recently; about 5; strong team

rows.finding: FY2027 consensus EPS of $9.79 implies a 12.3% rise from trailing $8.72, yet Apple guided September-quarter gross margin of 47-48% including 1 point of tariff refunds, against 48.1% in June ex-refund; two points of give-back on ~$490bn of revenue is $9.8bn pretax, 6.3% of net income, leaving EPS near $8.87.
rows.mechanism: Gross margin is the swing factor: memory costs above anything in the record and the refund rolling off compress the earnings base while opex, including R&D up 33% to $34.0bn in nine months, keeps growing; one point of margin equals 3.0% of net income, double one point of revenue growth.
rows.benchmark: Jefferies' $263.66 target of 2026-08-10 and the company's own 47-48% guide; consensus $9.79 assumes margin recovery that the guide contradicts.
rows.weakens: Apple has beaten estimates through the squeeze and has raised prices on iPad and Mac; if pass-through holds margin at 48%, $9.79 is achievable and the base returns to $296.
rows.implication: Value the base on $8.87 at 30.2x, about $268, not $296; do not buy above the margin-adjusted base.
rows.confidence: high on the arithmetic, medium on the FY2027 margin path because Apple's pricing response is undisclosed
rows.follow_up: What does the December-quarter guide on 2026-11-02 imply for gross margin ex-refund?

rows.finding: At $344.63 (NasdaqGS close, 2026-10-30), Apple trades at 39.5x trailing and 35.2x forward earnings against a 21.0x mega-cap peer median and a 30.2x five-year average, with a 2.7% free-cash-flow yield against a 4.93% ten-year Treasury.
rows.mechanism: A 39.5x multiple on a 2.7% cash yield requires the cash flow to compound; the reverse DCF needs 11.8% free-cash-flow growth for ten years against 1.5% delivered in FY2021-FY2025, so the price is a bet on re-rating persistence rather than on the franchise alone.
rows.benchmark: Ten-year P/E mean 25.35x, five-year average 30.2x, peer median 21.0x, S&P 500 21.76x trailing, ten-year Treasury 4.93%.
rows.weakens: Apple's 36.8x price-to-free-cash-flow is 43% below the peer median of 64.6x because capex is only $10.0bn a year; on cash the stock is the cheapest mega-cap in the set.
rows.implication: The asymmetry is in the entry price: a starter band at $240-265 and a full position at or below $225 offer a margin of safety that today's price does not.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Does the multiple hold if the ten-year yield stays near 4.93% and FY2027 EPS is cut?

rows.finding: Services produced 39.1% of gross profit in nine months to 2026-06-27, down from 42.2% in FY2025, because product gross profit grew 26.3% against 15.3% for Services; the reported ~$20bn Google payment is 22% of services gross profit.
rows.mechanism: The annuity is still the highest-margin layer at 76.3%, but it no longer grows faster than the hardware that creates it, and its most concentrated revenue line survives only on non-exclusive, one-year-or-shorter placement terms under appeal.
rows.benchmark: Services gross profit per dollar of product gross profit fell to $0.64 from $0.73; the D.D.C. remedies decision of 2025-09-02 refused a payment ban but barred exclusivity and terms over one year.
rows.weakens: Services revenue still grew 14.1% and Apple Intelligence registration in China on 2026-07-15 opens a market where the assistant was absent for 22 months.
rows.implication: Model the Google payment as an annually repriced asset, not a perpetuity, and cap the position for a single regulatory event worth 9.4% of market value.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: What terms does the first one-year renewal carry, and how much US link-out spending has moved off in-app purchase?

rows.finding: Greater China revenue rose 30.0% to $64.8bn in nine months to 2026-06-27 and Apple's unit share rose 4.2 points to 18.1% in Q2 2026, but Huawei holds 22.6% and IDC expects China shipments to fall about 20% in H2 2026.
rows.mechanism: The growth is a launch, price and currency effect on a withdrawn subsidy base; when the comparison laps a +30% base, the region that contributed 4.1 points of group growth becomes the largest source of downside.
rows.benchmark: China units fell 4.3% in Q2 2026, the fifth straight decline, and Huawei grew 19.9% on HarmonyOS and price discipline.
rows.weakens: Nine-month China revenue already exceeds all of FY2025, and the CAC approval of Apple Intelligence on 2026-07-15 narrows the AI gap in the market where it mattered most.
rows.implication: Stress China at -20% revenue: about $13bn, 3.9% of net income, before touching the multiple.
rows.confidence: high on the revenue figures, medium on the durability of the growth
rows.follow_up: How much of the Greater China increase is currency, and what does the December quarter show against the +30% base?

rows.finding: The closest analog is Microsoft after 2014: a legacy incumbent re-rated roughly eight-fold in a decade as cloud replaced declining licence revenue; the cautionary analog is Nokia, which held 40-50% of handsets in 2007 and under 5% by 2013 as the platform shifted to software it did not control.
rows.mechanism: Platform transitions destroy incumbent value when the new layer sits outside the incumbent's control; they enrich incumbents that own the distribution layer and can attach the new capability to an existing annuity.
rows.benchmark: Microsoft began its transition near 10-12x earnings, so re-rating supplied much of the return; Apple starts at 39.5x, where the same transformation would have to come from earnings alone.
rows.weakens: Apple owns its platform and distribution, unlike Nokia, and rents the frontier model rather than missing the shift, which is closer to Microsoft's early cloud years than to Nokia's collapse.
rows.implication: The franchise probably survives the AI shift; the multiple is the fragile part, so the decision rule is price, not technology.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: Does Apple's AI layer produce a measurable upgrade or ARPU lift by FY2028, or remain a licensed cost?

rows.finding: The market regime offers no valuation cushion: the S&P 500 is 3.4% below its 52-week high, the VIX is 19.42 at the 77th percentile, the ten-year Treasury yields 4.93% and technology is 7.4 points behind SPY over one month while energy and health care lead.
rows.mechanism: A high-multiple, long-duration cash-flow stock is sensitive to the discount rate and to rotation; with the risk-free rate near 5%, the 2.7% free-cash-flow yield demands growth that the margin guide puts at risk.
rows.benchmark: Ten-year Treasury 4.93%, 2-year 4.61%, fed funds 4.00%, IG spreads 89bp, HY 326bp.
rows.weakens: The Fed has stopped tightening and credit spreads are tight, so a soft-landing regime could support the multiple longer than the valuation arithmetic implies.
rows.implication: Size the position for a de-rating: zero now, 1-2% at $240-265, 3-4% at or below $225.
rows.confidence: high on the data, medium on regime persistence
rows.follow_up: Does a further rise in the ten-year yield above 5% coincide with FY2027 EPS cuts?

plan.decision_question: Does Apple at $344.63 offer a long-only fund an attractive expected return, or does the price already capitalise a margin peak and a decade of double-digit cash-flow growth?

rows.finding: Business quality is exceptional on the disclosed record: more than 2.5bn active devices, a record 23.6% iOS share of 2026 shipments, services at a 76.3% gross margin and return on assets of 36.1% against Microsoft's 35.9% ROIC and Alphabet's 37.0%.
rows.mechanism: The installed base plus the App Store and subscription layer produce a repeat-purchase annuity with negative working capital and minimal capex, which is why the franchise earns a premium multiple.
rows.benchmark: ROA 36.1% vs Microsoft 35.9% ROIC and Alphabet 37.0%; capex 2.2% of revenue vs 34.9% at Microsoft.
rows.weakens: The installed-base figure is company-reported and the app-economy pool is undisclosed, so the annuity's size cannot be independently verified.
rows.implication: Score business quality 9 and financial quality 9; these are the pillars that keep the name on a watchlist rather than in the avoid bucket.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: What share of services is commission versus subscription, and what is the measured replacement rate?

rows.finding: Valuation is the weakest dimension: 39.5x trailing and 35.2x forward against a 21.0x peer median, a 2.7% free-cash-flow yield against a 4.93% ten-year Treasury, and a reverse DCF that needs 11.8% free-cash-flow growth for a decade against 1.5% delivered.
rows.mechanism: The multiple, not the business, sets the forward return: at 35x forward the stock is fairly valued; at 30.2x it is worth $268; at 25x it is worth $205.
rows.benchmark: Peer median 21.0x, S&P 500 21.76x, five-year average 30.2x, ten-year mean 25.35x, ten-year Treasury 4.93%.
rows.weakens: On price-to-free-cash-flow Apple at 36.8x is 43% below the peer median of 64.6x, so the premium disappears on the metric that funds the buyback.
rows.implication: Score valuation 2; a 20-25% weight on this dimension is what makes the composite a watchlist score rather than a buy.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Does the multiple compress toward 30x as FY2027 EPS estimates are cut?

rows.finding: Earnings quality is weaker than the headline: FY2025's 22.7% EPS growth is 10.4% normalising the Irish charge, buybacks added 5.4 points over FY2023-FY2025 but only 1.9 in the trailing twelve months, 2.0 points of the June 2026 gross margin were tariff refunds and inventory rose 87% against 16.2% revenue growth.
rows.mechanism: The reported margin contains one-time refunds and a memory-cost tailwind, and the EPS denominator is shrinking; both flatter the base that the multiple capitalises.
rows.benchmark: Pretax income +7.5% against net income +19.5% in FY2025; free cash flow conversion 1.06x, but 0.88x in FY2025 on $43.4bn cash taxes.
rows.weakens: Cash conversion is strong and the refund is a real cash item, not an accounting invention; the balance sheet is net cash $62.2bn.
rows.implication: Score earnings quality 4 and treat trailing EPS $8.72 as a peak rather than a base.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Does the FY2026 10-K decompose the refund and inventory build?

rows.finding: Policy is a recurring cost to the highest-margin layer, not a licence-to-operate threat: the EU DMA fine was €500m on 2025-04-23, the US contempt finding dates from 2025-04-30, the DOJ case is in discovery toward a 2027 trial, and the Google payment survives on non-exclusive one-year terms under appeal.
rows.mechanism: Each remedy transfers pricing power from Apple's toll to developers, consumers or Google, and reaches services gross margin before it reaches revenue.
rows.benchmark: Peer fines are serial but modest: Meta €200m in the same DMA package, Google €890m on 2026-07-23, Alphabet's €4.1bn Android fine final in July 2026.
rows.weakens: China registered Apple Intelligence on 2026-07-15, Section 232 spared Apple products on 2026-01-14, and the IEEPA tariffs were struck down on 2026-02-20.
rows.implication: Score policy 6; cap any position at 4% because one regulatory event is worth 9.4% of market value.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: What does the D.C. Circuit do after argument from 2026-12-09, and does Article 6(4) produce a second fine?

rows.finding: Management and capital allocation are competent but not cheap: Ternus became CEO on 2026-09-01 with Cook as executive chair, and the company repurchased $62.1bn of stock in nine months at 39.5x, a 2.5% earnings yield against 4.93% on the ten-year.
rows.mechanism: Buybacks at a multiple above intrinsic value transfer value from continuing holders to sellers; the $100bn authorisation of April 2026 extends the practice.
rows.benchmark: Shareholder yield 1.9% against the ten-year Treasury 4.93%; diluted shares down from 16,865M in FY2021 to 14,715M.
rows.weakens: The succession is internal and complete, and net cash rose $28.4bn in nine months, so capital allocation has not damaged the balance sheet.
rows.implication: Score management 6; the buyback supports EPS, not value per share, at this price.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: Does the first Ternus year bring a new capital-allocation framework or another $100bn authorisation?

user_data_requests.database: PACER — U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey, dockets 2:24-cv-04055 (US et al. v. Apple Inc.) and MDL 2:24-md-03113
user_data_requests.query: The current scheduling order: trial date, fact- and expert-discovery cut-offs, the status of the three special discovery masters appointed in early 2026, and any stipulation defining the scope of equitable relief the DOJ and plaintiff states seek.
user_data_requests.why: The DOJ case is the largest unresolved structural threat to Apple's Services and iPhone economics. The public filings say only that discovery is under way and that the schedule points to a 2027 trial; the docket would date the trial and show how narrow or broad the requested remedy has become, which changes whether the risk belongs in a 2027 or a 2029 cash-flow case.
user_data_requests.how: Pull the docket sheets and the operative case management order from PACER (pacer.uscourts.gov, D.N.J.), or ask counsel with PACER access to export the docket and the scheduling order to PDF.

user_data_requests.database: USPTO Patent Center / EPO Espacenet (patent search and export)
user_data_requests.query: Patent families and grants naming Apple Inc. as assignee, filed 2024-2026, in four areas: on-device/cloud AI and model efficiency; wearable health sensing (blood pressure, glucose, sleep); foldable display and hinge; AR/VR optics and displays. Include application numbers, grant dates, status and forward citations.
user_data_requests.why: Apple discloses no patent count, so the technology section cannot quantify the IP moat or compare grant depth with Samsung, Huawei or Alphabet; without it the patent row stays 'unquantified' and the moat assessment rests on regulatory clearances and silicon know-how only.
user_data_requests.how: Export a CSV from USPTO Patent Center (or Espacenet) filtered by assignee 'Apple Inc.' and filing date 2024-01-01 to 2026-10-31, with CPC classes G06N, A61B5, H04M and G02B.

user_data_requests.query: Apple Operations International Limited, Apple Operations Limited and Apple Distribution International Limited: latest annual accounts, registered office, directors, shareholders and any transfer-pricing or IP-ownership notes.
user_data_requests.why: The 10-K gives no entity-level profit, ownership percentages or roles. These accounts would show which Irish entity books non-U.S. profit and set the durability of the 15.6% effective tax rate, the structure's main policy tail.
user_data_requests.how: Download the most recent annual accounts and company detail sheets for the three Irish entities from core.ie (some documents require a fee account) and upload them.

user_data_requests.database: Apple Q3 FY2026 earnings call transcript (2026-07-30), CFO prepared remarks
user_data_requests.query: The exact September-quarter 2026 guidance management gave: revenue growth range, gross-margin range, and the tariff-refund component of that margin range.
user_data_requests.why: The base case ($8.87 margin-adjusted EPS, $268) and the 47-48% September gross-margin assumption rest on a guide that Apple's 2026-07-30 release does not contain; only third-party coverage and a transcript page the server could not read report it. Without the transcript the margin give-back is trade-reported, not verified.
user_data_requests.how: Apple investor relations posts the earnings-call webcast and transcript; a licensed transcript from FactSet or LSEG also works. Please upload the PDF or text of the 2026-07-30 call.

notes.note: Two items for the unit economics and cash-flow lines: (1) intangible assets rose to $20.342bn at 2026-06-27 from $11.093bn at 2025-09-27, a $9.2bn increase that should add amortisation; Apple confirmed the Q.ai acquisition on 2026-01-29 (FT reported close to $2bn) and notified Ascend.io to the EC on 2026-06-30. (2) $25.8bn of buybacks in Q3 FY2026 plus $4.0bn dividends.

Your premiumisation case may understate the new price ceiling: iPhone 18 Pro launched 2026-09-09 at $1,199 and Pro Max at $1,299, and the first foldable iPhone Duo at $1,999 went on sale 2026-10-23 (pre-orders 2026-10-16). That is a new ASP tier above the prior range and supports the value-over-units argument for FY2027; first-quarter Duo volumes are undisclosed.

Evidence for the AI-delay and new-category risks: the next Apple Foundation Models will be based on Google Gemini under a multi-year deal announced 2026-01-12 (reported ~$1bn/yr), and Vision Pro shipped ~45,000 units in Q4 2025 after the M5 refresh, ~600,000 lifetime, with IDC forecasting ~290,000 units in 2026. Both are usable base rates for execution risk.

Greater China net sales rose 22% to $18,816m in the quarter ended 2026-06-27 and 30% to $64,839m for the nine months, from $49,884m, and China's CAC registered Apple Intelligence on 2026-07-15 with Alibaba's Qwen and Baidu. That cuts against a China share-loss thesis; the competitive question with Huawei remains. Watch 2027-01-10, when the Busan trade truce expires.

Google search-distribution remedies: the D.D.C. decision of 2025-09-02 refused to ban Google's payments to distributors and permitted default-placement payments that are non-exclusive and one year or less; a final judgment followed in December 2025 and both sides' appeals were pending at 2026-10-29. Model the search payment as intact but annually repriced, not expiring. Apple does not disclose the amount; the $20bn figure is unverified.

Two product-gating facts for the technology section: China's CAC registered Apple Intelligence on 2026-07-15 with Alibaba Qwen and Baidu after a ~22-month gap; and Apple's Q3 FY2026 10-Q warns DMA interoperability obligations have in the past, and may in future, caused it not to launch or maintain features "such as Siri AI" in certain jurisdictions. Availability is now a regulatory variable, not only an engineering one.

Checked S59: a MacRumors report dated 2026-09-09, so the $1,199 / $1,299 / $1,999 prices are media-reported, not Apple's own price list — I have labelled them "reported". Used the Duo price in the competition section and flagged the tension: $1,999 sits below the $2,550 foldable ASP IDC assumes, so IDC's $45.7bn 2027 foldable value estimate may be high. Duo volumes stay not disclosed. The market section keeps ASP as the key variable rather than quoting a new tier.

Your Greater China figures match mine exactly ($18,816m, +22%, quarter to 2026-06-27; $64,839m, +30%, nine months, from $49,884m), and I have added the 2026-07-15 CAC registration of Apple Intelligence with Qwen and Baidu to the China competition paragraph as evidence the AI gap narrows there without settling the Huawei question. I did not use the 2027-01-10 Busan truce date: no market-sizing or competitive mechanism in sections 4-5 turns on it, so it belongs in your policy section rather than mine.
